label: BiblIndex
description:
BiblIndex is an index of biblical references found in early Christian literature, both Western and Eastern, covering the first three centuries and part of the following centuries. The ultimate aim is to encompass the whole of Late Antiquity and the early Middle Ages in order to help renew the study of the interpretation and history of biblical texts.
In addition to a multi-criteria form enabling users to search for biblical passages in the patristic corpus analysed (around 650,000 biblical occurrences available at the end of 2024), it provides a browser in twelve Bibles, in Hebrew, Syriac, Greek, Latin, French and English, and a tool for displaying them in a synopsis that takes into account the differences in chapter and verse numbering.
It also gives access to an exhaustive index of authors and patristic works, aligned with different reference systems. For each work, a list of biblical quotations is compiled.

Access to the data is entirely free of charge.

label: Biblioteca anatomica
description: The project The “Civilization of Anatomy”: the genre of Literary Anatomies in seventeenth-century Italy (FNS 100012_204399) aims to verify, through an examination of literary documents, the thesis that anatomy permeates the style of thought and the cultural imagery of the early Modern Age. The research is based on a series of Italian works that include “anatomy” in their title and/or were inspired by anatomy, which have been analyzed and collected into a systematic corpus of “Literary Anatomies”: a multiform textual corpus codified here for the first time as a genre in its own right in the Italian tradition. The Anatomies cover multiple subjects – e.g., geography, astronomy, grammar, moral philosophy – yet all involve the same approach: the “dissection” of the body of a subject and its orderly classification.

label: Biblissima Authority Files
description:
The Biblissima Authority Files are a collaborative platform to manage, publish and expose Biblissima authority data. Its realization is part of the Biblissima+ programme, *Observatory of Written Cultures, from Clay to Print* (2021-2029). It follows Biblissima, *Observatory of the written heritage of the Middle Ages and the Renaissance from the 8th to the 18th century* (2012-2021). 

These authority files are based on data collected and processed within the framework of Biblissima+. They form the backbone of the [Biblissima portal](https://portail.biblissima.fr/) and the Biblissima [IIIF Collections of Manuscripts and Rare Books search engine](https://iiif.biblissima.fr/collections/).

They have been set up in order to identify, disambiguate, harmonize and align named entities from a wide range of data sources (digital libraries, catalogues and specialized databases on manuscripts and early printed books). This effort has been ongoing since the beginning of Biblissima in 2012. 

They create a hub of identifiers and structured data, that is accessible, interoperable and reusable for other projects. This platform therefore makes authority data available in a structured format according to the principles of Linked Open Data and accessible by computer programs using web services (or Web API).

relatedItems.label: Biblissima Resources
relatedItems.description: This page lists all the resources developed and maintained by Biblissima's founding partners: digital libraries of manuscripts and early printed books, various types of catalogues and scientific databases, specialised corpora and textual editions, as well as resources that can be found in the Biblissima toolkit. A large part of the resources listed below are intended to be integrated into the Biblissima portal, a unified access point to medieval and renaissance written cultural heritage (VIII-XVIII c.).

relatedItems.label: Biblissima IIIF Collections of Manuscripts and Rare Books
relatedItems.description:
IIIF Collections of Manuscripts and Rare Books is a cross-collections search and discovery environment for IIIF-compliant manuscripts and rare books dated before 1800.  Its realization is part of the Biblissima+ programme, *Observatory of Written Cultures, from Clay to Print* (2021-2029). It follows Biblissima, *Observatory of the written heritage of the Middle Ages and the Renaissance from the 8th to the 18th century* (2012-2021). 

The general approach of this platform is not only to harvest and index the Manifests’ metadata as present at the source, but also to reconcile, cluster and normalise some of the metadata elements in order to perform powerful search capabilities and facets. This data processing leverages the big cluster of authorities which forms the backbone of the interoperability of Biblissima's data. All “reconciled” entities enrich these same repositories, which are published on a dedicated platform accessible at [data.biblissima.fr](https://data.biblissima.fr). This work of reconciliation, disambiguation and alignment is thus exposed and freely reusable by the original libraries or other research projects, according to Linked Open Data principles.

relatedItems.label: Wikibase
relatedItems.description:
Wikibase is a set of MediaWiki extensions for working with versioned semi-structured data in a central repository. It is based upon JSON instead of the unstructured data of wikitext normally used in MediaWiki. Its primary components are the Wikibase Repository, an extension for storing and managing data, and the Wikibase Client which allows for the retrieval and embedding of structured data from a Wikibase repository. It was developed for and is used by Wikidata, by Wikimedia Deutschland. (from: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikibase)

concept.label: IIIF
concept.definition: The International Image Interoperability Framework (IIIF) is a set of shared application programming interface (API) specifications for interoperable functionality in digital image repositories. The IIIF is comprised of and driven by a community of libraries, museums, archives, software companies, and other organizations working together to create, test, refine, implement and promote the IIIF specifications. Using JSON-LD, linked data, and standard W3C web protocols such as Web Annotation, IIIF makes it easy to parse and share digital image data, migrate across technology systems, and provide enhanced image access for scholars and researchers. In short, IIIF enables better, faster and cheaper image delivery. It lets you leverage interoperability and the fabric of the Web to access new possibilities and new users for your image-based resources, while reducing long term maintenance and technological lock in. IIIF gives users a rich set of baseline functionality for viewing, zooming, and assembling the best mix of resources and tools to view, compare, manipulate and work with images on the Web, an experience made portableshareable, citable, and embeddable. (source: https://iiif.io/community/faq/)

relatedItems.label: Mandragore
relatedItems.description:
Mandragore is the iconographic database of illuminated manuscripts held by the Département des Manuscritst of the Bibliothèque nationale de France. Users search the database using the various indexes that accompany most of the searchable fields, and descriptors that enable contextual searches. The most direct way to start querying the database is to know the call number of the manuscript. There is both a simple search bar and an advanced search functionality which allows users to restrict by date, place, etc. 

To find a manuscript on Mandragore, several selection fields are available. If you don't know the call number of the manuscript, you can search by author. For example, in the author index, under the letter B, there are several entries for Boccacio, and by selecting Boccacio, decameron, all five available copies are proposed.

In the case of images, you can search by the associated keyword, as many folios are annotated by subject: each folio has one or more descriptors associated with it, which enable you to search for all folios containing the same keyword. When a folio contains several miniatures, each miniature is indexed.

label: Bibracte_Thesaurus
description:
Bibracte_Thesaurus is a specialised thesaurus developed for the archaeological research and documentation of Bibracte. It provides a structured vocabulary reflecting the terminology used by the scientific partners involved in research at the site, covering areas such as archaeological excavation and prospection, artefacts, chronology, research methods, conservation-restoration and dissemination. Managed through Opentheso, it supports the standardised description, organisation and interoperability of archaeological data.

Bibracte_Thesaurus est un thésaurus spécialisé développé pour la recherche et la documentation archéologiques de Bibracte. Il propose un vocabulaire structuré reflétant la terminologie utilisée par les partenaires scientifiques impliqués dans les recherches sur le site, couvrant notamment la prospection et la fouille archéologiques, les artefacts, la chronologie, les méthodes de recherche, la conservation-restauration et la valorisation. Géré avec Opentheso, il favorise la description et l'organisation normalisées des données archéologiques ainsi que leur interopérabilité.

relatedItems.label: Opentheso
relatedItems.description:
Opentheso is a web-based thesaurus management tool dedicated to the management of vocabularies. 
It conforms to ISO 25964-1 2011 and ISO 25964-2:2012 standards (Information and documentation. Thesauri and interoperability with other vocabularies).
It is developed at the CNRS (National Center for Scientific Research - France), financed by GDS FRANTIQ (https://www.frantiq.fr/), la MOM (https://www.mom.fr/) and IR* Huma-Num (https://www.huma-num.fr/) with Consortium (MASA) Mémoire des archéologues et des sites archéologiques (https://masa.hypotheses.org/). 


OpenTheso is used by a network of 39 research libraries (FRANTIQ. Archaeology, 32 000 concepts. Contact : Blandine Nouvel), research units (Zoomatia, archaelogical research project), les Hospices civils de Lyon (medicine, 60000 concepts), l’Institut des Sciences de l’Homme (part of Rameau vocabulary)…

Ses fonctionnalités actuelles :
- Gestion avancée des termes et des branches
- Drag and Drop
- Gestion collaborative avec 4 niveaux d'authentification (Superadmin, Admin, User et Traducteur)
- Interopérable : génération automatique d'identifiants Handle et ARK (ce service est assuré par le PSIR de la MOM)
- WebServices REST
- import : SKOS, Turtle, JsonLD
- export : SKOS, Turtle, JsonLD, CSV et PDF



OpenTheso is released under the terms of the CeCILL_C license, fully compatible with the GNU GPL.

relatedItems.label: Enrichir le candidat avec des alignements et des images
relatedItems.description:
Ajouter un alignement : il s’agit de créer une relation d’équivalence plus ou moins exacte entre le mot-clé Pactols et un item correspondant dans un autre référentiel du web. Pactols a fait le choix de préférer les relations exactes (skos:exactMatch). Les alignements ne sont possibles qu’avec des référentiels fournissant un identifiant pérenne à ses items (DOI, ARK,...) ou une adresse web stable (URI).

Les principaux référentiels des alignements Pactols sont : Wikidata, les thésaurus du ministère français de la Culture (http://data.culture.fr/thesaurus/), IdRef (oeuvres, personnes), le Art and Architecture Thesaurus de la Fondation Getty, Bibracte_thesaurus, Bnf, Pleiades (lieux anciens), Geonames (lieux), Insee (lieux de France). 

Deux modes d’alignement sont possibles : 
1. alignement : faites une recherche préalable dans le réservoir puis donnez l’URI distante de l’item et le nom du référentiel dans le formulaire.
Ex. URI distante : https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q6934696
      Nom de la source : Wikidata
2. alignement automatique : Opentheso opère une recherche sur le libellé dans les référentiels pré-enregistrés : Bibracte_thesaurus, Bnf, GeoNames, Wikidata. Selon le réservoir, la réponse peut être faussement négative sur le libellé en français, par exemple avec Wikidata dont les items peuvent ne pas avoir d’équivalent dans la langue de la recherche. Écrivez de préférence le terme de la requête dans la langue du référentiel visé. Sélectionnez la meilleure réponse affichée. La possibilité de rapatrier des métadonnées supplémentaires (traductions, images, définition) peut être un avantage mais nécessitera une relecture voire une correction après alignement. 

Image : Certains concepts, difficiles à définir, peuvent être illustrés avec profit d’une ou de plusieurs images. Celles-ci doivent être représentatives du concept et se positionner autant que possible dans le champ de l’archéologie sinon de l’histoire ancienne. Elles doivent impérativement être libres de droit (sélectionnez les réservoirs ad hoc, notamment Wikimedia Commons, et citables (avec une URI comme adresse web stable, un PID identifiant pérenne de type ARK, DOI, etc.).

Pour ajouter une image depuis Wikimedia Commons : sélectionnez l'image choisie, cliquez sur l'onglet "use this file" et recopiez le champ "File URL:". Remplissez les 4 champs de l'onglet Image de Pactols : l'URI, la légende de l'image (libellé), son auteur et la source. 
Ex. pour amphore attique : URI : https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/01/Amphore_attique_%C3%A0_figures_noires._Peintre_de_Rycroft_-_btv1b101044967_%282_of_2%29.jpg ; libellé : Amphore attique à figures noires. Peintre de Rycroft ; auteur : Bibliothèque nationale de France ; source : Wikimédia.

label: BibServer
description:
BibServer is an open-source RESTful bibliographic data server. BibServer makes it easy to create and manage collections of bibliographic records such as reading lists, publication lists and even complete library catalogs. Its main features include

Create and manage bibliographic collections simply and easily

Import (and export) your collection from bibtex, MARC, RIS, BibJSON, RDF or other bibliogrpaphic formats in a matter of seconds

Browse collection via an elegant faceted interface

Embed the collection browser in other websites

Full RESTful API
source.label: TAPoR

label: BibSonomy
description:
BibSonomy is a social bookmarking and publication-sharing system. It aims to integrate the features of bookmarking systems as well as team-oriented publication management. BibSonomy offers users the ability to store and organize their bookmarks and publication entries and supports the integration of different communities and people by offering a social platform for literature exchange.



Both bookmarks and publication entries can be tagged to help structure and re-find information. As the descriptive terms can be freely chosen, the assignment of tags from different users creates a spontaneous, uncontrolled vocabulary: a folksonomy. In BibSonomy, the folksonomy evolves from the participation of research groups, learning communities and individual users, organizing their information needs.



Publication posts in BibSonomy are stored in the BibTeX format. Export in other formats such as EndNote or HTML (e. g. for publication list creation) is possible.



The service was developed by a team of students and scientists working at the Institute of Knowledge and Data Engineering and is hosted by the University of Kassel in Germany.



\[Description taken from the Wikipedia article about BiBSonomy\]

label: Bibus
description:
Bibus is a bibliographic and reference management software. As with other such tools, Bibus allows one to search, edit, and sort bibliographic records. In addition, Bibus contains features that makes it unique among open source and even commercial bibliographic databases:

Hierarchical organization of the references with user defined keys

Designed for multiuser environments

Database sharing among an "unlimited" number of users

Individual classification for each user

Ability to define read-only and read-write users

Live queries; that is searches that update as the database changes

Online PubMed queries

Online eTBLAST queries

Insertion of references and formatting of bibliographies into three widely used Word Processors (LibreOffice.org,OpenOffice.org and Microsoft Word)

Foreign language support through Unicode and gettext. As of version 1.4, Bibus is available in English, Chinese, Czech, French, German, Hungarian, Portuguese, Slovenian, Spanish.

Blender is a free and open source 3D animation suite. The Blender Foundation (2002) is an independent public benefit organization. Its spin-off corporation Blender Institute (2007) hosts the foundation’s offices and currently employs 24 people who work on the Blender software and creative projects to validate and test Blender in production environments.

In 2020 the Institute split in two companies; Blender Institute now solely functions as working company for the Blender Foundation, and the new Blender Studio will contribute to the Blender mission producing content and testing production pipelines.

These organizations support the community of contributors on blender.org. That is where Blender is being made.

Mission
Get the world’s best 3D CG technology in the hands of artists as free/open source software.

Vision
Everyone should be free to create 3D CG content, with free technical and creative production means and free access to markets.

relatedItems.label: Create the 3D Model
relatedItems.description:
# 3D Modeling
This step involves the creation of an accurate 3D model based on the processed and georeferenced data from the digital survey. Using the cleaned and aligned point clouds or photogrammetric outputs, accurate geometric digital representations of the monument are generated. This process may include surface reconstruction, mesh generation, and texture mapping, depending on the level of detail required. 

# Data Enrichment
Once the base 3D model is created, and depending on the project’s goals, the model is enriched with additional data—such as historical context, material properties, or conservation status—as defined in the project's objectives, resulting in a 3D Data Model.

# Input:

* Processed point clouds / meshes from Step 6
* Historical and architectural data from Step 2
* Metadata from previous steps

# Output:

* Base 3D geometric model → .obj, .fbx, .stl, .ply, .glTF, .3ds
* Textured 3D model → .obj + .mtl + .jpg/png, .glb, .glTF
* Enriched 3D model with annotations or metadata → .ifc, .gltf, .json

relatedItems.label: Select computation systems and 3D model structuring protocols
relatedItems.description:
Following the creation of the 3D model, select and configure an appropriate computation system to enable and carry out the 3D geometric analysis process. This system is used to operationalise the geometric attribute parameters, compute the geometric attribute data, and extract the resulting data in an interoperable format for further analysis. If required, adopt or develop a 3D model structuring protocol to guide the preparatory structuring of the 3D model prior to computation.

# Input:

* Formalised geometric attribute parameter catalogue
* Technical properties of the 3D model: .json, .xml, .txt

# Output:

* Model structuring protocol: .json, .xml
* Computation environment specification: software, dependencies, libraries
* Executable computation tools: scripts, node graphs, plugins

relatedItems.label: Geometric attribute data computation
relatedItems.description:
Quantitative geometric attribute data, tied to the corresponding parameters, is computed from the structured 3D model. This data is then exported into an interoperable format for further analysis. This process can range from an operator systematically assessing (i.e. measuring) the attributes to customised scripts mass-computing and extracting attribute data, provided the model has been structured first.

# Input:

* Structured 3D model
* Attribute data computation system

# Output:

* Attribute data in an interoperable format: .csv, .json, .txt

relatedItems.label: 3D HBIM Modelling and Enrichment
relatedItems.description:
Create a 3D object-oriented parametric model hierarchically structured and linked to the heritage asset's components or spaces. Enrich the model with harmonized multidisciplinary data (step 3). Includes model creation, enrichment, and validation (step 1). 3D-HBIM modelled elements should adhere to Industry Foundation Class (IFC) open standards for maximum interoperability.

Specific issues should be specially addressed in the 3D-HBIM modelling, such as, common harmonised modelling rules, the information requirements (e.g., LOD, LOIN, standards for information management and data exchange) and data specificities, related with significant addressed categories, for model enhancement purposes.
For model enrichment with multidisciplinary data (e.g., structural data, material properties, historical events, conservation state analysis) collected (step 2), processed (step 3) and validated (step 1) is possible to link, embed or import data to the 3D-HBIM model ensuring compatibility with IFC data schema.
HBIM model validation and quality control should contribute to ensure enhanced outputs, including clash detection or geometry checks to identify inconsistencies, metadata validation (e.g., element categories, naming), and export tests (e.g., standard IDS - Information Delivery Specification, [buildingSMART IFC validation system](https://www.buildingsmart.org/users/services/ifc-validation-service/) ). Examples of basic workflows for BIM modelling are available at [buildingSMART International website](https://www.buildingsmart.org/clarifying-the-openbim-workflow/).

### Outputs / Deliverables

- Basic BIM model in open file format (.ifc)
- Documentation of modelling process
- Raw data acquisition reports for long‑term preservation
- Quality assurance report
- Drawings & documentation package

relatedItems.label: Research Design and Methodological Planning
relatedItems.description:
The treatment of oral sources begins with a carefully structured phase of research design and methodological planning, which shapes the quality of the data collected as well as its legal validity, long-term preservation, and future reuse. This phase brings together methodological reflection, technical, and ethical choices, legal awareness, and archival foresight.

At its core lies a solid grounding in the principles and practices of linguistics and oral history. Researchers—and, where applicable, collaborators—should develop a clear awareness of the legal, ethical, and deontological implications of working with oral testimonies. This includes familiarity with relevant international and national guidelines, such as those of the Oral History Society (OHS) and the Associazione Italiana di Storia Orale (AISO), and an understanding of the responsibilities linked to the collection, processing, and preservation of personal narratives. At this stage, the focus is on building awareness within the research team, rather than formally informing participants.

Methodological planning also involves defining the research framework, including research questions, scope, and participant selection. Interviews should be conceived as co-constructed communicative events; therefore, flexible interview guides are preferable to rigid questionnaires, allowing space for digressions that may open new lines of inquiry.

Researchers must also anticipate the conditions of the recording, including the choice of environment and the establishment of a relationship of trust with participants, which directly affects the quality and interpretability of the testimonies.

Technical planning is equally essential. Decisions regarding recording formats (audio or audio-video) and equipment should be made in relation to research objectives and future uses of the data. These choices are methodological as much as technical, as they shape the nature and reusability of the sources.

Finally, this phase includes preparing the documentation resources that will support the workflow, such as interview guides, information sheets, consent and authorization forms, and recording sheets for contextual data. Anticipating legal requirements, preservation strategies, and future access conditions ensures coherence across the process and supports the sustainable reuse of oral sources.

label: Bulgarian WordNet - BTB-WordNet
description:
The creation of BulTreeBank WordNet has a long history. It started initially as Bulgarian domain lexicons aligned to domain and upper ontologies used with the following European projects: LT4EL, AsIsKnown. The utility of these lexicons for semantic annotation of domain texts, and some other NLP tasks motivated us to start our own work on Bulgarian WordNet. When CLaDA-BG project started at the end of 2018 it contained a little more than 19000 synsets. During CLaDA-BG project 2019, 2020, 2021 and beginning of 2022 BTB-WN was checked by two people for consistency, the definitions were improved, it was mapped to Bulgarian Wikipedia, for many synsets new examples were added.

Thus, the current version of BTB-WN - 4.0 - was thoroughly revised using a specified software and extended with more than 10 000 new senses, so currently it contains more than 30 000 synsets.
Several explanatory dictionaries were consulted about the number of word senses in BTB-WN, definitions, etc.

description:
Command line tool for linking civil registries.

Historians use archival records to describe persons' lives. Each record (e.g. a marriage record) just describes a point in time. By doing so, pedigrees of humans can be created over multiple generations for research on social inequality, especially in the part of health sciences where the focus is on gene-social contact interactions.

relatedItems.label: Producing Structured Visual Data from Illustrated Heritage Corpora
relatedItems.description:
Illustrated heritage corpora bring together digitised pages, plates, photographs, prints, drawings, captions, inscriptions, handwritten notes, and catalogue records at different levels of granularity. This workflow provides a method for turning these heterogeneous sources into visual units that can be located, described, compared, and reused while preserving their connection to the original documents and collections.

Starting from a research question, the workflow guides the selection of a representative corpus, the preparation of images and metadata, and the definition of the visual and textual units to be identified. A reference sample establishes the expected structure and quality of the results. Automatic or semi-automatic processing can then be used to extract images and associated text, followed by expert review, correction, and evaluation. The validated results are converted into structured data that can support cataloguing, quantitative analysis, visual exploration, or the study of relationships between images, texts, people, places, and objects.

The workflow preserves source identifiers, processing history, uncertainty, and validation status throughout the process. Its outputs may include extracted image regions, annotations, transcriptions, structured metadata, authority links, similarity results, and documented datasets. These elements provide a reproducible basis for further research and enable the resulting data, methods, and evaluation criteria to be shared and adapted across heritage collections.

This process is particularly relevant to researchers working with visual or illustrated corpora; research engineers and data stewards; libraries, archives, museums and heritage institutions; digital humanities projects preparing training, evaluation or exploration datasets; and teaching and training teams introducing computer vision methods for cultural heritage.

relatedItems.label: Georeferencing the surveyed data: Using a GNSS            receiver for precise positioning of Ground Control Points
relatedItems.description: Using well materialized Ground Control Points (GCPs) and using the same set in all the performed flights will require the use of topographic instruments only for the first acquisition, as once measured, the GCPs will be re-used for the subsequents flights. It is important to underline the importance of acquiring a trustworthy set of GCPs to be used for all the surveys, instead of measuring new GCPs every time. It is more important, in fact, not to acquire the most accurate GNSS data, but to use the most precise set of GCPs, assuming for (at least locally) the validity of the first data acquired, cause repeating measures over time may lead to non extremely precise co-registration of the generated models. Instruments required: Total station D-GNSS antenna Action to perform: Defining and measuring a topographic network Materialization of the topographical vertices Materialization of the control points Ground control points displacement around and inside the site Natural points selection and digitization for future surveys Control points measurement and recording (via Total station or GNSS receiver) Softwares to use: Topographic network compensation (e.g. MicroSurvey StarNet)

relatedItems.label: Gallica
relatedItems.description:
Gallica is the online library of the Bibliothèque nationale de France and its partners. Online since 1997, thousands of new documents each week and offers access to many millions of digitized documents. Gallica is one of the major digital libraries available for free via the Internet. It provides access to any type of document: printed documents (books, press and magazines) in image and text mode, manuscripts, sound and iconographic documents, maps and plans.

Most of Gallica's collections have been converted into text format using optical character recognition (OCR-processing), which allows full-text search in the library materials. Users can access high quality zoom via IIIF. 

Each document has a digital identifier, the so-called ARK (Archival Resource Key) of the National Library of France and is accompanied by a bibliographic description. 

Gallica is intended to all readers, whether users just having a look, booklovers, students or academics.

relatedItems.label: Georeferencing historical maps from Gallica using Galligeo

label: CATMA: Computer Aided Textual Markup & Analysis
description:
CATMA is a free, open source markup and analysis tool from the University of Hamburg's Department of Languages, Literature and Media. 

It incorporates three interactive modules: 
1. The tagger enables flexible and individual textual markup and markup editing. 
2. The analyzer incorporates a query language and predefined functions. It also includes a query builder that allows users to construct queries from combinations of pre-defined questions while allowing for manual modification for more specific questions. 
3. The visualizer provides basic visualization options for texts and corpora. 

CATMA also interfaces with the Voyant toolset. As of version 4.1, CATMA is a web application with collaborative work functions, and improvements to its user interface, queries and corpus analysis capacity. Version 4.2 offers, among others, new visualization options.

Catmandu is a command line tool to access and convert data from your digital library, research services or any other open data sets. Catmandu provides a suite of Perl modules to ease the import, storage, retrieval, export and transformation of metadata records. Combine Catmandu modules with web application frameworks such as PSGI/Plack, document stores such as MongoDB and full text indexes such as Solr to create a rapid development environment for digital library services such as institutional repositories and search engines.

In the http://librecat.org/ project it is our goal to provide an open source set of programming components to build up digital libraries services suited to your local needs.

Pymarc is a python library for working with bibliographic data encoded in MARC21. It provides an API for reading, writing and modifying MARC records. It was mostly designed to be an emergency eject seat, for getting your data assets out of MARC and into some kind of saner representation. 

The tool can parse MARC data in MARC21, MARC, MARCXML and JSON format.

relatedItems.label: metafacture
relatedItems.description:
Metafacture is a toolkit for processing semi-structured data with a focus on library metadata. It provides a versatile set of tools for reading, writing and transforming data. Metafacture can be used as a stand-alone application or as a Java library in other applications. The name Metafacture is a portmanteau of the words metadata and manufacture.

Metafacture includes a large number of modules for operating on semi-structured data. These modules can be combined to build pipelines to perform complex metadata processing tasks. The pipelines can be constructed either in Java code or with the domain-specific language Flux. One of the core features of Metafacture is the Metamorph module. Metamorph is an xml-based language for specifying transformations of semi-structured data. It can be seamlessly integrated into Java code.

At its heart Metafacture is a framework for implementing modules for metadata processing. This makes Metafacture easily extendable with additional modules. The plugins and tools page on the wiki shows supplementary packages and projects which extend Metafacture.

Originally, Metafacture was developed as part of the Culturegraph platform but it is developed independently now and used by others, too: see who uses Metafacture.

Also Metafacture Fix, a non-xml Catmandu inspired language for specifying transformations, is being developed that is not stream-based but operates at record level.

Metafacture is maintained by the Team Offene Infrastruktur by hbz.

relatedItems.description: The E-Spectator course aims to train students to better understand and analyze the Performing Arts, mostly performance plays and dance performances but also perfomative activities such as fashion shows, providing new methods for their study along with digital technology. Performing Arts’ esthetic and poetry can be sometimes destabilizing at first glance and difficult to analyze because it is by nature ephemeral. Yet the Performative Arts are bearers of an alternative vision of the world that allows to maintain a critical view of events and our environment. In concrete terms, this project aims to the use of digital technology for analyzing live works, in particular through the study of videos of live shows.

relatedItems.label: L’annotation vidéo pour la recherche. Usages et outils numériques
relatedItems.description:
The creation, documentation, and analysis of digital audiovisual documents are central to numerous research projects in the humanities and social sciences. While the emergence of corpora comprised of audiovisual content is not novel, the advent of the digital era has greatly transformed their encoding, processing, sharing, and preservation, as well as the organization of researchers' work. This abundance of digital or digitized documents is accompanied by a shift in the relationship between users and digital audiovisual documents (DAD). Focusing on the concept of video annotation, this white paper from the CANEVAS consortium offers a (non-exhaustive) mapping of annotation practices and tools by employing the notion of personas to connect them. With a dual concern of contributing to the development of research on DAD annotation and engaging in an open conception of science, this toolkit aims to renew the instrumentation of research in the humanities and social sciences.

This French-language publication, created by the Canveas Consortium of IR* HumaNum, explores tools related to video annotation.

relatedItems.label: e-spect@tor
relatedItems.description:
From Stage to Screen: analyzing Performing Arts through e-spect@tor

e-spect@tor is an application dedicated to the annotation and interpretation of performing arts videos. It is designed to equip researchers, students, educators, and learners with tools to better understand and critically analyze video archives of the Performing Arts.

e-spect@tor, led by Cécile Chantraine Braillon (La Rochelle Université, Theatralia WG), was developed as a fork of Celluloid, a project originally created by Laurent Tessier (Institut Catholique de Paris) and Michaël Bourgatte (Université de Lorraine).

The application supports the study of a wide range of performing arts, including theatrical performances, dance, fashion shows, music concerts, and other performative genres. The aim is to propose innovative methods for studying these art forms by combining traditional analytical approaches with cutting-edge digital technologies and methodologies. Thanks to the e-spect@tor application and its functionalities to analyze video recordings of performative works, users will engage with an innovative digital tool that allows them to explore and analyze live works more thoroughly. 

The project is continuously evolving and is currently available in French, English, Spanish, and Indonesian, with upcoming support for Croatian and Portuguese.

Each instance hosts its users and their videos. In this way, every instance is created, moderated and maintained independently by various administrators. You can still watch from your account videos hosted by other instances though if the administrator of your instance had previously connected it with other instances.

label: CELT: Corpus of Electronic Texts
description:
CELT is an online database of contemporary and historical topics from many areas, including literature and the other arts. It is showcasing Ireland's heritage, and providing material for the greatest possible range of readers, researchers, academic scholars, teachers, students, and the general public. The texts can be searched, read on-screen, downloaded for later use, or printed out.


Texts are taken from the printed editions, scanned, and proofread. Markup for structural and analytic features is added according to the recommendations of the Text Encoding Initiative (TEI). Conversions to HTML are made for online reading, and the master files can be used to create versions in other formats, and for contextual searching, concordancing, and other analyses.


Note: This is thought to be one of the earliest examples of a Digital Humanities project in Ireland, originating in 1997. While the presentation format is dated the resource still offers value to the scholar.

The focus lies on manuscripts materials, but the Heritage of the Printed Book Database (HPB) and the English Short-Title Catalogue can be included in the search as well. More databases will be added in the near future, making this search portal a useful instrument for those researching manuscripts and other early written materials.

relatedItems.label: Kramerius
relatedItems.description:
Kramerius is an open source software for making digital documents accessible. It is primarily designed for digitalised library collections -- monographs and periodicals. 

It can be also used to make other types of documents accessible, such as maps, sheets of music, or old prints, if need be parts of documents, such as articles or chapters. The system is even suitable for „born digital“ documents, meaning those that come up in electronic form. The Kramerius system is being updated continuously, so that its metadata structure corresponds with the standards published by the National library of the Czech Republic.

The system provides an interface for end users, that enables them to search both in the metadata and in the full texts, to generate multi-page PDF documents from selected pages, download individual pages (JPEG) or print them.

From the management point of view, system Kramerius allows to create virtual collections, change accessibility, import, export, and other operations concerning the saved collection of digital documents.

label: CESNET DataCare - Object Based Storage
description: Object-based storage offered by CESNET is a simple and reliable service enhancing archiving of user data. CESNET provides two basic object-based services. Ceph RBD and S3. Ceph RBD (RADOS Block Device) images are simple block devices that are striped over objects and stored in a RADOS object store. Ceph RBD provides users with a network block device that looks like a local disk on the system where it is connected. The block device is fully managed by the user. An user can create a file system there and use it according to his needs. RBD image can be also encrypted. S3 is object-oriented storage accessible via HTTPS. Underneath S3 you can create so-called buckets where you can store your data. To manage your buckets and data you can use various clients like aws-cli, s3cmd, s5cmd. Most of the applications, e.g. backup tools, has their own built-in client, which can be configured directly against S3 storage using an access key and secret key.

It is owned and published by the Consortium of European Social Science Data Archives (CESSDA) and its national Service Providers. The thesaurus consists of over 3,300 concepts and covers the core social science disciplines: politics, sociology, economics, education, law, crime, demography, health, employment, information and communication technology and, increasingly, environmental science. ELSST is used for data discovery within CESSDA and facilitates access to data resources across Europe, independent of domain, resource, language or vocabulary. label: CESSDA Vocabularies Service (CVS)
description: The Vocabulary Service offers users the ability to discover, browse, and download controlled vocabularies in various languages. Downloads can be done in SKOS, HTML, and PDF formats, in the chosen languages.The CVS service also allows communities and organizations referred to as Agency to host and publish their own vocabularies for users to search and download. The communities have roles such as Editor, which enables them to create, manage, and translate the vocabularies. The editor also includes an access and user management interface and allows versioning with persistent identifiers and citation of the Controlled Vocabularies (CVs). The following link, https://docs.tech.cessda.eu/content-management/cvs-agency.html, provides guidance on registering a community as an Agency.Many of the vocabularies have been developed and maintained by the DDI Alliance and its Controlled Vocabularies Working Group. The Data Documentation Initiative (DDI) is a global standard used to describe data generated by surveys and other observational methods in social, behavioral, economic, and health sciences.Non-English versions of the vocabularies have been supplied by CESSDA members and associated organizations in different countries. The vocabularies allow for data descriptions to be harmonized, such as in the CESSDA Data Catalogue (CDC) service. As DDI vocabularies are utilized worldwide, organizations that want to produce and maintain a language not currently included are encouraged to do so. The same applies to the CESSDA Topic Classification vocabulary. Any interested organization is encouraged to submit their contact information to the DDI Controlled Vocabularies Working Group or via the "Send feedback" button on any page in the CESSDA Vocabulary Service.The service is also available through REST API at https://api.tech.cessda.eu/ by selecting the service in the dropbox.

label: Chronos Timeline
description:
HyperStudio's Chronos Timeline is designed specifically for needs in the humanities and social sciences to represent time-based data. Chronos allows scholars and students to dynamically present historical data in a flexible online environment. Switching easily between vertical and horizontal orientations, researchers can quickly scan large number of events, highlight and filter events based on subject matter or tags, and recontextualize historical data. The Chronos Timeline is one component in HyperStudio's emerging Repertoire platform and can easily be integrated with other tools such as faceted browsers, maps, and visualization modules.



Built in JavaScript on top of an extendable object-oriented architecture, Chronos is a flexible jQuery plug-in using the powerful jQuery library. Chronos is notable for its dynamic scaling, which allows the user to drill down into time periods to explore and compare events. Chronos connects flexibly to data sources via the JSON open standard, and will support XML data structures in a future version. Repertoire Chronos Timeline is currently in beta stage and will be released as free software under the GNU General Public License.

label: Cinco
description:
The "CINCO SCCE Meta Tooling Framework" is a generator-driven development environment for domain-specific graphical modeling tools. It is based on the Eclipse Modeling Framework and Graphiti Graphical Tooling Infrastructrure, but aims to hide much of their complexity and intricate APIs.



A graphical modeling tool developed with CINCO is completely generated from an intuitive higher-level abstract specification language. Semantics-inducing parts of the tool that are difficult to define in an abstract declarative way (such as model interpreters, transformations, or code generators) are written in Java against a simple model-based API. CINCO handles the inclusion of the right buttons in the GUI that trigger those actions.



Furthermore, CINCO supports the integration of the Java Application Building Center (jABC) into the development process, so that even people with little or no programming experience can express model behavior in a process-oriented fashion.

description:
Cirilo Client for GAMS (application for data curation in FEDORA-based repository systems)

Cirilo is an application developed for content preservation and data curation in FEDORA-based repository systems. Content preservation and data curation include object creation and management, versioning, normalization and standards, and the choice of data formats. The client offers functionalities which are especially prone to be used as tools for mass operations on FEDORA objects, such as ingest or replacement processes. Cirilo uses a collection of predefined content models, which can be used without further adjustments for standard workflow scenarios like the management of collections of TEI objects. It encapsulates functions for the resolvement of place names or ontology concepts, thus semantically enriching resources in the digital archive. Various dissemination options can also be assigned with the client.

The CLAN Programs are downloaded, installed, and used as a single application. Functionally, however, CLAN has two parts. The first part is the CLAN editor which can be used to edit files in either CHAT or CA (Conversation Analysis) format. relatedItems.label: Choix d'un outil de transcription
Transcribe and process the interview
relatedItems.description:
Produce a transcription of the recorded interview in order to enable analysis, indexing, and long-term accessibility. Transcription constitutes a key stage in the enrichment of the oral source, transforming an audio or audiovisual document into a textual resource that can be searched, annotated, and reused.

Define the level of transcription according to the objectives of the research. This may range from verbatim transcription (including hesitations, pauses, and non-verbal elements) to a more edited version that improves readability while preserving the meaning of the discourse. Where relevant, adopt established transcription conventions and ensure consistency across the corpus.

If required, integrate time-coding to align the transcription with the original recording, facilitating navigation between text and audio/video. Consider also the need for translation, particularly in multilingual research contexts.

During transcription, pay attention to the treatment of personal data and sensitive information. Anonymisation or pseudonymisation may be necessary, especially when preparing the material for dissemination or public access. Any modifications should be documented to ensure transparency and reproducibility.

The transcription should be treated as a distinct but related document within the oral source corpus. It must therefore be documented through a dedicated record, including its relationship to the original recording, the tools and methods used, and the identity of the transcriber.

This step may be carried out prior to, or in parallel with, the description and metadata creation phase, depending on the research design and available resources. In all cases, it significantly enhances the findability, accessibility, and reusability of the oral source in line with FAIR principles.

relatedItems.label: The Royal Society Corpus
relatedItems.description:
This corpus contains journal articles published in [Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London](http://rstl.royalsocietypublishing.org/) between 1665 and 1869. It includes all publications of the journal written mainly in English and containing running text. The Philosophical Transactions was the first periodical of scientific writing in England. Founded in 1665 by Henry Oldenburg, the first secretary of the Royal Society, it initially contained excerpts of letters of his scientific correspondence, reviews and summaries of recently-published books, and accounts of observations and experiments. 

The corpus is available for online querying through CQPweb and for download from the CLARIN-D repository of the University of Saarland.

relatedItems.label: The Old Bailey Corpus
relatedItems.description:
This historical corpus consists of [Proceedings of the Old Bailey](http://www.oldbaileyonline.org/); the Old Bailey was London’s central criminal court between 1674 and 1913. The corpus is annotated for detailed utterance-level sociolinguistic annotation at the following three levels: sociobiographical speaker information (gender, age, occupation, social class), pragmatic information (speaker role in the courtroom such as judge, witness, etc.), and metatextual information (the scribe, printer, and publisher of the individual Proceeding).

The corpus is available for download from CLARIN-D (Saarland University) and for online browsing through CQPWeb. 
For the corpus manual, see [Huber et al. (2016).](https://www.clarin.eu/resource-families/historical-corpora#Huber%20et%20al.%202016)

relatedItems.label: Linguistic Annotation
relatedItems.description: The corpus texts containing TEI text structuring can be further enhanced by adding linguistic markup, e.g. information on tokens, lemmas, Parts-of-Speech or results of higher level linguistic analysis). Here, a wide range of NLP tools are available to perform the task of linguistic analysis and tagging automatically. For example, the CLARIN infrastructure offers the WebLicht service which allows for data analysis with various NLP tools and for the building of analysis chains. In- and output format here is the Text Corpus Format (TCF; for conversion between TEI and TCF use the TEI2TCF-webservice). Another toolkit is e.g. Apache OpenNLP. As tools you may use e.g. the Stanford Tokenizer or TreeTagger for tokenization, POS tagging and more, or e.g. enrich corpus with Named Entity Recognition annotation (e.g. by usage of Apache Stanbol or Babelfy). Manual annotation may e.g. be performed in WebAnno.

relatedItems.label: Manual annotation
relatedItems.description: Sometimes, a research question requires a very specific annotation that can not be covered by the automatic annotation provided by NLP tools and frameworks. In this case, annotation has to be performed semi-automatically or entirely manually. This is often done in collaborative work and often requires several correction cycles. Fortunately, there are tools that support this work and also create formats that can be easily processed later on.

relatedItems.label: INCEpTION
relatedItems.description:
**INCEpTION** is an open-source, web-based platform for annotating text. It supports annotations of any span of text, from single words to whole documents, relations between annotations, coreference chains and document-level labels, on documents in formats such as plain text, PDF, HTML and TEI. INCEpTION is the successor of WebAnno and can import WebAnno projects.

* **Collaborative Annotation:** Multiple annotators can work on the same documents, with different workflow management schemes, built-in inter-annotator agreement measures, and curation of the individual annotations into a gold standard.
* **Customizable Annotation Layers:** Users define their own layers, features and tagsets in the browser, tailored to the needs of their project.
* **Knowledge Base Integration:** Annotations can be linked to knowledge bases and authority files such as Wikidata, the GND and SNOMED CT, to other resources in RDF, OWL, OBO or SKOS, and to remote SPARQL endpoints.
* **Machine Learning Integration:** Built-in recommenders learn from the annotations as users work and suggest new ones, active learning focuses attention on uncertain cases, and projects can connect their own models as external recommenders.
* **Interoperability:** It imports and exports a range of formats, including TEI, CoNLL-U and other CoNLL variants, WebAnno TSV, WebLicht TCF and UIMA XMI, and offers a REST API for integration into processing pipelines.
* **Flexible Deployment:** It runs on a single computer or on an institutional server with single sign-on. Hosted instances are offered through CLARIN:EL and CLARIN-IT.

These features make INCEpTION a comprehensive solution for building and managing annotated corpora.

relatedItems.label: Federated Content Search Tutorial
relatedItems.description:
The Aggregator application is a part of the CLARIN-FCS common federated content search infrastructure. It serves as a user interface to perform queries to CLARIN-
 resources and display search results. The Aggregator communicates with components called endpoints, which are provided as a service by all centres who participate in the federated content search. Each endpoint provides access to one or more searchable resources. The user can select a specific resource or resources, based on the resource name or on the language, or search through all of them. The content of these resources is searched with the query supplied to the endpoint. The endpoint returns results to this query and the aggregator collects the responses from all the endpoints and displays them to the user.

Glossa is also freely available for download from [GitHub](https://github.com/textlab/fglossa) and is easy to install on one's own server. Glossa is search engine agnostic and comes with support for the IMS Corpus Workbench and CLARIN Federated Content Search out of the box.

label: CLARIN Multilingual Metadata
description:
The  CLARIN  Multilingual  Metadata  resource  translates  into  different  languages  the  set  of  232 approved  metadata  from  the  CLARIN  Concept  Registry  (CCR),  which  are  originally  available  in English. Together with metadata, their definitions are translated as well.

CLARIN metadata aims at describing language resources. In particular, they are meant to map and harmonise metadata from various centres in the Virtual Language Observatory (VLO). Translating such metadata and their definitions allows to describe in many languages the different resources in the VLO, developed by different researchers from different countries, and to pursue the harmonisation intent with a multilingual approach. In this way, non-native English speakers will be able to describe their resources more easily, as they can adopt their own language. Similarly, SSH researchers will be able to find and access such resources in a simpler way.

The  CCR  232  approved  metadata  and  their  definition  are  translated  into  four  languages, namely Dutch, French, Greek and Italian. Translations are obtained by exploiting state-of-the-art Machine Translation tools (Deep-L, Google Translate, LINDAT Translation, Reverso) and manually checked by domain experts that are native speakers of the language.

relatedItems.label: 3D HBIM Modelling and Enrichment
relatedItems.description:
Create a 3D object-oriented parametric model hierarchically structured and linked to the heritage asset's components or spaces. Enrich the model with harmonized multidisciplinary data (step 3). Includes model creation, enrichment, and validation (step 1). 3D-HBIM modelled elements should adhere to Industry Foundation Class (IFC) open standards for maximum interoperability.

Specific issues should be specially addressed in the 3D-HBIM modelling, such as, common harmonised modelling rules, the information requirements (e.g., LOD, LOIN, standards for information management and data exchange) and data specificities, related with significant addressed categories, for model enhancement purposes.
For model enrichment with multidisciplinary data (e.g., structural data, material properties, historical events, conservation state analysis) collected (step 2), processed (step 3) and validated (step 1) is possible to link, embed or import data to the 3D-HBIM model ensuring compatibility with IFC data schema.
HBIM model validation and quality control should contribute to ensure enhanced outputs, including clash detection or geometry checks to identify inconsistencies, metadata validation (e.g., element categories, naming), and export tests (e.g., standard IDS - Information Delivery Specification, [buildingSMART IFC validation system](https://www.buildingsmart.org/users/services/ifc-validation-service/) ). Examples of basic workflows for BIM modelling are available at [buildingSMART International website](https://www.buildingsmart.org/clarifying-the-openbim-workflow/).

### Outputs / Deliverables

- Basic BIM model in open file format (.ifc)
- Documentation of modelling process
- Raw data acquisition reports for long‑term preservation
- Quality assurance report
- Drawings & documentation package

relatedItems.label: Organize, describe and conserve the oral sources
relatedItems.description:
Implement preservation measures as soon as field production is complete. Conservation is not a deferred activity: decisions taken at this stage determine the long-term accessibility and integrity of the source.

1. Organise and name files systematically: apply a consistent file-naming convention that reflects the project, the date, and the session identifier. Store files in a structured directory that mirrors the relationship between the field recording sheet and the individual document sheets. Keep all documents produced in a single recording event together.
2. Create preservation copies: produce at minimum: one high-resolution preservation copy (WAV/BWF, 96 kHz, 24-bit for audio; MPEG-4 AVC for video); one local copy on a redundant storage medium (NAS or equivalent); one off-site copy in a secure, trusted cloud repository. Optionally produce a lower-resolution access copy (MP3 or equivalent) for consultation purposes. Never delete original analogue supports after digitisation.
3. Add preservation metadata: attach to each digitised document the following preservation metadata: original support type and conservation state; playback equipment and technical parameters used for digitisation; digital format, codec, sampling rate, bit depth; software and operator information; date of digitisation. Preserve scans or photographs of original physical supports and their containers.
4. Digitise analogue supports (if applicable): for recordings on magnetic tape, vinyl, cylinders, or other analogue media, contract a specialist digitisation centre with documented expertise (public or private). Follow IASA TC-04 for audio and IASA TC-06 for video. The preservation copy must be a faithful transfer of the original signal: introduce no filtering, noise reduction, or signal enhancement. Retain the analogue original after digitisation.
5. Describe sources for discovery and access: describe each oral source within a network of relations: link the recording to its field recording sheet, to the research project, to the agents involved (interviewer, interviewee, archivist), and to any related documents. Use controlled vocabularies and authority files. Consult descriptive software in use at reference institutions (see "Vademecum"). Align description with Dublin Core or EAD standards where applicable, to support interoperability.
6. Identify or select a conservation institution: if you are an independent researcher or a small institution, identify a conservation centre suited to your collection by disciplinary affinity or geographic proximity. Prepare: (a) a project presentation sheet; (b) a transfer sheet specifying access conditions, use restrictions, reproduction rights, and loan terms. Transfer the collection in its entirety: avoid splitting a unified archival complex across multiple institutions.
7. Plan for refresh and format migration: digitisation alone does not guarantee long-term access. Establish a schedule for periodic refresh (copying files to new storage supports before degradation) and for format migration (moving files to new formats before obsolescence). If the collection is deposited in a conservation centre, clearly define which institution or department is responsible for carrying out these long-term preservation operations.

relatedItems.label: Prepare the repository (preliminary step)
relatedItems.description:
The first step is to create or configure a repository on a version control platform — GitLab or GitHub are the two standard options in SSH research contexts. However, GitHub is not a open-source platform, and it is preferable to use an open-source forge such as Codeberg (https://codeberg.org/). Your repository must include a set of mandatory files at its root, in Markdown format. A README.md file describes your software, its research context, and its usage. An AUTHORS.md file lists all authors with their institutional affiliations; contributors not intended to appear in citation metadata may be listed separately in a CONTRIBUTORS file. 

A LICENSE file specifies the reuse conditions of your source code. Licence selection should be carried out in consultation with the legal or valorisation service of your institution, as intellectual property rights may be shared between you and your employer. A codemeta.json file, generated with the CodeMeta Generator, provides machine-readable metadata that will pre-populate your HAL deposit form automatically. Both the copyright notice and the list of authors must appear explicitly in your repository at this stage, as they condition both citability and archiving eligibility in subsequent steps.

Finally, both Git repositories and Zenodo provide options to configure automatic archiving and synchronization between the repository and Zenodo. This integration enables version management and ensures that each software release deposited on Zenodo is assigned a persistent DOI, thereby facilitating citation, traceability, and long-term preservation of the code.

label: Coggle
description:
Coggle is an intuitive mind mapping tool that allows for collaboration between its users. It is free for public use and can be accessed in your browser or you can install the app on your Apple or Android device.
 
Though Coggle has been used for mind mapping, it is primarily a method of documenting branching and non-linear information, and encompassing multiple perspectives. It utlizes a drag and drop interface for integrating images, permits multiple users to edit at the same time without causing data conflicts, and supports Markdown and LaTeX formatting. Coggle diagrams can be interlinked, branches of one diagram can be spawned off into its own diagram connected back to the original, and individual branches can be linked via hashtags. The tool includes an API that permits users to interface their diagrams with other programs and manipulate or examine them, and diagrams can also be exported in various formats such as plain-text outline, vector PDFs or images. Coggle is free except where users require more than 100 monthly active users or a closed source version.

label: Concraft -> DependencyParser
description: The Polish dependency parser is trained on the extended version of the Polish dependency treebank (Składnica zależnościowa) with the publicly available parsing systems -- MaltParser or MateParser. MaltParser is a transition-based dependency parser that uses a deterministic parsing algorithm. The deterministic parsing algorithm builds a dependency structure of an input sentence based on transitions (shift-reduce actions) predicted by a classifier. The classifier learns to predict the next transition given training data and the parse history. MateParser, in turn, is a graph-based parser that defines a space of well-formed candidate dependency trees for an input sentence, scores them given an induced parsing model, and selects the highest scoring dependency tree as a correct analysis of the input sentence. Part of: Multiservice, a robust linguistic Web service for Polish.

relatedItems.label: Preserving 3D digital objects
relatedItems.description:
The long-term preservation of 3D digital objects raises some critical issues. Indeed, firstly, different kind of data can be archived: the original files depending on the method used to digitize; the final version, depending on the goal (simple acquisition or modelisation) and any relevant information (text, images, pdf , scenarios ...) added for a better comprehension of the 3D object. 

Secondly it is important that metadata accompany the archive to ensure that the 3D object will be human-readable in the long-term. These metadata have to be completed in distinct files.

The 3D consortium of Huma-Num developed a tool, aLTAG3D to easily produce metadata file for the full 3D archive. Lastly, a place to preserve 3D data in the long term has to be found. Many solutions exist, depending on the countries. In France, there are solutions such as the 3D conservatory for 3D data research for mid-term preservation, and the CINES in the continuity for long-term preservation.

relatedItems.label: Upload the archive in an official reliable repository
relatedItems.description: Submit the packet to a long-term storage service, preferably an official academic public permanent structure, like CINES for long term archiving or the French National 3D Data Repository for long term preservation, supported by Huma-Num in France.

relatedItems.label: Integrated Authority File (GND)
relatedItems.description:
The Integrated Authority File (GND) is a service facilitating the collaborative use and administration of authority data. These authority data represent and describe entities, i.e. persons, corporate bodies, conferences and events, geographic entities, topics and works relating to cultural and academic collections. Authority data make cataloguing easier, offer definitive search entries and forge links between different information resources.

It is operated cooperatively by the German National Library, all German-speaking library networks and the associated libraries, the German Union Catalogue of Serials (ZDB) and numerous other institutions. Contributions to the GND are made either via the networks or in direct agreement with the German National Library.

The Common Authority File (GND) is a service for the cooperative use and management of authority data. This authority data represents and describes entities, i.e. persons, corporate bodies, conferences, geographies, subject headings and works that are related to cultural and scientific collections. Standardised data facilitates indexing, provides clear search access points and links different information resources.

entityXML is (so far) a concept study in version 0.6.5 (BETA), which aims to model a standardised XML-based data format for the GND Agency Text+. The format is intended to cover three main aspects: The provision of a uniform (1) exchange and (2) storage format for describing entities, which can be mapped directly to the GND, and the Text+ GND agency also serves as a (3) workflow control instrument.

This resource is supported by [Text+](https://text-plus.org). In case of questions you may get in touch with the Text+ helpdesk at textplus-support@gwdg.de.

label: ContaWords
description:
With **ContaWords** you can quickly and easily get a frequency analysis of your texts (pdf, html, txt). The results can be downloaded and easily handled.

When you give **ContaWords** a task, it first reads the words of a text file and decides what part of speech to assign to each word (credit-Noun-credit but credit-Verb-to_credit). It then begins to count how many times a word appears in the text in every possible way (credits, credit, credited... etc).

**ContaWords** can also take into account that a sequence of words can, for example, be the name of an organization, a person or an entity (Named Entity Recognition).

Besides all this, **ContaWords** can find sequences of two words that seem to appear together more often than would be expected, such as "monetary policy " or "fiscal balance ".

label: Corpus de Referencia do Galego Actual (CORGA)
description:
The *Corpus de Referencia do Galego Actual* (CORGA) is a documentary corpus including different text-types representative of present-day Galician which are encoded in XML and cover the period ranging from 1975 to the present day. Codification is mainly applied to bibliographic information and document structure, and enables queries with or without regular expressions, by complete word, truncated word, and several words or word-parts, whether they are consecutive or not. Besides, users can restrict searches by applying a number of criteria such as time-span, subject field, type of document, or document area which can be combined depending on their needs.

CORGA has been improved by the automatic tagging of all documents, together with the addition of orthographic transcriptions of radio broadcasts where text and voice are aligned. Such alignment allows users to access audio clips matching the written text fragments retrieved as a result of their queries.

The present application facilitates the retrieval of linguistic data by means of a query tool that enables different search approaches: orthographic words, grammatical elements, word classes, tags, morphological features, lemmas or hyperlemmas. Based on these data, the system offers the possibility to extract simple and complete frequencies, to display the retrieved information in the form of concordances or to obtain the inventory of the requested elements for the whole corpus or for each of the classificatory parameters (period, source, origin, genre, subtype of document, subject area or author's gender). This version also includes the possibility of searching within a specific work and by a selected author or even by author's gender. Additionally, it offers a system for consulting the list of authors and works that make up the corpus, as well as a first version for searching for co-occurrences.

label: Corpus Documentale Latinum Cataloniae (CODOLCAT), v. 14 (2025)
description:
The creation of the Corpus Documentale Latinum Cataloniae (CODOLCAT) forms part of the Glossarium Mediae Latinitatis Cataloniae (GMLC) project—a dictionary of Latin and Romance terms documented within Catalan linguistic territories between the 9th and 12th centuries.

The GMLC aids philologists, historians, legal experts, and anyone interested in the Early Middle Ages in understanding the notarial documentation, as well as the literary, legal, and scientific Latin texts produced in the aforementioned regions and period. These texts serve as written testimony to both Medieval Latin and the emerging Romance language. In compiling our dictionary, we draw upon a manual index (comprising over 50,000 cards) as well as an extensive corpus of digitised texts (which currently encompasses more than 24,000 documents).

This latter corpus, converted into an externally searchable lexical database known as CODOLCAT, is intended as a tool to facilitate direct access to the Latin written output of early medieval Catalonia for those interested in the period. CODOLCAT allows for both simple and advanced lexical searches across the incorporated documentary corpus.

CODOLCAT is produced at the GMLC headquarters within the Milá y Fontanals Institution for Research in the Humanities.

label: Corpus Documentale Latinum Hispaniarum (CODOLHISP) 2
description:
The Corpus Documentale Latinum Hispaniarum (CODOLHISP and CODOLHISP 2) originated from the collaborative efforts of seven Spanish academic institutions—the CSIC and the universities of Santiago de Compostela, Barcelona, Valladolid, Alicante, Zaragoza, and the Balearic Islands—which share a commitment to research in Medieval Latin lexicography.

The primary objective of this project is to provide a common digital tool to facilitate access to Medieval Latin texts preserved across various territories of present-day Spain. CODOLHISP offers the scientific community and the general public a search platform for exploring, studying, and comparing Medieval Latin documents in an agile and rigorous manner. The implementation of CODOLHISP and its subsequent expansion with CODOLHISP 2 were made possible through the support and funding of the Government of Spain’s Ministry of Economy, Industry and Competitiveness, and the Ministry of Science, Innovation and Universities:

Network of Excellence FFI2016-81889-REDT (2017–2019), directed by Pere J. Quetglas (University of Barcelona).

Thematic Network RED2022-134432-T (2023–2025), coordinated by Ana Gómez Rabal (CSIC).

Both initiatives have driven the development of innovative digital resources, consolidating a shared infrastructure that promotes collaboration between researchers and facilitates access to Medieval Latin documentary heritage.

label: Corpus Paisà
description:
PAISÀ is a large corpus of authentic contemporary Italian texts from the web. It was created in the context of the project PAISÀ (Piattaforma per l’Apprendimento dell’Italiano Su corpora Annotati) with the aim to provide a large resource of freely available Italian texts for language learning by studying authentic text materials.

It constitutes a unique language resource for Italian in combining the following features:
- corpus of web texts (harvested in September/October 2010)
- composed entirely of freely available and freely distributable texts (under Creative Commons license, Attribution-ShareAlike and Attribution-Noncommercial-ShareAlike)
- dimension of about 250 mio tokens
- fully annotated in CoNLL format (lemmatized, POS-tagged (or also here) and annotated for syntactic dependencies)
- automatically cleaned-up and in part manually corrected (on different processing stages: retrieval of URLs, clean-up of harvested texts, and correction of annotations for adjustment of annotation tools)

Even though primarily created for language learning, the PAISÀ corpus also provides a rich resource for research.

This web site will serve a learner-oriented interface for online access to the corpus.

relatedItems.label: LetterSampo - Letters on the Semantic Web
relatedItems.description: Epistolary data about historical letters is typically distributed in different archives depending on where the letters were sent to and received, and the data are represented using local heterogeneous data models and different natural languages. To study such letter data on a global level, the heterogeneous, distributed data in local siloes need to be aggregated and harmonized into larger services where local metadata can enrich each other to complement missing information. LetterSampo a new framework for representing, publishing, and using epistolary data as Linked Open Data (LOD) on the Web for Digital Humanities (DH) research. The framework issued for creating LOD services and for building individual LetterSampo portals on top of them. To test and demonstrate the framework, it has been applied to the epistolary CKCC dataset of ca. 20 000 letters of the Huygens Institute, the Netherlands, to the correspSearchdataset of ca.151 000 letters aggregated by the Berlin-Brandenburg Academy of Sciences and Humanities, and to the Early ModernLetters Online (EMLO) data of ca.170 000letters published by the University of Oxford. The CKCC and correspSearch datasets were published as LOD services, SPARQL endpoints, and as data dumps at Zenodo.org for re-use, and a demonstrational portal LetterSampo: Historical Letters on the Semantic Web was created based on this data. A novelty of the LetterSampo portals is to use faceted semantic search for filtering data of interest in flexible ways from multiple perspectives on two conceptual levels, and then visualize and analyzethe results and data by seamlessly integrated data analytic tools - programming skills are not needed for using the portals. In addition to using the tools of the portal, the SPARQL endpoints can be used with modest knowledge about programming for DH research

label: Cos4Bio
description: \*\*\[Cos4Bio\](https://cos4bio.eu)\*\* It is a co-designed, interoperable and open source service that integrates biodiversity observations from multiple citizen observatories in one place allowing experts to save time in the species identification process and get access to an enormous number of biodiversity observations. Cos4Bio has been developed within the European Horizon 2020 Cos4Cloud project whose main objective is to improve citizen observatories technologies to help them increase the quantity and the quality of observations and, finally, to help ensure their long-term viability. Cos4Bio allows citizen science experts to view and identify all observations from a single place, interacting with the community and contributing their knowledge about each species. When an observation has been identified in Cos4Bio, this information is updated in the citizen observatory where it was published, awaiting final validation according to the algorithm defined in each observatory, in some cases, these validation algorithms require a Some degree of experience, but in others several identifications of the same observation are required to validate it definitively. The file of each observation can be seen by entering the detail of each one of them. # Main advantages - Reduce the time that citizen science experts spend on the identification process and therefore on citizens observatories. - Allow users to download observations from one portal without forgetting that the platform will recognize and notify each observation's authorship. - Train much better algorithms than if we have separate databases with only the partial information of a single citizen observatory. # Infographic !\[Cos4Bio\](https://cos4cloud-eosc.eu/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/Cos4Bio_Infografia-1024x723.png)
