label: Defacement Archive
description:
## The Defacement Archive is a collection of resources for academic engagement with web defacements. It has three main parts:

- The archive, based on the Attrition.org defacement mirror (coming soon, see the next section for more information)
- Research blog showing examples of using web defacements for research
- A collection of resources and publications

## What are web defacements?

Web defacements are unauthorized alterations or overwrites of existing web pages. While web pages might be defaced for a number of reasons ranging from cyber war campaigns to competitive hacking, web pages are also defaced for the expression and propagation of political content in the widest sense. Web defacements as a form of hacktivism are rarely archived and thus mostly lost for systematic study.

## The Archive

The data source used for this project is the defacement mirror provided by attrition.org. The site has been collecting defacement from 1999 until 2001 and in March 2021 has published their archive and some of their archiving tools on GitHub.

The release provides a novel data source for the research of web histories, social movements online and the history of political hacking in the pre-2002 era. Complementing this data source are custom finding aids such as an external link network. With this defacement archive publicly available, the archive may help further research and also offers the potential to be expanded in the future. The available data source - essentially the complete attrition.org website, including the defacement archive - presented a rare opportunity for the development of an archive. The defacements were old, in many cases predating the start of national collections, but defacements were also mostly political in content. Combining these two attributes, the defaced pages offered the opportunity to provide valuable insight into the history of political expression through illicit means.

relatedItems.label: Gate Cloud
relatedItems.description:
https://cloud.gate.ac.uk is a public REST API providing access to a wide variety of GATE text analysis pipelines and other services for use by third party software.  A simple web interface is available to test individual pipelines on small samples of text, and API documentation is provided for use by application integrators.  A tool is also available to run GATE Cloud services against text stored in Google Sheets.

Available pipelines cover a variety of tool types, levels of abstraction and target domains, ranging from simple low-level text analysis such as part-of-speech tagging, general named entity taggers for a variety of languages, domain-specific entity recognition services for archaeology & dendrochronology, various classifiers to assist with analysis of disinformation and hate speech, and an OCR service to extract text from images.  A basic quota sufficient to analyse ~1200 texts per day is available to anyone, with higher quotas available on request to research users.

DeReWo ist ein korpusbasiertes Forschungs‑Tool des IDS zur Erstellung von häufigkeitsbasierten Grund- und Wortformenlisten. Mithilfe von Verfahren auf virtuellen Korpora und dem Deutschen Referenzkorpus DeReKo generiert das Projekt unterschiedlichartige Grund- und Wortformenlisten des deutschen Sprachgebrauchs, z. B. die Lemmakandidatenliste für das Online-Wörterbuch zur deutschen Gegenwartssprache. DeReWo richtet sich an Linguist:innen, Korpusforscher:innen und alle Interessierten, die quantitative Einblicke in Wortgebrauch und Wortformen erhalten möchten.

---

DeReWo is a corpus-based research tool of IDS for creating frequency-based lists of base forms and word forms. Using methods applied to virtual corpora and the German Reference Corpus (DeReKo), the project generates various lists of base and word forms in contemporary German, such as the lemma candidate list for the Online Dictionary of Contemporary German. The generated word lists are available for download, including detailed documentation. DeReWo is aimed at linguists, corpus researchers, and anyone interested in gaining quantitative insights into word usage and word forms.

description: hocr-detect-columns is a Node.js module used in projects like the NYPL's NYC Space/Time Directory to analyze hOCR files, identifying columns and connecting indented lines. Utilizing Cheerio for parsing and Simple Statistics for clustering, it determines column counts per page based on OCR line distributions. RBush and rbush-knn enable connecting indented lines to their respective predecessors. Available via npm or as a standalone tool, it offers output formats including JSON and HTML visualization, with configurable options for column count, character width, and minimum lines per column. The resulting JSON object provides detailed page and line data, facilitating further analysis.

label: DH Press
description:
DH Press (originally called diPH) is a toolkit conceived as an easy-to-use WordPress plugin which allows potentially every kind of user to visualise and mashup historic and geographic information, documents and various types of multimedia content to develop digital humanities project.

The user cannot start from the toolkit itself, as the first step to set up a project, when the toolkit is already installed, is a CSV import. This means that the raw information has to be processed first, through any software like Microsoft Excel or Google Spreadsheet, following some conventions dictated by the toolkit, and once completed must be exported in CSV format. The file can then be imported into DH Press.

At this point, the user finally has full control over the data. First, the toolkit needs to be informed of what kind of data is in each column, as it can handle various types, such as Short Text, Long Text, Lat/Lon, Date, and Link. The steepest learning curve resides here, in the data management part, as the database must be set up very carefully, and fixing any problem later is complex. This does not mean that new users cannot approach the tool, but some basic research on data management is required to make correct use of it.

After setting up all this fields, called "motes" in the toolkit, a legend can be assigned to each of them, for example a field called "city" might contain, through multiple entries, ten different cities, and to each of those will correspond the colour chosen by the user. It is also possible to assign icons or png images instead of colours.

A single control panel then allows the user to create, set up and manage multiple visualisations of different kind, and in each of them the user can choose which information to display and how. This part is the most useful and is really straightforward.

The last section of the control panel lets the user set up custom fields for data and run a test of the whole project, and outputs detailed error information.

Following the training page, http://dhpress.org/training/, it is possible to take advantage of a pre-existing database, which can be used to quickly set up a project, so that one can instantly work on the main control panel. There is a detailed google document that guides the user through the process step by step, and also offers an even more detailed annex. A couple of hours is enough to go through all of it and get the necessary information to use it correctly. Then, any view can be quickly set up and customised in any desired way.

Overall, this toolkit is quite stable, reliable, user-friendly after the first entry barrier and gives you a varied set of tools to visualise and display a large amount of data in a neat, organised manner.

For a more detailed and personal review, please read http://claudiasartori.com/2015/01/tool-review-dh-press/

label: DH-Stipends
description:
Our DH fellowships foster research into our freely accessible data and collections using text and data mining methods. The yearly call is mainly directed at young, tech-savvy researchers in all disciplines who already have some experience with Digital Humanities‘ methods and tools. The call focusses on the German National Library's catalogue with more than 27 million datasets.

Mit den DH-Stipendien fördern wir die Erforschung unserer Daten und Bestände mit Methoden des Text- und Data-Minings. Die Ausschreibung richtet sich dabei vor allem an junge technikaffine Forscher*innen aller Fachgebiete, die sich bereits mit Methoden und Instrumenten der Digital Humanities beschäftigt und praktische Erfahrungen auf dem Gebiet gesammelt haben. Im Mittelpunkt stehen die Katalogdaten der DNB mit über 27 Millionen Datensätzen. Bewerbungen sind jährlich bis Ende April möglich.

relatedItems.description: DARIAH-EU Working Group DHwiki presents this White Paper about Wikibase and the Wikibase Ecosystem as a digest of its permanent activity in providing documentation about MediaWiki-based software solutions to researchers. The output of the Working group is accessible on its Wikibase instance at https://dhwiki.wikibase.cloud. As diverse as the Working Group itself is the target group of this report: DH researchers, GLAM institutions, contributors to the software platforms provided by Wikimedia, and software developers. label: DiCoGrA
description:
DiCoGrA (Dictionary of Ancient Greek Collocations) is an online dictionary that systematically and thoroughly compiles and describes verb-noun collocations in Ancient Greek, such as πόλεμον ποιεῖσθαι 'to make war, to fight', δίκην διδόναι 'to suffer punishment', διαβολῇ χρᾶσθαι 'to accuse falsely', or εἰς ἀπορίαν πίπτειν 'to get in trouble, to fall into distress', drawn from a broad corpus of authors and works ranging from the Homeric epics (8th century B.C.) to Postclassical Greek (3rd century A.D.).

This dictionary provides an exhaustive morphological, syntactic, and combinatorial analysis of each collocation, as well as real-world examples of usage (with Spanish translations), frequency of use, and diachronic evolution.

label: DiCoLat
description:
DiCoLat (Dictionary of Latin Collocations on the Internet) is an online dictionary that collects and describes in a systematic and detailed way all verbo-nominal collocations (of the type gratias agere, bellum gerere or in mentem venire) of the Latin language in a large corpus of authors and works from the 2nd century BC. until the 5th century AD.

This dictionary provides an exhaustive semantic, syntactic and combinatorial analysis of each of the collocations, as well as real examples of use (with their respective translations into Spanish), frequency of use, distribution by authors and literary genres and diachronic evolution.

label: digilib
description: Digilib is a web based client/server technology for images. The image content is processed on-the-fly by a Java Servlet on the server side so that only the visible portion of the image is sent to the web browser on the client side. It supports a wide range of image formats and viewing options on the server side while only requiring an internet browser with javascript and a low bandwidth internet connection on the client side. digilib enables very detailed work on an image as required by scientists with elaborate zoom features like an option to show images on the screen in their original size. digilib facilitates cooperation of scientists over the internet and novel uses of source material by image annotations and stable references that can be embedded in URLs. digilib is used in the ALCATRAZ framework of image, text and annotation tools and many other projects.

label: Digital Damaged Ceramics - web site files and data analysis and generation software
description:
This tool contains the script of a website exposing the research products concerning the Digital Damaged Ceramics project, available at https://bombedceramics.github.io/digital_damaged_ceramics/, and all the necessary code and materials to replicate the website semi-automatically from similar museum data catalogues.  
The website files include:
- A data visualisation landing page (index.html).
- A catalogue for each of the two collections (sevres.html, mic.html).
- An interface for semantically querying the dataset via a  SPARQL endpoint with some sample queries to select and run (sparql.html).
- A page for exposing the completed 3D models (3d.html), which currently only exposes a demo set of objects and keeps being updated as the project progresses. 
- A page for the object and digitisation process datasets (downloadable in CSV and TTL formats) and their provenance graph (in TTL format) (dataset.html).
- Documentation illustrating the methodology in detail with simplified diagrams (documentation.html). 
The Github repository on which the website is hosted (https://github.com/bombedceramics/digital_damaged_ceramics) is freely accessible, and the code is released under a MIT License, to allow broad reuse. A Python script for compressing catalogue images to be quickly loaded in the HTML page is also provided, in case the gallery’s byte size is not appropriate for web fruition (python_scripts/img_compressor.py). 
The entire code base can be easily reused as a template for any project based on metadata structured on the extended CHANGES tabular template, as it exploits well-documented and easily accessible JavaScript libraries for data visualisation (such as Chart.js and Google Charts) and web development frameworks (Bootstrap). Original Changes templates can be accessed at https://zenodo.org/records/14277220. The extended version of the templates used in this project is available at https://bombedceramics.github.io/digital_damaged_ceramics/documentation.html#ceramics-classification.
Similarly, the datasets of the Digital Damaged Ceramics can be used as a reference to fill in the spreadsheets. These are published on the website under a CC BY License and on Zenodo (https://zenodo.org/records/15854369). Since the dataset is meant to be further enlarged and possibly updated or corrected, all the previous versions will be maintained on the same page, alongside their provenance data.
The SPARQL endpoint is currently hosted on Oracle Cloud and is available at https://ddceramics.duckdns.org/ceramics/sparql. The SPARQL query interface (sparql.html) can be configured by updating the endpoint path. We included in the tool a minimal set of pre-compiled SPARQL queries to allow domain experts to benefit from a powerful tool for exploring and analysing the metadata collection even without being acquainted with Semantic Web Technologies. The pre-defined queries should be updated according to the structure of the graph exposed through the endpoint.

label: Digital Editions Technology Stack
description:
The Editions Technology Stack is a modular collection of APIs, backend services, and client-side viewer applications developed by the State and University Library Göttingen (SUB Göttingen) to support the creation, management, and dissemination of digital scholarly editions.
The stack enables the standardized yet flexible transformation, annotation, indexing, and presentation of textual data from heterogeneous sources (e.g. TEI, HTML, DocBook). It includes APIs for text delivery, annotation, search, and indexing, as well as interoperable viewer applications for exploring and comparing digital editions.
The technology stack is designed for researchers, research software engineers, and institutions working with historical texts and other complex textual corpora, providing FAIR, API-driven access to digital editions and their associated metadata and annotations.

label: Digital Humanities Call
description:
Digital Humanities Call (starting every year in March): We will gladly support you with your research project by providing metadata, digital objects and infrastructures. The provisions in section 60d UrhG apply. If you have ideas for research projects to which we can contribute with our data, we look forward to receiving your application, including a project outline providing information about:
- the questions and objectives pursued by the project,
- the data corpus,
- the technical equipment required (hardware, software) and
- the expected duration of the project.

relatedItems.label: Kramerius
relatedItems.description:
Kramerius is an open source software for making digital documents accessible. It is primarily designed for digitalised library collections -- monographs and periodicals. 

It can be also used to make other types of documents accessible, such as maps, sheets of music, or old prints, if need be parts of documents, such as articles or chapters. The system is even suitable for „born digital“ documents, meaning those that come up in electronic form. The Kramerius system is being updated continuously, so that its metadata structure corresponds with the standards published by the National library of the Czech Republic.

The system provides an interface for end users, that enables them to search both in the metadata and in the full texts, to generate multi-page PDF documents from selected pages, download individual pages (JPEG) or print them.

From the management point of view, system Kramerius allows to create virtual collections, change accessibility, import, export, and other operations concerning the saved collection of digital documents.

Next to the documents and translations, the edition offers an introduction to the countries the diplomatic staff came from, highlighting their diplomatic relations before and during the war, the general character of the reports and the role that the persecution of the Jews played in them.Currently, the edition includes reports of the diplomatic staff from Denmark, Italy, Japan and the US. description: Discursis is a tool for analyzing text-based natural language with a focus on sequential analysis. It is particularly desgined to work with texts that have an internal temporal structure, such as a transcribed conversation. For each text, it generates a statistics-based internal language model and applies tagging to each temporal unit detected. The model and tagging are then used as the basis for an interactive visualization which permits examination at a various levels of granularity, ranging from a whole-text to a unit-by-unit level; it can also show topic usage patterns within the text. Users must purchase a license; both student and academic trial licenses are available.

label: Discuss Data
description:
Discuss Data (www.discuss-data.net) is a new open repository for storing, sharing and discussing research data on Eastern Europe, South Caucasus and Central Asia. The platform, launched in September 2020, is funded by the German Research Foundation (DFG) and operated by the Research Centre for East European Studies at the University of Bremen (FSO) and the Göttingen State and University Library (SUB). Discuss Data goes beyond ordinary repositories and offers an interactive online platform for the discussion and quality assessment of research data. Our aim is to create a space for academic communication and for the community-specific publication, curation, annotation and discussion of research data on Eastern Europe, South Caucasus and Central Asia.

In view of an increasing debate within the academic community about the reliability and validity of research data, especially regarding the post-Soviet region, this is of crucial importance. Also, there is an increasing demand for research data management and transparency, manifested in initiatives like the FAIR Guiding Principles for scientific data management and stewardship. The major German scientific funding institution, the German Research Foundation (DFG), suggests in its "Proposals for Safeguarding Good Scientific Practice" to securely store primary research data for ten years. As a project funded by the DFG, Discuss Data is commited to this practice.

Discuss Data combines the upload and publication of data collections not only with documentations of data collection, but also enables in the same space the interactive evaluation of the data through the assessment of their quality, their contextualisation and discussion. Thus, we enable the international community of experts to report faulty data, in case of missing data to recommend alternative data sources, and to extensively discuss the interpretation and application of data. Discuss Data presents the opportunity to structure and present feedback to research data and to transform the evaluation of research data from an individualistic to a collective procedure that benefits the whole academic community.

For data storage and long-term digital preservation, Discuss Data is connected to the DARIAH-DE repository, where all open data will be archived, and prospectively the Humanities Data Centre services. Through cross-linkage with various external data sources, the knowledge and debates about research data shall be collected interactively and made accessible to both the academic community and the interested public. Thereby, Discuss Data contributes to the creation of a project-independent, transregional and sustainable information infrastructure.

relatedItems.label: Distant Viewing: Computational Exploration of Digital Images
relatedItems.description:
A new theory and methodology for the application of computer vision methods to the computational analysis of collected, digitized visual materials, called “distant viewing.”

Distant Viewing: Computational Exploration of Digital Images presents a new theory and methodology for the computational analysis of digital images, offering a lively, constructive critique of computer vision that you can actually use. What does it mean to say that computer vision “understands” visual inputs? Annotations never capture a whole image. The way digital images convey information requires what researchers Taylor Arnold and Lauren Tilton call “distant viewing”—a play on the well-known term “distant reading” from computational literary analysis.

Recognizing computer vision's limitations, Arnold and Tilton's spirited examination makes the technical exciting by applying distant viewing to the sitcoms Bewitched and I Dream of Jeannie, movie posters and other popular forms of advertising, and Dorothea Lange's photography. In the tradition of visual culture studies and computer vision, Distant Viewing's interdisciplinary perspective encompasses film and media studies, visual semiotics, and the sciences to create a playful, accessible guide for an international audience working in digital humanities, data science, media studies, and visual culture studies.

relatedItems.description:
The Distant Viewing Toolkit is a Python package for the computational analysis of visual culture. It addresses the challenges of working with moving images through the automated extraction and visualization of metadata summarizing the content (e.g., people/actors, dialogue, scenes, objects) and style (e.g., shot angle, shot length, lighting, framing, sound) of time-based media. This toolkit is optimized for two purposes: (1) scholarly inquiry of visual culture from the humanities and social sciences, and (2) search and discovery of collections within libraries, archives, and museums.

Many open-source projects provide implementations of state-of-the-art computer vision algorithms. However, there are limited options for users looking to quickly build end-to-end pipelines that link together common visual annotations. Those tools that do exist focus on specific subtasks, such as as FaceNet’s recognition of faces (Schroff, Kalenichenko, & Philbin, 2015), visual embedding with PixPlot (Duhaime, 2019), and FilmColors’ analysis of color (Flueckiger & Halter, 2018). Different algorithms require varying dependencies, different input formats, and produce outputs using different schemas. Because of the rapid pace of scholarship across the many sub-fields of computer vision, it can be difficult to determine which algorithms to use and a significant amount of work to manually test every option. These challenges are exacerbated when working with moving images because most available computer vision libraries take still images as inputs.

The Distant Viewing Toolkit addresses these needs by (1) constructing an object-oriented framework for applying a collection of algorithms to moving images, (2) packaging together common sound and computer vision algorithms in order to provide out-of-the-box functionality for common tasks in the computational analysis of moving images, and (3) allowing video files alongside still images as an input. Currently provided algorithms include functionality for: shot detection (Pal et al., 2015), object detection (Li, Zhao, & Zhang, 2018), face detection (Jiang & Learned-Miller, 2017), face identification (Cao, Shen, Xie, Parkhi, & Zisserman, 2018), color analysis (Karasek, Burget, Uher, Masek, & Dutta, 2015), image similarity (Szegedy, Ioffe, Vanhoucke, & Alemi, 2017), optical flow (Farnebäck, 2003), and shot distance analysis (Butler, 2012).

relatedItems.label: Producing Structured Visual Data from Illustrated Heritage Corpora
relatedItems.description:
Illustrated heritage corpora bring together digitised pages, plates, photographs, prints, drawings, captions, inscriptions, handwritten notes, and catalogue records at different levels of granularity. This workflow provides a method for turning these heterogeneous sources into visual units that can be located, described, compared, and reused while preserving their connection to the original documents and collections.

Starting from a research question, the workflow guides the selection of a representative corpus, the preparation of images and metadata, and the definition of the visual and textual units to be identified. A reference sample establishes the expected structure and quality of the results. Automatic or semi-automatic processing can then be used to extract images and associated text, followed by expert review, correction, and evaluation. The validated results are converted into structured data that can support cataloguing, quantitative analysis, visual exploration, or the study of relationships between images, texts, people, places, and objects.

The workflow preserves source identifiers, processing history, uncertainty, and validation status throughout the process. Its outputs may include extracted image regions, annotations, transcriptions, structured metadata, authority links, similarity results, and documented datasets. These elements provide a reproducible basis for further research and enable the resulting data, methods, and evaluation criteria to be shared and adapted across heritage collections.

This process is particularly relevant to researchers working with visual or illustrated corpora; research engineers and data stewards; libraries, archives, museums and heritage institutions; digital humanities projects preparing training, evaluation or exploration datasets; and teaching and training teams introducing computer vision methods for cultural heritage.

concept.label: ASCII
concept.definition: ASCII abbreviated from American Standard Code for Information Interchange, is a character encoding standard for electronic communication. ASCII codes represent text in computers, telecommunications equipment, and other devices. Most modern character-encoding schemes are based on ASCII, although they support many additional characters. ASCII is the traditional name for the encoding system.

concept.label: BMP
concept.definition: The BMP file format, also known as bitmap image file or device independent bitmap (DIB) file format or simply a bitmap, is a raster graphics image file format used to store bitmap digital images, independently of the display device (such as a graphics adapter), especially on Microsoft Windows and OS/2 operating systems. The BMP file format is capable of storing two-dimensional digital images both monochrome and color, in various color depths, and optionally with data compression, alpha channels, and color profiles. The Windows Metafile (WMF) specification covers the BMP file format. Among others, wingdi.h defines BMP constants and structures.

concept.label: COLLADA
concept.definition: COLLADA (COLLAborative Design Activity) is an interchange file format for interactive 3D applications. It is managed by the nonprofit technology consortium, the Khronos Group, and has been adopted by ISO as a publicly available specification, ISO/PAS 17506. COLLADA defines an open standard XML schema for exchanging digital assets among various graphics software applications that might otherwise store their assets in incompatible file formats. COLLADA documents that describe digital assets are XML files, usually identified with a .dae (digital asset exchange) filename extension.

concept.label: DUBLIN CORE
concept.definition: The Dublin Core Schema is a small set of vocabulary terms that can be used to describe web resources (video, images, web pages, etc.), as well as physical resources such as books or CDs, and objects like artworks. The full set of Dublin Core metadata terms can be found on the Dublin Core Metadata Initiative (DCMI) website.

concept.label: JPEG
concept.definition: JPEG ( JAY-peg) is a commonly used method of lossy compression for digital images, particularly for those images produced by digital photography. The degree of compression can be adjusted, allowing a selectable tradeoff between storage size and image quality. JPEG typically achieves 10:1 compression with little perceptible loss in image quality. JPEG compression is used in a number of image file formats. JPEG/Exif is the most common image format used by digital cameras and other photographic image capture devices; along with JPEG/JFIF, it is the most common format for storing and transmitting photographic images on the World Wide Web. These format variations are often not distinguished, and are simply called JPEG. The term "JPEG" is an initialism/acronym for the Joint Photographic Experts Group, which created the standard. The MIME media type for JPEG is image/jpeg, except in older Internet Explorer versions, which provides a MIME type of image/pjpeg when uploading JPEG images. JPEG files usually have a filename extension of .jpg or .jpeg. JPEG/JFIF supports a maximum image size of 65,53565,535 pixels, hence up to 4 gigapixels for an aspect ratio of 1:1.

concept.label: Multispectral Imaging
concept.definition: Multispectral imaging, like other spectral imaging, collects and processes information from across the electromagnetic spectrum. The goal of Multispectral imaging is to obtain the spectrum for each pixel in the image of a scene, with the purpose of finding objects, identifying materials, or detecting processes.

concept.label: PNG
concept.definition: Portable Network Graphics (PNG, pronounced PEE-en-JEE or PING) is a raster graphics file format that supports lossless data compression. PNG was created as an improved, non-patented replacement for Graphics Interchange Format (GIF), and is the most widely used lossless image compression format on the Internet. PNG supports palette-based images (with palettes of 24-bit RGB or 32-bit RGBA colors), grayscale images (with or without alpha channel for transparency), and full-color non-palette-based RGB/RGBA images (with or without alpha channel). PNG was designed for transferring images on the Internet, not for professional-quality print graphics, and therefore does not support non-RGB color spaces such as CMYK. A PNG file contains a single image in an extensible structure of "chunks", encoding the basic pixels and other information such as textual comments and integrity checks documented in RFC 2083. PNG files nearly always use file extension PNG or png and are assigned MIME media type image/png. PNG was published as informational RFC 2083 in March 1997 and as an ISO/IEC standard in 2004.

concept.label: TIFF
concept.definition: Tagged Image File Format, abbreviated TIFF or TIF, is a computer file format for storing raster graphics images, popular among graphic artists, the publishing industry, and photographers. TIFF is widely supported by scanning, faxing, word processing, optical character recognition, image manipulation, desktop publishing, and page-layout applications. The format was created by Aldus Corporation for use in desktop publishing. It published the latest version 6.0 in 1992, subsequently updated with an Adobe Systems copyright after the latter acquired Aldus in 1994. Several Aldus or Adobe technical notes have been published with minor extensions to the format, and several specifications have been based on TIFF 6.0, including TIFF/EP (ISO 12234-2), TIFF/IT (ISO 12639), TIFF-F (RFC 2306) and TIFF-FX (RFC 3949).

concept.label: XML
concept.definition: Extensible Markup Language (XML) is a markup language that defines a set of rules for encoding documents in a format that is both human-readable and machine-readable.

concept.label: .3ds
concept.definition: 3DS is one of the file formats used by the Autodesk 3ds Max 3D modeling, animation and rendering software. It was the native file format of the old Autodesk 3D Studio DOS (releases 1 to 4), which was popular until its successor (3D Studio MAX 1.0) replaced it in April 1996. Having been around since 1990 (when the first version of 3D Studio DOS was launched), it has grown to become a de facto industry standard for transferring models between 3D programs, or for storing models for 3D resource catalogs (along with OBJ, which is more frequently used as a model archiving file format). While the 3DS format aims to provide an import/export format, retaining only essential geometry, texture and lighting data, the related MAX format (now superseded by the PRJ format) also contains extra information specific to Autodesk 3ds Max, to allow a scene to be completely saved/loaded.

It enables composers to write music efficiently with flexible input and editing tools, allowing them to refine ideas freely at any stage. The software also offers powerful arranging features, making it easy to adapt music for different instruments, transpose, transform harmonies, or generate parts from chord symbols.

Dorico includes high-quality sounds, audio effects, and a full mixer, allowing users to produce realistic playback and fine-tune musical interpretation. It supports seamless import and export of formats such as MIDI and MusicXML, facilitating collaboration and sharing across platforms, including desktop and iPad.

Its advanced engraving engine automatically produces professional-quality scores, with extensive customization options when needed. Widely used in educational contexts, Dorico is also a valuable tool for teaching and learning music theory, thanks to its intuitive design and rich learning resources.

relatedItems.label: Guide to Digital Music Editing
relatedItems.description: The “Guide de l’édition musicale numérique” is a comprehensive, up-to-date manual designed to accompany researchers and practitioners through the intricacies of digital music editing, with a particular focus on scholarly critical editions and the European research context. It is the result of collaborative work within the Huma-Num MUSICA2 consortium in Tours.The Guide addresses the conceptual foundations, technical strategies, and best practices essential for conceiving, producing, and disseminating digital editions of notated music. It systematically distinguishes between “digitized” and genuinely “digital” editions, emphasizing the importance of interoperability, sustainability, and the FAIR principles that dominate the digital humanities landscape.Core topics include the selection and use of notation software, detailed descriptions of encoding formats such as MusicXML, MEI, and Humdrum, and guidance for the conversion, visualization, and long-term archiving of encoded music data. The Guide clarifies legal responsibilities, collaborative workflows, and the integration of metadata and source references—crucial elements for traceability and scholarly citation.It devotes substantial attention to the creation and management of critical apparatus, annotation spaces, and dynamic links between digital editions and primary sources, especially through IIIF protocols and digital “twins”. The text includes a typology of current notation and editing tools, recommendations for quality control, and active encouragement to use open standards and open-access practices to maximize reusability and impact.The Guide situates digital music editing in the wider landscape of European cultural policies, research funding expectations, and technological change, advocating for adaptability and technical literacy among editors. Practical elements include step-by-step checklists for project planning, metadata entry, visualization tools, and the identification of trusted data repositories for long-term preservation.By synthesizing recent research, technological developments, and institutional frameworks, the Guide provides a vital roadmap for both experienced musicologists and newcomers seeking to navigate the dynamic field of digital music publication.

relatedItems.description: DraCor (short for "drama corpora") is a growing collection of TEI-encoded plays in (mostly) European languages. The project showcases the concept of "Programmable Corpora", conceived as research ecosystems revolving around an API that provides access to bespoke slices of extracted data. DraCor also exposes a SPARQL endpoint to connect its semantic entities (authors, plays, characters, etc.) to the Linked Open Data cloud.

relatedItems.label: Shiny Dracor
relatedItems.description:
We maintain two in-house corpora, a Russian Drama Corpus (RusDraCor) and a German Drama Corpus (GerDraCor), both comprising plays from the 1730s to the 1930s. Both corpora are encoded in TEI, an XML vocabulary, which makes it easy to extract structural information.

RusDraCor comprises 80 plays, GerDraCor holds 465 plays at present (late December, 2017), but we will be growing both text collections throughout the next year. Featured authors of RusDraCor so far are Blok, Bulgakov, Chekhov, Fonvizin, Gogol, Gorky, Gumilyov, Krylov, Lermontov, Mayakovsky, Ostrovsky, Plavilshchikov, Prutkov, Pushkin, Sumarokov, Leo and Aleksey Tolstoy and Turgenev. German authors are too many to be listed here.

Our main purpose is the social network analysis of these dramatic texts: we extract social situations by collecting information on who is talking along with others in a given segment of a play (acts, scenes, other constellations). Via an API, we offer structural information, which we can analyse with a variety of tools. This website gives you the opportunity to explore the social structure of individual plays.

The analytical part for this page was done by Ivan Pozdniakov in R and is presented by help of the web application framework Shiny, hosted on our own server. Ultimately, we are interested in structural changes over time, the evolution of Russian and German drama, so to speak, for which we provide other tools.

WikiPack is a web based personal information organizer and Markdown editor that uses Dropbox for synced storage. Using plain text Markdown files and WikiWords, WikiPack gives information context and links entries together by turning your Markdown pages into a private, password protected wiki. The easy to use Markdown language lets you create and edit your wiki pages without having to learn complex wiki syntax. WikiPack features page history/versioning and visual change comparisons in the browser-based GUI and store all of your files in your Dropbox account.

You can import existing markdown files to sync WikiPack with other apps and services using Dropbox, or use the quick-start template to set up new wikis.

WikiPack includes a GUI markdown editor with syntax highlighting, built-in markdown reference, support for Multimarkdown table, and toolbar buttons with keyboard shortcuts and tools for common formatting. WikiPack works in the browser so you can use it on any desktop or mobile device that has an internet connection and Dropbox functionality.

relatedItems.label: WissKI
relatedItems.description:
As a full-featured virtual research environment WissKI is scalable from small single person ventures up to large institutional projects. WissKI is part of the open source content management system Drupal and therefore provides all the advantages of a constantly maintained and developed webapp. WissKI has everything to fulfill the research data lifecycle: beneath the fundamental possibilities to create, read, edit and delete content, users can create revisions and translations, open the access to the data with a wide range of interfaces and integration options, but also restrict it via detailed rights management. The data is stored in an external triple store, reachable trough own endpoints and therefore independent from Drupal or WissKIs architecture. The data modelling follow an ontological approach, preferably, but not exclusively according to the CIDOC CRM. Furthermore, the basic functions of WissKI can be extended with a variety of Drupal modules. This turns WissKI to a software optimized for research data management, and suitable for a wide range of application areas.

WissKI started as a joint venture of the Digital Humanities Research Group of the Department of Computer Science at Friedrich-Alexander University (FAU) in Erlangen, the Department of Museum Informatics at the Germanic National Museum (GNM) in Nuremberg and the Biodiversity Informatics Group at Zoological Research Museum Koenig (ZFMK) in Bonn. The Software development was funded by the German Research Foundation (DFG) from 2008 to 2012 and from 2014 to 2017 and is currently funded by the NFDI4Culture Consortium within the National Research Data Infrastructure (NFDI). WissKI is now supported by the Association for semantic data processing (IGSD e.V.) and has a continuously growing community.

label: Dublin Core for Performing Arts
description:
The Dublin Core for Performing Arts (DCPA) is a digital description language model specifically designed for performing arts archives. It aims to establish a common framework for describing performing arts collections while adhering to the FAIR principles—ensuring that data is Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable.

The Dublin Core for Performing Arts (DCPA) was developed by the THEATRALIA Working Group (DARIAH-ERIC) during its second phase, titled Performing Arts: Navigating through Digital Knowledge Models (2024–2025).

You can download the DCPA here: https://hal.science/hal-05214127 

The Dublin Core for Performing Arts (DCPA), developed by the THEATRALIA Working Group (DARIAH-ERIC), addresses the wide variation in vocabularies and metadata schemas used internationally in performing arts archives. Many practitioners lack expertise in archival standards and often create non-standardized descriptive systems, hindering data interoperability. To tackle these issues, THEATRALIA developed a common digital description model based on the Dublin Core Metadata Initiative (DCMI). 
To design this model, the THEATRALIA Working Group has built upon the Dublin Core Set, which provides 15 standardized metadata fields for a simple yet effective archival framework. Recognizing the complexity of performing arts archives, the group has also considered the more detailed “Qualified Dublin Core” (DCTERMS) to allow greater flexibility and customization. Performing arts collections include diverse materials—from paper documents to digital assets—requiring a tailored approach. This framework integrates core Dublin Core elements while allowing users to select only the fields relevant to their specific archival needs, ensuring both consistency and flexibility.

label: dür.air - digital unfolding of reality through augmented interpretative representation
description:
Dür.air is a mobile augmented reality application conceived as a field-based extension of the scientific and epistemological framework developed within the n-Dame_Heritage project. Its name reflects its core ambition: the digital unfolding of reality through augmented interpretative representation — reconciling observation, interpretation, and documentation at the place and moment where scientific observation is produced, by embedding spatial, temporal, and semantic information directly within in situ investigation.   

In archaeology, conservation–restoration, architectural history, materials science, and landscape studies, knowledge emerges through situated practices: inspection, comparison, measurement, annotation, and the progressive construction of interpretative hypotheses. Where 3D digitisation often separates acquisition and interpretation in time and space, dür.air keeps geometry, semantics, and observation tightly coupled in a single mobile and autonomous environment. 

Combining persistent augmented reality tracking, real-time LiDAR sensing, and on-device photogrammetric reconstruction, the platform supports a progressive “unfolding” of the object or site — an evolving augmented representation built across successive field sessions. On a single device (currently iPad Pro or iPhone Pro with LiDAR) and without network connectivity, it covers the full chain of field documentation: annotation, structured semantic description, metric measurement, dense 3D modelling, orthophoto and profile computation, interactive analysis, and the replay of spatio-temporal observation trajectories. Geometry remains a support for interpretation, memory, and cumulative reasoning.

When connectivity is available, projects can be deposited on a server node for institutional archive, sharing, and web publication — while field work itself stays fully offline.

dür.air is developed at the CNRS MAP laboratory (UPR 2002) within the ERC project n-Dame_Heritage (ERC-2021-Advanced Grant), in connection with the Notre-Dame de Paris scientific action. Complementary support has been provided by CNRS MITI, the French Ministry of Culture, the Fondation des Sciences du Patrimoine, EquipEx+ ESPADON, and E-RIHS ERIC.

relatedItems.label: dür.air multimodality process
relatedItems.description:
The dür.air application (see related items) constitutes a **workflow** in its own right, in that it encapsulates a number of activities, some of which could be regarded as a **fully-fledged workflow** in their own right (for example: photogrammetric data acquisition). Developed by Livio De Luca within the UPR 2002 MAP CNRS, dür.air operates at the intersection of heritage sciences and digital sciences, and is designed to manage data from acquisition through to publication. Through **three distinct acquisition modes** (3D by LiDAR, 3D by photogrammetry and 2D by photography), it is possible to digitise an object, process it, enrich it via spatial annotations, and save or publish it in an interoperable manner. These three modes are shown in the **illustration** using colours and an animation. The **diagram** has been designed to illustrate as clearly as possible the **relationships and specific features** of the tool in relation to these three modes. In particular, it highlights the necessary changes (*in situ vs. ex situ* as illustrated in the diagram showing the types of lines and the square brackets, round brackets or curly brackets surrounding the function names) with regard to the relationships between the various stages of a workflow. Feel free to **right-click** on the image to open it in a new tab so you can zoom in and read it whilst following the various stages of the workflow. For interface et in depth documentation see "User manual url" in metadata fields. \
This workflow is not intended to be a precise definition of implementation and usage, but rather a **general overview** of the functions and the relationships between them. In the animated illustration, the letters of the **Latin alphabet** denote the processes of acquisition, processing and enrichment relating to the three modes of dür.air acquisition and the production of data relating to a cultural artefact. The letters of the **Greek alphabet** denote the stages external to the production of the data, especially the ability to upload projects directly from the device to a node (server) specific to an institution. If the workflow **step** linked to the previous one is an iteration or a direct derivative, the numbering remains the same and **‘** / **°** / *, is then added to the letter. Finally, the type of circle for each step is link to a family of activity. \
To provide more concrete explanations of dür.air’s practical applications without limiting the potential of this **workflow-tool**, we prefer to leave it to **users** to envisage usage scenarios that correspond to their own practices. In this sense, a dür.air project may stop at the acquisition stage or extend as far as the curation of customised templates to enrich its annotations. Nevertheless, the application **use cases** (look for "see also" metadata on this page to find examples) will always fall within the scope of all the functions presented here .\
Currently in beta and distributed via an app installed on an iPad/Iphone Pro, this workflow may evolve in the futur.

relatedItems.label: BBT - BackBone Thesaurus
relatedItems.description: The BackBone Thesaurus (BBT for short) is the research outcome of work undertaken by the Thesaurus Maintenance Working Group (WG), which was established within the framework of DARIAH-EU. The BBT is an overarching meta-thesaurus for humanities research data. It offers top-level-concepts (facets and hierarchies) that serve as the common ground for thesaurus building. It relies on a faceted classification, which is considered valid and consistent from a cross-disciplinary perspective. Among the major advantages of such a classification, is its potential expansion into new scientific domains in a sustainable and manageable fashion. It is important to underline that the BBT, explicitly does not require domain experts to abandon their terminology in the name of some universally accepted terminology. Rather, the core feature of the BBT is that it promotes alignment of cutting-edge terminology to well-formed general terms of the meta-thesaurus capturing general meanings. This enables collaboration and cross-disciplinary resource discovery, while ensuring compatibility with thesauri that cover highly specific and developing areas of knowledge. By design, not only can the BBT function as an overarching thesaurus for the humanities, to be used by a gradually growing community of thesauri maintainers, but it can also evolve into a distributed federated thesaurus, bringing together several specialist thesauri, under one common scheme.

relatedItems.label: Copy the template
relatedItems.description:
Log in or create a GitHub account. 
Then, navigate to the Edith repository and click on the green button "use this template" and then "create a new repository" to copy the template into your account.

Note: It is also possible to download the template and work offline or without a GitHub account.

relatedItems.label: Add your encoded files
relatedItems.description:
In the repository, locate the "xml" folder. This is where your xml files will go. You do not need to make any changes to the files (See the technical section in the next step), as long as your files are TEI-compliant they should work without modifications.

Upload your files here.

relatedItems.label: Configure Edith to load your files
relatedItems.description: Locate the "poetry" folder - rename the folder as you like -. In this folder, find the "template.html" file. Now all you need to do is to change the link on line 12 ' ../xml/LinkToYourXmlHere.xml' so that it links to one of your xml files in the "xml" folder.

relatedItems.label: Add all remaining TEI-XML files
relatedItems.description:
Repeat the previous step, saving the template.html under a different name every time. 
Make sure the file paths are correct, or Edith can't load your XML files.

relatedItems.label: Customize the index page
relatedItems.description:
Open the 'index.html' file in the main folder of the repository. Change the links so that they point to the html files you created in the last step. Add as many links as you need. 
Under "photography", either add the scans/facsimiles you want to add to your edition or remove the element alltogether.

relatedItems.label: Edit and improve
relatedItems.description:
The look and behaviour of the edition is controlled by two CSS files:

- CETEIcean.css for the TEI-XML files
- stylesheet.css for the index.html page

Most TEI files should work fine "out of the box". But if you want to change or add something, do this: 

1. Edith uses CETEIcean to convert XLM to HTML. TEI tags will retain their name, but with the prefix "tei-". So for example, < becomes . To change the way your elements look on the page, find the entry for in the CSS file and change it. 2. The index.html page is styled according to the stylesheet.css file. Hint: If you want a quicker turnaround from making changed to waiting for Github actions to build your page, use a local web server for testing. Then, when you are happy with the result, upload your files to GitHub.

label: Edition der fränkischen Herrschererlasse
description:
The new edition of the Frankish capitularies, a corpus of pivotal medieval legal texts, aims to take their unique history of transmission into full consideration.

While capitularies originated as individual texts from deliberations and assemblies at court, they are transmitted exclusively in collections produced locally by royal agents. The edition will therefore pursue two goals during one joint process of exploration and editing: (1) each capitulary will be edited and translated as an individual text, reconstructing its original form, to be published in print; (2) each collection will be published as a digital edition online, making it easier for scholars everywhere to study the way in which capitularies were enacted locally and passed on.

The digital edition, with its transcriptions of the various collections, not only provides the material for the printed edition, but is meant as its permanent counterpart. For historians are not only interested in reconstructed original texts but also in their (re-)combination and (re-)ordering, and in the actual wording in which contemporaries transmitted, read and used these texts. The combination of digital and printed edition elucidates the road from individual manuscript to critical text while respecting the historical value of each collection. At the same time the project’s website provides the opportunity to combine and present new findings on the form and transmission of capitularies.

relatedItems.label: Edition Visualization Technology - a simple tool to publish digital editions and digital facsimiles
relatedItems.description:
The Digital Vercelli Book project aims at creating a digital edition of the Vercelli Book manuscript (MS CXVII, Biblioteca Capitolare di Vercelli, Italy), a fundamental document for the Old English language and literature area of studies. After the transcription of all the texts was completed using the TEI schemas, the researchers lacked a tool that would allow to publish a diplomatic edition of the former together with the digitized manuscript images. Many tools have been created in order to publish digital editions based on XML-encoded texts and meet the various needs of users. Some software tools (such as TEI Boilerplate) allow to publish TEI XML files directly in modern browsers. Even though this method is very light and user friendly, it is both unsuitable for publishing very large files and limited to XSLT 1.0; the typical output is a single web page for each XML document, which is not appropriate for the publication of image-based editions.

This led us to the design and implementation of EVT (Edition Visualization Technology), a lightweight software for that specific purpose. What started as a project, whose goal was the digital edition of a specific manuscript, has grown well beyond that, to the point of being available and usable as a general purpose publishing tool.

relatedItems.description: Although the final publication of your project may seem far away at this point, be aware that most publishing software expects your TEI-XML files to follow certain practices. Make your life easier by accounting for them at this early stage already.

concept.label: IIIF
concept.definition: The International Image Interoperability Framework (IIIF) is a set of shared application programming interface (API) specifications for interoperable functionality in digital image repositories. The IIIF is comprised of and driven by a community of libraries, museums, archives, software companies, and other organizations working together to create, test, refine, implement and promote the IIIF specifications. Using JSON-LD, linked data, and standard W3C web protocols such as Web Annotation, IIIF makes it easy to parse and share digital image data, migrate across technology systems, and provide enhanced image access for scholars and researchers. In short, IIIF enables better, faster and cheaper image delivery. It lets you leverage interoperability and the fabric of the Web to access new possibilities and new users for your image-based resources, while reducing long term maintenance and technological lock in. IIIF gives users a rich set of baseline functionality for viewing, zooming, and assembling the best mix of resources and tools to view, compare, manipulate and work with images on the Web, an experience made portableshareable, citable, and embeddable. label: Editors' Notes
description:
Editors' Notes is an open-source, web-based tool for recording, organizing, preserving, and opening access to research notes, built with the needs of documentary editing projects, archives, and library special collections in mind.

Projects that work closely with documents---researching, contextualizing, and ordering them---invariably produce massive amounts of thorough research notes which are too often locked away in filing cabinets or the minds of editors and curators, never to be seen by anyone. The Editors' Notes project is a collaboration between the editors of the Stanton-Anthony Papers, the Emma Goldman Papers, the Margaret Sanger Papers, and the Labadie Collection which aims to preserve those research notes in a way that makes them useful to future scholars and interested minds.

Research teams can use Editors' Notes to manage their research and note-taking. Project administrators can assign research tasks to other team members, and they can control who has permission to edit their project's notes.

Notes can be organized around documentary sources or thematically around topics (or both). Users can browse by topic, search full text, and filter using bibliographic metadata. Documents can be annotated with bibliographic metadata, topic keywords, and textual notations. Researchers can also upload scanned images of documents into the zoomable interface. Researchers can annotate specific passages in document transcripts. Annotations, like other notes, can include bibliographic metadata and topic keywords and are fully searchable. In addition to creating annotated transcripts, researchers can upload scanned images of documents, which can be viewed in a zoomable interface.

New accounts are by invitation only. Request an invitation. Editors' Notes is currently in limited beta release (Nov 10/14)

relatedItems.label: Telamon Project
relatedItems.description:
The AIAX platform initially developed for the Telamon collection of Ancient Greek inscriptions in Bulgaria (http://telamon.uni-sofia.bg) consists of two segments.
One segment is an SQL database for the storage of .xml files with front-end visualisation and indexing based on PHP. It was originally designed to work with the Telamon TEI XML template which is EpiDoc compatible and validates against the latest EpiDoc schema (https://epidoc.stoa.org/). It is similar in its basic architecture and functionalities to the native EpiDoc Front-End Service EFES (https://github.com/EpiDoc/EFES) but processes the XML data with PHP instead of XSLT.  
The other segment of the tool is a CMS-type platform for the management of the static parts of the visualisation platform, the menu and the content of the output, etc. 
The front-end has some additional functionalities such as embedded maps, more detailed indexes, and a tag-by-tag visualization of the code in parallel with the descriptions of the monuments and the authority files.  

The beta version of the service output displays a pilot collection of ancient inscriptions in Greek from Bulgaria. The source code is on GitHub together with the documentation.

label: eKultura portal
description:
The eKultura portal was developed within the eKultura project “Cultural heritage digitalisation”, funded by the European Regional Development Fund within the implementation of the Operational Programme “Competitiveness and Cohesion 2014-2020”. The project is implemented by the Ministry of Culture and Media in cooperation with partner institutions, the Croatian State Archives, the Croatian Radio-Television, the Museum of Arts and Crafts, and the National and University Library in Zagreb. The aim of the Project is to contribute to an increased use of information and communication technologies in communication between citizens and public administration by establishing an information system for coordinating communication and by developing a central software solution in the cultural heritage sector. The general goal of the Project is to increase the protection and online availability of digital cultural content, and the specific goal is to ensure the safe storage of digital cultural content in one place and provide users with a unique access to such stored content by establishing an appropriate ICT system.

The eKultura portal is the central website that provides access to and search of the existing digital collections of the Croatian cultural heritage. The collections presented on the portal are stored in heritage institutions in the Republic of Croatia that take professional care of them. The goal of the portal is to present the public with the heritage we are inheriting and leaving to future generations.
The eKultura portal enables all citizens to search and access various collections of digitalised material of museums, libraries, and archives in Croatia, regardless of whether they had been created within this project or are only registered and described here at the metadata level. You can search and examine the collections by topics, chronologically, or by material type, their location, or significant persons, items, or events to which they refer.

The eKultura portal provides additional services intended for cultural heritage institutions and citizens in order to systematically use the eKultura system, and to provide additional information on individual digitized cultural heritage objects on the eKultura Portal.

label: ELAN
description:
ELAN is a tool for creating annotations on multiple layers on audio and video resources. The textual content of annotations is in Unicode and the transcription is stored in XML.

With ELAN a user can add an unlimited number of textual annotations to audio and/or video recordings. An annotation can be a sentence, word or gloss, a comment, translation or a description of any feature observed in the media. Annotations can be created on multiple layers, called tiers. Tiers can be hierarchically interconnected. An annotation can either be time-aligned to the media or it can refer to other existing annotations. The content of annotations consists of Unicode text and annotation documents are stored in an XML format (EAF).

Main features and characteristics of ELAN:
* provides several ways to view the annotations, each view is connected to and synchronized with the media timeline
* supports creation of multiple tiers and tier hierarchies
* supports Controlled Vocabularies
* allows linking of up to 4 video files with an annotation document
* media support
   * builds on existing, native media frameworks, like Windows Media Player, QuickTime or VLC
   * support for audio and video formats depends on operating system, high performance media playback can usually be achieved
* technical
   * written in the Java programming language
   * distributions available for Windows, macOS and Linux
   * open source, the sources are available under a GPL 3 license 

The solution was developed by the Language Archive of the Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics.

relatedItems.label: Transcribe faithfully
relatedItems.description:
The traditional and methodologically recommended approach for dialect data is impressionistic transcription: the transcriber aims to represent, as faithfully as possible, their auditory impressions, mapping them onto the taxonomic categories provided by phonetic theory. This is neither a phonological idealisation nor an attempt to normalise pronunciation toward a reference model. Rather, the transcription records what is actually perceived as produced by the speaker in a given utterance at a specific moment.

Impressionistic transcription requires that the transcriber have a trained ear and a thorough command of the phonetic system being used. The availability of digital recordings and acoustic analysis software (see Tools section below) greatly facilitates this work by allowing the analyst to listen repeatedly to the sequence to transcribe and, where necessary, to complement auditory perception with the visual inspection of acoustic properties.

relatedItems.label: Post-process and normalise the transcription
relatedItems.description:
After the initial transcription, and having respected the phonetic reality produced by the speaker, it may be appropriate to intervene with simplification and normalisation operations to make the transcription usable for its intended purpose and audience. 

One common case concerns the normalisation of pronunciation variants. Minor fluctuations in the pronunciation of a given segment — which may have been transcribed with slightly different symbols across occurrences in the corpus — can often be unified under a single symbol after analysis, provided that the variation carries no contrastive or analytically significant function. For example, if a vowel is inconsistently realised between two slightly different articulatory positions, the analyst may choose either to preserve this difference by using two distinct phonetic notations, or to transcribe it uniformly using a single notation once it has been established that the variation is not meaningful to the analysis. The decision to normalise must follow, not precede, analysis: only after examining the distribution and function of a variable should you decide whether to represent its different variants with a single symbol. Normalisation should be conservative — when in doubt, preserve the variation.

A “narrow” transcription is appropriate for strictly phonetic research, or for studies in which phonetics constitutes a privileged level of analysis. Even in such cases, however, the transcriber may choose to represent certain phenomena in greater detail when they constitute the direct object of investigation, while paying less attention to other aspects. Although such choices may be acceptable for practical reasons related to time and resources, they must always be made explicit so that readers do not draw inaccurate conclusions from the transcription data. Any deviations from standard IPA symbols and conventions should likewise be clearly explained and properly justified, and should only be introduced when the IPA does not already provide a notation sufficiently adequate for what is being transcribed.

By contrast, in research that does not pursue specifically phonetic objectives, “broad” phonetic transcriptions are generally preferred. These omit most diacritics and tend to normalise minor fluctuations in pronunciation. More generally, every decision taken during transcription and post-processing should be documented clearly and transparently, so that users of the transcription can interpret the data correctly.

relatedItems.label: Choose the transcription environment and method (auditory vs. acoustic-supported)
relatedItems.description: Decide whether the transcription will be hosted and produced within a dedicated software environment, and whether it will be time-aligned to the acoustic signal or kept as a separate text. Two complementary methods of transcription exist. Auditory transcription relies on repeated listening to portions of the recording of varying length, letting the ear judge the identity of each sound. This method should be used with an explicit caveat: human auditory perception integrates a large number of acoustic cues simultaneously (spectral, temporal, and contextual), so isolating too short or too narrow a stretch of audio can distort perception and lead the transcriber to hear segments that are not actually representative of the sound in its natural context. Acoustic transcription complements auditory judgment with visual inspection of the acoustic signal, typically using Praat, which displays the waveform and spectrogram and allows fine-grained visualization and measurement of the signal. Two software tools are commonly used for this purpose. Praat is conceived primarily for acoustic analysis and offers advanced visualization (spectrogram, formants, pitch, intensity) together with an annotation (TextGrid) interface in which IPA symbols are already integrated, making it well suited to segmental and acoustic-phonetic work. ELAN is designed primarily for the annotation of conversational and multimodal data, but can be adapted to phonetic transcription purposes; it also captures the waveform reliably and is often preferred when transcription needs to be integrated with other layers of conversational or gestural annotation. The choice between the two (or the decision to use both) should be driven by whether the project's main analytic interest is fine acoustic-phonetic measurement (favoring Praat) or multi-layered discourse/interactional annotation (favoring ELAN).

relatedItems.label: Select and configure the ASR tool
Assess and correct the transcript
Encode the transcript in TEI-XML (optional. Recommended for archival deposit)
relatedItems.description:
1. For archival and interoperability purposes, encode the corrected transcript in TEI-XML using the TEI P5 guidelines, module 8 (Transcriptions of Speech). TEI-XML is the standard encoding format for primary textual sources in SSH digital humanities and is required by many European infrastructure repositories. Minimum TEI encoding for an oral source transcript includes: with full bibliographic and administrative metadata (interviewer, interviewee, date, location, project, language, transcription date, transcriber identity, encoding conventions); with ++(utterance) elements, who attribute for speaker attribution, and xml:id for segment identification; or @when attributes for timestamp anchoring; 
2. If full TEI encoding exceeds available resources, produce at minimum a well-structured plain text or SRT file with a separate metadata record in Dublin Core format; 3. Validate the TEI file against the TEI P5 schema using oXygen XML Editor or the TEI online validator before deposit.

relatedItems.label: Choix d'un outil de transcription
Configure ELAN
relatedItems.description:
A. Decide on the tiers you will create in ELAN

In ELAN, different dimensions of the interaction are organised into tiers — separate annotation layers that run in parallel and are aligned to the same time axis. Tiers can be given names, associated with specific participants, and arranged into hierarchies (a gloss tier may depend on a speech tier, for instance). It is also possible to add a transcriber comments tier for observations that should not be confused with the primary data.

B. Create the project and import media
Open ELAN and create a new annotation file (.eaf). Link your audio and/or video file(s) to the project. It is possible to link multiple media streams simultaneously, which is particularly useful for multi-party interaction data. The media files are not embedded in the .eaf file but referenced by path, so keep your folder structure stable throughout the project. PLEASE NOTE: to handle media files with different zero points or start times use synchonisation or adjust time offsets for secondary media files.

C. Define the tier hierarchy
Create your tiers according to the plan established in A. For each tier, specify: its name, the participant it is associated with (if applicable), its type (time-alignable, or dependent on a parent tier), and any linguistic type or vocabulary constraint you wish to apply. ELAN supports hierarchical relationships between tiers.

Assign clear, consistent names to your tiers from the outset. Renaming tiers later is possible but can create complications if tier names are referenced in templates or export settings.

relatedItems.label: Transcribe and process the interview
relatedItems.description:
Produce a transcription of the recorded interview in order to enable analysis, indexing, and long-term accessibility. Transcription constitutes a key stage in the enrichment of the oral source, transforming an audio or audiovisual document into a textual resource that can be searched, annotated, and reused.

Define the level of transcription according to the objectives of the research. This may range from verbatim transcription (including hesitations, pauses, and non-verbal elements) to a more edited version that improves readability while preserving the meaning of the discourse. Where relevant, adopt established transcription conventions and ensure consistency across the corpus.

If required, integrate time-coding to align the transcription with the original recording, facilitating navigation between text and audio/video. Consider also the need for translation, particularly in multilingual research contexts.

During transcription, pay attention to the treatment of personal data and sensitive information. Anonymisation or pseudonymisation may be necessary, especially when preparing the material for dissemination or public access. Any modifications should be documented to ensure transparency and reproducibility.

The transcription should be treated as a distinct but related document within the oral source corpus. It must therefore be documented through a dedicated record, including its relationship to the original recording, the tools and methods used, and the identity of the transcriber.

This step may be carried out prior to, or in parallel with, the description and metadata creation phase, depending on the research design and available resources. In all cases, it significantly enhances the findability, accessibility, and reusability of the oral source in line with FAIR principles.

relatedItems.label: Transcribing conversation in ELAN
relatedItems.description:
This workflow outlines the main steps involved in the transcription of conversational data using ELAN, a software environment designed for the annotation and synchronisation of audio and video recordings. ELAN is particularly suitable for multimodal transcription, as it allows the annotation of both verbal and non-verbal phenomena — such as gaze, gestures, pauses, and interactional dynamics — through multiple time-aligned annotation tiers.

The workflow includes the preliminary design of the transcription scheme and annotation hierarchy, the configuration of tiers and segmentation units, the automatic or manual transcription and annotation process, and the exportation of the final transcript in EAF or other formats. 

This workflow is based on Letizia Cirillo’s chapter “Trascrivere la conversazione” (pp. 181–188), part of the "Vademecum per il trattamento delle fonti orali" (Tavolo permanente per le fonti orali, 2020).

relatedItems.label: Annotating Proxemic Features in Audiovisual Document Using ELAN
relatedItems.description:
This workflow describes how to annotate proxemic features in audiovisual corpora using ELAN. It integrates multimodal annotation principles from linguistic and semiotic research, with particular reference to gesture classification frameworks (Kendon, McNeill) and facial annotation protocols (FACS, Ekman & Friesen).

This process is grounded on Meluzzi’s approach to annotation ("Annotare una trascrizione", in "Vademecum per il trattamento delle fonti orali", pp. 227-229).

label: EmoCorp: Tool for annotating and processing emotive expressions in parallel corpora
description:
Emotion Annotated Corpus
The tool enables users to identify and recognise the emotional content of a text on the basis of their own emotive expression annotations or those previously prepared by experts. An emotive expression comprises a sentence segment from a larger corpus, e.g. a literary text. The tagging of emotions is based on an emotion pattern. It contains nine basic emotions (joy, trust, fear, surprise, sadness, disgust, anger, foreboding, sympathy) and an emotional overtone (positive, neutral, positive). The user is able to annotate his or her own corpus independently as part of the emotional labelling. At the emotion processing stage, the annotated corpus is entered into the EmoCorp portal, which allows segments to be searched according to the set emotion. The user can also make use of ready-made literary corpora annotated by specialists. The service will be prepared primarily for Polish and German.

relatedItems.label: PaMuCo: Parallel Multilingual Corpus: Polish, German and Danish parallel langual corpus
relatedItems.description:
Parallel Multilingual Corpus
The PaMuCo resource offers annotated segments of film dialogues, fiction literature (novels and fairy tales) and EU legal texts in Polish, German and Danish, all annotated by a team of neophilologists, linked by translation relationships. The selection of texts is based on the principle of genre diversity and representative content that is socially, historically and culturally relevant internationally. The texts are placed in the MANTEL portal, which allows the user to assign linguistic equivalence relations to the texts. These are relations such as simple, merge / split, deletion, crossing, composition, compression, general paraphrase, reduction, expansion, substitution, disjunction. Corpus with translational relations are then uploaded to the PaMuCo portal, which is a search engine for these relations. It is based on existing or new corpora and allows to search comprehensively for segments and relations in corpora and make comparisons.
