relatedItems.label: Research Design and Methodological Planning
relatedItems.description:
The treatment of oral sources begins with a carefully structured phase of research design and methodological planning, which shapes the quality of the data collected as well as its legal validity, long-term preservation, and future reuse. This phase brings together methodological reflection, technical, and ethical choices, legal awareness, and archival foresight.

At its core lies a solid grounding in the principles and practices of linguistics and oral history. Researchers—and, where applicable, collaborators—should develop a clear awareness of the legal, ethical, and deontological implications of working with oral testimonies. This includes familiarity with relevant international and national guidelines, such as those of the Oral History Society (OHS) and the Associazione Italiana di Storia Orale (AISO), and an understanding of the responsibilities linked to the collection, processing, and preservation of personal narratives. At this stage, the focus is on building awareness within the research team, rather than formally informing participants.

Methodological planning also involves defining the research framework, including research questions, scope, and participant selection. Interviews should be conceived as co-constructed communicative events; therefore, flexible interview guides are preferable to rigid questionnaires, allowing space for digressions that may open new lines of inquiry.

Researchers must also anticipate the conditions of the recording, including the choice of environment and the establishment of a relationship of trust with participants, which directly affects the quality and interpretability of the testimonies.

Technical planning is equally essential. Decisions regarding recording formats (audio or audio-video) and equipment should be made in relation to research objectives and future uses of the data. These choices are methodological as much as technical, as they shape the nature and reusability of the sources.

Finally, this phase includes preparing the documentation resources that will support the workflow, such as interview guides, information sheets, consent and authorization forms, and recording sheets for contextual data. Anticipating legal requirements, preservation strategies, and future access conditions ensures coherence across the process and supports the sustainable reuse of oral sources.

relatedItems.label: Virtual Collection Registry
relatedItems.description:
A service that allows researchers to create their own citable digital bookmarks. A virtual collection is a coherent set of links to digital objects (e.g. annotated text, video) that can be easily created, accessed and cited. The links can originate from different archives, hence the term virtual. 

CLARIN provides a registry where scholars can create and publish their virtual collections. Each virtual collection comes with a persistent identifier and FAIR metadata.

The registry can be easily accessed via federated login. 

The collection metadata is openly available and accessible via the Virtual Language Observatory. The referenced digital objects can also be processed with the Language Resource Switchboard.

label: Language tags in HTML and XML
description: Language tags are used to indicate the language of text or other items in HTML and XML documents. Use the lang attribute to specify language tags in HTML, and the xml:lang attribute for XML In both cases, language information is inherited by elements inside the one where the declaration was made, unless one of those elements declares a different language (in the same way). RFCs are what the IETF calls its specifications. Each RFC has a unique number. Unfortunately, it is not possible to tell, when reading RFC 1766 or RFC 3066 that these specifications have been obsoleted and replaced by other specifications. Language tag syntax is defined by the IETF's BCP 47. BCP stands for 'Best Current Practice', and is a persistent name for a series of RFCs whose numbers change as they are updated. The latest RFC describing language tag syntax is RFC 5646, Tags for the Identification of Languages, and it obsoletes the older RFCs 4646, 3066 and 1766. You used to find subtags by consulting the lists of codes in various ISO standards, but now you can find all subtags in the IANA Language Subtag Registry. We will describe the new registry below.

relatedItems.label: Språkbanken
relatedItems.description: A free cloud service for OCR The project En fri molntjänst för OCR \`A free cloud service for OCR', funded by the National Library of Sweden (51-KB709-2012), ran from 1st September, 2013 until 31st August, 2014. The project was a collaboration between the University Library of University of Gothenburg and Språkbanken 'the Swedish Language Bank' at the Department of Swedish of University of Gothenburg, its aim to create a prototype Optical Character Recognition (OCR) web service for processing old Swedish texts that are printed in a blackletter (fraktur) or roman typeface, using one of two open source OCR engines. Our ultimate goal is to provide a service for libraries, museums and archives to upload any digitized document and retrieve an OCRed text with high quality, independent on the quality of the print. In the project, we have evaluated two open source OCR engines: OCRopus and Tesseract and further developed one of them, namely OCRopus. Using OCRopus we have set up a open webservice for OCR that can handle Swedish Blackletter print as well as Roman type print. The pilot cloud service and web API can be found here. The material and tools developed in the project are freely available for download from this site under the license CC-BY.

label: Latin-Bulgarian e-Dictionary
description: The electronic Latin-Bulgarian dictionary is an initiative of teachers and researchers from The Sofia University "St. Kliment Ohridski" and The Medical University - Sofia. Its goal is the creation of a modern and accessible lexicographic aid for all those interested in the Latin language. The creators of the dictionary use as a basis for their work various lexicographic sources located in the public domain. The project team updates the often obsolete language and spelling of the dictionary articles, corrects errors in them, and enriches their content with more accurate examples. The articles are supplemented with specific references to particular places in classical authors, and, unlike in many previous printed Latin dictionaries, all examples are provided with translations in Bulgarian. The lemmas are also enriched with appropriate illustrations where applicable. For the purposes of electronic processing, lemmas are encoded in XML according to the international digital lexicography standards of TEILex0  (https://dariah-eric.github.io/lexicalresources/pages/TEILex0/TEILex0.html). The Indexing and the visualization of the database are carried out using a modification of the ΑΙΑΧ service (https://telamon.uni-sofia.bg/page/project). Also, the dictionary is enriched with Latin maxims and phrases, as well as with useful lists of authors and works and of frequently used abbreviations. The dictionary will be expanded with terms from the fields of medical and legal Latin.

label: LATTE (Linking Annotations Through Textual Entities)
description: LATTE stands for ‘Linking Annotations Through Textual Entities’, a web-based application deployed on a project level which provides a frontend for a NEO4J hosted database. The application is paired with the LATTE connector, an end-to-end entity processing tool starting from the extraction of entities in a digitized flat text, to the annotation, disambiguation, linking and dissemination of entities by adding an optional Wikidata Q-identifier (based on string matching and internal frequency) and stable identifier. Data is exported in various ways, text-level exports are made possible using JSON and XML. Entity-level export is done by opening custom APIs which are configurable by net admins. The app allows annotations to be enriched with data from Wikidata based on the use of P-tags.

label: Latvian National Corpora Collection (LNCC)
description:
Latvian National Corpora Collection (LNCC) is a diverse collection of corpora representing both written and spoken language. LNCC covers various use cases and all the important text types and genres. It is a continuous multi-institutional and multi-project effort, supported by the digital humanities and language technology communities in Latvia.
Currently, 34 corpora developed by 13 institutions are available in the LNCC. Most of the corpora are annotated with a uniform morpho-syntactic annotation scheme and included in the federated search. The federated search combines multiple corpora from two corpus indexer instances (endpoints) maintained by [IMCS UL](https://nosketch.korpuss.lv/) and [NLL](https://nosketch.lnb.lv/). Federated search includes 28 corpora (2.4 billions tokens).

label: Le Maitron - Biographical Dictionary of the Social Movement
description:
*Le Maitron*, the bibliographic dictionary of the French labor movement, is a set of labor movement biographical dictionaries compiled by historian Jean Maitron and his successor Claude Pennetier, starting in the 1960s and continued onto today, now in an online format. The website is divided between the "Maitron Patrimonial," resources which were all published and digitized before 2024, and the "Active Corpora" that are ongoing projects. 

Initially published from 1964-2024 in paper versions, which have been digitized, *Le Maitron* is broken into editions by year, 1789-1864, 1864-1871, 1871-1914, 1914-1939, and 1940-1968. 

*Le Maitron*  website also includes other categories related to *Le Maitron*'s mission on building a bibliographic dictionary of groups related to the social movement in France. There are bibliographic entries for international social movements in Algeria, Tunisia, Germany, Austria, China, Great Britain & Ireland, Japan, the United States, and for the Komintern. Other sections of this webtool and *Le Maitron*'s mission include bibliographic dictionaries dedicated women active in social movement, to those executed as resistants during the Occupation, on volunteers for Republican Spain, rail workers, and immigrants, amongst others. 

In addition to bibliographic entries, there are also written resources to help guide researchers or interested readers.

label: Lemon - Lexicon Model for Ontologies
description:
Lemon is a proposed model for modeling lexicon and machine-readable dictionaries and linked to the Semantic Web and the Linked Data cloud. It was designed to meet the following challenges

RDF-native form to enable leverage of existing Semantic Web technologies (SPARQL, OWL, RIF etc.).
Linguistically sound structure based on LMF to enable conversion to existing offline formats.
Separation of the lexicon and ontology layers, to ensure compatability with existing OWL models.
Linking to data categories, in order to allow for arbitrarily complex linguistic description. In particular the LexInfo vocabulary is aligned to lemon and ISOcat.
A small model using the principle of least power - the less expressive the language, the more reusable the data.

label: Les vocabulaires du Ministère de la Culture
description:
The Vocabularies of the French Ministry of Culture are a set of controlled vocabularies, thesauri, authority lists, classifications and other scientific and technical reference resources developed or coordinated by the French Ministry of Culture. They are designed to support the standardised description, indexing and management of cultural heritage data.

These vocabularies provide a common terminology for describing cultural heritage objects, works, architectural elements, materials, techniques, periods, iconography and other relevant concepts. Their use helps to harmonise metadata, improve the consistency and quality of data, facilitate information retrieval, and enable interoperability between different cultural heritage databases and institutions.

FR: 

Les Vocabulaires du ministère de la Culture constituent un ensemble de référentiels scientifiques et techniques destinés à faciliter la description, l’indexation et la recherche des ressources et collections patrimoniales. Ils regroupent notamment des thésaurus, listes d’autorité, nomenclatures et autres vocabulaires contrôlés, élaborés par le ministère de la Culture et ses partenaires. Leur utilisation permet d’employer un langage commun et normalisé pour décrire les objets, les œuvres, les lieux, les techniques, les matériaux, les périodes ou encore les acteurs du patrimoine.

Ces vocabulaires jouent ainsi un rôle important dans l’harmonisation et l’interopérabilité des données patrimoniales : ils facilitent la cohérence de l’indexation, améliorent les possibilités de recherche et permettent de rapprocher des données provenant de différentes institutions ou bases documentaires. Certains sont notamment utilisés pour l’alimentation et l’interrogation de bases nationales telles que Joconde et sont diffusés dans des formats permettant leur réutilisation et leur intégration dans des environnements numériques.

relatedItems.label: Enrichir le candidat avec des alignements et des images
relatedItems.description:
Ajouter un alignement : il s’agit de créer une relation d’équivalence plus ou moins exacte entre le mot-clé Pactols et un item correspondant dans un autre référentiel du web. Pactols a fait le choix de préférer les relations exactes (skos:exactMatch). Les alignements ne sont possibles qu’avec des référentiels fournissant un identifiant pérenne à ses items (DOI, ARK,...) ou une adresse web stable (URI).

Les principaux référentiels des alignements Pactols sont : Wikidata, les thésaurus du ministère français de la Culture (http://data.culture.fr/thesaurus/), IdRef (oeuvres, personnes), le Art and Architecture Thesaurus de la Fondation Getty, Bibracte_thesaurus, Bnf, Pleiades (lieux anciens), Geonames (lieux), Insee (lieux de France). 

Deux modes d’alignement sont possibles : 
1. alignement : faites une recherche préalable dans le réservoir puis donnez l’URI distante de l’item et le nom du référentiel dans le formulaire.
Ex. URI distante : https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q6934696
      Nom de la source : Wikidata
2. alignement automatique : Opentheso opère une recherche sur le libellé dans les référentiels pré-enregistrés : Bibracte_thesaurus, Bnf, GeoNames, Wikidata. Selon le réservoir, la réponse peut être faussement négative sur le libellé en français, par exemple avec Wikidata dont les items peuvent ne pas avoir d’équivalent dans la langue de la recherche. Écrivez de préférence le terme de la requête dans la langue du référentiel visé. Sélectionnez la meilleure réponse affichée. La possibilité de rapatrier des métadonnées supplémentaires (traductions, images, définition) peut être un avantage mais nécessitera une relecture voire une correction après alignement. 

Image : Certains concepts, difficiles à définir, peuvent être illustrés avec profit d’une ou de plusieurs images. Celles-ci doivent être représentatives du concept et se positionner autant que possible dans le champ de l’archéologie sinon de l’histoire ancienne. Elles doivent impérativement être libres de droit (sélectionnez les réservoirs ad hoc, notamment Wikimedia Commons, et citables (avec une URI comme adresse web stable, un PID identifiant pérenne de type ARK, DOI, etc.).

Pour ajouter une image depuis Wikimedia Commons : sélectionnez l'image choisie, cliquez sur l'onglet "use this file" et recopiez le champ "File URL:". Remplissez les 4 champs de l'onglet Image de Pactols : l'URI, la légende de l'image (libellé), son auteur et la source. 
Ex. pour amphore attique : URI : https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/01/Amphore_attique_%C3%A0_figures_noires._Peintre_de_Rycroft_-_btv1b101044967_%282_of_2%29.jpg ; libellé : Amphore attique à figures noires. Peintre de Rycroft ; auteur : Bibliothèque nationale de France ; source : Wikimédia.

label: LetterSampo - Letters on the Semantic Web
description: Epistolary data about historical letters is typically distributed in different archives depending on where the letters were sent to and received, and the data are represented using local heterogeneous data models and different natural languages. To study such letter data on a global level, the heterogeneous, distributed data in local siloes need to be aggregated and harmonized into larger services where local metadata can enrich each other to complement missing information. LetterSampo a new framework for representing, publishing, and using epistolary data as Linked Open Data (LOD) on the Web for Digital Humanities (DH) research. The framework issued for creating LOD services and for building individual LetterSampo portals on top of them. To test and demonstrate the framework, it has been applied to the epistolary CKCC dataset of ca. 20 000 letters of the Huygens Institute, the Netherlands, to the correspSearchdataset of ca.151 000 letters aggregated by the Berlin-Brandenburg Academy of Sciences and Humanities, and to the Early ModernLetters Online (EMLO) data of ca.170 000letters published by the University of Oxford. The CKCC and correspSearch datasets were published as LOD services, SPARQL endpoints, and as data dumps at Zenodo.org for re-use, and a demonstrational portal LetterSampo: Historical Letters on the Semantic Web was created based on this data. A novelty of the LetterSampo portals is to use faceted semantic search for filtering data of interest in flexible ways from multiple perspectives on two conceptual levels, and then visualize and analyzethe results and data by seamlessly integrated data analytic tools - programming skills are not needed for using the portals. In addition to using the tools of the portal, the SPARQL endpoints can be used with modest knowledge about programming for DH research

relatedItems.label: Linked Data Technologies for Cultural Heritage and Digital Humanities: Introducing the Semantic Web in Video Lectures
relatedItems.description:
A paradigm shift is taking place in publishing and using Cutural Heritage (CH) content on the Web: in addition to publishing materials for the humans to read as usual, also the underlying data is published as Linked Open Data (LOD) using the FAIR principles. This facilitates

publishing ever larger aggregated datasets,
- enriching the Big Data with other publishers' data and by reasoning,
- development of more intelligent interfaces and applications for the end users, and
- using the data in Digital Humanities (DH) research for data analyses.

As a result, CH and DH have grown into and important application field of Semantic Web (SW) technologies.

Instead of a textual tutorial, this site provides an introduction based on videos, which hopefully lowers the barrier of getting grips with the opportunities and practical technical ideas underlying the paradigm change. The learning materials published in this online course are targeted to researches, collection managers and curators in memory organizations, students, and application developers interested in the opprotunities and challenges related to creating, aggregating, publishing, and using CH LOD on the SW.

relatedItems.label: Sampo-UI framework for developing semantic portal user interfaces
relatedItems.description: Sampo-UI is a framework for developing user interfaces for semantic portals. The underlying ideas of the framework are based on the "Sampo" model that contains a sustainable business model for publishing and sharing Linked Data based on a shared ontology infrastructure, the idea of providing the end user with multiple application perspectives to the Linked Data, and a two-step usage cycle based on faceted search combined with ready-to-use data-analytic tooling. The framework draws from longstanding research of the Semantic Computing Research Group since 2002 on developing semantic portals, which has resulted in publishing a series of "Sampo" portals, mostly related to the Cultural Heritage domain, that have had millions of end users on the Web. The Sampo-UI framework makes it possible to create highly customizable and responsive user interfaces that satisfy the requirements for such portals using current state-of-the-art JavaScript libraries and data from SPARQL endpoints, while saving substantial coding effort. Sampo-UI is published on GitHub under the open MIT License and has been utilized in several internal and external projects.

concept.label: IIIF
concept.definition: The International Image Interoperability Framework (IIIF) is a set of shared application programming interface (API) specifications for interoperable functionality in digital image repositories. The IIIF is comprised of and driven by a community of libraries, museums, archives, software companies, and other organizations working together to create, test, refine, implement and promote the IIIF specifications. Using JSON-LD, linked data, and standard W3C web protocols such as Web Annotation, IIIF makes it easy to parse and share digital image data, migrate across technology systems, and provide enhanced image access for scholars and researchers. In short, IIIF enables better, faster and cheaper image delivery. It lets you leverage interoperability and the fabric of the Web to access new possibilities and new users for your image-based resources, while reducing long term maintenance and technological lock in. IIIF gives users a rich set of baseline functionality for viewing, zooming, and assembling the best mix of resources and tools to view, compare, manipulate and work with images on the Web, an experience made portableshareable, citable, and embeddable. (source: https://iiif.io/community/faq/)

Importing, transforming, storing and indexing data should be easy.

label: LLM keyword mapping onto archaeological vocabularies (AMČR, TEATER) and born-digital PDF/DOCX conversion
description:
Maps archival text onto controlled archaeological vocabularies with a large language model, and converts born-digital documents into the ATRIUM document record.

**Vocabulary keywords.** Each text line (CSV, TEITOK) or each passage of a whole document (TXT, Markdown) is tagged with a term from the AMČR heslář and the TEATER thesaurus, with Czech and English keywords and a confidence score. The answer is held to the vocabulary: the term list becomes the enum of a JSON schema, decoding follows that schema where the backend supports it, and a category that is not in the vocabulary is dropped, not guessed.

**Born-digital conversion.** PDF and DOCX files with a usable text layer become the document record (JSON) without OCR.

Models run locally (transformers or vLLM, one or more GPUs) or through OpenRouter or Ollama. Every enrichment run writes a paradata JSON log. Command-line tools and container images, including a REST API (`ghcr.io/ufal/atrium-llm-enrich-api`).

relatedItems.label: ALTO XMLs post-processing and quality control (text lines categorization)
relatedItems.description:
Turns OCR output into clean, classified text lines. The pipeline splits documents into pages, builds page statistics tables, extracts text in reading order (LayoutReader by default; alto-tools, GLM-4v, JSON-key and plain-text readers as alternatives) and labels every line by language and OCR quality: Clear, Noisy, Trash, Non-text or Empty. The quality score combines structural detectors, perplexity (Qwen2.5-0.5B or distilgpt2) and character-level metrics; the language comes from FastText.

Input: ALTO XML, generic OCR JSON, or any text-bearing file (PDF, DOCX, TXT, HTML, TEI, PAGE XML and more). Output: per-line CSV tables, page statistics, plain text and the ATRIUM document record (JSON), with a paradata JSON log per run.

Command-line pipeline or REST API container image (`ghcr.io/ufal/atrium-alto-postprocess-api`, `/process`).

relatedItems.label: NLP enrichment of OCR text lines into TEITOK (UDPipe 2, NameTag 3)
relatedItems.description:
Adds linguistic annotation to text lines from ALTO post-processing (CSV or XLSX with a `text` column, or plain text). The lines go to the LINDAT UDPipe 2 service for tokens, lemmas, part-of-speech tags and syntax, and to NameTag 3 for named entities. The main output is TEITOK XML, a TEI-based format that keeps the annotation tied to the page layout when the ALTO files are supplied. CoNLL-U files, per-page entity tables, summary CSVs and the ATRIUM document record (JSON) are also written, with a paradata JSON log per run.

Optional keyword extraction per page or document uses YAKE (command-line default), KeyBERT (API default) or the legacy KER method. An optional LLM stage maps text onto the AMČR and TEATER vocabularies; the same engine is maintained as the separate tool atrium-llm-enrich, which the AMČR workflow uses.

relatedItems.label: Semi-automated extraction of information from textual documents in a domain-specific repository
relatedItems.description:
The workflow addresses the **machine processing and enhancement of archaeological textual documents** (e.g., grey literature, excavation reports, field forms) held in a domain-specific repository. It processes both **scanned documents**, through automatic text recognition, and **born-digital documents** (PDF, DOCX) that already carry a text layer. The goal is an integrated solution for **legacy data and new uploads within the selected repository system**: better search and reuse of the documents, and fewer manual steps in archiving and annotation.

The workflow chains **independent tools available as services through APIs**. Each tool performs one step: page classification, OCR quality control, linguistic annotation and named entity recognition, keyword extraction against the domain vocabularies, and translation. Each tool can also be used on its own. The repository calls the services asynchronously and stores every result as an **alternative distribution of the original file**, with a **paradata** record describing the run that produced it (tool version, parameters, licence).

The results of all steps also accumulate in **one JSON record per document** (the ATRIUM document record). Its blocks each have one producing tool, so any step can be re-run alone. The record carries the provenance of every contribution, and the licence of the combined result is derived from the most restrictive licence among them. It can later be exported as an RO-Crate.

The enriched data support:

* full-text and faceted search by page types, named entities and vocabulary keywords,
* assessment of OCR quality before further processing,
* linking of documents to controlled vocabularies and to each other,
* international access through English translations of metadata and texts,
* corpora for natural language processing, including the training and evaluation of models.

The tools were developed in the [ATRIUM project](https://atrium-research.eu/) by the Institute of Formal and Applied Linguistics (Charles University) with the Institutes of Archaeology of the Czech Academy of Sciences in Prague and Brno. They are open source, published as container images, and are described in their own Marketplace records. Their integration into [Galaxy](https://galaxyproject.org/) is being prepared with DARIAH.

The [Archaeological Map of the Czech Republic (AMCR)](https://digiarchiv.aiscr.cz/) repository serves as the **demonstrator** of the workflow.

**Diagram caption**: *Users and data curators work with a data repository (AMCR) that stores each document with its metadata, original file, ALTO XML, document record, enrichments and paradata, and the AMCR vocabularies. A processing orchestration (step 2) passes documents between the repository, a separate automatic text recognition workflow (step 4) and the ATRIUM tool services: page classification (3), ALTO post-processing and quality control (5), NLP enrichment with UDPipe and NameTag to TEITOK (7), vocabulary keywords by LLM (8) and XML translation (10). A dashed born-digital branch (6) replaces steps 4 and 5. NLP enrichment and translation call the LINDAT services; the vocabularies feed keyword extraction and translation. Annotators and data engineers train a custom NameTag model (9). A discovery service (11) serves users and feeds the OAI-PMH and File API, which feeds the ARIADNE Portal.*

relatedItems.label: Omeka
relatedItems.description:
Omeka is a content management system designed for the display of library, museum, archives, and scholarly collections and exhibitions.

Omeka falls at a crossroads of Web Content Management, Collections Management, and Archival Digital Collections Systems. Omeka is designed with non-IT specialists in mind, allowing users to focus on content and interpretation rather than programming. It brings Web 2.0 technologies and approaches to academic and cultural websites to foster user interaction and participation. It makes top-shelf design easy with a simple and flexible templating system. Its robust open-source developer and user communities underwrite Omeka's stability and sustainability.

Omeka allows users to publish cultural heritage objects, extend its functionality with themes and plugins, and curate online exhibits with digital objects.

label: LOD4HSS Initiative For the semantisation and reuse of research data in HSS
description:
The LOD4HSS initiative, promoted by the Laboratoire de Recherche Historique Rhône-Alpes (LARHRA, Lyon) and the Digital Humanities Chair at the University of Bern, aims to establish a sustainable and vibrant community that manages an ecosystem of projects and infrastructures for research in the Humanities and Social Sciences based on semantic web technologies. Open to all interested institutions and projects, the initiative dates back to 2017, with the creation of the OntoME web platform (ontome.net) and the launch of the Semantic Data for the Humanities and Social Sciences (SDHSS) project (sdhss.org).

The LOD4HSS initiative is built around four main pillars:

A common ontology ecosystem. At the heart of this endeavour is the SDHSS project. This project provides a methodology for ontology engineering based on OntoClean and DOLCE, as well as a common semantic backbone based on CIDOC CRM, a core ontology for describing events, actors, sources and other relevant information in the HSS domain. The SDHSS project meets the basic needs of most projects and provides a set of best practices for creating community-driven extensions for research subdomains. This ensures semantic consistency and interoperability across different datasets, enabling the construction of a research-driven, distributed giant knowledge graph.
Shared authority files. With a focus on Wikidata and IdRef, they enable the addition of entities not present in other repositories, as well as providing the information needed to identify them. They facilitate easy connection to other authority files (GND, BNF, etc.) if the entities are referenced there. Finally, this approach makes it possible to reuse apps and widgets that align existing data with Wikidata.
Adoption of existing virtual research environments This helps to enlarge and strengthen HSS research communities within the Semantic Web, making platforms more sustainable. We notably promote the use of the WissKI platform, an open-source infrastructure developed for semantic data management and publication, fully compatible with the LOD and Semantic Web standards and supported by the Germanisches Nationalmuseum.
Adopt and develop Open-Source Tools. The LOD4HSS initiative also promotes the reuse and development of innovative, specialised open-source tools such as the Local Graph Editor (LOGRE), which is based on a SHACL serialisation of application profiles managed in OntoME. These tools support the collaborative modelling and editing of knowledge graphs, enabling standardised, transparent, and reproducible research workflows.

description:
Logainm / the Placenames Database of Ireland is a comprehensive management system for the placenames data, records and research of the Irish State. It is a public resource for Irish people at home and abroad, and for all those who appreciate the rich heritage of Irish placenames.

A complementary site Sráidainm /Streetnames Database of Ireland (a bilingual directory of the correct forms of streetnames in Ireland) can be accessed at https://www.sraidainm.ie/en/

Logainm is a research project of the Gaois research group, Fiontar & Scoil na Gaeilge (DCU) and Dr Brian Ó Raghallaigh is the project Principal Investigator. The project's main objectives are (1) to provide state-of-the-art technology to facilitate the research of the Placenames Branch (Government of Ireland) and (2) to disseminate the State's toponymic data via logainm.ie.

The project is funded by the Department of Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht, with support from the National Lottery. The project was started in 2007 and the first version of the public website was launched in 2008. The current version of the website was launched in 2022. www.logainm.ie won the European Language Label in 2010 and was category winner at the Irish eGovernment Awards 2011 & 2016.

description: LoGaRT, or Local Gazetteers Research Tools, developed by Shih-Pei Chen, Qun Che, Calvin Yeh, and Sean Wang under the umbrella of the Max Planck Institute for the History of Science, aims to help scholars make the most out of the contents that local gazetteers can offer by encouraging the combination of close and distant reading. label: Lost Voices: The Chansons of Nicolas Du Chemin
description:
The Lost Voices project explores a little-studied repertory of sixteen sets of French polyphonic songs published in Paris by Nicolas Du Chemin between 1549 and 1568. Digital technologies are put to work in the service of these books in ways that will engender a broader discussion about style and structure in the sixteenth-century chanson.

This project features digital facsimiles of the set, freely available for display and download; complete modern editions of all the chansons, engraved as high quality PDF files; essays about the books, the music, and their historical context; and a searchable database of analytic observations about the music.

The project also allows users to contribute reconstructions of incomplete chansons (over 100 of them, to date). These are also available for dynamic display and comparison. All of these materials are combined in an innovative browser-based interface that permits users to search through the repertory, viewing (and collecting) musical excerpts of interest.

The MEI standard is a central resource for the project, serving as a medium of exchange between our original transcriptions (in Sibelius) and our dynamic editions (in any browser, using VexFlow). In addition, MEI is used to keep track of variant readings, emendations, and reconstructed voice parts contributed by different authors and editors. Various workflows and software tools have been developed that allow one to move back and forth among the transcriptions, MEI files, and dynamic renderings using Django (CMS), SOLR, and related technologies. All work is open-source, and available for re-use.

The Lost Voices Project. Companion resource to Les livres de Chansons Nouvelles de Nicolas Du Chemin (1549--1568), hosted by the Centre d'Études Supérieures de la Renaissance in Tours, France

label: Machine-learning-based interactive tool to identify the content of collective agreements (and other legal texts) in multiple languages
description:
Since 2012, the WageIndicator Foundation has maintained a Collective Agreements Database, where the texts of 1668 collective agreements (CBAs) from 61 countries and in 29 languages have been uploaded, coded and annotated. 
Under the SSHOC project and with the support of the CLARIN Research Infrastructure, the agreements have been manually and automatically annotated on several levels. Within this project, machine learning techniques and models are being used to identify where in a CBA a specific topic is addressed.
A guided notebook applies and compares different models and - for each language and each question - finds which model works better in spotting the right piece of text. The result is then used in this interactive tool, which allows the user to upload new collective agreements texts and find where a specific topic is addressed. 
As an extra feature, it also provides a worker friendliness score for the uploaded text.

relatedItems.description:
Since 2012, the WageIndicator Foundation has maintained a Collective Agreements Database, where the texts of 1600 collective agreements (CBAs) from 61 countries and in 27 languages have been uploaded, coded and annotated. This database is a unique example at global level: collective agreements are documents containing conditions of employment that result from negotiations between independent unions and employers, and their content is often surrounded by an atmosphere of secrecy. Under the SSHOC project and with the support of the CLARIN Research Infrastructure, the agreements have been manually and automatically annotated on several levels: for each agreement, the team answers a series of questions and selects the appropriate piece of text (clause) for each. 

One of the results of the collective agreements' annotation process is the dataset which is available here and includes all the clauses selected for each variable (WageIndicator_CBADatabase_Selected_Clauses). The full collective agreements' texts are stored in another dataset, also available here (WageIndicator_CBADatabase_Full_Texts_211019). A codebook is also included (210125-wageindicator-cba-codebook.pdf).

concept.label: IIIF
concept.definition: The International Image Interoperability Framework (IIIF) is a set of shared application programming interface (API) specifications for interoperable functionality in digital image repositories. The IIIF is comprised of and driven by a community of libraries, museums, archives, software companies, and other organizations working together to create, test, refine, implement and promote the IIIF specifications. Using JSON-LD, linked data, and standard W3C web protocols such as Web Annotation, IIIF makes it easy to parse and share digital image data, migrate across technology systems, and provide enhanced image access for scholars and researchers. In short, IIIF enables better, faster and cheaper image delivery. It lets you leverage interoperability and the fabric of the Web to access new possibilities and new users for your image-based resources, while reducing long term maintenance and technological lock in. IIIF gives users a rich set of baseline functionality for viewing, zooming, and assembling the best mix of resources and tools to view, compare, manipulate and work with images on the Web, an experience made portableshareable, citable, and embeddable. (source: https://iiif.io/community/faq/)

label: Maeshowe: The Application of RTI to Norse Runes
description: The chambered cairn and passage grave at Maeshowe is well known for its runic inscriptions. Since its construction around 2800 BC (Renfrew 1979: 203), the site has had a long history of re-use and disturbance (Davidson \& Henshall 1989: 61-2, 145). The presence of several runic inscriptions in the main chamber and the SE side-chamber indicates later Norse re-use, probably during the mid-12th century (Barnes 1994: 215). The ease with which these can be made out varies and some are now very difficult to see with the naked eye. Our work set out to examine how far Reflectance Transformation Imaging (RTI) could reveal the sequence of overlapping carvings, in order to help recognise runes that are difficult to see with the naked eye or indeed with a camera and raking light flash. This study examines the materiality of the Maeshowe runes.

relatedItems.label: Provide a suggested citation for the dataset so reusers are aware of how to cite it
relatedItems.description:
**Why**
A suggestion for the citation promotes access and reusability of data as well as helps reusers to properly cite the dataset, for example in the bibliographies of their publications. This gives credit, recognition and visibility to, for example, the culture heritage institution providing the dataset. 

**How**
For example, the National Library of Scotland’s Data Foundry provides a “Cite the data” section for each of its datasets, as well as a suggested citation, e.g. “Suggested citation: National Library of Scotland. A Medical History of British India. National Library of Scotland, 2019. [https://doi.org/10.34812/2w0t-3f08](https://doi.org/10.34812/2w0t-3f08)”. 
In addition, the National Library of the Netherlands provides a suggested citation: “When using this dataset we ask you to cite it as follows: Andreas van Cranenburgh, Sara Veldhoen, Michel De Gruijter (2022). Textual features and metadata for DBNL novels 1800-2000 [Data set]. Zenodo. [https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5786254](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5786254).” 
Ideally this data citation includes a Persistent Identifier, such as a DOI, ARK, Handle, etc.

relatedItems.label: Straight Talk! Automatic Recognition of Direct Speech in Nineteenth-Century French Novels
relatedItems.description: In fictional prose narrative such as novels and short stories, various forms of speech, thought, and writing representation are ubiquitous and have been studied in great detail in linguistics and literary studies. However, beyond quotation marks, what are linguistic markers of direct speech? And just how ubiquitous is direct speech really? Is there systematic variation in the amount of direct speech over time or across genres? Especially for the field of French literary history, where typography is not a reliable guide, we really don't know. This is regrettable, because being able to quickly and automatically detect direct speech in large collections of literary narrative texts is highly desireable for many areas in literary studies. In the history of literary genres, this allows to observe distributions and evolutions of a fundamental, formal aspect of the novel on a large scale. In narratology, differentiating narrator from character speech is a precondition for more detailed analyses of narrator speech, e.g. with regard to text type (descriptive, narrative, argumentative text). And in authorship attribution, it hereby becomes possible to discard character speech from a set of novels and perform authorship attribution on the narrator speech only, something which may improve attribution. Against this background, the work presented here addresses both the question of how to identify direct speech in French prose fiction and that of how prevalent direct speech is in different subgenres of the nineteenth-century French novel.

relatedItems.label: Concraft -> DependencyParser
relatedItems.description: The Polish dependency parser is trained on the extended version of the Polish dependency treebank (Składnica zależnościowa) with the publicly available parsing systems -- MaltParser or MateParser. MaltParser is a transition-based dependency parser that uses a deterministic parsing algorithm. The deterministic parsing algorithm builds a dependency structure of an input sentence based on transitions (shift-reduce actions) predicted by a classifier. The classifier learns to predict the next transition given training data and the parse history. MateParser, in turn, is a graph-based parser that defines a space of well-formed candidate dependency trees for an input sentence, scores them given an induced parsing model, and selects the highest scoring dependency tree as a correct analysis of the input sentence. Part of: Multiservice, a robust linguistic Web service for Polish.

label: Mandragore
description:
Mandragore is the iconographic database of illuminated manuscripts held by the Département des Manuscritst of the Bibliothèque nationale de France. Users search the database using the various indexes that accompany most of the searchable fields, and descriptors that enable contextual searches. The most direct way to start querying the database is to know the call number of the manuscript. There is both a simple search bar and an advanced search functionality which allows users to restrict by date, place, etc. 

To find a manuscript on Mandragore, several selection fields are available. If you don't know the call number of the manuscript, you can search by author. For example, in the author index, under the letter B, there are several entries for Boccacio, and by selecting Boccacio, decameron, all five available copies are proposed.

In the case of images, you can search by the associated keyword, as many folios are annotated by subject: each folio has one or more descriptors associated with it, which enable you to search for all folios containing the same keyword. When a folio contains several miniatures, each miniature is indexed.

relatedItems.label: Biblissima Portal
relatedItems.description:
The Biblissima Portal provides unique and simple access to a set of digital resources on the history of the transmission of texts produced from Antiquity to the Renaissance in the West and in the East, whatever the medium and whatever the language.

It is the entry point into the data of the Biblissima+ digital infrastructure (2021-2029), _Observatory of Ancient Written Cultures, from Clay to Print_ (ANR-21-ESRE-0005). For more information on the project as a whole, see [project.biblissima.fr](https://project.biblissima.fr).

This Portal brings together heterogeneous digital data produced by the partners of the Biblissima consortium (2012-2021) and then Biblissima+ (2021-2029). Its aim is to make interoperable heritage collections, research archives and scientific literature (original written documentation, collections of digitised sources, bibliography and research archives).

label: Manifold
description: Manifold Scholarship is an open-source publishing platform that enables authors and publishers a means to showcase and enhance the electronic content they already produce in their existing workflows: texts are displayed in a responsive, elegant reader crafted for all modern browsers and devices---desktop and mobile. Powerful built-in annotation and commenting systems allow readers to annotate, highlight, discuss, cite, and share passages from any Manifold text. Resources that are foundational to a particular discussion but that are often tabled because of physical, technical, logistic, or legal limitations can be layered dynamically and directly onto the digital text. And with Manifold, a new kind of publication is possible, one where authors create projects that grow iteratively and that are published online as they are created and then later in print, when they have been codified as versions of record. In short, Manifold transforms scholarly publications into living digital works.

label: Manuscripts with Irish Associations (MIrA)
description:
Manuscripts with Irish Associations (MIrA) - Evidence for early Irish book culture, c. AD 600–1000

MIrA contains two elements:

A catalogue of manuscripts relevant to the study of early Irish book culture (before AD 1000.) The core of the catalogue is c. 160 manuscripts probably written in Ireland and/or in Irish script (often written on the Continent). In addition, there are manuscripts written by named Irish scribes (not always in Irish script), thought to be from Irish exemplars, containing Irish texts, etc.

A web-based digital resource for viewing and exploring manuscripts. This is written in PHP and based on data supplied in XML files. The resource is intended to be lightweight and easy to adapt to other projects.

This resource aims to provide useful information for researchers on early Irish manuscript culture before c. AD 1000. ("Irish" here is shorthand for the broader Gaelic world, including early medieval Scotland.) The catalogue currently contains 301 manuscripts. Manuscripts are assigned to one or more categories. 

Written probably in Ireland
Written mostly in Irish script 
Containing vernacular (Old Irish) content (mostly glosses)

relatedItems.label: ST: Sport Thesaurus
relatedItems.description:
The World's First Multilingual Thesaurus of Sports
The Thesaurus of Sports is a hierarchically ordered structure of the names of competitions, disciplines and sports (Olympic and non-Olympic, including ancient and traditional) along with brief descriptions of the meaning of the main terms. It is linked to an ontology containing additional semantic categories. The presented thesaurus currently contains more than 1,300 main concepts arranged hierarchically in 3 trees, as well as additional categories (people, places, events, organizations synonyms, antonyms, associative terms). It allows searching for names of disciplines, competitions and types of occupations. The basic terminological relationship in the thesaurus is hyponymy (hyperonymy), and in addition there are also synonymy, antonymy, meronymy and fuzzynymes (includes attributes separately, e.g., wheel and net for hammer throw and proper fuzzynymes, e.g., athlete sculpture for discus throw). The thesaurus runs in the SKOSMOS environment.

relatedItems.label: AttentionHTR: Handwritten Text Recognition Based on Attention Encoder-Decoder Networks
relatedItems.description:
This work proposes an attention-based sequence-to-sequence model for handwritten word recognition and explores transfer learning for data-efficient training of HTR systems. To overcome training data scarcity, this work leverages models pre-trained on scene text images as a starting point towards tailoring the handwriting recognition models. ResNet feature extraction and bidirectional LSTM-based sequence modeling stages together form an encoder. The prediction stage consists of a decoder and a content-based attention mechanism. The effectiveness of the proposed end-to-end HTR system has been empirically evaluated on a novel multi-writer dataset Imgur5K and the IAM dataset. The experimental results evaluate the performance of the HTR framework, further supported by an in-depth analysis of the error cases. 

Source code and pre-trained models are available at GitHub (https://github.com/dmitrijsk/AttentionHTR).

relatedItems.label: Marginalia and machine learning: Handwritten text recognition for Marginalia Collections
relatedItems.description: The pressing need for digitization of historical document collections has led to a strong interest in designing computerised image processing methods for automatic hand-written text recognition (HTR). Handwritten text possesses high variability due to different writing styles, languages and scripts. Training an accurate and robust HTR system calls for data-efficient approaches due to the unavailability of sufficient amounts of annotated multi-writer text. A case study on an ongoing project “Marginalia and Machine Learning” is presented here that focuses on automatic detection and recognition of handwritten marginalia texts i.e., text written in margins or handwritten notes. Faster R-CNN network is used for detection of marginalia and AttentionHTR is used for word recognition. The data comes from early book collections (printed) found in the Uppsala University Library, with handwritten marginalia texts. Source code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/ektavats/Project-Marginalia.

relatedItems.label: Coggle
relatedItems.description:
Coggle is an intuitive mind mapping tool that allows for collaboration between its users. It is free for public use and can be accessed in your browser or you can install the app on your Apple or Android device.
 
Though Coggle has been used for mind mapping, it is primarily a method of documenting branching and non-linear information, and encompassing multiple perspectives. It utlizes a drag and drop interface for integrating images, permits multiple users to edit at the same time without causing data conflicts, and supports Markdown and LaTeX formatting. Coggle diagrams can be interlinked, branches of one diagram can be spawned off into its own diagram connected back to the original, and individual branches can be linked via hashtags. The tool includes an API that permits users to interface their diagrams with other programs and manipulate or examine them, and diagrams can also be exported in various formats such as plain-text outline, vector PDFs or images. Coggle is free except where users require more than 100 monthly active users or a closed source version.

relatedItems.label: WikiPack

WikiPack is a web based personal information organizer and Markdown editor that uses Dropbox for synced storage. Using plain text Markdown files and WikiWords, WikiPack gives information context and links entries together by turning your Markdown pages into a private, password protected wiki. The easy to use Markdown language lets you create and edit your wiki pages without having to learn complex wiki syntax. WikiPack features page history/versioning and visual change comparisons in the browser-based GUI and store all of your files in your Dropbox account.

You can import existing markdown files to sync WikiPack with other apps and services using Dropbox, or use the quick-start template to set up new wikis.

WikiPack includes a GUI markdown editor with syntax highlighting, built-in markdown reference, support for Multimarkdown table, and toolbar buttons with keyboard shortcuts and tools for common formatting. WikiPack works in the browser so you can use it on any desktop or mobile device that has an internet connection and Dropbox functionality.

label: Media-ecological Design Strategies for Improving Peri-urban Biodiversity : IoT Toolkit
description:
The increase in the human population and industrialization processes are leading to a worldwide loss of habitats and species. Industrial farming leads to agricultural desertification, which offers fewer living conditions to wild animals than human settlements with small-scale structures and gardens. Until now, however, green spaces in settlement design have been geared towards humans, while humans have been excluded from nature conservation biology. The supposed contradictions between nature, culture and technology should be brought into a constructive interplay to promote biodiversity in peri-urban areas. The attitude of the Mitwelten research project is post-humanistic and post-natural: it attempts to dissolve the central position of humans and to integrate them as a mere element into the more-than-human ecosystem. 
Based on the technologies of the Internet of Things (IoT), a generic IoT Toolkit was developed for field and design research. It consists of a network of nodes that are built from sensors, actuators, processors and other components. The sensors capture activities and changes in the state of the research areas (e.g. image, sound, movement, distance, temperature, humidity) and actuators (e.g. motors, loudspeakers, lamps) actively influence them. Energy supply units (e.g. batteries or solar panels) and network modules (e.g. LoRaWAN or 4/5G mobile networks) are used for power supply and networking.

relatedItems.label: Choose a Notation Software and an Encoding Strategy
relatedItems.description:
The second step involves selecting both an encoding format and a notational tool suited to the corpus and the edition's intended objectives. At this stage, the editor must determine whether the project calls for a diplomatic or a critical edition.

Regarding notational tools, MuseScore (open source) stands as the currently recommended choice: it supports direct export to MEI without requiring plugins. Sibelius and Finale, though still widely used in professional contexts, are no longer under active development and cannot be considered viable long-term solutions. For early or non-Western repertoires, specialized tools may prove necessary — among them Gregorio for neumatic notation, LuteScribe and Fronimo for tablature, and the ReTab module for lute tablature in MEI.

The choice of encoding format has major consequences for the interoperability and analytical potential of the edition. MEI (Music Encoding Initiative) is strongly recommended for scholarly digital editions: it allows the coexistence of graphical score visualization and semantic encoding of musical data, accommodates a critical apparatus and a metadata header, and opens the way to computational analysis via tools such as Music21 and Humdrum. MusicXML remains a widely supported interchange format, suitable at the data-transfer stage of the workflow. PDF, by contrast, is appropriate only for dissemination purposes and does not constitute a digital edition in the full sense of the term.

relatedItems.label: Convert to MEI (other softwares)
relatedItems.description:
For other software, there is no plugin to export directly to MEI. In this case, it is possible to use several online converters: Verovio, MEI Friend, MEI Garage. Follow the various resources below. 
Be aware that Verovio and MEI Friend (basically the same converter) preserve more metadata than MEI Garage. We advise you to use MEI Garage only if you encounter a problem with the other two converters.

relatedItems.label: Visualize the MEI file
relatedItems.description: During the conversion, it is possible that some musical data may be corrupted. To quickly view the MEI file in SVG format (music score), use Verovio, MEI Friend or MEISE. With Verovio and MEI Friend, you can open a MEI file online. Using MEISE requires however local software installation.

relatedItems.label: Fix and improve the music content
relatedItems.description:
In order to modify a MEI file to correct or improve it, you can use MEI Friend or MEISE. Both tools have a musical interface allowing modifying the score like a classic editor. However, the proposed changes remain limited. In order to edit a MEI file locally with MEI Friend, you can use the MEI Friend module in Atom.

To further modify the MEI file, it is necessary to modify the code. To do this, follow the MEI guidelines.

relatedItems.label: Add new metadata
relatedItems.description: To check, modify or add metadata, it is necessary to go to the MEI header. For this, you have to directly explore the code using MEI-Friend or MEISE. It is preferable to limit yourself to the basic fields proposed in the MEI header (;; , etc.). Make sure that the title of the work and the musical part (allegro, Kyrie, etc.) are not inverted. In order to fill in the metadata correctly, see the MEI guidelines.

label: MEI Score Editor --MEISE
description: The MEI Score Editor (MEISE) is an Eclipse-based client software for viewing and editing MEI-encoded music documents in CMN (Common Music Notation), facilitating proof reading as well as modifying and correcting MEI files. MEISE was designed to satisfy special requirements of research in musicology, currently unsupported by existing music notation software tools. MEISE should be used especially for working with MEI-data as a processing and editing tool, e.g. for creating variants, generating, completing and modifying MEI-files. As a key merit, MEISE gains of its homomorphic internal data structure to the MEI schema tree, allowing for native support for theoretically all MEI encoding principles. This allows for some unique features arising from the field of scholarly music edition, such as the encoding and visualization of variants of different musical sources in one digital MEI representation.

label: MerMEId MeLODy
description:
MerMEId MeLODy is an open-source, browser-based metadata editor designed specifically for creating well-formed MEI (Music Encoding Initiative) metadata for thematic work and source catalogues. It is the successor to MerMEId, the established metadata editor for thematic work catalogues originally developed at the Danish Centre for Music Editing.

The editor produces complex RDF/Turtle output that directly cooperates with MEI structures to ensure standards-compliant metadata. The RDF data model is precisely aligned with the MEI Schema (v5.1) and the FRBR (Functional Requirements for Bibliographic Records) conceptual model, so all structured metadata can be reliably transformed into MEI/XML for use in MEI-based workflows, research infrastructure, and digital editions. It is designed for musicologists, music librarians, and developers who need to create structured, interoperable, and FAIR-compliant metadata for musical works, sources, persons or events.

relatedItems.label: Process the captured data
relatedItems.description:
In this step, the raw data from step 5 is imported into processing software for cleaning, aligning, meshing, texturing and merging, and data optimisation. After raw data is collected through the digital survey, it enters a crucial post-processing phase where data optimisation takes place. This process involves aligning multiple datasets, georeferencing them to real-world coordinates, merging overlapping scans or images, and cleaning out noise or inaccuracies. The goal is to transform unstructured raw data into an accurate, cohesive, and usable dataset. During this phase, the data is refined to improve its quality, accuracy, and usability, ensuring it is suitable for analysis, modelling, or integration into GIS, CAD, or BIM systems. Without this optimisation phase, the raw data would remain fragmented and unreliable, greatly limiting its value in decision-making, design, and documentation. 

# Input:

* Raw scan and image data from Step 5
* Acquisition metadata

# Output:

* Cleaned and aligned point clouds → .e57, .las, .ply, .xyz
* Georeferenced datasets → .laz, .shp, .geojson
* Meshes (with or without texture) → .obj, .fbx, .stl, .3ds
* Orthophotos or DEMs (if generated) → .tiff, .jpg, .xyz, .asc
*  Metadata for processing steps → .xml, .json, .csv

label: Metadata Quality Assessment Framework
description:
Metadata Quality Assessment Framework is a generic metadata quality assessment tool. It accepts a metadata schema and metadata files, assess different quality dimensions, and produce output as CSV or JSON files. The framework measures the following features:
*  completeness: it says how complete your records, i.e. what ratio of data elements defined in the metadata schema is available in the records. It can also collect information about the extistence of the field, and their cardinality (how many times they occur in a record)
* uniqueness and TF-IDF score: it calculates the TF-IDF scores for field values. It is useful to learn how unique or how frequent the data values
* rule catalogue: one can set different rules or constraints against the data values. It checks if these rules are followed. One can set scores for failure and success cases.
* multilingual saturation: how multilingual your records. It requires XML or RDF based multilingual annotation. It reports the number of tagged literals, number of distinct language tags, number of tagged literals per language tag, average number of languages per property for which there is at least one language-tagged literal
* language extractor: it extracts the language tag of data elements if any.

above these there are some helper calculators:
* extractor: extracts and outputs values from the record
* annotator: injects metadata into the output (e.g. some values, which helps further processings, such as file name, date, identifier or other information about the measurement, which are not available within the records)
* indexer: index particular data elements with Solr before measurement. It is a necessary step for measuring TF-IDF or uniqueness

label: metafacture
description:
Metafacture is a toolkit for processing semi-structured data with a focus on library metadata. It provides a versatile set of tools for reading, writing and transforming data. Metafacture can be used as a stand-alone application or as a Java library in other applications. The name Metafacture is a portmanteau of the words metadata and manufacture.

Metafacture includes a large number of modules for operating on semi-structured data. These modules can be combined to build pipelines to perform complex metadata processing tasks. The pipelines can be constructed either in Java code or with the domain-specific language Flux. One of the core features of Metafacture is the Metamorph module. Metamorph is an xml-based language for specifying transformations of semi-structured data. It can be seamlessly integrated into Java code.

At its heart Metafacture is a framework for implementing modules for metadata processing. This makes Metafacture easily extendable with additional modules. The plugins and tools page on the wiki shows supplementary packages and projects which extend Metafacture.

Originally, Metafacture was developed as part of the Culturegraph platform but it is developed independently now and used by others, too: see who uses Metafacture.

Also Metafacture Fix, a non-xml Catmandu inspired language for specifying transformations, is being developed that is not stream-based but operates at record level.

Metafacture is maintained by the Team Offene Infrastruktur by hbz.

Importing, transforming, storing and indexing data should be easy.

Catmandu is a command line tool to access and convert data from your digital library, research services or any other open data sets. Catmandu provides a suite of Perl modules to ease the import, storage, retrieval, export and transformation of metadata records. Combine Catmandu modules with web application frameworks such as PSGI/Plack, document stores such as MongoDB and full text indexes such as Solr to create a rapid development environment for digital library services such as institutional repositories and search engines.

In the http://librecat.org/ project it is our goal to provide an open source set of programming components to build up digital libraries services suited to your local needs.

Read an in depth introduction into Catmandu programming at https://github.com/LibreCat/Catmandu/wiki/Introduction.

label: Metagrid Classic
description:
Metagrid is a networking initiative developped by Dodis, on behalf of the Swiss Academy of Humanities and Social Sciences (SAGW). It is designed to connect metadata and resources of research projects throughout the humanities and social sciences.

Metagrid Classic creates links between databases with information about historical persons. It relies on a federative system where about 35 projects make their data available. Currently, a pool of more than seven million items is available containing more than 1,000,000 links. Data management and linking is based on a multi-step, semi-automatic process. The Metagrid widget offers the possibility to embed the generated links on the partner websites. Moreover, you can access all persons in the Metagrid Network via a search interface. The participating projects thus increase their visibility and users can access further relevant information about a person with a single click. Metagrid is an initiative developped by Dodis, on behalf of the Swiss Academy of Humanities and Social Sciences (SAGW).
Features
Metagrid is format agnostic. It can work with APIs, plain HTML, XML, or CSV data sources.
We provide an internal matching tool to connect your data with other projects.
All links in Metagrid are shared with all partners.
The Metagrid Enhancer allows you to enrich your data, letting you pull structured data from different sources over a simple API.

relatedItems.description: This step is related to the surveyed object and to the software used for processing the data. Usually it is possible to refer to a traditional photogrammetric workflow: Data loading Tie points extraction (Sparse point cloud) Camera Calibration Relative orientation Absolute orientation (using georef. data) Densification (Dense point cloud) Meshing (Triangulated mesh) Texturing DSM generation 3D model exporting Software to use: Photogrammetric suite (MicMac, AgiSoft Metashape, Pix4D Mapper, etc.)

relatedItems.label: Georeferencing the surveyed data: Using a GNSS            receiver for precise positioning of Ground Control Points
relatedItems.description: Using well materialized Ground Control Points (GCPs) and using the same set in all the performed flights will require the use of topographic instruments only for the first acquisition, as once measured, the GCPs will be re-used for the subsequents flights. It is important to underline the importance of acquiring a trustworthy set of GCPs to be used for all the surveys, instead of measuring new GCPs every time. It is more important, in fact, not to acquire the most accurate GNSS data, but to use the most precise set of GCPs, assuming for (at least locally) the validity of the first data acquired, cause repeating measures over time may lead to non extremely precise co-registration of the generated models. Instruments required: Total station D-GNSS antenna Action to perform: Defining and measuring a topographic network Materialization of the topographical vertices Materialization of the control points Ground control points displacement around and inside the site Natural points selection and digitization for future surveys Control points measurement and recording (via Total station or GNSS receiver) Softwares to use: Topographic network compensation (e.g. MicroSurvey StarNet)

relatedItems.label: MicMacRoom - a plugin for running MicMac into Meshroom
relatedItems.description:
MicMacRoom is an open-source, community-driven prototype bridging the power of MicMac’s rigorous photogrammetric algorithms with Meshroom’s intuitive, node-based interface. Designed for humanities and social sciences (SHS) researchers, cultural heritage professionals, and digital humanists, this tool simplifies 3D reconstruction workflows while ensuring scientific precision, interoperability, and sustainability.
Why MicMacRoom?

User-Friendly & Customizable: Run complete photogrammetric pipelines (tie-point extraction, dense cloud generation, meshing, texturing, georeferencing) directly within Meshroom’s GUI, without command-line expertise.
Open & Collaborative: Fully open-source (code, tutorials, datasets) with a growing community of developers and users.
Cultural Heritage Focus: Optimized for CH applications (archaeology, museum digitization, architectural documentation) with color calibration (SHAFT2 integration) and georeferencing support.
Interoperable & Extensible: Compatible with existing FLOSS tools (PotreeConverter, SHAFT) and future integrations (AI-based annotation, SLAM capture).

For the SHS Community, MicMacRoom lowers the technical barrier to high-quality 3D modeling, enabling researchers to:

✔ Preserve & analyze cultural artifacts with metrological precision.

✔ Share & reuse workflows via preconfigured templates (e.g., MicMacOrtho, MicMacTexturedMesh).

✔ Collaborate & contribute to a sustainable open ecosystem for digital heritage.

relatedItems.label: Visualisation
relatedItems.description: Decide what the final user will be able to see of our work: i.e. formats, interactivity, access to metadata and sources, etc. Final outputs can include: images (that could be printed as well, which for a cultural heritage site is still important), videos (depending on a budget), interactive viewers (and which one), virtual reality (what type of device will be supported) if sources will be made available and in what formats website to host all the material Level of accuracy and details can be varied depending on: explicit annotations linking to sources resolution accessibility to documentation of the reconstruction process (technical metadata) context of the reconstruction (and possibility of updates)

relatedItems.label: Preservation
relatedItems.description: To convert and represent the information in a 3D reconstruction. In doing the model, each step implies choices about the representation and prioritisation of data in the sources. Consequently, it should be declared how this data is used and it should be clear that different methods highlight different aspects, responding to different research questions. Based on the aims and research questions, decisions (and clear statements) are needed on: the scale (1:1 is best) the level of details (e.g. all architectural details or just the volume) textures (procedural or mapping with a picture) lighting and shading (atmospherical, internal/external, time of the day, seasonality, etc.) soundscapes (specific audio, e.g. winds, acoustic of the building) annotations links to original sources: how are they connected and how is possible to verify the accuracy of the model

label: Mistakes as a source of knowledge: ACCSN 2.0
description:
The Digital Humanities project “Mistakes as a source of knowledge: ACCSN 2.0” lead by Assist. Prof. Lily Grozdanova, hosted by the Faculty of History, SU ”St. Kliment Ohridski”, was one of the five winning proposals, supported by DARIAH-ERIC for 2025. 
The project is the next stage of development of the Ancient Coins Counterfeits Scientific Network (ACCSN), funded by the Alexander von Humboldt Foundation. It addresses the pressing scientific and societal issue of the spread of numismatic counterfeits from a sustainability perspective, building on the first stage. The project offers a unique research angle, exploring mistakes (stylistic, technological, etc.) as a source of knowledge for developing expertise and identifying counterfeit markers.
The spread of counterfeits of ancient numismatic items leads to distortions in history, society, and identity. The most effective prevention against these processes is to create a stable, proactive academic network that enables enhanced knowledge exchange and transfer. Another central aspect is developing an IT-based digital tool that would be an active asset against the spread of objects identified as counterfeits. These are the two main goals of ACCSN 1.0, which are further developed in ACCSN 2.0 and will have a significant, positive impact on the preservation of cultural heritage.  

The project's central goal is to digitise the most significant collection of numismatic objects identified as counterfeits of the Coin Cabinet of the Royal Library of Belgium (1,242 forgeries of Greek and 2,123 of Roman coinages). This includes on-site processing of the objects using a specialised QuickPX hard- and software system provided by the partner projects Corpus Nummorum (CN) and DigiThrace. After initial processing, datasets are created for each object and entered into CN in accordance with the FAIR principles and LOD.    
A further goal is to perform the second stage of the digitisation of the “Callataÿ’ file of counterfeit Greek coins”. In the course of ACCSN 2, the digitisation of the entire collection of info cards as digital cultural heritage objects was finalised and it is currently published as open data on the ACCSN platform. The second stage will transform the data in the info cards into DB datasets, add them to the CN platform, and actively link the stable URIs of the CN platform to the digital heritage objects published on the ACCSN platform.
The third goal, which is currently being actively developed, is a “standardised identification expertise card” that can be internationally applied. A serious issue is the lack of an internationally standardised procedure for counterfeit identification. Activities are underway to define the terminology, including within the Nomisma Counterfeits Working group and the DARIAH Digital Numismatics working group, to address the challenges of terminology and ontology in the area.
Identifying forgeries of ancient numismatic material requires practical work and precise analysis of the counterfeits themselves. Until this project, there was no digitised collection of such objects to assist specialists in further developing their expertise in production techniques and forgery markers. Hence, the scientific community's ability to study mistakes and create proactive prevention strategies was severely limited. The ACCSN 2.0 is actively changing this concept by developing scientific, innovative digital prevention means.

label: MMM Sampo - Mapping Manuscript Migrations
description: Mapping Manuscript Migrations (MMM Sampo) is an in-use system for modeling, aggregating, publishing, and studying heterogeneous, distributed  premodern  manuscript  databases  on  the  Semantic  Web.  A  general “Sampo model” was applied to publishing and using linked data in Digital Humani-ties (DH) research and to creating the MMM Sampo system that includes a semantic portal and a Linked Open Data (LOD) service. The idea is to provide the manuscriptdata publishers with a novel collaborative way to enrich their contents with re-lated data of the other providers and by reasoning. For the end user, the MMMPortal facilitates semantic faceted search and exploration of the data, integrated seamlessly with data analytic tools for solving research problems in manuscriptstudies. In addition, the SPARQL endpoint of the LOD service can be used with external tools for customized use in DH research and applications. The MMM Sampo services  are  available  online,  based  on  metadata  of  over 220 000 manuscriptsfrom the Schoenberg Database of Manuscripts of the Schoenberg Institute for Manuscript Studies (University of Pennsylvania), the Medieval Manuscripts in Oxford  Libraries,  and  Bibale  of  Institut  de  recherche  et  d’histoire  des  textesin  Paris.  Evaluation  of  the  MMM  Portal  suggests  that  the  system  is  useful  in manuscript studies and outperforms current systems online in searching, exploring, and analyzing data.

relatedItems.label: WebLicht
relatedItems.description:
WebLicht is an execution environment for automatic annotation of text corpora. Linguistic tools such as tokenizers, part of speech taggers, and parsers are encapsulated as web services, which can be combined by the user into custom processing chains. The resulting annotations can then be visualized in an appropriate way, such as in a table or tree format. 

It is often the case that a tool relies on one or more annotation layers to exist in the input data before it can begin processing. WebLicht can assist the user in building a processing chain by determining which tools are able to operate on the data at any given point and offering only those tools as options to add to the chain. There are 2 modes for building tool chains: Easy Mode lets you choose pre-defined processing chains Advanced Mode allows you to build customized tool chains. 

Login is required to use the tools and corpora. Login with email addresses from most recognized European universities will be automatically accepted. Individuals with a Non-European email address need to create an account with clarin.eu Developed by the German language resource infrastructure (D-SPIN) and Common language resources and technology infrastructure (CLARIN).
