label: MorphAL (QGIS plugin)
description:
The MorphAL (Morphological Analysis) plugin for QGIS enriches vector shapefile data of the "parcel" type to facilitate the search for landscape structuring logic. It adds semantic attributes to segment and polygon data concerning their geometric properties (orientation, rectangularity, convexity). These attributes correspond to mathematical indicators that are automatically calculated and integrated into the shapefile attribute table.

Parcel data in polygons, most often from vectorized land registers, can be broken down into segments; the plugin then adds the orientation of each segment: researchers can then test or identify certain orientations that structure all or part of a space, and which are therefore more or less morphogenetic (for example, Roman centuriations that organize the Padanian plain of northern Italy even today more than in ancient times).

In addition, the geometry of polygonal parcel data can be characterized according to two morphological analysis criteria: rectangularity (parcels very far from or on the contrary very close to their minimum bounding rectangle) and convexity (parcels very far from or on the contrary very close to their convex hull). Mathematical indicators, with a value between 0 and 1, are automatically calculated and integrated into attributes of the shapefile data, which can then be classified. The concentration in a place of very rectangular parcels suggests a regularity that the historical discourse must then analyze: it makes it possible to identify an initial planning (for example a subdivision in an ancient period, including protohistoric) and the updating of this regular form over time in different periods (ancient, medieval, modern, etc.). The concentration in a place of parcels with a strong lack of convexity suggests conflicts of form and makes it possible to identify temporal shifts that result in an inadequacy of inherited spatial structures.

concept.label: BMP
concept.definition: The BMP file format, also known as bitmap image file or device independent bitmap (DIB) file format or simply a bitmap, is a raster graphics image file format used to store bitmap digital images, independently of the display device (such as a graphics adapter), especially on Microsoft Windows and OS/2 operating systems. The BMP file format is capable of storing two-dimensional digital images both monochrome and color, in various color depths, and optionally with data compression, alpha channels, and color profiles. The Windows Metafile (WMF) specification covers the BMP file format. Among others, wingdi.h defines BMP constants and structures.

concept.label: COLLADA

It is managed by the nonprofit technology consortium, the Khronos Group, and has been adopted by ISO as a publicly available specification, ISO/PAS 17506. COLLADA defines an open standard XML schema for exchanging digital assets among various graphics software applications that might otherwise store their assets in incompatible file formats. COLLADA documents that describe digital assets are XML files, usually identified with a .dae (digital asset exchange) filename extension.

concept.label: JPEG
concept.definition: JPEG ( JAY-peg) is a commonly used method of lossy compression for digital images, particularly for those images produced by digital photography. The degree of compression can be adjusted, allowing a selectable tradeoff between storage size and image quality. JPEG typically achieves 10:1 compression with little perceptible loss in image quality. JPEG compression is used in a number of image file formats. JPEG/Exif is the most common image format used by digital cameras and other photographic image capture devices; along with JPEG/JFIF, it is the most common format for storing and transmitting photographic images on the World Wide Web. These format variations are often not distinguished, and are simply called JPEG. The term "JPEG" is an initialism/acronym for the Joint Photographic Experts Group, which created the standard. The MIME media type for JPEG is image/jpeg, except in older Internet Explorer versions, which provides a MIME type of image/pjpeg when uploading JPEG images. JPEG files usually have a filename extension of .jpg or .jpeg. JPEG/JFIF supports a maximum image size of 65,53565,535 pixels, hence up to 4 gigapixels for an aspect ratio of 1:1.

relatedItems.label: ARIADNE Portal
relatedItems.description:
The ARIADNE Portal provides the main point of access for searching and browsing datasets and new services for processing and publishing archaeological datasets online. 

The Portal brings together existing archaeological research datasets from ARIADNE partners so that researchers can browse and access the various distributed datasets for use in their projects. The portal also provides a point of access for the new services developed by the project.

The datasets that are registered in the ARIADNE catalogue are held by its partners and have been created through research, in excavations, in fieldwork, laboratory and other projects. In recent years archaeologists have been making increasing use of sophisticated digital equipment and techniques. During the course of a research project large volumes of data are created and collected, and become part of the research archive. ARIADNE aims to make these archives available through its portal for researchers to consult when starting new research.

relatedItems.label: Gate Cloud
relatedItems.description:
https://cloud.gate.ac.uk is a public REST API providing access to a wide variety of GATE text analysis pipelines and other services for use by third party software.  A simple web interface is available to test individual pipelines on small samples of text, and API documentation is provided for use by application integrators.  A tool is also available to run GATE Cloud services against text stored in Google Sheets.

Available pipelines cover a variety of tool types, levels of abstraction and target domains, ranging from simple low-level text analysis such as part-of-speech tagging, general named entity taggers for a variety of languages, domain-specific entity recognition services for archaeology & dendrochronology, various classifiers to assist with analysis of disinformation and hate speech, and an OCR service to extract text from images.  A basic quota sufficient to analyse ~1200 texts per day is available to anyone, with higher quotas available on request to research users.

relatedItems.label: Choose a Notation Software and an Encoding Strategy
relatedItems.description:
The second step involves selecting both an encoding format and a notational tool suited to the corpus and the edition's intended objectives. At this stage, the editor must determine whether the project calls for a diplomatic or a critical edition.

Regarding notational tools, MuseScore (open source) stands as the currently recommended choice: it supports direct export to MEI without requiring plugins. Sibelius and Finale, though still widely used in professional contexts, are no longer under active development and cannot be considered viable long-term solutions. For early or non-Western repertoires, specialized tools may prove necessary — among them Gregorio for neumatic notation, LuteScribe and Fronimo for tablature, and the ReTab module for lute tablature in MEI.

The choice of encoding format has major consequences for the interoperability and analytical potential of the edition. MEI (Music Encoding Initiative) is strongly recommended for scholarly digital editions: it allows the coexistence of graphical score visualization and semantic encoding of musical data, accommodates a critical apparatus and a metadata header, and opens the way to computational analysis via tools such as Music21 and Humdrum. MusicXML remains a widely supported interchange format, suitable at the data-transfer stage of the workflow. PDF, by contrast, is appropriate only for dissemination purposes and does not constitute a digital edition in the full sense of the term.

relatedItems.label: Music Encoding Initiative from MusicXML
relatedItems.description: The Music Encoding Initiative is an open-source language to encode musical scores in a machine-readable structure. Its main strong point lies in the management of various metadata and its capacity to code the framework and the semantics of music works. In addition to these technical specificities, the MEI is perfectly proper for FAIR principles. In order to convert a MusicXML in MEI format, several ways are possible. This workflow aims to describe best practices, step by step, to preserve the initial file and to get a correct MEI. This workflow is suitable for both common Western notation and modern transcription of ancient works (Renaissance and Middle Ages).

relatedItems.label: Get MusicXML file ready
relatedItems.description:
The MEI require proper preparation of the MusicXML file, regardless of the software used (MuseScore, Sibelius, Finale, etc.). The recommendations are as follows: 
-	Use the partition models suggested in the software as well as the right instruments, especially in the case of transposing instruments or voices. 
-	Do not use an incipit at the beginning of the score (ancient music).
-	In the case of musica ficta and rhythmic ligature (ancient music), signs will not be preserved during export.

relatedItems.label: Add first metadata
relatedItems.description: It is already possible to add main metadata in the MusicXML file. In this case, use specifically the fields proposed by the software (work title, composer, parts, etc.). Do not directly add metadata in the code in order to facilitate their preservation during conversion.

label: musicaSearch
description:
MusicaSearch is the new digital resource for musicological research. Its innovative search engine connects students, scholars, researchers, music lovers and musicians to a unique network of musical and musicological collections drawn from partners in the Huma-Num Musica2 consortium. MusicaSearch aggregates data that was previously dispersed throughout France and worldwide, linked to a wide range of research units, institutions, organisations and foundations, some of which are entirely private. By centralising the documentation of these resources, MusicaSearch promotes true interoperability in musicological research and increases its visibility.

Hosted on the Huma-Num platform, MusicaSearch offers five main search options: individuals, musical ensembles, musical scores, events, and venues. Depending on the types of projects indexed, these filters can be used individually or combined to suit the specific characteristics of each search. Powered by ElasticSearch, the engine enables particularly effective cross-searching: accurate and exhaustive with up to three keywords (using ‘and’ logic), then more open and exploratory beyond this level (using ‘or’ logic), offering a degree of flexibility suited to all types of queries.

The collections retrieved by MusicaSearch cover various fields of study in musicology from the Renaissance to the present day. MusicaSearch accesses the Ricercar·data·lab website (CESR – UMR 7323 of the CNRS, University of Tours, Ministry of Culture), which in turn browses the various databases it now hosts, offering a musical repertoire of the Renaissance, a prosopography of singers, catalogues of works and various digital projects. The Mozart era is represented by the Référentiel historique de la France de l'Ancien Régime ReFar (IReMus – UMR 8223 of the CNRS; Centre de recherche du château de Versailles) and in part by the Dezède digital project (University of Rouen Normandy, CÉRÉdI – UR 3229; Paul-Valéry-Montpellier University, IRCL – UMR 5186; Toulouse-Jean Jaurès University, LLA CREATIS – UR 4152), which reconstitutes chronologies of concerts from the end of the Ancien Régime to the present day and archives the history of ensembles and orchestras in France. The Berlioz era is covered in particular by the Bru Zane Mediabase (Centre for French Romantic Music, Palazzetto Bru Zane Foundation), but also by Dezède. For the Boulez era, the IRCAM databases (CNRS, Ministry of Culture, Centre Pompidou) are now combined within its Documentation Centre (BRAHMS, Analyses, Médias, Sidney); the Centre Iannis Xenakis (University of Rouen Normandy, CÉRÉdI – UR 3229) enhances the UPIC archives held at the University of Rouen Normandy's Library of Arts and Humanities, while the Pierre Henry website (Son/Ré association, DRAC Île-de-France, Ministry of Culture, City of Paris, SACEM, SACEM Heart Committee) brings together comprehensive documentation on the composer. MusicaSearch also provides access to data from the Répertoire International des SourcesMusicales (RISM) – International Inventory of Musical Sources – (RISM), an international non-profit organisation founded in 1952 with the aim of documenting and locating musical sources held around the world.

Launched in 2024, MusicaSearch takes an open approach, gradually incorporating all digital projects that publish musicological or musical data accessible via their data centers (API, OAI-PMH, SPARQL Endpoint). This open structure allows for organic growth of the network, constantly enriching the available resources. Institutions, research centers and projects willing to join this collaborative adventure will find in MusicaSearch a leading technological and scientific partner, capable of promoting their collections while integrating them into a wider ecosystem.

Check out the JavaScript toolkit version of verovio running in the MEI Viewer as well as the app or tutorials for web integration and user interaction.

concept.label: CSV
concept.definition: A comma-separated values (CSV) file is a delimited text file that uses a comma to separate values. A CSV file stores tabular data (numbers and text) in plain text. Each line of the file is a data record. Each record consists of one or more fields, separated by commas. The use of the comma as a field separator is the source of the name for this file format. RFC 4180 formalized CSV. It defines the MIME type "text/csv", and CSV files that follow its rules should be very widely portable

concept.label: JPEG
concept.definition: JPEG ( JAY-peg) is a commonly used method of lossy compression for digital images, particularly for those images produced by digital photography. The degree of compression can be adjusted, allowing a selectable tradeoff between storage size and image quality. JPEG typically achieves 10:1 compression with little perceptible loss in image quality. JPEG compression is used in a number of image file formats. JPEG/Exif is the most common image format used by digital cameras and other photographic image capture devices; along with JPEG/JFIF, it is the most common format for storing and transmitting photographic images on the World Wide Web. These format variations are often not distinguished, and are simply called JPEG. The term "JPEG" is an initialism/acronym for the Joint Photographic Experts Group, which created the standard. The MIME media type for JPEG is image/jpeg, except in older Internet Explorer versions, which provides a MIME type of image/pjpeg when uploading JPEG images. JPEG files usually have a filename extension of .jpg or .jpeg. JPEG/JFIF supports a maximum image size of 65,53565,535 pixels, hence up to 4 gigapixels for an aspect ratio of 1:1.

concept.definition: The Music Encoding Initiative (MEI) is an open-source effort to create a system for representation musical documents in a machine-readable structure. concept.label: PNG
concept.definition: Portable Network Graphics (PNG, pronounced PEE-en-JEE or PING) is a raster graphics file format that supports lossless data compression. PNG was created as an improved, non-patented replacement for Graphics Interchange Format (GIF), and is the most widely used lossless image compression format on the Internet. PNG supports palette-based images (with palettes of 24-bit RGB or 32-bit RGBA colors), grayscale images (with or without alpha channel for transparency), and full-color non-palette-based RGB/RGBA images (with or without alpha channel). PNG was designed for transferring images on the Internet, not for professional-quality print graphics, and therefore does not support non-RGB color spaces such as CMYK. A PNG file contains a single image in an extensible structure of "chunks", encoding the basic pixels and other information such as textual comments and integrity checks documented in RFC 2083. PNG files nearly always use file extension PNG or png and are assigned MIME media type image/png. PNG was published as informational RFC 2083 in March 1997 and as an ISO/IEC standard in 2004.

relatedItems.label: Interoperability - a new horizon for data sharing in Humanities and Social Sciences. The input of three digital services developed by Huma-Num
relatedItems.description:
In the field of Humanities and Social Sciences, the production of digital or scanned data has increased considerably in recent years. These data, which are usually very expensive to produce, are often lost at the end of the project. They are therefore rarely reused, due to a lack of financial, human and technical resources of the communities that produced them.

The TGIR Huma-Num, whose mission is to facilitate the digital turn in Humanities and Social Sciences research, offers services dedicated to the production and reuse of data. These services aim at avoiding loss and facilitating the re-use of scientific data. To do this, Huma-Num supports research teams throughout their digital projects to allow the sharing, reuse and preservation of data thanks to a chain of devices focused on interoperability.

relatedItems.label: Deposit, Archive, and Ensure Long-Term Sustainability
relatedItems.description:
The final step of the workflow concerns the long-term sustainability of the edition: the choice of a trusted repository, the conditions of indexing, and the prevention of obsolescence. Data hosting on virtual machines provided by national research infrastructures is recommended for publicly funded projects. In France, Nakala (hosted by Huma-Num) provides a FAIR-compliant repository specifically designed for humanities and social sciences data produced by institutions affiliated with the French Ministry of Higher Education and Research. NEUMA (also hosted by Huma-Num) is a digital music library providing online access to encoded musical corpora. 

Interoperability should be considered from the earliest stages of the editorial project in order to ensure the edition's integration into the larger research ecosystem. The edition must be correctly indexed in relevant discovery portals: the SSH Open Marketplace, RISM, and the IIIF community's shared infrastructures. A stable persistent identifier (DOI via Zenodo, or a handle) must be assigned. Finally, the question of format obsolescence must be anticipated: MEI, like LaTeX, relies on plain text files with tags, a preservation strategy that is more robust than proprietary binary formats.

relatedItems.description:
Les transcriptions sont souvent faites pour être partagées avec d'autres utilisateurs. Le coût de leur création incite aussi à ce partage. Enfin les transcriptions réalisées et partagées peuvent être citées comme un travail de recherche et faire partie des travaux d'un chercheur ou d'une équipe de recherche.
Les dépôts et la diffusion de données se font de préférence dans des sites spécialisés comme COCOON, ORTOLANG, ou des sites généralistes comme NAKALA.

English translation

Transcriptions are often created to be shared with other users. The cost of producing them also encourages such sharing. Finally, completed and shared transcriptions can be cited as research output and form part of the work of a researcher or a research team.
Data deposition and dissemination are preferably carried out through specialised platforms such as COCOON, ORTOLANG, or more general-purpose repositories such as NAKALA.

relatedItems.label: Producing Structured Visual Data from Illustrated Heritage Corpora
relatedItems.description:
Illustrated heritage corpora bring together digitised pages, plates, photographs, prints, drawings, captions, inscriptions, handwritten notes, and catalogue records at different levels of granularity. This workflow provides a method for turning these heterogeneous sources into visual units that can be located, described, compared, and reused while preserving their connection to the original documents and collections.

Starting from a research question, the workflow guides the selection of a representative corpus, the preparation of images and metadata, and the definition of the visual and textual units to be identified. A reference sample establishes the expected structure and quality of the results. Automatic or semi-automatic processing can then be used to extract images and associated text, followed by expert review, correction, and evaluation. The validated results are converted into structured data that can support cataloguing, quantitative analysis, visual exploration, or the study of relationships between images, texts, people, places, and objects.

The workflow preserves source identifiers, processing history, uncertainty, and validation status throughout the process. Its outputs may include extracted image regions, annotations, transcriptions, structured metadata, authority links, similarity results, and documented datasets. These elements provide a reproducible basis for further research and enable the resulting data, methods, and evaluation criteria to be shared and adapted across heritage collections.

This process is particularly relevant to researchers working with visual or illustrated corpora; research engineers and data stewards; libraries, archives, museums and heritage institutions; digital humanities projects preparing training, evaluation or exploration datasets; and teaching and training teams introducing computer vision methods for cultural heritage.

label: NameTag
description:
NameTag is an open-source tool for named entity recognition (NER). NameTag identifies proper names in text and classifies them into predefined categories, such as names of persons, locations, organizations, etc. NameTag 2 recognizes nested entities (embedded entities) of arbitrary depth.

For Czech, it recognizes a [complex hierarchy of categories](http://ufal.mff.cuni.cz/~strakova/cnec2.0/ne-type-hierarchy.pdf). The English model, which is trained on CoNLL-2003 NER annotations (Sang and De Meulder [2003](https://www.clarin.eu/resource-families/tools-named-entity-recognition#Sang%20and%20De%20Meulder%202003)), distinguishes the following four NER classes: person, organisation, location and miscellaneous.

The trained model for Czech is available for through LINDAT: [Czech Models (CNEC) for NameTag](http://hdl.handle.net/11858/00-097C-0000-0023-7D42-8).
A [user manual](http://ufal.mff.cuni.cz/nametag/users-manual) is also available.

The **output** is a _JSON_ file, which contains details about the model used, acknowledgements, and the results of NER. This output should be then stored as another distribution of the document, providing a specific type of enrichment to the original data.

relatedItems.label: NLP enrichment of OCR text lines into TEITOK (UDPipe 2, NameTag 3)
relatedItems.description:
Adds linguistic annotation to text lines from ALTO post-processing (CSV or XLSX with a `text` column, or plain text). The lines go to the LINDAT UDPipe 2 service for tokens, lemmas, part-of-speech tags and syntax, and to NameTag 3 for named entities. The main output is TEITOK XML, a TEI-based format that keeps the annotation tied to the page layout when the ALTO files are supplied. CoNLL-U files, per-page entity tables, summary CSVs and the ATRIUM document record (JSON) are also written, with a paradata JSON log per run.

Optional keyword extraction per page or document uses YAKE (command-line default), KeyBERT (API default) or the legacy KER method. An optional LLM stage maps text onto the AMČR and TEATER vocabularies; the same engine is maintained as the separate tool atrium-llm-enrich, which the AMČR workflow uses.

Command-line pipeline or REST API container image (`ghcr.io/ufal/atrium-nlp-enrich-api`: `/enrich`, `/enrich_text`, background `/jobs`).

label: National Corpus of Irish / Corpas Náisiúnta na Gaeilge
description:
Corpas Náisiúnta na Gaeilge (CNG) is a balanced corpus of 100 million words, both written and spoken. All texts compiled for the corpus span the 2000-2024 period with the intention of being representative of contemporary Irish. It contains a large variety of genres, sources, and dialects, weighted in a way that avoids any one person, genre, or particular work having an excessive influence on the corpus as a whole. CNG will be used to investigate general questions of language, for example, how often a particular word or phrase is used, which preposition is most commonly used with a particular verb etc. Such questions often occur to us while learning, writing or translating and a search in CNG will provide reliable evidence that may lead to a satisfactory answer. Not only that, computer scientists can also process the corpus data in various ways to generate language models or make frequency lists.

---------------

Is corpas cothromaithe é Corpas Náisiúnta na Gaeilge (CNG) a bhfuil 100 milliún focal ann, idir ábhar scríofa agus ábhar labhartha. Baineann na téacsanna go léir a tiomsaíodh don chorpas leis an tréimhse 2000–2024 agus é i gceist go mbeadh sé ionadaíoch ar an nGaeilge chomhaimseartha.

Tá meascán mór seánraí, foinsí, agus canúintí in CNG agus iad ualaithe ar bhealach a sheachnaíonn róthionchar a bheith ag duine, seánra, nó saothar ar leith ar an gcorpas trí chéile. Úsáidfear CNG chun ceisteanna ginearálta teanga a fhiosrú, mar shampla, cé chomh minic is a úsáidtear focal nó frása áirithe, cén réamhfhocal is mó a úsáidtear le briathar áirithe etc. Is iomaí duine a ritheann ceisteanna den sórt sin leo agus iad ag foghlaim, ag scríobh nó ag aistriú agus cuirfidh cuardach in CNG fianaise iontaofa ar fáil dóibh a chabhródh leo freagra sásúil a aimsiú. Ní hamháin sin ach is féidir le ríomheolaithe na sonraí corpais a phróiseáil ar bhealaí éagsúla chun samhlacha teanga a ghiniúint nó chun liostaí minicíochta a dhéanamh.

relatedItems.label: An Bunachar Náisiúnta Téarmaíochta don Ghaeilge / The National Terminology Database for Irish
relatedItems.description:
The téarma.ie project
This is the national terminology database for Irish, managed by the Gaois research group in Fiontar & Scoil na Gaeilge (DCU) in partnership with the Terminology Committee, Foras na Gaeilge.

Around 186,000 bilingual entries are available in the database. They can be queried in various ways, and the material can also be downloaded in TBX or TXT format. If you don’t find the term you are looking for, you can use the query form to ask the Terminology Committee, Foras na Gaeilge, for advice.

The project has been running since 2004. The system is based on Terminologue, an open-source platform developed by Gaois for the National Terminology Database and as a resource for other projects. 

Tionscadal téarma.ie
Seo é an bunachar náisiúnta téarmaíochta don Ghaeilge, á bhainistiú ag grúpa taighde Gaois, Fiontar & Scoil na Gaeilge (DCU) i gcomhar leis an gCoiste Téarmaíochta, Foras na Gaeilge.

Tá c.186,000 iontráil dhátheangach ar fáil sa bhunachar. Is féidir dul i ngleic leis na téarmaí ar bhealaí éagsúla agus is féidir chomh maith an t-ábhar a íoslódáil i bhformáid TBX no TXT. Má tá téarma nach bhfuil ar fáil sa bhunachar seo á lorg agat, is féidir leagan a iarraidh ar an gCoiste Téarmaíochta, Foras na Gaeilge, ach an fhoirm fiosraithe a líonadh.

Táthar anois i mbun chéim VII den tionscadal seo (tionscadal atá ar bun ó 2004 i leith). Seoladh suíomh nua agus córas úrnua eagarthóireachta ar an 14 Márta 2019. Tá an córas seo bunaithe ar Terminologue, ardán foinse oscailte a d’fhorbair Gaois don Bhunachar Náisiúnta Téarmaíochta agus mar áis do thionscadail eile.

relatedItems.label: Foclóir.ie / Foclóirí ár linne
relatedItems.description:
Foclóirí ár linne, Foras na Gaeilge’s dictionary website contains both An Foclóir Nua Gaeilge [the new monolingual Irish Dictionary] (2025) and the New English-Irish Dictionary (2013-2017). 

Both dictionaries are available free of charge and have been adapted to work on both desktop computers and mobile devices. The universal search allows users to search both dictionaries at the same time.

If you are unable to find a word please also search: www.tearma.ie (if it’s a technical term) or else English-Irish Dictionary (1959). Both resources are linked to this record.

Project milestones
December 2025
The new monolingual Irish dictionary was launched. The first tranche of material comprised 20,000 entries and 40,000 senses.

September 2020
The print edition of the New English-Irish Dictionary, Concise English-Irish Dictionary, was published. The printed dictionary contains 30,000 entries and 85,000 word senses. 

January 2017
The online version of the New English-Irish Dictionary was completed. The total number of entries in the dictionary is 48,000 (140,000 senses).

October 2013
Online versions of de Bhaldraithe's English-Irish Dictionary (1959) and Ó Dónaill's Foclóir Gaeilge-Béarla (1977) launched, as well as a grammar database and a pronunciation database. (Access website: https://www.teanglann.ie/en/)

January 2013
The first version of the New English-Irish Dictionary launched, with over 7,000 headwords. This version covered approximately 70% of general English-language usage, and contained 30% of the eventual content in terms of word senses.

label: Nation, Genre & Gender
description:
Combining literary and data science expertise, Nation, Genre, Gender maps and analyses social networks in Irish and English fiction, 1800-1922. 

It explores how writers and readers have imagined the connections between people in their society and turned those connections into plots. The project, funded by the Irish Research Council, has completed work on 46 novels to date. The Nation, Genre & Gender project is a unique collaboration between researchers in literature and data analytics. The research team combines UCD’s strengths in cultural criticism and social network analysis, traditional humanities and new computational approaches, established and early stage researchers.

Nation, Genre & Gender: Data
As part of this project, we have manually annotated a corpus of 19th-20th century Irish and British novels. Sample data for three case study novels is provided on the website. A full downloadable corpus will follow in the second phase of the project.

Data Format
Each annotated novel contains the following data files and directories:

fulltext.txt: a single file containing a version of the novel text with manual annotations to aid character identification.
dictionary.txt: file containing list of all unique characters in the novel, along with their aliases.
stopwords.txt: file containing list of words/phrases which should not be identified as characters.
attributes.txt: file containing list of attributes for the characters in the novel.
notes.txt: notes regarding the edition and annotation process for the specific novel.
networks: directory containing the individual chapter and overall character networks for the novel, in GEXF format.

Downloads are available at: http://erdos.ucd.ie/nggproject/

Data for each of the three case study novels is provided in a separate ZIP archive:

>> Pride and Prejudice by Jane Austen
>> Phineas Finn by Anthony Trollope
>> A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man by James Joyce

This data emanating from the Nation, Genre, Gender SNA Project by Gerardine Meaney, Derek Greene, Karen Wade, Maria Mulvany, Siobhan Grayson, Jennie Rothwell is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International License. Permissions beyond the scope of this license may be available.

relatedItems.description:
Omeka is a content management system designed for the display of library, museum, archives, and scholarly collections and exhibitions.

Omeka falls at a crossroads of Web Content Management, Collections Management, and Archival Digital Collections Systems. Omeka is designed with non-IT specialists in mind, allowing users to focus on content and interpretation rather than programming. It brings Web 2.0 technologies and approaches to academic and cultural websites to foster user interaction and participation. It makes top-shelf design easy with a simple and flexible templating system. Its robust open-source developer and user communities underwrite Omeka's stability and sustainability.

Omeka allows users to publish cultural heritage objects, extend its functionality with themes and plugins, and curate online exhibits with digital objects.

description:
The NeDiMAH Methods Ontology (NeMO) is a comprehensive ontological model of scholarly practice in the arts and humanities, the development of which is undertaken through the ESF Research Network NeDiMAH.

NeMO is a CIDOC CRM - compliant ontology which explicitly addresses the interplay of factors of agency (actors and goals), process (activities and methods) and resources (information resources, tools, concepts) manifest in the scholarly process. It builds on the results of extensive empirical studies and modelling of scholarly practices performed by the Digital Curation Unit in projects DARIAH and EHRI.

NeMO incorporates existing relevant taxonomies of scholarly methods and tools, such as TaDIRAH, the arts-humanities.net and Oxford taxonomies of ICT methods, DHCommons, CCC-IULA-UPF and DiRT, through appropriate mappings of the concepts defined therein onto a semantic backbone of NeMO concepts. It thus enables combining documentary elements on scholarly practices of different perspectives and using different vocabularies.

The development of NeMO is an on-going project that greatly benefits from the discussions in related workshops and meetings and the generous intellectual contributions of participants. Interested individuals are invited to continue participating, and also to contribute comments through this site.

label: NLP enrichment of OCR text lines into TEITOK (UDPipe 2, NameTag 3)
description:
Adds linguistic annotation to text lines from ALTO post-processing (CSV or XLSX with a `text` column, or plain text). The lines go to the LINDAT UDPipe 2 service for tokens, lemmas, part-of-speech tags and syntax, and to NameTag 3 for named entities. The main output is TEITOK XML, a TEI-based format that keeps the annotation tied to the page layout when the ALTO files are supplied. CoNLL-U files, per-page entity tables, summary CSVs and the ATRIUM document record (JSON) are also written, with a paradata JSON log per run.

Optional keyword extraction per page or document uses YAKE (command-line default), KeyBERT (API default) or the legacy KER method. An optional LLM stage maps text onto the AMČR and TEATER vocabularies; the same engine is maintained as the separate tool atrium-llm-enrich, which the AMČR workflow uses.

Command-line pipeline or REST API container image (`ghcr.io/ufal/atrium-nlp-enrich-api`: `/enrich`, `/enrich_text`, background `/jobs`).

relatedItems.label: UDPipe: tool for lemmatization, morphological analysis, POS tagging and dependency parsing in multiple languages
relatedItems.description: UDPipe is a software tool and service that analyzes (plain) text in about 100 different natural languages up to the dependency syntax level. Users specify the desired function (tokenization, segmentation, morphological analysis, lemmatization, POS tagging, dependency parsing), output format, and input text (file(s)). The resulting analysis can be used to index and search documents by lemmas instead of multiple word forms, extract syntactic dependencies with POS information to get relations between words or lemmas, or get grammatical information for every word in the text. While in many cases the results can be used directly (statistical analysis on part of speech, lemmas and words), in many other applications the results of UDPipe serve as intermediate input to more sophisticated analysis, such as information extraction, knowledge representation, term extraction etc. UDPipe software allow to train on any language for which a treebank is available in the CoNLL-U format, such as all the Universal Dependencies corpora.

relatedItems.label: NameTag
relatedItems.description:
NameTag is an open-source tool for named entity recognition (NER). NameTag identifies proper names in text and classifies them into predefined categories, such as names of persons, locations, organizations, etc. NameTag 2 recognizes nested entities (embedded entities) of arbitrary depth.

For Czech, it recognizes a [complex hierarchy of categories](http://ufal.mff.cuni.cz/~strakova/cnec2.0/ne-type-hierarchy.pdf). The English model, which is trained on CoNLL-2003 NER annotations (Sang and De Meulder [2003](https://www.clarin.eu/resource-families/tools-named-entity-recognition#Sang%20and%20De%20Meulder%202003)), distinguishes the following four NER classes: person, organisation, location and miscellaneous.

The trained model for Czech is available for through LINDAT: [Czech Models (CNEC) for NameTag](http://hdl.handle.net/11858/00-097C-0000-0023-7D42-8).
A [user manual](http://ufal.mff.cuni.cz/nametag/users-manual) is also available.

relatedItems.label: ALTO XMLs post-processing and quality control (text lines categorization)
relatedItems.description:
Turns OCR output into clean, classified text lines. The pipeline splits documents into pages, builds page statistics tables, extracts text in reading order (LayoutReader by default; alto-tools, GLM-4v, JSON-key and plain-text readers as alternatives) and labels every line by language and OCR quality: Clear, Noisy, Trash, Non-text or Empty. The quality score combines structural detectors, perplexity (Qwen2.5-0.5B or distilgpt2) and character-level metrics; the language comes from FastText.

Input: ALTO XML, generic OCR JSON, or any text-bearing file (PDF, DOCX, TXT, HTML, TEI, PAGE XML and more). Output: per-line CSV tables, page statistics, plain text and the ATRIUM document record (JSON), with a paradata JSON log per run.

relatedItems.label: Semi-automated extraction of information from textual documents in a domain-specific repository
relatedItems.description:
The workflow addresses the **machine processing and enhancement of archaeological textual documents** (e.g., grey literature, excavation reports, field forms) held in a domain-specific repository. It processes both **scanned documents**, through automatic text recognition, and **born-digital documents** (PDF, DOCX) that already carry a text layer. The goal is an integrated solution for **legacy data and new uploads within the selected repository system**: better search and reuse of the documents, and fewer manual steps in archiving and annotation.

The workflow chains **independent tools available as services through APIs**. Each tool performs one step: page classification, OCR quality control, linguistic annotation and named entity recognition, keyword extraction against the domain vocabularies, and translation. Each tool can also be used on its own. The repository calls the services asynchronously and stores every result as an **alternative distribution of the original file**, with a **paradata** record describing the run that produced it (tool version, parameters, licence).

The results of all steps also accumulate in **one JSON record per document** (the ATRIUM document record). Its blocks each have one producing tool, so any step can be re-run alone. The record carries the provenance of every contribution, and the licence of the combined result is derived from the most restrictive licence among them. It can later be exported as an RO-Crate.

The enriched data support:

* full-text and faceted search by page types, named entities and vocabulary keywords,
* assessment of OCR quality before further processing,
* linking of documents to controlled vocabularies and to each other,
* international access through English translations of metadata and texts,
* corpora for natural language processing, including the training and evaluation of models.

The tools were developed in the [ATRIUM project](https://atrium-research.eu/) by the Institute of Formal and Applied Linguistics (Charles University) with the Institutes of Archaeology of the Czech Academy of Sciences in Prague and Brno. They are open source, published as container images, and are described in their own Marketplace records. Their integration into [Galaxy](https://galaxyproject.org/) is being prepared with DARIAH.

The [Archaeological Map of the Czech Republic (AMCR)](https://digiarchiv.aiscr.cz/) repository serves as the **demonstrator** of the workflow.

**Diagram caption**: *Users and data curators work with a data repository (AMCR) that stores each document with its metadata, original file, ALTO XML, document record, enrichments and paradata, and the AMCR vocabularies. A processing orchestration (step 2) passes documents between the repository, a separate automatic text recognition workflow (step 4) and the ATRIUM tool services: page classification (3), ALTO post-processing and quality control (5), NLP enrichment with UDPipe and NameTag to TEITOK (7), vocabulary keywords by LLM (8) and XML translation (10). A dashed born-digital branch (6) replaces steps 4 and 5. NLP enrichment and translation call the LINDAT services; the vocabularies feed keyword extraction and translation. Annotators and data engineers train a custom NameTag model (9). A discovery service (11) serves users and feeds the OAI-PMH and File API, which feeds the ARIADNE Portal.*

relatedItems.description:
Maps archival text onto controlled archaeological vocabularies with a large language model, and converts born-digital documents into the ATRIUM document record.

**Vocabulary keywords.** Each text line (CSV, TEITOK) or each passage of a whole document (TXT, Markdown) is tagged with a term from the AMČR heslář and the TEATER thesaurus, with Czech and English keywords and a confidence score. The answer is held to the vocabulary: the term list becomes the enum of a JSON schema, decoding follows that schema where the backend supports it, and a category that is not in the vocabulary is dropped, not guessed.

**Born-digital conversion.** PDF and DOCX files with a usable text layer become the document record (JSON) without OCR.

Models run locally (transformers or vLLM, one or more GPUs) or through OpenRouter or Ollama. Every enrichment run writes a paradata JSON log. Command-line tools and container images, including a REST API (`ghcr.io/ufal/atrium-llm-enrich-api`).

relatedItems.label: NoSketch Engine Docker
relatedItems.description:
Sketch Engine is a corpus analysis and query system popular with linguists and lexicographers, which allows computer-assisted linguistic examinations on loaded text corpora. Two versions are available:
1. A full-fledged version of Sketch Engine running in the cloud with preloaded corpora. A proprietary service and can be used for a fee on a [subscription basis](https://www.sketchengine.eu/price-list/#academic) and can be tried for free with limited features for a limited time at [this link](https://www.sketchengine.eu/price-list/#free-trial).
2. [The NoSketch Engine, an open-source version](https://nlp.fi.muni.cz/trac/noske/wiki/WikiStart) that can be installed on your own machine, with no preloaded corpora, but need expert level technical skills to install and operate.

[The Department of Digital Humanities of Eötvös Loránd University](https://elte-dh.hu/en/) runs its copy of NoSketch Engine, into which they have loaded the corpora they have used and created (for more information see the list of corpora in system). The loaded corpora are not available at [Sketch Engine](www.sketchengine.eu), however, they are available free of charge to citizens of Hungarian and foreign institutions with eduID. The loaded corpora can only be used indirectly for non-profit scientific purposes!

To facilitate the on-premises usage, [an unofficial Docker image](https://github.com/ELTE-DH/NoSketch-Engine-Docker) is also developed by the Department of Digital Humanities of Eötvös Loránd University, with the same features they use in their service (https://sketchengine.elte-dh.hu/). With this containerised version the installation and operation requirements are significantly reduced. The detailed guide and examples make the setup a bliss. As the installation is reduced to issuing a few commands. The format also allows customisation and creation of downstream variants, but that needs a more in-depth technical expertise.

The most important feature of the NoSketch Engine is the concordance search. Concordance-based searching allows you to search for words, phrases, tags, documents, text types or corpus structures in loaded corpora to display each result with their context underneath each other, i.e. as concordances. The search can be fine-tuned in several ways and the resulting concordance that is displayed can be varied (e.g. sorted, filtered, aggregated) and exported as standard formats for further processing. The precise definition of search conditions is essential because, in the case of large corpora, a search may produce a large number of results which cannot be handled manually.
The most precise way to fine-tune the queries is the Corpus Query Language (CQL), a special format language designed specifically for Sketch Engine queries. CQL can be used to search for complex grammatical and lexical patterns while allowing to supply conditions that cannot be directly set on the basic user interface of the service. 

Within the CQL queries, one can use standard regular expressions to define fuzzy character sequences, while CQL can set constraints on tokens. The classic wildcard characters (which are a subset of the regular expression syntax) can also be used within the CQL query expressions. These options offer many extras compared to the basic search. A detailed guide on the syntax is available at: https://www.sketchengine.eu/documentation/cql-basics/

relatedItems.label: Sketch Engine
relatedItems.description: Sketch Engine is a tool to explore how language works. Its algorithms analyze authentic texts of billions of words (text corpora) to identify instantly what is typical in language and what is rare, unusual or emerging usage. It is also designed for text analysis or text mining applications.Sketch Engine is used by linguists, lexicographers, translators, students and teachers. It is a first choice solution for publishers, universities, translation agencies and national language institutes throughout the world.Sketch Engine contains 500 ready-to-use corpora in 90+ languages, each having a size of up to 30 billion words to provide a truly representative sample of language.Some of its functions are: word sketch, sketch difference, thesaurus, concordance, parallel concordance, wordlist, n-grams, keywords \& terms, bilingual term extractiontrends and OneClick Dictionary.

relatedItems.label: tg-model - TextGrid Import Modeller
relatedItems.description:
Whats the aim?
This project focuses on attemps for a simple import of text corpora (encoded in XML/TEI) to TextGrid Repository by modeling the required metadata file structure.

To generate the TextGrid metadata files, the tool tg-model was developed, which can be used as a Python library and on the command line. The metadata files are important for good searchability and presentation of the imported data. The more detailed and precise the metadata in these files is, the better the data can be found in the portal and search results can be faceted. Typically, TEI files already contain metadata in the teiHeader element. These can be used for the content of the metadata files. However, since TEI allows many ways to mark the same information, the automated mapping of TEI metadata to the corresponding TextGrid metadata presents a challenge. The tg-model tool supports this task in several ways: In the first step, configuration files are generated that contain settings for the TextGrid metadata and indicate what values they have or where they can be found in the teiHeader (specified as an XPath expression). As far as the same information is found in the same place in the teiHeader in several files in a corpus, the corresponding XPath expression is written into the configuration files. The configuration files can then be adjusted. Subsequently, based on the configuration files and the input data, the metadata files are generated. Now everything necessary is available to import data into TextGridRep.

relatedItems.label: tgadmin - TextGrid repository administration cli tool, based on tgclients
relatedItems.description:
What is the aim?
A command line tool for managing your projects in the TextGrid repository without TextGridLab.

The actual data import is finally carried out by the Python tools tgadmin and tgclients, which in turn communicate with the TextGrid backend via the various TextGridRep APIs. Altogether, this forms the foundation for the new, simple way to comfortably import and ultimately publish data in TextGridRep. The tools, libraries, and also the TextGridRep API were expanded and revised on the occasion of the Code Sprint.

relatedItems.label: The TextGrid Repository Documentation
relatedItems.description:
The TextGrid Repository is a long-term archive for humanities research data. It provides an extensive, searchable, and reusable repository of texts and images. Aligned with the principles of Open Access and FAIR, the TextGrid Repository was awarded the CoreTrustSeal in 2020. For researchers, the TextGrid Repository offers a sustainable, durable, and secure way to publish their research data in a citable manner and to describe it in an understandable way through required metadata. Read more about sustainability, FAIR and Open Access in the Mission Statement of the TextGrid Repository.

On this site you can find information on organizational infrastructure, data policies, and digital object management of the DARIAH-DE Repository, user guides and public APIs are documented as well. They provide information on access, import, dissemination, and resolving. You can find more information about the TextGrid Repository on the TextGrid Website.

relatedItems.description:
New research methods have caused exponential growth in the creation of research data, requiring new approaches to data curation in the humanities. IT-based research techniques and collaborative
ways of working with data sets require secure and flexible research infrastructures. The TextGrid Repository, as part of the TextGrid Virtual Research Environment, enables researchers to publish and
share their data in ways that support long-term availability and re-use

relatedItems.label: TextGrid - Import Workflow for Data aka The Fluffy Import
relatedItems.description:
How do I import textual research data in the TextGrid Repository?

Researchers repeatedly articulate their need for well-usable tools and infrastructures for the easy creation and publication of text-based research data. This also applies to Text+ and is exemplified by the Text+ User Stories. The partners involved in Text+, including SUB Göttingen, GWDG, and TU Dresden, contribute to this—for example, with the new developments tested at the 2024 Code Sprint for Humanities Data.

Thanks to its extensive, searchable, and reusable collection of texts and images, TextGridRep is an important and relevant repository for humanities research data.

For researchers, it offers a sustainable, permanent, and secure means of citable publication of their research data and a clear description of the same through necessary and extended metadata so that the publication in TextGridRep can be presented and reused. Results were achieved on various levels, which were presented and used on the occasion of the Code Sprint. TextGridRep was further developed in terms of authentication, the presentation of unpublished projects, and data intake. A new tool was developed for generating the required TextGrid metadata files, which detects the metadata in the teiHeader elements of the input files and also allows the manual setting of values and rules for their discovery. A web-based tool enabling convenient workflow operation was implemented as a Jupyter Notebook. For easy use of this tool, the Text+ JupyterHub is available. It was also adapted on this occasion so that the mentioned tools are already installed and can be used without further ado.

This workflow describes the new fluffy import in the TextGrid Repository.

relatedItems.label: TextGrid Repository & Laboratory
relatedItems.description:
TextGrid is a virtual research environment for text-based humanities scholarship. It offers a variety of tools and services for collaboratively creating, analyzing, editing, and publishing texts. The TextGrid environment is split into two components, the Laboratory housing the tools and services, and the Repository for preserving reserach data and making it available to other scholars.

The [TextGrid Laboratory](https://textgrid.de/werkzeuge/) : Open source tools and services support Humanities scholars during the entire process of research, especially in digital scholarly editing.

The [TextGrid Repository](https://textgridrep.org/?lang=en) : The long-term research data archive offers safe storing, publishing and researching versatile digital material (XML/TEI formatted text and images), e.g., in the Digital Library of TextGrid. Certified with the Core Trust Seal.

The TextGrid Community: An online help, tutorials, mailing lists, a bug tracker and the source code enable users and developers to quickly start working with TextGrid.

This resource is supported by Text+. In case of questions you may get in touch with the Text+ helpdesk at textplus-support@gwdg.de.

concept.label: ASCII
concept.definition: ASCII abbreviated from American Standard Code for Information Interchange, is a character encoding standard for electronic communication. ASCII codes represent text in computers, telecommunications equipment, and other devices. Most modern character-encoding schemes are based on ASCII, although they support many additional characters. ASCII is the traditional name for the encoding system.

concept.label: ALTO-XML
concept.definition: ALTO (Analyzed Layout and Text Object) is an open XML Schema developed by the EU-funded project called METAe. The standard was initially developed for the description of text OCR and layout information of pages for digitized material. The goal was to describe the layout and text in a form to be able to reconstruct the original appearance based on the digitized information - similar to the approach of a lossless image saving operation. ALTO is often used in combination with Metadata Encoding and Transmission Standard (METS) for the description of the whole digitized object and creation of references across the ALTO files, e.g. reading sequence description.

concept.label: JPEG
concept.definition: JPEG ( JAY-peg) is a commonly used method of lossy compression for digital images, particularly for those images produced by digital photography. The degree of compression can be adjusted, allowing a selectable tradeoff between storage size and image quality. JPEG typically achieves 10:1 compression with little perceptible loss in image quality. JPEG compression is used in a number of image file formats. JPEG/Exif is the most common image format used by digital cameras and other photographic image capture devices; along with JPEG/JFIF, it is the most common format for storing and transmitting photographic images on the World Wide Web. These format variations are often not distinguished, and are simply called JPEG. The term "JPEG" is an initialism/acronym for the Joint Photographic Experts Group, which created the standard. The MIME media type for JPEG is image/jpeg, except in older Internet Explorer versions, which provides a MIME type of image/pjpeg when uploading JPEG images. JPEG files usually have a filename extension of .jpg or .jpeg. JPEG/JFIF supports a maximum image size of 65,53565,535 pixels, hence up to 4 gigapixels for an aspect ratio of 1:1.

concept.label: PNG
concept.definition: Portable Network Graphics (PNG, pronounced PEE-en-JEE or PING) is a raster graphics file format that supports lossless data compression. PNG was created as an improved, non-patented replacement for Graphics Interchange Format (GIF), and is the most widely used lossless image compression format on the Internet. PNG supports palette-based images (with palettes of 24-bit RGB or 32-bit RGBA colors), grayscale images (with or without alpha channel for transparency), and full-color non-palette-based RGB/RGBA images (with or without alpha channel). PNG was designed for transferring images on the Internet, not for professional-quality print graphics, and therefore does not support non-RGB color spaces such as CMYK. A PNG file contains a single image in an extensible structure of "chunks", encoding the basic pixels and other information such as textual comments and integrity checks documented in RFC 2083. PNG files nearly always use file extension PNG or png and are assigned MIME media type image/png. PNG was published as informational RFC 2083 in March 1997 and as an ISO/IEC standard in 2004.

concept.label: TIFF
concept.definition: Tagged Image File Format, abbreviated TIFF or TIF, is a computer file format for storing raster graphics images, popular among graphic artists, the publishing industry, and photographers. TIFF is widely supported by scanning, faxing, word processing, optical character recognition, image manipulation, desktop publishing, and page-layout applications. The format was created by Aldus Corporation for use in desktop publishing. It published the latest version 6.0 in 1992, subsequently updated with an Adobe Systems copyright after the latter acquired Aldus in 1994. Several Aldus or Adobe technical notes have been published with minor extensions to the format, and several specifications have been based on TIFF 6.0, including TIFF/EP (ISO 12234-2), TIFF/IT (ISO 12639), TIFF-F (RFC 2306) and TIFF-FX (RFC 3949).

concept.label: XML
concept.definition: Extensible Markup Language (XML) is a markup language that defines a set of rules for encoding documents in a format that is both human-readable and machine-readable.

concept.label: hOCR
concept.definition: hOCR is an open standard for representing document layout analysis and OCR results as a subset of HTML. The goal is to reuse as much existing technology as possible, and to arrive at a representation that makes it easy to store, share, process and display OCR results. This specification defines many features that can represent a variety of OCR-related information. However, being built on top of HTML, hOCR is designed to make it easy to start simple and gradually use more complex constructs when necessary. Consider you have an HTML document that encodes a book: Wrapping page elements in <div class="ocr_page"> tags will convey the page boundaries to hOCR-capable agents and turn the HTML document into an hOCR document.

It is a Java application that reads a formatting object (FO) tree and renders the resulting pages to a specified output. Output formats currently supported include PDF, PS, PCL, AFP, XML (area tree representation), Print, AWT and PNG, and to a lesser extent, RTF and TXT. The primary output target is PDF

relatedItems.label: Transcribe and process the interview
relatedItems.description:
Produce a transcription of the recorded interview in order to enable analysis, indexing, and long-term accessibility. Transcription constitutes a key stage in the enrichment of the oral source, transforming an audio or audiovisual document into a textual resource that can be searched, annotated, and reused.

Define the level of transcription according to the objectives of the research. This may range from verbatim transcription (including hesitations, pauses, and non-verbal elements) to a more edited version that improves readability while preserving the meaning of the discourse. Where relevant, adopt established transcription conventions and ensure consistency across the corpus.

If required, integrate time-coding to align the transcription with the original recording, facilitating navigation between text and audio/video. Consider also the need for translation, particularly in multilingual research contexts.

During transcription, pay attention to the treatment of personal data and sensitive information. Anonymisation or pseudonymisation may be necessary, especially when preparing the material for dissemination or public access. Any modifications should be documented to ensure transparency and reproducibility.

The transcription should be treated as a distinct but related document within the oral source corpus. It must therefore be documented through a dedicated record, including its relationship to the original recording, the tools and methods used, and the identity of the transcriber.

This step may be carried out prior to, or in parallel with, the description and metadata creation phase, depending on the research design and available resources. In all cases, it significantly enhances the findability, accessibility, and reusability of the oral source in line with FAIR principles.

label: ODISSEI Knowledge Graph
description:
We aim to better support data- and computational-intensive research in the social sciences and humanities (SSH). One way to do so is by collecting which SSH research outputs are available so researchers can easily find what is relevant, and if they find something, assess to what extent it fits their needs.
Traditionally, the focus has been on books and articles as the main research output types, but in data-centric and computational approaches, researchers also are interested in which datasets are available, background material such as code books and question banks that help to better interpret these datasets, research software that has been used to analyse the data, information on the researchers involved and their institutes, etc. Making sure that all these research outputs are findable and reusable for others while giving their creators the credits they deserve is one of the key aspects of Open Science and FAIR data.

relatedItems.label: spaCy
relatedItems.description: spaCy is an open-source software library for advanced natural language processing, written in the programming languages Python and Cython. The library is published under the MIT license and currently offers statistical neural network models for English, German, Spanish, Portuguese, French, Italian, Dutch and multi-language NER, as well as tokenization for various other languages. Unlike NLTK, which is widely used for teaching and research, spaCy focuses on providing software for production usage. As of version 1.0, spaCy also supports deep learning workflows that allow connecting statistical models trained by popular machine learning libraries like TensorFlow, Keras, Scikit-learn or PyTorch. spaCy's machine learning library, Thinc, is also available as a separate open-source Python library. It features convolutional neural network models for part-of-speech tagging, dependency parsing and named entity recognition, as well as API improvements around training and updating models, and constructing custom processing pipelines.

Gemma is a family of open models built by Google DeepMind. Gemma 4 models are multimodal, handling text and image input and generating text output.

Gemma 4 introduces key capability and architectural advancements:

Reasoning – All models in the family are designed as highly capable reasoners, with configurable thinking modes.
Extended Multimodalities – Processes Text, Image with variable aspect ratio and resolution support (all models)
Diverse & Efficient Architectures – Offers Dense and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) variants of different sizes for scalable deployment.
Optimized for On-Device – Smaller models are specifically designed for efficient local execution on laptops and mobile devices.
Increased Context Window – The small models feature a 128K context window, while the medium models support 256K.

label: Omeka
description:
Omeka is a content management system designed for the display of library, museum, archives, and scholarly collections and exhibitions.

Omeka falls at a crossroads of Web Content Management, Collections Management, and Archival Digital Collections Systems. Omeka is designed with non-IT specialists in mind, allowing users to focus on content and interpretation rather than programming. It brings Web 2.0 technologies and approaches to academic and cultural websites to foster user interaction and participation. It makes top-shelf design easy with a simple and flexible templating system. Its robust open-source developer and user communities underwrite Omeka's stability and sustainability.

Omeka allows users to publish cultural heritage objects, extend its functionality with themes and plugins, and curate online exhibits with digital objects.

concept.label: JPEG
concept.definition: JPEG ( JAY-peg) is a commonly used method of lossy compression for digital images, particularly for those images produced by digital photography. The degree of compression can be adjusted, allowing a selectable tradeoff between storage size and image quality. JPEG typically achieves 10:1 compression with little perceptible loss in image quality. JPEG compression is used in a number of image file formats. JPEG/Exif is the most common image format used by digital cameras and other photographic image capture devices; along with JPEG/JFIF, it is the most common format for storing and transmitting photographic images on the World Wide Web. These format variations are often not distinguished, and are simply called JPEG. The term "JPEG" is an initialism/acronym for the Joint Photographic Experts Group, which created the standard. The MIME media type for JPEG is image/jpeg, except in older Internet Explorer versions, which provides a MIME type of image/pjpeg when uploading JPEG images. JPEG files usually have a filename extension of .jpg or .jpeg. JPEG/JFIF supports a maximum image size of 65,53565,535 pixels, hence up to 4 gigapixels for an aspect ratio of 1:1.

The term "MEI", like "TEI", describes the governing organization and the markup language.

relatedItems.label: Automatic Transcription of Oral Sources
relatedItems.description:
This workflow guides you through the automatic transcription of oral source recordings in SSH research contexts. It covers the full pipeline: audio preparation, model selection and configuration, transcription, speaker diarisation, quality control, manual post-correction, and the export of timestamped, structured transcripts suitable for archival deposit and open publication.
The central tool is Whisper, a multilingual, open-source automatic speech recognition (ASR) model developed by OpenAI and released under the MIT licence. The workflow also integrates complementary tools for audio preprocessing (Audacity, FFmpeg), enhanced transcription (WhisperX, faster-whisper), annotation (ELAN), and text encoding (TEI-XML). It applies equally to newly recorded interviews and to the retrospective transcription of archival holdings.

relatedItems.label: Select and configure the ASR tool
Transcribe and process the interview
relatedItems.description:
Produce a transcription of the recorded interview in order to enable analysis, indexing, and long-term accessibility. Transcription constitutes a key stage in the enrichment of the oral source, transforming an audio or audiovisual document into a textual resource that can be searched, annotated, and reused.

Define the level of transcription according to the objectives of the research. This may range from verbatim transcription (including hesitations, pauses, and non-verbal elements) to a more edited version that improves readability while preserving the meaning of the discourse. Where relevant, adopt established transcription conventions and ensure consistency across the corpus.

If required, integrate time-coding to align the transcription with the original recording, facilitating navigation between text and audio/video. Consider also the need for translation, particularly in multilingual research contexts.

During transcription, pay attention to the treatment of personal data and sensitive information. Anonymisation or pseudonymisation may be necessary, especially when preparing the material for dissemination or public access. Any modifications should be documented to ensure transparency and reproducibility.

The transcription should be treated as a distinct but related document within the oral source corpus. It must therefore be documented through a dedicated record, including its relationship to the original recording, the tools and methods used, and the identity of the transcriber.

This step may be carried out prior to, or in parallel with, the description and metadata creation phase, depending on the research design and available resources. In all cases, it significantly enhances the findability, accessibility, and reusability of the oral source in line with FAIR principles.

label: OpenArchaeo - Semantic web plateform for archaeological data
description:
MASA (Mémoire des Archéologues et des Sites Archéologiques), a consortium of the TGIR Huma-Num, in partnership with the SPARNA company, specialized in semantic web, and the Laboratoire d’Informatique Fondamentale et Appliquée de Tours (LIFAT), has developed the OpenArchaeo semantic web platform. Exploiting the archaeological triplestores paired with the CIDOC in a federated way, OpenArchaeo has been designed with two distinct interfaces.
The Explorer, resolutely user-friendly, is based on a system of icons and concepts well understood by archaeologists (Stratigraphic Unit, Artifact, Feature, Site...). In order to produce a SPARQL query from the natural language, OpenArchaeo has been the subject of the development of the SPARNATURAL component, which is modular and reusable. This system enables to generate a SPARQL query intuitively, without knowledge of the SPARQL language, but with knowledge of the main concepts of archaeology.
The SPARQL endpoint is a query service to write federated queries to multiple sources in SPARQL language (query language dedicated to the semantic web). This interface is associated with web services to exploit the MASA Triplestore. Its purpose is to be operated by machines and is therefore more accessible to computer specialists.

relatedItems.label: SHACL (Shapes Constraint Language)
relatedItems.description:
The Shapes Constraint Language (SHACL) is a widely-supported W3C standard that lets us describe conditions that a dataset must meet. As with RDFS schemas and OWL ontologies, SHACL contains metadata about datasets, but this metadata serves a different purpose: to help validate the data instead of enabling inferencing.

Because RDFS schemas and OWL ontologies describe a dataset’s structure by listing classes, properties, and their relationships, many people have thought that these were describing a schema the same way the schema of a relational database or an object-oriented system does — by describing constraints that data must conform to if it will be used in that dataset.

But, they do not. RDFS schemas and OWL ontologies describe these structures to enable inferencing. For example, if an RDFS schema says that the familyName property has a domain of Person, then we can infer that any resource with a familyName property is an instance of the class Person. Neither RDFS nor OWL give you a way to say that familyName is a required property of Person, so that if an instance of Person lacks a familyName value then it is an invalid instance.

This is where SHACL comes in. If you want to say that familyName is a required property for the Person class, or that a Review class’s rating value must be an integer value between 1 and 5, then SHACL lets you do this. This makes SHACL invaluable for ensuring data quality when you manage your RDF knowledge graph using a tool that supports SHACL such as GraphDB.

[from:https://www.ontotext.com/knowledgehub/fundamentals/what-is-shacl/]

relatedItems.label: CIDOC-CRM
relatedItems.description: The "CIDOC object-oriented Conceptual Reference Model" (CRM), was developed by the ICOM/CIDOC Documentation Standards Group. Since September 2000, the CIDOC CRM is being developed into an ISO standard in a joined effort of the CIDOC CRM SIG and ISO/TC46/SC4/WG9. Since September 2006 it has been accepted as ISO 21127. The CIDOC CRM represents an 'ontology' for cultural heritage information i.e. it describes in a formal language the explicit and implicit concepts and relations relevant to the documentation of cultural heritage. The primary role of the CIDOC CRM is to serve as a basis for mediation of cultural heritage information and thereby provide the semantic 'glue' needed to transform today's disparate, localised information sources into a coherent and valuable global resource. The CIDOC CRM is intended to promote a shared understanding of cultural heritage information by providing a common and extensible semantic framework that any cultural heritage information can be mapped to. It is intended to be a common language for domain experts and implementers to formulate requirements for information systems and to serve as a guide for good practice of conceptual modelling. In this way, it can provide the "semantic glue" needed to mediate between different sources of cultural heritage information, such as that published by museums, libraries and archives.

relatedItems.label: Define and implement software solutions for data processing and access
relatedItems.description:
There are two main software options that support processing of a literary bibliography and they depend on whether a literary bibliography is being created fully automatically or the workflow includes manual creation of entries.
In the first scenario a software for discovery service is needed which does not need to have support for manual creation of entries (e.g. Vufind). It allows importing data into it and the user gets access to the data through a search engine, faceted browsing etc. These kinds of software solutions usually allow for machine access to data (e.g. OAI-PMH, Z39.50, API). For small scale projects solutions like Zotero or even spreadsheets might be of use.
The second scenario demands a software solution that supports manual creation of records and this could be an integrated solution. There is a number of Integrated Library Systems (ILS) on the market available under various business models or one can use open source solutions such as Koha or Folio.  More universal systems such as Wikibase create another option. Finally custom-made solutions are also prevalent, but building such a system from scratch is demanding and comes with sustainability challenges.

relatedItems.label: Develop relationships with existing initiatives and ensure discoverability
relatedItems.description:
When your service is more defined and operating then more collaboration options open up. It is recommended for a literary bibliography to seek collaborations with research infrastructures on national (e.g. DARIAH ERIC nodes, OPERAS nodes), international (DARIAH, e.g. DARIAH Bibliographical Data WG, OPERAS, etc.) and disciplinary levels (literary researchers associations, other infrastructures e.g. CLS etc.). 
Services like literary bibliographies should be presented and discussed both on disciplinary events (conferences, workshops), but also on digital humanities and scholarly communication events. On many occasions poster sessions are a good way to present your tool. 
An operating service might also be an interesting resource for other parts of the research infrastructure ecosystem, e.g. metadata aggregators such as GoTriple or European Literary Bibliography. Making your data available through a protocol like OAI-PMH or API will allow other services to aggregate your data and reach wider audiences. Although, some service providers might also worry about the negative impact of such aggregation on the traffic on their platform. Reuse of your data by services can be, however, monitored if proper relationships with aggregators are established (e.g. allowing for access to some usage statistics).

relatedItems.description: Using well materialized Ground Control Points (GCPs) and using the same set in all the performed flights will require the use of topographic instruments only for the first acquisition, as once measured, the GCPs will be re-used for the subsequents flights. It is important to underline the importance of acquiring a trustworthy set of GCPs to be used for all the surveys, instead of measuring new GCPs every time. It is more important, in fact, not to acquire the most accurate GNSS data, but to use the most precise set of GCPs, assuming for (at least locally) the validity of the first data acquired, cause repeating measures over time may lead to non extremely precise co-registration of the generated models. Instruments required: Total station D-GNSS antenna Action to perform: Defining and measuring a topographic network Materialization of the topographical vertices Materialization of the control points Ground control points displacement around and inside the site Natural points selection and digitization for future surveys Control points measurement and recording (via Total station or GNSS receiver) Softwares to use: Topographic network compensation (e.g. MicroSurvey StarNet)

Hypotheses is a non-commercial blog portal for the humanities and social sciences. The portal provides a free service that facilitates scientific blogging and ensures greater visibility as well as archiving of content. The German branch of Hypotheses is provided by [OpenEdition](https://openedition.org/) in cooperation with the [Max Weber Foundation](https://www.maxweberstiftung.de/index.php?id=startseite). It contains contributions selected by the [community management](https://de.hypotheses.org/community-management) based at Max Weber Foundation. In a wider context, under the umbrella of OpenEdition [hypotheses.org](https://hypotheses.org/) publishes content in a wide range of languages. It is possible to browse the platform in the most commonly used languages on Hypotheses: French, German, Spanish and English.

The German branch of Hypotheses offers:
+ Technical assistance online via the [bloghaus](https://bloghaus.hypotheses.org/), by mail, as well as training offers.
+ Visibility of the posts on the homepage as well as via the social media channels of the portal
+ Archiving of content
+ Migration of already existing blogs

For further assistance please write to: blogs@maxweberstiftung.de

Check out some examples of community and research data infrastructure blogs: [Text+ Blog](https://textplus.hypotheses.org/) or [OPERAS-GER](https://operas-ger.hypotheses.org/)
