label: Participad
description:
Participad is a WordPress plugin that allows multiple people to edit the same WP content at the same time. Powered by Etherpad Lite, Participad gives you: notepads for collaborative notetaking; synchronous authoring of any content in the WordPress Dashboard; front-end editing. You can download it from the WordPress plugin repository.

Participad has three modules:

Dashboard -- The Dashboard module puts Etherpad editors into the WordPress Dashboard. Participad removes the "Visual" and "HTML" tabs from the standard WP editor, and replaces them with a "Participad" tab.

Frontend -- The Frontend module allows users to edit WordPress content from the front end of your website -- no Dashboard required. Participad modifies the Edit links on your posts and pages so that, instead of leading to the Dashboard, the static content of your post is swapped with an editable Etherpad window.

Notepad -- The Notepad module enables a new WordPress Post Type called Notepads. Notepads are collaborative note-taking documents, which can optionally be linked to existing static posts or pages. Participad provides several shortcodes and widgets that make it easy to create new Notepads from the front end of your website.

N.B. Participad requires a separate Etherpad Lite Installation.

label: ParZu - The Zurich Dependency Parser for German
description:
The Zurich Dependency Parser for German ParZu is a free software

ParZu is a dependency parser for German. This means that it analyzes the linguistic structure of sentences and, among other things, identifies the subject and object(s) of a verb.

It is a fork of Gerold Schneider's English Pro3Gres parser. Its architecture is hybrid and consists of both a hand-written grammar and a statistics module that returns the most likely analysis of a sentence. The primary difference to the English parser is the German grammar and statistics module. Architecturally, it is different in that it supports the use of morphological information, and does not use a chunker. ParZu also has a python wrapper that supports various input/output formats and multiprocessing.

label: PastMaps / Maps with the Past
description:
In 2011, Cartomatic launched the geoportal ‘Maps with the Past’, which presents mosaicked and georeferenced old maps, including topographic maps of the Polish Military Geographical Institute from the interwar period, Prussian and German maps from the 19th century, Prussian and German maps or old city maps. The materials were created by students of cartography at the Faculty of Geography and Regional Studies at the University of Warsaw as part of their internship at Cartomatic. Access to the maps was possible not only via the Geoportal, but also via the Web Map Service (WMS) geodata services. The interest in the data was great: it was not only used by scientists (archaeologists, geographers, historians), but also by anyone interested in geohistory.

In mid-2022, the geoportal was shut down for technical reasons, denying many people access to this extremely valuable and precious material. Shortly afterwards, the Department of Historical Atlases at the Institute of History of the Polish Academy of Sciences in Warsaw (ZAH) offered to take over the maintenance of the maps developed and made available by Cartomatic until then. Work began in August 2022 and the data was transferred to new servers and made available as WMS services by Warsaw University of Technology through CENAGIS infrastructure. A WebGIS application was then developed to access the maps. The application allows zooming in and out, enabling/disabling layers, changing transparency and searching for locations. To the maps provided by Cartomatic, ZAH staff have added others: the Gaul/Raczyński map (1:125 000, 1807-1812), the Schroetter map (1:150 000, 1796-1802), the Gilly map (1:150 000, 1802-1803) and the Chrzanowski map (1:300 000, 1859). It is planned to add further cartographic works to the services and applications.

relatedItems.label: Atlas Fontium
relatedItems.description:
“Atlas Fontium” is a website dedicated to the publications of historical sources, research results and sharing materials and data from the period of the old Poland and the old Republic of Poland that have a spatial dimension. The main purpose of the project is to create a uniform system for gathering, analysing, and making available of information and sources for research in the field of historical geography of Polish lands within borders prior to 1772. The results of historical and geographical research conducted in various scientific centres, in Poland and abroad, will be presented on an IT platform. The project is based on the framework of settlement network and territorial divisions, both church and secular, in the period before the Partitions. As such, its main aim is to present materials related with this period.

Technological development connected with the introduction of historical spatial databases and GIS tools to research offers interesting possibilities not only when we speak about the presentation of research results, but also for the entire field of editing of historical sources, written, cartographic, and iconographic. Geographic space is an excellent reference plane for the humanities, allowing scholars to integrate large stocks of information, as well as determining future collaborated syntheses of historical and social phenomena. The materials, as well as source information related to particular topics, are linked with a digital map, thus allowing for a statistical and spatial analysis, and a direct visualization of results on thematic maps.

Lafuente Ferrari Photographic Collection is part of the heritage of the Complutense University of Madrid Library and was donated by the distinguished professor to the Department of Art History of the Faculty of Fine Arts, which carefully guarded, studied, and preserved it for years. Since 2011, it has been housed in the Historical Library and consists of 11,545 glass plate slides belonging to the most famous photographic studios dedicated to the commercialization of slides of artistic reproductions for educational purposes in the late 19th century and the first third of the 20th century. In 2012, with the support of the Director General of Books, Archives, and Libraries of the Spanish Culture Ministry, the process of digitizing this photographic archive began. In its first phase, a total of 1,161 images were digitized, covering only 10% of the total and including collections from the studios Braun et Cie, Franz and Edgar Hanfstaengl, Lévy et ses Fils, Pestalozzi Educational View Institute, Dr. Franz Stoedtner, and several others, all of which are dedicated to artistic reproduction photography.
The Digital and Web Service of the Complutense Library has converted the original metadata (available in Cisne search engine in Marc21 format) into different interoperable vocabularies (tsv, txt, ods, xml) to make it available to the public

This description has been reviewed by the Historical Library of the UCM, where they are physically deposited. As for their digital version, they have been deposited in the portal Patrimonio Digital Complutense by the Digital and Web Service of the Complutense Library. This Service has carried out the conversion of the original metadata available in the Cisne search engine in Marc21 format to the different interoperable vocabularies to make them available to the public. relatedItems.label: Workflow to work with the PATRIMONIVM-Editor
relatedItems.description:
The PATRIMONIVM-Editor has been created by Alberto Dalla Rosa and Vincent Razanajao (https://patrimonium.huma-num.fr/atlas/editor/) to be a modular, customizable and integrated web application for the management of epigraphic corpora, based on the eXist-db platform. It creates TEI XML on the basis of EpiDoc, allowing the data to be used in digital editions. Based on our experiences with a customized version of the “eStudium. A virtual research environment for Historians” for the epigraphic project “Celtic Divine Names in Latin Inscriptions of the Military Zone in Germania Superior on the Left Bank of the River Rhine. Religious Phenomena in a Cultural Contact Zone“ (FWF funded project P 34422-G), this workflow will document the process both for the scientific, and probably non-tech savvy user, who is filling the editor with information, as well as for the user tasked with postprocessing the information available in the editor for the online publication.

For our first project “Celtic Divine Names in the Inscriptions of the Roman Province Germania Inferior. A Case Study on Religion in the Context of Cultural Contacts and Cultural Transfer” (FWF funded project P 29274-G25) we used single MC Word documents for every entry, which then were consolidated into a single MC Excel document for the conversion to XML by our partners at ZIM (Zentrum für Informationsmodellierung – Centre for Information Modelling) and the following online publication on GAMS (Geisteswissenschaftliches Asset Management System – Humanities’ Asset Management System; https://gams.uni-graz.at/context:fercan ; see picture 10). This method was redundant, cumbersome and prone to errors, especially with regard to required changes. With the PATRIMONIVM-Editor, these redundancies are removed and problems occurring during the postprocessing are easily identified, communicated and solved. (For the process of adapting the PATRIMONIVM-Editor, see either the GitHub documentation https://github.com/DigitalHumanitiesCraft/PatrimoniumEditorFercan/, or "Customizing the Patrimonium-Editor" on SSHOM)

relatedItems.label: Customizing the Patrimonium-Editor
relatedItems.description:
This document serves as a guide for customizing the Patrimonium Editor  using the example of the Fercan projects at the University of Graz, that study the Celtic divine names in roman inscriptions in antiquity (see also GitHub https://github.com/DigitalHumanitiesCraft/PatrimoniumEditorFercan/). These projects utilizes the Patrimonium Editor to collect and manage epigraphic data. Supported by the Austrian Science Fund (FWF) through grants. The first project “Celtic Divine Names in the Inscriptions of the Roman Province Germania Inferior. A Case Study on Religion in the Context of Cultural Contacts and Cultural Transfer” researched the Celtic divine names in the Roman provinces of Germania Inferior (P 29274-G25) and the second one “Celtic Divine Names in Latin Inscriptions of the Military Zone in Germania Superior on the Left Bank of the River Rhine. Religious Phenomena in a Cultural Contact Zone“ (P 34422-G) focused on the northern Germania Superior. These two projects examined how local Celtic traditions were integrated into Roman practices, using epigraphic evidence to trace changes and continuities in religious expression. The customization and application of the Patrimonium Editor was done during the second project and retroactively applied to the data management of the first project too.

The Patrimonium Editor is a web application suite designed for academic use, focusing on the encoding, management, and analysis of epigraphic and historical textual sources. It includes an XML editor for text encoding, conversion tools adhering to the Leiden Conventions, and data management capabilities for places, people, and thematic categories. Its modular architecture provides flexibility for customization and leverages the eXist-db XML database. The editor supports TEI (Text Encoding Initiative) and EpiDoc (Epigraphic Documents) guidelines, ensuring compatibility with international standards in digital humanities.

label: PDFAnnotations
description:
PDFAnnotations is a browser-based tool for extracting and reusing annotations from PDF documents. It is designed for researchers, students, and other readers who annotate academic papers, books, reports, or other research documents and need to move those annotations into their research and writing workflows.

The tool extracts highlights, comments, notes, underlines, strikeouts, and other PDF annotations, together with relevant metadata such as page numbers, authors, timestamps, and annotation colours. Users can filter and organise annotations before exporting them to Markdown, CSV, plain text, or JSON.

PDFAnnotations processes PDF files locally in the browser using WebAssembly, so the documents do not need to be uploaded to a server. This makes it suitable for workflows involving unpublished research materials, personal notes, and other documents where local processing is preferred.

The tool is particularly useful for literature review, close reading, research note-taking, and transferring information from annotated PDFs into knowledge-management or writing environments such as Markdown-based workflows, Obsidian, or Notion.

label: Performing Arts Thesaurus
description:
During its second phase (2024–2025), the THEATRALIA working group has developed a prototype of a multilingual thesaurus for the performing arts. Covering theatre, dance, performance, and circus arts, the thesaurus is for now available only in English, with future extensions planned in French, Spanish, Croatian, Portuguese and Indonesian. It provides a coherent conceptual framework to support the description, indexing, and interoperability of archival resources, foster multilingual database research, and promote the valorization of intangible cultural heritage. This prototype marks an exploratory step toward a shared, evolving tool, open to contributions from researchers and professionals.
The thesaurus in progress can be downloaded here: https://hal.science/halshs-05156229v1
The project is carried out within two international research initiatives: THEATRALIA, supported by DARIAH-EU, and PERFORMA, funded by the Institut des Amériques. For implementation, OpenTheso, was used, an open-source, RDF-compatible platform hosted by HumaNum, balancing usability and interoperability.
The initial corpus was built from online glossaries (American Association of Community Theatre, Theatre Development Fund) and printed dictionaries, mainly those by Patrice Pavis, which have been translated into several languages. After extraction and normalization, about 1,400 terms were integrated into OpenTheso, including around 100 entries with fully developed, context-specific definitions for performing arts archiving and research.

relatedItems.label: Construct and configure the text processing pipeline
relatedItems.description:
For maximum flexibility the text processing components have been developed as flexible, configurable and reusable [Python](https://www.python.org/) modules which can be combined within a [spaCy](https://spacy.io/) pipeline architecture to perform various tasks including text normalisation and vocabulary-driven concept recognition. The temporal components accommodate multilingual data, the vocabulary-driven components as described here use English language vocabularies.

Construction and configuration of pipelines is illustrated in a series of exemplar demonstrator [Jupyter notebooks](https://github.com/cbinding/rematch2) accompanying the source code, where more details of the configuration options are also present.

### Configuration

Much of the lower-level configuration is initialised with sensible defaults making the pipeline components usable ‘out of the box’, however as the components can be combined in various ways there are some choices to be made:

- Choose which controlled vocabularies to match on. This involves choosing from a set of pre-defined vocabulary-matching pipeline components. These include:
   - Facets of the [Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus (AAT)](https://www.getty.edu/research/tools/vocabularies/aat/)
      - [AAT Associated Concepts facet](http://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300264086)
      - [AAT Materials facet](http://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300264091)
      - [AAT Objects facet](http://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300264092)
      - [AAT Physical Attributes facet](http://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300264087)
      - [AAT Styles & Periods facet](http://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300264088)
   - Vocabularies originating from the [Forum on Information Standards in Heritage (FISH)](https://heritage-standards.org.uk/fish-vocabularies/)
      - [FISH Archaeological Objects thesaurus](http://purl.org/heritagedata/schemes/mda_obj)
      - [FISH Archaeological Sciences thesaurus](http://purl.org/heritagedata/schemes/560)
      - [FISH Building Materials thesaurus](http://purl.org/heritagedata/schemes/eh_tbm)
      - [FISH Components thesaurus](http://purl.org/heritagedata/schemes/eh_com)
      - [FISH Event Types thesaurus](http://purl.org/heritagedata/schemes/agl_et)
      - [FISH Evidence thesaurus](http://purl.org/heritagedata/schemes/eh_evd)
      - [FISH Maritime Craft Types thesaurus](http://purl.org/heritagedata/schemes/eh_tmc)
      - [FISH Monument Types thesaurus](http://purl.org/heritagedata/schemes/eh_tmt2)
      - [FISH Object Materials thesaurus](http://purl.org/heritagedata/schemes/73)
- Choose a [PeriodO](https://perio.do/) authority identifier. The pipeline component to identify named periods in the text utilises the (entire) PeriodO dataset. When configured with a valid PeriodO authority identifier (e.g. “p0xxt6t” - [Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA)](http://n2t.net/ark:/99152/p0xxt6t)), the component will identify matches within the text for any of the labels of periods contained in that specified authority. e.g. *Chalcolithic*, *Early Bronze Age*, *Antonine* etc.

- Choose whether to include tokenisation results in the output (default: false). The tokenisation is a key step in the NLP pipeline. The results of the tokenisation can be useful information in diagnosing and understanding how the NLP part of the pipeline has worked. However, these results can be large and detailed and are not required for the overall goal of the workflow, so you may optionally choose to omit them from the output (by default they will be omitted).

relatedItems.label: Configure and apply information extraction NLP pipeline
relatedItems.description: The next step creates and applies a [spaCy](https://spacy.io/) information extraction NLP pipeline to identify named periods and year spans within the body of the abstract text. The named periods originate from a chosen [PeriodO](https://perio.do/) authority. This workflow includes an exemplar source code demonstrator in the form of [a Jupyter notebook](https://github.com/cbinding/rematch2/blob/main/ATRIUM_T3_4_IE_gotriple_abstracts.ipynb), and the techniques are described more fully in the workflow *Vocabulary-driven Information Extraction*.

relatedItems.label: Vocabulary-driven Information Extraction
relatedItems.description:
This workflow concerns information extraction from textual documents with the aim of enriching existing subject indexing with Linked Open Data (LOD) identifiers for concepts drawn from published controlled vocabularies (such as thesauri) specific to the domain. The overall goal is to improve findability and interoperability in accordance with FAIR principles. 

The primary use-case (in the context of the ATRIUM project) is to suggest enrichments for the subject indexing of English language reports and journal articles describing archaeological investigations and interventions, as supplied by ATRIUM partner Archaeology Data Service (ADS). The workflow accommodates structured text inputs and PDF documents (provided textual data can be extracted). Jupyter notebook demonstrators illustrate the application of the tools developed.

Importing, transforming, storing and indexing data should be easy.

Catmandu is a command line tool to access and convert data from your digital library, research services or any other open data sets. Combine Catmandu modules with web application frameworks such as PSGI/Plack, document stores such as MongoDB and full text indexes such as Solr to create a rapid development environment for digital library services such as institutional repositories and search engines.

label: Persistent Identifier Service
description:
In all aspects of research, the amount of digitally stored data is increasing continuously. Thereby the management will be more and more complex, so that the sustainable reference to data and thus their permanent censibility represent a challenge. By a persistent identifier taking a mediator role, references, for example in scientific publications, can remain stable, even if the location of the data changes.

With our persistent identifier services you have the possibility to generate PIDs for your research results (data, texts, images, etc.) or to receive institutional prefixes that make all generated PIDs recognisable as belonging to your institution. You can create and maintain PIDs via GUI or REST interface. We operate a local resolver to resolve the PID and, as a partner of the ePIC consortium, give access to at least two mirror resolvers within Europe to guarantee the resolvability of the PID with high availability. If your PID holds the metadata required by DataCite, a DOI can be derived from it.
We offer quick and easy access to the creation of individual PIDs in our self-service area. There you have the possibility to create and edit PIDs via the browser and to output a list of your PIDs. If you need a larger number of PIDs or would like to integrate the generation into your application, you can contact [us](support@de.dariah.eu).

This resource is supported by Text+. In case of questions you may get in touch with the Text+ helpdesk at textplus-support@gwdg.de.

relatedItems.label: Provide a suggested citation for the dataset so reusers are aware of how to cite it
relatedItems.description:
**Why**
A suggestion for the citation promotes access and reusability of data as well as helps reusers to properly cite the dataset, for example in the bibliographies of their publications. This gives credit, recognition and visibility to, for example, the culture heritage institution providing the dataset. 

**How**
For example, the National Library of Scotland’s Data Foundry provides a “Cite the data” section for each of its datasets, as well as a suggested citation, e.g. “Suggested citation: National Library of Scotland. A Medical History of British India. National Library of Scotland, 2019. [https://doi.org/10.34812/2w0t-3f08](https://doi.org/10.34812/2w0t-3f08)”. 
In addition, the National Library of the Netherlands provides a suggested citation: “When using this dataset we ask you to cite it as follows: Andreas van Cranenburgh, Sara Veldhoen, Michel De Gruijter (2022). Textual features and metadata for DBNL novels 1800-2000 [Data set]. Zenodo. [https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5786254](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5786254).” 
Ideally this data citation includes a Persistent Identifier, such as a DOI, ARK, Handle, etc.

label: Personal Data Repository (PDR)
description:
Repository for managing, integrating and linking scholarly biographical and personal data.

The Personal Data Repository (PDR) is a research infrastructure for the management, storage and integration of scholarly biographical information. It enables research projects to maintain individual workspaces on a shared platform while linking data from different research contexts. The repository is designed to support heterogeneous personal data by using a flexible semantic data model in which persons are represented through collections of referenced statements rather than fixed records. The PDR interacts with the Archive Editor for data creation and editing and provides additional tools for structuring, enriching and publishing personal data. The infrastructure is operated by the Berlin-Brandenburg Academy of Sciences and Humanities (BBAW) and supports collaborative research on historical and biographical data.

Further information about the service is available on the DARIAH-DE Personal Data Repository page:
https://de.dariah.eu/en/web/guest/personendatenrepositorium

Technical documentation and user information are available in the Personal Data Repository Wiki:
https://pdrprod.bbaw.de/wiki/doku.php?id=de:start

relatedItems.label: DARIAH-DE Collection Registry
DARIAH-DE Generic Search
relatedItems.description:
Search engine that allows to search in the metadata records of the [Collection Registry](https://colreg.de.dariah.eu/colreg/?lang=en)

The [Generic Search](https://search.de.dariah.eu/search/?lang=en) creates a comprehensive search facility in DARIAH-DE. For this purpose, the individual metadata records of the collections described in the Collection Registry are combined. The Generic Search is available free and without registration.

With the myCollections function, users can create their own individual selection of these collections and save them permanently. This allows researches in a precisely defined environment. An "own" search engine created this way can be shared with other users.

The Generic Search combines the features of breadth-first and depth-first search so that a dynamic adaptation of the search - e.g. in regards to a faceting - but also the application of different visualization techniques becomes possible. The Generic Search allows a detailed examination of the considered data (depth-first search). With a growing number of included collections, the granularity of the consideration and the faceting of the search can be reduced and assume the form of a breadth-first search.

Click [here](https://search.de.dariah.eu/search/?lang=en) to go to the Generic Search 

Are there still unresolved issues or would you like further information? You can reach us at info@de.dariah.eu.

This resource is supported by Text+. In case of questions you may get in touch with the Text+ helpdesk at textplus-support@gwdg.de.

relatedItems.label: DARIAH-DE Repository
relatedItems.description:
The DARIAH-DE Repository is a central component of the DARIAH-DE research data federation architecture. The DFA aggregates various services and, thus, ensures a convenient use. The repository makes it possible to store research data sustainably and securely, to provide them with metadata, and to find them through the generic search. Options for additional features and linking with other infrastructures are permanently under consideration.
Each object described and stored in the DARIAH-DE Repository gets a unique and lasting Persistent Identifier (DOI) with which it is permanently referenced, cited, and kept available for the long term. In addition, the DARIAH-DE Repository enables the sustainable and secure archiving of data collections. 

This resource is supported by Text+. In case of questions you may get in touch with the Text+ helpdesk at textplus-support@gwdg.de.

label: Phonographic Resources of Polish Traditional Music
description:
The Phonographic Collection of The Institute of Art is the oldest sound archive of traditional music in Poland. It contains nearly 200 000 recordings of folk songs and instrumental tunes from all over Poland, including borderlands and national minorities. Apart from folk music, there are also recordings of speeches and interviews with folk artists. The earliest recordings date back to the beginning of the 20th century. The collection keeps growing, with new recordings being made also in the context of the present-day culture, e.g. stage concerts, festivals, but also in traditional rituals and customs. The oldest recorded performers were singers born in 1854, and a large number of recorded artists were born in the second half of the 19th century.  

The collection is currently being digitized, examined, described, catalogued, administered, developed and made accessible with a dedicated system that has been developed in the long-term project ETNOFON (Polish traditional music – a phonographic heritage. The present state, preservation and sharing). The aim of the system is to support the development of the Institute of Art own ethno-phonographic collections as well as those obtained from 30 other institutions such as universities, museums, archives of radio stations, regional organizations and societies and private collections.

concept.label: JPEG
concept.definition: JPEG ( JAY-peg) is a commonly used method of lossy compression for digital images, particularly for those images produced by digital photography. The degree of compression can be adjusted, allowing a selectable tradeoff between storage size and image quality. JPEG typically achieves 10:1 compression with little perceptible loss in image quality. JPEG compression is used in a number of image file formats. JPEG/Exif is the most common image format used by digital cameras and other photographic image capture devices; along with JPEG/JFIF, it is the most common format for storing and transmitting photographic images on the World Wide Web. These format variations are often not distinguished, and are simply called JPEG. The term "JPEG" is an initialism/acronym for the Joint Photographic Experts Group, which created the standard. The MIME media type for JPEG is image/jpeg, except in older Internet Explorer versions, which provides a MIME type of image/pjpeg when uploading JPEG images. JPEG files usually have a filename extension of .jpg or .jpeg. JPEG/JFIF supports a maximum image size of 65,53565,535 pixels, hence up to 4 gigapixels for an aspect ratio of 1:1.

concept.label: PNG
concept.definition: Portable Network Graphics (PNG, pronounced PEE-en-JEE or PING) is a raster graphics file format that supports lossless data compression. PNG was created as an improved, non-patented replacement for Graphics Interchange Format (GIF), and is the most widely used lossless image compression format on the Internet. PNG supports palette-based images (with palettes of 24-bit RGB or 32-bit RGBA colors), grayscale images (with or without alpha channel for transparency), and full-color non-palette-based RGB/RGBA images (with or without alpha channel). PNG was designed for transferring images on the Internet, not for professional-quality print graphics, and therefore does not support non-RGB color spaces such as CMYK. A PNG file contains a single image in an extensible structure of "chunks", encoding the basic pixels and other information such as textual comments and integrity checks documented in RFC 2083. PNG files nearly always use file extension PNG or png and are assigned MIME media type image/png. PNG was published as informational RFC 2083 in March 1997 and as an ISO/IEC standard in 2004.

concept.label: TIFF
concept.definition: Tagged Image File Format, abbreviated TIFF or TIF, is a computer file format for storing raster graphics images, popular among graphic artists, the publishing industry, and photographers. TIFF is widely supported by scanning, faxing, word processing, optical character recognition, image manipulation, desktop publishing, and page-layout applications. The format was created by Aldus Corporation for use in desktop publishing. It published the latest version 6.0 in 1992, subsequently updated with an Adobe Systems copyright after the latter acquired Aldus in 1994. Several Aldus or Adobe technical notes have been published with minor extensions to the format, and several specifications have been based on TIFF 6.0, including TIFF/EP (ISO 12234-2), TIFF/IT (ISO 12639), TIFF-F (RFC 2306) and TIFF-FX (RFC 3949).

concept.label: IIIF
concept.definition: The International Image Interoperability Framework (IIIF) is a set of shared application programming interface (API) specifications for interoperable functionality in digital image repositories. The IIIF is comprised of and driven by a community of libraries, museums, archives, software companies, and other organizations working together to create, test, refine, implement and promote the IIIF specifications. Using JSON-LD, linked data, and standard W3C web protocols such as Web Annotation, IIIF makes it easy to parse and share digital image data, migrate across technology systems, and provide enhanced image access for scholars and researchers. In short, IIIF enables better, faster and cheaper image delivery. It lets you leverage interoperability and the fabric of the Web to access new possibilities and new users for your image-based resources, while reducing long term maintenance and technological lock in. IIIF gives users a rich set of baseline functionality for viewing, zooming, and assembling the best mix of resources and tools to view, compare, manipulate and work with images on the Web, an experience made portableshareable, citable, and embeddable. (source: https://iiif.io/community/faq/)

label: Pinboard
description:
Pinboard is a social bookmarking website that describes itself as "a fast, no-nonsense bookmarking site for people who value privacy and speed." The service lets users bookmark content from any web browser, offers browser plugins, and a way to save open tabs in a minimal, fast, and secure environment.



You can connect up to three Twitter accounts (search the archives of your tweets), and configure Pinboard to automatically mirror public bookmarks from your accounts on Instapaper, Pocket and Readability. All of your bookmarks from Delicious, Google Bookmarks, Diigo, Firefox, Safari, and many other sources can be imported to your Pinboard account. Everything on the site is available as an RSS feed and you can import and export data in a wide variety of formats.



Unlike other popular bookmarking services, Pinboard caters to users who value privacy. You do not need to have any public bookmarks to use the site. Pinboard does not serve any third-party content to logged-in users---that means no scripts, images, analytics trackers, and no ads. You do not have to provide any personally identifying information to open a Pinboard account. The only requirement is a working email address.



There is a third-party clients.



There is a one time fee of $11.



In addition to the basic features, Pinboard offers a bookmark archiving service for an annual fee of $25. The site will crawl and store a copy of every bookmark in your account, and display a special icon you can click to see a cached copy. If the page you bookmarked goes offline, you'll still be able to see the archived copy indefinitely.



Pinboard is a small site that features easy access to customer support and communicating with the developer. He is easy to reach through Twitter, IRC or email,.

description: PIRIDI is an open-access Digital Humanities research project and Virtual Research Environment (VRE) dedicated to the study of Roman instrumenta Inscripta. It provides a relational database and a suite of smart tools for the prosopographical analysis of inscriptions found on household artifacts, such as amphorae, lamps, and utensils. Currently, the project centers on the tituli picti of Dressel 20 amphorae from Monte Testaccio (Rome), offering a specialized ecosystem to manage Artifacts, Objects, Inscriptions, and Prosopography.

relatedItems.label: Georeferencing the surveyed data: Using a GNSS            receiver for precise positioning of Ground Control Points
relatedItems.description: Using well materialized Ground Control Points (GCPs) and using the same set in all the performed flights will require the use of topographic instruments only for the first acquisition, as once measured, the GCPs will be re-used for the subsequents flights. It is important to underline the importance of acquiring a trustworthy set of GCPs to be used for all the surveys, instead of measuring new GCPs every time. It is more important, in fact, not to acquire the most accurate GNSS data, but to use the most precise set of GCPs, assuming for (at least locally) the validity of the first data acquired, cause repeating measures over time may lead to non extremely precise co-registration of the generated models. Instruments required: Total station D-GNSS antenna Action to perform: Defining and measuring a topographic network Materialization of the topographical vertices Materialization of the control points Ground control points displacement around and inside the site Natural points selection and digitization for future surveys Control points measurement and recording (via Total station or GNSS receiver) Softwares to use: Topographic network compensation (e.g. MicroSurvey StarNet)

relatedItems.description: In UAV photogrammetric acquisition the flight plan is a crucial part for guarantee the success of the subsequent 3D object reconstruction. In this step it is important to decide the level of details you want to reach. The flight plan will influence different parameters of the reconstructed object, such as GSD (influenced by flight altitude), camera orientation (depending on the object conformation). It is also important to consider a sufficient overlap between images (usually 80%-60%). Instruments required: UAV platform DSLR camera (for close range acquisition) Action to perform: Flight Planning Flight Execution Softwares to use: Flight planning software (Pix4D capture, DJI DSPRO, UGCS, etc.)

relatedItems.label: Carry out the digital survey
relatedItems.description:
The digital survey phase involves the data acquisition process, where spatial information is captured using technologies such as 3D laser scanning, photogrammetry, Differential GPS (DGPS), and Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs). These tools work together to collect high-resolution spatial and visual data from various perspectives, ensuring comprehensive coverage of the surveyed area or object. During this step, it is essential to record acquisition parameters as metadata, including equipment specifications, camera calibration settings, flight altitude, image overlap, and Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) accuracy.

# Input:
* Work plan
* Calibrated equipment (laser scanner, cameras, UAVs, DGPS)

# Output:

* Raw spatial data:
 * Laser scans → .e57, .las, .pts, .rcs
 * Photogrammetry → .jpeg, .tiff (images), .exif (metadata)
 * GNSS/GPS logs → .csv, .gpx
 * UAV flight data → .log, .csv, .json

* Paradata : equipment settings, flight data, etc.

* Field notes and photo logs

relatedItems.label: Configure the annotation tool
relatedItems.description:
With the environment set up, you can now configure the annotation tool to align with the project’s collaborative structure, research goals and annotation schema. Naturally, the configuration is directly linked to the selected tool. For the purposes of this workflow, the steps outlined are based on the [Recogito Studio](https://recogitostudio.org/) platform.
- Implement collaboration roles and access according to your annotation schema and the roles explicitly assigned by the tool.
- Choose/import basemap layer: If the map(s) have been georeferenced or georectified (see Step 3), the output could be imported and used as a basemap layer in the GeoTagger plugin of the annotation tool.   
- Set the annotation vocabulary: Determine whether an annotation vocabulary that fits your purposes already exists. If a suitable vocabulary is available, select it or import it into the annotation tool. If not, **run the Vocabulary Creation Workflow** [workflow currently under development — more elaborate description will be delivered soon] and develop a custom vocabulary that reflects your project’s needs, considering the integration or extension of domain-specific ontologies (e.g., [CIDOC CRM](https://cidoc-crm.org/)) or thesauri (e.g., [Getty AAT](https://www.getty.edu/research/tools/vocabularies/aat/)). Once the new vocabulary is defined, import it into the annotation platform. In all cases, consider the desired level of annotation granularity (as defined in your annotation schema) as well as interoperability with other datasets and systems. 
- Set gazetteer(s) for geo-tagging: Determine whether a suitable gazetteer already exists for your project’s geographical and historical context, as defined in your annotation schema (e.g., [Pleiades](https://pleiades.stoa.org/) for ancient places, [World Historical Gazetteer](https://whgazetteer.org/) for historical places, [GeoNames](https://www.geonames.org/) for modern locations, or even [Wikidata](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:Main_Page)). If no appropriate gazetteer exists, or if existing gazetteers only partially cover your needs, consider seeking support — for example, from the [World Historical Gazetteer](https://whgazetteer.org/) team or the [Pelagios Gazetteer Activity](https://pelagios.org/activities/gazetteers/). If these options are not applicable, you may need to compile or create a custom gazetteer, tailored to your project needs. In that case, run the **Gazetteer Creation Workflow** [workflow currently under development — more elaborate description will be delivered soon] and once finalized, import it in the appropriate format into the annotation environment.

relatedItems.label: ToposText
relatedItems.description:
ToposText is a mobile application designed to provide users with access to an extensive collection of ancient Greek texts and mapped locations spanning from the Neolithic era through the 2nd century CE. The concept was inspired by the founder's two decades of exploration in Greece and the need to organize information gathered from primary sources like Pausanias. Leveraging the advancement of mobile electronic devices and the availability of ancient texts online, ToposText was developed to index these texts geographically, using a map of Greece as the primary interface.

Upon opening the application, users are presented with a scrolling alphabetical list of over 5000 Greek cities, colonies, sanctuaries, archaeological sites, museums, and other points of interest. These are accompanied by a location-aware map displaying nearby places and the number of ancient references in the database. The application operates offline, storing texts, indexes, and a basic map on the device.

Selecting a site from the list or map provides users with a table of two-line snippets from ancient authors, often supplemented by modern descriptions where available. Users can then access the full text of approximately 240 works in English translation, with some including the original Ancient Greek. The interface allows for filtering by date, genre, and relevance, facilitating quick access to relevant passages.

Translations included in the application are older works in the public domain, stripped of footnotes and scholarly apparatus. Users are reminded that ToposText is not a substitute for the most recent scholarly editions. Each paragraph in the texts is accompanied by a date and event date, though caution is advised regarding historical accuracy.

The application also features links to Travelogues, a sister website offering early traveler illustrations of Greece and its antiquities, complementing the ancient texts.

Places listed in ToposText are categorized by confidence level, with coordinates corrected for accuracy where possible. The application aims for comprehensiveness within the territory of modern Greece, with additional coverage of key areas in the ancient Greek world. Expansion plans include the inclusion of more texts and translations, depending on the availability of scholarly resources.

relatedItems.label: Ancient Place-Name Extractor for Turkish Excavation Reports
relatedItems.description: This open‑source toolkit automatically extracts ancient place‑names from the annual proceedings of [“Kazı Sonuçları Toplantısı”](https://ukaas.ktb.gov.tr/TR-389973/kazi-sonuclari-toplantisi.html) that are the excavation reports published as PDFs on the Turkish Ministry of Culture website. It uses the Pleiades gazetteer (filtered to modern‐Turkey coordinates), page‑by‑page text extraction (with a PyPDF2→PyMuPDF fallback), and Turkish lemmatization via Zemberek.  The final output is a single JSON file listing every detected place‑name along with its Pleiades ID, coordinates, source PDF, page number, and surrounding snippet.

relatedItems.label: Geotagging of texts
relatedItems.description:
The goal of this workflow is to identify historical place names in texts and assign geo-coordinates by linking them to gazetteers (e.g., [ToposText](https://topostext.org/), [Pleiades](https://pleiades.stoa.org/), [GeoNames](https://www.geonames.org/), [World Historical Gazetteer](https://whgazetteer.org/)). By resolving these place references to gazetteer URIs, the workflow enables the retrieval of standardized geographic coordinates, allowing the enriched data to be integrated and published as Linked Open Data (LOD).

This workflow is designed to:
* Combine automatic and manual steps to improve the accuracy of geotagging.
* Explore the application of Named Entity Recognition (NER) for place identification.
* Develop a mechanism to resolve ambiguities.
* Support different input data formats.

relatedItems.label: Select external vocabularies and authority sources
relatedItems.description:
This step defines how the vocabulary relates to existing vocabularies, gazetteers, period authorities, and domain vocabularies. The aim is to avoid unnecessary duplication while keeping the vocabulary appropriate for the map corpus, annotation goals, and project scope. The strategy is recorded per facet or term family, so different approaches may be combined within the same vocabulary.

**Input**: Facet model, term families, Vocabulary Design Brief, project scope, sample map content, and relevant external vocabularies or authority sources.

**Main actions**:
1. Identify external resources relevant to each facet or term family. For example, spatial or geographic references may draw on gazetteers such as Pleiades, GeoNames, or relevant regional gazetteers, temporal references may draw on PeriodO or other period authorities and map features, monuments, buildings, land use, or object types may be compared with domain vocabularies such as the Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus or the FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types. 
2. For each relevant facet or term family, record whether external resources will be used as reference only, whether local terms will be mapped to external resources, whether external identifiers will be reused directly, or whether local terms only will be maintained. 
3. Define a mapping policy, including when to use exact, close, broader, or narrower matches.
4. Record source and citation information for external vocabularies and authority sources. 
5. Document cases where local terms are needed because no suitable external authority exists or because the concept is project specific.

**Output**: External authority list, reuse or mapping decision for each relevant facet, mapping policy, source and citation notes, and local vocabulary requirements where external resources are not sufficient.

**Format**: Mapping table, spreadsheet sheet, README section, authority list, or SKOS mapping fields where relevant.

relatedItems.label: Enrichir le candidat avec des alignements et des images
relatedItems.description:
Ajouter un alignement : il s’agit de créer une relation d’équivalence plus ou moins exacte entre le mot-clé Pactols et un item correspondant dans un autre référentiel du web. Pactols a fait le choix de préférer les relations exactes (skos:exactMatch). Les alignements ne sont possibles qu’avec des référentiels fournissant un identifiant pérenne à ses items (DOI, ARK,...) ou une adresse web stable (URI).

Les principaux référentiels des alignements Pactols sont : Wikidata, les thésaurus du ministère français de la Culture (http://data.culture.fr/thesaurus/), IdRef (oeuvres, personnes), le Art and Architecture Thesaurus de la Fondation Getty, Bibracte_thesaurus, Bnf, Pleiades (lieux anciens), Geonames (lieux), Insee (lieux de France). 

Deux modes d’alignement sont possibles : 
1. alignement : faites une recherche préalable dans le réservoir puis donnez l’URI distante de l’item et le nom du référentiel dans le formulaire.
Ex. URI distante : https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q6934696
      Nom de la source : Wikidata
2. alignement automatique : Opentheso opère une recherche sur le libellé dans les référentiels pré-enregistrés : Bibracte_thesaurus, Bnf, GeoNames, Wikidata. Selon le réservoir, la réponse peut être faussement négative sur le libellé en français, par exemple avec Wikidata dont les items peuvent ne pas avoir d’équivalent dans la langue de la recherche. Écrivez de préférence le terme de la requête dans la langue du référentiel visé. Sélectionnez la meilleure réponse affichée. La possibilité de rapatrier des métadonnées supplémentaires (traductions, images, définition) peut être un avantage mais nécessitera une relecture voire une correction après alignement. 

Image : Certains concepts, difficiles à définir, peuvent être illustrés avec profit d’une ou de plusieurs images. Celles-ci doivent être représentatives du concept et se positionner autant que possible dans le champ de l’archéologie sinon de l’histoire ancienne. Elles doivent impérativement être libres de droit (sélectionnez les réservoirs ad hoc, notamment Wikimedia Commons, et citables (avec une URI comme adresse web stable, un PID identifiant pérenne de type ARK, DOI, etc.).

Pour ajouter une image depuis Wikimedia Commons : sélectionnez l'image choisie, cliquez sur l'onglet "use this file" et recopiez le champ "File URL:". Remplissez les 4 champs de l'onglet Image de Pactols : l'URI, la légende de l'image (libellé), son auteur et la source. 
Ex. pour amphore attique : URI : https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/01/Amphore_attique_%C3%A0_figures_noires._Peintre_de_Rycroft_-_btv1b101044967_%282_of_2%29.jpg ; libellé : Amphore attique à figures noires. Peintre de Rycroft ; auteur : Bibliothèque nationale de France ; source : Wikimédia.

relatedItems.label: Pinboard
relatedItems.description:
Pinboard is a social bookmarking website that describes itself as "a fast, no-nonsense bookmarking site for people who value privacy and speed." The service lets users bookmark content from any web browser, offers browser plugins, and a way to save open tabs in a minimal, fast, and secure environment.



You can connect up to three Twitter accounts (search the archives of your tweets), and configure Pinboard to automatically mirror public bookmarks from your accounts on Instapaper, Pocket and Readability. All of your bookmarks from Delicious, Google Bookmarks, Diigo, Firefox, Safari, and many other sources can be imported to your Pinboard account. Everything on the site is available as an RSS feed and you can import and export data in a wide variety of formats.



Unlike other popular bookmarking services, Pinboard caters to users who value privacy. You do not need to have any public bookmarks to use the site. Pinboard does not serve any third-party content to logged-in users---that means no scripts, images, analytics trackers, and no ads. You do not have to provide any personally identifying information to open a Pinboard account. The only requirement is a working email address.



There is a third-party clients.



There is a one time fee of $11.



In addition to the basic features, Pinboard offers a bookmark archiving service for an annual fee of $25. The site will crawl and store a copy of every bookmark in your account, and display a special icon you can click to see a cached copy. If the page you bookmarked goes offline, you'll still be able to see the archived copy indefinitely.



Pinboard is a small site that features easy access to customer support and communicating with the developer. He is easy to reach through Twitter, IRC or email,.

relatedItems.label: Georeferencing the surveyed data: Using a GNSS            receiver for precise positioning of Ground Control Points
relatedItems.description: Using well materialized Ground Control Points (GCPs) and using the same set in all the performed flights will require the use of topographic instruments only for the first acquisition, as once measured, the GCPs will be re-used for the subsequents flights. It is important to underline the importance of acquiring a trustworthy set of GCPs to be used for all the surveys, instead of measuring new GCPs every time. It is more important, in fact, not to acquire the most accurate GNSS data, but to use the most precise set of GCPs, assuming for (at least locally) the validity of the first data acquired, cause repeating measures over time may lead to non extremely precise co-registration of the generated models. Instruments required: Total station D-GNSS antenna Action to perform: Defining and measuring a topographic network Materialization of the topographical vertices Materialization of the control points Ground control points displacement around and inside the site Natural points selection and digitization for future surveys Control points measurement and recording (via Total station or GNSS receiver) Softwares to use: Topographic network compensation (e.g. MicroSurvey StarNet)

label: Polish Literary Bibliography (PBL)
description:
The Polish Literary Bibliography (PBL) (in Polish: Polska Bibliografia Literacka) is a service and database providing access to data on literary, theatrical and film culture for 1989-2003. It documents books published in Poland in Polish and other languages as well as books published abroad in Polish and other languages when they pertain to Polish writers or when their author is Polish.

The service is curated by the PBL team — the Department of Current Bibliography of the Institute of Literary Research of the Polish Academy of Sciences (Pracownia Bibliografii Bieżącej Instytutu Badań Literackich Polskiej Akademii Nauk). The department has operated in Poznań since 1948. The „Polish Literary Bibliography” publishing series has been printed since 1954, with 45 annuals published by 2000, containing materials for the years 1944/45–1988. The printed volumes of the PBL have been digitalized and they are available in the public repository. 2001 was a breakthrough year for the presentation of the materials from the „Polish Literary Bibliography” as it saw the launch of the online PBL database, available at www.pbl.ibl.poznan.pl and spanning the years 1989–2003. 

For every year the PBL team examines approx. 850 periodicals: nation-wide dailies; domestic literary, cultural, and cultural-social periodicals; series published by scholarly institutions; selected émigré press titles; and foreign scholarly journals devoted to the subject matter of Slavic countries. A significant percentage of these records are also annotated. An important aspect of the PBL tradition is that it is a bibliography of not only texts, but also theater, film, radio, and television works (when connected with literature or theater) and also that it keeps indexes of people, institutions, works, series, and periodicals.

description:

Mrežno izdanje Portal hrvatske tehničke baštine, obogaćeno dodatnim sadržajima i prednostima novih informacijskih tehnologija, jest portal znanja i polazišna točka za istraživanje. Tiskano je izdanje usmjereno korisnicima naklonjenima tradicionalnom mediju te omogućuje trajnu pohranu ostvarenja ovoga projekta u fizičkom obliku, u knjižnicama i kućnim bibliotekama.

---

The IDS online portal provides information on the German language in Russia and the peculiarities of the dialects spoken in Western Russia and in German language islands of the eastern Soviet Union. Users can research in the original corpus, listen to recordings, and explore differences with modern dialects. The dialects developed independently as “language island varieties” and differ in many ways from standard German dialects. The portal is aimed at language enthusiasts, Russian Germans, as well as linguists and university lecturers. It offers a comprehensive insight into the development and characteristics of Russian German dialects.

concept.label: IIIF
concept.definition: The International Image Interoperability Framework (IIIF) is a set of shared application programming interface (API) specifications for interoperable functionality in digital image repositories. The IIIF is comprised of and driven by a community of libraries, museums, archives, software companies, and other organizations working together to create, test, refine, implement and promote the IIIF specifications. Using JSON-LD, linked data, and standard W3C web protocols such as Web Annotation, IIIF makes it easy to parse and share digital image data, migrate across technology systems, and provide enhanced image access for scholars and researchers. In short, IIIF enables better, faster and cheaper image delivery. It lets you leverage interoperability and the fabric of the Web to access new possibilities and new users for your image-based resources, while reducing long term maintenance and technological lock in. IIIF gives users a rich set of baseline functionality for viewing, zooming, and assembling the best mix of resources and tools to view, compare, manipulate and work with images on the Web, an experience made portableshareable, citable, and embeddable. (source: https://iiif.io/community/faq/)

relatedItems.label: SPPAS
relatedItems.description:
SPPAS - the automatic annotation and analyses of speech is a scientific computer software package. SPPAS is daily developed with the aim to provide a robust and reliable software. Available for free, with open source code, there is simply no other package for linguists to simple use in both the automatic annotations of speech, the analyses of any kind of annotated data and the conversion of annotated file formats. You can imagine the annotations or analyses you need, SPPAS does the rest!

SPPAS ensures flexibility rather than a one-size-fits all approach in the implementation of the proposed features. There are no fixed or unique solutions, but a bunch of customizable features to make choices according to the user requirements.

Annotating recordings is very labor-intensive and cost-ineffective since it has to be performed manually by experienced researchers with many hours of work. As the primary functionality, SPPAS proposes a set of automatic or semi-automatic annotations of recordings. In the present context, annotations are "defined as the practice of adding interpretative, linguistic information to an electronic corpus of spoken and/or written language data. "Annotation" can also refer to the end-product of this process" (Leech, 1997). SPPAS automatizes the annotation processes and allows users to save time. In order to be used efficiently, SPPAS expects a rigorous methodology to collect data and to prepare them.

Linguistics annotation, especially when dealing with multiple domains, makes use of different tools within a given project. This implies a rigorous annotation framework to ensure compatibilities between annotations and time-saving. SPPAS annotation files are in a specific XML format with extension xra. Annotations can be imported from and exported to a variety of other formats including Praat (TextGrid, PitchTier, IntensityTier), Elan (eaf), Transcriber (trs), Annotation Pro (antx), Phonedit (mrk), Sclite (ctm, stm), HTK (lab, mlf), subtitles formats (srt, sub), CSV files…

relatedItems.label: Using Praat for Linguistic Research
relatedItems.description:
Using Praat for Linguistic Research by Will Styler is a practical guidebook and information package designed to help you use the Praat phonetics software package more effectively in Phonetic or Phonological research. Although it was originally written in the Spring/Summer of 2011 for the 2011 Linguistic Institute’s Praat workshop, it’s now available for anybody who’s interested, and is being updated over time, both as Praat changes and as the author adds new information.

The guidebook itself is an 85+ page compilation of walkthroughs, explanations, and tutorials explaining how to use Praat for a variety of measurements and tasks. Although the guide does start with “basic” tasks like opening sound files, measuring duration, formants, pitch, it also covers more “advanced” tasks like source-filter resynthesis, A1-P0 nasality measurement, formula manipulation of sounds and even Praat scripting.

relatedItems.label: Transcribe faithfully
relatedItems.description:
The traditional and methodologically recommended approach for dialect data is impressionistic transcription: the transcriber aims to represent, as faithfully as possible, their auditory impressions, mapping them onto the taxonomic categories provided by phonetic theory. This is neither a phonological idealisation nor an attempt to normalise pronunciation toward a reference model. Rather, the transcription records what is actually perceived as produced by the speaker in a given utterance at a specific moment.

Impressionistic transcription requires that the transcriber have a trained ear and a thorough command of the phonetic system being used. The availability of digital recordings and acoustic analysis software (see Tools section below) greatly facilitates this work by allowing the analyst to listen repeatedly to the sequence to transcribe and, where necessary, to complement auditory perception with the visual inspection of acoustic properties.

relatedItems.label: Post-process and normalise the transcription
relatedItems.description:
After the initial transcription, and having respected the phonetic reality produced by the speaker, it may be appropriate to intervene with simplification and normalisation operations to make the transcription usable for its intended purpose and audience. 

One common case concerns the normalisation of pronunciation variants. Minor fluctuations in the pronunciation of a given segment — which may have been transcribed with slightly different symbols across occurrences in the corpus — can often be unified under a single symbol after analysis, provided that the variation carries no contrastive or analytically significant function. For example, if a vowel is inconsistently realised between two slightly different articulatory positions, the analyst may choose either to preserve this difference by using two distinct phonetic notations, or to transcribe it uniformly using a single notation once it has been established that the variation is not meaningful to the analysis. The decision to normalise must follow, not precede, analysis: only after examining the distribution and function of a variable should you decide whether to represent its different variants with a single symbol. Normalisation should be conservative — when in doubt, preserve the variation.

A “narrow” transcription is appropriate for strictly phonetic research, or for studies in which phonetics constitutes a privileged level of analysis. Even in such cases, however, the transcriber may choose to represent certain phenomena in greater detail when they constitute the direct object of investigation, while paying less attention to other aspects. Although such choices may be acceptable for practical reasons related to time and resources, they must always be made explicit so that readers do not draw inaccurate conclusions from the transcription data. Any deviations from standard IPA symbols and conventions should likewise be clearly explained and properly justified, and should only be introduced when the IPA does not already provide a notation sufficiently adequate for what is being transcribed.

By contrast, in research that does not pursue specifically phonetic objectives, “broad” phonetic transcriptions are generally preferred. These omit most diacritics and tend to normalise minor fluctuations in pronunciation. More generally, every decision taken during transcription and post-processing should be documented clearly and transparently, so that users of the transcription can interpret the data correctly.

relatedItems.label: Complement Transcription with Acoustic Analysis Tools
relatedItems.description: Recognize that musical transcription functions as one tool among several for representing and analyzing musical sound, and has historically been used alongside other methods. Where appropriate, make use of specific acoustic analysis software capable of extracting data and generating graphic representations of the sound parameters relevant to musicological and ethnomusicological analysis — for example, tools such as Sonic Visualizer or Praat. These tools can complement written transcription by providing additional layers of analysis for the same performance.

relatedItems.label: Choose the transcription environment and method (auditory vs. acoustic-supported)
relatedItems.description: Decide whether the transcription will be hosted and produced within a dedicated software environment, and whether it will be time-aligned to the acoustic signal or kept as a separate text. Two complementary methods of transcription exist. Auditory transcription relies on repeated listening to portions of the recording of varying length, letting the ear judge the identity of each sound. This method should be used with an explicit caveat: human auditory perception integrates a large number of acoustic cues simultaneously (spectral, temporal, and contextual), so isolating too short or too narrow a stretch of audio can distort perception and lead the transcriber to hear segments that are not actually representative of the sound in its natural context. Acoustic transcription complements auditory judgment with visual inspection of the acoustic signal, typically using Praat, which displays the waveform and spectrogram and allows fine-grained visualization and measurement of the signal. Two software tools are commonly used for this purpose. Praat is conceived primarily for acoustic analysis and offers advanced visualization (spectrogram, formants, pitch, intensity) together with an annotation (TextGrid) interface in which IPA symbols are already integrated, making it well suited to segmental and acoustic-phonetic work. ELAN is designed primarily for the annotation of conversational and multimodal data, but can be adapted to phonetic transcription purposes; it also captures the waveform reliably and is often preferred when transcription needs to be integrated with other layers of conversational or gestural annotation. The choice between the two (or the decision to use both) should be driven by whether the project's main analytic interest is fine acoustic-phonetic measurement (favoring Praat) or multi-layered discourse/interactional annotation (favoring ELAN).

relatedItems.label: Choix d'un outil de transcription
Transcribe and process the interview
relatedItems.description:
Produce a transcription of the recorded interview in order to enable analysis, indexing, and long-term accessibility. Transcription constitutes a key stage in the enrichment of the oral source, transforming an audio or audiovisual document into a textual resource that can be searched, annotated, and reused.

Define the level of transcription according to the objectives of the research. This may range from verbatim transcription (including hesitations, pauses, and non-verbal elements) to a more edited version that improves readability while preserving the meaning of the discourse. Where relevant, adopt established transcription conventions and ensure consistency across the corpus.

If required, integrate time-coding to align the transcription with the original recording, facilitating navigation between text and audio/video. Consider also the need for translation, particularly in multilingual research contexts.

During transcription, pay attention to the treatment of personal data and sensitive information. Anonymisation or pseudonymisation may be necessary, especially when preparing the material for dissemination or public access. Any modifications should be documented to ensure transparency and reproducibility.

The transcription should be treated as a distinct but related document within the oral source corpus. It must therefore be documented through a dedicated record, including its relationship to the original recording, the tools and methods used, and the identity of the transcriber.

This step may be carried out prior to, or in parallel with, the description and metadata creation phase, depending on the research design and available resources. In all cases, it significantly enhances the findability, accessibility, and reusability of the oral source in line with FAIR principles.

PRISM is a standardised way for academic publishers to display information about their peer review processes across their entire catalogue. At the publisher level, all their peer review processes are visible (as they may have more than one process in use across all their series and titles). PRISM’s goal is to provide transparency about the peer review process(es) that apply to their works. This helps build trust in open access academic book publishing.How can PRISM help me?- If you’re a publisher, PRISM helps you display the peer review process that has been applied to works in your collection. This helps you showcase how you apply best practices in peer review.- If you’re a librarian, PRISM allows you to see the quality control process that applies to a given work. This will give you confidence in recommending the work as a reliable source to your researchers and students.- If you’re a funder, PRISM gives you more detailed information about the quality assurance process of the research outputs you’ve funded.- If you’re a researcher, student, or a general reader, PRISM allows you to see the quality control process that applies to a given work. This will give you more information about the publisher.

concept.label: CSV
concept.definition: A comma-separated values (CSV) file is a delimited text file that uses a comma to separate values. A CSV file stores tabular data (numbers and text) in plain text. Each line of the file is a data record. Each record consists of one or more fields, separated by commas. The use of the comma as a field separator is the source of the name for this file format. RFC 4180 formalized CSV. It defines the MIME type "text/csv", and CSV files that follow its rules should be very widely portable

concept.label: IIIF
concept.definition: The International Image Interoperability Framework (IIIF) is a set of shared application programming interface (API) specifications for interoperable functionality in digital image repositories. The IIIF is comprised of and driven by a community of libraries, museums, archives, software companies, and other organizations working together to create, test, refine, implement and promote the IIIF specifications. Using JSON-LD, linked data, and standard W3C web protocols such as Web Annotation, IIIF makes it easy to parse and share digital image data, migrate across technology systems, and provide enhanced image access for scholars and researchers. In short, IIIF enables better, faster and cheaper image delivery. It lets you leverage interoperability and the fabric of the Web to access new possibilities and new users for your image-based resources, while reducing long term maintenance and technological lock in. IIIF gives users a rich set of baseline functionality for viewing, zooming, and assembling the best mix of resources and tools to view, compare, manipulate and work with images on the Web, an experience made portableshareable, citable, and embeddable. 3D render files

Photoshop's native PSD format can be previewed and compared to previous versions of the same file.

Documentation and wikis

Small websites can be hosted from public repositories on GitHub. The URL format is http://projectname.github.io.

Issue tracking (including feature requests)

Gantt charts

GitHub is a heavily used in the opensource development community but does not require hosted projects to meet the definition of Open Source.

label: Protégé
description:
The Protege Project offers WebProtege and Protege Desktop, which are free and open source ontology editing applications.

WebProtégé is an ontology development environment for the Web that makes it easy to create, upload, modify, and share ontologies for collaborative viewing and editing. WebProtégé fully supports the latest OWL 2 Web Ontology Language. The highly configurable user interface creates the perfect environment for beginners and experts alike. Collaboration features abound, including sharing and permissions, threaded notes and discussions, watches and email notifications. RDF/XML, Turtle, OWL/XML, OBO, and other formats available for ontology upload and download.

Protégé Desktop is a feature rich ontology editing environment with full support for the OWL 2 Web Ontology Language, and direct in-memory connections to description logic reasoners like HermiT and Pellet. Protégé Desktop supports creation and editing of one or more ontologies in a single workspace via a completely customizable user interface. Visualization tools allow for interactive navigation of ontology relationships. Advanced explanation support aids in tracking down inconsistencies. Refactor operations available including ontology merging, moving axioms between ontologies, rename of multiple entities, and more.

THISTLE is a pipeline for post-OCR error correction developed to improve the accuracy of machine-readable text extracted from nineteenth-century issues of The Scotsman newspaper. At this stage, the pipeline is code-based; future work may explore the development of a no-code front-end UI to increase accessibility, as well as interoperability with other archives, genres, languages and historical periods.

THISTLE is provided as a research prototype / proof-of-concept. Some components remain in draft or experimental form. This repo reflects the state of the project as of 4 February 2026.

This work has received support from UKRI (Grant No. APP4595) through the ‘Digital Skills in Arts and Humanities (DISKAH): Transforming Access to Digital Infrastructure and Skills’ project.

label: Protovis
description:
Protovis composes custom views of data with simple marks such as bars and dots. Unlike low-level graphics libraries that quickly become tedious for visualization, Protovis defines marks through dynamic properties that encode data, allowing inheritance, scales and layouts to simplify construction.

Protovis is free and open-source, provided under the BSD License. It uses JavaScript and SVG for web-native visualizations; no plugin required (though you will need a modern web browser)! Although programming experience is helpful, Protovis is mostly declarative and designed to be learned by example.

Protovis is no longer being developed. The developers have moved on to a new visualization library, D3.

label: Ptolemaic
description: Ptolemaic is a computer application for music visualization and analysis written in the Java programming language. The software is designed to aid in the analysis of all types of Western music using established analytical techniques, including tonal functional analysis (Harrison 1994), pitch-class set analysis (Forte 1973), hierarchical linear analysis (Schenker 1935, Jones 2002), tonal pitch-space analysis on the Tonnetz (Riemann 1915), pitch-class set analysis (Forte 1973), and transformation analysis (Lewin 1987). Musical works and excerpts may be opened and saved using the de-facto standard music notation interchange format, MusicXML. To assist in analysis, Ptolemaic can display the music on a pitch/time graph, on a pitch-class/time graph, on a step-class/time graph (also called a diatonic lattice) (Jones 2002), on the Tonnetz, or using filtered point-symmetry (Douthett 2008). Pitch classes and chords are color coded so that the user can easily correlate them across each graph. The benefit of having a software tool to visualize and perform certain analysis tasks is in automating processes that are normally time-consuming for the musician, thus allowing the music scholar to focus on the musical issues, rather than the technical issues of graphing, and calculating chord classes. Ptolemaic provides useful ways of visualizing a piece of music and tools for gaining more information about that music, so that the user can efficiently make informed musical decisions about the music and preserve that analysis for future study.

relatedItems.label: The DARIAH ELDAH consent form wizard
relatedItems.description:
In this poster, we would like to introduce the “consent form wizard” developed by the DARIAH-EU working group “Ethics and Legality in Digital Arts and Humanities” (ELDAH). This tool is currently under development and will be finalized and available in time for the DH2020 conference. It will enable digital scholars as well as the wider research infrastructure community to quickly and easily obtain a standardized consent form that is conforming to the obligations and regulations of the European Union General Data Protection regulation (GDPR) and therefore legally valid in all of the European Union.

Depending on the context for which consent is obtained (e.g. use of images of people at academic events, processing of information shared in surveys, collection / processing of personal data), the wizard users will receive a consent form tailored to their specific needs after answering a series of questions. The different scenarios are the result of discussions with participants of the DH2019 in Utrecht and the DARIAH Annual Meeting 2019 in Warsaw and hence driven by the needs of the research community. Additional meetings with stakeholders from cultural heritage organisations (e.g. ICARUS) and the DARIAH-EU community will ensure a critical evaluation as well as a pragmatic, user-friendly implementation of the tool.

It will be inspired by the code of the CLARIN LINDAT Public License Selector (cf. Kamocki et al. 2016) which offers the same service for license selection that we would like to develop for obtaining a consent form. Software developers, legal experts and (digital) humanities researchers will cooperate in the development of this tool, which - while legally addressing the strict data protection regulations of the European Union - will also be of use for the international research community outside Europe, since the consent forms will provide a best-practice template for ethical research conduct when processing personal data, and hence address the increasingly prominent topic of ethical research practice and scientific behaviour, especially in a largely digital, Internet-based research context (cf. Markham & Buchanan 2012, McKee & Porter 2009).

The presentation of the poster at the DH2020 conference will allow us to present the wizard to colleagues outside our European network, discuss their needs and experiences with the protection of personal data and hence, if appropriate, adapt the wizard to reflect a global rather than European common perspective on research ethics and the processing of personal data.
