label: Pundit: a semantic powered web annotation service
description: Pundit (https://thepund.it) is a cloud service that allows users to *“take notes”* on web documents, like a web page or a PDF file. It consists of a set of components, amongst them the **Annotator**, a free extension for the Google Chrome browser used by users to create the annotations. ![Pundit in action](https://thepund.it/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/img-hero-smaller.png)Annotations can be **highlights** of text parts or **comments**, applied either on a selection of the text or on the whole document. It is also possible to create annotations to **tag** a selected text or an entire web page. This creates a free-form personal category that can be reused in other annotations.Pundit has also some very distinguished features. First of all it supports **semantic annotations**, real RDF triples (subject - predicate -> object) to specify formal, structured and reusable statements associated to the annotated content. Specialized ontologies/vocabularies can be defined, in situations in which a higher precision is needed, e.g. research scenarios in specific domains, identification of concepts in medical reports or even tagging text for machine learning training.Pundit annotations are then collected in “containers” called **Notebooks**. Users can have as many notebooks as they like and can make them “public” or “private”: all annotations contained in them can be, respectively, freely seen or not in their original web pages by using Pundit. Soon Notebooks can also be shared with specific users.Users can access the **Pundit WebApp** to see and manage in a centralized place all their annotations done “on the web”. Here they can search and filter annotations with a faceted interface and also export them in a variety of standard/open formats, including Microsoft Office and Open Office files (.xlsx, .docx and .odt) and, for a technical audience, JSON-LD files, fully compliant with the **W3C Web Annotation Data Model** specification.For those who don’t want to install the Chrome Extension or prefer to use another web browser, the **FeedThePundit** “proxy service” is available. It allows users to open web pages from every browser, also from mobile devices, with Pundit being automatically activated.Finally, for developers and system integrators, a set of **APIs** are also publicly available, that allows the development of custom integration scenarios with the Pundit service.The tool at present can be **freely used** by everyone as a cloud service managed by Net7. Users can register at https://thepund.it either directly or by using external authentication services, including EGI Check-In.A part of its codebase is also available as **open source** software with the AGPL 3.0 license.  Pundit is currently **one of the EOSC DIH pilot** (see https://eosc-dih.eu/pundit/ ). The pilot has the following objectives: (1) supporting Net7 to onboard Pundit in the EOSC Marketplace, which will give to this tool a significant boost in visibility, especially amongst European researchers; (2) studying other possible use cases and business exploitation options for Pundit, including the release of the service with a Freemium model (free to use for basic functionalities while for more advanced and professional features the user must pay a recurrent subscription); (3) analysing the technical feasibility for deploying Pundit, which is currently hosted at AWS, in an EOSC infrastructure.

label: PyDistintoX
description:
A Python tool for **contrastive text analysis** using 16 statistical distinctiveness measures (based on [Pydistinto](https://github.com/Zeta-and-Company/pydistinto), see [Project Status](https://gitlab.com/pydistintox/pydistintox/#project-status) for details).

PyDistintoX is designed to compare and analyze **two text corpora** using a comprehensive set of 16 statistical measures (e.g., TF-IDF, Zeta, Chi-squared, LLR, Eta). Built as a **command-line interface (CLI) tool**, it enables researchers, linguists, and data analysts to efficiently quantify and visualize lexical distinctiveness between corpora.

**Key Features:**

- **16 distinctiveness measures** for robust contrastive analysis.
- **CLI** for quick, scriptable workflows.
- **Python Library** for custom workflows (see [documentation](https://pydistintox-993c39.gitlab.io/api/))
- **Visualization support** (e.g., heatmaps) for intuitive interpretation.
- **Lightweight and scalable**—optimized for large corpora using Gensim and NumPy/SciPy.sparse.

relatedItems.label: gensim
relatedItems.description: Gensim is an open-source library for unsupervised topic modeling and natural language processing, using modern statistical machine learning. Gensim is implemented in Python and Cython. Gensim is designed to handle large text collections using data streaming and incremental online algorithms, which differentiates it from most other machine learning software packages that target only in-memory processing. Gensim includes streamed parallelized implementations of fastText, word2vec and doc2vec algorithms, as well as latent semantic analysis (LSA, LSI, SVD), non-negative matrix factorization (NMF), latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA), tf-idf and random projections.

relatedItems.label: spaCy
relatedItems.description: spaCy is an open-source software library for advanced natural language processing, written in the programming languages Python and Cython. The library is published under the MIT license and currently offers statistical neural network models for English, German, Spanish, Portuguese, French, Italian, Dutch and multi-language NER, as well as tokenization for various other languages. Unlike NLTK, which is widely used for teaching and research, spaCy focuses on providing software for production usage. As of version 1.0, spaCy also supports deep learning workflows that allow connecting statistical models trained by popular machine learning libraries like TensorFlow, Keras, Scikit-learn or PyTorch. spaCy's machine learning library, Thinc, is also available as a separate open-source Python library. It features convolutional neural network models for part-of-speech tagging, dependency parsing and named entity recognition, as well as API improvements around training and updating models, and constructing custom processing pipelines.

Moreover, Pygmalion can work with any language and script, so opening the possibility to compare the evolution of meaning in different languages.

description:
PyLaia is a toolkit specialized for handwritten text document analysis. More specifically, for Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) and Keyword Spotting (KWS).

PyLaia is flexible, open-source, device-agnostic, and can be used to express a wide variety of experiments, including (but not limited to) training and inference over Convolutional and Recurrent based deep Neural Network models. The software is extensible and easily configurable and provides a rich set of functional layers with a particular focus on HTR.

It has been used for conducting research over several historic text databases. Additionally, it is one of the main engines used by the Transkribus project where thousands of handwritten and printed pages are transcribed every week by both individuals and organizations around the world. Tested in many languages: English, Spanish, Latin, Bengali, Hebrew, Arabic, Swedish, German, Italian, ...

relatedItems.label: Extract text contents of the input document(s)
relatedItems.description:
The information extraction pipeline works on textual documents, so the next requirement is to obtain the textual contents of the input documents. For extraction of text from PDF files, text extraction libraries (such as [PyPDF2](https://pypi.org/project/PyPDF2/)) can be employed. The output of this step is intended to be a JSON formatted element corresponding to each record or document. This JSON element will hold the text content plus some suitable associated metadata, to be successively enriched in subsequent steps. The expected JSON format for the output of this step is detailed in the schema [Textual Information Data Extraction Schema (TIDES)](https://github.com/cbinding/rematch2/blob/main/tides_schema.json). An example illustrative minimal document is shown below (additional fields may also be present):

```json
{
   "text": "obtained text content to be further processed",
   "meta": {
       "filename": "name_of_file_the_text_was_extracted_from.pdf"
  	   "description": "about the original source of the text and the information extraction process",
  	   "created": "2025-06-26T10:33:36Z"
   }, 
   "tokens": [],
   "spans": [],
   "sections": []
}
```

A [tool created by University of Sheffield](https://github.com/GateNLP/atrium-text_extraction/) performs text extraction from PDF and will create output conforming to this JSON schema. The script also includes an option to re-do OCR on the original PDF document if required.

relatedItems.label: Construct and configure the text processing pipeline
relatedItems.description:
For maximum flexibility the text processing components have been developed as flexible, configurable and reusable [Python](https://www.python.org/) modules which can be combined within a [spaCy](https://spacy.io/) pipeline architecture to perform various tasks including text normalisation and vocabulary-driven concept recognition. The temporal components accommodate multilingual data, the vocabulary-driven components as described here use English language vocabularies.

Construction and configuration of pipelines is illustrated in a series of exemplar demonstrator [Jupyter notebooks](https://github.com/cbinding/rematch2) accompanying the source code, where more details of the configuration options are also present.

### Configuration

Much of the lower-level configuration is initialised with sensible defaults making the pipeline components usable ‘out of the box’, however as the components can be combined in various ways there are some choices to be made:

- Choose which controlled vocabularies to match on. This involves choosing from a set of pre-defined vocabulary-matching pipeline components. These include:
   - Facets of the [Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus (AAT)](https://www.getty.edu/research/tools/vocabularies/aat/)
      - [AAT Associated Concepts facet](http://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300264086)
      - [AAT Materials facet](http://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300264091)
      - [AAT Objects facet](http://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300264092)
      - [AAT Physical Attributes facet](http://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300264087)
      - [AAT Styles & Periods facet](http://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300264088)
   - Vocabularies originating from the [Forum on Information Standards in Heritage (FISH)](https://heritage-standards.org.uk/fish-vocabularies/)
      - [FISH Archaeological Objects thesaurus](http://purl.org/heritagedata/schemes/mda_obj)
      - [FISH Archaeological Sciences thesaurus](http://purl.org/heritagedata/schemes/560)

- Choose a [PeriodO](https://perio.do/) authority identifier. The pipeline component to identify named periods in the text utilises the (entire) PeriodO dataset. When configured with a valid PeriodO authority identifier (e.g. “p0xxt6t” - [Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA)](http://n2t.net/ark:/99152/p0xxt6t)), the component will identify matches within the text for any of the labels of periods contained in that specified authority. e.g. *Chalcolithic*, *Early Bronze Age*, *Antonine* etc.

- Choose whether to include tokenisation results in the output (default: false). The tokenisation is a key step in the NLP pipeline. The results of the tokenisation can be useful information in diagnosing and understanding how the NLP part of the pipeline has worked. However, these results can be large and detailed and are not required for the overall goal of the workflow, so you may optionally choose to omit them from the output (by default they will be omitted).

relatedItems.label: Apply the configured pipeline to the input text(s) and produce output
relatedItems.description:
The Python spaCy pipeline components perform operations including text normalisation, tokenization, POS tagging, lemmatization, and vocabulary-driven concept recognition. The input for this step will be the JSON file as produced in the first step of the workflow, plus the built and configured pipeline. Various output report formats are available, including TXT, CSV, JSON, HTML and PDF. 

* The CSV output lists the concept entities identified in the text, with their locations in the text.
* The JSON output will be the JSON input enriched with additional fields containing the results of applying the configured pipeline to the input text. This allows for further processing or for flexible aggregation and reporting on the results.
* The HTML output visualises and lists concept entities identified in the text, with summaries of counts for each concept.
* The TXT output is a text version of the HTML output.
* The PDF output is a PDF version of the HTML output.

Examples of applying configured pipelines to data are available as a series of [Jupyter (Python) notebooks](https://github.com/cbinding/rematch2) that accompany the source code.

relatedItems.label: Configure and apply information extraction NLP pipeline
relatedItems.description: The next step creates and applies a [spaCy](https://spacy.io/) information extraction NLP pipeline to identify named periods and year spans within the body of the abstract text. The named periods originate from a chosen [PeriodO](https://perio.do/) authority. This workflow includes an exemplar source code demonstrator in the form of [a Jupyter notebook](https://github.com/cbinding/rematch2/blob/main/ATRIUM_T3_4_IE_gotriple_abstracts.ipynb), and the techniques are described more fully in the workflow *Vocabulary-driven Information Extraction*.

relatedItems.label: Unify the spelling for the main tier
relatedItems.description: INEL uses a near-phonological Latin transcription convention. The rules are language-specific. The source data usually in Cyrillic or Latin scripts, with many idiosyncratic conventions used in that particular source. While keeping the original spelling on a separate tier, duplicate and convert it to the standardized  spelling to be useed on the « baseline » transcription tier.

relatedItems.label: Formalise geometric attribute parameters
relatedItems.description:
Geometric attributes describe the morphological properties of an architectural structure (e.g., a building), its constituent elements (e.g., a wall within that building), and the individual components of those elements (e.g., the stones within that wall), as well as the inter-elemental (e.g., an array of pillars) and inter-componential relationships (e.g., bonding between stones). For example, a geometric attribute of a building may be its height; of a wall its thickness; of a stone its angularity; the spacing between pillars for an inter-elemental relationship; and the degree of overlap between superposed stones for an inter-componential relationship. Geometric attributes can serve as meaningful proxies in a range of broader analyses of structural integrity, construction quality, invested labour, typology, and construction choices. The selected geometric attributes are therefore determined by the research premise and question defined within the project objectives and expected outcomes (Step 1 of “3D Digital Representations of Heritage Assets” workflow). In order to enable their measurement and extraction from a 3D model in the form of quantitative data, the selected geometric attributes are mathematically formalised into parameters, which can be analytically operationalised in a digital environment. How and in what way the geometric attributes are formalised into corresponding geometric attribute parameters is informed by the available data and documentation on both the architectural structure and the types of attributes under investigation (Step 2 of “3D Digital Representations of Heritage Assets” workflow). In turn, the resulting parameters inform, in part, the plan of work for reality-based data acquisition (Step 4 of the “3D Digital Representations of Heritage Assets” workflow), as the minimum perceptibility of relevant morphologies and relationships dictates key technical and logistical requirements.

# Input:

* Project objectives and expected outcomes: .docx, .pdf, .md, .xml
* Data and documentation on the architectural structure: .pdf, .tiff, .jpg, .dwg, .dxf, .ifc
* Reference typologies and measurement conventions for geometrical attributes: .pdf, .docx

# Output:

* Formalised geometric attribute parameter catalogue: .pdf, .docx, .md, .json, .csv, .py, .txt

relatedItems.label: Select computation systems and 3D model structuring protocols
relatedItems.description:
Following the creation of the 3D model, select and configure an appropriate computation system to enable and carry out the 3D geometric analysis process. This system is used to operationalise the geometric attribute parameters, compute the geometric attribute data, and extract the resulting data in an interoperable format for further analysis. If required, adopt or develop a 3D model structuring protocol to guide the preparatory structuring of the 3D model prior to computation.

# Input:

* Formalised geometric attribute parameter catalogue
* Technical properties of the 3D model: .json, .xml, .txt

# Output:

* Model structuring protocol: .json, .xml
* Computation environment specification: software, dependencies, libraries
* Executable computation tools: scripts, node graphs, plugins

relatedItems.label: Geometric attribute data computation
relatedItems.description:
Quantitative geometric attribute data, tied to the corresponding parameters, is computed from the structured 3D model. This data is then exported into an interoperable format for further analysis. This process can range from an operator systematically assessing (i.e. measuring) the attributes to customised scripts mass-computing and extracting attribute data, provided the model has been structured first.

# Input:

* Structured 3D model
* Attribute data computation system

# Output:

* Attribute data in an interoperable format: .csv, .json, .txt

relatedItems.label: Geometric attribute data analysis
relatedItems.description:
Subsequent data analysis, such as statistical and comparative analyses, is performed on the extracted geometric attribute data to allow further evaluation and interpretation. The attribute data analysis method is inherently interconnected with the selected geometric attributes and their corresponding parameters. Ultimately, by extension, it is also connected to the predefined research premise and question embedded within the overarching project objectives and expected outcomes.

# Input:

* Attribute data in an interoperable format
* Chosen attribute data analysis method and associated systems

# Output:

* Analytical results ready for evaluation and interpretation
* Visualisations
* Annotated analytical models
* Analysis report

relatedItems.label: Vocabulary-driven Information Extraction
relatedItems.description:
This workflow concerns information extraction from textual documents with the aim of enriching existing subject indexing with Linked Open Data (LOD) identifiers for concepts drawn from published controlled vocabularies (such as thesauri) specific to the domain. The overall goal is to improve findability and interoperability in accordance with FAIR principles. 

The primary use-case (in the context of the ATRIUM project) is to suggest enrichments for the subject indexing of English language reports and journal articles describing archaeological investigations and interventions, as supplied by ATRIUM partner Archaeology Data Service (ADS). The workflow accommodates structured text inputs and PDF documents (provided textual data can be extracted). Jupyter notebook demonstrators illustrate the application of the tools developed.

relatedItems.label: Text Extraction From PDF Files
relatedItems.description:
This workflow describes the process for extracting the textual content of PDF files, and performing some basic segmentation of the extracted text.

The workflow is intended to be used as the first step in larger workflows that process the text (such as geographic named entity extraction etc,) and is unlikely to be particularly useful as a stand-alone workflow. Specifically it was designed in the context of the ATRIUM project to aid in the indexing of English language reports and journal articles describing archaeological investigations and interventions, as supplied by ATRIUM partner Archaeology Data Service (ADS).

label: Python Tools for Text-Analysis
description:
This is a set of simple, free tools for analyzing, exploring, and dividing plain texts. The tools are available in the simple, menu-driven Python program. Some are rather trivial and none of them claims to be perfect or optimized. 

Probably the most important tool is the **Apostrophe_Project**, which accepts a plain text file, partially corrects it to prevent potential problems in text-analysis, and marks it up for further semi-automated correction. It addresses the long-standing and usually ignored problem that the single quotation mark and the apostrophe are indistinguishable in plain text files. It replaces the following characters with separate symbols that are not already in the text: 
- Internal apostrophes: presumably real apostrophes 
- Non-internal apostrophes preceding capital letters: usually scare quotes or dialogue marked with single quotation marks 
- Non-internal apostrophes following a word-final "s": usually plural possessives 
- Non-internal apostrophes in very commonly used contracted forms: 'em, an', 'twas, and so forth 
- Non-internal apostrophes between other breaking characters: essentially never anything but single quotation marks

relatedItems.label: MorphAL (QGIS plugin)
relatedItems.description:
The MorphAL (Morphological Analysis) plugin for QGIS enriches vector shapefile data of the "parcel" type to facilitate the search for landscape structuring logic. It adds semantic attributes to segment and polygon data concerning their geometric properties (orientation, rectangularity, convexity). These attributes correspond to mathematical indicators that are automatically calculated and integrated into the shapefile attribute table.

Parcel data in polygons, most often from vectorized land registers, can be broken down into segments; the plugin then adds the orientation of each segment: researchers can then test or identify certain orientations that structure all or part of a space, and which are therefore more or less morphogenetic (for example, Roman centuriations that organize the Padanian plain of northern Italy even today more than in ancient times).

In addition, the geometry of polygonal parcel data can be characterized according to two morphological analysis criteria: rectangularity (parcels very far from or on the contrary very close to their minimum bounding rectangle) and convexity (parcels very far from or on the contrary very close to their convex hull). Mathematical indicators, with a value between 0 and 1, are automatically calculated and integrated into attributes of the shapefile data, which can then be classified. The concentration in a place of very rectangular parcels suggests a regularity that the historical discourse must then analyze: it makes it possible to identify an initial planning (for example a subdivision in an ancient period, including protohistoric) and the updating of this regular form over time in different periods (ancient, medieval, modern, etc.). The concentration in a place of parcels with a strong lack of convexity suggests conflicts of form and makes it possible to identify temporal shifts that result in an inadequacy of inherited spatial structures.

relatedItems.label: Online workshop: Using the Geographical Information System QGIS for data analysis [Video]
relatedItems.description:
This record presents the video from the CESSDA online workshop "Using the Geographical Information System QGIS for data analysis", a hands-on workshop on Geographic Information Systems for social scientists with no experience in QGIS (12 July 2022).
Geographical and georeferenced data are gaining increasing importance in social science research. For example, it is becoming more common to add geographical data related to the social or physical environment as contextual variables to social surveys or to aggregate social survey results at various geographical scales. Using geographical data in our research necessitates additional analytical skills and workflows, usually related to some sort of Geographical Information System (GIS). GIS can be defined as a collection of tools to process, analyze and visualize data containing spatial information; such tools have been developed as “packages” for statistical software R or for the programming language Python, but these require intermediate to advanced coding skills. On the other hand, there are also GIS software solutions by various corporations which may be unaffordable for certain contexts, such as independent researchers of non-governmental organisations.

For this workshop we was using the free and open source software QGIS, which is widely available and fully maintained by a strong community of volunteers and supporting organisations. In addition to the main QGIS software, there is a wide range of training material produced by the QGIS community and many educational and research institutes.

In this workshop, participants learnt how to use QGIS for basic data processing and introductory spatial analysis. They also learnt about common GIS formats, importing data, processing them for further analysis and mapping their results.

Objective: Training events to broaden data analytical skills.

label: QHoD - Digital Scholarly Editions of Habsburg-Ottoman Diplomatic Sources 1500–1918
description:
This project revolves around the production of a historical and critical digital edition of sources on Habsburg–Ottoman diplomacy from the beginnings of diplomatic relations between the Habsburg and the Ottoman Empires at the turn of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries to the demise of both empires at the end of the First World War. This undertaking is a “born-digital edition” and hence makes use of the full potential of digital editing technology. The edited sources are published open access as freely licensed open research data for further use.

The editions include multiple sources of Western and Ottoman origin documenting the diplomatic contacts, namely reports, correspondence, instructions, minutes, invoices, Seyahatnâme and Sefâretnâme, but also published sources (pamphlets and newspaper articles), contractual agreements, maps (or cartographic depictions) and travel reports and diaries. It also includes pictorial sources (legation portraits, allegories, historical paintings etc.) and material culture (e.g. gifts). Sources written in Ottoman Turkish are transliterated and also translated into English.

Due to the broad range of their content, these sources are of great importance to the history of the Habsburg Empire and its successor states, the Ottoman Empire and the Balkan region. They contain a wealth of information on anthropological and cultural topics, the circulation of knowledge, trans-culturalism and empire building. Furthermore, they are of great societal and political relevance beyond the world of scholarship, since they offer profound insights into the historical dimensions of relations between Christianity and Islam and between Europe and Asia as well as Turkey’s involvement in European history.

description:
The RAD-on system is a part of the Integrated Network of Information on Science and Higher Education, which is the biggest, in terms of the scope of collected data, public system in Poland supporting the Ministry of Education and Science and other state agencies in shaping the scientific policy.

The RAD-on system is intended to be used primarily by scientists, students, entrepreneurs, political decision-makers and journalists looking for reliable and up to date information on scientific institutions and on their research. The system offers the following services and functionalities:

Reports. Interactive reports on higher education institutions, students, graduates, academic staff, and research conducted in Poland and abroad. They can be used as one of the tools to create an evidence-based policy

Analyses. Reliable information on issues connected with science and higher education supplemented with extensive comments

Data. Knowledge base on scientific institutions, scientific and artistic activities, academic staff and promotion procedures may prove useful for anyone looking for up to date information and news from the science and higher education sector

User account. Users, whose data are stored in the RAD-on system and its source systems, can view, update and verify their data. To access your personal data, please log in using the login.gov.pl system.

relatedItems.label: Studies on science and higher education system in Poland using the RAD-on platform
relatedItems.description:
In order to answer questions regarding the science or higher education system quality datasets are needed. In this workflow, we guide you through the process of gathering and analysing data about the Polish system of science and higher education using the most up-to-date and reliable open data platform, which is called RAD-on.

The RAD-on system presents reports, analyses, and data on science and higher education in Poland. RAD-on was developed by the National Information Processing Institute in collaboration with the Polish Ministry of Education and Science.

In terms of the data it collects and shares, RAD-on is currently the largest national IT system in science and higher education in Europe. It stores information on nearly all scientific institutions in Poland, as well as their scientists. This includes academic teachers and other individuals who conduct classes at higher education institutions. RAD-on also offers comprehensive lists of scholarly publications, national and international patents, research projects funded by various sources, and institutional investments. It contains extensive information on students, graduates, and on tertiary education programmes.

We hope that the information presented in this workflow will inspire valuable research on science and higher education in Poland. This workflow also serves as an invitation to discuss the future of RAD-on. We are confident that our efforts to promote more widespread understanding of RAD-on will inspire stakeholders to collaborate in the portal’s development and in the enhancement of its efficacy.

label: R Analyzer for Large-Scale Assessments (RALSA)
description:
The R Analyzer for Large-Scale Assessments (RALSA) is an open-source and free cross-platform R package for preparation and analysis of data from large-scale assessments and surveys which use complex sampling and assessment design. Currently, RALSA supports a number of studies with different design and a number of analysis types. RALSA has a comprehensive graphical user interface (GUI) for the non-technical user.
RALSA supports preparation and analysis of data from all cycles of the following studies:
- CivED
- ICCS
- ICILS
- RLII
- PIRLS (including PIRLS Literacy and ePIRLS)
- TIMSS (including TIMSS Numeracy and eTIMSS)
- TiPi (TIMSS and PIRLS joint study)
- TIMSS Advanced
- SITES
- TEDS-M
- PISA
- PISA for Development
- TALIS
- TALIS Starting Strong Survey
- REDS
Currently, RALSA supports the following functionality:
- Prepare data for analysis
  - Download (and optionally convert) studies’ data
  - Convert data (SPSS, or text in case of PISA prior 2015)
  - Merge study data files from different countries and/or respondents
  - View variable properties (name, class, variable label, response categories/unique values, user-defined missings)
  - Data diagnostic tables (quick weighted or unweighted frequencies and descriptives for data inspection and elaborating hypotheses)
   - Recode variables
- Perform analyses (more analysis types will be added in future)
  - Percentages of respondents in groups and their averages on variables of interest
  - Percentiles of continuous variables within groups of respondents
  - Percentages of respondents reaching or surpassing benchmarks of achievement
  - Crosstabulations with Rao-Scott first- and second-order chi-square adjustments
  - Correlations (Pearson or Spearman)
  - Linear regression
  - Binary logistic regression

label: RDMO in Text+
description:
The institutions involved in [Text+ consortium](https://text-plus.org/en/) offer advise to researchers from the very beginning of the research process in all steps of the systematic organisation of their research data. In doing so, we draw on the expertise of our certified data repositories. To guide you through this process and to document your research data in the form of a data management plan, Text+ offers a questionnaire which is closely based on the [Max Weber Foundation’s question catalogue for humanities](https://github.com/rdmorganiser/rdmo-catalog/blob/main/shared/MaxWeberStiftung) and the [standard catalogue of the Research Data Management Organiser (RDMO)](https://github.com/rdmorganiser/rdmo-catalog). It was adapted in collaboration with participants of the Text+ consortium  and expanded with discipline-specific examples. Recently, it also has been revised as part of an [incubator project with DMP4NFDI](https://dmp.services.base4nfdi.de/incubator/).
 The questionnaire is closely linked to our [consulting services](https://text-plus.org/en/daten-dienste/consulting/). Researchers can answer the questions independently or as part of an accompanying consultation with the [Text+ Helpdesk](https://text-plus.org/en/helpdesk/) and deal with the challenges that potentially arise together with one of our Helpdesk Agents. The questionnaire supports you with your self-organisation, but it also helps raising awareness of how to handle research data reasonably and FAIR. 
This offer is explicitly targeted at our community which focusses on language and text-based data. Potential use cases include applications for projects, preparation for the (long-term) storage of research data in corresponding repositories, and the basic organisation of research data.

relatedItems.label: Research Data Management Organiser (RDMO)
relatedItems.description:
The Research Data Management Organiser (RDMO) supports research projects in the planning, implementation and administration of all research data management tasks. 

RDMO is a community effort. The key to the further development of the software is the active participation of interested parties. A selection of working groups with different focuses is therefore available to those who are interested. Becoming part of the community and participating in the technical or content-related further development of RDMO in one of the working groups is highly encouraged. 

All RDMO users and institutions that have their own instance can seek advice and support from the RDMO community.
At the same time, this network of cooperation enables RDMO to take into account requirements and feedback from the specialist sciences, as well as to ensure the exchange and coordination with infrastructure initiatives for data management.

relatedItems.label: RDMO - Max Weber Foundation's platform for research data management
relatedItems.description:
RDMO (Research Data Management Organizer) is a tool that supports you in the structured planning of your data management and the creation of data management plans and text modules for your funding application. Through a structured interview in the form of a suitable questionnaire, the following are thereby

+ considers all important aspects of data management (such as responsibilities, data description, archiving and publication),
+ put collaborative data management on a common basis for agreements,
+ enables the output of a data management plan or individual text modules for your funding application,
+ versioned data management plans for your funding body (e.g. for EU Horizon 2020 projects) via snapshot function.

The Max Weber Foundation - German Humanities Institutes Abroad provides an instance of the RDMO service.

In doing so, we draw on the expertise of our certified data repositories. To guide you through this process and to document your research data in the form of a data management plan, Text+ offers a questionnaire which is closely based on the [Max Weber Foundation’s question catalogue for humanities](https://github.com/rdmorganiser/rdmo-catalog/blob/main/shared/MaxWeberStiftung) and the [standard catalogue of the Research Data Management Organiser (RDMO)](https://github.com/rdmorganiser/rdmo-catalog). It was adapted in collaboration with participants of the Text+ consortium  and expanded with discipline-specific examples. Recently, it also has been revised as part of an [incubator project with DMP4NFDI](https://dmp.services.base4nfdi.de/incubator/).
 The questionnaire is closely linked to our [consulting services](https://text-plus.org/en/daten-dienste/consulting/). Researchers can answer the questions independently or as part of an accompanying consultation with the [Text+ Helpdesk](https://text-plus.org/en/helpdesk/) and deal with the challenges that potentially arise together with one of our Helpdesk Agents. The questionnaire supports you with your self-organisation, but it also helps raising awareness of how to handle research data reasonably and FAIR. 
This offer is explicitly targeted at our community which focusses on language and text-based data. Potential use cases include applications for projects, preparation for the (long-term) storage of research data in corresponding repositories, and the basic organisation of research data.

A selection of working groups with different focuses is therefore available to those who are interested. Becoming part of the community and participating in the technical or content-related further development of RDMO in one of the working groups is highly encouraged. 

All RDMO users and institutions that have their own instance can seek advice and support from the RDMO community.
At the same time, this network of cooperation enables RDMO to take into account requirements and feedback from the specialist sciences, as well as to ensure the exchange and coordination with infrastructure initiatives for data management.

relatedItems.label: Produce and document the communicative event
relatedItems.description:
Conduct the interview session with methodological rigour. The recording, together with all simultaneously produced documents, constitutes the founding document of the oral source.

1. Choose and prepare recording equipment: select recording format according to research type and intended preservation use. Recommended audio format: WAV (uncompressed PCM), sampling frequency 96 kHz (minimum 48 kHz, up to 192 kHz), 24-bit resolution. Recommended video format: MPEG-4 AVC (H.264). Recommended photographic format: RAW at maximum camera resolution. Test all equipment before the session. 
2. Prepare and control the recording environment: minimise ambient noise and interference. Choose a space that allows uninterrupted exchange. Position the microphone to capture the speaker clearly. Where video recording is used, frame and light the space appropriately. Notify all parties present of the recording.
3. Open the recording with contextual identification: at the start of each recording, state aloud the date, location, names of interviewer(s) and interviewee(s) (or a pseudonym code if anonymity is required), the research project title, and confirmation of the participant's authorisation. This spoken header embeds essential metadata directly into the audio or video document.
4. Conduct the interview: practise attentive listening. Do not impose rigid structures. Allow for digressions, which often open unforeseen lines of inquiry. Document non-verbal elements (gestures, pauses, emotional tone) in field notes immediately after the session, while memory is fresh.
5. Close the recording: at the end of the session, restate the participant's authorisation and confirm any conditions they have placed on use. Note the close of the recording aloud. Collect any additional materials the participant may share (photographs, letters, objects for digitisation).
6. Complete the field recording sheet: fill in the field recording sheet immediately after the session. Record: event date and location; names and roles of all persons present; equipment used and recording format; contextual annotations impossible to reconstruct later; references to all documents produced during the same session (audio, video, photographs, written materials). This sheet is the archival backbone of the entire oral source package.
7. Complete individual document sheets: for each distinct document produced (each audio file, each video file, each photograph), fill in a document sheet that functions as a sub-unit of the field recording sheet. Record: unique identifier, file name, format and technical parameters, duration or size, relationship to other documents in the same recording event. Preserve the archival bond between all documents of a single event.

relatedItems.label: Choose tool(s)
relatedItems.description:
Selecting the right tool is a critical step, as it shapes the entire annotation workflow, from data input and collaboration to output formats and interoperability. The choice should be guided by your project’s goals, technical requirements, and the skills of your team. 
- Assess tool compatibility: Compare key tools according to specific requirements. Prioritize tools that natively integrate IIIF manifests and linking with gazetteers and other authority files, support collaborative workflows, comply with standards (e.g., the [Web Annotation Data Model](https://www.w3.org/TR/annotation-model/)), and ensure output interoperability, such as [Recogito Studio](https://recogitostudio.org/). Additional key considerations are: cost and access, training needs and scalability.
- Assess tool extensibility: Evaluate whether the tool allows for customization or expansion through additional services, plugins, APIs, etc. This can be important for adapting the platform to specialized needs, such as gazetteer linking.
- Integrate specialized tools as needed: E.g., if the labels on the map are in an alphabet different from Latin, you might consider using a tool or service for text transliteration/romanization, such as the [Transliteration of Greek characters into Latin](https://transliteration.nlg.gr/?lang=en) tool of the National Library of Greece.

relatedItems.label: Set up the tool(s)
relatedItems.description:
Once you have selected the appropriate tools, it is important to set up the environment that will support effective collaboration, data management, and workflow integration throughout the project. Depending on whether you can have access to an already existing instance of the chosen platform or you need to install the software to your own server (and configure the necessary applications), you might need access to servers and ideally the support of a capable server administrator.
- Set up a collaborative workspace: Establish a shared workspace for coordination, data storage, and version control to streamline teamwork and maintain transparency.
- Finalize tool stack/pipeline: Confirm the tools to be used and how they will interact within your workflow.
- Add plugins if needed: Install any extensions or add-ons required for enhanced functionality, e.g., the [GeoTagger](https://github.com/recogito/plugin-geotagging) plugin for RecogitoStudio.
- Document the tool setup to support reproducibility and long-term maintenance.

relatedItems.label: Collaborative Reusable Map Annotation
relatedItems.description:
Historical maps are valuable resources for humanities research, offering insights into past landscapes and patterns of human activity. Maps are more than images; they represent spatial and cultural relationships that may be anchored to the physical world, and often embed narratives of power, identity, and change, such as shifts in place names or symbolic representations. They vary widely in form, type, content, level of detail, and granularity of the information they present. At the same time they are material objects, cultural artifacts, with distinct physical characteristics and complex biographies of their own. Historical maps also come with challenges: they often lack modern geographic precision, may contain outdated or biased perspectives (which are nonetheless of historical significance), or show signs of physical wear, among other issues. Moreover, access to the information they contain is often limited, as searching through map collection catalogues typically relies on record metadata (i.e., basic information, such as title, creator, or date) and not the full content of the map.
Map annotation provides a means to address these issues by enabling scholars to encode features, comment on the content, link place names to gazetteers or other authority files, transcribe text on maps, document historical or cartographic context, etc. Apart from supporting scholarly analysis, this process can transform static maps into searchable and machine-readable resources, by enriching the map metadata and allowing text search indices (Rainer et al. 2019). 
Developed within the ATRIUM project, this workflow supports collaborative annotation and geo-tagging of historical maps, transforming them into rich multilayer resources. It addresses both technical interoperability and data reusability, with outcomes that can enhance catalog records, improve search capabilities, feed into analytical pipelines, and support data visualizations, or even enable the creation of critical editions of maps. While primarily tested in [Recogito Studio](https://recogitostudio.org/), the workflow is designed as tool-agnostic, ensuring flexibility and reusability across different tools, projects and teams. Its steps are not strictly linear; annotation is an iterative process and teams may revisit earlier phases (e.g., revising vocabularies during annotation) or run tasks in parallel or in alternation (e.g., linking to vocabularies and gazetteers). This iterative design allows teams to adapt to evolving insights and technical constraints. 
Note: This workflow is intended for manual annotation.

**References:**
- Reckziegel, M., Wrisley, D. J., Hixson, T. W., & Jänicke, S. (2021). Visual exploration of historical maps, *Digital Scholarship in the Humanities*, 36 (Supplement_2), ii251–ii272, https://doi.org/10.1093/llc/fqaa059 
- Rainer, S., Vitale, V., Kahn, R., Barker, E. & Isaksen, L. (2019). Revisiting Linking Early Geospatial Documents with Recogito, *e-Perimetron* 14 (3), 152–63, https://www.e-perimetron.org/Vol_14_3/Simon_et_al.pdf

relatedItems.label: Choose how the vocabulary will be maintained and used
relatedItems.description:
This step defines the practical environment in which the vocabulary will be created, edited, used during annotation, and prepared for release. It follows a tool agnostic but tool aware approach: the vocabulary should remain reusable beyond a single annotation tool, while still taking into account how the selected annotation environment can import, display, apply, export, and check vocabulary terms.

**Input**: Vocabulary Design Brief, annotation facets and term sets, Collaborative Reusable Map Annotation Workflow, annotation schema, intended annotation environment, available tools, project resources, team expertise, and publication aims.

**Main actions**: 
1. Review how the annotation environment [^1] can import, display, apply, export, and check vocabulary terms. 
2. Decide what will be treated as the authoritative working source of the vocabulary. 
3. Define the format needed for use in the annotation tool and the intended release or publication format. 
4. Choose the maintenance path that best fits the project. In a tabular and document driven path, the authoritative working source is maintained as a structured table or spreadsheet, with fields such as identifier, preferred label, definition, scope note, broader concept, mapping target, status, source, and editorial note. This path is suitable for projects with limited time, small teams, or no dedicated Semantic Web infrastructure, while still keeping the vocabulary reusable and prepared for possible later SKOS conversion. In a SKOS native path, the vocabulary is managed from the beginning in a vocabulary editor or RDF environment, where concepts, labels, hierarchy, mappings, and identifiers are maintained as part of a semantic resource. 

**Output**: Tooling and implementation profile, selected maintenance path, authoritative working source, annotation tool format, intended release or publication format.

**Format**: Short tooling note, configuration table, README section, spreadsheet documentation sheet, or project documentation page.

[^1]: Recogito Studio is one possible annotation environment for applying or testing the vocabulary. If the selected tool supports only a flat tag list, this list should be treated as a practical derivative of the maintained vocabulary source, not as the authoritative vocabulary itself. Hierarchy, semantic notes, mappings, and documentation should remain in the maintained source.

label: Re.Data
description:
The Re.Data website makes available to the Portuguese research community a set of services related to research data management. 

The Re.Data consortium emerges in the context of the growing importance of managing and sharing data in research and development, and the consequent need to create services and training programs that support the research data lifecycle, in the different planning phases – documenting, processing and analyzing, storing, preserving, publishing and reusing data – establishing these best practices as a priority in scientific institutions in Portugal.
The creation of the Re.Data consortium thus represents a central contribution to ensuring alignment with the development of the EOSC, integration with European electronic infrastructures such as OpenAIRE, EGI, PRACE, GEANT and EUDAT, in a convergence of actions with the main infrastructures of the ESFRI roadmap with a national presence, such as OPERAS, CESSDA, DARIAH, SHARE, MIRRI, LifeWatch, EPOS, ELIXIR and CLARIN, including the implementation of the recommendations and results of the Research Data Alliance (RDA), paving the way for the implementation of national networks within the framework of a European Federation of Open Science.
The Re.Data Project aims to establish and operationalize the Portuguese network to support Research Data Management (RDM) together with the RDM capacity building platform, enabling a networked community of practice to operate three centers of competence in policy, training and support for data curation, with the objective of developing a national research data culture aligned with the FAIR principles to converge with the EOSC.

description:

Users can automatically insert references from their database into their papers and generate formatted bibliographies and manuscripts in seconds.

RefWorks allows you to...

Organize and create a personal database online -- no more index cards to write out and organize. Everything is done automatically as you import the reference into RefWorks.

Format bibliographies and manuscripts in seconds -- this saves hours of typing time and decreases the number of errors in creating tedious bibliographies. Easily make changes to your paper and reformat in seconds.

Import references from a variety of databases using the already created Import Filters.

Manage Alerts -- RefWorks has incorporated a RSS feed reader to allow you to establish links to your favorite RSS feeds and import data from those feeds directly into RefWorks.

Searching your RefWorks database is fast and easy -- RefWorks automatically creates author, descriptor and periodical indexes when importing so you just click on the word to perform the retrieval. The Répertoire International des Sources Musicales (RISM) - International Inventory of Musical Sources - is an international, non-profit organization that aims to comprehensively document extant musical sources worldwide. These primary sources are music manuscripts or printed music editions, writings on music theory, and libretti. They are preserved in libraries, archives, churches, schools and private collections.

RISM was founded in Paris in 1952 and is the largest and only international organization that documents written musical sources. RISM records what exists and where it can be found. As a result, by virtue of being cataloged in a comprehensive inventory, music traditions are protected while also being made available to musicologists and musicians alike. Such work is thus not an end in itself, but leads directly to practical applications.

relatedItems.label: Creation of a Digital Music Edition
relatedItems.description:
A digital edition encodes musical information as structured, machine-readable, and semantically rich data, a transformation that requires a series of methodological and technical decisions. This workflow addresses the full range of operations involved, including the choice of encoding format, the management of metadata, the establishment of relationships with sources, the integration of a critical apparatus, and the conditions for sustainable online publication.
It outlines the essential steps required to produce a scholarly digital music edition, from the initial scoping of the corpus to its long-term archiving and dissemination. Structured around the three pillars of digital editing—tools, content, and presentation—it is designed to ensure compliance with FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) principles throughout the entire lifecycle of the edition.

Developed from the Guide to Digital Music Editing produced by the Consortium-HN MUSICA within the French research infrastructure Huma-Num, this workflow also aligns with the requirements of the European ECHOES project (European Cloud for Heritage Open Science), which frames digital editions as components of digital twins integrating source digitization, musical encoding, and audio recording. It is intended for researchers, digital humanists, and engineers working in institutional contexts shaped by Open Access policies and European research funding frameworks.

label: Repository of Psychological Instruments in Serbian
description: **REPOPSI – Repository of Psychological Instruments in Serbian / Repozitorijum psiholoških instrumenta na srpskom jeziku** is an open repository that enables users to freely access and share psychological instruments in Serbian and other languages. It was established in 2020 by the [Laboratory for Research of Individual Differences (LIRA)](https://lira.f.bg.ac.rs/en/) at the University of Belgrade – Faculty of Philosophy.REPOPSI holds psychological measures, scales, tests, and other instruments commonly used in social and behavioural science research. While it is primarily intended for Serbian instruments (that is, instruments translated/adapted into Serbian or originally developed by local scientists), it also documents English and multilingual instruments. REPOPSI is a growing collection – it currently contains around 200 instrument records, half of which are available in both Serbian and English.REPOPSI increases the visibility and availability of psychological instruments in Serbian and prevents overlapping translation efforts. Being a good starting point for any project, REPOPSI helps researchers and students quickly find the materials they need. Bilingual and multilingual instruments it offers have proven to facilitate participation in multi-country research projects.Instruments found in REPOPSI may be used under the Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International ([CC BY-NC-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/4.0/)) licence. They can be freely accessed and used without permission for noncommercial purposes, provided instrument authors and translators are cited.[Learn how to search REPOPSI.](https://www.repopsi.f.bg.ac.rs/en/how-to-search-repopsi/)[Learn how to contribute to REPOPSI.](https://www.repopsi.f.bg.ac.rs/en/how-to-contribute-to-repopsi/)In 2022, REPOPSI received support from the [EOSC Future](https://eoscfuture.eu/) through the [Research Data Alliance (RDA)](https://www.rd-alliance.org/) Open Call for Cross Disciplinary Science Adoption Grants, for a [project](https://www.rd-alliance.org/repopsi) focused on building the Repository’s technologies needed to improve its user focus, sustainability, findability, and interoperability.Find REPOPSI in  [Open Science Framework](http://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/5ZB8P)  [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/communities/repopsi-rda/)  [re3data](http://doi.org/10.17616/R31NJMV5)  [FAIRsharing](https://fairsharing.org/4918)

label: Research Data Management Organiser (RDMO)
description:
The Research Data Management Organiser (RDMO) supports research projects in the planning, implementation and administration of all research data management tasks. 

RDMO is a community effort. The key to the further development of the software is the active participation of interested parties. A selection of working groups with different focuses is therefore available to those who are interested. Becoming part of the community and participating in the technical or content-related further development of RDMO in one of the working groups is highly encouraged. 

All RDMO users and institutions that have their own instance can seek advice and support from the RDMO community.
At the same time, this network of cooperation enables RDMO to take into account requirements and feedback from the specialist sciences, as well as to ensure the exchange and coordination with infrastructure initiatives for data management.

relatedItems.label: RDMO in Text+
relatedItems.description:
The institutions involved in [Text+ consortium](https://text-plus.org/en/) offer advise to researchers from the very beginning of the research process in all steps of the systematic organisation of their research data. In doing so, we draw on the expertise of our certified data repositories. To guide you through this process and to document your research data in the form of a data management plan, Text+ offers a questionnaire which is closely based on the [Max Weber Foundation’s question catalogue for humanities](https://github.com/rdmorganiser/rdmo-catalog/blob/main/shared/MaxWeberStiftung) and the [standard catalogue of the Research Data Management Organiser (RDMO)](https://github.com/rdmorganiser/rdmo-catalog). It was adapted in collaboration with participants of the Text+ consortium  and expanded with discipline-specific examples. Recently, it also has been revised as part of an [incubator project with DMP4NFDI](https://dmp.services.base4nfdi.de/incubator/).
 The questionnaire is closely linked to our [consulting services](https://text-plus.org/en/daten-dienste/consulting/). Researchers can answer the questions independently or as part of an accompanying consultation with the [Text+ Helpdesk](https://text-plus.org/en/helpdesk/) and deal with the challenges that potentially arise together with one of our Helpdesk Agents. The questionnaire supports you with your self-organisation, but it also helps raising awareness of how to handle research data reasonably and FAIR. 
This offer is explicitly targeted at our community which focusses on language and text-based data. Potential use cases include applications for projects, preparation for the (long-term) storage of research data in corresponding repositories, and the basic organisation of research data.

relatedItems.label: RDMO - Max Weber Foundation's platform for research data management
relatedItems.description:
RDMO (Research Data Management Organizer) is a tool that supports you in the structured planning of your data management and the creation of data management plans and text modules for your funding application. Through a structured interview in the form of a suitable questionnaire, the following are thereby

+ considers all important aspects of data management (such as responsibilities, data description, archiving and publication),
+ put collaborative data management on a common basis for agreements,
+ enables the output of a data management plan or individual text modules for your funding application,
+ versioned data management plans for your funding body (e.g. for EU Horizon 2020 projects) via snapshot function.

The Max Weber Foundation - German Humanities Institutes Abroad provides an instance of the RDMO service.

label: Research Infrastructure for Automatic Text Recognition (ForATR)
description:
ForATR is a pilot project funded by the University of Zurich. Its goal is to establish technical support services for the digital processing of historical sources. The project responds to the growing need for OCR/HTR technologies, data management, and secure archiving in source-based humanities research, and it promotes the implementation of the FAIR principles in the digital processing of text data.
Our methodological approach is based on automatic text recognition (ATR). The use of AI-supported technologies enables more efficient research, the automated creation of standardized text and metadata, and their provision for reuse. We do not develop our own software; instead, we rely on existing solutions, such as commercial tools like Transkribus and open-source applications like eScriptorium, Kraken, OCR4all, and Tesseract, which we adapt to the individual needs of researchers.

label: Research Object Crate (RO-Crate)
description:
RO-Crate is a community effort to establish a lightweight approach to packaging research data with their metadata. It is based on schema.org annotations in JSON-LD, and aims to make best-practice in formal metadata description accessible and practical for use in a wider variety of situations, from an individual researcher working with a folder of data, to large data-intensive computational research environments.

The RO-Crate effort brings together practitioners from very different backgrounds, and with different motivations and use-cases. Among our core target users are: a) researchers engaged with computation and data-intensive, workflow-driven analysis; b) digital repository managers and infrastructure providers; c) individual researchers looking for a straight-forward tool or how-to guide to “FAIRify” their data; d) data stewards supporting research projects in creating and curating datasets.

label: Research Software Directory for Editions Tools
description:
Version 6.4.0 of a curated software platform for scholarly editions developed in Text+/NFDI is now available. 
The platform improves the visibility of software (and its authors) used in the field of scholarly editions. The platform also has the following objectives for the community:

* It provides a curated set of tools and software for working on and with scholarly editions.
* It provides metadata on software for the [Text+ Registry](https://registry.text-plus.org/), especially one of its functions, i.e. an [open registry for scholarly editions](https://registry.text-plus.org/docs/docs/backend-extras/editions).
* It serves as a hub for the further networking of software-related resources such as tutorials, teaching materials and workflows within Text+.
* It is integrated into the overall Text+ portfolio of services, such as the web portal, the Text+ Registry, [Text+ Consulting](https://text-plus.org/en/daten-dienste/consulting/) and the [Text+ Helpdesk](https://text-plus.org/en/helpdesk/).
* The curated data can be integrated into the larger NFDI infrastructure and beyond (e.g. NFDI4Culture Registry and SSH Open Marketplace, EOSC Marketplace)
The participation of the development team in the NFDI basic service [‘NFDI.software’](https://base4nfdi.de/projects/nfdi-software) emphasises the sustainability and interoperability of the platform in order to be able to provide the data beyond the project duration and integrate it into existing databases. This prevents unnecessary parallel structures and isolated solutions from the outset.

label: Research Spotlight
description:
Research Spotlight is an automated workflow designed to demonstrate how texts from scholarly publications can be gradually transformed into structured knowledge graphs. The entire process is ontology driven, meaning that the types of entities and relations to be created are defined in a conceptual framework specifically designed for modeling scholarly work, so that the information is described consistently and can be easily understood and reused by different systems. Along this line, for the population of Scholarly Ontology's core entities and relations, Research Spotlight provides a series of interconnected modules, each dealing with a specific step of the workflow. Using a modular notebook-based setup, it shows how complex academic writing can be broken down into meaningful components such as research methods, activities, and goals, helping learners better understand both the research content and the underlying process.

The workflow is organized into clear, consecutive steps that mirror how humans make sense of research. It begins by identifying important elements in the text, then resolving ambiguities where terms may have multiple meanings, and linking those elements to widely used reference sources. From there, the system highlights how the extracted entities are semantically related to one another, for example which methods are used in which activities and what goals they aim to achieve. Finally all the extracted and interrelated information is transformed into a scholarly knowledge graph adhering to Semantic Web’s linked data standards. Each step is implemented as a separate module, making the process transparent and easy to follow.

By presenting research analysis as a sequence of understandable steps, Research Spotlight serves as a practical teaching tool for topics such as text analysis, knowledge organization, and semantic technologies. It allows learners to experiment with each module of the workflow, observe intermediate results, and gain hands-on insight into how scholarly knowledge can be structured and connected in a systematic and meaningful way.

Registry and recommendation system for controlled vocabularies and authority data in the humanities.

R:hovono is a registry and recommendation system that supports researchers in discovering, creating and reusing controlled vocabularies for humanities research. relatedItems.label: GND Agency Text+
relatedItems.description:
The GND Agency Text+  is a service that is being set up at the Göttingen State and University Library (SUB Göttingen) as part of the NFDI consortium Text+. As a partner of the GND (Integrated Authority File), the agency acts as a central point of contact, initially for projects in the humanities and cultural sciences that are funded by Text+.
This resource is supported by Text+. In case of questions, you may get in touch with the Text+ Helpdesk at textplus-support@gwdg.de.

Die GND-Agentur Text+ ist ein Service, der im Rahmen des NFDI-Programms Text+ an der SUB Göttingen aufgebaut wird. Als Partner der GND (Gemeinsame Normdatei) fungiert die Agentur als zentrale Anlaufstelle zunächst für geistes- und kulturwissenschaftliche Projekte, die im Rahmen des NFDI-Konsortiums Text+ gefördert werden. Langfristig ist geplant, sowohl den Service zu verstetigen als auch das Angebot auf eine breitere Projektlandschaft auszuweiten.

Was machen wir?
Ziel der Agentur ist es, Projekte dabei zu unterstützen, ihre Forschungsdaten als Normdaten in die GND einzubringen.

Dazu gehören:

Die inhaltliche Beratung hinsichtlich der Eignungskriterien von Daten für die GND.
Die Bereitstellung und Weiterentwicklung von entityXML, dem Datenformat für den Austausch von Normdaten zwischen Projekten und Agentur.
Die Bereitstellung einer technischen Umgebung für die Datenverarbeitung auf Grundlage von entityXML .
Das Einspielen von potentiellen Kandidaten in die GND.
Die Bereitstellung von GND-IDs für die Projekte.
Wie unterstützen wir?
Kontaktstelle: Wir sind die erste Anlaufstelle, wenn Sie Ihre Daten in die GND einbringen möchten. Bei projektspezifischem Bedarf vermitteln wir Sie ggf. an eine unserer GND-Partneragenturen weiter.

Beratungsstelle (im Aufbau): Wir beraten Sie bei Fragen rund um die GND und stellen Ihnen Informationsmaterial zur Verfügung.

Datenservice: Wir unterstützen Sie bei der Erstellung von GND-konformen Normdaten. Ihre Daten werden validiert, bereinigt, angereichert und in das für den Dateningest in die GND erforderliche Format konvertiert. Die mit einem GND-ID angereicherten Daten werden von uns an Sie zurückgespielt.

Kontakt: gnd-agentur[at]sub.uni-goettingen.de

relatedItems.label: Integrated Authority File (GND)
relatedItems.description:
The Integrated Authority File (GND) is a service facilitating the collaborative use and administration of authority data. These authority data represent and describe entities, i.e. persons, corporate bodies, conferences and events, geographic entities, topics and works relating to cultural and academic collections. Authority data make cataloguing easier, offer definitive search entries and forge links between different information resources.

It is operated cooperatively by the German National Library, all German-speaking library networks and the associated libraries, the German Union Catalogue of Serials (ZDB) and numerous other institutions. Contributions to the GND are made either via the networks or in direct agreement with the German National Library.

The Common Authority File (GND) is a service for the cooperative use and management of authority data. This authority data represents and describes entities, i.e. persons, corporate bodies, conferences, geographies, subject headings and works that are related to cultural and scientific collections. Standardised data facilitates indexing, provides clear search access points and links different information resources.

relatedItems.label: Musicology and artificial intelligence
relatedItems.description:
This report provides an overview of Artificial Intelligence in European musicological research, addressed to musicologists, librarians, archivists, curators, educators, research-policy officers, infrastructure coordinators, and tool developers. Moving from conceptual foundations to institutional implications, it maps the affordances and limitations of AI-based models and tools for the discipline, while situating them within the European normative landscape defined by the ALLEA European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity, the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, and the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence.

The six complementary sections successively address: (1) methodological foundations, clarifying notions of model, tool, and critical posture, and surveying audio-, image-, encoding-, and language-model-based applications such as automatic music transcription, optical music recognition, score-audio alignment, automated analysis, reconstruction, and LLM prompt­ing; (2) data infrastructure, covering FAIR/CARE governance, ontologies and persistent identifiers, European federated infra­structures, auditory digital twins, and risks of fragmentation, representational bias, quality variability, and copyright; (3) a continuation of the disciplinary stakes involved in source and corpus processing; (4) musicological education in the age of AI, including curricular redesign, AI literacy, and design models such as the Two-Lane Approach; (5) professional practices and responsibilities, examining scholarly credibility, intellectual property, academic integrity frameworks, cultural and creative industry collaborations, institutional and legal risks, gender equality, and lessons from organised labour; and (6) best practic­es, articulating methodological pluralism against technological determinism and formalising principles of ethical reflexivity, human oversight, explainability, reproducibility, and accountability.

relatedItems.label: Historical Musicology and European Research Infrastructures and Initiatives: A Practical Guide and Strategic Integration Framework
relatedItems.description:
This publication addresses a major structural challenge facing historical musicology: although the field has developed rich bodies of sources, methods, and scholarly traditions, it remains only partially integrated into the European research infrastructure ecosystem that increasingly shapes access to data, tools, funding, collaboration, and long-term preservation. Focusing on five key European infrastructures and initiatives—the European Open Science Cloud (EOSC), the European Collaborative Cloud for Cultural Heritage (ECCCH/ECHOES), the Common European Data Space for Cultural Heritage, DARIAH ERIC, and E-RIHS ERIC—the report examines how these frameworks can support historical musicology through digitisation, encoding, analysis, interoperability, data sharing, and sustainable reuse.

The publication maps these infrastructures against the concrete workflows and needs of musicological research, from source study and editorial practice to heritage science, digital annotation, and collaborative knowledge production. It combines a systematic presentation of the European infrastructural landscape with a series of use cases designed to test how different categories of users—researchers, librarians, curators, musicians, students, policymakers, and journalists—engage with existing tools and where significant gaps remain. On this basis, it proposes a strategic framework for integrating musicology more fully into European digital and heritage infrastructures without abandoning the disciplinary expertise that defines the field.

The report argues that such integration is not only possible but increasingly urgent. As European research becomes more strongly organized around openness, interoperability, shared standards, and collaborative environments, historical musicology risks marginalisation if it does not strengthen its presence within these infrastructures. By identifying practical entry points, institutional pathways, and methodological opportunities, this publication presents research infrastructures not as external technical systems, but as essential conditions for the future visibility, sustainability, and transformation of musicological scholarship in Europe and beyond.

label: Ricgraph - Research in context graph
description:
Ricgraph, also known as Research in context graph, enables the exploration of researchers, teams, their results, collaborations, skills, projects, and the relations between these items.
Ricgraph can store many types of items into a single graph.  These items can be obtained from various systems and from multiple organizations. Ricgraph facilitates reasoning about these items because it infers new relations between items, relations that are not present in any of the separate source systems. It is flexible and extensible, and can be adapted to new application areas.
Throughout this text, we illustrate how Ricgraph works by applying it to the application area research information.

Motivation
Ricgraph, also known as Research in context graph, is software that is about relations between items. These items can be collected from various source systems and from multiple organizations. We explain how Ricgraph works by applying it to the application area research information. We show the insights that can be obtained by combining information from various source systems, insight arising from new relations that are not present in each separate source system.
Research information is about anything related to research: research results, the persons in a research team, their collaborations, their skills, projects in which they have participated, as well as the relations between these entities. Examples of research results are publications, data sets, and software.
Example use cases from the application area research information are:
(1) As a journalist, I want to find researchers with a certain skill and their publications, so that I can interview them for a newspaper article.
(2) As a librarian, I want to enrich my local research information system with research results that are in other systems but not in ours, so that we have a more complete view of research at our university.
(3) As a researcher, I want to find researchers from other universities that have co-authored publications written by the co-authors of my own publications, so that I can read their publications to find out if we share common research interests.
These use cases use different types of information (called items): researchers, skills, publications, etc. Most often, these types of information are not stored in one system, so the use cases may be difficult or time-consuming to answer. However, by using Ricgraph, these use cases (and many others) are easy to answer.
Although this text illustrates Ricgraph in the application area research information, the principle "relations between items from various source systems" is general, so Ricgraph can be used in other application areas.

Main contributions of Ricgraph
(1) Ricgraph can store many types of items in a single graph.
(2) Ricgraph harvests multiple source systems into a single graph.
(3) Ricgraph Explorer is the exploration tool for Ricgraph.
(4) Ricgraph facilitates reasoning about items because it infers new relations between items.
(5) Ricgraph can be tailored for an application area.

Read more about Ricgraph
For a gentle introduction in Ricgraph, read the reference publication: Rik D.T. Janssen (2024). Ricgraph: A flexible and extensible graph to explore research in context from various systems. SoftwareX, 26(101736). https://doi.org/10.1016/j.softx.2024.101736
The website for Ricgraph can be found at https://www.ricgraph.eu
The documentation website for Ricgraph can be found at https://docs.ricgraph.eu
Extensive documentation, publications, videos and source code can be found in the GitHub repository https://github.com/UtrechtUniversity/ricgraph

relatedItems.label: ROSSIO Infrastructure: a digital research tool for Social Sciences, Arts and Humanities
relatedItems.description: ROSSIO Infrastructure is building an open-access and free platform that aims to aggregate, organise and connect digital resources related to Social Sciences, Arts and Humanities located in Portuguese educational and cultural institutions. This paper aims to present ROSSIO infrastructure, the institutions involved, its main goals and the services it will provide, such as a discovery portal, exhibitions, collections and a virtual research environment. Underlying these services is a metadata aggregation approach that brings into ROSSIO the metadata on digital objects from the providing institutions. The aggregated dataset is transformed into linked data and enriched with entities from controlled vocabularies, which are defined by ROSSIO. We will detail this process, including the applications employed and how they interoperate. Finally, we will conclusively reflect on the potentialities of these services for public dissemination of science, taking into account the FAIR principles.
