relatedItems.label: Choose a transcription system
relatedItems.description:
Multiple transcription systems have been developed for the documentation of Italian dialects. Each reflects different theoretical assumptions and historical traditions of study. The choice of system must be made deliberately, as it conditions both the nature of the categories used and the interoperability of the resulting data.

Widely used among Italian dialectologists is the “Ascoli–Merlo” system. With some modifications, this system was employed in a major documentation project of the Italian dialect heritage known as the “Carta dei Dialetti Italiani”. Substantially different transcription systems were used in works of fundamental importance for Italian dialectology, namely the “Atlante Italo Svizzero” (AIS) and the “Atlante Linguistico Italiano” (ALI). To this plurality of systems, the IPA was added in the second half of the twentieth century, initially facing resistance among Italian dialectologists and only becoming widely established in recent decades. The "Rivista Italiana di Dialettologia" adopts the IPA system. However, its first issue also proposed a simplified transcription system based on Italian orthography.

The existence of multiple systems does not merely represent a variation in symbols: each embodies a different approach to the categorisation and classification of phonetic reality, and must be understood within the historical and theoretical context in which it was developed.

For any new transcription project, the use of the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) is strongly recommended. The IPA is the most widely used phonetic transcription system internationally, grounded in a modern and consolidated phonetic theory. It offers extensive documentation of its symbols and principles, remains relatively stable over time, and provides a flexible yet relatively simple system: the most phonologically relevant distinctions are represented through alphabetic symbols, while diacritics allow for finer phonetic detail. It is also supported by extensive reference materials, including the Illustrations of the IPA series.

If your project is already underway and uses a non-IPA or mixed transcription system, you are not required to convert it to IPA. However, you should provide clear and exhaustive documentation of all symbols employed and of the transcription practices adopted. In this context, the IPA can serve as a metalinguistic reference to clarify the phonetic values of non-standard symbols. If you decide to attempt a conversion to IPA, you should keep in mind that transcription systems are not strictly isomorphic, and that a one-to-one correspondence between symbols is not always possible. Any conversion should therefore preserve the original transcriptions, which users should always remain able to consult.

In some contexts — particularly for dialects with an existing written tradition — transcriptions seek a compromise between orthographic local spelling conventions and phonetic notation; in such cases, all non-standard symbols used must be explicitly listed and linked to their IPA equivalent to ensure interpretability for any reader.

An example of a mixed approach is the orthographic system used to render Neapolitan dialect dialogue in Italian cinema. Stromboli ("Il dialetto sul grande schermo. Il napoletano nella storia del cinema italiano", Firenze, Cesati, 2022) follows the written tradition of Neapolitan, itself based on Italian orthography, while adding a small number of phonetic symbols from different sources. The following extract is from a scene in Massimo Troisi's "Ricomincio da tre":

"E cchéllə ca dico iə, cu tutt' 'a ggènte ca čə sta a Nnapulə pròpio nu móstrə éva vənì 'e cas' affianc' a mme?'"

Here, the schwa symbol [ə] is used to represent the unstressed indistinct vowels typical of Neapolitan, and ‹č› stands for IPA [tʃ] (as in čə = 'there is' where čə = [tʃ]). These conventions must be explicitly glossed in any published transcription.

relatedItems.label: Learn or review your transcription system
relatedItems.description: Whichever system you adopt, a solid command of its symbols and conventions is essential before beginning. Study the relevant charts and reference materials carefully, paying particular attention to the sounds present in the dialect you are documenting. If working with IPA — the recommended choice — the authoritative references are the "Handbook of the International Phonetic Association" (Cambridge UP, 1999) and the Illustrations series published in the Journal of the International Phonetic Association, which provides transcribed samples of many languages and dialect varieties. For a broader and more comprehensive understanding of the modern phonetic theory underlying the IPA system, you should also consult J. Laver ("Principles of Phonetics", Cambridge UP, 1994).

label: HBIM and Information Management for Knowledge and Conservation of Architectural Heritage: A Review
description:
Abstract

This paper presents a comprehensive review of research on Historic Building Information Modeling (HBIM), focusing on its role as a tool for managing knowledge and supporting conservation practices of Architectural Heritage. While previous review articles and most research works have predominantly addressed geometric modeling—given its significant challenges in the context of historic buildings—this study places greater emphasis on the integration of non-geometric data within the BIM environment. A systematic search was conducted in the Scopus database to extract the 451 relevant publications analyzed in this review, covering the period from 2008 to mid-2024. A bibliometric analysis was first performed to identify trends in publication types, geographic distribution, research focuses, and software usage. The main body of the review then explores three core themes in the development of the information system: the definition of model entities, both semantic and geometric; the data enrichment phase, incorporating historical, diagnostic, monitoring and conservation-related information; and finally, data use and sharing, including on-site applications and interoperability. For each topic, the review highlights and discusses the principal approaches documented in the literature, critically evaluating the advantages and limitations of different information management methods with respect to the distinctive features of the building under analysis and the specific objectives of the information model.

relatedItems.label: 3D-HBIM workflow
relatedItems.description:
The 3D-Heritage Building Information Modelling (HBIM) workflow provides a comprehensive approach for the 3D geometric and parametric modelling of built heritage, and its subsequent enrichment with diverse discipline data related to a built asset’s context, environment, conservation reports and other scientific analysis materials, as well as historical information. It contributes to structuring and enhancing the value of information about built heritage enabling integrated, multidisciplinary, and cross-sectoral collaboration on built heritage preservation and conservation. It recommends the use of accessible open science practices, services and tools that respect existing interoperability standards for streamlining the process of built heritage digitisation, modelling, and information sharing.

### Requirements

- Open science (e.g., use of open standards and metadata schemas for improving data and models interoperability)
- Accessible, open‑source services and tools

### Implementation

Use of open standards and testing of free tools and services for built heritage advanced digitisation, integrating reality capture, scan-to-BIM, and multidisciplinary structured information aggregation. It includes data FAIRness (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) enhancement, geometric modelling and enrichment, and consolidated digital representation of built heritage.

label: Heritage building information modeling (HBIM) for heritage conservation: Framework of challenges, gaps, and existing limitations of HBIM
description:
Abstract
This study investigates the pivotal role of Heritage Building Information Modeling (HBIM) in conservation of cultural heritage buildings. Utilizing a systematic literature review and in-depth analysis of 59 studies within 2013–23 period, the study underscores HBIM's capacity to document, analyze, and manage heritage structures. It delineates the workflow from data acquisition through laser scanning and photogrammetry, to the modeling of historic fabric, highlighting the integration of digital technologies in conservation practices. The paper identifies key challenges in HBIM adoption, including technical limitations, the need for specialized skills, and the complexity of accurately modeling historical details. It proposes avenues for future research focused on enhancing data acquisition techniques, improving the interoperability of HBIM with other digital tools, and developing standards for the effective documentation of heritage sites. The findings advocate for a collaborative approach, leveraging HBIM to foster interdisciplinary partnerships between architects, historians, and conservationists, for sustainable preservation of cultural heritage.

label: Historical Musicology and European Research Infrastructures and Initiatives: A Practical Guide and Strategic Integration Framework
description:
This publication addresses a major structural challenge facing historical musicology: although the field has developed rich bodies of sources, methods, and scholarly traditions, it remains only partially integrated into the European research infrastructure ecosystem that increasingly shapes access to data, tools, funding, collaboration, and long-term preservation. Focusing on five key European infrastructures and initiatives—the European Open Science Cloud (EOSC), the European Collaborative Cloud for Cultural Heritage (ECCCH/ECHOES), the Common European Data Space for Cultural Heritage, DARIAH ERIC, and E-RIHS ERIC—the report examines how these frameworks can support historical musicology through digitisation, encoding, analysis, interoperability, data sharing, and sustainable reuse.

The publication maps these infrastructures against the concrete workflows and needs of musicological research, from source study and editorial practice to heritage science, digital annotation, and collaborative knowledge production. It combines a systematic presentation of the European infrastructural landscape with a series of use cases designed to test how different categories of users—researchers, librarians, curators, musicians, students, policymakers, and journalists—engage with existing tools and where significant gaps remain. On this basis, it proposes a strategic framework for integrating musicology more fully into European digital and heritage infrastructures without abandoning the disciplinary expertise that defines the field.

The report argues that such integration is not only possible but increasingly urgent. As European research becomes more strongly organized around openness, interoperability, shared standards, and collaborative environments, historical musicology risks marginalisation if it does not strengthen its presence within these infrastructures. By identifying practical entry points, institutional pathways, and methodological opportunities, this publication presents research infrastructures not as external technical systems, but as essential conditions for the future visibility, sustainability, and transformation of musicological scholarship in Europe and beyond.

GitHub is a web-based repository service which offers the distributed revision control and source code management (SCM) functionality of GIT with a graphical user interface, desktop, and mobile integration. Projects on GitHub can be accessed and manipulated using the git command-line interface and all of the standard git commands work with it. GitHub also allows registered and non-registered users to browse public repositories on the site. Multiple desktop clients have also been created by GitHub and other third parties which integrate with the platform.

GitHub is mainly used for code but can also be used for non-code files, it supports the following formats and features:

3D render files

Photoshop's native PSD format can be previewed and compared to previous versions of the same file.

Nested task-lists

Documentation and wikis

Small websites can be hosted from public repositories on GitHub. The URL format is http://projectname.github.io.

Issue tracking (including feature requests)

Visualization of geospatial data

Gantt charts

GitHub is a heavily used in the opensource development community but does not require hosted projects to meet the definition of Open Source.

label: ICON: An Ontology for Comprehensive Artistic Interpretations
description: In this work, we introduce ICON, an ontology that models artistic interpretations of artworks’ subject matter (i.e., iconographies) and meanings (i.e., symbols, iconological aspects). Developed by conceptualizing authoritative knowledge and notions taken from Panofsky’s levels of interpretation theory, ICON ontology focuses on the granularity of interpretations. It can be used to describe an interpretation of an artwork from the pre-iconographical, icongraphical, and iconological levels. Its main classes have been aligned to ontologies that come from the domains of cultural descriptions (ArCo, CIDOC-CRM, VIR), semiotics (DOLCE), bibliometrics (CITO), and symbolism (Simulation Ontology), to grant a robust schema that can be extendable using additional classes and properties coming from these ontologies. The ontology was evaluated through competency questions that range from simple recognition on a specific level of interpretation to complex scenarios. Data written using this model was compared to state-of-the-art ontologies and schemas to both highlight the current lack of a domain-specific ontology on art interpretation and show how our work fills some of the current gaps. The ontology is openly available and compliant with FAIR principles. With our ontology, we hope to encourage digital art historians working for cultural institutions in making more detailed linked open data about the content of their artifacts, to exploit the full potential of Semantic Web in linking artworks through not only subjects and common metadata but also specific symbolic interpretations, intrinsic meanings, and the motifs through which their subjects are represented. Additionally, by basing our work on theories made by different art history scholars in the last century, we make sure that their knowledge and studies will not be lost in the transition to the digital, linked open data era.

For publishing, it is recommended to adhere to the FAIR principles. These include using open standard file formats (.IFC) and persistent identifiers (e.g., DOIs) to enhance findability and ensure long-term interoperability, open licences for enabling reuse, and open or accessible and secure data repositories.
The repository selection should account for best data management and information system practices, as compliance with relevant standards (e.g., ISO 14721 - OAIS reference model), including comprehensive documentation, security, and integrity. relatedItems.label: Learn or review your transcription system
relatedItems.description: Whichever system you adopt, a solid command of its symbols and conventions is essential before beginning. Study the relevant charts and reference materials carefully, paying particular attention to the sounds present in the dialect you are documenting. If working with IPA — the recommended choice — the authoritative references are the "Handbook of the International Phonetic Association" (Cambridge UP, 1999) and the Illustrations series published in the Journal of the International Phonetic Association, which provides transcribed samples of many languages and dialect varieties. For a broader and more comprehensive understanding of the modern phonetic theory underlying the IPA system, you should also consult J. Laver ("Principles of Phonetics", Cambridge UP, 1994).

relatedItems.label: Become familiar with the IPA transcription system
relatedItems.description: Before transcribing, annotators should familiarize themselves with the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA), the most widely used phonetic alphabet, developed and maintained by the International Phonetic Association. The IPA Chart organizes consonants, vowels, and diacritics into tables structured according to phonetic-theoretical parameters (place and manner of articulation, voicing, vowel height and backness, rounding, etc.) rather than as an arbitrary inventory of symbols; understanding this underlying theoretical structure makes the choice of symbols more principled and consistent. The IPA Chart itself, together with downloadable fonts, a phonetic keyboard for Unicode text input, and a broad census of freely available phonetic resources (audio and video illustrations, pronunciation dictionaries, teaching materials), can be consulted and freely downloaded from the International Phonetic Association's website under a CC BY-SA 3.0 licence. A particularly useful external resource is the Seeing Speech portal, which offers interactive IPA tables: clicking on each symbol gives access to an audio example and to visualizations of the moving articulatory organs producing that sound.

label: Il sistema di trascrizione dell’Atlante Linguistico Mediterraneo  tra principi teorico-metodologici e prassi trascrittorie
description: This contribution traces the history of the Atlante Linguistico Mediterraneo transcription system, from its first formulation to the subsequent modifications that needed to be made after the fieldwork campaigns. The theoretical-methodological choices made by the promoters of this enterprise are investigated, as well as the phonetic practices of the fieldworkers who often departed from the original prescriptions. In the context of the works for the recovery and publication of the Atlas, and in relation to the strategies of normalization and simplification of the transcriptions that we are planning, it is more than ever appropriate to mature an overview of the evolution of the ALM transcription system and of the theoretical-methodological principles on which this was grounded. Every intervention on the transcriptions must indeed be consistent with these principles, so as to ensure the philological correctness of the operations. The main differences with the IPA transcription system are also summarized. This comparison will help to clarify the specificities of the ALM transcription system, and to correctly evaluate the opportunity and the modalities of a procedure for converting the ALM transcriptions into the IPA system.

relatedItems.label: Choose a transcription system
relatedItems.description:
Multiple transcription systems have been developed for the documentation of Italian dialects. Each reflects different theoretical assumptions and historical traditions of study. The choice of system must be made deliberately, as it conditions both the nature of the categories used and the interoperability of the resulting data.

Widely used among Italian dialectologists is the “Ascoli–Merlo” system. With some modifications, this system was employed in a major documentation project of the Italian dialect heritage known as the “Carta dei Dialetti Italiani”. Substantially different transcription systems were used in works of fundamental importance for Italian dialectology, namely the “Atlante Italo Svizzero” (AIS) and the “Atlante Linguistico Italiano” (ALI). To this plurality of systems, the IPA was added in the second half of the twentieth century, initially facing resistance among Italian dialectologists and only becoming widely established in recent decades. The "Rivista Italiana di Dialettologia" adopts the IPA system. However, its first issue also proposed a simplified transcription system based on Italian orthography.

The existence of multiple systems does not merely represent a variation in symbols: each embodies a different approach to the categorisation and classification of phonetic reality, and must be understood within the historical and theoretical context in which it was developed.

For any new transcription project, the use of the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) is strongly recommended. The IPA is the most widely used phonetic transcription system internationally, grounded in a modern and consolidated phonetic theory. It offers extensive documentation of its symbols and principles, remains relatively stable over time, and provides a flexible yet relatively simple system: the most phonologically relevant distinctions are represented through alphabetic symbols, while diacritics allow for finer phonetic detail. It is also supported by extensive reference materials, including the Illustrations of the IPA series.

If your project is already underway and uses a non-IPA or mixed transcription system, you are not required to convert it to IPA. However, you should provide clear and exhaustive documentation of all symbols employed and of the transcription practices adopted. In this context, the IPA can serve as a metalinguistic reference to clarify the phonetic values of non-standard symbols. If you decide to attempt a conversion to IPA, you should keep in mind that transcription systems are not strictly isomorphic, and that a one-to-one correspondence between symbols is not always possible. Any conversion should therefore preserve the original transcriptions, which users should always remain able to consult.

In some contexts — particularly for dialects with an existing written tradition — transcriptions seek a compromise between orthographic local spelling conventions and phonetic notation; in such cases, all non-standard symbols used must be explicitly listed and linked to their IPA equivalent to ensure interpretability for any reader.

An example of a mixed approach is the orthographic system used to render Neapolitan dialect dialogue in Italian cinema. Stromboli ("Il dialetto sul grande schermo. Il napoletano nella storia del cinema italiano", Firenze, Cesati, 2022) follows the written tradition of Neapolitan, itself based on Italian orthography, while adding a small number of phonetic symbols from different sources. The following extract is from a scene in Massimo Troisi's "Ricomincio da tre":

"E cchéllə ca dico iə, cu tutt' 'a ggènte ca čə sta a Nnapulə pròpio nu móstrə éva vənì 'e cas' affianc' a mme?'"

Here, the schwa symbol [ə] is used to represent the unstressed indistinct vowels typical of Neapolitan, and ‹č› stands for IPA [tʃ] (as in čə = 'there is' where čə = [tʃ]). These conventions must be explicitly glossed in any published transcription.

label: Impact of Image Enhancement Methods on Automatic Transcription Trainings with eScriptorium
description: This study stems from the Desenrollando el cordel (Untangling the cordel) project, which focuses on 19th-century Spanish prints editing. It evaluates the impact of image enhancement methods on the automatic transcription of low-quality documents, both in terms of printing and digitisation. We compare different methods (binarisation, deblur) and present the results obtained during the training of models with the Kraken tool. We demonstrate that binarisation methods give better results than the other, and that the combination of several techniques did not significantly improve the transcription prediction. This study shows the significance of using image enhancement methods with Kraken. It paves the way for further experiments with larger and more varied corpora to help future projects design their automatic transcription workflow.

relatedItems.label: FoNDUE - Une infrastructure HTR pour Genève
relatedItems.description:
L’HTR (​Handwritten Text Recognition​), parfois aussi appelé OCR (​Optical character recognition​), devient un besoin de plus en plus urgent des équipes de l’UNIGE. L’enjeu est le suivant : extraire rapidement et efficacement un maximum d’informations d’une page numérisée, dont évidemment la transcription mais pas uniquement (illustrations, mise en page...), et reproduire cette opération sur des grandes quantités de documents. L'obtention de ces données, désormais cruciales pour concevoir les grands corpus nécessaires à la recherche en lettres, implique des besoins informatiques nouveaux et très importants.

Plutôt que de sous-traiter un besoin essentiel à des sociétés (semi-)privées offrant des conditions scientifiques et légales parfois insatisfaisantes, l'Université de Genève a décidé de proposer un service local a adapté à tous les besoins (du travail de fin d'études au projet FNS). Concernant la partie logiciel, le choix s’est porté sur ​eScriptorium, une application en ligne proposant une solution intégralement ​open source​, déjà mature d’un point de vue technique (plusieurs années de développement) et bénéficiant de soutiens internationaux (France, USA, Allemagne…) qui en garantissent la fiabilité et l'efficacité.

L'outil final devrait être inclus dans l’offre du Portail DH de l’UNIGE, qui dispose déjà d’éléments d’infrastructure permettant d’envisager une articulation intelligente de ses outils pour les chercheurs.ses : un serveur IIIF qui sert des documents numérisés en format image, une instance de TEI Publisher pour la publication de documents (édition et corpus) en TEI.

This local service, based on eScriptorium, allows researchers at UNIGE and other Swiss universities to use HTR services.

relatedItems.label: DaSCH - Swiss National Data and Service Center for the Humanities
relatedItems.description: DaSCH is the trusted platform and partner for open research data in the Humanities. DaSCH develops and operates a FAIR long-term repository and a generic virtual research environment for open research data in the humanities in Switzerland. We provide long-term direct access to the data, enable their continuous editing and allow for precise citation of single objects within a dataset. We ensure interoperability with tools used by the Humanities and Cultural Sciences communities and foster the use of standards. The development of our platform happens in close cooperation with these communities. We provide training and advice in the area of research data management, promote open data and the use of standards. DaSCH is the coordinating institution and representative of Switzerland in the European Research Infrastructure Consortium ‘Digital Research Infrastructure for the Arts and Humanities’ (DARIAH ERIC). Within this mandate, we actively engage in community building within Switzerland and abroad. DaSCH cooperates with national and international organizations and initiatives in order to provide services that are fit for purpose within the broader Swiss open research data landscape and that are coordinated with other institutions such as FORS. We base our actions on the values reliability, flexibility, appreciation, curiosity, and persistence. Furthermore, DARIAH’s activities in Switzerland are coordinated by DaSCH and DaSCH is acting as DARIAH-CH Coordination Office.

relatedItems.label: Indexing an Audio Resource
relatedItems.description: Conceived and employed by the ORMETE project (Oralità, Memoria, Teatro), directed by Donatella Orecchia (Università di Roma Tor Vergata), this workflow allows a researcher or curator to produce a segment-based index of an audio or an audiovisual resource. Rather than replacing the recording with a transcription, this process structures the resource into titled, synopsised, and keyworded segments, enabling users to navigate directly to specific points in the interview and locate content by person, place, or institution. By preserving the double voice of interviewer and interviewee at segment level and by using indexing — rather than transcription — as the primary access tool, the workflow supports listening to the original recording as the main mode of engagement with the source, in line with the stated aim of guiding and educating listening. This kind of indexing can be carried out either through OHMS (Oral History Metadata Synchronizer) or without the support of any dedicated application. The output is a reviewed, structured index suitable for publication.

relatedItems.label: Oral History Metadata Synchronizer
relatedItems.description:
OHMS (Oral History Metadata Synchronizer) inexpensively and efficiently enhances access to oral history by providing users with word-level search capability and a time-correlated transcript or indexed interview connecting the textual search term to the corresponding moment in the recorded interview online.

OHMS is an open source, web-based application designed to improve the user experience you provide for oral history, no matter what CMS or repository you use. There are 2 main components of the OHMS system

OHMS Application: The OHMS application is where the work is done. This is the back-end, web-based application where interviews are imported, and metadata is created. In the OHMS application transcripts are time-coded and/or interviews are indexed. Upon completion, the interview record (including the synchronized transcript and/or time-coded index) are exported as an XML file. When located on a web server, the OHMS XML file is what interfaces with your content management system through the OHMS Viewer.

OHMS Viewer: The OHMS viewer is the user interface of ohms. When an interview is called by the repository, the OHMS viewer loads, calling select interview level metadata and the intra interview level metadata created in the OHMS Application from the corresponding xml file.

label: Information Organization and Access in Digital Humanities: TaDiRAH Revised, Formalized and FAIR
description:
Classifying and categorizing the activities that comprise the digital humanities (DH) has been a longstanding area of interest for many practitioners in this field, fueled by ongoing attempts to define the field both within the academic and public sphere. Several European initiatives are currently shaping advanced research infrastructures that would benefit from an implementation of a suiting taxonomy. Therefore, new humanities and information science collaborations have been formed to provide a service that meets their needs. 

This working paper presents the transformation of the Taxonomy of Digital Research Activities in the Humanities (TaDiRAH) in order to make it machine-readable and become a formalized taxonomy. This includes the methodology and realization containing a complete revision of the original version, decisions in modelling, the implementation as well as organization of ongoing and future tasks. TaDiRAH addresses a wide range of humanities disciplines and integrates application areas from philologies as well as epigraphy, and musicology to name just a few. For this reason, the decision in favor of SKOS was made purely pragmatically in terms of technology, concept and domains. New language versions can now be easily integrated and low-threshold term extensions can be carried out via Wikidata. The new TaDiRAH not only represents a knowledge organization system ( KOS ) which has recently been released as version 2.0. According to the FAIR principles this new version improves the Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, and Reuse of research data and digital assets in the digital humanities.

label: Integrating Semantic and Statistical Features for Authorial Clustering of Qumran Scrolls
description: We present a novel framework for authorial classification and clustering of the Qumran Dead Sea Scrolls (DSS). Our approach com-bines modern Hebrew BERT embeddings with traditional natural language processing features in a graph neural network (GNN) architecture. Our results outperform baseline methods on both the Dead Sea Scrolls and a validation dataset of the Hebrew Bible. In particular, we leverage our model to provide significant insights into long-standing debates, including the classification of sectarian and non-sectarian texts and the division of the Hodayot collection of hymns.

label: Integrating Terminological and Ontological Principles into a Lexicographic Resource
description:
This paper/presentation addresses the research being held at the NOVA FCSH-CLUNL within MORDigital - a lexicographic project that aims to produce digital versions of the first three editions (1789; 1813; 1823) of the Diccionario da Lingua Portugueza by António de Morais Silva. The Morais dictionary represents a great legacy, since it marks the beginning of Portuguese dictionaries, having served as a model for all subsequent lexicographic production throughout the 19th and 20th centuries. MORDigital follows a new paradigm in lexicography, which results from the convergence between lexicography, terminology, computational linguistics, and ontologies as an integral part of digital humanities and linked (open) data, aligned with the FAIR principles. In the Portuguese context, this research project fills a gap with regard to searchable online retrodigitised dictionaries, built on current standards and methodologies which promote data sharing and harmonisation, namely TEI Lex-0, LMF and Ontolex-Lemon. This research project is connected to ROSSIO Infrastructure’s Controlled Vocabularies, and it aims to further ensure the connection to other existing systems and lexical resources, particularly in the Portuguese-speaking world.

The ROSSIO vocabularies are a set of concept schemes in the social sciences, arts and humanities for facilitating knowledge organization in the platform. There are presently core vocabularies for Agents, Places, Periods and Topics. The ROSSIO Infrastructure may also host vocabularies provided by its partners, or for specific functions within the platform.

Controlled vocabularies
A controlled vocabulary is an authorized list of concepts in a discipline or subject designated by terms or codes. The concepts in a controlled vocabulary are often placed in hierarchies of broader/narrower concepts and networks of related concepts.

Thesauri, classifications, name authority lists and gazetteers are types of controlled vocabularies. Their function is to organize knowledge and provide linguistic and/or non-linguistic means of accessing the concepts in a discipline or subject.

Services for controlled vocabularies
The ROSSIO Infrastructure enables the construction and management of vocabularies in SKOS through VocBench 3 for authorized users.

The vocabularies are hosted through Skosmos. This tool allows users to browse the vocabularies and allows them to be published on the Web as linked data.

description:
In the field of Humanities and Social Sciences, the production of digital or scanned data has increased considerably in recent years. These data, which are usually very expensive to produce, are often lost at the end of the project. They are therefore rarely reused, due to a lack of financial, human and technical resources of the communities that produced them.

The TGIR Huma-Num, whose mission is to facilitate the digital turn in Humanities and Social Sciences research, offers services dedicated to the production and reuse of data. These services aim at avoiding loss and facilitating the re-use of scientific data. To do this, Huma-Num supports research teams throughout their digital projects to allow the sharing, reuse and preservation of data thanks to a chain of devices focused on interoperability.

Some of the challenges of Digital Humanities are tasks related to interoperability between databases, such as documentation, alignment, migration and publication. **HEIMDALL** is a tool for converting more easily one or more databases from one format to another.

If, for example, you find yourself in one of the following situations…

- you need to **access** data, but it is not stored in a format compatible with your favorite software…
- you’d prefer to **merge** several heterogeneous databases into a single corpus, easier to analyze…
- you’re considering which format to use for your software or database…
- you want to make data more **accessible** and **interoperable**…

… then HEIMDALL can offer you an exchange format, and abstract the details of data implementation: yours, but also those of others.
Thanks to HEIMDALL, you can also switch from one technology to another in a matter of moments, as and when you need to, without ever losing, disorganizing or corrupting your data –or even by improving them over time, documenting them and linking them to current standards in your field.

In a nutshell, HEIMDALL is your **H**igh-**E**nd **I**nteroperability **M**odule when **D**ata is **ALL** over the place. It’s a bridge between scattered islands of data. ⚔️🌉🌈

relatedItems.label: KATI - Katasterdokumente
relatedItems.description:
Das Projekt Pro-Kat-Digital – Die Protokolle des Franziszeischen Katasters in Tirol. Digitalisierung-Sicherung-Aufbereitung (KATI-digital) wird vom Land Tirol als Leuchtturmprojekt im Bereich Digitalisierung finanziert und in den Jahren 2019 bis 2021 realisiert. Projektpartner sind die Universität Innsbruck und die Europäische Genossenschaft READ-COOP SCE mit Unterstützung des Bundesamts für Eich- und Vermessungswesen, des Tiroler Landesarchivs sowie des Tiroler Bildungsforums.

Im Projekt Pro-Kat-Digital werden die Urmappen (Kartenblätter) des Franziszeischen Katasters und die dazugehörigen Detailvermessungsoperate (Protokolle) für eine breite Öffentlichkeit im Internet zugänglich gemacht und die darin enthaltenen Informationen erschlossen und miteinander verschränkt. Es handelt sich für das heutige Bundesland Tirol um 7.650 Mappenblätter (ca. 22 pro Katastralgemeinde) und etwa 160.000 Seiten Protokolle (ca. 457 pro Katastralgemeinde). Die Protokolle enthalten neben den Grund- und Bauparzellenprotokollen ein alphabetisches Verzeichnis, Grenzbeschreibungen, ein Häuser- und Flurnamenverzeichnis, einen Bodennutzungsausweis, etc.

Die digitalisierten Mappenblätter und die Grund- und Bauparzellenprotokolle liegen – sortiert nach Katastralgemeinden – in dieser Webplattform zur Bearbeitung auf. Ziel ist es, durch die Markierung der Parzellennummern sowohl in der Urmappe als auch in den Protokollen eine Verschränkung zwischen den beiden Quellen zu erreichen. Damit wird die Voraussetzung für weitere wissenschaftliche Auswertungen, aber auch für Nutzungen durch die Öffentlichkeit geschaffen. Ab Herbst 2020 sind daher alle Ortschronist*innen und andere Interessierte dazu eingeladen, jeweils ihre Gemeinde zu bearbeiten. Das große Ziel einer möglichst flächendeckenden Verknüpfung von Urmappe und Protokollen kann nur von vielen Händen gestemmt werden!

Vertiefende Informationen zum Franziszeischen Kataster und zum Projekt sind in der Zeitschrift Tiroler Chronist, Ausgabe Nr. 155/156 (2020), nachzulesen! Weitere, allgemeine Informationen zum Franziszeischen Kataster können unter der Adresse www.franziszeischerkataster.at abgerufen werden. 

---

The Pro-Kat-Digital project – The records of the Franciscan cadastre in Tyrol. Digitization, preservation, and processing (KATI-digital) is funded by the province of Tyrol as a flagship project in the field of digitization and will be implemented between 2019 and 2021. The project partners are the University of Innsbruck and the European cooperative READ-COOP SCE, with support from the Federal Office of Metrology and Surveying, the Tyrolean State Archives, and the Tyrolean Education Forum.

The Pro-Kat-Digital project makes the original cadastral maps ("Urmappen") and detailed survey records (protocols) of the Franziszeischer Kataster publicly accessible online. For Tyrol, this includes 7,650 map sheets and around 160,000 pages of records, featuring parcel data, indexes, boundary descriptions, house and field names, and land use certificates. The digitized materials are organized by cadastral municipality and can be edited via a web platform. The goal is to link maps and records by matching plot numbers, enabling deeper research and public use. Since fall 2020, local historians and volunteers are invited to contribute. The major goal of linking the original map and records as comprehensively as possible can only be achieved with many hands!

More detailed information on the Franciscan cadastre and the project can be found in the magazine Tiroler Chronist, issue no. 155/156 (2020)! Further general information on the Franciscan cadastre can be found at www.franziszeischerkataster.at.

OHMS (Oral History Metadata Synchronizer) inexpensively and efficiently enhances access to oral history by providing users with word-level search capability and a time-correlated transcript or indexed interview connecting the textual search term to the corresponding moment in the recorded interview online.

OHMS is an open source, web-based application designed to improve the user experience you provide for oral history, no matter what CMS or repository you use. There are 2 main components of the OHMS system

OHMS Application: The OHMS application is where the work is done. This is the back-end, web-based application where interviews are imported, and metadata is created. In the OHMS application transcripts are time-coded and/or interviews are indexed. Upon completion, the interview record (including the synchronized transcript and/or time-coded index) are exported as an XML file. When located on a web server, the OHMS XML file is what interfaces with your content management system through the OHMS Viewer.

OHMS Viewer: The OHMS viewer is the user interface of ohms. When an interview is called by the repository, the OHMS viewer loads, calling select interview level metadata and the intra interview level metadata created in the OHMS Application from the corresponding xml file.

label: L’annotation vidéo pour la recherche. Usages et outils numériques
description:
The creation, documentation, and analysis of digital audiovisual documents are central to numerous research projects in the humanities and social sciences. While the emergence of corpora comprised of audiovisual content is not novel, the advent of the digital era has greatly transformed their encoding, processing, sharing, and preservation, as well as the organization of researchers' work. This abundance of digital or digitized documents is accompanied by a shift in the relationship between users and digital audiovisual documents (DAD). Focusing on the concept of video annotation, this white paper from the CANEVAS consortium offers a (non-exhaustive) mapping of annotation practices and tools by employing the notion of personas to connect them. With a dual concern of contributing to the development of research on DAD annotation and engaging in an open conception of science, this toolkit aims to renew the instrumentation of research in the humanities and social sciences.

This French-language publication, created by the Canveas Consortium of IR* HumaNum, explores tools related to video annotation.

label: Learning attention for historical text normalization by learning to pronounce
description: Automated processing of historical texts often relies on pre-normalization to modern word forms. Training encoder-decoder architectures to solve such problems typically requires a lot of training data, which is not available for the named task. We address this problem by using several novel encoder-decoder architectures, including a multi-task learning (MTL) architecture using a grapheme-to-phoneme dictionary as auxiliary data, pushing the state-of-theart by an absolute 2% increase in performance. We analyze the induced models across 44 different texts from Early New High German. Interestingly, we observe that, as previously conjectured, multi-task learning can learn to focus attention during decoding, in ways remarkably similar to recently proposed attention mechanisms. This, we believe, is an important step toward understanding how MTL works.

label: Les outils d’annotation vidéo pour la recherche
description:
White paper, drafted by the French Consortium-HN Canevas, that examines and compares research tools for video annotation. 

Les Humanités Numériques portent leur attention sur différents types de corpus textuels et de jeux de données. Pour autant, les cultures numériques se façonnent aussi en dehors du livre et de l’écrit. L’un des enjeux fondamentaux pour ce champ émergent réside dans le traitement de corpus d’images, et notamment d’images animées. En effet, grâce aux outils numériques, il est de plus en plus facile de produire et de regarder des vidéos. Comment les chercheurs peuvent-ils concrètement investiguer, traiter, catégoriser, analyser cette profusion inédite d’images ? Nous nous concentrons ici sur la question de l’annotation. L’une des pratiques fondatrices du travail de recherche, on le sait, réside dans l’annotation de matériaux. Annoter un texte est une pratique aussi vieille que l’écrit lui-même et démultipliée par les possibilités du numérique. En revanche, annoter un film, en particulier à des fins de recherche, est resté jusqu’à une période récente une opération complexe. Cet article présente et analyse les usages et les nouveaux outils numériques qui permettent de travailler avec la vidéo et de l’annoter.

label: Lexical and Non-lexical Tone and Prosodic Typology
description:
Prosodic typology has generally concentrated on those aspects of prosodic representation which are assumed to be represented in the lexicon. It is argued here that non-lexical representation at various levels, underlying phonological, surface phonological and phonetic, can also constitute a basis for prosodic typology. An example is given of a low-level comparison of English and French pitch patterns. A prosodic model integrating these different levels is presented which, it
argued can provide a useful tool for the investigation of prosodic typology and for a more robust basis for establishing the more abstract levels including those of lexical representations.

relatedItems.label: How to Transcribe Phonetically
relatedItems.description: This workflow describes the successive methodological decisions and operations required to produce a phonetic transcription of oral/spoken data for research and documentation purposes in the social sciences and humanities (linguistics, dialectology, sociolinguistics, psycholinguistics, language documentation, conversation analysis, etc.). It is designed for researchers, students, and archivists who need to convert an audio recording into a phonetically annotated resource, whether for a single case study or for a larger, shareable, and reusable corpus. The workflow was elaborated on the basis of practical teaching and research notes on phonetic transcription (auditory and acoustic-supported transcription, use of Praat and ELAN, IPA/SAMPA conventions, inter-annotator agreement, and data publication), and integrates reference information on the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) and its alternative ASCII-based encoding, X-SAMPA. The workflow can be adapted to individual projects or to team-based research infrastructures, and it explicitly foresees the possibility of publishing the resulting transcriptions, together with the source audio, as a citable open dataset (e.g. via Zenodo or a comparable repository).

relatedItems.label: Pundit: Semantic web annotation tool
relatedItems.description:
Pundit is a cloud service that allows users to 'take notes' on web documents, like a web page or a PDF file. It consists of a set of components, amongst them the Annotator, a free extension for the Google Chrome browser used by users to create the annotations. Annotations can be highlights of text parts or comments, applied either on a selection of the text or on the whole document. It is also possible to create annotations to tag a selected text or an entire web page. Pundit supports semantic annotations, real RDF triples (subject - predicate -> object) to specify formal, structured and reusable statements associated to the annotated content. 

Other notable features of Pundit are: 
- Notebooks to collect annotations, which can be public, private and (soon) sharable with other users 
- Pundit WebApp to see and manage in a centralized place all the annotations done 'on the web'
- FeedThePundit proxy service, to use Pundit when the Chrome extension is not available and also from mobile browsers 
- APIs to develop custom integration scenarios. 

Since November 2022 Pundit is a service of the EOSC marketplace.

3D render files

Documentation and wikis

label: Marginalia and machine learning: Handwritten text recognition for Marginalia Collections
description: The pressing need for digitization of historical document collections has led to a strong interest in designing computerised image processing methods for automatic hand-written text recognition (HTR). Handwritten text possesses high variability due to different writing styles, languages and scripts. Training an accurate and robust HTR system calls for data-efficient approaches due to the unavailability of sufficient amounts of annotated multi-writer text. A case study on an ongoing project “Marginalia and Machine Learning” is presented here that focuses on automatic detection and recognition of handwritten marginalia texts i.e., text written in margins or handwritten notes. Faster R-CNN network is used for detection of marginalia and AttentionHTR is used for word recognition. The data comes from early book collections (printed) found in the Uppsala University Library, with handwritten marginalia texts. Source code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/ektavats/Project-Marginalia.

relatedItems.label: AttentionHTR: Handwritten Text Recognition Based on Attention Encoder-Decoder Networks
relatedItems.description:
This work proposes an attention-based sequence-to-sequence model for handwritten word recognition and explores transfer learning for data-efficient training of HTR systems. To overcome training data scarcity, this work leverages models pre-trained on scene text images as a starting point towards tailoring the handwriting recognition models. ResNet feature extraction and bidirectional LSTM-based sequence modeling stages together form an encoder. The prediction stage consists of a decoder and a content-based attention mechanism. The effectiveness of the proposed end-to-end HTR system has been empirically evaluated on a novel multi-writer dataset Imgur5K and the IAM dataset. The experimental results evaluate the performance of the HTR framework, further supported by an in-depth analysis of the error cases. 

Source code and pre-trained models are available at GitHub (https://github.com/dmitrijsk/AttentionHTR).

relatedItems.label: Choose a Notation Software and an Encoding Strategy
relatedItems.description:
The second step involves selecting both an encoding format and a notational tool suited to the corpus and the edition's intended objectives. At this stage, the editor must determine whether the project calls for a diplomatic or a critical edition.

Regarding notational tools, MuseScore (open source) stands as the currently recommended choice: it supports direct export to MEI without requiring plugins. Sibelius and Finale, though still widely used in professional contexts, are no longer under active development and cannot be considered viable long-term solutions. For early or non-Western repertoires, specialized tools may prove necessary — among them Gregorio for neumatic notation, LuteScribe and Fronimo for tablature, and the ReTab module for lute tablature in MEI.

The choice of encoding format has major consequences for the interoperability and analytical potential of the edition. MEI (Music Encoding Initiative) is strongly recommended for scholarly digital editions: it allows the coexistence of graphical score visualization and semantic encoding of musical data, accommodates a critical apparatus and a metadata header, and opens the way to computational analysis via tools such as Music21 and Humdrum. MusicXML remains a widely supported interchange format, suitable at the data-transfer stage of the workflow. PDF, by contrast, is appropriate only for dissemination purposes and does not constitute a digital edition in the full sense of the term.

label: Metadata Quality Improvement \& Portal Progress Report
description: The aim of this task was to analyse and compare the different metadata strategies of CLARIN, DARIAH and CESSDA, and to identify possibilities of cross-fertilization to take profit from each other solutions where possible. To have a better understanding in which stages of the research lifecycle metadata comes to the fore, we looked at several research data lifecycles and business process models. However the current research data lifecycle odels have the 'static' data object as basis, whereas metadata design, redesign, creation and management can continue to be 'live' issues within the research lifecycle. We therefore developed a metadata lifecycle based closely on familiar lifecycle models but extended to support the more dynamic metadata issues. To describe the metadata management of the different infrastructures we took a double approach. We looked on a more general level and outlined the policies and strategies regarding metadata of the three infrastructures. We evaluated these strategies on metadata quality issues with the Bruce and Hillmann criteria. On the other hand we looked with more detail how the work on metadata management is done by the individual data repositories. The infrastructures of CESSDA, CLARIN and DARIAH differ in visions, strategies and initiatives regarding metadata issues; similarly there is a difference in metadata management among the various repositories. Despite these differences, cross fertilisation by coordination on common lists of metadata elements, sharing of knowledge, and linking resources would leverage the overall metadata quality. Evaluation of the prototype of the joint CLARIN, DARIAH and CESSDA metadata portal endorses the opinion that more coordination is needed. Metadata quality must be discussed in relation to the activities for which they are used. We suggest that the infrastructures DARIAH and CLARIN prioritise future collaboration about standardisation efforts, which have already been initialised in dialogue between the CLARIN Standards Committee and the DARIAH representatives. Similar initiatives could be established with CESSDA

relatedItems.label: Planning and Management
relatedItems.description:
Set up based on scope, major objectives, and primary requirements of the digitisation and modelling process established by the involved stakeholders. Efficient management and enhanced significance of the whole process can be achieved by customizing project and data requirements, allocating resources, and establishing collaborative protocols. Established best practices include the BIM framework (e.g., agreeing on Exchange Information Requirements (EIR), draft and implementing Building Execution Plan (BEP), and Information Exchange Protocols (IEP)).

Common activities of planning and management include:

- Establish the main objectives of the heritage digitisation (e.g., documentation, research, management, restoration planning) considering legal constraints and compliance requirements on assets.

- Establish information requirements, including:
    - level of information need (LOIN) or level of development (LOD) for the 3D model
    - data categories (e.g., historical documentation, site surveys, conservation state analysis, environmental monitoring data)
    - data types and file formats (e.g., IFC, CSV, PDF)
    - data security
    - standards (e.g., ISO 19650) and metadata schemas (e.g., CIDOC CRM, Ao-Cat) for interoperability
    - milestones and deliverables

- Draft and implement the execution plans and information protocols, including:
    - Roles and responsibilities (e.g., survey specialists, historians, BIM modellers, researchers, data managers, BIM coordinators)
    - Communication and information exchange protocols (e.g., online repositories, naming conventions, version control)
    - Checks for quality, progress track and ensure alignment with objectives
    - Collaboration tools

### Outputs / Deliverables
- Information requirements (e.g., project information requirements, EIR)
- Execution plans (e.g., project execution plan, BEP)
- Project management documentation (e.g., charts, diagrams, reports)
- Information Exchange Matrix
- Conservation Management Plan (CMP)
- Heritage Asset Information Requirements (AIR)
- Organisation Information Requirements (OIR)

label: METHODOLOGY FOR THE ENERGY RENOVATION OF HERITAGE BUILDINGS USING BIM
description: This guidelines’ document was developed within the ENI CBC Med BEEP project and aims to enhance the capacity of public local administrations to design, and realise innovative energy and environmental improvement on historic public buildings, through a multidisciplinary and integrated digital approach (using Building Information Modelling and performance-based design to develop an Energy Efficient Heritage Building Information Model - EE-HBIM). The guideline is based on the testing of this emerging technology on built heritage in eight different EU and non EU Mediterranean countries to demonstrate its scalability to the entire building stock of the Med area. The project will provide public administrations with a powerful method for the energy rehabilitation of public buildings to be supported with private funds through the Energy Performance Contracting. The HBIM model should integrate previously collected information on the building (geometric, diagnostic, environmental data), to create a comprehensive documentation of the building's current state. Moreover, the HBIM model will be used as a basis to inform the subsequent simulation-based energy-environmental improvement concept, through energy renovation scenarios that are both compatible with the identified historic buildings and capable to enhance its energy and environmental performance.

Set up based on scope, major objectives, and primary requirements of the digitisation and modelling process established by the involved stakeholders. Efficient management and enhanced significance of the whole process can be achieved by customizing project and data requirements, allocating resources, and establishing collaborative protocols. Established best practices include the BIM framework (e.g., agreeing on Exchange Information Requirements (EIR), draft and implementing Building Execution Plan (BEP), and Information Exchange Protocols (IEP)).

Common activities of planning and management include:

- Establish the main objectives of the heritage digitisation (e.g., documentation, research, management, restoration planning) considering legal constraints and compliance requirements on assets.

- Establish information requirements, including:
    - level of information need (LOIN) or level of development (LOD) for the 3D model
    - data categories (e.g., historical documentation, site surveys, conservation state analysis, environmental monitoring data)
    - data types and file formats (e.g., IFC, CSV, PDF)
    - data security
    - standards (e.g., ISO 19650) and metadata schemas (e.g., CIDOC CRM, Ao-Cat) for interoperability
    - milestones and deliverables

- Draft and implement the execution plans and information protocols, including:
    - Roles and responsibilities (e.g., survey specialists, historians, BIM modellers, researchers, data managers, BIM coordinators)
    - Communication and information exchange protocols (e.g., online repositories, naming conventions, version control)
    - Checks for quality, progress track and ensure alignment with objectives
    - Collaboration tools

### Outputs / Deliverables
- Information requirements (e.g., project information requirements, EIR)
- Execution plans (e.g., project execution plan, BEP)
- Project management documentation (e.g., charts, diagrams, reports)
- Information Exchange Matrix
- Conservation Management Plan (CMP)
- Heritage Asset Information Requirements (AIR)
- Organisation Information Requirements (OIR)

3D render files

Photoshop's native PSD format can be previewed and compared to previous versions of the same file.

Nested task-lists

Documentation and wikis

Small websites can be hosted from public repositories on GitHub. The URL format is http://projectname.github.io.

Issue tracking (including feature requests)

Visualization of geospatial data

Gantt charts

GitHub is a heavily used in the opensource development community but does not require hosted projects to meet the definition of Open Source.

CATMA is a free, open source markup and analysis tool from the University of Hamburg's Department of Languages, Literature and Media. 

It incorporates three interactive modules:

2. The analyzer incorporates a query language and predefined functions. It also includes a query builder that allows users to construct queries from combinations of pre-defined questions while allowing for manual modification for more specific questions. 
3. The visualizer provides basic visualization options for texts and corpora. 

CATMA also interfaces with the Voyant toolset. As of version 4.1, CATMA is a web application with collaborative work functions, and improvements to its user interface, queries and corpus analysis capacity. Version 4.2 offers, among others, new visualization options.

label: Multiple Temporalities of Language and Body in Interaction: Challenges for Transcribing Multimodality
description:
The article focuses on the principles of multimodal CA, the way they can be operationalized in a transcription system, and the analytical and conceptual consequences of transcription choices. Elaborating on the foundations of multimodal CA and on the basis of video recordings of French and Swiss German encounters, as well as animal interactions, the article discusses classic and contemporary challenges for transcription and analysis, such as beyond gesture and gaze, body arrangements in interactional spaces, larger groups, material environments, mobile settings, silent activities, and animal encounters. It also highlights the diversity of multimodal practices involved: mobilizing occasioned
material resources, movements not only of the upper (head, gesture) but also the lower (feet, legs, posterior) parts of the body, haptic contacts touching objects and coparticipants, and camera movements. The precise transcription of relevant details reveals complex arrangements of multimodal resources and
gestalts. Their fine-grained, distinct, multiple temporalities constitute the basis of their sequential order—for sequentiality as a fundamental organizational principle of action. Data are in French and Swiss German.

relatedItems.label: Import a transcription or transcribe
relatedItems.description:
Annotate speech, prosody, non-verbal behaviour, and paralinguistic features. 

A. Transcribe speech using Jefferson conventions
Enter the verbal transcription in the speech tiers, one turn at a time, following the Jefferson system (G. Jefferson, Glossary of 'Transcript Symbols with an Introduction', in G.H. Lerner (ed.), "Conversation Analysis. Studies from the First Generation", Amsterdam/Philadelphia, John Benjamins, 2004, pp. 13-31.). The transcript is laid out vertically according to turn sequence; each turn is associated with a speaker identifier and, in ELAN, aligned to a time interval in the recording. Overlapping talk is marked with square brackets [ ] at the point where it begins and ends across the relevant tiers. It should be noted, however, that these brackets are not automatically generated by ELAN but are added manually. This point is important because conversation analysts working within the Jeffersonian transcription tradition—where the alignment of overlapping speech is visually reproduced on the page using vertically synchronized square brackets—may expect a comparable output. In ELAN, overlap is instead primarily represented through separate tiers and synchronized timestamps. Reproducing the conventional Jefferson-style layout therefore requires exporting the transcript (for instance into Word), using a monospaced font such as Courier, and often manually adjusting the alignment of the strings. 
Prosodic and voice quality features are noted inline using the standard symbols.

ELAN allows you to play short loops, slow down the audio, and zoom into the waveform display while annotating, which considerably aids the transcription of rapid, overlapping, or unclear speech.

B. Transcribe non-verbal behaviour
For audio-visual data, annotate non-verbal actions — gesture, gaze, posture, object manipulation — in the corresponding tiers, following the Mondada conventions. Each embodied action is described in plain language within angle-bracket-delimited strings, synchronised with the speech tier via time codes and shared symbols. The symbols mark the preparation, apex, and retraction phases of a movement, and indicate whether the action begins before the extract, continues beyond it, or is captured at a precise moment by a video frame reference (#).

Non-verbal actions often do not map neatly onto turn boundaries: a gesture may begin several syllables before the relevant word, or continue after the turn has ended. ELAN's multi-tier, time-aligned interface is designed precisely to capture this temporal complexity.

C. Add a working translation if needed
For multilingual data, or when the corpus will be shared with readers unfamiliar with the language of the interaction, it is useful to add a translation tier aligned to each speech tier. This working translation is not part of the primary transcription data but serves as an access tool. It should be clearly labelled as a gloss and not confused with the transcription itself.

relatedItems.label: Annotating Proxemic Features in Audiovisual Document Using ELAN
relatedItems.description:
This workflow describes how to annotate proxemic features in audiovisual corpora using ELAN. It integrates multimodal annotation principles from linguistic and semiotic research, with particular reference to gesture classification frameworks (Kendon, McNeill) and facial annotation protocols (FACS, Ekman & Friesen).

This process is grounded on Meluzzi’s approach to annotation ("Annotare una trascrizione", in "Vademecum per il trattamento delle fonti orali", pp. 227-229).

relatedItems.label: Choose a Notation Software and an Encoding Strategy
relatedItems.description:
The second step involves selecting both an encoding format and a notational tool suited to the corpus and the edition's intended objectives. At this stage, the editor must determine whether the project calls for a diplomatic or a critical edition.

Regarding notational tools, MuseScore (open source) stands as the currently recommended choice: it supports direct export to MEI without requiring plugins. Sibelius and Finale, though still widely used in professional contexts, are no longer under active development and cannot be considered viable long-term solutions. For early or non-Western repertoires, specialized tools may prove necessary — among them Gregorio for neumatic notation, LuteScribe and Fronimo for tablature, and the ReTab module for lute tablature in MEI.

The choice of encoding format has major consequences for the interoperability and analytical potential of the edition. MEI (Music Encoding Initiative) is strongly recommended for scholarly digital editions: it allows the coexistence of graphical score visualization and semantic encoding of musical data, accommodates a critical apparatus and a metadata header, and opens the way to computational analysis via tools such as Music21 and Humdrum. MusicXML remains a widely supported interchange format, suitable at the data-transfer stage of the workflow. PDF, by contrast, is appropriate only for dissemination purposes and does not constitute a digital edition in the full sense of the term.

relatedItems.label: Encode the Musical Data
relatedItems.description:
Encoding is the central intellectual and technical operation of the digital edition. It involves transcribing musical information into structured, machine-readable data, capturing not only the visual symbols of the score but also their semantic significance. Before encoding, the editor must define which signs are essential and which are complementary: staves, pitches, rhythmic values, dynamics, and measures constitute primary data; ficta accidentals, ornaments, and performance indications may be treated as secondary layers, depending on whether the edition prioritizes analytical use or performer accessibility. Good encoding practice avoids an excessive accumulation of customized or unconventional graphical elements, which compromise file integrity and interoperability. 

The choice between prioritizing logical readability (for analytical purposes) and visual fidelity must be made deliberately and applied consistently. For works with text (vocal music), particular care must be taken to align syllables precisely with their corresponding notes. MEI's attribute allows each element to be uniquely identified, enabling subsequent linkage to sources and audio recordings via thesauruses and reference systems. For some notational symbols (e.g. musica ficta), Python scripts can automate corrections across the encoded corpus, provided the initial encoding has been properly prepared.

relatedItems.label: Build the Critical Apparatus and Annotation Spaces
relatedItems.description: For critical editions, this step involves the systematic encoding of textual variants, editorial emendations, and scholarly annotations within the MEI file or an associated annotation layer. MEI supports a dedicated critical apparatus (using the , , and elements), which enables multiple readings to be encoded within a single master file and linked to their respective sources. The editor must decide in advance on a minimal yet meaningful set of annotation criteria, so that the significance of each source remains clearly perceptible without overloading the file with cross-references. Online platforms implementing collaborative annotation workflows --- such as Gesualdo Online digital edition, both hosted at the RicercarDataLab --- provide established models: annotating users are identified by contributor level, annotations are categorized by type (Duration, Emendation, Pitch, etc.) and validated by an administrator before integration into the master file. The critical apparatus can also incorporate audio files (MIDI or live recordings), provided the relevant rights have been cleared. Synchronization between encoded files and audio recordings remains technically challenging and is currently achieved by only a small number of projects (e.g. the Marenzio edition).

relatedItems.label: Fix and improve the music content
relatedItems.description:
In order to modify a MEI file to correct or improve it, you can use MEI Friend or MEISE. Both tools have a musical interface allowing modifying the score like a classic editor. However, the proposed changes remain limited. In order to edit a MEI file locally with MEI Friend, you can use the MEI Friend module in Atom.

To further modify the MEI file, it is necessary to modify the code. To do this, follow the MEI guidelines.

relatedItems.label: Add new metadata
relatedItems.description: To check, modify or add metadata, it is necessary to go to the MEI header. For this, you have to directly explore the code using MEI-Friend or MEISE. It is preferable to limit yourself to the basic fields proposed in the MEI header (;; , etc.). Make sure that the title of the work and the musical part (allegro, Kyrie, etc.) are not inverted. In order to fill in the metadata correctly, see the MEI guidelines.

label: Musicology and artificial intelligence
description:
This report provides an overview of Artificial Intelligence in European musicological research, addressed to musicologists, librarians, archivists, curators, educators, research-policy officers, infrastructure coordinators, and tool developers. Moving from conceptual foundations to institutional implications, it maps the affordances and limitations of AI-based models and tools for the discipline, while situating them within the European normative landscape defined by the ALLEA European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity, the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, and the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence.

The six complementary sections successively address: (1) methodological foundations, clarifying notions of model, tool, and critical posture, and surveying audio-, image-, encoding-, and language-model-based applications such as automatic music transcription, optical music recognition, score-audio alignment, automated analysis, reconstruction, and LLM prompt­ing; (2) data infrastructure, covering FAIR/CARE governance, ontologies and persistent identifiers, European federated infra­structures, auditory digital twins, and risks of fragmentation, representational bias, quality variability, and copyright; (3) a continuation of the disciplinary stakes involved in source and corpus processing; (4) musicological education in the age of AI, including curricular redesign, AI literacy, and design models such as the Two-Lane Approach; (5) professional practices and responsibilities, examining scholarly credibility, intellectual property, academic integrity frameworks, cultural and creative industry collaborations, institutional and legal risks, gender equality, and lessons from organised labour; and (6) best practic­es, articulating methodological pluralism against technological determinism and formalising principles of ethical reflexivity, human oversight, explainability, reproducibility, and accountability.

label: Musicology as data science and heritage science
description: This collective guide explores the transformative intersections of musicology with data science and heritage science in theEuropean context. It positions musicological research as both a model for and contributor to broader cultural heritage, analyzingits tangible and intangible dimensions. The report  reviews advances in research infrastructures, including the European Open Science Cloud, ECHOES, and E-RIHS, highlighting challenges and opportunities for integrating music into transnational heritage frameworks. It surveys the complexity of music data — notation, audio, metadata, and visual sources — and emphasizes standardized methods for cataloging and preservation. The text critically assesses legal, policy, and technical barriers to digitizing and reusing musical materials, advocating for legal reforms and open science principles. New publication paradigms are proposed, leveraging digital tools to expand access and impact. The role of musicologists in public engagement, education, and fostering research communities is underscored as crucial for sustainability. Best practices and collaborative models link musicological data to broader digital humanities and preservation strategies. Ultimately, the guide calls for active participation in European policy and research networks to enhance musicology’s role in shaping and disseminating cultural heritage for future generations.

relatedItems.label: Guide to Digital Music Editing
relatedItems.description: The “Guide de l’édition musicale numérique” is a comprehensive, up-to-date manual designed to accompany researchers and practitioners through the intricacies of digital music editing, with a particular focus on scholarly critical editions and the European research context. It is the result of collaborative work within the Huma-Num MUSICA2 consortium in Tours.The Guide addresses the conceptual foundations, technical strategies, and best practices essential for conceiving, producing, and disseminating digital editions of notated music. It systematically distinguishes between “digitized” and genuinely “digital” editions, emphasizing the importance of interoperability, sustainability, and the FAIR principles that dominate the digital humanities landscape.Core topics include the selection and use of notation software, detailed descriptions of encoding formats such as MusicXML, MEI, and Humdrum, and guidance for the conversion, visualization, and long-term archiving of encoded music data. The Guide clarifies legal responsibilities, collaborative workflows, and the integration of metadata and source references—crucial elements for traceability and scholarly citation.It devotes substantial attention to the creation and management of critical apparatus, annotation spaces, and dynamic links between digital editions and primary sources, especially through IIIF protocols and digital “twins”. The text includes a typology of current notation and editing tools, recommendations for quality control, and active encouragement to use open standards and open-access practices to maximize reusability and impact.The Guide situates digital music editing in the wider landscape of European cultural policies, research funding expectations, and technological change, advocating for adaptability and technical literacy among editors. Practical elements include step-by-step checklists for project planning, metadata entry, visualization tools, and the identification of trusted data repositories for long-term preservation.By synthesizing recent research, technological developments, and institutional frameworks, the Guide provides a vital roadmap for both experienced musicologists and newcomers seeking to navigate the dynamic field of digital music publication.

relatedItems.label: Creation of a Digital Music Edition
relatedItems.description:
A digital edition encodes musical information as structured, machine-readable, and semantically rich data, a transformation that requires a series of methodological and technical decisions. This workflow addresses the full range of operations involved, including the choice of encoding format, the management of metadata, the establishment of relationships with sources, the integration of a critical apparatus, and the conditions for sustainable online publication.
It outlines the essential steps required to produce a scholarly digital music edition, from the initial scoping of the corpus to its long-term archiving and dissemination. Structured around the three pillars of digital editing—tools, content, and presentation—it is designed to ensure compliance with FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) principles throughout the entire lifecycle of the edition.

Developed from the Guide to Digital Music Editing produced by the Consortium-HN MUSICA within the French research infrastructure Huma-Num, this workflow also aligns with the requirements of the European ECHOES project (European Cloud for Heritage Open Science), which frames digital editions as components of digital twins integrating source digitization, musical encoding, and audio recording. It is intended for researchers, digital humanists, and engineers working in institutional contexts shaped by Open Access policies and European research funding frameworks.
