relatedItems.description: ROSSIO Infrastructure is building an open-access and free platform that aims to aggregate, organise and connect digital resources related to Social Sciences, Arts and Humanities located in Portuguese educational and cultural institutions. This paper aims to present ROSSIO infrastructure, the institutions involved, its main goals and the services it will provide, such as a discovery portal, exhibitions, collections and a virtual research environment. Underlying these services is a metadata aggregation approach that brings into ROSSIO the metadata on digital objects from the providing institutions. The aggregated dataset is transformed into linked data and enriched with entities from controlled vocabularies, which are defined by ROSSIO. We will detail this process, including the applications employed and how they interoperate. Finally, we will conclusively reflect on the potentialities of these services for public dissemination of science, taking into account the FAIR principles.

relatedItems.label: Data Catalog Vocabulary (DCAT) - Version 3
relatedItems.description:
Data Catalog Vocabulary (DCAT) is an [Resource Description Framework (RDF)](https://www.w3.org/RDF/) vocabulary designed to facilitate interoperability between data catalogs published on the Web. 

DCAT enables a publisher to describe datasets and data services in a catalog using a standard model and vocabulary that facilitates the consumption and aggregation of metadata from multiple catalogs. This can increase the discoverability of datasets and data services. It also makes it possible to have a decentralized approach to publishing data catalogs and makes federated search for datasets across catalogs in multiple sites possible using the same query mechanism and structure. Aggregated DCAT metadata can serve as a manifest file as part of the digital preservation process.

relatedItems.label: Rijksmuseum data
relatedItems.description:
Published by the Rijksmuseum, this dataset provides controlled vocabularies and includes a list of actors (e.g., persons and organisations) and a thesaurus (e.g., concepts, places and events) as two different data packages. According to the content provided by each of them, the metadata is described by means of a particular vocabulary. A brief description is provided below.

**Actors**
The controlled vocabulary of actors is a list of persons and organisations. The data is structured according to the [Europeana Data Model](https://pro.europeana.eu/edm-documentation), Linked Data compatible and available in XML.

**Thesaurus**
The thesaurus includes concepts, places and events. Data is structured according to the [Simple Knowledge Organization System](https://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/), Linked Data compatible and available in XML.

relatedItems.label: Create SKOS Application Profiles
relatedItems.description: Creating an application profile from different SKOS vocabularies involves combining and aligning multiple SKOS vocabularies to create a unified and customized vocabulary that suits your specific requirements. This is a step-by-step approach to help you create an application profile.

relatedItems.label: Include machine-readable metadata about the content provided in the dataset
relatedItems.description:
**Why**
The use of interoperable machine-readable metadata enhances discoverability and use since the data can be processed by a computer. Interoperability helps in the aggregation of datasets to search across several catalogues.

**How**
For example, controlled vocabularies such as [Data Catalog Vocabulary DCAT](https://marketplace.sshopencloud.eu/tool-or-service/1Y0yKp) enables a publisher to describe datasets using a standard model that facilitates the consumption and aggregation of metadata from multiple catalogues (e.g., the [DCAT GLAM Catalogue](https://github.com/hibernator11/dcat-glam-catalog)). Other examples of vocabularies are [Dublin Core](https://marketplace.sshopencloud.eu/training-material/bxWKhV), [Schema.org](https://schema.org/) and [Simple Knowledge Organization System (SKOS)](https://marketplace.sshopencloud.eu/training-material/mUQw6r).

relatedItems.label: Créer un nouveau  « Candidat »
relatedItems.description:
La fiche « Candidat » comprend plusieurs champs issus principalement du standard SKOS, Simple Knowledge Organisation System (https://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/). 

1. Renseigner dans un premier temps les deux champs obligatoires qui apparaissent (voir image 1).

Ils obéissent à des règles d’écriture précises : 

a. Intitulé (skos:prefLabel@fr) : il représente le libellé préférentiel donné au concept. C’est un substantif (mot simple ou mot composé) écrit en français, langue par défaut du thésaurus, et au singulier dans cette langue sauf usage particulier. Le libellé n’est ni un verbe ni un adjectif. Ceux-ci peuvent être substantivés pour répondre aux règles d’écriture. 
Ex. : brillance plutôt que briller ou brillant.

Le mot commence par une lettre minuscule, sauf s’il s'agit d’une entité nommée (nom de personnage, de lieu, d'œuvre, etc.).
Ex. : catacombes ; épigraphie ; arsenal naval ; grotte de Lascaux ; Les Troyennes (Sénèque).

Le libellé doit être explicite, au besoin en conservant la langue d’origine s’il n’y a pas d’équivalent en français (ou dans une autre des langues du thésaurus).
Ex. : dolium (dans toutes les langues du thésaurus).

Pour éviter toute ambiguïté, il est possible d’ajouter entre parenthèses une précision.
Ex. : Dialogues (Tacite).

b. Définition (skos:definition) : explicitation du concept en une phrase commençant par un substantif avec initiale en majuscule et qui reprend idéalement la position du concept dans l’arbre. La définition ne contient ni le terme défini ni aucun exemple et n’est pas une notice d’information. Elle est une aide pour sélectionner le mot-clé le plus juste dans l’indexation d’une ressource.
Voir les recommandations sur https://hal.inrae.fr/hal-03153824v1/document. 

La source de la définition peut être signalée entre parenthèses à la fin du texte. Elle sera de préférence issue de dictionnaires ou de publications imprimées ou numériques faisant foi.
Ex. : bouilloire (TG récipient culinaire) : Pot verseur utilisé pour chauffer de l'eau (Balfet et al. 1989, p. 19).

2. Valider la demande de création du candidat.

description:
Diese Ressource stellt den Austria Media Corpus (amc) und seine Nutzungsmöglichkeiten vor. Sie erklärt die Durchführung von Abfragen in der corpus query engine namens Sketch Engine. Im Besonderen geht es um die Einführung in Sketch Engine's "Corpus Query Language" (CQL). Daher ist das Tutorial bewusst in deutscher Sprache gehalten. Alle Beispiele im Tutorial sind direkt dem amc entnommen.

---

This resource introduces the Austria Media Corpus (amc) and its possible uses. It explains how to perform queries in the corpus query engine called Sketch Engine. In particular, it provides an introduction to Sketch Engine's “Corpus Query Language” (CQL). The aim of the tutorial is to give users of the Austrian Media Corpus (amc) an easy introduction to querying the amc with Sketch Engine and CQL. For this reason, the tutorial is deliberately written in German. All examples in the tutorial are taken directly from the amc.

relatedItems.label: Surveys to Ethnic and Migrant Minorities across Europe. Identifying Knowledge Strengths and Gaps Using Survey Metadata
relatedItems.description:
This report, the second in the series of reports produced by COST Action 16111 Ethmigsurveydata, presents the results from the analysis of the survey metadata compiled through the Ethnic and Migrant Minorities (EMM) Survey Registry launched by the COST Action and with the support of the H2020 project Social Sciences and Humanities Open Cloud (SSHOC). The current version of the report focuses on six countries for which the metadata is complete and controlled for quality: Croatia, Norway, Switzerland, Romania, Germany and Turkey. 

The report begins with an introduction about the survey metadata compilation undertaken by Ethmigsurveydata, followed by a detailed overview of the methodological approaches used to develop the EMM Survey Registry. The report is then structured into five additional sections that present the findings for the EMM surveys in these six countries in relation to their geographical and target group coverage, the definition and measurement of EMMs, the topics covered by the surveys, their technical characteristics, and their accessibility and reusability. The final section offers conclusions and recommendations for funders, data producers and data analysis.

The materials have been created so that they can be leveraged and used by various users and stakeholders of quantitative survey data on EMMs’ integration.

relatedItems.label: Ethnic and Migrant Minorities (EMM) Survey Registry
relatedItems.description:
The EMM Survey Registry—which has been co-created by COST Action 16111 - ETHMIGSURVEYDATA, the H2020 SSHOC project, and the ANR project FAIRETHMIGQUANT—is a free online tool for discovering and learning about existing quantitative surveys undertaken with EMM (sub)populations in Europe and beyond. This tool not only brings together previously scattered information about these surveys but also offers detailed and structured metadata for each of the surveys. Designed with the end-users in mind, this tool can also easily be leveraged by anyone interested in doing research or policy-related work using quantitative surveys on EMMs' integration and inclusion.

The EMM Survey Registry is currently live and available in beta version. This version is fully functional and displays metadata about 870+ surveys from 21 different countries. In the coming months, the tool will not only expand its metadata offerings (to cover at least an additional 100-200 surveys from roughly 10 additional countries), but also enrich its various user-friendly features and functionalities.

relatedItems.label: Make your oral sources accessible and reusable
relatedItems.description:
Make your oral sources accessible to researchers and, where legally permissible, to the wider public. Apply FAIR principles throughout.

1. Structure data and metadata for FAIR compliance: structure metadata to ensure Findability (assign persistent identifiers; use rich descriptive metadata), Accessibility (store in open or widely supported formats; ensure long-term availability of metadata even if access to data is restricted), Interoperability (use shared vocabularies and standards such as Dublin Core, EAD, or domain-specific thesauri), and Reusability (attach clear licence information; document provenance and context). Consult the FAIR Principles documentation for a full specification.
2. Publish online with an explicit release form: where an explicit "liberatoria" exists, publish the oral source online. Protect third parties mentioned in the recording: de-index their names from search engines where the information could damage their reputation; place sensitive content behind a registration-protected access area. Provide rich contextual metadata for all published materials.
3. Apply appropriate access restrictions where no release form exists: where no explicit release exists, choose among the following graduated approaches: (a) exclude the recording from online publication; (b) publish only excerpts already available in other public forms (print, documentary, educational DVD); (c) publish a pseudonymised transcript, ensuring the individual cannot be re-identified through cross-referencing; (d) publish a keyword index (thesaurus-based) omitting personal names; (e) provide authenticated access for research and educational purposes only; (f) state publicly the willingness to remove content on explicit request. Recall that these restrictions do not apply to recordings of public figures whose personal opinions, religious affiliation, or public acts are already widely known.
4. Assign a Creative Commons licence: choose and attach a Creative Commons licence to each published oral source. Select the licence that best reflects the rights-assignment conditions established with the interviewer and interviewee: CC BY (attribution only), CC BY-NC (non-commercial), CC BY-ND (no derivatives), or more restrictive combinations. Note that CC licences govern the circulation of the work online; they do not supersede GDPR obligations, which govern the processing of personal data independently.
5. Deposit in a trusted digital repository: deposit the oral source collection — including recordings, documentation, and metadata — in a trusted digital repository aligned with open science principles. Ensure the repository assigns persistent identifiers (DOI, Handle, or equivalent). Verify that the repository's preservation commitments cover refresh, format migration, and long-term access. Cross-link the deposit record with related publications and project documentation.

label: Creative Commons Lizenzen bei Digitalen Editionen
description:
EMPFEHLUNGEN OPEN ACCESS Als Open Access Standard, mithin als «echte» Open-Access Lizenzen, gelten bei digitalen Editionen nur CC-0, CC-BY und CC-BY-SA. Der Zusatz NC (Non Commercial) etwa schränkt die Nachnutzbarkeit bereits so stark ein, dass nicht mehr von «Open Access Publikationen/Daten» gesprochen werden kann. Diese Auslegung entspricht auch den Grundsätzen des SNF, der für jede Einschränkung der Nutzungsrechte, die über CC-BY hinausgeht, eine Begründung erwartet. Wir empfehlen deshalb, wenn immer möglich die Verwendung von CC-BY. 

---

RECOMMENDATIONS OPEN ACCESS Only CC-0, CC-BY, and CC-BY-SA are considered open access standards, i.e., “genuine” open access licenses, for digital editions. The addition of NC (Non Commercial), for example, restricts reusability to such an extent that it can no longer be referred to as “open access publications/data.” This interpretation is also in line with the principles of the SNSF, which expects justification for any restriction of usage rights that goes beyond CC-BY. We therefore recommend the use of CC-BY whenever possible.

label: DARIAH can help researchers to use digital methods at every stage of their research
description: Maija Paavolainen explains the challenges of finding a 'common language' in the digital humanities. She finds that simply talking about this issue helps. Thus, experience in communicating across disciplines is a positive outcome of training initiatives in itself. The role of research infrastructures, she argues, is certainly in sharing tools and best practices. However, most importantly, it is also to create opportunities for people to meet and learn face-to-face. She explains that humanities scholars are more accustomed to using digital methods and tools in the initial (information gathering) and final (publication) stages of research. However, DARIAH, specifically, can help them to also use them in the core part of the research process - i.e. in organising, annotating, and enriching data.

DARIAH-DE Data Modeling Environment
relatedItems.description:
Environment for modeling data and their relationships.

The Data Modeling Environment (DME) is a tool for modeling and associating data. By means of the DME, data models and mappings between them are defined and provided in terms of interfaces (REST-API). Integrative services such as the generic search access data models and mappings of the DME and utilize them for further processing, transformation and integration of data. A special feature of the DME is that data can be modeled regardless of its disciplinary context, its degree of structure and complexity, and its further use. Thus, in addition to standards such as [TEI](https://dme.mww-forschung.de/dme/model/editor/5f69fc384c7b040386a9239c/), [MODS](https://dme.de.dariah.eu/dme/model/editor/5a2e893061432f28f8254523/) and [DataCite](https://teaching.clariah.de/dme/model/editor/5eb11e106117b10b7b6c7c11/), data models and mappings of the DME also adress local and specifically developed schemas for which, for example, compliance with FAIR principles is to be achieved. The particular powerfulness of the DME with regard to the modeling of complex research data of the humanities and cultural sciences is based on the language-based approach to the definition of complex data and the associated explication of domain knowledge.

The DME source code is available under an open source license: https://gitlab.rz.uni-bamberg.de/dariah/dme 

Further information on the main concepts of DME can be found in the following publications:

Henrich, Andreas; Gradl, Tobias (2021): The Integration of Research Data. How Can Research Infrastructures Help? In Eva-Marie Seng, Frank Göttmann (Eds.): DOKUMENT - OBJEKT - GENESE: DE GRUYTER, S. 767–802.
Steyer, Timo; Gradl, Tobias (2019): A research-oriented and case-based data federation for the Humanities. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.2536107
Gradl, Tobias/Henrich, Andreas (2016): „Data Integration for the Arts and Humanities: A Language Theoretical Concept“. In: Fuhr, Norbert et al. (Hg.): Research and Advanced Technology for Digital Libraries: 20th International Conference on Theory and Practice of Digital Libraries, TPDL 2016, Hannover, Germany, September 5?9, 2016, Proceedings. Cham: Springer International Publishing, S. 281–293
Gradl, Tobias/Henrich, Andreas (2016): „Extending Data Models by Declaratively Specifying Contextual Knowledge“. In: Sablatnig, Robert/Hassan, Tamir (Hg.): DocEng '16 Proceedings of the 2016 ACM Symposium on Document Engineering. New York, NY, USA: ACM: ACM, S. 123–126

relatedItems.label: DARIAH-DE Publikator
relatedItems.description:
For whom?
Researchers who want to deposit their research data safe, persistent, and referencable in a research data repository.

The DARIAH-DE Publikator offers the possibility to prepare, manage and import research data for the import into the DARIAH-DE Repository.
The DARIAH-DE Repository allows for storing your research data in a sustainable and secure way, providing it with metadata and eventually publishing it. Your research data, called "collections" in the following, as well as each individual file are long-term available in the DARIAH-DE repository and get a unique and permanently valid persistent identifier (DOI). Your data can be referenced permanently and will be quotable with this identifier. In addition, you can register your collections with the Collection Registry, which are then also found in the Generic Search.

The DARIAH-DE Publikator is the access point for importing collections which offers the possibility to prepare and manage your collections for an import into the DARIAH-DE Repository, and finally import them into the repository. Your research data …

* is safely stored in the repository,

* gets a Persistent Identifier (DOI),

* is permanently referenceable and quotable,

* is publicly accessible,

* can be described in the Collection Registry as a collection, and

* is finally searchable in the generic search.

This means that your research data is included in the research data lifecycle and thus available for subsequent use.

Documentation
For more information on usage of the Publikator and the DARIAH-DE Repository, please refer to the DARIAH-DE Documentation at https://doc.repository.de.dariah.eu/submodules/publikator/docs/index.html. The technical documentation and API descriptions for each repository service can be found on the documentation page of the Repository server on https://repository.de.dariah.eu/doc/services/.

Are there still unresolved issues or would you like further information? You can reach us at info@de.dariah.eu.

This resource is supported by Text+. In case of questions you may get in touch with the Text+ helpdesk at textplus-support@gwdg.de.

relatedItems.label: Netnography Open Educational Resource
relatedItems.description:
Netnography is an adaptation of ethnography to the study of digital interactions. In this course, the ethnographic perspective underpinning Netnography is introduced together with the netnographic approach and different types of netnographic material. Ethnographic procedures adapted to digital settings, such as participant observations, interviews and taking field notes, are described together with Social Network Analysis. Employing both qualitative elements (such as participant observations) and quantitative (Social Network Analysis), learners will work hands-on with pre-selected datasets to do a small-scale netnographic study. This study will depart from questions connected to equality, cultural diversity and public health.

The course includes four units that are designed to gradually introduce the learner to Netnography as a research field and a methodology, but the units can also be studied separately. Each unit includes theoretical content and practical assignments that will allow the learner to develop a thorough understanding of Netnography and a useful skillset for doing netnographies.

relatedItems.label: #dariahTeach - online teaching, MOOCs and beyond
relatedItems.description: The #dariahTeach project (funded by an Erasmus+ Strategic Partnership) is developing a  network based in seven partner countries exploring the production, dissemination, and promotion of high quality, dynamic, extensible, localisable, and integrated educational materials for the digital humanities specifically tailored for third level education. It is adopting a cMOOC philosophy which focuses on ‘creation, creativity, autonomy, and social networked learning’ (Siemens, 2012) to provide pedagogical content that can be easily integrated into diverse teaching and learning situations.

relatedItems.label: The E-spect@tor Tool Open Educational Resource
relatedItems.description: The E-Spectator course aims to train students to better understand and analyze the Performing Arts, mostly performance plays and dance performances but also perfomative activities such as fashion shows, providing new methods for their study along with digital technology. Performing Arts’ esthetic and poetry can be sometimes destabilizing at first glance and difficult to analyze because it is by nature ephemeral. Yet the Performative Arts are bearers of an alternative vision of the world that allows to maintain a critical view of events and our environment. In concrete terms, this project aims to the use of digital technology for analyzing live works, in particular through the study of videos of live shows.

- knowledge organisation systems and professional subject indexing, 
- social tagging as another approach to knowledge organisation, and
- automatic subject indexing as the third approach to knowledge organisation.


Starting from the case studies analysed in the course, you will be able to transfer the knowledge obtained to any digital humanities context anywhere in the world.

description:
This online resource provides practical recommendations for interdisciplinary and highly collaborative research (IHCR) teams in managing and curating their data. IHCR is defined broadly as research that combines resources and expertise across disciplines and institutions. The recommendations come from a research collaboration between Indiana University Bloomington, Virginia Tech, and the University of Colorado Boulder funded by the Institute of Museum and Library Services (Award #LG-246400-OLS-20).

The resource has five main recommendations:

 - Implementing a Charter 
 - Organizing Information and Data 
 - Creating and Maintaining a Catalog of Data Assets
 - Processing Collected Quantitative Data for Easy Analysis Input
 - Preserving Data from Digital Projects Published Online

In addition to the main recommendations, the resource offers a primer and a data management guide for IHCR data.

relatedItems.label: Research Design and Methodological Planning
relatedItems.description:
The treatment of oral sources begins with a carefully structured phase of research design and methodological planning, which shapes the quality of the data collected as well as its legal validity, long-term preservation, and future reuse. This phase brings together methodological reflection, technical, and ethical choices, legal awareness, and archival foresight.

At its core lies a solid grounding in the principles and practices of linguistics and oral history. Researchers—and, where applicable, collaborators—should develop a clear awareness of the legal, ethical, and deontological implications of working with oral testimonies. This includes familiarity with relevant international and national guidelines, such as those of the Oral History Society (OHS) and the Associazione Italiana di Storia Orale (AISO), and an understanding of the responsibilities linked to the collection, processing, and preservation of personal narratives. At this stage, the focus is on building awareness within the research team, rather than formally informing participants.

Methodological planning also involves defining the research framework, including research questions, scope, and participant selection. Interviews should be conceived as co-constructed communicative events; therefore, flexible interview guides are preferable to rigid questionnaires, allowing space for digressions that may open new lines of inquiry.

Researchers must also anticipate the conditions of the recording, including the choice of environment and the establishment of a relationship of trust with participants, which directly affects the quality and interpretability of the testimonies.

Technical planning is equally essential. Decisions regarding recording formats (audio or audio-video) and equipment should be made in relation to research objectives and future uses of the data. These choices are methodological as much as technical, as they shape the nature and reusability of the sources.

Finally, this phase includes preparing the documentation resources that will support the workflow, such as interview guides, information sheets, consent and authorization forms, and recording sheets for contextual data. Anticipating legal requirements, preservation strategies, and future access conditions ensures coherence across the process and supports the sustainable reuse of oral sources.

label: Data management planning for long-term preservation
description: Data management planning (DMP) concerns the development, execution and supervision of plans, policies, programs and practices that control, protect, deliver and enhance the value of data and information assets. The certification of digital repositories (the subject of D13.4) is an important instrument to improve the quality of the data management infrastructure. Both DMP and certification of repositories are closely related and covered in this report. This deliverable contains the strategy and planning to create and disseminate expertise on DMP for the EHRI community. Input from the research data community on DMP is discussed with and assessed by policy makers from IT-savvy EHRI partners. This input consists of the FAIR data principles, the certification of repositories by means of a certification framework, the data management services provided by the EUDAT Collaborative Data Infrastructure, and the current relevant practices of the invited partners as well as the Dutch National Archives. All these will be used as building blocks for the final roadmap for a long-term access infrastructure of Holocaust digital objects (D13.2).

relatedItems.label: Establish the legal and ethical framework
relatedItems.description:
Complete all legal groundwork before any recording takes place. This phase is mandatory and non-negotiable.

1. Determine the legal basis for data processing: identify the applicable legal basis under GDPR Art. 6 (e.g. consent of the data subject, public interest, scientific research). Consult applicable national legislation (e.g. Italy: "Codice in materia di protezione dei dati personali"; "Regole deontologiche per il trattamento a fini di archiviazione nel pubblico interesse"). Align your choice with the institutional mandate of the data controller.
2. Draft and distribute the privacy notice: prepare a privacy notice compliant with GDPR Arts. 12–14. Write it in plain, accessible language. Deliver it to each participant before any data collection begins. The notice must specify the legal basis, the purposes and modalities of processing, data retention periods, and participant rights. It may be provided in writing or, where identity is verifiable by other means, orally.
3. Obtain interview authorisation: collect the participant's authorisation to take part in the research — distinct from GDPR consent — either in writing or as a recorded oral declaration at the opening of the session. Confirm the authorisation at the close of the interview. Incorporate this declaration directly into the audio or video recording where possible.
4. Address copyright: clarify authorship and exploitation rights. The interviewer, as the party who structures the encounter and formulates questions, generally holds copyright over the interview as a creative work (Italian Law no. 633/1941; EU Directive 2019/790). Include a rights-assignment clause in the participant waiver, covering both image rights and intellectual property rights. Define contractual terms with any commissioning institution or conservation archive before fieldwork begins.
5. Prepare documentation templates: assemble the following before entering the field: (a) privacy notice; (b) interview authorisation form; (c) participant waiver with rights-assignment clause; (d) field recording sheet; (e) individual document sheet. Use models provided by the "Vademecum".

label: Digital Humanities 2019 Workshop: The Case Of Interview Data
description:
**Date:** 09 July 2019
**Location:** Utrecht, The Netherlands
 
# DH2019 Workshop: The Case Of Interview Data
A multidisciplinary approach to the use of technology in research using interview methods
 
## Lecturers

Arjan van Hessen, Stefania Scagliola, Louise Corti, Silvia Calamai, Norah Karrouche, Christoph Draxler, Henk van den Heuvel
 
## The workshop

The event took place in the frame of the Digital Humanities Conference 2019, in Utrecht from the 9th to the 12th of July and it was organised by [Oralhistory.eu](https://oralhistory.eu/) in collaboration with the SSHOC project, with [CLARIN ERIC](https://www.clarin.eu/) and with the [UK Data Service](https://ukdataservice.ac.uk/).

This pre-conference workshop at DH2019 in Utrecht presented the complete workflow for processing spoken interview data, e.g. from the domain of Oral History. The workshop focused on free web services and tools.

-    Preprocessing of audio signal data
-    Automatic speech recognition for the transcription of speech data
-    Manual correction of the transcript
-    Automatic time-alignment of the transcript
-    Additional analysis and annotation of the data, e.g. emotion recognition

## SSHOC' Involvement

This workshop addresses the data creation phase of the data lifecycle within the Social Sciences and Humanities, which is one of the major goals of the SSHOC project, tackled within WP4 where SSHOC partners, who are also lecturers at the workshop, are collecting, processing and analyzing audio data in the form of voice recorded interviews with automatic speech recognition and are developing a survey module specifically adapted to integrate audio recordings and their processing into the traditional data collection process.

## About the Oralhistory.eu Group:

The Oralhistory.eu Group is a multidisciplinary group of European scholars, tools and data professionals, spanning the fields of speech technology, social sciences, human computer interaction, oral history and linguistics, interested in strengthening the position of interview data in Digital Humanities. Since 2016 they have organized a series of workshops, supported by CLARIN on this topic ([See this website](https://oralhistory.eu/workshops)).

Their first concrete output was the development of the **T-Chain**, a tool that supports transcription and alignment of audio and text in multiple languages. Second, they developed a format for experimenting with a variety of annotation, text analysis and emotion recognition tools as they apply to interview data.

-    Christoph Draxler, University of Munchen

relatedItems.label: Creation of a Digital Music Edition
relatedItems.description:
A digital edition encodes musical information as structured, machine-readable, and semantically rich data, a transformation that requires a series of methodological and technical decisions. This workflow addresses the full range of operations involved, including the choice of encoding format, the management of metadata, the establishment of relationships with sources, the integration of a critical apparatus, and the conditions for sustainable online publication.
It outlines the essential steps required to produce a scholarly digital music edition, from the initial scoping of the corpus to its long-term archiving and dissemination. Structured around the three pillars of digital editing—tools, content, and presentation—it is designed to ensure compliance with FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) principles throughout the entire lifecycle of the edition.

Developed from the Guide to Digital Music Editing produced by the Consortium-HN MUSICA within the French research infrastructure Huma-Num, this workflow also aligns with the requirements of the European ECHOES project (European Cloud for Heritage Open Science), which frames digital editions as components of digital twins integrating source digitization, musical encoding, and audio recording. It is intended for researchers, digital humanists, and engineers working in institutional contexts shaped by Open Access policies and European research funding frameworks.

relatedItems.label: Make your oral sources accessible and reusable
relatedItems.description:
Make your oral sources accessible to researchers and, where legally permissible, to the wider public. Apply FAIR principles throughout.

1. Structure data and metadata for FAIR compliance: structure metadata to ensure Findability (assign persistent identifiers; use rich descriptive metadata), Accessibility (store in open or widely supported formats; ensure long-term availability of metadata even if access to data is restricted), Interoperability (use shared vocabularies and standards such as Dublin Core, EAD, or domain-specific thesauri), and Reusability (attach clear licence information; document provenance and context). Consult the FAIR Principles documentation for a full specification.
2. Publish online with an explicit release form: where an explicit "liberatoria" exists, publish the oral source online. Protect third parties mentioned in the recording: de-index their names from search engines where the information could damage their reputation; place sensitive content behind a registration-protected access area. Provide rich contextual metadata for all published materials.
3. Apply appropriate access restrictions where no release form exists: where no explicit release exists, choose among the following graduated approaches: (a) exclude the recording from online publication; (b) publish only excerpts already available in other public forms (print, documentary, educational DVD); (c) publish a pseudonymised transcript, ensuring the individual cannot be re-identified through cross-referencing; (d) publish a keyword index (thesaurus-based) omitting personal names; (e) provide authenticated access for research and educational purposes only; (f) state publicly the willingness to remove content on explicit request. Recall that these restrictions do not apply to recordings of public figures whose personal opinions, religious affiliation, or public acts are already widely known.
4. Assign a Creative Commons licence: choose and attach a Creative Commons licence to each published oral source. Select the licence that best reflects the rights-assignment conditions established with the interviewer and interviewee: CC BY (attribution only), CC BY-NC (non-commercial), CC BY-ND (no derivatives), or more restrictive combinations. Note that CC licences govern the circulation of the work online; they do not supersede GDPR obligations, which govern the processing of personal data independently.
5. Deposit in a trusted digital repository: deposit the oral source collection — including recordings, documentation, and metadata — in a trusted digital repository aligned with open science principles. Ensure the repository assigns persistent identifiers (DOI, Handle, or equivalent). Verify that the repository's preservation commitments cover refresh, format migration, and long-term access. Cross-link the deposit record with related publications and project documentation.

relatedItems.label: Defining and implementing data models
relatedItems.description:
The definition and implementation of the specific data model is of high importance for the further use of the data. The curator should take into account the needs of the specific community, cataloguing standards, and authority files as well as systems of persistent identifiers and descriptive thesauri and ontologies for the needs of the subject description.
The current bibliographic data processing is dominated by the standardised exchange coming from the librarianship sphere. The most popular format is undoubtedly MARC21 and its different variants. MARC21 is a specific hybrid format which might not be easy to understand outside the librarian community. Another option is BIBFRAME, LOD-based format coming from the librarian sphere as well. With regard to the interoperability, the common data standards can be used (e. g. Dublin Core). Specific option is to process the bibliography in the form of linked data/wikidata format. We would not recommend using proprietary data format unless there is no other option available, because it highly complicates the data interoperability.
Next to the format, the list of processed information (database fields) should be prepared. For most of the data, the relevant fields should be available in the standardised formats. There is a possibility to use nationally or locally defined fields as well. If any relevant field is not defined within the standard, it is possible to use e. g. note field in a consistent way.
For the needs of interconnection of the data it is crucial to implement the system of persistent identifiers. These identifiers are crucial for data interoperability and data enrichment from the external sources. National authorities files should be taken into account as PID general knowledge databases adapted for the given country. Individual authorities systems are mapped on the international Virtual Authority File (VIAF) which enables interconnection between various systems of national authority system as well as to wikidata. Subject description might be realised with the set of national authorities as well, but for the needs of specialised discipline bibliographies they might be too general and more granular hierarchy might be needed. The examples of such thesauri might be MESH or AGROVOC.
Finally, a crucial task is to understand the licensing of your data – both those that are being reused and those which are created manually. Proper licensing decision have decisive implications on future data reuse. For open digital literary bibliography Creative Commons licences could be recommended.

The use of interoperable machine-readable metadata enhances discoverability and use since the data can be processed by a computer. Interoperability helps in the aggregation of datasets to search across several catalogues.

**How**
For example, controlled vocabularies such as [Data Catalog Vocabulary DCAT](https://marketplace.sshopencloud.eu/tool-or-service/1Y0yKp) enables a publisher to describe datasets using a standard model that facilitates the consumption and aggregation of metadata from multiple catalogues (e.g., the [DCAT GLAM Catalogue](https://github.com/hibernator11/dcat-glam-catalog)). Other examples of vocabularies are [Dublin Core](https://marketplace.sshopencloud.eu/training-material/bxWKhV), [Schema.org](https://schema.org/) and [Simple Knowledge Organization System (SKOS)](https://marketplace.sshopencloud.eu/training-material/mUQw6r).

relatedItems.label: Post-process and normalise the transcription
relatedItems.description:
After the initial transcription, and having respected the phonetic reality produced by the speaker, it may be appropriate to intervene with simplification and normalisation operations to make the transcription usable for its intended purpose and audience. 

One common case concerns the normalisation of pronunciation variants. Minor fluctuations in the pronunciation of a given segment — which may have been transcribed with slightly different symbols across occurrences in the corpus — can often be unified under a single symbol after analysis, provided that the variation carries no contrastive or analytically significant function. For example, if a vowel is inconsistently realised between two slightly different articulatory positions, the analyst may choose either to preserve this difference by using two distinct phonetic notations, or to transcribe it uniformly using a single notation once it has been established that the variation is not meaningful to the analysis. The decision to normalise must follow, not precede, analysis: only after examining the distribution and function of a variable should you decide whether to represent its different variants with a single symbol. Normalisation should be conservative — when in doubt, preserve the variation.

A “narrow” transcription is appropriate for strictly phonetic research, or for studies in which phonetics constitutes a privileged level of analysis. Even in such cases, however, the transcriber may choose to represent certain phenomena in greater detail when they constitute the direct object of investigation, while paying less attention to other aspects. Although such choices may be acceptable for practical reasons related to time and resources, they must always be made explicit so that readers do not draw inaccurate conclusions from the transcription data. Any deviations from standard IPA symbols and conventions should likewise be clearly explained and properly justified, and should only be introduced when the IPA does not already provide a notation sufficiently adequate for what is being transcribed.

By contrast, in research that does not pursue specifically phonetic objectives, “broad” phonetic transcriptions are generally preferred. These omit most diacritics and tend to normalise minor fluctuations in pronunciation. More generally, every decision taken during transcription and post-processing should be documented clearly and transparently, so that users of the transcription can interpret the data correctly.

relatedItems.label: Vom Suchen und Finden: Einführung in die Recherche mit der Gemeinsamen Normdatei / Searching and finding: Introduction to searching with the Common Authority File (GND))
relatedItems.description:
Wie kann man mittels der Verwendung von Normdaten seine Suchergebnisse nach Literatur und Daten verbessern. Was sind Normdaten und welche Funktion haben sie bei der Beschreibung von Objekten wie Publikationen, Forschungsdaten oder Sammlungsgut? Im Fokus dieser Einführung stehen die Normdaten der Gemeinsamen Normdatei (GND), das zentrale kontrollierte Vokabular für Kultur und Forschung im deutschsprachigen Raum. Im Text werden dann verschiedene Anwendungen vorgestellt, mit denen man in der GND passende Suchbegriffe beispielsweise für die Suche nach geeigneter Literatur zum eigenen Thema findet. Zugleich erfährt man, wie man seine eigenen Texte und Daten durch die Verwendung von Normdaten für Dritte leichter auffindbar und damit sichtbarer machen kann.

Diese Ressource wird von Text+ unterstützt. Bei Fragen können Sie sich an den Text+ Helpdesk wenden: textplus-support@gwdg.de
Text von Moritz Strickert (UB HU Berlin) in einer von Barbara Fischer (DNB AfS) überarbeiteten Fassung.

- - -

How can you improve your search results for literature and data by using standardised data? What is authority data and what function does it have in the description of objects such as publications, research data or collections? This introduction focuses on the authority files of the Gemeinsame Normdatei (GND), the central controlled vocabulary for culture and research in German-speaking countries. The text then presents various applications for finding suitable search terms in the GND, for example, when searching for appropriate literature on one's topic. At the same time, it explains how to make one's own texts and data more easily discoverable and thus more visible to others by using authority data.

This resource is supported by Text+. In case of questions you may get in touch with the Text+ helpdesk at textplus-support@gwdg.de.

relatedItems.description:
The GND Agency Text+  is a service that is being set up at the Göttingen State and University Library (SUB Göttingen) as part of the NFDI consortium Text+. As a partner of the GND (Integrated Authority File), the agency acts as a central point of contact, initially for projects in the humanities and cultural sciences that are funded by Text+.
This resource is supported by Text+. In case of questions, you may get in touch with the Text+ Helpdesk at textplus-support@gwdg.de.

Die GND-Agentur Text+ ist ein Service, der im Rahmen des NFDI-Programms Text+ an der SUB Göttingen aufgebaut wird. Als Partner der GND (Gemeinsame Normdatei) fungiert die Agentur als zentrale Anlaufstelle zunächst für geistes- und kulturwissenschaftliche Projekte, die im Rahmen des NFDI-Konsortiums Text+ gefördert werden. Langfristig ist geplant, sowohl den Service zu verstetigen als auch das Angebot auf eine breitere Projektlandschaft auszuweiten.

Was machen wir?
Ziel der Agentur ist es, Projekte dabei zu unterstützen, ihre Forschungsdaten als Normdaten in die GND einzubringen.

Dazu gehören:

Die inhaltliche Beratung hinsichtlich der Eignungskriterien von Daten für die GND.
Die Bereitstellung und Weiterentwicklung von entityXML, dem Datenformat für den Austausch von Normdaten zwischen Projekten und Agentur.
Die Bereitstellung einer technischen Umgebung für die Datenverarbeitung auf Grundlage von entityXML .
Das Einspielen von potentiellen Kandidaten in die GND.
Die Bereitstellung von GND-IDs für die Projekte.
Wie unterstützen wir?
Kontaktstelle: Wir sind die erste Anlaufstelle, wenn Sie Ihre Daten in die GND einbringen möchten. Bei projektspezifischem Bedarf vermitteln wir Sie ggf. an eine unserer GND-Partneragenturen weiter.

Beratungsstelle (im Aufbau): Wir beraten Sie bei Fragen rund um die GND und stellen Ihnen Informationsmaterial zur Verfügung.

Datenservice: Wir unterstützen Sie bei der Erstellung von GND-konformen Normdaten. Ihre Daten werden validiert, bereinigt, angereichert und in das für den Dateningest in die GND erforderliche Format konvertiert. Die mit einem GND-ID angereicherten Daten werden von uns an Sie zurückgespielt.

Kontakt: gnd-agentur[at]sub.uni-goettingen.de

relatedItems.label: Integrated Authority File (GND)
relatedItems.description:
The Integrated Authority File (GND) is a service facilitating the collaborative use and administration of authority data. These authority data represent and describe entities, i.e. persons, corporate bodies, conferences and events, geographic entities, topics and works relating to cultural and academic collections. Authority data make cataloguing easier, offer definitive search entries and forge links between different information resources.

It is operated cooperatively by the German National Library, all German-speaking library networks and the associated libraries, the German Union Catalogue of Serials (ZDB) and numerous other institutions. Contributions to the GND are made either via the networks or in direct agreement with the German National Library.

The Common Authority File (GND) is a service for the cooperative use and management of authority data. This authority data represents and describes entities, i.e. persons, corporate bodies, conferences, geographies, subject headings and works that are related to cultural and scientific collections. Standardised data facilitates indexing, provides clear search access points and links different information resources.

relatedItems.label: Organize, describe and conserve the oral sources
relatedItems.description:
Implement preservation measures as soon as field production is complete. Conservation is not a deferred activity: decisions taken at this stage determine the long-term accessibility and integrity of the source.

1. Organise and name files systematically: apply a consistent file-naming convention that reflects the project, the date, and the session identifier. Store files in a structured directory that mirrors the relationship between the field recording sheet and the individual document sheets. Keep all documents produced in a single recording event together.
2. Create preservation copies: produce at minimum: one high-resolution preservation copy (WAV/BWF, 96 kHz, 24-bit for audio; MPEG-4 AVC for video); one local copy on a redundant storage medium (NAS or equivalent); one off-site copy in a secure, trusted cloud repository. Optionally produce a lower-resolution access copy (MP3 or equivalent) for consultation purposes. Never delete original analogue supports after digitisation.
3. Add preservation metadata: attach to each digitised document the following preservation metadata: original support type and conservation state; playback equipment and technical parameters used for digitisation; digital format, codec, sampling rate, bit depth; software and operator information; date of digitisation. Preserve scans or photographs of original physical supports and their containers.
4. Digitise analogue supports (if applicable): for recordings on magnetic tape, vinyl, cylinders, or other analogue media, contract a specialist digitisation centre with documented expertise (public or private). Follow IASA TC-04 for audio and IASA TC-06 for video. The preservation copy must be a faithful transfer of the original signal: introduce no filtering, noise reduction, or signal enhancement. Retain the analogue original after digitisation.
5. Describe sources for discovery and access: describe each oral source within a network of relations: link the recording to its field recording sheet, to the research project, to the agents involved (interviewer, interviewee, archivist), and to any related documents. Use controlled vocabularies and authority files. Consult descriptive software in use at reference institutions (see "Vademecum"). Align description with Dublin Core or EAD standards where applicable, to support interoperability.
6. Identify or select a conservation institution: if you are an independent researcher or a small institution, identify a conservation centre suited to your collection by disciplinary affinity or geographic proximity. Prepare: (a) a project presentation sheet; (b) a transfer sheet specifying access conditions, use restrictions, reproduction rights, and loan terms. Transfer the collection in its entirety: avoid splitting a unified archival complex across multiple institutions.
7. Plan for refresh and format migration: digitisation alone does not guarantee long-term access. Establish a schedule for periodic refresh (copying files to new storage supports before degradation) and for format migration (moving files to new formats before obsolescence). If the collection is deposited in a conservation centre, clearly define which institution or department is responsible for carrying out these long-term preservation operations.

label: Evaluation of the analytical potential of laser-induced breakdown spectrometry (LIBS) for the analysis of historical glasses
description: The novel and---for archaeometrical applications---still rarely used Laser-Induced Breakdown Spectrometry (LIBS) was tested on various standard glasses for its spectrometric performance. LIBS is an almost non-destructive method based on the time-resolved detection of optical emission following direct laser ablation. A frequency-quadrupoled Nd:YAG laser at 266 nm was found to cause a hardly visible crater of c. 200 µm in diameter. The application of an innovative high-resolution Echelle spectrograph allows the fast and simultaneous determination of up to 90 elements in the spectral range from 200 to 780 nm, with a resolution of 10--30 pm under ambient conditions. In principle, LIBS has a high analytical potential for archaeometry; in particular, for the determination of light elements (Li, Be, B and others). Because the measurement parameters (laser energy, delay time and number of pulses) do not independently influence the emission signal, their optimization proved to be complex and is rather a compromise for the range of elements. The effects of sample distance, surface roughness and the accumulation of depth profiles were studied. Problems arose for the determination of sodium and potassium in higher contents due to self-absorption effects. Quantification tests using a silicon line as internal standard yielded a precision range between 3% and 20% relative, but in general no satisfying accuracy for a number of elements. However, these problems might be overcome in the near future by improved spectrometer set-ups and matrix correction approaches

relatedItems.label: Make your oral sources accessible and reusable
relatedItems.description:
Make your oral sources accessible to researchers and, where legally permissible, to the wider public. Apply FAIR principles throughout.

1. Structure data and metadata for FAIR compliance: structure metadata to ensure Findability (assign persistent identifiers; use rich descriptive metadata), Accessibility (store in open or widely supported formats; ensure long-term availability of metadata even if access to data is restricted), Interoperability (use shared vocabularies and standards such as Dublin Core, EAD, or domain-specific thesauri), and Reusability (attach clear licence information; document provenance and context). Consult the FAIR Principles documentation for a full specification.
2. Publish online with an explicit release form: where an explicit "liberatoria" exists, publish the oral source online. Protect third parties mentioned in the recording: de-index their names from search engines where the information could damage their reputation; place sensitive content behind a registration-protected access area. Provide rich contextual metadata for all published materials.
3. Apply appropriate access restrictions where no release form exists: where no explicit release exists, choose among the following graduated approaches: (a) exclude the recording from online publication; (b) publish only excerpts already available in other public forms (print, documentary, educational DVD); (c) publish a pseudonymised transcript, ensuring the individual cannot be re-identified through cross-referencing; (d) publish a keyword index (thesaurus-based) omitting personal names; (e) provide authenticated access for research and educational purposes only; (f) state publicly the willingness to remove content on explicit request. Recall that these restrictions do not apply to recordings of public figures whose personal opinions, religious affiliation, or public acts are already widely known.
4. Assign a Creative Commons licence: choose and attach a Creative Commons licence to each published oral source. Select the licence that best reflects the rights-assignment conditions established with the interviewer and interviewee: CC BY (attribution only), CC BY-NC (non-commercial), CC BY-ND (no derivatives), or more restrictive combinations. Note that CC licences govern the circulation of the work online; they do not supersede GDPR obligations, which govern the processing of personal data independently.
5. Deposit in a trusted digital repository: deposit the oral source collection — including recordings, documentation, and metadata — in a trusted digital repository aligned with open science principles. Ensure the repository assigns persistent identifiers (DOI, Handle, or equivalent). Verify that the repository's preservation commitments cover refresh, format migration, and long-term access. Cross-link the deposit record with related publications and project documentation.

relatedItems.label: Federated Content Search Tutorial
relatedItems.description:
The Aggregator application is a part of the CLARIN-FCS common federated content search infrastructure. It serves as a user interface to perform queries to CLARIN-
 resources and display search results. The Aggregator communicates with components called endpoints, which are provided as a service by all centres who participate in the federated content search. Each endpoint provides access to one or more searchable resources. The user can select a specific resource or resources, based on the resource name or on the language, or search through all of them. The content of these resources is searched with the query supplied to the endpoint. The endpoint returns results to this query and the aggregator collects the responses from all the endpoints and displays them to the user.

relatedItems.label: CLARIN Federated Content Search
relatedItems.description: The Federated Content Search (FCS) is an established search platform that allows accessing distributed linguistic resources using a common specification of technical interfaces, data formats, and query languages. The framework was developed in the European CLARIN project and is based on standard protocols like OASIS searchRetrieve and the Contextual Query Language (CQL).

relatedItems.label: FCS Endpoint Validator
relatedItems.description: The Federated Content Search (FCS) is a specification and technical infrastructure for querying and aggregating distributed research data. FCS Endpoints implement this specification to offer search through local resources for the infrastructure (FCS Clients). The FCS Endpoint Validator is a service to check conformance to the FCS and SRU protocols of FCS endpoints to help developers and endpoint operators.

relatedItems.label: Text+ Federated Content Search (FCS)
relatedItems.description:
The Federated Content Search (FCS) is a specification and technical infrastructure for querying and aggregating distributed research data. It enables access to a wide range of resource types across the various Text+ data domains and is integrated into the Text+ portal as the consortium's central search function in a user-friendly way.
This resource is supported by Text+. In case of questions you may get in touch with the Text+ helpdesk at textplus-support@gwdg.de.

label: Federated Content Search Tutorial
description:
The Aggregator application is a part of the CLARIN-FCS common federated content search infrastructure. It serves as a user interface to perform queries to CLARIN-
 resources and display search results. The Aggregator communicates with components called endpoints, which are provided as a service by all centres who participate in the federated content search. Each endpoint provides access to one or more searchable resources. The user can select a specific resource or resources, based on the resource name or on the language, or search through all of them. The content of these resources is searched with the query supplied to the endpoint. The endpoint returns results to this query and the aggregator collects the responses from all the endpoints and displays them to the user.

relatedItems.label: Configure the annotation tool
relatedItems.description:
With the environment set up, you can now configure the annotation tool to align with the project’s collaborative structure, research goals and annotation schema. Naturally, the configuration is directly linked to the selected tool. For the purposes of this workflow, the steps outlined are based on the [Recogito Studio](https://recogitostudio.org/) platform.
- Implement collaboration roles and access according to your annotation schema and the roles explicitly assigned by the tool.
- Choose/import basemap layer: If the map(s) have been georeferenced or georectified (see Step 3), the output could be imported and used as a basemap layer in the GeoTagger plugin of the annotation tool.   
- Set the annotation vocabulary: Determine whether an annotation vocabulary that fits your purposes already exists. If a suitable vocabulary is available, select it or import it into the annotation tool. If not, **run the Vocabulary Creation Workflow** [workflow currently under development — more elaborate description will be delivered soon] and develop a custom vocabulary that reflects your project’s needs, considering the integration or extension of domain-specific ontologies (e.g., [CIDOC CRM](https://cidoc-crm.org/)) or thesauri (e.g., [Getty AAT](https://www.getty.edu/research/tools/vocabularies/aat/)). Once the new vocabulary is defined, import it into the annotation platform. In all cases, consider the desired level of annotation granularity (as defined in your annotation schema) as well as interoperability with other datasets and systems. 
- Set gazetteer(s) for geo-tagging: Determine whether a suitable gazetteer already exists for your project’s geographical and historical context, as defined in your annotation schema (e.g., [Pleiades](https://pleiades.stoa.org/) for ancient places, [World Historical Gazetteer](https://whgazetteer.org/) for historical places, [GeoNames](https://www.geonames.org/) for modern locations, or even [Wikidata](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:Main_Page)). If no appropriate gazetteer exists, or if existing gazetteers only partially cover your needs, consider seeking support — for example, from the [World Historical Gazetteer](https://whgazetteer.org/) team or the [Pelagios Gazetteer Activity](https://pelagios.org/activities/gazetteers/). If these options are not applicable, you may need to compile or create a custom gazetteer, tailored to your project needs. In that case, run the **Gazetteer Creation Workflow** [workflow currently under development — more elaborate description will be delivered soon] and once finalized, import it in the appropriate format into the annotation environment.

label: Fluorescence and Raman spectra on painting materials:reconstruction of spectra with mathematical methods
description: SERDS (shift excitation difference spectroscopy) and SSRS (subtracted shifted Raman spectroscopy) methods were applied for fluorescence-background rejection in the Raman spectra of colored materials. These techniques are based on the assumption that the fluorescence contribution can be completely eliminated by subtracting two Raman spectra acquired at two shifted laser excitation frequencies. For the SERDS method a micro-Raman experimental apparatus coupled with a tunable diode laser (central emission at 684 nm) was set up. SSRS measurements were made on a commercial micro-Raman instrument; in this case the shifted spectrum was obtained by moving the spectrometer grating. Raman spectra were then reconstructed by applying the difference deconvolution method that automatically converts the difference signals in Raman peaks through a deconvolution operation. These techniques were tested on two reference colors (ultramarine and 6,6′-dibromoindigotine) and two colored samples of unknown composition (a Pompeian pink powder and a blue paint from a XVII century painting). Fluorescence-background subtraction and the following operation of spectra reconstruction took place successfully with no errors in Raman peaks, width and wavenumber position. In addition, even weak spectral details were revealed favoring the comparison with reference data for a molecular identification

relatedItems.label: Research Design and Methodological Planning
relatedItems.description:
The treatment of oral sources begins with a carefully structured phase of research design and methodological planning, which shapes the quality of the data collected as well as its legal validity, long-term preservation, and future reuse. This phase brings together methodological reflection, technical, and ethical choices, legal awareness, and archival foresight.

At its core lies a solid grounding in the principles and practices of linguistics and oral history. Researchers—and, where applicable, collaborators—should develop a clear awareness of the legal, ethical, and deontological implications of working with oral testimonies. This includes familiarity with relevant international and national guidelines, such as those of the Oral History Society (OHS) and the Associazione Italiana di Storia Orale (AISO), and an understanding of the responsibilities linked to the collection, processing, and preservation of personal narratives. At this stage, the focus is on building awareness within the research team, rather than formally informing participants.

Methodological planning also involves defining the research framework, including research questions, scope, and participant selection. Interviews should be conceived as co-constructed communicative events; therefore, flexible interview guides are preferable to rigid questionnaires, allowing space for digressions that may open new lines of inquiry.

Researchers must also anticipate the conditions of the recording, including the choice of environment and the establishment of a relationship of trust with participants, which directly affects the quality and interpretability of the testimonies.

Technical planning is equally essential. Decisions regarding recording formats (audio or audio-video) and equipment should be made in relation to research objectives and future uses of the data. These choices are methodological as much as technical, as they shape the nature and reusability of the sources.

Finally, this phase includes preparing the documentation resources that will support the workflow, such as interview guides, information sheets, consent and authorization forms, and recording sheets for contextual data. Anticipating legal requirements, preservation strategies, and future access conditions ensures coherence across the process and supports the sustainable reuse of oral sources.

label: forTEXT & CATMA - YouTube Channel
description:
Worum geht es in Goethes Werther? Wie schlagen sich Freundschaften zwischen Schriftstellern in ihren Texte nieder? Wie sieht das Netzwerk der Figuren in Hoffmanns Sandmann aus?  

Diesen und anderen Fragen aus der Literaturgeschichte gehen wir hier nach. Dabei nähern wir uns der wunderbaren Welt der Bücher immer mit digitalen Methoden. So erfährst du, wie sich Literatur in Daten und Daten in Interpretationen verwandeln lassen. Von der digitalen Annotation über die Netzwerkanalyse, die Stilometrie und bis hin zum Topic Modeling findest du hier zahlreiche Methoden. Wenn du danach gleich loslegen möchtest mit deiner eigenen digitalen Literaturanalyse, findest du in unseren Tutorials und Screencasts auch gleich Anleitungen dazu. 

Ob in der Schule oder in der Uni, forTEXT-Videos helfen dir dabei, Literatur einmal anders zu betrachten. Du bist Lehrer oder gibst Seminare an der Uni? Gerne kannst du unsere Videos kostenfrei für deine Lehre nutzen, denn alle Inhalte stehen unter cc-by Lizenz.

PLEASE NOTE: The videos are available in various languages, predominantly in German.

What is Goethe's *Werther* about? How are friendships between writers reflected in their texts? What does the network of characters look like in Hoffmann's *The Sandman*?

We explore these and other questions from literary history here. As we approach the wonderful world of books, we always use digital methods. You'll discover how literature can be transformed into data and data into interpretations. From digital annotation and network analysis to stylometry and topic modeling, you’ll find a variety of methods here. If you’re ready to dive into your own digital literary analysis, our tutorials and screencasts offer step-by-step guides.

Whether in school or university, forTEXT videos help you see literature in a new way. Are you a teacher or running seminars at a university? Feel free to use our videos in your teaching, as all content is licensed under cc-by and available for free use.

relatedItems.label: forTEXT Journal
relatedItems.description:
Die deutschsprachige Online-Zeitschrift forTEXT publiziert fundierte Beiträge zu Forschung und Lehre der textbasierten Digital Humanities.

Mit dem Ziel, Wissensaustausch zu fördern und Digital Humanities-Ansätze in Forschung und Lehre zu etablieren, bietet forTEXT eine Plattform für Veröffentlichungen von Beiträgen zu Methoden, Ressourcen und Tools der Digital Humanities. Als Diamond Open-Access-Zeitschrift steht forTEXT für eine offene Wissenschaftskultur, die den FAIR-Prinzipien folgt, um Transparenz, Nachnutzbarkeit und langfristige Verfügbarkeit sicherzustellen.

Die Calls for Papers für Digital-Humanities-Themen in Forschung und Lehre werden etwa halbjährlich veröffentlicht. Die eingereichten Beiträge durchlaufen ein Open-Review-Verfahren und werden dabei von unserer Fachredaktion begutachtet. Ausgewählte Ausgaben werden von Gastherausgeber*innen initiiert und betreut. 

Alle Ausgaben der forTEXT-Zeitschrift erscheinen als thematisch organisierte, sogenannte Rolling Issues, die fortlaufend um neue Beiträge ergänzt werden.

Ab der 13. Ausgabe werden erstmals Beiträge veröffentlicht, die im Rahmen eines Call for Papers eingereicht wurden und insbesondere nachnutzbare, praxiserprobte Lehrkonzepte für verschiedene Lehrformate vorstellen.

---

With the aim of promoting knowledge exchange and establishing digital humanities approaches in research and teaching, forTEXT offers a platform for publishing articles on methods, resources and tools in the digital humanities. As a diamond open access journal, forTEXT stands for an open scientific culture that follows the FAIR principles to ensure transparency, reusability and long-term availability.

Calls for papers on digital humanities topics in research and teaching are published approximately every six months. Submitted contributions undergo an open review process and are evaluated by our editorial team. Selected issues are initiated and supervised by guest editors. 

All issues of the forTEXT journal are published as thematically organised, so-called rolling issues, which are continuously supplemented with new contributions.

Starting with the 13th issue, contributions submitted as part of a call for papers will be published for the first time, presenting reusable, tried-and-tested teaching concepts for various teaching formats.

relatedItems.label: forTEXT Portal
relatedItems.description:
Das forTEXT-Portal bietet seit 2017 frei zugängliche, deutschsprachige Einführungen in digitale Tools und Methoden an. Unsere Einführungen sind für Interessierte, Studierende und traditionell geisteswissenschaftlich Forschende konzipiert, die wenig bis gar keine technischen Vorkenntnisse haben und sich für Ansätze der digitalen Geisteswissenschaften (Digital Humanitites, kurz DH) interessieren. Sie eignen sich sowohl zum Selbststudium als auch zum Einsatz in der Schul- und Hochschullehre (für Lehrende). Ergänzt wird das Angebot durch verschiedene Ressourcen wie Korpora, Tagsets, ein DH-Glossar, Jupyter Notebooks und Videotutorials auf Youtube und Zenodo.

Seit 2024 gehört auch unser Open-Access-Journal forTEXT dazu, in dem ein stärkerer Fokus auf Lehre gesetzt wird und nachnutzbare Digital Humanities-Lehrkonzepte (für Lehrende) veröffentlicht werden – mit dem Ziel, den Austausch über digitale Lehre weiter zu fördern. Im Journal haben wir außerdem alle Portalartikel als Zweitveröffentlichungen im Zeitschriftenformat veröffentlicht. Dort stehen die Webseitenartikel als PDFs zum Download zur Verfügung.

---

Since 2017, the forTEXT portal has been offering freely accessible, German-language introductions to digital tools and methods. Our introductions are designed for interested parties, students and traditional humanities researchers who have little or no prior technical knowledge and are interested in approaches to digital humanities (DH). They are suitable for self-study as well as for use in school and university teaching (for educators). The offering is supplemented by various resources such as corpora, tag sets, a DH glossary, Jupyter notebooks, and video tutorials on YouTube and Zenodo.

Since 2024, our open access journal forTEXT has also been part of the portal, placing a stronger focus on teaching and publishing reusable digital humanities teaching concepts (for teachers) with the aim of further promoting exchange on digital teaching. We have also published all portal articles as secondary publications in journal format in the journal. The website articles are available for download as PDFs.

relatedItems.label: Vistorian - A Network Analysis Tool for Digital Historians
relatedItems.description:
The Vistorian is an online tool for interactive exploration of dynamic, multivariate, and geographic networks. It is an active research project at the Vishub at the University of Edinburgh and Inria, France.

The Vistorian includes four different interactive visualizations – node-link, TimeArcs, matrix, and map with network – in the attempt of mediating between two different instances, the user intent and the usage context, which are often difficult to harmonize and are not always tackled by other network tools.

The Vistorian thus allows digital humanists, and especially historians, to analyze complex geolocated and temporal networks of individuals.

description: In this two-part lesson, we will build on what you’ve learned about Downloading Web Pages with Python, learning how to remove the HTML markup from the webpage of Benjamin Bowsey’s 1780 criminal trial transcript. Finally, we convert content from a long string to a list of words that can later be sorted, indexed, and counted.

relatedItems.label: Prepare the repository (preliminary step)
relatedItems.description:
The first step is to create or configure a repository on a version control platform — GitLab or GitHub are the two standard options in SSH research contexts. However, GitHub is not a open-source platform, and it is preferable to use an open-source forge such as Codeberg (https://codeberg.org/). Your repository must include a set of mandatory files at its root, in Markdown format. A README.md file describes your software, its research context, and its usage. An AUTHORS.md file lists all authors with their institutional affiliations; contributors not intended to appear in citation metadata may be listed separately in a CONTRIBUTORS file. 

A LICENSE file specifies the reuse conditions of your source code. Licence selection should be carried out in consultation with the legal or valorisation service of your institution, as intellectual property rights may be shared between you and your employer. A codemeta.json file, generated with the CodeMeta Generator, provides machine-readable metadata that will pre-populate your HAL deposit form automatically. Both the copyright notice and the list of authors must appear explicitly in your repository at this stage, as they condition both citability and archiving eligibility in subsequent steps.

Finally, both Git repositories and Zenodo provide options to configure automatic archiving and synchronization between the repository and Zenodo. This integration enables version management and ensures that each software release deposited on Zenodo is assigned a persistent DOI, thereby facilitating citation, traceability, and long-term preservation of the code.

label: Guidelines for adding Text+ Services to the SSH Open Marketplace
description:
This short guideline document how services affiliated with Text+ may be described in the SSH Open Marketplace.

With its portfolio, Text+ as an NFDI consortium for language- and text-based research data addresses various tasks within scientific research data management. A significant part of this portfolio consists of services that are provided by the participating data and competence centers as well as developments within Text+. These services – with the term "service" defined broadly – are to be provided through the Text+ portal in a simple, understandable, and contextualized manner.

The approach chosen by Text+ for making services visible therefore relies on:

SSH Open Marketplace as the actual provisioning and curation site of the descriptive metadata of the services,

Text+ Registry as the delivering service in the Text+ portal, which harvests the metadata from the SSH Open Marketplace,
And the Text+ portal itself as the presentation layer on top of the registry.
Overall, both Marketplace and Registry remain as machine-harvestable sources, with the Marketplace being the authoritative source.
