relatedItems.label: Transkribus Text Tagging
relatedItems.description:
The workflow describes the strategic development and deployment of a text tagging scheme for transcribed historical prints and / or handwritten resources. It aims primarily at larger collections that consist of relatively homogenous resource types. That means they are similar compared to each other regarding their historic context, structure, extent, language, etc.

If you’ve done transcriptions using Transkribus, it may be the ideal platform to implement your tagging scheme, but the approach is transferable.

Key objectives of the workflow are:
- manage quality and consistency for basic text analysis in the light of limited resources of academic research projects
- make large collections more manageable
- iteratively build up a comprehensible and consistent dataset
- adapt to the specific and generic characteristics of the source material on one side and 
- adapt early to key research questions and analytical dimensions on the other side
- provide the foundation for further data enrichment and higher levels of analysis such as normalized collection dictionaries, NER, Geo-Referencing, etc.
- create a model tagging scheme adapted to your needs for further scalability
- create ground truth data set for domain-specific AI text tagging

Please mind:
1. The workflow was developed in the context of a specific research project at the University of Basel, please visit ["VOCAL POWER"](https://dg.philhist.unibas.ch/de/bereiche/fruehe-neuzeit/snf-professur-macht-der-stimme/) for more information.
2. For the Open Marketplace it was shaped to address challenges that will very likely arise in similar projects. However: We strongly suggest thoroughly discussing all the steps with key stakeholders and project staff in order to adapt the parameters according to your own needs on the ground.
3. Work on data projects is prone to get out of hand easily, so plan your steps carefully, test and iterate small portions early on and finish one step at a time.

relatedItems.label: Transkribus - Handwritten Text Recognition technology for historical documents
relatedItems.description:
Transkribus is a platform for the automated recognition, transcription and searching of handwritten historical documents. Transkribus is part of the EU-funded Recognition and Enrichment of Archival Documents (READ) project. The core mission of the READ project is to make archival material more accessible through the development and dissemination of Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) and other cutting-edge technologies.

The workshop is aimed at researchers and students who are interested in the transcription, searching and publishing of historical documents. It will introduce participants to the technology behind the READ project and demonstrate the Transkribus transcription platform. Our team has already conducted 30 similar workshops over the course of 2016, including several sessions with digital humanities scholars and students.

relatedItems.label: Enrichir le candidat avec des alignements et des images
relatedItems.description:
Ajouter un alignement : il s’agit de créer une relation d’équivalence plus ou moins exacte entre le mot-clé Pactols et un item correspondant dans un autre référentiel du web. Pactols a fait le choix de préférer les relations exactes (skos:exactMatch). Les alignements ne sont possibles qu’avec des référentiels fournissant un identifiant pérenne à ses items (DOI, ARK,...) ou une adresse web stable (URI).

Les principaux référentiels des alignements Pactols sont : Wikidata, les thésaurus du ministère français de la Culture (http://data.culture.fr/thesaurus/), IdRef (oeuvres, personnes), le Art and Architecture Thesaurus de la Fondation Getty, Bibracte_thesaurus, Bnf, Pleiades (lieux anciens), Geonames (lieux), Insee (lieux de France). 

Deux modes d’alignement sont possibles : 
1. alignement : faites une recherche préalable dans le réservoir puis donnez l’URI distante de l’item et le nom du référentiel dans le formulaire.
Ex. URI distante : https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q6934696
      Nom de la source : Wikidata
2. alignement automatique : Opentheso opère une recherche sur le libellé dans les référentiels pré-enregistrés : Bibracte_thesaurus, Bnf, GeoNames, Wikidata. Selon le réservoir, la réponse peut être faussement négative sur le libellé en français, par exemple avec Wikidata dont les items peuvent ne pas avoir d’équivalent dans la langue de la recherche. Écrivez de préférence le terme de la requête dans la langue du référentiel visé. Sélectionnez la meilleure réponse affichée. La possibilité de rapatrier des métadonnées supplémentaires (traductions, images, définition) peut être un avantage mais nécessitera une relecture voire une correction après alignement. 

Image : Certains concepts, difficiles à définir, peuvent être illustrés avec profit d’une ou de plusieurs images. Celles-ci doivent être représentatives du concept et se positionner autant que possible dans le champ de l’archéologie sinon de l’histoire ancienne. Elles doivent impérativement être libres de droit (sélectionnez les réservoirs ad hoc, notamment Wikimedia Commons, et citables (avec une URI comme adresse web stable, un PID identifiant pérenne de type ARK, DOI, etc.).

Pour ajouter une image depuis Wikimedia Commons : sélectionnez l'image choisie, cliquez sur l'onglet "use this file" et recopiez le champ "File URL:". Remplissez les 4 champs de l'onglet Image de Pactols : l'URI, la légende de l'image (libellé), son auteur et la source. 
Ex. pour amphore attique : URI : https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/01/Amphore_attique_%C3%A0_figures_noires._Peintre_de_Rycroft_-_btv1b101044967_%282_of_2%29.jpg ; libellé : Amphore attique à figures noires. Peintre de Rycroft ; auteur : Bibliothèque nationale de France ; source : Wikimédia.

relatedItems.label: ArkeoGIS
relatedItems.description:
ARKEOGIS, SHARING AND USE OF SPATIALIZED DATA ABOUT THE PAST
ArkeoGIS enables to pool and query – thanks to a mapping interface – the spatialized scientific data about the past (archaeology, environment…). ArkeoGIS is an online platform accessible in four languages (German, English, Spanish and French).

ArkeoGIS is a multidisciplinary application. The databases come from different sources: institutional researchers’ work (either personal or contractual researches), graduate students’ researches, private companies and archaeological heritage management services. They also come from palaeoenvironementalists’, geographers’ and historians’ work. Multidisciplinarity is spurred and promoted All these shared (import protocol) databases are available and can be queried online (webGIS) by ArkeoGIS’ users.
Each user have its own personal and customizable project interface. One can query online all or only a part of these databases, display the results on multiple backgrounds maps, save and export them towards other tools one might use (CSV export).

The chronological frame of the tool is now both customizable and multiple. ArkeoGIS’ multi-chronologies system enables to aggregate, for different areas, information from the Prehistory to the Present. About ten chronologies are already available, from the Iberian Peninsula and the Mediterranean to the Middle East or continental Europe. ArkeoGIS’ geographical frame enables to display information about all of these regions. As today, the most documented areas are the Upper Rhine Valley, the Mediterranean and the Middle East.

ArkeoGIS can be used for many different forms of research, individual or collective. It allows, among other things, to handle the data management plan (DMP) for contractual researches. ArkeoGIS is a powerful tool to use during different kind of studies (excavations, synthesis or PhD thesis, etc.).
Several tens of thousands of sites, objects and analysis are already available. ArkeoGIS is also linking several digital tools, allowing its users to be aware of their existence.
Every author submitting his localized data into ArkeoGIS keeps the control over them and is the only one who can amend them. Any user can easily access to other contributors’ data and improve its own database. A directory allows researchers to contact each other. This initiative helps to develop scientific exchanges between countries and institutions.

Hosted by Huma-NUM IR*, ArkeoGIS is a lasting solution, the datasets are available in the NAKALA repository.

The ArkeoGIS’ project is run by the University of Strasbourg.

relatedItems.label: The Pactols Thesaurus
relatedItems.description:
Controlled, standardized and multilingual vocabulary for archaeology, from prehistory to the contemporary period and for the sciences of antiquity in all their aspects.

Pactols is a reservoir of controlled and multilingual keywords.

If it serves historically the indexing of the CCI (Frantiq's indexed collective catalog), its richness and its scalability seduced other communities. For several years, it has been used as a thematic repository for diversified resources (academic journals, scientific databases, heritage enhancement programs).

It was created by Frantiq (Federation and Resources on Antiquity constituted as a CNRS Service Group no. 3378), which brings together around fifty units CNRS, services of the Ministry of Culture, archaeological museums, local authorities and other public establishments.

It was developed with the support of MASA consortium, Memory of archaeologists and archaeological sites.

relatedItems.label: VIAF: The Virtual International Authority File
relatedItems.description: The VIAF (Virtual International Authority File) service provides libraries and library users with convenient access to the world's major name authority files. VIAF Contributors regularly supply authority data that VIAF matches, links, and groups. All descriptions for a given entity are merged into a cluster that brings together the different names for that entity. This service allows researchers to identify names, locations, works, and expressions while preserving regional preferences for language, spelling, and script.

relatedItems.label: Enrichir le candidat avec des alignements et des images
relatedItems.description:
Ajouter un alignement : il s’agit de créer une relation d’équivalence plus ou moins exacte entre le mot-clé Pactols et un item correspondant dans un autre référentiel du web. Pactols a fait le choix de préférer les relations exactes (skos:exactMatch). Les alignements ne sont possibles qu’avec des référentiels fournissant un identifiant pérenne à ses items (DOI, ARK,...) ou une adresse web stable (URI).

Les principaux référentiels des alignements Pactols sont : Wikidata, les thésaurus du ministère français de la Culture (http://data.culture.fr/thesaurus/), IdRef (oeuvres, personnes), le Art and Architecture Thesaurus de la Fondation Getty, Bibracte_thesaurus, Bnf, Pleiades (lieux anciens), Geonames (lieux), Insee (lieux de France). 

Deux modes d’alignement sont possibles : 
1. alignement : faites une recherche préalable dans le réservoir puis donnez l’URI distante de l’item et le nom du référentiel dans le formulaire.
Ex. URI distante : https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q6934696
      Nom de la source : Wikidata
2. alignement automatique : Opentheso opère une recherche sur le libellé dans les référentiels pré-enregistrés : Bibracte_thesaurus, Bnf, GeoNames, Wikidata. Selon le réservoir, la réponse peut être faussement négative sur le libellé en français, par exemple avec Wikidata dont les items peuvent ne pas avoir d’équivalent dans la langue de la recherche. Écrivez de préférence le terme de la requête dans la langue du référentiel visé. Sélectionnez la meilleure réponse affichée. La possibilité de rapatrier des métadonnées supplémentaires (traductions, images, définition) peut être un avantage mais nécessitera une relecture voire une correction après alignement. 

Image : Certains concepts, difficiles à définir, peuvent être illustrés avec profit d’une ou de plusieurs images. Celles-ci doivent être représentatives du concept et se positionner autant que possible dans le champ de l’archéologie sinon de l’histoire ancienne. Elles doivent impérativement être libres de droit (sélectionnez les réservoirs ad hoc, notamment Wikimedia Commons, et citables (avec une URI comme adresse web stable, un PID identifiant pérenne de type ARK, DOI, etc.).

Pour ajouter une image depuis Wikimedia Commons : sélectionnez l'image choisie, cliquez sur l'onglet "use this file" et recopiez le champ "File URL:". Remplissez les 4 champs de l'onglet Image de Pactols : l'URI, la légende de l'image (libellé), son auteur et la source. 
Ex. pour amphore attique : URI : https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/01/Amphore_attique_%C3%A0_figures_noires._Peintre_de_Rycroft_-_btv1b101044967_%282_of_2%29.jpg ; libellé : Amphore attique à figures noires. Peintre de Rycroft ; auteur : Bibliothèque nationale de France ; source : Wikimédia.

relatedItems.label: Omeka.net
relatedItems.description:
Omeka.net provides a web-publishing platform to curate collections and create exhibitions of digitized content. Omeka.net has grown out of the Omeka project. Omeka.net provides some of the same functionality as Omeka, but does not require the user to provide hosting or to maintain their installation in any way. However, use of Omeka.net limits customization, and hosting more than 500MB of content requires a paid account.

Objects in the collection can be cataloged with Dublin core metadata fields and georeferenced for display on a map. Omeka.net includes several plugins, including COinS (which makes objects in Omeka accessible to citations management software, like Zotero), HTML5 Media (to play audio and video), and Library of Congress Suggest (which will auto-populate fields with LoC authority and subject headings).

label: Use and Re-use of Scientific Data in Archaeology and Heritage
description:
**Date:** 02 April 2020
**Location:** Online

An opportunity to learn about novel policy and best practice around use and re-use of scientific data within the heritage science and archaeology contexts in this half-day webinar jointly organised by SSHOC, SEADDA and E-RIHS. We presented the new heritage science data curation policy developed by E-RIHS and SEADDA, discussed practice challenges and shared best tools to support on data re-use. Participation (live) by invitation.

## Speakers

Dr **Holly Wright** is International Projects Manager for the Archaeology Data Service, including participation in the SEADDA, ArchAIDE, NEARCH, E-RIHS, ARIADNE, ARIADNEplus, LoCloud, CARARE, and SENESCHAL projects. Her research focuses on archaeological field drawing and the Semantic Web, including specialisation in visual documentation and communication, archaeological data management, the use of Web standards and the Semantic Web in archaeology. 

Dr **Jessica Hendy** is Lecturer in Palaeoproteomics at the University of York. Her research focuses on the study of ancient proteins, and how these biomolecules can be used for understanding the past. She is interested in developing and applying proteomic methods to a diverse range of multidisciplinary projects, particularly in the study of past foods and diets. Her research seeks to characterise the culinary diversity of past societies, and in particular her research explores the antiquity and modern diversity of dairying practices, as well as food fermentation.

Dr **Scott Allan Orr** is a Lecturer in Heritage Data Science at the UCL Institute for Sustainable Heritage. He is the Deputy Course Director on the MSc in Data Science for Cultural Heritage, a programme pioneering a new way of teaching data science through application in a cross-disciplinary context. Scott’s research within heritage science uses data-driven methods to further understanding, improve management, and widen participation within the heritage sector. He primarily works on assessing climate impacts on buildings, the use of non-destructive tools, and incorporating value and perception into scientific evaluations.

relatedItems.label: Archaeology Data Service / Digital Antiquity Guides to Good Practice
relatedItems.description:
Modern archaeological projects have the capacity to create large quantities of digital information, whether from the on-site recording of excavation and survey data, specialist datasets developed during pre and post-excavation analysis, or publication of interpretative maps and plans. Digital information is created at every stage of a project, from fieldwork to assessment, analysis, and finally reporting and dissemination. Within the discipline, there has been an increasing awareness that data, not just artefacts and paper records, are part of the primary collection and should be preserved and archived as such. The current trend of moving away from physical and toward digital recording of information has made the lack of thoughtful preservation of digital data an even larger issue. In fact, in many cases, a digital dataset may be the only product of a project, and without thoughtful preservation, all context for any archaeological resources will be lost. 

The primary aim of these Guides to Good Practice is to provide information on the best way to create, manage, and document digital material produced during the course of an archaeological project. The ultimate aim of the Guides is to improve the practice of depositing and preserving digital information safely within an archive for future use.

relatedItems.label: Directory of the 111 ProBleu Funded School Projects
relatedItems.description:
This publication presents a collection of 111 school projects supported by the European project ProBleu (ProBleu Project, Grant agreement No. 101113001), focused on promoting water and ocean literacy across educational communities.

The projects included in this volume have enabled participating schools to develop learning experiences connected to aquatic ecosystems, sustainability, and environmental responsibility. Through these initiatives, many institutions have progressed towards accreditation as European Blue Schools and have become part of the Network of European Blue Schools, a growing community committed to advancing ocean literacy in education.

The collection reflects a wide diversity of educational contexts, including primary education, secondary education, special education and vocational and technical education and training (VET).

Each project is presented as an individual case study, combining:

- Descriptions of activities and objectives

- Real-world implementation examples

- Photographic documentation

- Reflections and insights from teachers

Together, these contributions illustrate how schools across Europe are integrating water and ocean literacy into their curricula, fostering student engagement, critical thinking, and environmental awareness. This compilation serves as a record of funded initiatives, and as a source of inspiration for educators and institutions interested in strengthening water literacy.

label: Use of secondary data in scientific research [Online Workshop, Presentation]
description:
In the last ten years, Serbia has been involved in the Open Science Movement, which is a policy priority for the European Commission and a method of collaboration and sharing within the scientific community. Despite the efforts made by the Ministry and research infrastructures, Serbian researchers, regardless of the scientific field or discipline, insufficiently use the data collected by other researchers, which is available through digital archives or repositories. 

The concept for the workshop originated from DCS's collaboration with colleagues from the Observatory of Social Innovations and the OPENAir movement in Serbia when it was determined that researchers in Serbia do not utilise available secondary data. Also, the CESSDA Data Catalogue, a resource intended for social science scholars, is similarly underutilised. 

The workshop “Use of secondary data within scientific research” primarily aimed to promote CESSDA Data Catalogue (CDC) with other services available in CESSDA Tools & Services portfolio. In addition, it intended to bring together and educate scientists in Serbia on locating and exploiting secondary data from various sources and what to consider while sharing research data. 

The workshop opened with an explanation of microdata from international studies like the Community Innovation Survey, European Social Survey, PISA, Labour force survey and others. The workshop continued with practical advice on how to prepare data to be easily discoverable and accessible on the web, as well as ideas on how to locate the data of others, along with an in-depth explanation of FAIR principles. The last part of the workshop presented the CESSDA ERIC as a European consortium for data in the social sciences. Primarily, the CESSDA Agenda was explained with coverage of the main pillars – Trust, Training, Technology and Tools & Services. The main data hub in CESSDA is the Data Catalogue (CDC) which was presented thoroughly. Additionally, the presentation covered other CESSDA services, ELLST (European Language Social Science Thesaurus), CESSDA Vocabulary Service, CESSDA Resource Directory, CESSDA Metadata Validator and European Question Bank.

The event was held in national language (Serbian).

relatedItems.label: Make your oral sources accessible and reusable
relatedItems.description:
Make your oral sources accessible to researchers and, where legally permissible, to the wider public. Apply FAIR principles throughout.

1. Structure data and metadata for FAIR compliance: structure metadata to ensure Findability (assign persistent identifiers; use rich descriptive metadata), Accessibility (store in open or widely supported formats; ensure long-term availability of metadata even if access to data is restricted), Interoperability (use shared vocabularies and standards such as Dublin Core, EAD, or domain-specific thesauri), and Reusability (attach clear licence information; document provenance and context). Consult the FAIR Principles documentation for a full specification.
2. Publish online with an explicit release form: where an explicit "liberatoria" exists, publish the oral source online. Protect third parties mentioned in the recording: de-index their names from search engines where the information could damage their reputation; place sensitive content behind a registration-protected access area. Provide rich contextual metadata for all published materials.
3. Apply appropriate access restrictions where no release form exists: where no explicit release exists, choose among the following graduated approaches: (a) exclude the recording from online publication; (b) publish only excerpts already available in other public forms (print, documentary, educational DVD); (c) publish a pseudonymised transcript, ensuring the individual cannot be re-identified through cross-referencing; (d) publish a keyword index (thesaurus-based) omitting personal names; (e) provide authenticated access for research and educational purposes only; (f) state publicly the willingness to remove content on explicit request. Recall that these restrictions do not apply to recordings of public figures whose personal opinions, religious affiliation, or public acts are already widely known.
4. Assign a Creative Commons licence: choose and attach a Creative Commons licence to each published oral source. Select the licence that best reflects the rights-assignment conditions established with the interviewer and interviewee: CC BY (attribution only), CC BY-NC (non-commercial), CC BY-ND (no derivatives), or more restrictive combinations. Note that CC licences govern the circulation of the work online; they do not supersede GDPR obligations, which govern the processing of personal data independently.
5. Deposit in a trusted digital repository: deposit the oral source collection — including recordings, documentation, and metadata — in a trusted digital repository aligned with open science principles. Ensure the repository assigns persistent identifiers (DOI, Handle, or equivalent). Verify that the repository's preservation commitments cover refresh, format migration, and long-term access. Cross-link the deposit record with related publications and project documentation.

label: Using LLM for Data Extraction with Historical Documents
description: This program offers a clear introduction to the mathematical and technical foundations of Large Language Models (LLMs), covering vectors, word embeddings, and the Transformer architecture. It builds practical skills through advanced prompting methods such as Few‑Shot and Chain‑of‑Thought, as well as direct interaction with APIs and parameters like Temperature for output control. Tutorials demonstrate systematic evaluation of LLM results using metrics such as Precision, Recall, and Character Error Rate against a manually created Gold Standard. The course also outlines how research data and code can be documented, licensed, and published on platforms like Zenodo in line with Open Science principles. Finally, it highlights critical issues including bias in training data, hallucinations, and effective handling of content filters when working with historical sources.

label: Using Praat for Linguistic Research
description:
Using Praat for Linguistic Research by Will Styler is a practical guidebook and information package designed to help you use the Praat phonetics software package more effectively in Phonetic or Phonological research. Although it was originally written in the Spring/Summer of 2011 for the 2011 Linguistic Institute’s Praat workshop, it’s now available for anybody who’s interested, and is being updated over time, both as Praat changes and as the author adds new information.

The guidebook itself is an 85+ page compilation of walkthroughs, explanations, and tutorials explaining how to use Praat for a variety of measurements and tasks. Although the guide does start with “basic” tasks like opening sound files, measuring duration, formants, pitch, it also covers more “advanced” tasks like source-filter resynthesis, A1-P0 nasality measurement, formula manipulation of sounds and even Praat scripting.

relatedItems.label: Post-process and normalise the transcription
relatedItems.description:
After the initial transcription, and having respected the phonetic reality produced by the speaker, it may be appropriate to intervene with simplification and normalisation operations to make the transcription usable for its intended purpose and audience. 

One common case concerns the normalisation of pronunciation variants. Minor fluctuations in the pronunciation of a given segment — which may have been transcribed with slightly different symbols across occurrences in the corpus — can often be unified under a single symbol after analysis, provided that the variation carries no contrastive or analytically significant function. For example, if a vowel is inconsistently realised between two slightly different articulatory positions, the analyst may choose either to preserve this difference by using two distinct phonetic notations, or to transcribe it uniformly using a single notation once it has been established that the variation is not meaningful to the analysis. The decision to normalise must follow, not precede, analysis: only after examining the distribution and function of a variable should you decide whether to represent its different variants with a single symbol. Normalisation should be conservative — when in doubt, preserve the variation.

A “narrow” transcription is appropriate for strictly phonetic research, or for studies in which phonetics constitutes a privileged level of analysis. Even in such cases, however, the transcriber may choose to represent certain phenomena in greater detail when they constitute the direct object of investigation, while paying less attention to other aspects. Although such choices may be acceptable for practical reasons related to time and resources, they must always be made explicit so that readers do not draw inaccurate conclusions from the transcription data. Any deviations from standard IPA symbols and conventions should likewise be clearly explained and properly justified, and should only be introduced when the IPA does not already provide a notation sufficiently adequate for what is being transcribed.

By contrast, in research that does not pursue specifically phonetic objectives, “broad” phonetic transcriptions are generally preferred. These omit most diacritics and tend to normalise minor fluctuations in pronunciation. More generally, every decision taken during transcription and post-processing should be documented clearly and transparently, so that users of the transcription can interpret the data correctly.

relatedItems.label: Transcribe and process the interview
relatedItems.description:
Produce a transcription of the recorded interview in order to enable analysis, indexing, and long-term accessibility. Transcription constitutes a key stage in the enrichment of the oral source, transforming an audio or audiovisual document into a textual resource that can be searched, annotated, and reused.

Define the level of transcription according to the objectives of the research. This may range from verbatim transcription (including hesitations, pauses, and non-verbal elements) to a more edited version that improves readability while preserving the meaning of the discourse. Where relevant, adopt established transcription conventions and ensure consistency across the corpus.

If required, integrate time-coding to align the transcription with the original recording, facilitating navigation between text and audio/video. Consider also the need for translation, particularly in multilingual research contexts.

During transcription, pay attention to the treatment of personal data and sensitive information. Anonymisation or pseudonymisation may be necessary, especially when preparing the material for dissemination or public access. Any modifications should be documented to ensure transparency and reproducibility.

The transcription should be treated as a distinct but related document within the oral source corpus. It must therefore be documented through a dedicated record, including its relationship to the original recording, the tools and methods used, and the identity of the transcriber.

This step may be carried out prior to, or in parallel with, the description and metadata creation phase, depending on the research design and available resources. In all cases, it significantly enhances the findability, accessibility, and reusability of the oral source in line with FAIR principles.

relatedItems.label: INCEpTION
relatedItems.description:
**INCEpTION** is an open-source, web-based platform for annotating text. It supports annotations of any span of text, from single words to whole documents, relations between annotations, coreference chains and document-level labels, on documents in formats such as plain text, PDF, HTML and TEI. INCEpTION is the successor of WebAnno and can import WebAnno projects.

* **Collaborative Annotation:** Multiple annotators can work on the same documents, with different workflow management schemes, built-in inter-annotator agreement measures, and curation of the individual annotations into a gold standard.
* **Customizable Annotation Layers:** Users define their own layers, features and tagsets in the browser, tailored to the needs of their project.
* **Knowledge Base Integration:** Annotations can be linked to knowledge bases and authority files such as Wikidata, the GND and SNOMED CT, to other resources in RDF, OWL, OBO or SKOS, and to remote SPARQL endpoints.
* **Machine Learning Integration:** Built-in recommenders learn from the annotations as users work and suggest new ones, active learning focuses attention on uncertain cases, and projects can connect their own models as external recommenders.
* **Interoperability:** It imports and exports a range of formats, including TEI, CoNLL-U and other CoNLL variants, WebAnno TSV, WebLicht TCF and UIMA XMI, and offers a REST API for integration into processing pipelines.
* **Flexible Deployment:** It runs on a single computer or on an institutional server with single sign-on. Hosted instances are offered through CLARIN:EL and CLARIN-IT.

These features make INCEpTION a comprehensive solution for building and managing annotated corpora.

label: Video: CESSDA Series on Variable Harmonization: An Overview of Concepts and Strategies
description:
Dr. Kristi Winters (GESIS) and Janek Bruker (formerly of GESIS) discuss social science variable harmonization and harmonized data documentation practices. This is video 1 in a series of 4 videos and the video provides introductory information on social science variable harmonization. Topics in this four-part educational video series include: an introduction to social science variable harmonization, ex ante and ex post harmonization strategies, examples from international social science surveys (including the European Values Survey), the use of international standard classifications, and how to use metadata to construct FAIR variable harmonization documentation. This video was created for the Consortium of European Social Science Archives (CESSDA).
The course material comprises the presentation "Variable Harmonization in the Social Sciences" (http://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.3924955) and the full series of 4 videos:

Objective: This video aimed to discuss social science metadata and standards for documenting harmonized social science data.

relatedItems.label: Make your oral sources accessible and reusable
relatedItems.description:
Make your oral sources accessible to researchers and, where legally permissible, to the wider public. Apply FAIR principles throughout.

1. Structure data and metadata for FAIR compliance: structure metadata to ensure Findability (assign persistent identifiers; use rich descriptive metadata), Accessibility (store in open or widely supported formats; ensure long-term availability of metadata even if access to data is restricted), Interoperability (use shared vocabularies and standards such as Dublin Core, EAD, or domain-specific thesauri), and Reusability (attach clear licence information; document provenance and context). Consult the FAIR Principles documentation for a full specification.
2. Publish online with an explicit release form: where an explicit "liberatoria" exists, publish the oral source online. Protect third parties mentioned in the recording: de-index their names from search engines where the information could damage their reputation; place sensitive content behind a registration-protected access area. Provide rich contextual metadata for all published materials.
3. Apply appropriate access restrictions where no release form exists: where no explicit release exists, choose among the following graduated approaches: (a) exclude the recording from online publication; (b) publish only excerpts already available in other public forms (print, documentary, educational DVD); (c) publish a pseudonymised transcript, ensuring the individual cannot be re-identified through cross-referencing; (d) publish a keyword index (thesaurus-based) omitting personal names; (e) provide authenticated access for research and educational purposes only; (f) state publicly the willingness to remove content on explicit request. Recall that these restrictions do not apply to recordings of public figures whose personal opinions, religious affiliation, or public acts are already widely known.
4. Assign a Creative Commons licence: choose and attach a Creative Commons licence to each published oral source. Select the licence that best reflects the rights-assignment conditions established with the interviewer and interviewee: CC BY (attribution only), CC BY-NC (non-commercial), CC BY-ND (no derivatives), or more restrictive combinations. Note that CC licences govern the circulation of the work online; they do not supersede GDPR obligations, which govern the processing of personal data independently.
5. Deposit in a trusted digital repository: deposit the oral source collection — including recordings, documentation, and metadata — in a trusted digital repository aligned with open science principles. Ensure the repository assigns persistent identifiers (DOI, Handle, or equivalent). Verify that the repository's preservation commitments cover refresh, format migration, and long-term access. Cross-link the deposit record with related publications and project documentation.

label: Voices of the Parliament: A Corpus Approach to Parliamentary Discourse Research
description: While corpus methods are widely used in linguistics, including gender analysis, this tutorial shows the potential of richly annotated language corpora for research of the socio-cultural context and changes over time that are reflected through language use. The tutorial encourages students and scholars of modern languages, as well as users from other fields of digital humanities and social sciences who are interested in the study of socio-cultural phenomena through language, to engage with user-friendly digital tools for the analysis of large text collections. The tutorial is designed in such a way that it takes full advantage of both linguistic annotations and the available speaker and text metadata to formulate powerful quantitative queries that are then further extended with manual qualitative analysis in order to ensure adequate framing and interpretation of the results.The tutorial demonstrates the potential of parliamentary corpora research via concordancers without the need for programming skills. No prior experience in using language corpora and corpus querying tools is required in order to follow this tutorial. While the same analysis could be carried out on any parliamentary corpus with similar annotations and metadata, in this tutorial we will use the siParl 2.0 corpus which contains parliamentary debates of the National Assembly of the Republic of Slovenia from 1990 to 2018. Knowledge of Slovenian is not required to follow the tutorial. To reproduce the analyses in other languages, we invite you to explore a parliamentary corpus of your choice from those available through CLARIN. Taken from: Teaching with CLARIN:

label: Vom Suchen und Finden: Einführung in die Recherche mit der Gemeinsamen Normdatei / Searching and finding: Introduction to searching with the Common Authority File (GND))
description:
Wie kann man mittels der Verwendung von Normdaten seine Suchergebnisse nach Literatur und Daten verbessern. Was sind Normdaten und welche Funktion haben sie bei der Beschreibung von Objekten wie Publikationen, Forschungsdaten oder Sammlungsgut? Im Fokus dieser Einführung stehen die Normdaten der Gemeinsamen Normdatei (GND), das zentrale kontrollierte Vokabular für Kultur und Forschung im deutschsprachigen Raum. Im Text werden dann verschiedene Anwendungen vorgestellt, mit denen man in der GND passende Suchbegriffe beispielsweise für die Suche nach geeigneter Literatur zum eigenen Thema findet. Zugleich erfährt man, wie man seine eigenen Texte und Daten durch die Verwendung von Normdaten für Dritte leichter auffindbar und damit sichtbarer machen kann.

Diese Ressource wird von Text+ unterstützt. Bei Fragen können Sie sich an den Text+ Helpdesk wenden: textplus-support@gwdg.de
Text von Moritz Strickert (UB HU Berlin) in einer von Barbara Fischer (DNB AfS) überarbeiteten Fassung.

- - -

How can you improve your search results for literature and data by using standardised data? What is authority data and what function does it have in the description of objects such as publications, research data or collections? This introduction focuses on the authority files of the Gemeinsame Normdatei (GND), the central controlled vocabulary for culture and research in German-speaking countries. The text then presents various applications for finding suitable search terms in the GND, for example, when searching for appropriate literature on one's topic. At the same time, it explains how to make one's own texts and data more easily discoverable and thus more visible to others by using authority data.

This resource is supported by Text+. In case of questions you may get in touch with the Text+ helpdesk at textplus-support@gwdg.de.
Text by Moritz Strickert (UB HU Berlin) in a revised version by Barbara Fischer (DNB AfS).

concept.definition: The Integrated Authority File (German: Gemeinsame Normdatei, also known as: Universal Authority File) or GND is an international authority file for the organisation of personal names, subject headings and corporate bodies from catalogues. It is used mainly for documentation in libraries and increasingly also by archives and museums.

relatedItems.label: Einfach normiert - Mit der GND die Qualität von Sammlungsdaten verbessern / Simply Standardized – Improving the Quality of Collection Data with the GND
relatedItems.description:
Die modulare auf ca. 30 bis 50 Minuten konzipierte Lerneinheit führt mittels des GND Explorers in die Nutzung der GND ein. Es wendet sich an die Menschen, die vorwiegend wissen wollen, was Normdaten sind, wo sie sie finden und wie sie die GND in ihrer Arbeit am Museum, im Archiv oder in Forschungsprojekten nutzen können. Den Entdeckungen der [Persona](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persona_(Mensch-Computer-Interaktion)) Dr. Anna Mayer folgen die Lernenden in diesen Abschnitten:

- Was ist die GND?
- Vorteile der Nutzung
- Die GND Suche
- Kurzer Blick auf technische Belange
- Quiz


Die Vertonung des Moduls erfolgte durch eine KI-Stimme. Das vereinfacht spätere Änderungen oder Aktualisierungen.

---

The modular learning unit, designed to last approximately 30 to 50 minutes, introduces users to the GND through the GND Explorer.
It is aimed at individuals who primarily want to understand what authority data is, where to find it, and how to use the GND in their work at museums, archives, or research projects.
The module is narrated using an AI-generated voice, allowing for easier updates and modifications.

relatedItems.label: Mitarbeiten in der GND - Einführung in die kooperative Pflege von Normdaten in der GND / Collaborating in the GND – Introduction to Cooperative Authority Data Curation
relatedItems.description:
Diese Lerneinheit wendet sich an alle, die bereits die GND kennen und schon nutzen. Sie ist modular aufgebaut und auf ca. 30 bis 50 Minuten konzipiert. Zielgruppe sind diejenigen, die selbst aktiver die GND anwenden möchten, sei es weil sie neue Datensätze anlegen wollen, oder sich fragen, wie sie ihre Bedarfe in Bezug auf Formate, Datenschemata und Regeln in die GND einbringen könnten. Daher auch der vollständige Titel “Mitarbeiten in der GND – Einführung in die kooperative Pflege von Normdaten in der GND”. Das Modul verfolgt die GND-Story der [Persona](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persona_(Mensch-Computer-Interaktion)) Beate Batic über folgende Kapitel:

- Quiz zu Modul 1 ("Einfach normiert - Mit der GND die Qualität von Sammlungsdaten verbessern“)

- die GND als Organisation

- Eignungskriterien & Relevanz 

- eine Auswahl in die GND einbringen 

- Abschlussquiz

Die Vertonung des Moduls erfolgte durch eine KI-Stimme. Das vereinfacht spätere Änderungen oder Aktualisierungen.

relatedItems.label: GND Agency Text+
relatedItems.description:
The GND Agency Text+  is a service that is being set up at the Göttingen State and University Library (SUB Göttingen) as part of the NFDI consortium Text+. As a partner of the GND (Integrated Authority File), the agency acts as a central point of contact, initially for projects in the humanities and cultural sciences that are funded by Text+.
This resource is supported by Text+. In case of questions, you may get in touch with the Text+ Helpdesk at textplus-support@gwdg.de.

Die GND-Agentur Text+ ist ein Service, der im Rahmen des NFDI-Programms Text+ an der SUB Göttingen aufgebaut wird. Als Partner der GND (Gemeinsame Normdatei) fungiert die Agentur als zentrale Anlaufstelle zunächst für geistes- und kulturwissenschaftliche Projekte, die im Rahmen des NFDI-Konsortiums Text+ gefördert werden. Langfristig ist geplant, sowohl den Service zu verstetigen als auch das Angebot auf eine breitere Projektlandschaft auszuweiten.

Was machen wir?
Ziel der Agentur ist es, Projekte dabei zu unterstützen, ihre Forschungsdaten als Normdaten in die GND einzubringen.

Dazu gehören:

Die inhaltliche Beratung hinsichtlich der Eignungskriterien von Daten für die GND.
Die Bereitstellung und Weiterentwicklung von entityXML, dem Datenformat für den Austausch von Normdaten zwischen Projekten und Agentur.
Die Bereitstellung einer technischen Umgebung für die Datenverarbeitung auf Grundlage von entityXML .
Das Einspielen von potentiellen Kandidaten in die GND.
Die Bereitstellung von GND-IDs für die Projekte.
Wie unterstützen wir?
Kontaktstelle: Wir sind die erste Anlaufstelle, wenn Sie Ihre Daten in die GND einbringen möchten. Bei projektspezifischem Bedarf vermitteln wir Sie ggf. an eine unserer GND-Partneragenturen weiter.

Beratungsstelle (im Aufbau): Wir beraten Sie bei Fragen rund um die GND und stellen Ihnen Informationsmaterial zur Verfügung.

Datenservice: Wir unterstützen Sie bei der Erstellung von GND-konformen Normdaten. Ihre Daten werden validiert, bereinigt, angereichert und in das für den Dateningest in die GND erforderliche Format konvertiert. Die mit einem GND-ID angereicherten Daten werden von uns an Sie zurückgespielt.

Kontakt: gnd-agentur[at]sub.uni-goettingen.de

relatedItems.label: Integrated Authority File (GND)
relatedItems.description:
The Integrated Authority File (GND) is a service facilitating the collaborative use and administration of authority data. These authority data represent and describe entities, i.e. persons, corporate bodies, conferences and events, geographic entities, topics and works relating to cultural and academic collections. Authority data make cataloguing easier, offer definitive search entries and forge links between different information resources.

It is operated cooperatively by the German National Library, all German-speaking library networks and the associated libraries, the German Union Catalogue of Serials (ZDB) and numerous other institutions. Contributions to the GND are made either via the networks or in direct agreement with the German National Library.

The Common Authority File (GND) is a service for the cooperative use and management of authority data. This authority data represents and describes entities, i.e. persons, corporate bodies, conferences, geographies, subject headings and works that are related to cultural and scientific collections. Standardised data facilitates indexing, provides clear search access points and links different information resources.

relatedItems.label: Make your oral sources accessible and reusable
relatedItems.description:
Make your oral sources accessible to researchers and, where legally permissible, to the wider public. Apply FAIR principles throughout.

1. Structure data and metadata for FAIR compliance: structure metadata to ensure Findability (assign persistent identifiers; use rich descriptive metadata), Accessibility (store in open or widely supported formats; ensure long-term availability of metadata even if access to data is restricted), Interoperability (use shared vocabularies and standards such as Dublin Core, EAD, or domain-specific thesauri), and Reusability (attach clear licence information; document provenance and context). Consult the FAIR Principles documentation for a full specification.
2. Publish online with an explicit release form: where an explicit "liberatoria" exists, publish the oral source online. Protect third parties mentioned in the recording: de-index their names from search engines where the information could damage their reputation; place sensitive content behind a registration-protected access area. Provide rich contextual metadata for all published materials.
3. Apply appropriate access restrictions where no release form exists: where no explicit release exists, choose among the following graduated approaches: (a) exclude the recording from online publication; (b) publish only excerpts already available in other public forms (print, documentary, educational DVD); (c) publish a pseudonymised transcript, ensuring the individual cannot be re-identified through cross-referencing; (d) publish a keyword index (thesaurus-based) omitting personal names; (e) provide authenticated access for research and educational purposes only; (f) state publicly the willingness to remove content on explicit request. Recall that these restrictions do not apply to recordings of public figures whose personal opinions, religious affiliation, or public acts are already widely known.
4. Assign a Creative Commons licence: choose and attach a Creative Commons licence to each published oral source. Select the licence that best reflects the rights-assignment conditions established with the interviewer and interviewee: CC BY (attribution only), CC BY-NC (non-commercial), CC BY-ND (no derivatives), or more restrictive combinations. Note that CC licences govern the circulation of the work online; they do not supersede GDPR obligations, which govern the processing of personal data independently.
5. Deposit in a trusted digital repository: deposit the oral source collection — including recordings, documentation, and metadata — in a trusted digital repository aligned with open science principles. Ensure the repository assigns persistent identifiers (DOI, Handle, or equivalent). Verify that the repository's preservation commitments cover refresh, format migration, and long-term access. Cross-link the deposit record with related publications and project documentation.

relatedItems.label: Provide a clear license and terms of use allowing reuse of the dataset without restrictions
relatedItems.description:
**Why**
The use of permissive licences as well as the inclusion of terms of use are crucial to ease an understanding of the reuse possibilities, as well as to facilitate the reuse of the digital collections by the community and to encourage responsible data use.

**How**
For example, the National Library of Scotland’s Data Foundry provides “Rights Information” for each of the datasets published on their website. For each dataset licensing information is provided in a README file (e.g. for the Moving Image Archive dataset: “Licence: [Creative Commons Zero 1.0 Universal (CC0 1.0)](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/)”. Additionally, a link is provided to the [National Library’s copyright page](https://www.nls.uk/copyright/). 
Similarly, the National Library of Luxembourg publishes a variety of datasets on their Open Data Portal under a Public Domain CC0 licence. For example, [a number of datasets](https://data.bnl.lu/data/historical-newspapers/) extracted from their digitised historical newspaper collections. [Clear guidance](https://data.bnl.lu/data/rights/) on rights and copyright is also provided.

label: Webinar: Archiving Social Media Data: Challenges and Proposed Solutions
description:
While much effort has gone into developing tools and methods for collecting and analyzing social media data, there still is considerable uncertainty regarding the archiving of these data. This webinar brought together experts from various institutions that have experience in working with social media data to discuss practical, ethical, and legal challenges.
In the opening presentations, Libby Hemphill (ICPSR) addressed ICPSR's efforts to enhance metadata for social media objects, integrating social media data into the restricted data ecosystem at ICPSR, and the changes to technical infrastructure that social media data require. Janez Štebe (Slovenian Social Sciences Data Archives) discussed the application of FAIR indicators to social media archiving and provide an overview of existing cases of social media archiving from the SERISS project. Sara D. Thomson (University of Edinburgh) presented on common challenges and potential shared solutions across different archive sectors to ethically preserving and sharing social media. Libby Bishop (GESIS) presented metadata challenges regarding social media data, and present draft recommendations of metadata elements and documentation developed from examples of ingesting such data at GESIS. Sebastian Karcher (Qualitative Data Repository) discussed the distinct opportunities and challenges of archiving small-n social media data commonly used in qualitative social science research with a special focus on tools for archivists and researchers. Oliver Watteler (GESIS) addressed the challenges presented by cases in which researchers have circumvented legal restrictions, like license agreements or usage contracts, in order to get to the data they need. These presentations were followed by a roundtable discussion with the attendees.

Objective: This webinar aimed to present challenges and proposed solutions for archiving social media data.

Besides an overview of the guide and how to navigate it, the webinar covers data management planning and key legal and ethical considerations in creating shareable data.
Let European data experts take you on a tour around the research data lifecycle to learn about best practices in data management to make research data findable, understandable, sustainably accessible and reusable.

This webinar will introduce you to the recently published Expert Tour Guide on Data Management, developed by fifteen data experts from the Consortium of European Social Science Data Archives (CESSDA). Travel with us for an hour and we will show you how to use the guide for self-study or how to use it for delivering face-to-face data management training. Besides an overview of the guide and how to navigate it, the trip will zoom in on data management planning and key legal and ethical considerations in creating shareable data. Overall, the expert tour guide provides guidance to early career social scientists, from planning, organising, documenting, processing, storing and protecting data to sharing and publishing them. Along the way, illustrations and examples, as well as expert tips and insights into data management practices in different European countries lighten up the journey.

Objective: Introduce the Data Management Expert Guide.

label: Webinar: Making Social Science Research Transparent
description:
High-quality data have the potential to be reused in many ways. Archiving and publishing your data properly is at the core of making your data FAIR and will enable both your future self as well as others to get the most out of your data. Recently, more and more scientific journals are implementing open data policies, leading to researchers' dilemmas about where, when and how to publish the data.
Replicability, reproducibility, questionable research practices, and related issues are becoming increasingly important in the social sciences. Consequently, the way that social science research is conducted and disseminated is gradually changing. A crucial element of that change is research transparency. This entails, among other things, making research data, analysis code, and study materials openly available. In this talk, we will present a short overview of some of the elements of research transparency, and their contribution to an open, and credible body of scientific knowledge.

In the second part, we will present in-depth the processes, policies and tools implemented for facilitating transparent research in the social sciences. The presenters will discuss the processes that need to be in place for an open research cycle, the role of data archives and repositories in sharing research data and materials, tools for reproducing research findings in practice, collaborations between archives and social science journals, and implementing Transparency and Openness Promotion Guidelines in different social science disciplines. The event will conclude with wider reflections on the progress of social science research transparency and the way forward.

relatedItems.label: Establish the legal and ethical framework
relatedItems.description:
Complete all legal groundwork before any recording takes place. This phase is mandatory and non-negotiable.

1. Determine the legal basis for data processing: identify the applicable legal basis under GDPR Art. 6 (e.g. consent of the data subject, public interest, scientific research). Consult applicable national legislation (e.g. Italy: "Codice in materia di protezione dei dati personali"; "Regole deontologiche per il trattamento a fini di archiviazione nel pubblico interesse"). Align your choice with the institutional mandate of the data controller.
2. Draft and distribute the privacy notice: prepare a privacy notice compliant with GDPR Arts. 12–14. Write it in plain, accessible language. Deliver it to each participant before any data collection begins. The notice must specify the legal basis, the purposes and modalities of processing, data retention periods, and participant rights. It may be provided in writing or, where identity is verifiable by other means, orally.
3. Obtain interview authorisation: collect the participant's authorisation to take part in the research — distinct from GDPR consent — either in writing or as a recorded oral declaration at the opening of the session. Confirm the authorisation at the close of the interview. Incorporate this declaration directly into the audio or video recording where possible.
4. Address copyright: clarify authorship and exploitation rights. The interviewer, as the party who structures the encounter and formulates questions, generally holds copyright over the interview as a creative work (Italian Law no. 633/1941; EU Directive 2019/790). Include a rights-assignment clause in the participant waiver, covering both image rights and intellectual property rights. Define contractual terms with any commissioning institution or conservation archive before fieldwork begins.
5. Prepare documentation templates: assemble the following before entering the field: (a) privacy notice; (b) interview authorisation form; (c) participant waiver with rights-assignment clause; (d) field recording sheet; (e) individual document sheet. Use models provided by the "Vademecum".

relatedItems.label: Configure the annotation tool
relatedItems.description:
With the environment set up, you can now configure the annotation tool to align with the project’s collaborative structure, research goals and annotation schema. Naturally, the configuration is directly linked to the selected tool. For the purposes of this workflow, the steps outlined are based on the [Recogito Studio](https://recogitostudio.org/) platform.
- Implement collaboration roles and access according to your annotation schema and the roles explicitly assigned by the tool.
- Choose/import basemap layer: If the map(s) have been georeferenced or georectified (see Step 3), the output could be imported and used as a basemap layer in the GeoTagger plugin of the annotation tool.   
- Set the annotation vocabulary: Determine whether an annotation vocabulary that fits your purposes already exists. If a suitable vocabulary is available, select it or import it into the annotation tool. If not, **run the Vocabulary Creation Workflow** [workflow currently under development — more elaborate description will be delivered soon] and develop a custom vocabulary that reflects your project’s needs, considering the integration or extension of domain-specific ontologies (e.g., [CIDOC CRM](https://cidoc-crm.org/)) or thesauri (e.g., [Getty AAT](https://www.getty.edu/research/tools/vocabularies/aat/)). Once the new vocabulary is defined, import it into the annotation platform. In all cases, consider the desired level of annotation granularity (as defined in your annotation schema) as well as interoperability with other datasets and systems. 
- Set gazetteer(s) for geo-tagging: Determine whether a suitable gazetteer already exists for your project’s geographical and historical context, as defined in your annotation schema (e.g., [Pleiades](https://pleiades.stoa.org/) for ancient places, [World Historical Gazetteer](https://whgazetteer.org/) for historical places, [GeoNames](https://www.geonames.org/) for modern locations, or even [Wikidata](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:Main_Page)). If no appropriate gazetteer exists, or if existing gazetteers only partially cover your needs, consider seeking support — for example, from the [World Historical Gazetteer](https://whgazetteer.org/) team or the [Pelagios Gazetteer Activity](https://pelagios.org/activities/gazetteers/). If these options are not applicable, you may need to compile or create a custom gazetteer, tailored to your project needs. In that case, run the **Gazetteer Creation Workflow** [workflow currently under development — more elaborate description will be delivered soon] and once finalized, import it in the appropriate format into the annotation environment.

relatedItems.label: Establish the legal and ethical framework
relatedItems.description:
Complete all legal groundwork before any recording takes place. This phase is mandatory and non-negotiable.

1. Determine the legal basis for data processing: identify the applicable legal basis under GDPR Art. 6 (e.g. consent of the data subject, public interest, scientific research). Consult applicable national legislation (e.g. Italy: "Codice in materia di protezione dei dati personali"; "Regole deontologiche per il trattamento a fini di archiviazione nel pubblico interesse"). Align your choice with the institutional mandate of the data controller.
2. Draft and distribute the privacy notice: prepare a privacy notice compliant with GDPR Arts. 12–14. Write it in plain, accessible language. Deliver it to each participant before any data collection begins. The notice must specify the legal basis, the purposes and modalities of processing, data retention periods, and participant rights. It may be provided in writing or, where identity is verifiable by other means, orally.
3. Obtain interview authorisation: collect the participant's authorisation to take part in the research — distinct from GDPR consent — either in writing or as a recorded oral declaration at the opening of the session. Confirm the authorisation at the close of the interview. Incorporate this declaration directly into the audio or video recording where possible.
4. Address copyright: clarify authorship and exploitation rights. The interviewer, as the party who structures the encounter and formulates questions, generally holds copyright over the interview as a creative work (Italian Law no. 633/1941; EU Directive 2019/790). Include a rights-assignment clause in the participant waiver, covering both image rights and intellectual property rights. Define contractual terms with any commissioning institution or conservation archive before fieldwork begins.
5. Prepare documentation templates: assemble the following before entering the field: (a) privacy notice; (b) interview authorisation form; (c) participant waiver with rights-assignment clause; (d) field recording sheet; (e) individual document sheet. Use models provided by the "Vademecum".

relatedItems.label: Think about a structure for the dataset for a better understanding of how to reuse the content
relatedItems.description:
**Why**
A coherent internal organisation of a dataset is essential for researchers wishing to explore and query the dataset. This includes giving descriptive and consistent folder and file names as well as providing a dataset structure to include metadata in several formats and the content.

**How**
Several initiatives provide detailed approaches to packaging research data with their metadata such as [Research Object Crate (RO-Crate)](https://www.researchobject.org/ro-crate/), the [BagIt File Packaging Format](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8493) and the [Data Package specification](https://specs.frictionlessdata.io/data-package/). 
For example, the [National Library of Luxembourg](https://data.bnl.lu/data/historical-newspapers/) published historical newspapers as open data using a zip file. Other approaches are based on metadata and provide a set of documents with different formats (e.g., Dublin Core and MARC) such as the [Data Foundry’s Moving Image Archive dataset](https://data.nls.uk/data/metadata-collections/moving-image-archive/).

label: 3D Digital Representations of Heritage Assets
description:
The developed 3D workflow aims to provide a comprehensive, step-by-step methodology for the digitisation of built heritage, guiding projects from initial planning to the final publication of high-quality, interoperable 3D data models. Its primary goal is to ensure accurate, consistent, and context-rich digital documentation of monuments, buildings, and historical sites for purposes such as conservation, research, education, virtual exhibitions, and heritage management.

In current practice, many digital documentation initiatives suffer from fragmentation - researchers  often struggle to bring together technical precision with the historical and architectural depth that built heritage demands.  As a result, 3D models are often disconnected from their interpretative context. This workflow guides practitioners through a structured sequence that integrates archival research, field assessment, advanced survey techniques, and post-processing into a coherent and reusable approach.

The workflow encompasses nine structured stages, from defining objectives and metadata to on-site inspection, digital survey, data processing, 3D modelling, validation, and final dissemination. Each phase is designed to build upon the previous one, ensuring a seamless transition from raw data to usable, shareable, and long-term preservable digital assets.

The application of this workflow is particularly suited to multidisciplinary heritage projects where diverse stakeholders—architects, conservators, historians, and digital technicians—collaborate. It supports the production of interoperable models, that comply with open standards and can be integrated into systems like GIS, BIM, or online repositories, enhancing accessibility, transparency, and reuse.

![3D Digital Representations of Heritage Assets](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AniaNast/WORKFLOW/main/3D%20Digital%20Representations%20of%20Heritage%20Assets.png)

3DHOP: 3D Heritage Online Presenter
relatedItems.description:
3DHOP (3D Heritage Online Presenter) is an open-source framework for the creation of interactive Web presentations of high-resolution 3D models, oriented to the Cultural Heritage field. 3DHOP target audience ranges from the museum curators with some IT experience to the experienced Web designers who want to embed 3D contents in their creations, from students in the CH field to small companies developing web applications for museum and CH institutions.

3DHOP allows the creation of interactive visualization of 3D models directly inside a standard web page, just by adding some HTML and JavaScript components in the web page source code. The 3D scene and the user interaction can be easily configured using a simple "declarative programming" approach. By using a multi-resolution 3D model management 3DHOP is able to work with high-resolution 3D models (hundreds millions of triangles/points) with ease, also on low-bandwidth. 3DHOP does not need a specialized server, nor server-side computation: simply some space on a web server, and does work directly inside modern web browsers, no plug-ins or additional components are necessary.

relatedItems.label: 3D-HBIM workflow
relatedItems.description:
The 3D-Heritage Building Information Modelling (HBIM) workflow provides a comprehensive approach for the 3D geometric and parametric modelling of built heritage, and its subsequent enrichment with diverse discipline data related to a built asset’s context, environment, conservation reports and other scientific analysis materials, as well as historical information. It contributes to structuring and enhancing the value of information about built heritage enabling integrated, multidisciplinary, and cross-sectoral collaboration on built heritage preservation and conservation. It recommends the use of accessible open science practices, services and tools that respect existing interoperability standards for streamlining the process of built heritage digitisation, modelling, and information sharing.

### Requirements

- Open science (e.g., use of open standards and metadata schemas for improving data and models interoperability)
- Accessible, open‑source services and tools

### Implementation

Use of open standards and testing of free tools and services for built heritage advanced digitisation, integrating reality capture, scan-to-BIM, and multidisciplinary structured information aggregation. It includes data FAIRness (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) enhancement, geometric modelling and enrichment, and consolidated digital representation of built heritage.

composedOf.label: Carry out the digital survey
composedOf.description:
The digital survey phase involves the data acquisition process, where spatial information is captured using technologies such as 3D laser scanning, photogrammetry, Differential GPS (DGPS), and Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs). These tools work together to collect high-resolution spatial and visual data from various perspectives, ensuring comprehensive coverage of the surveyed area or object. During this step, it is essential to record acquisition parameters as metadata, including equipment specifications, camera calibration settings, flight altitude, image overlap, and Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) accuracy.

# Input:
* Work plan
* Calibrated equipment (laser scanner, cameras, UAVs, DGPS)

# Output:

* Raw spatial data:
 * Laser scans → .e57, .las, .pts, .rcs
 * Photogrammetry → .jpeg, .tiff (images), .exif (metadata)
 * GNSS/GPS logs → .csv, .gpx
 * UAV flight data → .log, .csv, .json

* Paradata : equipment settings, flight data, etc.

* Field notes and photo logs

relatedItems.label: 3D fotogrametria: 3D models of any objects (photogrammetric method)
relatedItems.description:
Everything can be scanned
The photogrammetric method makes it possible to make 3D models of various objects, from small objects (e.g. archaeological artefacts) to entire architectural complexes. Models are made based on a series of photographs, which are processed in several stages to obtain the model: combining the photographs, point cloud, mesh, and textures. In the case of portable objects, this is done in a photographic studio, for larger and stationary objects on site, in which case access from all sides is important. Photogrammetric models should be seen as a complement to other scanning technologies (laser scanning, structured light) and should be performed when other methods are not available. Scans can be used in a variety of fields, from quality control, reverse engineering, graphics, gaming and art to making digital copies of monuments, where photogrammetry technology is safe.

relatedItems.label: Twin3D: 3D scanning and photogrammetry
relatedItems.description:
Create detailed digital copies of 3D objects and terrain
Creating digital copies of 3D objects and terrain maps for scientific research and commercial applications (creative industry, VR/XR, 3D printing, entertainment, games, film, advertising, tourism).
Scanning of various types of 3D objects and terrain with laser 3D scanners and structured light scanners - both small objects (museal artifacts, archaeological finds), large objects (e.g. monuments), buildings (both exterior and interior), scanning and photogrammetry of terrain (buildings, archaeological sites) from the air using a drones.
Use of: Leica RTC350, Leica BLK2GO, Einscan HX scanners, DJI Matrice M300 flying platform with P1 photogrammetric camera and others. Processing of point clouds and 3D models using software: Cyclone Register, Cyclone Register 360, Leica Cyclone 3DR, Bentley Context Capture, DJI Terra, TerraSolid and others.

relatedItems.label: UAV LiDAR
relatedItems.description:
See everything from the air
Terrain scanning using UVA and a LiDAR sensor to prepare a colour point cloud with a density of several hundred to several thousand points per square metre and register up to 3 reflections. This data is used to create a precise Digital Elevation Model. The point cloud and its derivatives can be used for presentation, promotion, analysis, inspection and registration purposes. The service can cover landscape elements, archaeological sites, buildings (including monuments), large areas of land. It is performed using an UAV (DJI Matrice 300 RTK) with a LiDAR camera (DJI Zenmuse L1). The point cloud and its derivatives are given georeferences.

relatedItems.label: UAV data acquisition and management for          multitemporal surveys of archaeological sites.
relatedItems.description: Aerial photogrammetry is a powerful technique that can be used for recording and analyzing excavation phases of archaeological sites. Based on the authors experience, there are some strategies that can speed up the data acquisition, processing and analysis steps. This works aims to underline best practices and lesson learned in the scenario of UAV data acquisition and management for multitemporal surveys of archaeological sites with a photogrammetric approach.

composedOf.label: Process the captured data
composedOf.description:
In this step, the raw data from step 5 is imported into processing software for cleaning, aligning, meshing, texturing and merging, and data optimisation. After raw data is collected through the digital survey, it enters a crucial post-processing phase where data optimisation takes place. This process involves aligning multiple datasets, georeferencing them to real-world coordinates, merging overlapping scans or images, and cleaning out noise or inaccuracies. The goal is to transform unstructured raw data into an accurate, cohesive, and usable dataset. During this phase, the data is refined to improve its quality, accuracy, and usability, ensuring it is suitable for analysis, modelling, or integration into GIS, CAD, or BIM systems. Without this optimisation phase, the raw data would remain fragmented and unreliable, greatly limiting its value in decision-making, design, and documentation. 

# Input:

* Raw scan and image data from Step 5
* Acquisition metadata

# Output:

* Cleaned and aligned point clouds → .e57, .las, .ply, .xyz
* Georeferenced datasets → .laz, .shp, .geojson
* Meshes (with or without texture) → .obj, .fbx, .stl, .3ds
* Orthophotos or DEMs (if generated) → .tiff, .jpg, .xyz, .asc
*  Metadata for processing steps → .xml, .json, .csv

It offers features for processing raw data produced by 3D digitization tools/devices and for preparing models for 3D printing.

relatedItems.description: RealityCapture is a software solution which automatically produces high resolution 3D models from photographs or laser-scans. RealityCapture can process thousands of images and scans in few minutes and can produce very detailed 3D models suitable for wide range of applications - cultural heritage, visual effects, computer games, GIS, 3D maps, industry, 3D print content, measurements and analysis.

composedOf.label: Create the 3D Model
composedOf.description:
# 3D Modeling
This step involves the creation of an accurate 3D model based on the processed and georeferenced data from the digital survey. Using the cleaned and aligned point clouds or photogrammetric outputs, accurate geometric digital representations of the monument are generated. This process may include surface reconstruction, mesh generation, and texture mapping, depending on the level of detail required. 

# Data Enrichment
Once the base 3D model is created, and depending on the project’s goals, the model is enriched with additional data—such as historical context, material properties, or conservation status—as defined in the project's objectives, resulting in a 3D Data Model.

# Input:

* Processed point clouds / meshes from Step 6
* Historical and architectural data from Step 2
* Metadata from previous steps

# Output:

* Base 3D geometric model → .obj, .fbx, .stl, .ply, .glTF, .3ds
* Textured 3D model → .obj + .mtl + .jpg/png, .glb, .glTF
* Enriched 3D model with annotations or metadata → .ifc, .gltf, .json
