relatedItems.label: Classification of 3D Digital Heritage
relatedItems.description: In recent years, the use of 3D models in cultural and archaeological heritage for documentation and dissemination purposes is increasing. The association of heterogeneous information to 3D data by means of automated segmentation and classification methods can help to characterize, describe and better interpret the object under study. Indeed, the high complexity of 3D data along with the large diversity of heritage assets themselves have constituted segmentation and classification methods as currently active research topics. Although machine learning methods brought great progress in this respect, few advances have been developed in relation to cultural heritage 3D data. Starting from the existing literature, this paper aims to develop, explore and validate reliable and efficient automated procedures for the classification of 3D data (point clouds or polygonal mesh models) of heritage scenarios. In more detail, the proposed solution works on 2D data ("texture-based" approach) or directly on the 3D data ("geometry-based approach) with supervised or unsupervised machine learning strategies. The method was applied and validated on four different archaeological/architectural scenarios. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach is reliable and replicable and it is effective for restoration and documentation purposes, providing metric information e.g. of damaged areas to be restored.

composedOf.label: Validate and check data consistency
composedOf.description:
Perform a final review of the 3D model to ensure completeness, technical integrity, and consistency before publication.This step involves a comprehensive internal review of the 3D model and its associated data prior to dissemination. The goal is to verify that all elements—geometries, textures, metadata, and semantic annotations—have been properly integrated and documented. The model is checked for structural completeness, potential misalignments, missing components, or inconsistent labeling. Metadata must conform to the project's schema, and semantic segmentation should be uniformly applied throughout the model. Additionally, this step ensures that the exported file formats, coordinate systems, and data layers are compatible with the selected repositories and web platforms. Completing this final check guarantees a clean, well-structured, and interoperable dataset ready for publication and long-term reuse.

# Input:

* Final 3D model and associated metadata
* Project schema and guidelines

# Output:

* Validation report (model integrity, completeness, metadata checks)
* Final ready-for-publication dataset

composedOf.label: Publish the 3D Model for data access and sharing
composedOf.description:
The publication and dissemination of the 3D model and associated data. This includes selecting appropriate repositories, web viewers, and collaborative platforms that align with the project's technical standards and accessibility requirements. The 3D model should be exported in standardized file formats (e.g., OBJ, glTF, IFC) suitable for both visualization and interoperability. Once prepared, the model and any related datasets are uploaded to the chosen platforms along with comprehensive metadata, including information on data acquisition methods, processing workflows, georeferencing details, and semantic annotations.

# Input:

* Validated 3D data and enriched metadata
* Project documentation

# Output:

* Uploaded 3D models to repositories or viewers
* Public access page or dataset
* Metadata records compliant with standards (e.g., Dublin Core, CIDOC CRM)

# Export formats for dissemination:

* Visualization: .glTF, .glb, .obj, .fbx
* HBIM: .ifc
* Documentation: .pdf, .xml, .json

relatedItems.label: ARIADNE EpHEMERA
ARIADNE Portal
relatedItems.description:
The ARIADNE Portal provides the main point of access for searching and browsing datasets and new services for processing and publishing archaeological datasets online. 

The Portal brings together existing archaeological research datasets from ARIADNE partners so that researchers can browse and access the various distributed datasets for use in their projects. The portal also provides a point of access for the new services developed by the project.

The datasets that are registered in the ARIADNE catalogue are held by its partners and have been created through research, in excavations, in fieldwork, laboratory and other projects. In recent years archaeologists have been making increasing use of sophisticated digital equipment and techniques. During the course of a research project large volumes of data are created and collected, and become part of the research archive. ARIADNE aims to make these archives available through its portal for researchers to consult when starting new research.

relatedItems.label: 3DHOP: 3D Heritage Online Presenter
relatedItems.description:
3DHOP (3D Heritage Online Presenter) is an open-source framework for the creation of interactive Web presentations of high-resolution 3D models, oriented to the Cultural Heritage field. 3DHOP target audience ranges from the museum curators with some IT experience to the experienced Web designers who want to embed 3D contents in their creations, from students in the CH field to small companies developing web applications for museum and CH institutions.

3DHOP allows the creation of interactive visualization of 3D models directly inside a standard web page, just by adding some HTML and JavaScript components in the web page source code. The 3D scene and the user interaction can be easily configured using a simple "declarative programming" approach. By using a multi-resolution 3D model management 3DHOP is able to work with high-resolution 3D models (hundreds millions of triangles/points) with ease, also on low-bandwidth. 3DHOP does not need a specialized server, nor server-side computation: simply some space on a web server, and does work directly inside modern web browsers, no plug-ins or additional components are necessary.

label: 3D Geometric Analysis of Historical Structures
description: The developed workflow provides a comprehensive, step-by-step methodological framework for the 3D geometric analysis of historical architectural structures, with applications in archaeological and art historical research, conservation, and heritage management. Starting from objective formulation and project planning, the workflow ensures that the initial data acquisition process considers subsequent 3D geometric analysis. Moreover, it presents the 3D geometric analysis process by highlighting the prerequisite and subsequent steps involved in computing and extracting relevant architectural attribute data (i.e. features) from 3D models for data analysis and interpretation. Rather than presenting a specific type of 3D geometric analysis, the workflow provides a methodological framework within which practitioners can integrate and use the most appropriate type of 3D geometric analysis for their research objectives.

relatedItems.label: 3D Digital Representations of Heritage Assets
relatedItems.description:
The developed 3D workflow aims to provide a comprehensive, step-by-step methodology for the digitisation of built heritage, guiding projects from initial planning to the final publication of high-quality, interoperable 3D data models. Its primary goal is to ensure accurate, consistent, and context-rich digital documentation of monuments, buildings, and historical sites for purposes such as conservation, research, education, virtual exhibitions, and heritage management.

In current practice, many digital documentation initiatives suffer from fragmentation - researchers  often struggle to bring together technical precision with the historical and architectural depth that built heritage demands.  As a result, 3D models are often disconnected from their interpretative context. This workflow guides practitioners through a structured sequence that integrates archival research, field assessment, advanced survey techniques, and post-processing into a coherent and reusable approach.

The workflow encompasses nine structured stages, from defining objectives and metadata to on-site inspection, digital survey, data processing, 3D modelling, validation, and final dissemination. Each phase is designed to build upon the previous one, ensuring a seamless transition from raw data to usable, shareable, and long-term preservable digital assets.

The application of this workflow is particularly suited to multidisciplinary heritage projects where diverse stakeholders—architects, conservators, historians, and digital technicians—collaborate. It supports the production of interoperable models, that comply with open standards and can be integrated into systems like GIS, BIM, or online repositories, enhancing accessibility, transparency, and reuse.

![3D Digital Representations of Heritage Assets](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AniaNast/WORKFLOW/main/3D%20Digital%20Representations%20of%20Heritage%20Assets.png)

composedOf.label: Formalise geometric attribute parameters
composedOf.description:
Geometric attributes describe the morphological properties of an architectural structure (e.g., a building), its constituent elements (e.g., a wall within that building), and the individual components of those elements (e.g., the stones within that wall), as well as the inter-elemental (e.g., an array of pillars) and inter-componential relationships (e.g., bonding between stones). For example, a geometric attribute of a building may be its height; of a wall its thickness; of a stone its angularity; the spacing between pillars for an inter-elemental relationship; and the degree of overlap between superposed stones for an inter-componential relationship. Geometric attributes can serve as meaningful proxies in a range of broader analyses of structural integrity, construction quality, invested labour, typology, and construction choices. The selected geometric attributes are therefore determined by the research premise and question defined within the project objectives and expected outcomes (Step 1 of “3D Digital Representations of Heritage Assets” workflow). In order to enable their measurement and extraction from a 3D model in the form of quantitative data, the selected geometric attributes are mathematically formalised into parameters, which can be analytically operationalised in a digital environment. How and in what way the geometric attributes are formalised into corresponding geometric attribute parameters is informed by the available data and documentation on both the architectural structure and the types of attributes under investigation (Step 2 of “3D Digital Representations of Heritage Assets” workflow). In turn, the resulting parameters inform, in part, the plan of work for reality-based data acquisition (Step 4 of the “3D Digital Representations of Heritage Assets” workflow), as the minimum perceptibility of relevant morphologies and relationships dictates key technical and logistical requirements.

# Input:

* Project objectives and expected outcomes: .docx, .pdf, .md, .xml
* Data and documentation on the architectural structure: .pdf, .tiff, .jpg, .dwg, .dxf, .ifc
* Reference typologies and measurement conventions for geometrical attributes: .pdf, .docx

# Output:

* Formalised geometric attribute parameter catalogue: .pdf, .docx, .md, .json, .csv, .py, .txt

label: 3D-HBIM workflow
description:
The 3D-Heritage Building Information Modelling (HBIM) workflow provides a comprehensive approach for the 3D geometric and parametric modelling of built heritage, and its subsequent enrichment with diverse discipline data related to a built asset’s context, environment, conservation reports and other scientific analysis materials, as well as historical information. It contributes to structuring and enhancing the value of information about built heritage enabling integrated, multidisciplinary, and cross-sectoral collaboration on built heritage preservation and conservation. It recommends the use of accessible open science practices, services and tools that respect existing interoperability standards for streamlining the process of built heritage digitisation, modelling, and information sharing.

### Requirements

- Open science (e.g., use of open standards and metadata schemas for improving data and models interoperability)
- Accessible, open‑source services and tools

### Implementation

Use of open standards and testing of free tools and services for built heritage advanced digitisation, integrating reality capture, scan-to-BIM, and multidisciplinary structured information aggregation. It includes data FAIRness (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) enhancement, geometric modelling and enrichment, and consolidated digital representation of built heritage.

The application of this workflow is particularly suited to multidisciplinary heritage projects where diverse stakeholders—architects, conservators, historians, and digital technicians—collaborate. It supports the production of interoperable models, that comply with open standards and can be integrated into systems like GIS, BIM, or online repositories, enhancing accessibility, transparency, and reuse.

relatedItems.label: A structured framework for HBIM standardization: Integrating scan-to-BIM methodologies and heritage conservation standards
relatedItems.description:
Abstract
Heritage conservation demands innovative approaches that integrate advanced technologies with traditional principles to protect monuments and historic buildings. This research investigates the potential of Building Information Modeling (BIM) in heritage conservation, with a focus on developing and adapting workflows tailored to Heritage Building Information Modeling (HBIM). Through a systematic analysis of literature, the research highlights the adaptation of scan-to-BIM methodologies for HBIM creation and their significant role in enhancing preservation efforts. Key technologies, including laser scanning, photogrammetry, and machine learning, are discussed for their contributions to generate accurate and information-rich digital models of heritage structures. Furthermore, this work discovers critical specifications and proposes a structured framework for balancing these specifications within HBIM workflows. This framework addresses challenges such as standardization, scalability, and adaptability, which are essential for accurately capturing the complexity of heritage buildings. By examining these issues, the study identifies opportunities to improve HBIM's capability to monitor, document, and manage culturally significant assets. The findings provide a comprehensive understanding of HBIM processes and their potential to support the effective conservation of heritage.

relatedItems.label: Heritage building information modeling (HBIM) for heritage conservation: Framework of challenges, gaps, and existing limitations of HBIM
relatedItems.description:
Abstract
This study investigates the pivotal role of Heritage Building Information Modeling (HBIM) in conservation of cultural heritage buildings. Utilizing a systematic literature review and in-depth analysis of 59 studies within 2013–23 period, the study underscores HBIM's capacity to document, analyze, and manage heritage structures. It delineates the workflow from data acquisition through laser scanning and photogrammetry, to the modeling of historic fabric, highlighting the integration of digital technologies in conservation practices. The paper identifies key challenges in HBIM adoption, including technical limitations, the need for specialized skills, and the complexity of accurately modeling historical details. It proposes avenues for future research focused on enhancing data acquisition techniques, improving the interoperability of HBIM with other digital tools, and developing standards for the effective documentation of heritage sites. The findings advocate for a collaborative approach, leveraging HBIM to foster interdisciplinary partnerships between architects, historians, and conservationists, for sustainable preservation of cultural heritage.

relatedItems.label: V-HBIM: A Vulnerability-Oriented Heritage BIM Workflow for Cultural Heritage Conservation
relatedItems.description:
Abstract

Heritage Building Information Modelling (H-BIM) is increasingly used for the documentation, conservation and management of historical assets. However, the integration of geometric singularities, degradation phenomena and vulnerability-related information within H-BIM environments remains only partially addressed, as current workflows are often manual, fragmented and poorly connected to structured conservation assessment procedures. This paper introduces V-HBIM, a vulnerability-oriented Heritage BIM approach aimed at integrating geometric data, defect mapping and conservation parameters into a single digital model. A semi-automated scan-to-model workflow is proposed, combining point cloud processing, geometric modelling, mesh-based defect representation, BIM conversion, structural vulnerability calculations and automated information enrichment. The workflow uses CloudCompare, Rhinoceros 3D, Rhino.Inside.Revit, Autodesk Revit and Dynamo scripts to connect digital survey outputs with a structured database derived from the Italian Ministry of Culture Risk Map. The method is validated on the Roman Arch of San Damiano, in the Archeological Park of Carsulae, Italy. Results show that defects can be represented as queryable BIM entities and associated with severity, extent and urgency parameters. The proposed approach supports conservation planning, inspection updating and vulnerability-oriented management of cultural heritage assets.

relatedItems.label: HBIM and Information Management for Knowledge and Conservation of Architectural Heritage: A Review
relatedItems.description:
Abstract

This paper presents a comprehensive review of research on Historic Building Information Modeling (HBIM), focusing on its role as a tool for managing knowledge and supporting conservation practices of Architectural Heritage. While previous review articles and most research works have predominantly addressed geometric modeling—given its significant challenges in the context of historic buildings—this study places greater emphasis on the integration of non-geometric data within the BIM environment. A systematic search was conducted in the Scopus database to extract the 451 relevant publications analyzed in this review, covering the period from 2008 to mid-2024. A bibliometric analysis was first performed to identify trends in publication types, geographic distribution, research focuses, and software usage. The main body of the review then explores three core themes in the development of the information system: the definition of model entities, both semantic and geometric; the data enrichment phase, incorporating historical, diagnostic, monitoring and conservation-related information; and finally, data use and sharing, including on-site applications and interoperability. For each topic, the review highlights and discusses the principal approaches documented in the literature, critically evaluating the advantages and limitations of different information management methods with respect to the distinctive features of the building under analysis and the specific objectives of the information model.

composedOf.label: Planning and Management
composedOf.description:
Set up based on scope, major objectives, and primary requirements of the digitisation and modelling process established by the involved stakeholders. Efficient management and enhanced significance of the whole process can be achieved by customizing project and data requirements, allocating resources, and establishing collaborative protocols. Established best practices include the BIM framework (e.g., agreeing on Exchange Information Requirements (EIR), draft and implementing Building Execution Plan (BEP), and Information Exchange Protocols (IEP)).

Common activities of planning and management include:

- Establish the main objectives of the heritage digitisation (e.g., documentation, research, management, restoration planning) considering legal constraints and compliance requirements on assets.

- Establish information requirements, including:
    - level of information need (LOIN) or level of development (LOD) for the 3D model
    - data categories (e.g., historical documentation, site surveys, conservation state analysis, environmental monitoring data)
    - data types and file formats (e.g., IFC, CSV, PDF)
    - data security
    - standards (e.g., ISO 19650) and metadata schemas (e.g., CIDOC CRM, Ao-Cat) for interoperability
    - milestones and deliverables

- Draft and implement the execution plans and information protocols, including:
    - Roles and responsibilities (e.g., survey specialists, historians, BIM modellers, researchers, data managers, BIM coordinators)
    - Communication and information exchange protocols (e.g., online repositories, naming conventions, version control)
    - Checks for quality, progress track and ensure alignment with objectives
    - Collaboration tools

### Outputs / Deliverables
- Information requirements (e.g., project information requirements, EIR)
- Execution plans (e.g., project execution plan, BEP)
- Project management documentation (e.g., charts, diagrams, reports)
- Information Exchange Matrix
- Conservation Management Plan (CMP)
- Heritage Asset Information Requirements (AIR)
- Organisation Information Requirements (OIR)

relatedItems.description: This guidelines’ document was developed within the ENI CBC Med BEEP project and aims to enhance the capacity of public local administrations to design, and realise innovative energy and environmental improvement on historic public buildings, through a multidisciplinary and integrated digital approach (using Building Information Modelling and performance-based design to develop an Energy Efficient Heritage Building Information Model - EE-HBIM). The guideline is based on the testing of this emerging technology on built heritage in eight different EU and non EU Mediterranean countries to demonstrate its scalability to the entire building stock of the Med area. The project will provide public administrations with a powerful method for the energy rehabilitation of public buildings to be supported with private funds through the Energy Performance Contracting. The HBIM model should integrate previously collected information on the building (geometric, diagnostic, environmental data), to create a comprehensive documentation of the building's current state. Moreover, the HBIM model will be used as a basis to inform the subsequent simulation-based energy-environmental improvement concept, through energy renovation scenarios that are both compatible with the identified historic buildings and capable to enhance its energy and environmental performance.

relatedItems.label: Naming Convention
relatedItems.description:
The example naming convention proposed in this document follows the requirements specified in BS1192: 2007 (Collaborative production of architectural, engineering and construction information – Code of practice) and will be used to name all kinds of FILES referring to the HBIM models, namely 3D BIM models, point clouds, mesh, models, CAD files, drawings, reports, simulation files, etc., that are stored in the Common Data Environment (CDE).

Even if somewhat more complex than other systems the choice of the BS1192 regulation is based on its widespread diffusion. The new ISO 19650-3 should provide an international standard for the naming convention in the foreseeable future.

The naming convention does not apply to a huge amount of data collected together, like geometric survey files (photographs, scan files), mesh models files, historical data, LCA files, or internal documents; in this case, the naming convention could apply to the folder in where the data are stored. The naming convention should generally be applied to the files directly produced within the project that are most important for the HBIM process (such as all the files linked to the HBIM models, simulation files, etc.). Nevertheless, a general name coding has been set for the internal needs of the UP project.

The name will be composed of single fields of code, representing the file’s metadata so that the name itself will provide information without the file being opened. Names should be created by joining together the codes in the specified fields, in the specified order, using the “-” hyphen character.

relatedItems.label: PORTAL FOR HERITAGE BUILDINGS' INTEGRATION INTO THE CONTEMPORARY BUILT ENVIRONMENT. Guidebook for the preplanning and development of Heritage BIM models
relatedItems.description:
In an era of rapid technological improvements, state-of-the-art methodologies and tools dedicated to the protection and promotion of our cultural heritage should be developed and extensively employed in the management of our built environment. At the same time, sustainability principles underline the importance of the continuous use of historic or vernacular buildings as part of the building stock of our cities. The adoption of a holistic, integrated, multi-disciplinary strategy can bridge technological innovation with the conservation and restoration of heritage buildings.

The project “Portal for heritage buildings' integration into the contemporary built environment” (Urban PERIsCOPE) provides an innovative platform for the identification, classification, documentation, and renovation of heritage buildings - a tool that can be exploited by a variety of stakeholders related to the conservation and retrofit activities. Urban PERIsCOPE enables the exploitation of state-of-the-art techniques in the scientific fields of Building Information Modelling (BIM), remote sensing, terrestrial and aerial 3D modelling techniques, and non-destructive onsite testing, pursued by the leading research and academic institutions of Cyprus in these fields. The Urban PERIsCOPE platform addresses specific stakeholders to impact culturally and economically the society of Cyprus, including public authorities and policymakers (Town Planning and Housing Department, Department of Antiquities, Municipalities) and professionals (archaeologists, engineers, architects, and chartered surveyors).

The implementation of Urban PERIsCOPE in practice involves the pilot application of an innovative, holistic, integrated methodology on a select number of heritage buildings in Nicosia and Limassol (including examples located in both Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot neighbourhoods), which were selected based on their location in the contemporary fabric of the city, architectural typology, use, as well as their current structural condition.

The Urban PERIsCOPE platform and its associated tools bring added value and benefits to the Public Authorities and professionals in Cyprus. The proposed methodology approaches the challenges and identified issues of heritage buildings in the contemporary urban fabric from multiple points of view, including (i) the mapping and parametric management of data of heritage buildings through BIM, (ii) the documentation of architectural typology and architectonic features, (iii) the method of construction, (iv) the definition of their structural condition, and (v) the restoration and renovation requirements.

composedOf.label: Data Collection
composedOf.description:
Gather relevant information and data on the heritage asset according to the requirements established in step 1 of this workflow. Collection of legal, regulatory, historical, geographical, environmental, social, structural, and material related information is recommended. Collection of geospatial and geometric survey data on the asset is mandatory.

Relevant data, according to information requirements (step 1), should be collected in open standard file formats (e.g., PDF, CSV, JSON, JPEG, TIFF) or processed (step 3), structured and archived in an accessible, secure and frequently updated repository (e.g., PIDs, structured databases, metadata tags).
Absent, purpose specific, relevant data should be acquired (e.g., GIS, materials, structural, and environmental data), especially, digital survey data (on-site survey and reality capture, using either 3D laser scanning or photogrammetry).
Each method used for data collection is expected to follow its own specific workflow, depending on system and information requirements, data sources, object of analysis (e.g., products function, materials properties), and resources (e.g., standards, equipment, software). Examples of basic workflows for geometric survey can be found under the related items.

Preliminary checks for completeness and reporting on data quality should be done, according to the requirements established in step 1. Data processing (step 3) for assuring specified data quality and interoperability (step 1) may be required before data archiving.
A shared data environment is recommended for managing and linking information from various sources to facilitate collaborative work and improve interoperability (e.g., Common Data Environment - CDE in BIM).
Apply naming conventions to all source files and folders.
Populate a central repository with raw data and metadata. Data management documentation should be kept updated.

### Outputs / Deliverables

- Records of data, after quality checks, in open standard file formats (including raw point clouds or raw photogrammetry data, and significant data, as required in step 1, such as, historical, geographical, environmental, social, structural, and material related data)
- Data annotations and structured data
- Interoperable data
- Accessible and secure data
- Preliminary data quality reports
- Data management documentation

relatedItems.label: A Continuous Scan-to-HBIM Workflow Based on Integrated Multisensor Acquisition and Real-Time Semantic Modelling
relatedItems.description:
Abstract

The increasing adoption of Building Information Modeling (BIM) in the AECO sector has highlighted persistent limitations in Scan-to-HBIM workflows, particularly related to fragmentation, manual processing, and lack of continuity between data acquisition and modeling. This study proposes and validates a continuous Scan-to-HBIM workflow based on integrated multisensor acquisition and real-time semantic modeling, aiming to reduce these discontinuities and improve data consistency. The method is implemented through an all-in-one platform combining mobile LiDAR, photogrammetry, sensor fusion (IMU–SLAM), machine learning for semantic segmentation, and extended reality (XR) for in-field validation, enabling the direct generation of parametric BIM elements during acquisition. The approach is tested on the ex Mulino Gallisai, a complex and degraded heritage building, using a controlled benchmarking protocol against a traditional pipeline. Results show high metric reliability (MAE = 1.68 cm), semantic recognition accuracy of 88.2%, and a Manual Correction Ratio of 11.8%, indicating reduced human intervention. The integrated workflow also achieves a 29% reduction in total processing time while improving spatial continuity and topological coherence. These findings demonstrate that a continuous, integrated Scan-to-HBIM paradigm is technically feasible and can shift modeling from a post-process reconstruction to a real-time generative process, supporting more efficient and reliable digital representations and contributing to the development of Digital Twin-oriented workflows.

relatedItems.label: Documentation strategies for HBIM model parameterization: A case study of the José de Alencar Theater
relatedItems.description:
Abstract
This study presents HBIMPath, a methodology designed to address the challenges of documenting and managing complex historic buildings. The approach is demonstrated through a case study of the José de Alencar Theater. Historic structures often present intricate architectural details and diverse material compositions that require precise documentation for effective maintenance and conservation. HBIMPath aims to integrate Building Information Modeling (BIM) with systematic historical research, on-site investigations, and non-destructive testing to create an accurate and comprehensive digital representation of heritage assets. The methodology combines historical data and advanced visualization techniques, including virtual tours, to facilitate detailed analysis of materials and structural elements. This approach minimizes the need for invasive procedures while ensuring the reliability of geometric and material data. The study emphasizes the importance of computational efficiency, balancing model accuracy and performance, particularly when dealing with highly ornate features. Results demonstrate the potential of HBIMPath in documenting and preserving complex historic buildings and its adaptability for less intricate structures, including modernist architecture. The study also highlights the critical role of interdisciplinary collaboration in capturing historical accuracy and architectural intent. Future research opportunities include improving the integration of detailed ornamentation into digital models without compromising computational performance and expanding the methodology's application to modern and contemporary constructions. HBIMPath contributes to the field of heritage management by providing a robust, systematic framework that supports sustainable conservation and enhances decision-making processes for maintaining built heritage across diverse architectural contexts.

composedOf.label: Data Processing
composedOf.description:

Different operations, such as cleaning, validation, transformation, enrichment and analysis may be included depending on the data characteristics. Data validation (step 3), harmonization (steps 2 and 3), and storage (step 2) are primary requirements for the seamless integration of multidisciplinary data in step 4.

Unvalidated or poor-quality data should be processed according to the established information requirements (step 1). Some data should also be transformed to streamline 3D-HBIM modelling and enrichment (step 4) using harmonized and interoperable data. Cleaning and merging of point cloud data, improved quality of textured 3D meshes, and related data transformation, assuring the use of consistent coordinate references, are processing stages especially decisive for this broad 3D-HBIM workflow. Examples of basic workflows for 3D data processing can be found under the related items tab.

composedOf.label: 3D HBIM Modelling and Enrichment
composedOf.description:
Create a 3D object-oriented parametric model hierarchically structured and linked to the heritage asset's components or spaces. Enrich the model with harmonized multidisciplinary data (step 3). Includes model creation, enrichment, and validation (step 1). 3D-HBIM modelled elements should adhere to Industry Foundation Class (IFC) open standards for maximum interoperability.

Specific issues should be specially addressed in the 3D-HBIM modelling, such as, common harmonised modelling rules, the information requirements (e.g., LOD, LOIN, standards for information management and data exchange) and data specificities, related with significant addressed categories, for model enhancement purposes.
For model enrichment with multidisciplinary data (e.g., structural data, material properties, historical events, conservation state analysis) collected (step 2), processed (step 3) and validated (step 1) is possible to link, embed or import data to the 3D-HBIM model ensuring compatibility with IFC data schema.
HBIM model validation and quality control should contribute to ensure enhanced outputs, including clash detection or geometry checks to identify inconsistencies, metadata validation (e.g., element categories, naming), and export tests (e.g., standard IDS - Information Delivery Specification, [buildingSMART IFC validation system](https://www.buildingsmart.org/users/services/ifc-validation-service/) ). Examples of basic workflows for BIM modelling are available at [buildingSMART International website](https://www.buildingsmart.org/clarifying-the-openbim-workflow/).

### Outputs / Deliverables

- Basic BIM model in open file format (.ifc)
- Documentation of modelling process
- Raw data acquisition reports for long‑term preservation
- Quality assurance report
- Drawings & documentation package

relatedItems.label: CloudCompare
relatedItems.description: CloudCompare is a 3D point cloud (and triangular mesh) processing software. It has been originally designed to perform comparison between two dense 3D points clouds (such as the ones acquired with a laser scanner) or between a point cloud and a triangular mesh. It relies on a specific octree structure dedicated to this task. Afterwards, it has been extended to a more generic point cloud processing software, including many advanced algorithms (registration, resampling, color/normal/scalar fields handling, statistics computation, sensor management, interactive or automatic segmentation, display enhancement, etc.).

composedOf.label: Publishing
composedOf.description:
Publish and share the outputs (of steps 2, 3 and 4), particularly the enriched 3D-HBIM model (step 4). The significance and impact of structured information are enhanced by its various potential applications, including heritage preservation and research across different fields of knowledge, such as exemplified by the ATRIUM project and its demonstrators.

For publishing, it is recommended to adhere to the FAIR principles. These include using open standard file formats (.IFC) and persistent identifiers (e.g., DOIs) to enhance findability and ensure long-term interoperability, open licences for enabling reuse, and open or accessible and secure data repositories.
The repository selection should account for best data management and information system practices, as compliance with relevant standards (e.g., ISO 14721 - OAIS reference model), including comprehensive documentation, security, and integrity. Provision or support for 3D viewers from web-based solutions (e.g., XeoKit), for interactive 3D-HBIM previews and exploration, is also advisable.
Improved impact should result from freely sharing data and relevant findings with stakeholders and the heritage community (e.g., via demonstrators, presentations, webinars, or conferences) and by inviting user interactions for data reusability feedback and collaboration.

Users can access technical studies regarding historical context, geometric documentation, conservation state analysis, building provenance, structural changes and urban context transformations. The Urban PERIScOPE Platform offers the next step in the development of built heritage digitisation methods and it focuses on expanding the scope of study beyond the single built heritage structure by allowing deeper understanding and interdisciplinary interpretation of a heritage building’s condition within its topographical context and the surrounding built environment. Specifically, the Urban PERIScOPE Platform aims to support the three key phases of heritage safeguarding and urban transitions, including (1) observation and monitoring at neighbourhood scale, (2) building diagnosis and analysis, and (3) implementation of technical procedures by means of good practices, guidelines and instructions.

relatedItems.label: 3DHOP: 3D Heritage Online Presenter
relatedItems.description:
3DHOP (3D Heritage Online Presenter) is an open-source framework for the creation of interactive Web presentations of high-resolution 3D models, oriented to the Cultural Heritage field. 3DHOP target audience ranges from the museum curators with some IT experience to the experienced Web designers who want to embed 3D contents in their creations, from students in the CH field to small companies developing web applications for museum and CH institutions.

3DHOP allows the creation of interactive visualization of 3D models directly inside a standard web page, just by adding some HTML and JavaScript components in the web page source code. The 3D scene and the user interaction can be easily configured using a simple "declarative programming" approach. By using a multi-resolution 3D model management 3DHOP is able to work with high-resolution 3D models (hundreds millions of triangles/points) with ease, also on low-bandwidth. 3DHOP does not need a specialized server, nor server-side computation: simply some space on a web server, and does work directly inside modern web browsers, no plug-ins or additional components are necessary.

label: Acquiring Images for Automatic Text Recognition
description: Whether photographed in an archive or discovered in the digital collections of memory institutions like libraries or museums, for many humanities scholars, images of text sources form the basis of their academic work. Finding, creating and collecting images of textual material is often the first step in the research process.

concept.label: Collecting
concept.definition: purposefully gathering items (Wikidata contributors, "Q208165," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q208165&oldid=1249560517 (accessed September 4, 2020).

relatedItems.label: Automatic Text Recognition Roadmap
relatedItems.description:
**Automatic Text Recognition** (ATR) uses Artificial Intelligence (AI), in particular **machine learning** (ML), to **extract text from a scanned image**. It encompasses two main techniques: **Optical Character Recognition** (OCR), extracting text from printed documents, and **Handwritten Text Recognition** (HTR), extracting text from manusripts.  
This workflow presents the main steps of an ATR workflow and how to integrate it in your research project.

composedOf.label: Find Images in Repositories
composedOf.description:
### Public Domain
Sources that have entered the public domain can often be found online on digital libraries like the [Internet Archive](https://archive.org/) or [Google Books](https://books.google.fr/). These sources consist of a collection of scans with an added layer of optical character recognition (OCR) which is, in most cases, not of any usable quality. Both types of data are combined into a PDF that can be downloaded.

### Archives
Archives and other memory institutions offer a wealth of material that has not yet been digitised. If you are struggling to obtain digital copies of the documents you are interested in, visiting the institution and requesting the digitisation of specific items may be necessary.  

As most memory institutions – slowly but surely – move into the digital age, your digitisation journey will usually begin in the comfort of your own home, searching through digital finding aids and preparing lists of the relevant institutions and archival materials to request for digital copies.  

Once the archival staff has prepared the required files for you, your work of selecting relevant archival materials begins. It is rare that an entire archival folder will be relevant to you. Here, a careful selection might save not only the time of the archivists doing the digitisation, but also your wallet.  

Most archives and other memory institutions have clearly defined conditions under which digital copies of archival material can be provided and how they can be used. These rules may be part of a general contract between the user and the particular archive, but in the case of a larger digitisation project it might be necessary to create a separate contract with project-specific rules.

composedOf.label: Define your Goals
composedOf.description:
Questions to ask yourself:
* What type of data do you need from the PDF? (text, paratext, digital object)
* Are you planning to research the sources or are you planning to republish the sources? (e.g. as part of training data for other ATR projects)

Depending on your objectives, you may be satisfied with:
* Using the Google Books PDF directly
* Obtaining a permissive license from the partner cultural heritage institution
* Creating an envelope dataset that does not contain the actual copyrighted object but enriches it with quality annotation such as transcriptions and only references the copyrighted digital object.

composedOf.label: Digitise Texts
composedOf.description:
Digitisation of archival materials may be done directly by the user, but often the digitisation is carried out by a specialized department within the archive or an external provider. In this case, the user should specify the preferred quality of the digitised material so that it can fit the criteria for the subsequent ATR process. This service is usually chargeable and the final price is based on the number of items digitized.

### Specifications to take into account when digitising:
    * **Resolution**: 300 to 400 dpi (dots per inch).
    * **Colour space**: If you are scanning images yourself, make sure you are scanning in colour. It is the most effective way of recognising things in pictures, such as stamps or strange bleed-through effects, but also the script itself is much more cleaner in colour than bitonal. Colour can also help to make things clearer – boosting contrasts or even flipping colours around can make details stand out.
    * **File format**: For long-term archiving, formats such as ```TIFF``` of ```JPEG2000``` are often recommended or even required by research funders. They are very rich and large file formats. However, for processing image files with ATR, formats such as ```JPG```, ```PNG```, or ```PDF``` work just fine. If you need to change an image format into another, you can use converters. We recommend [ImageMagick](https://imagemagick.org/index.php), which is open source and free of charge.

composedOf.label: Pay Attention to Copyright and Reuse Conditions: the Heritage Data Reuse Charter
composedOf.description:
When you are planning to publish your research outcomes, it might be helpful to consult the [Heritage Data Reuse Charter](https://www.dariah.eu/activities/open-science/data-re-use/), a DARIAH initiative. It contains 6 points on which cultural heritage institutions and researchers should agree upon when working together:
* **Reciprocity**: Do both cultural heritage institutions and researchers agree to share content and knowledge equally with each other, making use of data centres and research infrastructures?
* **Interoperability**: Cultural heritage data will be made accessible in a form that facilitates reuse of the data for research Formats should work and be interoperable for both scholars and cultural heritage institutions.
* **Citability**: Cultural heritage data and any resulting research need to be fully citable to increase their visibility and impact. Relevant data citation standards should be applied.
* **Openness**: Cultural heritage data should be shared under an open license whenever possible, taking into account existing copyright and any restrictions due to national legislation and privacy issues.
* **Stewardship**: Long-term preservation, persistence, accessibility, and legibility of cultural heritage data should be a priority.
* **Trustworthiness**: The provenance of cultural heritage data and any consequent research should be clear, up to date, openly available and therefore trustworthy.

label: Annotating Proxemic Features in Audiovisual Document Using ELAN
description:
This workflow describes how to annotate proxemic features in audiovisual corpora using ELAN. It integrates multimodal annotation principles from linguistic and semiotic research, with particular reference to gesture classification frameworks (Kendon, McNeill) and facial annotation protocols (FACS, Ekman & Friesen).

This process is grounded on Meluzzi’s approach to annotation ("Annotare una trascrizione", in "Vademecum per il trattamento delle fonti orali", pp. 227-229).

relatedItems.label: Indexing an Audio Resource
relatedItems.description: Conceived and employed by the ORMETE project (Oralità, Memoria, Teatro), directed by Donatella Orecchia (Università di Roma Tor Vergata), this workflow allows a researcher or curator to produce a segment-based index of an audio or an audiovisual resource. Rather than replacing the recording with a transcription, this process structures the resource into titled, synopsised, and keyworded segments, enabling users to navigate directly to specific points in the interview and locate content by person, place, or institution. By preserving the double voice of interviewer and interviewee at segment level and by using indexing — rather than transcription — as the primary access tool, the workflow supports listening to the original recording as the main mode of engagement with the source, in line with the stated aim of guiding and educating listening. This kind of indexing can be carried out either through OHMS (Oral History Metadata Synchronizer) or without the support of any dedicated application. The output is a reviewed, structured index suitable for publication.

relatedItems.label: MultiCo: MultiCo Multimodal Corpus
relatedItems.description:
Multico - a uniqe multimodal corpus
The MultiCo Corpus consists of three Persuasion, Dialogue, and Sports subcorpora, and covers three categories of communicative events: monologues, dialogues, and multilogues. The audiovisual material comes, respectively, from the Polish TEDx and parliamentary speeches, from the recordings of task-oriented dialogues, and from a sports television broadcast. Each subcorpus offers approximately five hours of audio and video recordings along with time-aligned orthographic transcriptions and gesture annotation. The latter is done manually for the Persuasion and Sports subcorpora, and is based on motion capture technology for the Dialogue subcorpus. The dialogues are recorded with multiple camcorders and high-quality microphones. The MultiCo corpus is a freely available resource. Its potential applications range from research (e.g., studies on multimodal interaction), to design (e.g., the design of virtual agents), and education (e.g., training in interpersonal communication or rhetorics).

relatedItems.label: Multimodal corpus EVA 1.0
relatedItems.description:
This corpus contains one episode of an audio/video session plus corresponding orthographic transcriptions with a duration of 57 minutes. The multi-party spontaneous discourse in the recording is from an entertaining evening TV-talk show [A si ti tut not padu](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt6384412/), broadcasted by the POP-TV Slovene commercial TV station in 2008, and represents a part of the [Slovene spoken corpus GOS](http://hdl.handle.net/11356/1040).
In addition to the original transcription and morphosyntactic annotation from the GOS corpus, the following layers of information are added:* statement sentiment
* phrase breaks within statements
* prominence of statements
* sentences within the statement
* sentence sentiment
* sentence type
* speaker visibility on the scene
* gesture units
* gesture phrases
* emotions
* semiotic intent
* dialogue role
The corpus is available for download from the CLARIN.SI repository.

relatedItems.label: BAS SmartKom Public Video and Gesture corpus
relatedItems.description: This corpus contains multi modal recordings of 86 actors who use the SmartKom system. SmartKom Public is comparable to a traditional public phone booth but equipped with additional intelligent communication devices. Naive users were asked to test a 'prototype' for a market study not knowing that the system was in fact controlled by two human operators. They were asked to solve two tasks in a period of 4,5 min while they were left alone with the system. The instruction was kept to a minimum, in fact the user only knew that the system is able to understand speech, gestures and even mimic expressions and should more or less communicate like a human.

relatedItems.label: Multiple Temporalities of Language and Body in Interaction: Challenges for Transcribing Multimodality
relatedItems.description:
The article focuses on the principles of multimodal CA, the way they can be operationalized in a transcription system, and the analytical and conceptual consequences of transcription choices. Elaborating on the foundations of multimodal CA and on the basis of video recordings of French and Swiss German encounters, as well as animal interactions, the article discusses classic and contemporary challenges for transcription and analysis, such as beyond gesture and gaze, body arrangements in interactional spaces, larger groups, material environments, mobile settings, silent activities, and animal encounters. It also highlights the diversity of multimodal practices involved: mobilizing occasioned
material resources, movements not only of the upper (head, gesture) but also the lower (feet, legs, posterior) parts of the body, haptic contacts touching objects and coparticipants, and camera movements. The precise transcription of relevant details reveals complex arrangements of multimodal resources and
gestalts. Their fine-grained, distinct, multiple temporalities constitute the basis of their sequential order—for sequentiality as a fundamental organizational principle of action. Data are in French and Swiss German.

relatedItems.label: Enhanced gaze-following behavior in Deaf infants of Deaf parents
relatedItems.description: Gaze following plays a role in parent–infant communication and is a key mechanism by which infants acquire information about the world from social input. Gaze following in Deaf infants has been understudied. Twelve Deaf infants of Deaf parents (DoD) who had native exposure to American Sign Language (ASL) were gender-matched and age-matched (±7 days) to 60 spoken-language hearing control infants. Results showed that the DoD infants had significantly higher gaze-following scores than the hearing infants. We hypothesize that in the absence of auditory input, and with support from ASL-fluent Deaf parents, infants become attuned to visual-communicative signals from other people, which engenders increased gaze following. These findings underscore the need to revise the ‘deficit model’ of deafness. Deaf infants immersed in natural sign language from birth are better at understanding the signals and identifying the referential meaning of adults’ gaze behavior compared to hearing infants not exposed to sign language. Broader implications for theories of social-cognitive development are discussed. A video abstract of this article can be viewed at https://youtu.be/QXCDK_CUmAI

relatedItems.label: ELAN
relatedItems.description:
ELAN is a tool for creating annotations on multiple layers on audio and video resources. The textual content of annotations is in Unicode and the transcription is stored in XML.

With ELAN a user can add an unlimited number of textual annotations to audio and/or video recordings. An annotation can be a sentence, word or gloss, a comment, translation or a description of any feature observed in the media. Annotations can be created on multiple layers, called tiers. Tiers can be hierarchically interconnected. An annotation can either be time-aligned to the media or it can refer to other existing annotations. The content of annotations consists of Unicode text and annotation documents are stored in an XML format (EAF).

Main features and characteristics of ELAN:
* provides several ways to view the annotations, each view is connected to and synchronized with the media timeline
* supports creation of multiple tiers and tier hierarchies
* supports Controlled Vocabularies
* allows linking of up to 4 video files with an annotation document
* media support
   * builds on existing, native media frameworks, like Windows Media Player, QuickTime or VLC
   * support for audio and video formats depends on operating system, high performance media playback can usually be achieved
* technical
   * written in the Java programming language
   * distributions available for Windows, macOS and Linux
   * open source, the sources are available under a GPL 3 license 

The solution was developed by the Language Archive of the Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics.

relatedItems.label: The benefit of gestures during communication: Evidence from hearing and hearing-impaired individuals
relatedItems.description:
in «Cortex», 48 (2012), 7, pp. 857-870.Christian Obermeier
, 
There is no doubt that gestures are communicative and can be integrated online with speech. Little is known, however, about the nature of this process, for example, its automaticity and how our own communicative abilities and also our environment influence the integration of gesture and speech. In two Event Related Potential (ERP) experiments, the effects of gestures during speech comprehension were explored. In both experiments, participants performed a shallow task thereby avoiding explicit gesture–speech integration. In the first experiment, participants with normal hearing viewed videos in which a gesturing actress uttered sentences which were either embedded in multi-speaker babble noise or not. The sentences contained a homonym which was disambiguated by the information in a gesture, which was presented asynchronous to speech (1000 msec earlier). Downstream, the sentence contained a target word that was either related to the dominant or subordinate meaning of the homonym and was used to indicate the success of the disambiguation. Both the homonym and the target word position showed clear ERP evidence of gesture–speech integration and disambiguation only under babble noise. Thus, during noise, gestures were taken into account as an important communicative cue. In Experiment 2, the same asynchronous stimuli were presented to a group of hearing-impaired students and age-matched controls. Only the hearing-impaired individuals showed significant speech–gesture integration and successful disambiguation at the target word. The age-matched controls did not show any effect. Thus, individuals who chronically experience suboptimal communicative situations in daily life automatically take gestures into account. The data from both experiments indicate that gestures are beneficial in countering difficult communication conditions independent of whether the difficulties are due to external (babble noise) or internal (hearing impairment) factors.

relatedItems.label: “The Egg and Jerry”: Narration and Gesture In L1 and L2 By Italian Schoolchildren
relatedItems.description: In  this paper,we  present  sociolinguistic  research  conducted  on  Italian  schoolchildren  learning  English  as  L2. Following  on  from  renowned  researchers,  we  focused  on  a  less  studied population,  whichis  school-aged  monolingual children.Our participants consistedof15 students of a fourth-grade class at a primary school in Pavia;all aged around 9 years  of  age -7  boys  and  8  girls. Noneof  the childrenpresent  any  recorded  cognitive  problems;they  are  all  Italian  L1 speakers with little or no use of other languages at home, and English has been learnt as L2since the beginning of primary school at age 6. We recorded all the children performing a task of re-narration of a “Tom & Jerry” cartoon, firstly in Italian and then, after one week, in English. The corpus consistsofabout 2h 45’ of recordings, transcribed and annotated in ELAN. Lexical knowledge in English was also tested through a questionnaire before the recordings.The results were analyzed both qualitatively and, partly, quantitatively. During qualitative analysis, two elements were observed: (1) general tendencies in speakers’general  behavior  and  (2)  differences  in  the  relationship  between  syntactic-conversational  system  and  gesture system in relation to L1/L2. The quantitative analysis showsa difference in theuse of beats gestures and iconic ones between L1 and L2, but also between boys and girls. Themain findings of the current research are: (1) frequent use of gesture during L1  recordings,  in  contrast  to  a  general  decrease  of  gesture  during  L2  recordings;  (2)  gesture  as  linguistic  reinforcing  or replacement  of  speech  production  during  L1  recordings,  in  contrast  to  gesture  as a problem-solving  strategy  during  L2 recordings; (3) generally, offline knowledge in L2 is not reflected in online knowledge.

relatedItems.label: Transcribing conversation in ELAN
relatedItems.description:
This workflow outlines the main steps involved in the transcription of conversational data using ELAN, a software environment designed for the annotation and synchronisation of audio and video recordings. ELAN is particularly suitable for multimodal transcription, as it allows the annotation of both verbal and non-verbal phenomena — such as gaze, gestures, pauses, and interactional dynamics — through multiple time-aligned annotation tiers.

The workflow includes the preliminary design of the transcription scheme and annotation hierarchy, the configuration of tiers and segmentation units, the automatic or manual transcription and annotation process, and the exportation of the final transcript in EAF or other formats. 

This workflow is based on Letizia Cirillo’s chapter “Trascrivere la conversazione” (pp. 181–188), part of the "Vademecum per il trattamento delle fonti orali" (Tavolo permanente per le fonti orali, 2020).

relatedItems.label: Treating Oral Sources in SSH Research
relatedItems.description:
This workflow, developed in Italy, guides SSH researchers, archivists, and institutions through the full lifecycle of oral sources: from initial legal and ethical preparation, through fieldwork and documentation, to long-term preservation, archival transfer, access, and valorisation, including responsible online publication. It covers the production of audio or audiovisual recordings, their contextual documentation, and their integration into archival systems.

The workflow applies equally to newly initiated oral data gathering campaigns and to the retrospective treatment of pre-existing collections. It draws on the "Vademecum per il trattamento delle fonti orali" (Ministero della Cultura, Direzione Generale Archivi, 2023), a multidisciplinary reference document developed by specialists from different domains, including oral historians, linguists, ethnologists, librarians and archivists.

While it integrates European data protection requirements (GDPR) and established professional standards, it also refers at certain points to the Italian legal framework. Researchers operating in other national contexts should therefore consult the relevant legislation and guidelines applicable in their own country.

relatedItems.label: Vademecum per il trattamento delle fonti orali
relatedItems.description: Starting from a broader definition of oral sources and from the assumption of the unity of the communicative event that generates the source—and, consequently, the archive of oral sources—this Vademecum provides a coherent theoretical framework, not merely prescriptive, to which methods and practices for the treatment of oral documentation can be anchored.

composedOf.label: Create annotation categories (tiers)
Create labels for each tier
composedOf.description:
Controlled label sets for each tier are defined by grounding the annotation scheme in established frameworks, while maintaining sufficient constraint to ensure comparability across datasets and to avoid both over- and under-categorisation, a tension captured by the so-called “setaccio problem” discussed by Meluzzi.

For the hand gesture tier, the label system is organised as follows. Handedness is encoded through a closed set comprising right, left, and both, ensuring consistent identification of the articulating effector across annotations. Directionality is defined in relation to Kendon’s typology of palm orientation, with controlled values such as palm_up and palm_down; these categories are deliberately restricted in order to reduce interpretative dispersion while preserving a key semiotic dimension of gesture organisation. A further functional layer can be integrated on the basis of McNeill’s framework, distinguishing deictic, iconic, metaphoric, and beat gestures. Given its higher level of interpretive abstraction, this layer remains optional and is applied only where analytically robust across datasets.

For the facial gesture tier, the annotation system is anchored in the Facial Action Coding System (FACS) developed by Ekman and Friesen. The primary unit of analysis is the Action Unit (AU), defined in relation to specific underlying facial muscle activations. Each AU is described through three controlled parameters: the muscle group involved, following FACS nomenclature; the movement direction, operationalised as activation or deactivation where relevant; and intensity, coded on a fixed ordinal scale from 1 to 5, ranging from minimal visible activation to maximal intensity. This structure supports a fine-grained yet standardised representation of facial behaviour.

Across all tiers, the design balances three principles. The first is theoretical precision, ensured through the integration of established frameworks (FACS for facial movements, McNeill for gesture typology, and Kendon for spatial and orientational parameters). The second is comparability across datasets, achieved through the use of closed or semi-closed label sets that support reproducibility in multimodal corpora. The third is controlled granularity, which directly addresses the “setaccio problem” (Meluzzi): excessive segmentation leads to fragmentation and loss of consistency, whereas overly coarse categories obscure meaningful variation. The resulting system therefore remains deliberately selective, privileging analytically robust distinctions over exhaustive descriptive coverage.

composedOf.label: Perform annotation and time alignment
composedOf.description:
Gesture annotation can be carried out directly on the temporal axis of the video within ELAN, where gestures are segmented and aligned with observable multimodal events. Segmentation may follow the internal dynamics of the interaction, with gesture units identified according to their onset, apex, and offset, rather than relying on externally imposed units. In this way, gestures can be represented as temporally structured events rather than as static annotations.

Alignment with the speech transcription tier can rely on temporal anchoring, which enables systematic comparison between verbal and non-verbal modalities. Strict simultaneity does not need to be assumed. The annotation system can accommodate non-synchronous relations, including anticipatory gestures that precede lexical items and post-stroke gestures that extend beyond speech completion.

Partial overlap between speech and gesture can also be treated as a frequent and analytically meaningful configuration in natural interaction. In such cases, temporal intersections may be encoded without enforcing full equivalence between modalities, allowing each tier to preserve its own internal temporal logic. This approach acknowledges that multimodal alignment is often imperfect and that asynchrony itself can be interpreted as a relevant dimension of communicative organisation rather than as an annotation error.

relatedItems.label: Bielefeld Speech and Gesture Alignment Corpus
relatedItems.description:
This corpus contains 25 dialogues of interlocutors (50), who engage in a spatial communication task combining direction-giving and sight description. The stimulus is a model of a town presented in a Virtual Reality (VR) environment. Upon finishing a “bus ride” through the VR town along five landmarks, a router explained the route as well as the wayside landmarks to an unknown and naive follower. Six of those dialogues with data only from the direction giver are available including audio (*.wav) and video (*.mp4) data.  There are 1764 isolated gestures in the corpus. 
The corpus is available for download from the BAS CLARIN-D repository.

composedOf.label: Add comments and analytic notes (optional)
composedOf.description:
Qualitative comments and analytic notes can be included in ELAN as an optional layer that complements the structured annotation tiers, without modifying their formal structure. This space can be used for contextual interpretation, particularly when aspects of meaning, framing, or interactional relevance are not easily captured through controlled labels.

It can also be useful to document uncertainty markers. In cases where segmentation is ambiguous, where gesture categorisation is partial, or where FACS-based identification remains open to interpretation, noting the degree and source of uncertainty can help clarify later analytical decisions and make the annotation process more transparent.

This layer can further support the recording of interactional observations, such as turn-taking organisation, alignment or misalignment between modalities, shifts in attention, or emerging pragmatic effects across speech and gesture. These dimensions often exceed the descriptive scope of formal tiers but remain important for interpreting the interaction as a whole.

Finally, the comment field can be used to capture multimodal co-occurrence patterns, for instance recurring associations between specific gesture forms and lexical items, or systematic synchronisations between facial expressions, prosody, and bodily orientation. Over time, these notes can help identify patterns that are not pre-encoded in the annotation scheme but emerge inductively from the data.

Overall, this layer can function as a flexible interpretative space that supports later theoretical analysis while keeping the structured annotation system stable and comparable.

composedOf.label: Export annotated data
composedOf.description:
For the export phase, ELAN annotations can be exported into formats that support different levels of downstream analysis. CSV format is particularly suitable for quantitative processing, as it allows structured manipulation of tiers, time codes, and categorical labels in statistical software or programming environments. This format is especially useful for operations such as frequency counts, duration analysis, or alignment comparisons across tiers. TXT export, by contrast, can support qualitative inspection or transfer into coding environments, where linear readability and manual coding remain important. It is often used when the analytical focus shifts from structured quantification to interpretative reading or when annotations need to be integrated into broader qualitative workflows.

Once exported, the dataset can support multiple lines of analysis. Gesture frequency can be computed across speakers, contexts, or interactional settings, enabling comparative perspectives on multimodal behaviour. Co-occurrence between gesture and speech can be systematically examined by aligning temporal segments, making it possible to identify recurrent synchronisation patterns or systematic divergences between modalities. In addition, gesture types can be compared across speakers or communicative contexts, allowing for both intra- and inter-speaker variation to be analysed within a unified annotated framework.

composedOf.label: Publication and data sharing
composedOf.description:
For publication and data sharing, annotated datasets can be prepared in line with FAIR principles, ensuring that data are findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable. Accessibility strategies may vary depending on ethical constraints and project design. Institutional repositories or dedicated project servers can be used for controlled dissemination, particularly when data remain within a research group or consortium. CLARIN-compatible repositories offer a particularly suitable infrastructure for linguistically annotated multimodal corpora, especially when access conditions need to be regulated. Dataverse provides a robust solution for structured long-term preservation, ensuring both versioning and metadata stability over time.

Ethical and access considerations form a central component of this stage. Participant anonymisation may be required depending on consent agreements and the sensitivity of audiovisual materials, with particular attention to face visibility, voice identification, and contextual traceability. Access conditions can be adjusted accordingly, ranging from open access to restricted or request-based access. Comprehensive metadata documentation is essential at this stage, particularly regarding consent procedures, usage limitations, and any constraints on redistribution or reuse. This ensures that the dataset remains both ethically compliant and methodologically transparent for future research use.

composedOf.description:
Decide whether to deposit your data:  
-	in a [CLARIN-B certified data centre](https://www.clarin.eu/content/certified-b-centres), or
-	in your university's research data repository, or
-	in an inter-institutional repository like [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/).

relatedItems.label: Zenodo
relatedItems.description: Zenodo is a catch-all repository for research data. It accepts all research data, with no requirements on format, size, access restrictions, or license. It is intended to support storage, curation, and publication of big research data. It was developed by the OpenAIRE partner CERN, responding to a request by the European Commission to create an open catch-all repository for all EC funded research.

composedOf.label: Get requirements concerning file formats
composedOf.description: If you did not choose Zenodo in step n. 1, ask the repository for requirements concerning accepted file formats. A [CLARIN-B certified data centre](https://www.clarin.eu/content/certified-b-centres) might solely accept some file formats.

composedOf.label: Migrate your data to accepted, open-source file format(s)
composedOf.description:
Depending on the requirements or guidelines you received, you might have to migrate (i.e., convert) your data to new, accepted file format(s). Do not migrate your data to proprietary file formats. Keep your source data for documentation purposes. 
You can find a detailed list of file formats for archival purposes [here](https://kost-ceco.ch/).
In any case, it would be beneficial to deposit your corpus in more than one file format.

composedOf.label: Check and improve your metadata
Deposit data and metadata
composedOf.description: Tranfer your textual corpus, your data management plan and your documentation to the repository. Make sure you are depositing the latest version of both your data management plan and of your documentation.

relatedItems.label: ArkeoGIS
relatedItems.description:
ARKEOGIS, SHARING AND USE OF SPATIALIZED DATA ABOUT THE PAST
ArkeoGIS enables to pool and query – thanks to a mapping interface – the spatialized scientific data about the past (archaeology, environment…). ArkeoGIS is an online platform accessible in four languages (German, English, Spanish and French).

ArkeoGIS is a multidisciplinary application. The databases come from different sources: institutional researchers’ work (either personal or contractual researches), graduate students’ researches, private companies and archaeological heritage management services. They also come from palaeoenvironementalists’, geographers’ and historians’ work. Multidisciplinarity is spurred and promoted All these shared (import protocol) databases are available and can be queried online (webGIS) by ArkeoGIS’ users.
Each user have its own personal and customizable project interface. One can query online all or only a part of these databases, display the results on multiple backgrounds maps, save and export them towards other tools one might use (CSV export).

The chronological frame of the tool is now both customizable and multiple. ArkeoGIS’ multi-chronologies system enables to aggregate, for different areas, information from the Prehistory to the Present. About ten chronologies are already available, from the Iberian Peninsula and the Mediterranean to the Middle East or continental Europe. ArkeoGIS’ geographical frame enables to display information about all of these regions. As today, the most documented areas are the Upper Rhine Valley, the Mediterranean and the Middle East.

ArkeoGIS can be used for many different forms of research, individual or collective. It allows, among other things, to handle the data management plan (DMP) for contractual researches. ArkeoGIS is a powerful tool to use during different kind of studies (excavations, synthesis or PhD thesis, etc.).
Several tens of thousands of sites, objects and analysis are already available. ArkeoGIS is also linking several digital tools, allowing its users to be aware of their existence.
Every author submitting his localized data into ArkeoGIS keeps the control over them and is the only one who can amend them. Any user can easily access to other contributors’ data and improve its own database. A directory allows researchers to contact each other. This initiative helps to develop scientific exchanges between countries and institutions.

Hosted by Huma-NUM IR*, ArkeoGIS is a lasting solution, the datasets are available in the NAKALA repository.

The ArkeoGIS’ project is run by the University of Strasbourg.

relatedItems.label: ArkeOpen
relatedItems.description:
ArkeOpen is an open-access interface that lets you consult, query, and cross-reference open data from the ArkeoGIS research platform.

 - The left-hand pane lets you change the chronology and filter the results visible on the map according to various criteria (Periods, Thesaurus, Authors, etc.).
 - Detailed information is presented in the right-hand pane.

Creation of the tools under the supervision of Université de Strasbourg and under Free Software license following funding from the French Ministry of Higher Education, Research and Innovation (2022).

The platform is run and administered by the University of Strasbourg and the Maison Inter-universitaire des Sciences de l'Homme - Alsace (MISHA) on the Huma-Num digital humanities IR infrastructures, by a multidisciplinary team.

**Shared data**

The data accessible (datasets, chronologies, images and documentation) comes from research work, theses, inventories and books in the humanities, social sciences (archaeology, history) and environmental sciences.
Following an alignment carried out on the ArkeoGIS research platform, accessible only to professionals, these data are presented here to all readers by their authors and publishers.

composedOf.label: Create an Account on ArkeoGIS
composedOf.description: If You want to share a dataset on the ArkeoGIS platform, You need to have an account with a higher level as "student", i.e. "researcher" or "admin". Of course, You also need a dataset of spatialised informations (X/Y or Geonames) with characterisations and chronology that You intend to share to the community or open through ArkeOpen. It can be in any format (spreadsheet, database, geographical information system, even a list in a text format can do).
