relatedItems.label: ArkeoGIS
relatedItems.description:
ARKEOGIS, SHARING AND USE OF SPATIALIZED DATA ABOUT THE PAST
ArkeoGIS enables to pool and query – thanks to a mapping interface – the spatialized scientific data about the past (archaeology, environment…). ArkeoGIS is an online platform accessible in four languages (German, English, Spanish and French).

ArkeoGIS is a multidisciplinary application. The databases come from different sources: institutional researchers’ work (either personal or contractual researches), graduate students’ researches, private companies and archaeological heritage management services. They also come from palaeoenvironementalists’, geographers’ and historians’ work. Multidisciplinarity is spurred and promoted All these shared (import protocol) databases are available and can be queried online (webGIS) by ArkeoGIS’ users.
Each user have its own personal and customizable project interface. One can query online all or only a part of these databases, display the results on multiple backgrounds maps, save and export them towards other tools one might use (CSV export).

The chronological frame of the tool is now both customizable and multiple. ArkeoGIS’ multi-chronologies system enables to aggregate, for different areas, information from the Prehistory to the Present. About ten chronologies are already available, from the Iberian Peninsula and the Mediterranean to the Middle East or continental Europe. ArkeoGIS’ geographical frame enables to display information about all of these regions. As today, the most documented areas are the Upper Rhine Valley, the Mediterranean and the Middle East.

ArkeoGIS can be used for many different forms of research, individual or collective. It allows, among other things, to handle the data management plan (DMP) for contractual researches. ArkeoGIS is a powerful tool to use during different kind of studies (excavations, synthesis or PhD thesis, etc.).
Several tens of thousands of sites, objects and analysis are already available. ArkeoGIS is also linking several digital tools, allowing its users to be aware of their existence.
Every author submitting his localized data into ArkeoGIS keeps the control over them and is the only one who can amend them. Any user can easily access to other contributors’ data and improve its own database. A directory allows researchers to contact each other. This initiative helps to develop scientific exchanges between countries and institutions.

Hosted by Huma-NUM IR*, ArkeoGIS is a lasting solution, the datasets are available in the NAKALA repository.

The ArkeoGIS’ project is run by the University of Strasbourg.

relatedItems.label: The Pactols Thesaurus
relatedItems.description:
Controlled, standardized and multilingual vocabulary for archaeology, from prehistory to the contemporary period and for the sciences of antiquity in all their aspects.

Pactols is a reservoir of controlled and multilingual keywords.

If it serves historically the indexing of the CCI (Frantiq's indexed collective catalog), its richness and its scalability seduced other communities. For several years, it has been used as a thematic repository for diversified resources (academic journals, scientific databases, heritage enhancement programs).

It was created by Frantiq (Federation and Resources on Antiquity constituted as a CNRS Service Group no. 3378), which brings together around fifty units CNRS, services of the Ministry of Culture, archaeological museums, local authorities and other public establishments.

It was developed with the support of MASA consortium, Memory of archaeologists and archaeological sites.

composedOf.label: Upload into the ArkeoGIS platform
composedOf.description: Once Your dataset is ready, use the online tool to upload and check it. More details (so far in french language only) are to be find here https://www.nakala.fr/data/11280/bafc9eb0 . Make sure the spreadsheet is a .csv (Comma Separated Value)file in UTF8 format with ";" as separators -and also that you have no semicolons in "Comments" or "Bibliography" fields.

composedOf.label: Correct any errors
composedOf.description: Your file might have errors in it. The online debug tells You where the corrections are needed in the report (on down on the screen). Debug and resent until You have reached a correct file. If you are using GEONAMES for coordinates (on some or all the lines), switch the "using Geoname" curser to the right. Once done, You are ready to fill the metadata

composedOf.label: Fill in metadata as completely as possible
composedOf.description:
You will find several steps of metadata in order to describe Your dataset. Make sure those are as completed as possible in order to ensure proper citation and reuse of Your work.

Once your dataset is online, it should appear in the Databases' list (in the menu on top right of the screen)

composedOf.label: (OPTIONAL) Open your dataset in ArkeOpen
composedOf.description:
once online, if You wish to open Your dataset in ArkeOpen, You just have to go on the "information for the publication" screen of the "databases' list" and switch the button "public" to the right. An admin will then use the internal app in order to add Your dataset in ArkeOpen once a DOI has been created. NB You can add images in ArkeOpen, using the "WEB_IMAGES" column of the spreadsheet. Images must be in an open repository usign IIIF, NAKALA for example.

This is workflow 1.1, we will improve, feel free to send feedback and ideas here https://arkeogis.org/contact-2/

relatedItems.description:
ArkeOpen is an open-access interface that lets you consult, query, and cross-reference open data from the ArkeoGIS research platform.

Creation of the tools under the supervision of Université de Strasbourg and under Free Software license following funding from the French Ministry of Higher Education, Research and Innovation (2022).

label: Automatic Image Annotation Workflow
description:
## Steps to fine-tune pre-trained image recognition model for domain-specific applications

This workflow outlines a process for fine-tuning a pre-trained image recognition model to enhance its ability to recognize specific object categories that are underrepresented or entirely absent in its original training dataset. The primary goal is to create a lightweight machine learning (ML) model capable of annotating images using terms from domain-specific controlled vocabularies. 
This facilitates more accurate and consistent image annotation in specialized contexts.

The workflow serves the dual purpose of improving the model's performance on domain-specific data and streamlining the image annotation process. 
By iteratively combining manual annotation, automated annotation using the fine-tuned model, and model re-training, the workflow supports efficient creation of high-quality annotations, even for large and complex datasets. 

Key methods implemented include:

* Data preparation and harmonization, division into training and testing datasets.
* Fine-tuning: Re-training a pre-trained ML model on the manually annotated dataset.
* Automated annotation: Using the fine-tuned model to annotate unlabeled images.
* Verification and iteration: Refining the model by verifying and correcting its outputs, followed by additional training rounds.

The workflow follows an iterative cycle: starting with manual annotations, training the model, applying it to unlabeled data, validating its outputs, and re-training to achieve incremental improvements.
This approach is applicable to any general-purpose image recognition model and enables domain-specific adaptation of image recognition models, making them effective tools for tasks like object classification and metadata generation in specialized fields.

### Requirements

* The resulting model is lightweight and versatile, i.e. can be used in various places, applications and workflows.
* The annotated dataset can be used to further fine-tune the model, as the amount of annotated images grows. The ground-truth dataset is in a widely used format and structured according to good practice in the field.
* Image metadata is enriched with terms from domain-specific controlled vocabularies enhancing their general FAIRness.
    * It is possible to find images according to their contents described using controlled vocabulary terms.
    * Interoperability is increased by using shared controlled vocabularies and formal mappings between various vocabularies.
    * Re-usability of the data is enhanced because the contents of images are formally annotated.

## Use-case

In case of the [ATRIUM project](https://atrium-research.eu/) sub-task **Automatic Image Recognition**, the goal is to annotate images from archaeological archives with terms from domain-specific controlled vocabularies, e.g. types of artifacts present in the photographs, types of objects etc. 
This greatly improves usability of archaeological image archives, as metadata of the images are enriched with specific terms from controlled vocabularies, findability of images with specific contents is enhanced, and metadata description of photographs is simplified and automated.

Two types of images are used in the process:

1. photographs of (mostly) **single finds** (artefacts) photographed on (often) standardized backgrounds with a scale, 
2. **archival** (legacy) **photographs** with various contents, mostly photographs of fieldwork and archaeological objects (trenches, burials etc.)

The intended outcome is two-fold, firstly process vast amounts of archival archaeological images and thus improve their metadata descriptions in the Archaeological Map of the Czech Republic (AMCR) repository and discovery service (parts of the [Archaeological Information System of the Czech Republic (AIS CR)](https://www.aiscr.cz/)) and in the [ARIADNE Knowledge Base and Portal](https://www.ariadne-infrastructure.eu/), and secondly, automate the metadata description of photographs submitted to the AMCR repository by metal detectorists through the AMCR-PAS portal.

relatedItems.label: ARIADNE Portal
relatedItems.description:
The ARIADNE Portal provides the main point of access for searching and browsing datasets and new services for processing and publishing archaeological datasets online. 

The Portal brings together existing archaeological research datasets from ARIADNE partners so that researchers can browse and access the various distributed datasets for use in their projects. The portal also provides a point of access for the new services developed by the project.

The datasets that are registered in the ARIADNE catalogue are held by its partners and have been created through research, in excavations, in fieldwork, laboratory and other projects. In recent years archaeologists have been making increasing use of sophisticated digital equipment and techniques. During the course of a research project large volumes of data are created and collected, and become part of the research archive. ARIADNE aims to make these archives available through its portal for researchers to consult when starting new research.

relatedItems.label: ARIADNEplus Linked Open Data (GraphDB)
relatedItems.description: GraphDB provides researchers with access to the ARIADNEpPlus Knowledge Base, including all the partner data as a Linked Open Data set and modelled according to the ARIADNE ontology. With GraphDB, researchers can explore the knowledge base with the available web GUI or programmatically with SPARQL queries.

relatedItems.label: AMCR Digital Archive
relatedItems.description: The Digital Archive of the Archaeological Map of the Czech Republic (AMCR) is a web application designed for viewing information about archaeological investigations, sites and finds, operated by the Archaeological Institutes of the CAS in Prague and Brno. The archives of these institutions contain documentation of archaeological fieldwork on the territory of the Czech Republic from 1919 to the present day, and they continue to enrich their collections. The AMCR database and related documents form the largest collection of archaeological data concerning the Czech Republic and are therefore an important part of our cultural heritage.

composedOf.label: Consider the goal and use-case
composedOf.description:
Firstly, consider the goal and individual use-case of the model application. 
This workflow describes how to **fine-tune a pre-trained image recognition model** (e.g. [ResNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.03385v1)) to recognize objects and annotate the images with terms from controlled vocabularies, which is a relatively **light-weight** solution. 
If cost-effectiveness, price etc. are not of concern or natural language description of the contents of the image plays a role in your use-case, consider using a solution from a family of large language models (LLMs), their usability for tasks as described here is increasing, including outputs in machine-readable formats etc.

relatedItems.label: Computer Vision for the Humanities: An Introduction to Deep Learning for Image Classification (Part 1)
relatedItems.description: This is the first of a two-part lesson introducing deep learning based computer vision methods for humanities research. Using a dataset of historical newspaper advertisements and the fastai Python library, the lesson walks through the pipeline of training a computer vision model to perform image classification.

relatedItems.label: Computer Vision for the Humanities: An Introduction to Deep Learning for Image Classification (Part 2)
relatedItems.description: This is the second of a two-part lesson introducing deep learning based computer vision methods for humanities research. This lesson digs deeper into the details of training a deep learning based computer vision model. It covers some challenges one may face due to the training data used and the importance of choosing an appropriate metric for your model. It presents some methods for evaluating the performance of a model.

relatedItems.label: Distant Viewing: Computational Exploration of Digital Images
relatedItems.description:
A new theory and methodology for the application of computer vision methods to the computational analysis of collected, digitized visual materials, called “distant viewing.”

Distant Viewing: Computational Exploration of Digital Images presents a new theory and methodology for the computational analysis of digital images, offering a lively, constructive critique of computer vision that you can actually use. What does it mean to say that computer vision “understands” visual inputs? Annotations never capture a whole image. The way digital images convey information requires what researchers Taylor Arnold and Lauren Tilton call “distant viewing”—a play on the well-known term “distant reading” from computational literary analysis.

Recognizing computer vision's limitations, Arnold and Tilton's spirited examination makes the technical exciting by applying distant viewing to the sitcoms Bewitched and I Dream of Jeannie, movie posters and other popular forms of advertising, and Dorothea Lange's photography. In the tradition of visual culture studies and computer vision, Distant Viewing's interdisciplinary perspective encompasses film and media studies, visual semiotics, and the sciences to create a playful, accessible guide for an international audience working in digital humanities, data science, media studies, and visual culture studies.

composedOf.label: Gather and harmonize image data
composedOf.description:
Initial step in the workflow is to obtain and harmonize the image data. 
Image data come in different formats, resolutions, and sizes, these should be normalized before the training of a model. 

- Format: Images must be in the same bitmap format for the training, the most common choice for image recognition models is JPEG, as it has a good balance of image quality and size efficiency and thus is a default choice if you are dealing with large datasets.  On the other hand, if preservation of fine details, high fidelity, or transparency is important in your case, PNG might be more suitable.
- Color Channels: Ensure images are in RGB format, as most image-recognition models expect 3-channel input.

Further image processing (resizing, pixel normalization, etc.), is an inherent part of the fine-tuning step of the workflow and will depend on the chosen model.

relatedItems.label: GIMP (GNU Image Manipulation Program)
relatedItems.description:
GIMP is a free and open source image editing software. It is a multi-platform software application primarily used for image composition and editing. The basic tool may be augmented by plug-ins and extensions that allow the use of new file formats, effects filters and batch processing capabilities. GIMP was initially created to manipulate raster images, but has been extended to provide limited vector image and moving image support. A number of free extensions are available in the plugin registry.

GIMP is a cross-platform image editor available for GNU/Linux, OS X, Windows and more operating systems.

relatedItems.label: ImageMagick
relatedItems.description: ImageMagick is free software delivered as a ready-to-run binary distribution or as source code that you may use, copy, modify, and distribute in both open and proprietary applications. ImageMagick utilizes multiple computational threads to increase performance and can read, process, or write mega-, giga-, or tera-pixel image sizes.

composedOf.label: Align controlled vocabulary terms
composedOf.description:
**Metadata**, especially **controlled vocabulary terms**, must be aligned, ie. mapped to a common standard, if image data from various data sources do not use identical controlled vocabularies. This is best done by creating Simple Knowledge Organization System ([SKOS](https://www.w3.org/TR/skos-reference/)) mappings  between different vocabularies. 

To map to GETTY Art & Architecture Thesaurus (AAT), ARIADNE Vocabulary Matching Tool can be used. 

The mapping process is described in detail in the workflow [*Create SKOS Application Profiles*](https://marketplace.sshopencloud.eu/workflow/yLX6Bd).

## SKOS mapping relations

`skos:mappingRelation` has following properties:

-  `skos:exactMatch` -- the two terms are exact matches and can be used interchangeably
- `skos:closeMatch` -- the two terms are not exact matches, but have similar meaning
- `skos:broadMatch` -- the target term has more general meaning than the source (hierarchical relationship, inverse of `skos:narrowMatch`)
- `skos:narrowMatch` -- the target term has more specific meaning than the source (hierarchical relationship, inverse of `skos:broadMatch`)
- `skos:relatedMatch` -- the target and source terms are somehow related, but the relation is not hierarchical

relatedItems.label: Create SKOS Application Profiles
relatedItems.description: Creating an application profile from different SKOS vocabularies involves combining and aligning multiple SKOS vocabularies to create a unified and customized vocabulary that suits your specific requirements. This is a step-by-step approach to help you create an application profile.

relatedItems.label: ARIADNE Vocabulary Matching Tool
relatedItems.description: The Vocabulary Matching Tool allows users to align Linked Data vocabulary concepts with Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus concepts. The tool is a browser based application that presents concepts from chosen source and target vocabularies side by side, exposing additional contextual evidence to allow the user to make an informed choice when deciding on potential mappings (expressed as SKOS mapping relationships). The tool is intended for vocabularies already expressed in RDF/SKOS and can work directly with the data – querying external SPARQL endpoints rather than storing any local copies of complete vocabularies. The set of mappings developed can be saved locally, reloaded and exported to a number of different output formats.

relatedItems.label: Controlled Vocabularies and SKOS
relatedItems.description: Thesauri, taxonomies and other forms of controlled vocabularies represent a conceptual backbone of the research, playing an ever-increasing role in various aspects of the data management process.  These resources are indispensable to determine common understanding allowing to systematically categorize and enrich research data in a consistent manner, as well as foster the data interoperability and integration among projects and web applications.

relatedItems.label: GETTY Art & Architecture Thesaurus (AAT)
relatedItems.description: The Getty Thesaurus of Geographic Names ® (TGN), The Art & Architecture Thesaurus ® (AAT), the Union List of Artist Names ® (ULAN), the Cultural Objects Name Authority ® (CONA), and the Iconography Authority (IA) are structured resources that can be used to improve access to information about art, architecture, and material culture. Through rich metadata and links, it is hoped that the Getty vocabularies will provide a powerful conduit for research and discovery for digital art history and related disciplines.

composedOf.label: Annotate images
composedOf.description:
Once both the **image data** and **metadata** are ready, annotate fist batch of the images. 
There are many tools that can be used to annotate images, for instance *Computer Vision Annotation Tool* ([CVAT](https://www.cvat.ai/)), *VGG Image Annotator* ([VIA](https://www.robots.ox.ac.uk/~vgg/software/via/)), [makesense.ai](https://www.makesense.ai/) etc.

Annotation can be divided into two sub-steps:

1. **Segmentation**  
Segment the images manually or using *Segment Anything Model 2* ([SAM2](https://ai.meta.com/sam2/)). 
The result of segmentation using SAM2 is a (binary) mask assigning each pixel of the image into the given segment or not, a polygonal representation of the segment or its bounding box for each segmented object in the image. 
The result of segmentation is recorded in JSON file compatible with the [COCO](https://cocodataset.org/) (*Common Objects in Context*) format.

2. **Labeling**  
Tag the segmented objects in the images with terms from controlled vocabularies. These are saved in the COCO compatible JSON file as well.
Typically, a human readable and understandable label is used in computer vision datasets.

concept.definition: the act of labelling a piece of data or content wth a short string to express some metadata (Wikidata contributors, "Q43401994," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q43401994&oldid=1198888121 (accessed September 4, 2020)

composedOf.label: Split into train, test and val datasets
composedOf.description:
Split the annotated data into three parts, first one will be a **training** dataset, second one a **validation** dataset and the last one a **testing** dataset. 
The training dataset is usually around 60–80 % of the whole and it is used to re-train the model. 
The validation dataset is then used to guide the training of the model not to overfit parameters etc., this portion is commonly around 10–20  % of the training dataset. 
The testing dataset is then 20–25 % of the whole and it is used to test the model accuracy on images the model has not seen before. 

The training, validation and testing datasets **do not overlap**, i.e. each consists of **distinct images**. 
Each dataset should consist of a representative proportion of all the classes present in the whole dataset, i.e. the real world-application. 
If the dataset is imbalanced, i.e. there is a significantly different number of representatives of each class, the proportion of classes in each dataset should be kept consistent with the original dataset.

composedOf.label: Re-train model
composedOf.description:
The fine-tuning of the selected model is done using existing libraries and tools like [*TensorFlow*](https://www.tensorflow.org/) or [*PyTorch*](https://pytorch.org/).

After the training, test the model performance on the testing dataset. 
Use the model to automatically annotate the images, then automatically verify the annotations. 
There are many ways of measuring model performance and/or accuracy, i.e. the proportion of the correctly classified instances (successes) out of all instances in the testing dataset is the simplest one. 
Expected accuracy is between 80–95 %. 
If the accuracy is lower, go back to annotating more images and reiterate the whole process. 

In case of sufficient performance, you reached the end of the training phase, now you have a ML model ready to use on other datasets and a ground-truth dataset consisting of image files and a COCO compatible JSON file with the results of segmentation and annotations.

composedOf.label: Apply the ML model
composedOf.description:
Use the model to automatically annotate previously unannotated (unlabeled) images, either from your original dataset, if there are any yet unannotated images, or a completely new set of image files without metadata. 
Once the images are automatically annotated, you can manually verify the annotations and if these are correct, these data can be added to the ground-truth dataset. 
The model can now be used in various contexts and the annotations can be extracted from the JSON file and attached to the image files in repositories in appropriate metadata fields etc.

label: Automatic Text Recognition Roadmap
description:
**Automatic Text Recognition** (ATR) uses Artificial Intelligence (AI), in particular **machine learning** (ML), to **extract text from a scanned image**. It encompasses two main techniques: **Optical Character Recognition** (OCR), extracting text from printed documents, and **Handwritten Text Recognition** (HTR), extracting text from manusripts.  
This workflow presents the main steps of an ATR workflow and how to integrate it in your research project.

relatedItems.label: Making Data Reusable in the Context of Automatic Text Recognition
relatedItems.description:
The most common reason behind an export is to create backups of the data because digital tools and servers are not 100% reliable. Export can be done even with unfinished transcriptions when your project is still considered work in progress.  

In the cases where it is possible to change software, you will want to move your data from the current software to the one you want to migrate to. Similarly, by exporting the transcription, you can feed the data to another tool, which can be one of the reuse options. Exporting can also be done to publish finished transcriptions, whether it is the whole corpus or simply a sample. Finally, if you want to transform your transcribed corpus, an export will be necessary.

relatedItems.label: Model Training for Automatic Text Recognition
relatedItems.description:
Automatic Text Recognition (ATR) describes the convergent usage of Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR).  

OCR is aimed at treating printed media, such as books. This technology has only improved over time, and systems nowadays can have an accuracy of 99% in recognising text from printed documents. HTR, as the name suggests, is used for handwritten documents, improve their accessibility, and allow for efficient data extraction. Human handwriting poses a challenge even for modern technology, as manuscripts encompass a near-endless range of fonts and styles. It is out of range for traditional approaches of pattern matching, which is the crux of OCR.  

Evolving technologies have allowed for text recognition systems to now to do both HTR and OCR simultaneously. Modern models can recognise printed as well as handwritten text, and process segments in lines or entire paragraphs. These technologies are especially appealing to historians, librarians, archival staff, and scholars in general who want to convert, analyse, store, or maintain their documents in a novel way, adopting global digital trends.

relatedItems.label: Pre-Processing Images for Automatic Text Recognition
relatedItems.description:
Pre-processing is optional and, in some cases, not necessary at all. This is usually the case if you receive your images directly from a cultural heritage institution. However, if you are faced with double-sided copies or crooked and poorly cropped images, pre-processing may be necessary. 

If you cannot avoid pre-processing, test the results on a small dataset before performing large-scale pre-processing.  

#### Pros and Cons of Pre-Processing
* Pros: 
    * Can drastically reduce the amount of time spent correcting segmentation results;
    * Can increase your chances of achieving better transcription results.
* Cons: 
    * Can be time consuming;
    * Can have a negative impact on the results if done incorrectly
    * Can be less effective than model training in some cases (e.g. low contrasts or translucent pages).

This workflow uses GIMP, which is a free and easy to use graphic editor.

relatedItems.label: Acquiring Images for Automatic Text Recognition
relatedItems.description: Whether photographed in an archive or discovered in the digital collections of memory institutions like libraries or museums, for many humanities scholars, images of text sources form the basis of their academic work. Finding, creating and collecting images of textual material is often the first step in the research process.

relatedItems.label: Performing Layout Analysis for Automatic Text Recognition
relatedItems.description:
Layout analysis is a computer vision tasks that allows us to identify the structure of a document and localize the lines of text. We generate a series of _x_ and _y_ coordinates corresponding to regions/lines on the image, which we associate to a corresponding labels.  

Text line segmentation is mandatory in most ATR systems, but without a good line segmentation, transcription performances will not be sufficient. For example, lines can be missed, read in the wrong order, or even broken down into several lines. 

Synonyms: "segmentation", "zoning", "document analysis", "optical layout analysis".

media.caption: Getting Started with Automatic Text Recognition

composedOf.label: Defining goals and objective(s)
composedOf.description:
#### Why use ATR?
* To **speed up text acquisition** → Identify the tools and ATR models available for a **ready-to-use** solution to apply to your corpus directly.
* **Impossibility of transcribing the corpus by hand** → Either opt for a **ready-to-use** solution or **fine-tune** an ATR model by collecting or creating training data to form your own template.  

_Please note that building an ATR model from scratch is **expensive** (costs of data creation and gathering), **time-consuming**, and **energy-intensive**. In addition, processing complex layouts remains a major challenge._ 


#### Your objective(s)

|                           | Precision | Accuracy | Model               |
| :------------------------ | :-------: | :------: | :------------------ |
| **Quantitative Analysis** | Low       | ~85%     | Generic             |
| **Text Repository**       | Medium    | ~90%     | Specific or Generic |
| **Scientific Editing**    | High      | ~95%     | Specific            |

If the quality of ATR predictions is not sufficient to reach your research objectives, the quality of the generated text can be improved by introducing a **human proofreading** phase, creating **more training data**, or implementing **post-treatment checks**.

composedOf.label: Assessing resources
composedOf.description:
_The larger the project, the easier to find resources and expertise._  

##### Individual vs. Collective
* My project is an **individual** project → Keep it simple and try to look for as many **ready-to-use solutions** as possible.
* My project is a **collective** project → Use the **expertise and resources** (infrastructures, models, data) **of your partners** to build your project on solid ground.

##### Not Funded vs. Funded
* My project is **not funded** → Keep it simple and try to look for as many **ready-to-use solutions** as possible.
* My project is **funded** → The project can grow depending on your budget and project objectives. You can **train your own team or call experts in**, **hire engineer(s) to create or optimize your pipeline**, **finance the creation of training data**, or even **buy/pay for access to compute servers** in order to train new generic models. 

##### Team Training
* My team **cannot be trained** in ATR techniques → Keep it simple and try to look for as many **ready-to-use solutions** as possible.
* My tean **can be trained** in ATR techniques → You can **expand** your use of ATR, **fine-tune** or **create your own** models, in order to adapt the ATR techniques as much as possible to your research objectives.

composedOf.label: Integrating ATR in your workflow
composedOf.description:
As ATR facilitates the acquisition of texts, it should be the **first step** in your project. It is preferable to **anticipate** having to dedicate a considerable amount of time for this part of the project workflow since it **determines the quality of the textual data**. Set aside **at least 6 months** in order to **prepare the training data**, **correct the transcriptions**, and anticipate segmentation problems. Do not forget to **include checkpoints** to verify data quality at **each step of the workflow**. This is likely to impact the text output in your corpus.

#### Choosing your tool
* **[eScriptorium](https://escriptorium.inria.fr/)** ([contact](https://cremmacall.sciencescall.org)) is an ATR web application which allows you to annotate and transcribe your documents. It is not a totally ready-to-use solution since you need to **either train or download a model**. However, your are completely free to train your model through your chosen parameters with _Kraken_.
* **[OCR-D](https://ocr-d.de/en)** is an open source software that covers a full OCR workflow as long as you provide digitized images. It is optimized for old prints (16th-18th centuries).
* **[Transkribus](https://www.transkribus.org/)** is a ready-to-use solution, even though it is not totally open. It requires that you stay in the _Transkribus_ environment, which means that you cannot run your training on the command line and choose your training parameters.
* Other: Please note that the less common your solution is, the fewer ready-to-use resources will be available to you.  

_Once you have chosen a tool, you should stay in the same environment for compatibility reasons. Data and models are not totally compatible between different tools._  

#### Training data
You can find available data and models in the **[HTR-United](https://htr-united.github.io/)** catalog, on **GitHub** or **Zenodo**. With _Transkribus_, models are accessible via the interface. When you collect data or reuse a model, make sure that the transcription guidelines used are appropriate for your project.  
* If your transcriptions are to be aligned, you will need to spend time creating data for segmentation and text alignment, for example.
* Training data in an XML format (**ALTO** or **PAGE**) are ready to use. You can gather data from different projects, but be careful about compatibility.  

#### Is there an appropriate generic model?
* YES → You can use the model directly or fine-tune it on your corpus. Most of the time, 5 images with aligned text are enough to achieve results of around 95% accuracy if the generic model is appropriate. 
* NO → You have to create a model from scratch by reusing and/or create new data. For a simple document, 20 images with aligned text may be enough.  

#### Transcription rules and outputs
* Your pipeline should include the **type of text output** you want, which will **determine your transcription rules**. These rules are extremely important to ensure the homogeneity of your data. See for example the [CATMuS](https://catmus-guidelines.github.io/) transcription guidelines.
* Your research objectives are key in designing your pipeline and making sure that you have integrated all the necessary textual features.
* **Text post-processing protocols** (_word segmentation, lemmatisation, named entity recognition, etc._) are determined by the type of text output you want, either raw (for quantitative analysis) or pre-edited text.
* It is crucial to decide what you can share and where you will do so in order to design your pipeline and data management plan.  
_You do not have to keep everything_.

relatedItems.label: HTR-United
relatedItems.description:
HTR-United is a catalog of metadata on training datasets (ground truth datasets) available for the creation of transcription or segmentation models. The metadata are provided by the creators of these datasets. 
HTR-United offers a schema to homogenize descriptions of datasets, as well as recommendations on how to organize a data repository, and tools for quality control and continuous documentation. 
HTR-United is an ecosystem relying on a Github organization, transparent and open to all, using minimalistic developments to facilitate its maintenance. 
HTR-United was born from the necessity -for projects- to have access to various types of ground truth to rapidly train models on smaller corpora.

relatedItems.label: Transkribus
relatedItems.description:
Transcribe. Collaborate. Share... and benefit from cutting edge research in Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR)! 

Transkribus is an OCR platform for transcribing hand-written text. After manually transcribing 100 images, scholars can use a trained HTR engine to automate the transcription of the remaining pages of their documents. The platform has a number of tools and features for users in different disciplines. /

relatedItems.label: eScriptorium
relatedItems.description:
eScriptorium means to provide researchers in the humanities with an integrated set of tools to transcribe, annotate, translate and publish historical documents.
The eScriptorium app itself is at the 'center'. It is a work in progress but will implement at least automatic transcriptions through kraken, indexation for complex search and filtering, annotation and some simple forms of collaborative working such as sharing and versioning.

composedOf.label: Acquiring images
composedOf.description: Images of text sources are the basis of many Humanities scholars' academic work. Finding, creating and/or collecting images of textual material is often the **first step of the research process**. Users may digitize archival materials themselves, but digitization is **often carried out by the archival administration or an external provider**.

composedOf.label: Pre-processing images
composedOf.description: The **pre-processing** step is **optional**, and sometimes not necessary. Image optimization includes processes like **adjusting** brightness and contrast, cropping, splitting, rotating, and dewarping.

composedOf.label: Analysing the layout of the images
composedOf.description:
Once the images are ready and uploaded onto a transcription platform (e.g. eScriptorium), the **software recognizes the different zones on the page** like text, non-textual content, or no content at all. This process is called **segmentation**. It can itself be broken down into two different steps:
1. Recognition of text zones;
2. Recognition of lines within the text zones.  

The layout analysis step is essential for defining the layout of the text and **locating the titles, subtitles, margins, or annotations** that accompany the main body of text.

relatedItems.label: Performing Layout Analysis for Automatic Text Recognition
relatedItems.description:
Layout analysis is a computer vision tasks that allows us to identify the structure of a document and localize the lines of text. We generate a series of _x_ and _y_ coordinates corresponding to regions/lines on the image, which we associate to a corresponding labels.  

Text line segmentation is mandatory in most ATR systems, but without a good line segmentation, transcription performances will not be sufficient. For example, lines can be missed, read in the wrong order, or even broken down into several lines. 

Synonyms: "segmentation", "zoning", "document analysis", "optical layout analysis".

media.caption: Segmentation example from Gallic(orpor)a project with three different zones (Credit: Ariane Pinche)

composedOf.label: Training a model and applying it to the text recognition
composedOf.description:
Once the zones have been segmented, the model recognizes the **text within the zones**. The machine does not actually read the text, but rather **predicts the probability of a combination of letters or for a specific word to appear**. A model is trained and improved based on **manually curated** pre-existing training data, also known as **ground truth** data.  

The model can either be created from scratch, or be a fine-tuning of an existing model:
* Building a model from scratch demands a substantial volume of training data and involves significant investment in terms of time, computing resources, and technical expertise.
* Fine-tuning a model involves incorporating your own data into a generic ATR model before customizing it to suit the specific corpus.

media.caption: Example of text recognition (Credit: Ariane Pinche)

composedOf.label: Assessing the quality of the output
composedOf.description:
Once the model has produced the transcription, you need to **check its performance**. Several types of errors can occur in ATR transcriptions: addition, deletion, or replacement of characters, for example.  
Scores to evaluate the performance of a model include:
* **Word Error Rate** (WER) is the sum of the three types of transcription errors divided by the total number of words in the ground truth.
* **Character Error Rate** (CER) compares the total number of characters in the test set (including spaces) with the total number of additions, deletions, and substitutions of characters required to obtain the ground truth results.  

These scores do not have the same significance depending on the diversity of the training corpus. The greater the diversity in the model's training corpus, the more data it requires to achieve higher accuracy. However, with a diverse training corpus, the model is more likely to successfully adapt to an unknown document.

media.caption: Types of transcription errors (Credit: Ariane Pinche)
Formula for the character error rate (Credit: Ariane Pinche)
Use according to accuracy rate in per cent (Credit: Ariane Pinche)

composedOf.label: Choosing an end format and facilitating reuse
composedOf.description:
Once the transcription has been predicted by the machine and corrected by a human, the final stage is to **export the results** from the transcription platform. There are several possible formats for this, such as raw text or XML formats, depending on what the transcription is needed for.  

**Sharing your data will help the community to grow and build more generic models while attracting greater visibility for your project**. You may need to share images in order to share training data, so make sure that you have the rights to do so. You can link your repositories to [HTR-United](https://htr-united.github.io/) for greater visibility.

label: Automatic Text Recognition using Object Detection with eScriptorium
description:
_Please note that this workflow is bound to change once the new version of eScriptorium is released._

This workflow performs Automatic Text Recognition (ATR) with an object detection approach. It uses a YOLO object detection model for segmenting regions, the kraken library for line segmentation, and performs text recognition on the eScriptorium platform. Please note that some prior knowledge in the application of these tools is expected, like using a command-line interface or having a free Roboflow account.

relatedItems.label: Roboflow
relatedItems.description: Roboflow is a comprehensive computer vision platform designed to streamline every stage of building and deploying vision-based applications, from data collection and labelling, to model training and deployment.

relatedItems.label: eScriptorium
relatedItems.description:
eScriptorium means to provide researchers in the humanities with an integrated set of tools to transcribe, annotate, translate and publish historical documents.
The eScriptorium app itself is at the 'center'. It is a work in progress but will implement at least automatic transcriptions through kraken, indexation for complex search and filtering, annotation and some simple forms of collaborative working such as sharing and versioning.

composedOf.label: Annotating Training Data in Roboflow
composedOf.description:
#### Importing your Images
Create your object detection project in Roboflow and start importing your data. We recommend that you import images in a **JPEG, JPG or PNG** format rather than in a PDF format.  
_For this step, a free account on Roboflow is sufficient._  
_Please note that Roboflow does not support the TIFF format._

#### Defining your Annotation Classes
When training an object detection model, you need to determine what are the objects you wish to detect. Each object refers to a **class** associated with a **label**.  
Example of classes: paragraphs, headings, form fields, tables, images, etc.  

#### Using Bounding Boxes
We recommend that you use rectangular bounding boxes rather than polygons to annotate your data because it makes detection easier.

composedOf.label: Exporting the Annotated Training Data
composedOf.description:
#### Generating your Dataset
Once your images are annotated according to your defined classes, generate your dataset by clicking on "Add _n_ images to dataset".

#### Exporting the Data
Go to the "Versions" tab and create a new version of your dataset. Disable augmentation if you want your data as they appear in the web application of Roboflow.  
Export your data using the "Export Dataset" button. Choose a **YOLO export format**.

composedOf.label: Training a YOLO Object Detection Model
composedOf.description:
Train a YOLO model using the ultralytics Python library.  
_For more information, please check the [ultralytics documentation](https://docs.ultralytics.com/modes/train/#how-do-i-train-an-object-detection-model-using-ultralytics-yolo11)._

concept.label: Machine Learning
concept.definition: branch of statistics and computer science, which studies algorithms and architectures that learn from observed facts (Wikidata contributors, "Q2539," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q2539&oldid=1228523395 (accessed July 30, 2020).

composedOf.label: Segmenting Data with YALTAi
composedOf.description:
[YALTAi](https://github.com/PonteIneptique/YALTAi) (_You Actually Look Twice At it_) is a Python library that provides an adapter for kraken to use the YOLOv8 object detection routine.  

* Install YALTAi on your machine: ```pip install yaltai```
* In the shell, use the following command to segment the lines with kraken with the zones from the YOLO model: ```yaltai kraken -I "*.jpg" --suffix ".xml" segment --yolo /path/to/yolo/model```

composedOf.label: Text Recognition with eScriptorium
composedOf.description:
#### Importing your Dataset
At this point, your data should be in an ALTO format (output from YALTAi). Import your data in eScriptorium.  

#### Training the Text Recognition Model
Thanks to the previous steps, your data has already been segmented (regions with YOLO on Roboflow, and lines with kraken via YALTAi). You can either create your own text recognition model with your training data, or fine-tune an existing model.  

#### Evaluating your Model
It is very important to check the performances of your transcription model, in order to finetune it if necessary. Evaluation scores include Word Error Rate (WER) and Character Error Rate (CER).

_For more information, please check Steps 7 and 8 of the "Automatic Text Recognition Roadmap"._

The representation is generally textual for the verbal aspects of recordings and structured for example by speech turns. It can also contain multimodal information like gestures or events and multimedia information like time synchronization and relation to media files.

relatedItems.label: Automatic Text Recognition Roadmap
relatedItems.description:
**Automatic Text Recognition** (ATR) uses Artificial Intelligence (AI), in particular **machine learning** (ML), to **extract text from a scanned image**. It encompasses two main techniques: **Optical Character Recognition** (OCR), extracting text from printed documents, and **Handwritten Text Recognition** (HTR), extracting text from manusripts.  
This workflow presents the main steps of an ATR workflow and how to integrate it in your research project.

label: Automatic Text Recognition Workflow
description:
This is workflow for using OCR/HTR itself without  using dashboard, because this workflow is dedicated to mass processing 

The main purpose of the workflow presented here is to recognize a text that has been printed or handwritten. This text was then scanned, photographed, or its image was digitally represented or obtained in any other way (e.g., digitally generated image, NOT text). It is important that we have an image of the text, but not the content of the text itself. What we want to obtain is the content of the text. This will allow us to further process the content obtained in this way, e.g., search for specific words or phrases. NLP tools will allow us to attempt to read the meaning of the text, e.g., NER, sentiment analysis, etc. There is also the potential to translate the recognized text. Recognizing text from images is usually the first step in data processing. This workflow DOES NOT DO this on its own, but it provides input for such processing in other workflows.

This workflow can be part of a larger workflow that receives an image of text at the input and needs the text content (its values) for processing. This workflow can handle both simple text images, i.e., those consisting of a single column, and only that column is on the page. The text can also consist of multiple columns, and the page can contain many different (essentially rectangular) areas with different texts that do not form a single coherent whole. This workflow can be performed for a single page or even a fragment of a page, as well as for multiple pages of an entire document. 

In addition to recognizing the text itself, this workflow can recognize typical page layouts. In this case, it will be the page layout recognized by the OCR/HTR engine. Page layout recognition can also be performed by a dedicated external service.


++Requirements++

1. One or more files that represent a single document. These can be one or more image files in common formats such as jpeg, tiff, or png. If there is more than one file, then all files together form a single multi-page document, and the order in which the files are delivered to the workflow is important and determines the order of the pages in the document.

When we deliver a pdf file, it can be a single file consisting of one or more pages. pdf files can be scanned or digitally created (digital-born). However, text recognition in such files is always performed as if it were an image. This is because some digitally born files may have an internal structure that is not suitable for simple text extraction.

2. When recognizing handwritten text, a trained AI model is required to recognize a specific type of handwriting. This is not necessary for typical printed texts, as most fonts, even if there are differences between them, are well recognized by typical OCR/HTR engines. When it comes to recognizing handwritten texts, it is necessary to train the handwriting model in advance. Training the system is a separate workflow, depending on the software used. In our workflow, we use Kraken software for HTR and recommend using eScriptorium to train models.

3. Optionally, this workflow can use a tool for recognizing page layout.
4. At the output, the workflow delivers:

alto format files   OR
txt (plain text)   files OR
pdf with text layer.

NOTE: Implementation's steps connected with image attached as a media.

composedOf.label: Preparing input
composedOf.description: A set of images with text to be recognized is provided at the input. Such a set is a single document. In particular, the set may consist of a single file

composedOf.label: Preprocessing pdf files
composedOf.description: If a pdf file is submitted, it should be a single file, and the subsequent pages are pages of that file. In this case, the file is pre-processed and the subsequent pages are converted into images with a resolution of at least 300 dpi.

concept.label: Preprocessing
concept.definition: Wikidata contributors, "Q28838080," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q28838080&oldid=941780726 (accessed September 4, 2020).

composedOf.label: External layout recognizer is used?
composedOf.description: Should a dedicated service be used to recognize the page layout? Answering YES means going to step (WITH_ELR), answering NO means going to step (WITHOUT_ELR).

composedOf.label: (WITH_ELR) Transefer data to layout recognition service
composedOf.description: Data is transferred to this service (the workflow of this service should be described separately). This service should return information about the division of the page into individual regions. These areas are rectangular in shape and the resulting data is expressed in a page coordinate system.

composedOf.label: Reading/storing External Layout Recognition results
composedOf.description: After the page division recognition service has been performed, these pages are divided into smaller fragments according to the results obtained from the page layout recognition service. These fragments will be separate images for processing in the OCR engine, but they will form a logical whole of a single page, and the coordinates of their position on the page will be retained and used at a later stage to assemble the page into a whole. When creating the final ALTO output file, the order of the fragments obtained from the layout recognition service and the coordinates in the page reference layout will be important. When creating the TXT output file, the order of the obtained page regions will be important.

composedOf.label: (WITHOUT_ELR) Proper text recognition
composedOf.description: There may be different HTR/OCR engines performing this service. All these engines will be programmed in such a way that they have one and the same interface, but if an engine does not perform a given function, then – depending on the context, either the default implementation will be used (e.g., if a language is missing, the default language will be used) or the function will not be performed (e.g., if fonts/styles/text decorations can be recognized, this data will not be included in the output file). If the recognition concerns handwritten texts and the engine used allows it, a trained text recognition model will be used at this stage. Such a model is in practice a data file and at this stage it can be provided from outside. The model training workflow itself is described separately.

composedOf.label: Reading results
composedOf.description:
The result of processing may be an ALTO file, which contains the content and information about the location of individual elements on the page. Some engines also allow text style recognition. Another option is a result in the form of TXT files.  Pages will be separated by the ASCII FF (0xC) character. If an external page layout recognition service is used, then subsequent page elements will be saved to the TXT file in the order in which these fragments are returned by the service.
Additionally, it is possible to generate a PDF file containing the original images with an added text layer. This option will not be available for PDF input files (d-b).

label: Automatic Transcription of Oral Sources
description:
This workflow guides you through the automatic transcription of oral source recordings in SSH research contexts. It covers the full pipeline: audio preparation, model selection and configuration, transcription, speaker diarisation, quality control, manual post-correction, and the export of timestamped, structured transcripts suitable for archival deposit and open publication.
The central tool is Whisper, a multilingual, open-source automatic speech recognition (ASR) model developed by OpenAI and released under the MIT licence. The workflow also integrates complementary tools for audio preprocessing (Audacity, FFmpeg), enhanced transcription (WhisperX, faster-whisper), annotation (ELAN), and text encoding (TEI-XML). It applies equally to newly recorded interviews and to the retrospective transcription of archival holdings.

Les données de langage oral enregistrées avec un magnétophone ou une caméra vidéo peuvent être transcrites de manière orthographique (pour les langues ayant une écriture) ou phonétique. Ces transcriptions se font en alignant le résultat de la transcription et du son (ou des gestes).  Le résultat des transcriptions est largement utilisé dans la recherche en sciences du langage.

English translation

The oral language data recorded with a tape recorder or video camera can be transcribed either orthographically (for languages that have a writing system) or phonetically. These transcriptions are produced by aligning the transcription output with the sound (or gestures). The resulting transcriptions are widely used in linguistic research.

relatedItems.label: Import a transcription or transcribe
relatedItems.description:
Annotate speech, prosody, non-verbal behaviour, and paralinguistic features. 

A. Transcribe speech using Jefferson conventions
Enter the verbal transcription in the speech tiers, one turn at a time, following the Jefferson system (G. Jefferson, Glossary of 'Transcript Symbols with an Introduction', in G.H. Lerner (ed.), "Conversation Analysis. Studies from the First Generation", Amsterdam/Philadelphia, John Benjamins, 2004, pp. 13-31.). The transcript is laid out vertically according to turn sequence; each turn is associated with a speaker identifier and, in ELAN, aligned to a time interval in the recording. Overlapping talk is marked with square brackets [ ] at the point where it begins and ends across the relevant tiers. It should be noted, however, that these brackets are not automatically generated by ELAN but are added manually. This point is important because conversation analysts working within the Jeffersonian transcription tradition—where the alignment of overlapping speech is visually reproduced on the page using vertically synchronized square brackets—may expect a comparable output. In ELAN, overlap is instead primarily represented through separate tiers and synchronized timestamps. Reproducing the conventional Jefferson-style layout therefore requires exporting the transcript (for instance into Word), using a monospaced font such as Courier, and often manually adjusting the alignment of the strings. 
Prosodic and voice quality features are noted inline using the standard symbols.

ELAN allows you to play short loops, slow down the audio, and zoom into the waveform display while annotating, which considerably aids the transcription of rapid, overlapping, or unclear speech.

B. Transcribe non-verbal behaviour
For audio-visual data, annotate non-verbal actions — gesture, gaze, posture, object manipulation — in the corresponding tiers, following the Mondada conventions. Each embodied action is described in plain language within angle-bracket-delimited strings, synchronised with the speech tier via time codes and shared symbols. The symbols mark the preparation, apex, and retraction phases of a movement, and indicate whether the action begins before the extract, continues beyond it, or is captured at a precise moment by a video frame reference (#).

Non-verbal actions often do not map neatly onto turn boundaries: a gesture may begin several syllables before the relevant word, or continue after the turn has ended. ELAN's multi-tier, time-aligned interface is designed precisely to capture this temporal complexity.

C. Add a working translation if needed
For multilingual data, or when the corpus will be shared with readers unfamiliar with the language of the interaction, it is useful to add a translation tier aligned to each speech tier. This working translation is not part of the primary transcription data but serves as an access tool. It should be clearly labelled as a gloss and not confused with the transcription itself.

relatedItems.label: Treating Oral Sources in SSH Research
relatedItems.description:
This workflow, developed in Italy, guides SSH researchers, archivists, and institutions through the full lifecycle of oral sources: from initial legal and ethical preparation, through fieldwork and documentation, to long-term preservation, archival transfer, access, and valorisation, including responsible online publication. It covers the production of audio or audiovisual recordings, their contextual documentation, and their integration into archival systems.

The workflow applies equally to newly initiated oral data gathering campaigns and to the retrospective treatment of pre-existing collections. It draws on the "Vademecum per il trattamento delle fonti orali" (Ministero della Cultura, Direzione Generale Archivi, 2023), a multidisciplinary reference document developed by specialists from different domains, including oral historians, linguists, ethnologists, librarians and archivists.

While it integrates European data protection requirements (GDPR) and established professional standards, it also refers at certain points to the Italian legal framework. Researchers operating in other national contexts should therefore consult the relevant legislation and guidelines applicable in their own country.

relatedItems.label: ELAN
relatedItems.description:
ELAN is a tool for creating annotations on multiple layers on audio and video resources. The textual content of annotations is in Unicode and the transcription is stored in XML.

With ELAN a user can add an unlimited number of textual annotations to audio and/or video recordings. An annotation can be a sentence, word or gloss, a comment, translation or a description of any feature observed in the media. Annotations can be created on multiple layers, called tiers. Tiers can be hierarchically interconnected. An annotation can either be time-aligned to the media or it can refer to other existing annotations. The content of annotations consists of Unicode text and annotation documents are stored in an XML format (EAF).

Main features and characteristics of ELAN:
* provides several ways to view the annotations, each view is connected to and synchronized with the media timeline
* supports creation of multiple tiers and tier hierarchies
* supports Controlled Vocabularies
* allows linking of up to 4 video files with an annotation document
* media support
   * builds on existing, native media frameworks, like Windows Media Player, QuickTime or VLC
   * support for audio and video formats depends on operating system, high performance media playback can usually be achieved
* technical
   * written in the Java programming language
   * distributions available for Windows, macOS and Linux
   * open source, the sources are available under a GPL 3 license 

The solution was developed by the Language Archive of the Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics.

composedOf.label: Encode the transcript in TEI-XML (optional. Recommended for archival deposit)
composedOf.description:
1. For archival and interoperability purposes, encode the corrected transcript in TEI-XML using the TEI P5 guidelines, module 8 (Transcriptions of Speech). TEI-XML is the standard encoding format for primary textual sources in SSH digital humanities and is required by many European infrastructure repositories. Minimum TEI encoding for an oral source transcript includes: with full bibliographic and administrative metadata (interviewer, interviewee, date, location, project, language, transcription date, transcriber identity, encoding conventions); with ++(utterance) elements, who attribute for speaker attribution, and xml:id for segment identification; or @when attributes for timestamp anchoring; 
2. If full TEI encoding exceeds available resources, produce at minimum a well-structured plain text or SRT file with a separate metadata record in Dublin Core format; 3. Validate the TEI file against the TEI P5 schema using oXygen XML Editor or the TEI online validator before deposit.

label: A workflow to publish Collections as Data: the case of Cultural Heritage data spaces
description:
Cultural Heritage institutions have been making their digital collections available for the public for several decades. Advances in technology such as Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning have provided a new context in which digital collections can be analysed using computational methods. Initiatives such as [Collections as data](https://collectionsasdata.github.io) and the [FAIR data principles](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201618), have emerged to provide best practices and guidelines for publishing [digital collections suitable for computational use](https://zenodo.org/record/7897735). These initiatives are complemented with the [CARE principles](https://www.gida-global.org/care) to strengthen ethical considerations in data governance and reuse. In parallel, experimental [Labs](https://www.glamlabs.io/publications/open-a-glam-lab) have been implemented in Galleries, Libraries, Archives and Museums (GLAM) in order to reuse the digital collections.

[Data spaces](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/strategy-data) have emerged as an innovative way to publish and reuse digital collections. Based on [previous work undertaken in the context of the GLAM Labs Community](https://www.glamlabs.io/checklist), this workflow provides a set of steps to publish Collections as data. It aims to guide and encourage cultural heritage institutions, step by step, in publishing their collections, so that they are suitable for computational use. It is important to note that the checklist items are iterative in nature and there is no particular order to apply them. Each institution can choose which items to use. Priorities depend on the purpose, the context, the content, the intended use or target users of the dataset.

This workflow has been developed in the context of the [common European data space for cultural heritage](https://pro.europeana.eu/page/common-european-data-space-for-cultural-heritage). It builds on the International GLAM Labs’ [Checklist to Publish Collections as Data in GLAM Institutions](https://marketplace.sshopencloud.eu/publication/uviY8r). Our intention is to further enhance and refine this workflow based on community feedback and contributions to facilitate the publication of Collections as data.

relatedItems.label: A Checklist to Publish Collections as Data in GLAM Institutions
relatedItems.description:
Large-scale digitization in Galleries, Libraries, Archives and Museums (GLAM) created the conditions for providing access to collections as data. It opened new opportunities to explore, use and reuse digital collections. Strong proponents of collections as data are the Innovation Labs which provided numerous examples of publishing datasets under open licenses in order to reuse digital content in novel and creative ways. Within the current transition to the emerging data spaces, clouds for cultural heritage and open science, the need to identify practices which support more GLAM institutions to offer datasets becomes a priority, especially within the smaller and medium-sized institutions.

This work answers the need to support GLAM institutions in facilitating the transition into publishing their digital content and to introduce collections as data services; this will also help their future efficient contribution to data spaces and cultural heritage clouds. It offers a checklist that can be used for both creating and evaluating digital collections suitable for computational use. The main contributions of this paper are i) a methodology for devising a checklist to create and assess digital collections for computational use; ii) a checklist to create and assess digital collections suitable for use with computational methods; iii) the assessment of the checklist against the practice of institutions innovating in the Collections as data field; and iv) the results obtained after the application and recommendations for the use of the checklist in GLAM institutions.

relatedItems.label: A Workflow to publish Collections as Data
relatedItems.description:
## Looking back at Europeana.eu and forward to the common European data space for cultural heritage

For decades, cultural heritage (CH) institutions have been making their digital collections available for potential communities of users. Recent advances in technology, such as machine learning, have provided a new context in which digital collections are a rich resource that can be analysed and reused by means of computational methods, for example in the humanities. Initiatives such as Collections as Data, the FAIR (findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable and CARE (collective benefit, authority to control, responsibility, ethics) data principles, and experimental Labs provide best practices and guidelines for publishing digital collections suitable for responsible computational use. In addition, data spaces have recently emerged as a new concept to foster creation, access and reuse of heritage data in which CH institutions play a key role as data providers. In this work we present a workflow for adopting Collections as Data in CH data spaces. The workflow has been developed in the context of the common European data space for cultural heritage and published on the Social Sciences and Humanities (SSH) Open Marketplace. It aims to support CH institutions, humanities researchers and computer scientists interested in making CH data available in data spaces. The article illustrates how the workflow can be adopted by CH institutions or applied by researchers wishing to publish digital collections suitable for computational use. We also demonstrate how the workflow is being adopted in the common European data space for cultural heritage, and describe a selection of potential areas that we believe will most benefit from the wide application of the workflow in the CH domain.

composedOf.label: Provide a clear license and terms of use allowing reuse of the dataset without restrictions
composedOf.description:
**Why**
The use of permissive licences as well as the inclusion of terms of use are crucial to ease an understanding of the reuse possibilities, as well as to facilitate the reuse of the digital collections by the community and to encourage responsible data use.

**How**
For example, the National Library of Scotland’s Data Foundry provides “Rights Information” for each of the datasets published on their website. For each dataset licensing information is provided in a README file (e.g. for the Moving Image Archive dataset: “Licence: [Creative Commons Zero 1.0 Universal (CC0 1.0)](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/)”. Additionally, a link is provided to the [National Library’s copyright page](https://www.nls.uk/copyright/). 
Similarly, the National Library of Luxembourg publishes a variety of datasets on their Open Data Portal under a Public Domain CC0 licence. For example, [a number of datasets](https://data.bnl.lu/data/historical-newspapers/) extracted from their digitised historical newspaper collections. [Clear guidance](https://data.bnl.lu/data/rights/) on rights and copyright is also provided.

relatedItems.label: SSHOC Workshop: Copyright Issues in Secondary Data Use
relatedItems.description:
**Date:** 24 to 25 January 2022
**Location:** Online
 
This was a two-day interactive workshop that took place on the 24th and 25th of January 2022.
 
## Event Overview

There is a **misconception in the research community** that the **use of secondary data** does not entail **legal considerations**. Secondary data is an intellectual property of the data owner, so any use of that data may require the data owner’s permission or may be subject to certain terms and conditions. Therefore, this online workshop was specifically designed to highlight these issues and help you overcome these.

In this two-day online workshop, **participants understood what needs to be taken into account when creating, using and sharing data**. It covered the following topics:

-    What is secondary data?
-    Introduction to the copyright
-    Layers and duration of copyright
-    Copyright licenses
-    Copyright in an international context
-    Copyright exceptions
-    Other rights

The two-day workshop included **lectures and presentations** with **individual exercises and group discussions**.
 
## Learning objectives
 
-    Gain a **better understanding of copyright** such as what is copyright, what is covered, who owns it and what is the duration?
-    Identify **copyright exemptions** and gain a better appreciation of fair dealing
-    Be able to differentiate between available **copyright licences** and assess these licences when publishing their own data
-    Be able to identify **country-level diversity in copyright laws** and gain a basic understanding of other types of rights in data
 
## Target Audience

This workshop was intended for anyone who wants to learn about basic copyright principles and is interested in creating, sharing and using data.

## Speakers

**Hina Zahid** is the Senior Research Data Services Officer working in the UK Data Service's Research Data Management section based at the UK Data Archive, University of Essex. She leads on the ethical aspects of research data management, sharing and reuse. She works proactively with researchers, and research centres to provide guidance, advice and training to achieve the implementation of good data management practices, and to optimise the sharing and archiving of data for research.

**Hannah Pyman** joined the University of Essex Library team in September 2016 as a Graduate Trainee, going on to become Interlending and Document Delivery Assistant in April 2017. From September 2019 until July 2020 she was an Information Literacy Co-ordinator. She began her new role as Scholarly Communications Co-ordinator in July 2020. Hannah’s role covers support across the research lifecycle, ranging from literature searching and evaluating resources, to publishing (including open access publishing), copyright, and citations.

**Cristina Magder** manages the UK Data Service's Data Collections Development and Research Data Management teams at the UK Data Archive. She leads the research data management portfolio of support and training for the UK Data Service. Her main teaching interests are data management planning, sharing and archiving data with a specific focus on licencing, data quality assurance, disclosure risk assessment, and reproducibility.

**Maureen Haaker** is a scholar in the field of qualitative methodology. She has worked with the UK Data Service for 10 years as a senior qualitative training officer and is a lecturer in the School of Social Sciences and Humanities at University of Suffolk. Her work has involved the ingest and digitisation of qualitative data, development of training for the management, deposit, and re-use of qualitative data, and the re-use of qualitative datasets for teaching and learning. She is a key contributor to Sage’s Managing and Sharing Research Data (2nd edition) and Qualitative Secondary Analysis. She is currently completing a PhD in Sociology at University of Essex.

relatedItems.label: Copyright and Licencing for Cultural Heritage Collections As Data
relatedItems.description: Cultural Heritage (CH) institutions have been exploring innovative ways to publish digital collections to facilitate reuse, through initiatives like Collections as data and the International GLAM Labs Community. When making a digital collection available for computational use, it is crucial to have reusable and machine-readable open licences and copyright terms. While existing studies address copyright for digital collections, this study focuses specifically on the unique requirements of collections as data. This research highlights both the legal and technical aspects of copyright concerning collections as data. It discusses permissible uses of copyrighted collections, emphasising the need for interoperable, machine-readable licences and open licences. By reviewing current literature and examples, this study presents best practices and examples to help CH institutions better navigate copyright and licencing issues, ultimately enhancing their ability to convert their content into collections as data for computational research. It is expected that the research will contribute to increasing CH institutions’ awareness of copyright and licencing concerning CH collections as data.

composedOf.label: Provide a suggested citation for the dataset so reusers are aware of how to cite it
composedOf.description:
**Why**
A suggestion for the citation promotes access and reusability of data as well as helps reusers to properly cite the dataset, for example in the bibliographies of their publications. This gives credit, recognition and visibility to, for example, the culture heritage institution providing the dataset. 

**How**
For example, the National Library of Scotland’s Data Foundry provides a “Cite the data” section for each of its datasets, as well as a suggested citation, e.g. “Suggested citation: National Library of Scotland. A Medical History of British India. National Library of Scotland, 2019. [https://doi.org/10.34812/2w0t-3f08](https://doi.org/10.34812/2w0t-3f08)”. 
In addition, the National Library of the Netherlands provides a suggested citation: “When using this dataset we ask you to cite it as follows: Andreas van Cranenburgh, Sara Veldhoen, Michel De Gruijter (2022). Textual features and metadata for DBNL novels 1800-2000 [Data set]. Zenodo. [https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5786254](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5786254).” 
Ideally this data citation includes a Persistent Identifier, such as a DOI, ARK, Handle, etc.
