relatedItems.label: Formalise geometric attribute parameters
relatedItems.description:
Geometric attributes describe the morphological properties of an architectural structure (e.g., a building), its constituent elements (e.g., a wall within that building), and the individual components of those elements (e.g., the stones within that wall), as well as the inter-elemental (e.g., an array of pillars) and inter-componential relationships (e.g., bonding between stones). For example, a geometric attribute of a building may be its height; of a wall its thickness; of a stone its angularity; the spacing between pillars for an inter-elemental relationship; and the degree of overlap between superposed stones for an inter-componential relationship. Geometric attributes can serve as meaningful proxies in a range of broader analyses of structural integrity, construction quality, invested labour, typology, and construction choices. The selected geometric attributes are therefore determined by the research premise and question defined within the project objectives and expected outcomes (Step 1 of “3D Digital Representations of Heritage Assets” workflow). In order to enable their measurement and extraction from a 3D model in the form of quantitative data, the selected geometric attributes are mathematically formalised into parameters, which can be analytically operationalised in a digital environment. How and in what way the geometric attributes are formalised into corresponding geometric attribute parameters is informed by the available data and documentation on both the architectural structure and the types of attributes under investigation (Step 2 of “3D Digital Representations of Heritage Assets” workflow). In turn, the resulting parameters inform, in part, the plan of work for reality-based data acquisition (Step 4 of the “3D Digital Representations of Heritage Assets” workflow), as the minimum perceptibility of relevant morphologies and relationships dictates key technical and logistical requirements.

# Input:

* Project objectives and expected outcomes: .docx, .pdf, .md, .xml
* Data and documentation on the architectural structure: .pdf, .tiff, .jpg, .dwg, .dxf, .ifc
* Reference typologies and measurement conventions for geometrical attributes: .pdf, .docx

# Output:

* Formalised geometric attribute parameter catalogue: .pdf, .docx, .md, .json, .csv, .py, .txt

relatedItems.label: Select computation systems and 3D model structuring protocols
relatedItems.description:
Following the creation of the 3D model, select and configure an appropriate computation system to enable and carry out the 3D geometric analysis process. This system is used to operationalise the geometric attribute parameters, compute the geometric attribute data, and extract the resulting data in an interoperable format for further analysis. If required, adopt or develop a 3D model structuring protocol to guide the preparatory structuring of the 3D model prior to computation.

# Input:

* Formalised geometric attribute parameter catalogue
* Technical properties of the 3D model: .json, .xml, .txt

# Output:

* Model structuring protocol: .json, .xml
* Computation environment specification: software, dependencies, libraries
* Executable computation tools: scripts, node graphs, plugins

relatedItems.label: 3D model structuring
relatedItems.description:
If necessary, preparatory model structuring entails processing and/or modifying the generated 3D model to the appropriate format to execute geometric attribute data computation. 3D Model structuring may involve actions such as segmentation, isolating elements and components into separate analytical units, and subsequent classification to enrich these units and their associated geometric attribute data with qualitative descriptors that are relevant for further statistical and comparative analysis.

# Input:

* Generated geometric digital representation (3D model)
* Model structuring schema: .json, .xml

# Output:

* Structured 3D model: .fbx, .glTF, .obj, .ply
* Segmentation-classification maps: .csv, .json

concept.label: PLY
concept.definition: PLY is a computer file format known as the Polygon File Format or the Stanford Triangle Format. It was principally designed to store three-dimensional data from 3D scanners. concept.label: PNG
concept.definition: Portable Network Graphics (PNG, pronounced PEE-en-JEE or PING) is a raster graphics file format that supports lossless data compression. PNG was created as an improved, non-patented replacement for Graphics Interchange Format (GIF), and is the most widely used lossless image compression format on the Internet. PNG supports palette-based images (with palettes of 24-bit RGB or 32-bit RGBA colors), grayscale images (with or without alpha channel for transparency), and full-color non-palette-based RGB/RGBA images (with or without alpha channel). PNG was designed for transferring images on the Internet, not for professional-quality print graphics, and therefore does not support non-RGB color spaces such as CMYK. A PNG file contains a single image in an extensible structure of "chunks", encoding the basic pixels and other information such as textual comments and integrity checks documented in RFC 2083. PNG files nearly always use file extension PNG or png and are assigned MIME media type image/png. PNG was published as informational RFC 2083 in March 1997 and as an ISO/IEC standard in 2004.

concept.label: JPEG
concept.definition: JPEG ( JAY-peg) is a commonly used method of lossy compression for digital images, particularly for those images produced by digital photography. The degree of compression can be adjusted, allowing a selectable tradeoff between storage size and image quality. JPEG typically achieves 10:1 compression with little perceptible loss in image quality. JPEG compression is used in a number of image file formats. JPEG/Exif is the most common image format used by digital cameras and other photographic image capture devices; along with JPEG/JFIF, it is the most common format for storing and transmitting photographic images on the World Wide Web. These format variations are often not distinguished, and are simply called JPEG. The term "JPEG" is an initialism/acronym for the Joint Photographic Experts Group, which created the standard. The MIME media type for JPEG is image/jpeg, except in older Internet Explorer versions, which provides a MIME type of image/pjpeg when uploading JPEG images. JPEG files usually have a filename extension of .jpg or .jpeg. JPEG/JFIF supports a maximum image size of 65,53565,535 pixels, hence up to 4 gigapixels for an aspect ratio of 1:1.

concept.label: TIFF
concept.definition: Tagged Image File Format, abbreviated TIFF or TIF, is a computer file format for storing raster graphics images, popular among graphic artists, the publishing industry, and photographers. TIFF is widely supported by scanning, faxing, word processing, optical character recognition, image manipulation, desktop publishing, and page-layout applications. The format was created by Aldus Corporation for use in desktop publishing. It published the latest version 6.0 in 1992, subsequently updated with an Adobe Systems copyright after the latter acquired Aldus in 1994. Several Aldus or Adobe technical notes have been published with minor extensions to the format, and several specifications have been based on TIFF 6.0, including TIFF/EP (ISO 12234-2), TIFF/IT (ISO 12639), TIFF-F (RFC 2306) and TIFF-FX (RFC 3949).

relatedItems.label: DIGITALIZATION CULTURE VS ARCHAEOLOGICAL VISUALIZATION: INTEGRATION OF PIPELINES AND OPEN ISSUES
relatedItems.description: **Abstract.** Scholars with different backgrounds have carried out extensive surveys centred on how 3D digital models, data acquisition and processing have changed over the years in fields of archaeology and architecture and more in general in the Cultural Heritage panorama: the current framework focused on reality-based modelling is then split in several branches: acquisition, communication and analysis of buildings (Pintus et alii, 2014). Despite the wide set of well-structured and all-encompassing surveys on the IT application in Cultural Heritage, several open issues still seem to be present, in particular once the purpose of digital simulacra is the one to fit with the "pre-informatics" legacy of architectural/archaeological representation (historical drawings with their graphic codes and aesthetics). Starting from a series of heterogeneous matters that came up studying two Italian UNESCO sites, this paper aims at underlining the importance of integrating different pipelines from different technological fields, in order to achieve multipurpose models, capable to comply with graphic codes of traditional survey, as well as semantic enrichment, and last but not least, data compression/portability and texture reliability under different lighting simulation.

relatedItems.label: Supervised segmentation of 3D cultural heritage
relatedItems.description: The use of 3D models nowadays is widely diffused for the documentation and dissemination of cultural and archaeological heritage. Nevertheless to provide an useful model it is necessary to associate to it some materials that can help operators to understand the object. This study aims at carrying out an optimal, repeatable and reliable segmentation procedure to manage various types of 3D survey data and associate them with heterogeneous information and attributes to characterize and describe the surveyed object. In particular the method starts from 2D supervised machine learning segmentation of the textured UV maps then projected on the 3D models. Three different archaeological case studies are here presented for restoration and documentation purposes. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach is effective and with many further potentials.

A variety of properties can be stored, including: color and transparency, surface normals, texture coordinates and data confidence values. The format permits one to have different properties for the front and back of a polygon. There are two versions of the file format, one in ASCII, the other in binary.

relatedItems.label: Classification of 3D Digital Heritage
relatedItems.description: In recent years, the use of 3D models in cultural and archaeological heritage for documentation and dissemination purposes is increasing. The association of heterogeneous information to 3D data by means of automated segmentation and classification methods can help to characterize, describe and better interpret the object under study. Indeed, the high complexity of 3D data along with the large diversity of heritage assets themselves have constituted segmentation and classification methods as currently active research topics. Although machine learning methods brought great progress in this respect, few advances have been developed in relation to cultural heritage 3D data. Starting from the existing literature, this paper aims to develop, explore and validate reliable and efficient automated procedures for the classification of 3D data (point clouds or polygonal mesh models) of heritage scenarios. In more detail, the proposed solution works on 2D data ("texture-based" approach) or directly on the 3D data ("geometry-based approach) with supervised or unsupervised machine learning strategies. The method was applied and validated on four different archaeological/architectural scenarios. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach is reliable and replicable and it is effective for restoration and documentation purposes, providing metric information e.g. of damaged areas to be restored.

label: Cleaning tabular data with OpenRefine
description: This workflow provides a step-by-step guide to cleaning messy tabular data using OpenRefine. It was developed for a workshop organised by the DARIAH-EU Working Group on Community Engagement as part of the project Empowering Future Scholars: Supporting PhD Students’ Training Needs, funded by the DARIAH-EU Funding Scheme for Working Group Activities (2023–2025).

composedOf.label: Download and Launch OpenRefine
composedOf.description: If necessary, download OpenRefine (https://openrefine.org/) and launch.

relatedItems.label: OpenRefine
relatedItems.description: OpenRefine (formerly Google Refine) is a free, open-source tool for working with messy data. It enables users to clean data, transform it between a variety of formats, extend it with web services, and link it to databases. This tool is available for Windows, Mac and Linux.

composedOf.label: Create project
composedOf.description:
## Step 1: Import your data

Upload your dataset into OpenRefine. You can import files from your computer in a variety of formats, including TSV, CSV, other *SV formats, Excel files (`.xls` and `.xlsx`), JSON, XML, RDF (as XML), and Google Data documents.  
Alternatively, you can paste your data directly using the **Clipboard** option.

## Step 2: Configure parsing options

Check that OpenRefine has parsed your data correctly before proceeding. In particular:

- Verify that column headers are correctly identified. If necessary, use **“Ignore first … lines”** or **“Parse next … lines as column headers”** to specify which rows should be treated as headers.
- Confirm that the character encoding is correct (UTF-8 usually works well).

## Step 3: Name your project, add tags if wanted and click on "Create project"

relatedItems.label: Cleaning Data with OpenRefine
relatedItems.description: This tutorial focuses on how scholars can diagnose and act upon the accuracy of data.

composedOf.label: Use facets and filters
composedOf.description:
To understand the contents of your dataset and identify messy or inconsistent data, you can use **facets** and **filters** on individual columns.

1. Click the drop-down arrow next to the column header you want to analyse.
2. Select **Facet** and choose the appropriate facet type based on the data in the column:
   - **Text facet** (recommended for text columns):  
     Displays all unique text values in the column and shows how often each value occurs.
   - **Numeric facet** (for columns containing numbers):  
     Allows you to explore value ranges and detect outliers.
   - **Timeline facet** (for date columns):  
     Visualises dates along a timeline and helps identify missing or inconsistent date values.

composedOf.label: Explore your data carefully
composedOf.description:
Before making any changes, take time to understand your dataset.

- Use **facets** and **filters** on each column to see which values occur and how often.
- Look for common problems such as:
  - Different spellings of the same value
  - Inconsistent capitalisation
  - Extra spaces before or after text
  - Empty or missing cells
- Values that appear only once are often good candidates for closer inspection.

composedOf.label: Make small manual corrections
composedOf.description:
If you notice only a few incorrect values:

- Hover over a cell and click **Edit**.
- Correct the value manually and click **Apply**.
- This method is useful for isolated errors but should be avoided for cleaning large numbers of cells.

composedOf.label: Remove extra spaces and normalise text
composedOf.description:
Many datasets contain unwanted spaces or inconsistent text formatting.

- Click the drop-down arrow next to the column you want to clean.
- Select **Edit cells → Common transforms**.
- Choose **Trim leading and trailing whitespace** to remove extra spaces.
- If needed, use **To lowercase** or **To uppercase** to make text consistent.

composedOf.label: Transform values using GREL
composedOf.description:
For more advanced or customised cleaning tasks, you can use **GREL (General Refine Expression Language)**. GREL allows you to transform values using simple expressions.

- Open the column menu and select **Edit cells → Transform**.
- In the expression box, write a GREL expression to modify the column values.
- The preview on the right shows how the transformation will affect your data before you apply it.

Common beginner-friendly examples include:
- `value.trim()` – removes extra spaces
- `value.toLowercase()` – converts text to lowercase
- `value.replace("old value","new value")` – replaces specific text
- `value.split(";")[0]` – extracts part of a value

> 💡 Tip: Always check the preview before clicking **OK**.

To learn more about GREL syntax and examples, see the official tutorial:  
👉 https://openrefine.org/docs/manual/grelfunctions

composedOf.label: Find and merge similar values using clustering
composedOf.description:
- Open a **Text facet** on the column.
- Click the **Cluster** button.
- Review the suggested clusters carefully.
- For each group, choose the correct or preferred form of the value.
- Click **Merge selected & re-cluster** to apply the changes.

> ⚠️ Always review clusters before merging to avoid combining values that should remain separate.

composedOf.label: Clean numeric and date columns
composedOf.description:
For columns containing numbers or dates:

- Use a **Numeric facet** to identify unusual values or outliers.
- Use a **Timeline facet** to check whether dates are missing, incomplete, or incorrectly formatted.
- If necessary, convert text to numbers or dates using **Edit cells → Transform**.

composedOf.label: Deal with blank or missing values
composedOf.description:
To identify empty cells:

- Open a **Facet → Customized facets → Facet by blank**.
- Decide how to handle missing values:
  - Leave them empty if the information is unavailable
  - Replace them with a standard value (e.g. “Unknown”)
  - Remove rows that do not contain enough information

composedOf.label: Remove unnecessary rows or columns
composedOf.description:
If your dataset contains irrelevant information:

- Use filters to select rows you want to remove.
- Choose **Edit rows → Remove matching rows**.
- To delete a column, open the column menu and select **Edit column → Remove this column**.

composedOf.label: Review and document your changes
composedOf.description:
OpenRefine keeps track of every action you perform.

- Open the **Undo / Redo** panel to review all cleaning steps.
- Use this panel to undo mistakes or understand how your data was transformed.
- This history can also be used to document your cleaning process for transparency and reproducibility.

composedOf.label: Export your cleaned data
composedOf.description:
Once you are satisfied with the results:

- Click **Export** in the top-right corner.
- Choose a suitable format (e.g. CSV or Excel).
- Save the cleaned dataset for further analysis or sharing.

relatedItems.label: What Can I Do With This Messy Spreadsheet? Converting from Excel Sheets to Fully Compliant EAD-XML files
relatedItems.description: Many Galleries, Libraries, Archives, and Museums (GLAMs) face difficulties sharing their collections metadata in standardised and sustainable ways, meaning that staff rely on more familiar general purpose office programs such as spreadsheets. However, while these tools offer a simple approach to data registration and digitisation they don’t allow for more advanced uses. label: Collaborative Digital Edition of a Musical Corpus
description: A project aims to do a digital edition of a musical corpus. The researchers need to be able to encode a broad range of musical documents in a machine-readable structure. The data to be encoded may include the musical content as provided by the composer (notes, pitches, durations, dynamics, etc.), information on the score (incipit, lyrics writer, etc.), information added by a performer when interpreting the content (timing, phrasing, various annotations, etc.), information on the visual appearance of the score (page layout, musical font, etc.) and analyses of the content in any of the other domains. The edition will be structured around a database in order to allow the users to explore it more easily. Furthermore, the project intends to be collaborative, which means it will offer anyone interested the possibility to contribute.

concept.label: Consortium-HN
concept.definition: The Consortiums-HN are networks of experts financed for 4 years by the IR* Huma-Num (HN), bringing together staff from French SSH research units and teams, with a variety of professions (researchers, engineers, archivists, documentalists, etc.) around common themes and/or objects for which they define shared digital procedures and standards (methods, tools, sharing of experiences). In connection with HN, they aim to create synergies within the SSH research communities to encourage their appropriation of digital tools and their insertion in Open Science, while responding to the FAIR principles.

relatedItems.label: Creation of a Digital Music Edition
relatedItems.description:
A digital edition encodes musical information as structured, machine-readable, and semantically rich data, a transformation that requires a series of methodological and technical decisions. This workflow addresses the full range of operations involved, including the choice of encoding format, the management of metadata, the establishment of relationships with sources, the integration of a critical apparatus, and the conditions for sustainable online publication.
It outlines the essential steps required to produce a scholarly digital music edition, from the initial scoping of the corpus to its long-term archiving and dissemination. Structured around the three pillars of digital editing—tools, content, and presentation—it is designed to ensure compliance with FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) principles throughout the entire lifecycle of the edition.

Developed from the Guide to Digital Music Editing produced by the Consortium-HN MUSICA within the French research infrastructure Huma-Num, this workflow also aligns with the requirements of the European ECHOES project (European Cloud for Heritage Open Science), which frames digital editions as components of digital twins integrating source digitization, musical encoding, and audio recording. It is intended for researchers, digital humanists, and engineers working in institutional contexts shaped by Open Access policies and European research funding frameworks.

relatedItems.label: Music Encoding Initiative from MusicXML
relatedItems.description: The Music Encoding Initiative is an open-source language to encode musical scores in a machine-readable structure. Its main strong point lies in the management of various metadata and its capacity to code the framework and the semantics of music works. In addition to these technical specificities, the MEI is perfectly proper for FAIR principles. In order to convert a MusicXML in MEI format, several ways are possible. This workflow aims to describe best practices, step by step, to preserve the initial file and to get a correct MEI. This workflow is suitable for both common Western notation and modern transcription of ancient works (Renaissance and Middle Ages).

It is developed at the Musicology Seminar Detmold/Paderborn, University of Paderborn (http://muwi-detmold-paderborn.de) as part of the german part of the research project "Digital Research Infrastructure for the Arts and Humanities" -- DARIAH-DE (http://de.dariah.eu).

relatedItems.label: MEI Score Editor --MEISE
relatedItems.description: The MEI Score Editor (MEISE) is an Eclipse-based client software for viewing and editing MEI-encoded music documents in CMN (Common Music Notation), facilitating proof reading as well as modifying and correcting MEI files. MEISE was designed to satisfy special requirements of research in musicology, currently unsupported by existing music notation software tools. MEISE should be used especially for working with MEI-data as a processing and editing tool, e.g. for creating variants, generating, completing and modifying MEI-files. As a key merit, MEISE gains of its homomorphic internal data structure to the MEI schema tree, allowing for native support for theoretically all MEI encoding principles. This allows for some unique features arising from the field of scholarly music edition, such as the encoding and visualization of variants of different musical sources in one digital MEI representation.

relatedItems.label: Omeka
relatedItems.description:
Omeka is a content management system designed for the display of library, museum, archives, and scholarly collections and exhibitions.

Omeka falls at a crossroads of Web Content Management, Collections Management, and Archival Digital Collections Systems. Omeka is designed with non-IT specialists in mind, allowing users to focus on content and interpretation rather than programming. It brings Web 2.0 technologies and approaches to academic and cultural websites to foster user interaction and participation. It makes top-shelf design easy with a simple and flexible templating system. Its robust open-source developer and user communities underwrite Omeka's stability and sustainability.

Omeka allows users to publish cultural heritage objects, extend its functionality with themes and plugins, and curate online exhibits with digital objects.

relatedItems.label: MerMEId. Tool for editing MEI header data
relatedItems.description:
MerMEId is superseded by MerMEId MeLODy.

MerMEId is a system for the editing, handling, and (pre-)viewing of music metadata, based on the the Music Encoding Initiative (MEI) XML schema. As of April 2017 MerMEId supports MEI 3.0.0. MerMEId is developed at the Danish Centre for Music Editing (DCM) both for the production of thematic catalogues of works and for organizing source- and work-related information during the preparation of scholarly editions of music.

relatedItems.label: MerMEId MeLODy
relatedItems.description:
MerMEId MeLODy is an open-source, browser-based metadata editor designed specifically for creating well-formed MEI (Music Encoding Initiative) metadata for thematic work and source catalogues. It is the successor to MerMEId, the established metadata editor for thematic work catalogues originally developed at the Danish Centre for Music Editing.

The editor produces complex RDF/Turtle output that directly cooperates with MEI structures to ensure standards-compliant metadata. The RDF data model is precisely aligned with the MEI Schema (v5.1) and the FRBR (Functional Requirements for Bibliographic Records) conceptual model, so all structured metadata can be reliably transformed into MEI/XML for use in MEI-based workflows, research infrastructure, and digital editions. It is designed for musicologists, music librarians, and developers who need to create structured, interoperable, and FAIR-compliant metadata for musical works, sources, persons or events.

relatedItems.label: Gesualdo Online
relatedItems.description: The Gesualdo Online project, developed by the Programme Ricercar at the Centre for Renaissance Studies in Tours, represents an innovative way to conceive and to publish a musical edition. Through the application of new web technologies to musicology, in particular in the domain of "dynamic" editions, the project allows musicologists and editors to re-think traditional editorial praxis. The Gesualdo Online Project at the Center for Renaissance Studies invites those in the musicological and musical community interested in Gesualdo's music to their create their own user account in the project website and to contribute to this online edition.

relatedItems.label: Lost Voices: The Chansons of Nicolas Du Chemin
relatedItems.description:
The Lost Voices project explores a little-studied repertory of sixteen sets of French polyphonic songs published in Paris by Nicolas Du Chemin between 1549 and 1568. Digital technologies are put to work in the service of these books in ways that will engender a broader discussion about style and structure in the sixteenth-century chanson.

This project features digital facsimiles of the set, freely available for display and download; complete modern editions of all the chansons, engraved as high quality PDF files; essays about the books, the music, and their historical context; and a searchable database of analytic observations about the music.

The project also allows users to contribute reconstructions of incomplete chansons (over 100 of them, to date). These are also available for dynamic display and comparison. All of these materials are combined in an innovative browser-based interface that permits users to search through the repertory, viewing (and collecting) musical excerpts of interest.

The MEI standard is a central resource for the project, serving as a medium of exchange between our original transcriptions (in Sibelius) and our dynamic editions (in any browser, using VexFlow). In addition, MEI is used to keep track of variant readings, emendations, and reconstructed voice parts contributed by different authors and editors. Various workflows and software tools have been developed that allow one to move back and forth among the transcriptions, MEI files, and dynamic renderings using Django (CMS), SOLR, and related technologies. All work is open-source, and available for re-use.

The Lost Voices Project. Companion resource to Les livres de Chansons Nouvelles de Nicolas Du Chemin (1549--1568), hosted by the Centre d'Études Supérieures de la Renaissance in Tours, France

Verovio is written in standard 2020 C++ and can be compiled as a standalone command-line tool, used as a compiled music-rendering library for applications (Qt, python), or compiled into Javascript using the Emscripten LLVM-to-JavaScript compiler. Check out the JavaScript toolkit version of verovio running in the MEI Viewer as well as the app or tutorials for web integration and user interaction.

relatedItems.label: GioQoso, Gestion de la Qualité des partitions musicales ouvertes
relatedItems.description:
A French language resource that helps researchers digitize musical partitions 

L'objectif de GioQoso est l'élaboration de méthodes et outils de gestion de la qualité des données dans des corpus collaboratifs de partitions musicales numérisées. Les verrous scientifiques à lever concernent (1) la définition et la mesure de la qualité de ce type particulier de données, (2) la prise en compte de la qualité dans les processus (incluant notamment la recherche et la publication) et (3) la mise au point d'une méthodologie générale pour la gestion de la qualité dans les bases documentaires en SHS. Les compétences scientifiques mobilisées concernent les domaines de recherche de la musicologie, de la gestion de données volumineuses et des méthodes de suivi et de contrôle de la qualité dans les systèmes d'information. Le projet comprend une validation de la méthodologie proposée consistant à appliquer des procédures de mesure, d'évaluation et de prise en compte de la qualité dans l'une des principales bibliothèques numériques s'appuyant sur les principes de la Music Encoding Initiative (MEI). Nous ambitionnons un impact potentiel important sur la constitution en pleine émergence de larges corpus de musique notée, et au-delà, sur les bases documentaires patrimoniales SHS.

label: Collaborative Multilingual Translation Workflow for a Hackathon
description: This workflow defines a structured and reproducible procedure for conducting a collaborative multilingual translation and review exercise in hackathon format. The primary use case is the translation and review of GoTriple ontology labels (controlled vocabularies), while simultaneously assessing the MONDAECUS platform under real operational conditions. The workflow is designed to be publishable as a generic methodological reference for collaborative translation exercises on demand.

relatedItems.label: GoTriple Discovery Platform
relatedItems.description: The GoTriple platform is an innovative multilingual and multicultural discovery solution for the social sciences and humanities (SSH). It will provide a single access point that allows researchers to explore, find, access and reuse materials such as literature, data, projects and researcher profiles at a European scale. Conceived as an entry point to the EOSC, it is one of the dedicated services of OPERAS, the Research Infrastructure supporting Open Scholarly Communication in the SSH in the European Research Area.

composedOf.label: 1. Define strategic translation scope and infrastructure goals
2. Deliver platform training and prepare operational documents
composedOf.description:
Operational preparation of the hackathon through a single online training session composed of two complementary training moments, together with the preparation of supporting documents required for the smooth execution and evaluation of the translation exercise.
Training moment 1 – Discovery platform familiarisation:
Participants are introduced to GoTriple with the aim of visualising how selected ontology terms are used within the platform. Rather than providing exhaustive instruction, this moment enables participants to explore the platform autonomously, observe how ontology elements appear in practice (e.g. in discovery, filtering, and navigation), and gain a clearer understanding of the platform’s logic and functionalities through direct interaction.
Training moment 2 – Collaborative translation platform onboarding:
In the same online session, participants receive a general presentation of MONDAECUS, covering its basic features and workflows. This onboarding allows users to access the platform in advance of the hackathon, become familiar with its interface, and understand how it will be used during the translation activity.
In parallel, this step includes the preparation of operational support documents, namely:
	•	a MONDAECUS user guide, tailored to the specific needs and practical requirements of this translation exercise;
	•	a checklist for moderators, used to verify that all technical and procedural aspects are operational, to monitor translation workflows, and to support participants during the hackathon;
	•	a participant survey, designed to collect feedback on both the platform and the translation exercise, supporting later evaluation and refinement.
These elements ensure that both participants and moderators are adequately prepared, and that the hackathon is supported by clear procedures and evaluation mechanisms.

composedOf.label: 4. Carry out collaborative translation and moderation
composedOf.description:
Execution phase of the hackathon, where the collaborative translation exercise is carried out using the validated materials, defined roles, and agreed procedures.
Participants translate the finalised list of terms within the collaborative translation platform (e.g. MONDAECUS), following the guidelines circulated in previous steps. Translation work is performed in a hybrid format, combining online participation with in-person collaboration, while maintaining consistent workflows across both modalities.
Translators focus on producing translations for the assigned terms, documenting uncertainties, ambiguities, or alternative renderings when relevant.
Moderators oversee the process, ensuring that procedures are followed, supporting participants, and addressing technical or organisational issues as they arise.
Moderator-translators combine both roles, contributing to translation while facilitating coordination and clarification, particularly in mixed or distributed working groups.
Throughout the exercise, moderators:
	•	monitor progress and workflow consistency;
	•	use the checklist to verify that operational conditions are met;
	•	support communication between online and in-person participants;
	•	document issues, observations, and procedural deviations for later assessment.
Translations are produced with attention to how terms are used within the discovery platform (e.g. GoTriple), ensuring that outputs are suitable for later integration and evaluation.

label: Collaborative Reusable Map Annotation
description:
Historical maps are valuable resources for humanities research, offering insights into past landscapes and patterns of human activity. Maps are more than images; they represent spatial and cultural relationships that may be anchored to the physical world, and often embed narratives of power, identity, and change, such as shifts in place names or symbolic representations. They vary widely in form, type, content, level of detail, and granularity of the information they present. At the same time they are material objects, cultural artifacts, with distinct physical characteristics and complex biographies of their own. Historical maps also come with challenges: they often lack modern geographic precision, may contain outdated or biased perspectives (which are nonetheless of historical significance), or show signs of physical wear, among other issues. Moreover, access to the information they contain is often limited, as searching through map collection catalogues typically relies on record metadata (i.e., basic information, such as title, creator, or date) and not the full content of the map.
Map annotation provides a means to address these issues by enabling scholars to encode features, comment on the content, link place names to gazetteers or other authority files, transcribe text on maps, document historical or cartographic context, etc. Apart from supporting scholarly analysis, this process can transform static maps into searchable and machine-readable resources, by enriching the map metadata and allowing text search indices (Rainer et al. 2019). 
Developed within the ATRIUM project, this workflow supports collaborative annotation and geo-tagging of historical maps, transforming them into rich multilayer resources. It addresses both technical interoperability and data reusability, with outcomes that can enhance catalog records, improve search capabilities, feed into analytical pipelines, and support data visualizations, or even enable the creation of critical editions of maps. While primarily tested in [Recogito Studio](https://recogitostudio.org/), the workflow is designed as tool-agnostic, ensuring flexibility and reusability across different tools, projects and teams. Its steps are not strictly linear; annotation is an iterative process and teams may revisit earlier phases (e.g., revising vocabularies during annotation) or run tasks in parallel or in alternation (e.g., linking to vocabularies and gazetteers). This iterative design allows teams to adapt to evolving insights and technical constraints. 
Note: This workflow is intended for manual annotation.

**References:**
- Reckziegel, M., Wrisley, D. J., Hixson, T. W., & Jänicke, S. (2021). Visual exploration of historical maps, *Digital Scholarship in the Humanities*, 36 (Supplement_2), ii251–ii272, https://doi.org/10.1093/llc/fqaa059 
- Rainer, S., Vitale, V., Kahn, R., Barker, E. & Isaksen, L. (2019). Revisiting Linking Early Geospatial Documents with Recogito, *e-Perimetron* 14 (3), 152–63, https://www.e-perimetron.org/Vol_14_3/Simon_et_al.pdf

relatedItems.label: Controlled Vocabulary for Annotation of Historical Maps
relatedItems.description:
Historical maps contain many different kinds of information that are not always captured by catalogue metadata alone. Place names, symbols, legends, inscriptions, marginal notes, cartouches, views, tables, and other visual or textual elements may all be relevant for research, but they are often difficult to search, compare, or reuse unless they are described in a consistent way.

Annotation workflows make it possible to record information directly on or in relation to the map. Yet collaborative annotation also creates a practical problem: different annotators may use different words for similar features, describe them at different levels of detail, or record information such as certainty, identification status, and review status in inconsistent ways. Controlled vocabularies support consistency in annotation across annotators, maps, and use contexts by standardising what can be expressed, how it should be expressed, and how it should be applied through term sets, definitions, scope notes, and usage constraints.

This workflow provides a method for creating and maintaining controlled vocabularies for historical map annotation. It supports teams in defining the purpose and scope of the vocabulary, modelling facets and term families, deciding when to use external vocabularies or local terms, building a documented term list, testing it through annotation, and preparing it for governance, maintenance, and release.

Developed within the ATRIUM project, the workflow is designed to work together with the Collaborative Reusable Map Annotation Workflow, while focusing specifically on the vocabulary layer of the annotation process. Its output is a documented and versioned vocabulary resource that can be used during annotation and prepared for reuse beyond a single project or tool. Depending on the project’s aims, capacity, and publication strategy, the vocabulary may be kept for internal project use, published as a documented vocabulary package, or released as a semantic vocabulary using standards such as Simple Knowledge Organization System (SKOS). In this way, the workflow supports more consistent annotation practice, clearer documentation, and, where appropriate, FAIR oriented and semantically interoperable data outputs.

relatedItems.label: Define vocabulary purpose, scope, and requirements
relatedItems.description:
This step defines why the vocabulary is needed and what it should support. It translates the needs of the parent workflow, the *Collaborative Reusable Map Annotation Workflow*, into an initial vocabulary plan by identifying which parts of the annotation process require controlled vocabulary support.

The vocabulary is not designed in the abstract. It is derived from the annotation tasks, map features, and coordination needs defined in the parent workflow, such as distinguishing inscriptions, legend-based symbols, paratextual elements, interpretive comments, certainty levels, or review categories.

**Input**: Collaborative Reusable Map Annotation Workflow, research goals, selected historical maps, annotation targets, annotation schema, intended annotation environment, annotator roles, review needs, and sample map content.

**Main actions**: 
1. Review the Collaborative Reusable Map Annotation Workflow and identify where controlled vocabulary support is needed. 
2. Define the annotation facets[^1]  that require controlled terms, such as inscription function, legend category, paratext object type, commentary category, certainty, identification status, period, or place reference. For each facet, identify the corresponding vocabulary term set needed to support annotation. 
3. Distinguish between terms that describe map content and terms that support collaborative annotation practice, such as certainty levels, review categories, or quality control flags. 
4. Define scope boundaries, identify areas where external vocabularies or authorities may be relevant, and set initial granularity, user, and project constraints.

**Output**: Vocabulary Design Brief, including the initial list of required annotation facets and term sets, scope statement, granularity guidelines, and a short note explaining how the vocabulary supports the Collaborative Reusable Map Annotation Workflow.

**Format**: Short text document, Markdown/README section, DOCX/PDF, or structured planning table.

[^1]: **Terminology**: In this workflow, a facet is an annotation dimension or property that needs controlled description, such as inscription function, certainty, identification status, period, or place reference. A vocabulary term set is the list or structured set of controlled terms used for that facet. The term scheme is reserved for more formally organised vocabularies, such as a Simple Knowledge Organization System (SKOS) ConceptScheme.

composedOf.label: Acquire data
composedOf.description:
Before any annotation or other processing activity can take place, it is essential to identify and secure access to suitable digitized historical maps, ensuring the relevance, quality, and usability of the data. The following steps are recommended:
- Evaluate sources: Assess the scholarly value of the maps and verify that the file formats and usage licenses align with your project’s technical and legal requirements.
- Retrieve data:
  - For IIIF-compatible maps — obtain IIIF manifest URLs from trusted digital repositories (for a list of IIIF map collections see [IIIF Map Collections GitHub repository](https://github.com/allmaps/iiif-map-collections) and [Navigating the IIIF Landscape blog post](https://liiive.now/blog/2025-02-navigating-the-iiif-landscape/)).
  - For non-IIIF images — download high-resolution files directly from institutional portals or archival databases.
  - For undigitized materials — coordinate with holding institutions (libraries, museums, archives) to request digitization, ensuring the Open Access compliance of the digitized files.
- Retrieve metadata: Collect the metadata of each map, in support of interoperability.

composedOf.label: Assess georeferencing feasibility
composedOf.description:
Identifying control points on a map and aligning them with real-world geographic coordinates can be considered a form of (geographic) annotation (Reckziegel et al. 2021). In this step, the idea is to determine whether the map can be accurately georeferenced (assigned real-world coordinates) or georectified (geometrically adjusted to correct distortions and aligned with a spatial reference system). Consider that early modern maps — created before the adoption of precise topographic survey techniques — and certain categories (e.g., imaginary maps) often lack geospatial accuracy and may be unsuitable for full georeferencing or georectification.
- Check for existing georeference/georectification: To avoid duplication of effort, determine if the map is already georeferenced or georectified (e.g., in [Allmaps Explore](https://dev.explore.allmaps.org/), [MapWarper](https://mapwarper.net/maps?show_warped=1), [OldMapsOnline](https://www.oldmapsonline.org/)) and whether it can be exported in the desired format.
- Review metadata: Assess whether the map’s creation date, creator, or stated purpose points to geographic precision. For example, maps created after the adoption of standardized surveying techniques, especially by official agencies or trained cartographers, are generally more accurate. The map’s intended purpose can also indicate its precision, e.g., cadastral or administrative maps are typically reliable, while illustrative or decorative maps tend to be less so.
- Assess image quality: Check for damage (e.g., tears, fading) that could obstruct analysis. Verify scale, resolution and legibility (e.g., text labels) for Ground Control Point placement.
- Assess feasibility: Determine whether the map is schematic (e.g., symbolic) vs. cartographically precise. Look for distortions caused by historical projection methods or artistic license.
- Check for ground control points: Identify recognizable landmarks (e.g., coastlines, rivers, towns) that match modern or historical basemaps. Evaluate whether the map includes a coordinate system or scale bar.

**Decision**: If the assessment determines that the map can be georeferenced or georectified (and has not already been), proceed to the **Run Georeferencing Workflow** step [workflow currently under development]; otherwise, skip this step.

composedOf.label: Run Georeferencing Workflow
composedOf.description: If the map is suitable for georeferencing or georectification, this step transforms it from a static image into geospatial data, resulting in a raster that can be used as a basemap layer for analysis and visualization. Execute the georeferencing workflow and export the output in a supported format (e.g., XYZ tiles), depending on the tool you plan to use for annotation (see Step 5). [Workflow currently under development. More elaborate description will be delivered soon]

composedOf.label: Define goals and annotation schema
composedOf.description:
What is the purpose of annotation, which features will be annotated, and how will this be done? Clarifying these questions is essential to ensuring that the annotation process is systematic and aligned with the project’s broader research goals. A well-defined annotation schema and clear guidelines help maintain consistency across annotators, support interoperability, and enable meaningful analysis of the outputs. This step is also closely tied to the tools selected, as their capabilities will shape the methodology and how guidelines are applied in practice. The output of this step should be documents capturing the decisions and providing guidelines about following aspects:
- Define scope and outputs: Determine the primary objectives (e.g., addressing a specific research question) and specify the intended outputs (e.g., an index of place names, enriched metadata, data for further analysis and visualization, etc.). Identify and categorize features to annotate, such as: places (e.g., cities, rivers, regions); objects (e.g., ships, fortifications, symbols); historical events (e.g. battles, migrations, treaties); comments (e.g., descriptions, marginalia, creator biases, errors, historical context), elements of cartography (e.g., legend, cartouche, compass rose), physical and material properties of the map as artifact (e.g., damage, repairs), etc.
- Establish annotation rules, e.g., define how to handle temporal or multilingual name variants.
- Define reference resources: Determine whether you will link to authority files (e.g., controlled vocabularies or gazetteers), depending on the type of map(s) and the scope of annotation. It is also important to assess if and which tools can support this.
- Set critical analysis protocols: Decide on bias and error documentation (e.g., cartographic distortions, omissions, or ideological framing) and contextual linking (e.g., connecting annotations to primary sources or historiographical debates).
- Manage uncertainty and ambiguity: Decide on how to handle uncertainty and ambiguity, and examine flagging such elements with confidence levels. Decide on debate tracking to document team disagreements and resolutions.
- Define collaboration roles: Assign specific roles (e.g., annotators, validators) and clearly outline responsibilities–such as transcription, gazetteer linking, tagging, commenting, cross-checking annotations against external sources, and resolving conflicts (e.g., place-name disputes) using predefined rules (e.g., “prioritize contemporary place names”). Establish a suitable workflow for collaboration. Keep in mind that this process is closely tied to the tool selected (see Step 5), as some platforms require at least certain roles to be explicitly assigned.

composedOf.label: Choose tool(s)
composedOf.description:
Selecting the right tool is a critical step, as it shapes the entire annotation workflow, from data input and collaboration to output formats and interoperability. The choice should be guided by your project’s goals, technical requirements, and the skills of your team. 
- Assess tool compatibility: Compare key tools according to specific requirements. Prioritize tools that natively integrate IIIF manifests and linking with gazetteers and other authority files, support collaborative workflows, comply with standards (e.g., the [Web Annotation Data Model](https://www.w3.org/TR/annotation-model/)), and ensure output interoperability, such as [Recogito Studio](https://recogitostudio.org/). Additional key considerations are: cost and access, training needs and scalability.
- Assess tool extensibility: Evaluate whether the tool allows for customization or expansion through additional services, plugins, APIs, etc. This can be important for adapting the platform to specialized needs, such as gazetteer linking.
- Integrate specialized tools as needed: E.g., if the labels on the map are in an alphabet different from Latin, you might consider using a tool or service for text transliteration/romanization, such as the [Transliteration of Greek characters into Latin](https://transliteration.nlg.gr/?lang=en) tool of the National Library of Greece.

composedOf.label: Set up the tool(s)
composedOf.description:
Once you have selected the appropriate tools, it is important to set up the environment that will support effective collaboration, data management, and workflow integration throughout the project. Depending on whether you can have access to an already existing instance of the chosen platform or you need to install the software to your own server (and configure the necessary applications), you might need access to servers and ideally the support of a capable server administrator.
- Set up a collaborative workspace: Establish a shared workspace for coordination, data storage, and version control to streamline teamwork and maintain transparency.
- Finalize tool stack/pipeline: Confirm the tools to be used and how they will interact within your workflow.
- Add plugins if needed: Install any extensions or add-ons required for enhanced functionality, e.g., the [GeoTagger](https://github.com/recogito/plugin-geotagging) plugin for RecogitoStudio.
- Document the tool setup to support reproducibility and long-term maintenance.

relatedItems.label: Recogito Studio
relatedItems.description: An Extensible Platform for Collaborative, Standards-Based Annotation of TEI Text, IIIF Images, and PDFs. Modern, Open Source, and Easy to Use.

composedOf.label: Configure the annotation tool
composedOf.description:
With the environment set up, you can now configure the annotation tool to align with the project’s collaborative structure, research goals and annotation schema. Naturally, the configuration is directly linked to the selected tool. For the purposes of this workflow, the steps outlined are based on the [Recogito Studio](https://recogitostudio.org/) platform.
- Implement collaboration roles and access according to your annotation schema and the roles explicitly assigned by the tool.
- Choose/import basemap layer: If the map(s) have been georeferenced or georectified (see Step 3), the output could be imported and used as a basemap layer in the GeoTagger plugin of the annotation tool.   
- Set the annotation vocabulary: Determine whether an annotation vocabulary that fits your purposes already exists. If a suitable vocabulary is available, select it or import it into the annotation tool. If not, **run the Vocabulary Creation Workflow** [workflow currently under development — more elaborate description will be delivered soon] and develop a custom vocabulary that reflects your project’s needs, considering the integration or extension of domain-specific ontologies (e.g., [CIDOC CRM](https://cidoc-crm.org/)) or thesauri (e.g., [Getty AAT](https://www.getty.edu/research/tools/vocabularies/aat/)). Once the new vocabulary is defined, import it into the annotation platform. In all cases, consider the desired level of annotation granularity (as defined in your annotation schema) as well as interoperability with other datasets and systems. 
- Set gazetteer(s) for geo-tagging: Determine whether a suitable gazetteer already exists for your project’s geographical and historical context, as defined in your annotation schema (e.g., [Pleiades](https://pleiades.stoa.org/) for ancient places, [World Historical Gazetteer](https://whgazetteer.org/) for historical places, [GeoNames](https://www.geonames.org/) for modern locations, or even [Wikidata](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:Main_Page)). If no appropriate gazetteer exists, or if existing gazetteers only partially cover your needs, consider seeking support — for example, from the [World Historical Gazetteer](https://whgazetteer.org/) team or the [Pelagios Gazetteer Activity](https://pelagios.org/activities/gazetteers/). If these options are not applicable, you may need to compile or create a custom gazetteer, tailored to your project needs. In that case, run the **Gazetteer Creation Workflow** [workflow currently under development — more elaborate description will be delivered soon] and once finalized, import it in the appropriate format into the annotation environment.

relatedItems.label: Finding Places in Text with the World Historical Gazetteer
relatedItems.description: Researchers often need to be able to search a corpus of texts for a defined list of terms and historians are often interested in certain places named in a text or texts. This lesson details how to programmatically search documents for a list of terms, including place names and then how to obtain coordinates and map historical place names with the World Historical Gazetteer.

relatedItems.label: Working with Named Places: How and Why to Build a Gazetteer
relatedItems.description: A digital gazetteer records information associated with specific places. This lesson teaches you how to create a gazetteer from a historical text, using the Linked Places Delimited (LP-TSV) format.

relatedItems.label: GeoNames
relatedItems.description:
A global geographical database that may be used to identify and tag all references to location. The database contains over 8 million entries, each of which possesses a geographic name (in various languages), latitude, longitude, elevation, population, administrative subdivision and postal codes and information on unique features.

Features:

Built upon web service, enabling transparent look-up and use of content through third-party tools and sites

Browse by geographic location, country name, size of geographic region and other categories.

Full text search support





Extensible, enabling users to expand existing information or contribute new content

Support for the World Geodetic System 1984 (WGS84) co-ordinate system

relatedItems.label: Pleiades: A community-built gazetteer and graph of ancient places
relatedItems.description: Pleiades gives scholars, students, and enthusiasts worldwide the ability to use, create, and share historical geographic information about the ancient world in digital form.

composedOf.label: Import image data
composedOf.description: Once the annotation environment is set up and while tool configuration is underway, you can bring in the map content that will be annotated (see Step 1). Import or upload the digitized images of the maps (in the supported formats) or load the IIIF manifests in the annotation tool. Also don’t forget to add the associated metadata.

composedOf.label: Annotate the map(s)
composedOf.description:
This is the core task of the workflow. It involves enriching the map(s) with structured information based on your annotation schema and the established guidelines (see Step 4) . Annotations may range from simple tags to complex data entries and semantic links (e.g., semantic annotation of places — alignment to URI-based gazetteers — for linking data). Because humanities data is inherently complex, full standardization of the annotation process may not always be possible. However, following your predefined guidelines will help ensure the greatest possible consistency, accuracy, and scholarly value across all annotations. 
- Apply the annotation schema and guidelines: Use the structure and categories defined in your annotation schema to guide the annotation process, in alignment with the collaboration roles assigned to the contributors. This includes identifying the types of features to annotate, and following any critical analysis protocols and rules you established.
- Transcribe text (if needed): If you annotate text on maps (e.g., placenames) you may  transcribe the text to make it machine-readable and searchable. While transcribing, maintain fidelity to the original spelling and script, but consider adding normalized or transliterated forms where needed.
- Add comments and contextual notes: Depending on the goals of your project and your annotation schema, you may include interpretative notes, observations, descriptions or comments that e.g., provide context, document uncertainties, or highlight issues such as creator bias, ideological framing, or inconsistencies.
- Link to vocabulary(-ies): Create structured data by tagging the content you annotate with terms from the vocabulary you have selected or created (see Step 7). Ensure consistent use of terminology across the team and follow your project's agreed rules for vocabulary usage. While new tagging terms may be introduced as the annotation progresses, any additions should be agreed upon by the team and incorporated systematically into the vocabulary.  
- Link to gazetteer(s): Connect place references to gazetteers to geo-annotate map content. Make sure the appropriate place is selected, keeping in mind that historical maps may refer to places using outdated or multilingual names, requiring careful cross-checking. Try to maintain a consistent and context-sensitive approach to geo-tagging. When necessary, alternate between multiple gazetteers to ensure coverage and accuracy. If a match cannot be found, flag the place for later review or custom gazetteer entry.

concept.label: Transcribing
concept.definition: transcribing describes  the activity of creating a representation of a manuscript or of audio or video recordings. The representation is generally textual for the verbal aspects of recordings and structured for example by speech turns. It can also contain multimodal information like gestures or events and multimedia information like time synchronization and relation to media files.

composedOf.label: Review and refine
composedOf.description: As the annotation progresses, it is important to evaluate the process and review the results, making any necessary adjustments. This may include assessing the quality and consistency of annotations, addressing unexpected annotation cases, resolving ambiguities, refining the annotation schema, vocabulary, and gazetteer links, and informing the guidelines. Keep in mind that this is an iterative process and you may need to alternate between the annotation and reviewing steps several times, until you are satisfied with the results and you can finalize and export your annotations. This step is also closely linked to the collaboration roles assigned within the team (see Step 4).

concept.label: Improving
concept.definition: process of a thing moving from one state to another that is considered to be better, usually through some action intended to bring about that better state (Wikidata contributors, "Q21255975," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q21255975&oldid=1264546813 (accessed September 4, 2020).

composedOf.label: Export
composedOf.description: Once all annotations have been reviewed and finalized, export the annotated data in appropriate formats/protocols for your intended use (e.g., visualization, analysis, publication, etc.). Naturally, the available export formats depend on the tool you have chosen. Since annotations may form a potentially complex dataset, exporting the data in multiple formats and complying with standards, such as the [Web Annotation Data Model](https://www.w3.org/TR/annotation-model/), is the optimum and should have been a criterion for the selection of the annotation tool. If the desired format is not directly supported, consider converting the output using appropriate transformation tools or scripts. Similarly, the structure of the exported data may need some refinement or normalization and you may need to further process your exported data using tools such as [OpenRefine](https://openrefine.org/), for example. If the annotation tool you are using includes built-in sharing or publishing capabilities, and depending on the goals of your project, you may want to skip this step and proceed directly to the next one (**Share/publish data**).

composedOf.label: Share/publish data
composedOf.description: You may now proceed to share or publish the annotated data. Before making the data publicly available, ensure that you comply with any necessary licensing or permissions. Depending on your goals, you may share the data to initiate a new workflow, for example to conduct further analysis (e.g., in a GIS tool) or visualization (see **Interactive Visualization Workflow**) [workflow currently under development; will be linked later]. You can also deposit or publish your dataset and research outputs in a suitable/trusted repository, such as institutional repositories or [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/), to ensure long-term accessibility, reusability, and preservation.

label: Collaborative Video Annotation with Celluloid
description: Celluloid Video Annotation Plateform is part of CANEVAS Huma-Num Consortium for the ANnotation, Analysis and Archiving of Video applied to Scientific Activities which supports research in Social Sciences and Humanities mobilizing video corpora on the following topics: annotating, commenting, analyzing, searching, sharing or archiving video. Members of the consortium contribute to the development of standards (FAIR), best practices and tools dedicated to the disciplines concerned: Media Studies, Sociology, Education, History, Film Studies and Theatre Studies.

relatedItems.description: A webservice to annotate, comment and analyze audiovisual content (movies, series, TV shows or your own videos – interviews, ethnographic documentary…), alone or as a team

composedOf.label: Opening Remarks
composedOf.description: Celluloid is a web platform that accompanies and supports the collaborative research uses of online video. The service promotes interactions between researchers through the practice of collaborative annotation. It allows them to develop the observation and the analysis of video contents ( movies, reports, conferences, online courses...).

relatedItems.label: Les outils d’annotation vidéo pour la recherche
relatedItems.description:
White paper, drafted by the French Consortium-HN Canevas, that examines and compares research tools for video annotation. 

Les Humanités Numériques portent leur attention sur différents types de corpus textuels et de jeux de données. Pour autant, les cultures numériques se façonnent aussi en dehors du livre et de l’écrit. L’un des enjeux fondamentaux pour ce champ émergent réside dans le traitement de corpus d’images, et notamment d’images animées. En effet, grâce aux outils numériques, il est de plus en plus facile de produire et de regarder des vidéos. Comment les chercheurs peuvent-ils concrètement investiguer, traiter, catégoriser, analyser cette profusion inédite d’images ? Nous nous concentrons ici sur la question de l’annotation. L’une des pratiques fondatrices du travail de recherche, on le sait, réside dans l’annotation de matériaux. Annoter un texte est une pratique aussi vieille que l’écrit lui-même et démultipliée par les possibilités du numérique. En revanche, annoter un film, en particulier à des fins de recherche, est resté jusqu’à une période récente une opération complexe. Cet article présente et analyse les usages et les nouveaux outils numériques qui permettent de travailler avec la vidéo et de l’annoter.

composedOf.label: Define the framework of a collaborative work around video with Celluloid
composedOf.description: After logging in, a user creates a project by giving it a title and setting research goals. It includes the URL of the video that will be streamed in Celluloid, as well as descriptive data. He chooses to make the project visible or not on the Celluloid platform (to give it media coverage, to inspire other users, etc.).

composedOf.label: Create a Peertube instance to host your video materials
composedOf.description: PeerTube is the free and decentralized video platforms. Anyone with a modicum of technical skills can host a PeerTube server, aka an instance. Each instance hosts its users and their videos. In this way, every instance is created, moderated and maintained independently by various administrators. You can still watch from your account videos hosted by other instances though if the administrator of your instance had previously connected it with other instances.

composedOf.label: Share the project with a group of researchers

composedOf.description: Once contributors are connected, they can create annotations as comments, descriptions or questions. label: Controlled Vocabulary for Annotation of Historical Maps
description:
Historical maps contain many different kinds of information that are not always captured by catalogue metadata alone. Place names, symbols, legends, inscriptions, marginal notes, cartouches, views, tables, and other visual or textual elements may all be relevant for research, but they are often difficult to search, compare, or reuse unless they are described in a consistent way.

Annotation workflows make it possible to record information directly on or in relation to the map. Yet collaborative annotation also creates a practical problem: different annotators may use different words for similar features, describe them at different levels of detail, or record information such as certainty, identification status, and review status in inconsistent ways. Controlled vocabularies support consistency in annotation across annotators, maps, and use contexts by standardising what can be expressed, how it should be expressed, and how it should be applied through term sets, definitions, scope notes, and usage constraints.

This workflow provides a method for creating and maintaining controlled vocabularies for historical map annotation. It supports teams in defining the purpose and scope of the vocabulary, modelling facets and term families, deciding when to use external vocabularies or local terms, building a documented term list, testing it through annotation, and preparing it for governance, maintenance, and release.

Developed within the ATRIUM project, the workflow is designed to work together with the Collaborative Reusable Map Annotation Workflow, while focusing specifically on the vocabulary layer of the annotation process. Its output is a documented and versioned vocabulary resource that can be used during annotation and prepared for reuse beyond a single project or tool. Depending on the project’s aims, capacity, and publication strategy, the vocabulary may be kept for internal project use, published as a documented vocabulary package, or released as a semantic vocabulary using standards such as Simple Knowledge Organization System (SKOS). In this way, the workflow supports more consistent annotation practice, clearer documentation, and, where appropriate, FAIR oriented and semantically interoperable data outputs.

relatedItems.label: Collaborative Reusable Map Annotation
relatedItems.description:
Historical maps are valuable resources for humanities research, offering insights into past landscapes and patterns of human activity. Maps are more than images; they represent spatial and cultural relationships that may be anchored to the physical world, and often embed narratives of power, identity, and change, such as shifts in place names or symbolic representations. They vary widely in form, type, content, level of detail, and granularity of the information they present. At the same time they are material objects, cultural artifacts, with distinct physical characteristics and complex biographies of their own. Historical maps also come with challenges: they often lack modern geographic precision, may contain outdated or biased perspectives (which are nonetheless of historical significance), or show signs of physical wear, among other issues. Moreover, access to the information they contain is often limited, as searching through map collection catalogues typically relies on record metadata (i.e., basic information, such as title, creator, or date) and not the full content of the map.
Map annotation provides a means to address these issues by enabling scholars to encode features, comment on the content, link place names to gazetteers or other authority files, transcribe text on maps, document historical or cartographic context, etc. Apart from supporting scholarly analysis, this process can transform static maps into searchable and machine-readable resources, by enriching the map metadata and allowing text search indices (Rainer et al. 2019). 
Developed within the ATRIUM project, this workflow supports collaborative annotation and geo-tagging of historical maps, transforming them into rich multilayer resources. It addresses both technical interoperability and data reusability, with outcomes that can enhance catalog records, improve search capabilities, feed into analytical pipelines, and support data visualizations, or even enable the creation of critical editions of maps. While primarily tested in [Recogito Studio](https://recogitostudio.org/), the workflow is designed as tool-agnostic, ensuring flexibility and reusability across different tools, projects and teams. Its steps are not strictly linear; annotation is an iterative process and teams may revisit earlier phases (e.g., revising vocabularies during annotation) or run tasks in parallel or in alternation (e.g., linking to vocabularies and gazetteers). This iterative design allows teams to adapt to evolving insights and technical constraints. 
Note: This workflow is intended for manual annotation.

**References:**
- Reckziegel, M., Wrisley, D. J., Hixson, T. W., & Jänicke, S. (2021). Visual exploration of historical maps, *Digital Scholarship in the Humanities*, 36 (Supplement_2), ii251–ii272, https://doi.org/10.1093/llc/fqaa059 
- Rainer, S., Vitale, V., Kahn, R., Barker, E. & Isaksen, L. (2019). Revisiting Linking Early Geospatial Documents with Recogito, *e-Perimetron* 14 (3), 152–63, https://www.e-perimetron.org/Vol_14_3/Simon_et_al.pdf

composedOf.label: Define vocabulary purpose, scope, and requirements
composedOf.description:
This step defines why the vocabulary is needed and what it should support. It translates the needs of the parent workflow, the *Collaborative Reusable Map Annotation Workflow*, into an initial vocabulary plan by identifying which parts of the annotation process require controlled vocabulary support.

The vocabulary is not designed in the abstract. It is derived from the annotation tasks, map features, and coordination needs defined in the parent workflow, such as distinguishing inscriptions, legend-based symbols, paratextual elements, interpretive comments, certainty levels, or review categories.

**Input**: Collaborative Reusable Map Annotation Workflow, research goals, selected historical maps, annotation targets, annotation schema, intended annotation environment, annotator roles, review needs, and sample map content.

**Main actions**: 
1. Review the Collaborative Reusable Map Annotation Workflow and identify where controlled vocabulary support is needed. 
2. Define the annotation facets[^1]  that require controlled terms, such as inscription function, legend category, paratext object type, commentary category, certainty, identification status, period, or place reference. For each facet, identify the corresponding vocabulary term set needed to support annotation. 
3. Distinguish between terms that describe map content and terms that support collaborative annotation practice, such as certainty levels, review categories, or quality control flags. 
4. Define scope boundaries, identify areas where external vocabularies or authorities may be relevant, and set initial granularity, user, and project constraints.

**Output**: Vocabulary Design Brief, including the initial list of required annotation facets and term sets, scope statement, granularity guidelines, and a short note explaining how the vocabulary supports the Collaborative Reusable Map Annotation Workflow.

**Format**: Short text document, Markdown/README section, DOCX/PDF, or structured planning table.

[^1]: **Terminology**: In this workflow, a facet is an annotation dimension or property that needs controlled description, such as inscription function, certainty, identification status, period, or place reference. A vocabulary term set is the list or structured set of controlled terms used for that facet. The term scheme is reserved for more formally organised vocabularies, such as a Simple Knowledge Organization System (SKOS) ConceptScheme.

composedOf.label: Choose how the vocabulary will be maintained and used
composedOf.description:
This step defines the practical environment in which the vocabulary will be created, edited, used during annotation, and prepared for release. It follows a tool agnostic but tool aware approach: the vocabulary should remain reusable beyond a single annotation tool, while still taking into account how the selected annotation environment can import, display, apply, export, and check vocabulary terms.

**Input**: Vocabulary Design Brief, annotation facets and term sets, Collaborative Reusable Map Annotation Workflow, annotation schema, intended annotation environment, available tools, project resources, team expertise, and publication aims.

**Main actions**: 
1. Review how the annotation environment [^1] can import, display, apply, export, and check vocabulary terms. 
2. Decide what will be treated as the authoritative working source of the vocabulary. 
3. Define the format needed for use in the annotation tool and the intended release or publication format. 
4. Choose the maintenance path that best fits the project. In a tabular and document driven path, the authoritative working source is maintained as a structured table or spreadsheet, with fields such as identifier, preferred label, definition, scope note, broader concept, mapping target, status, source, and editorial note. This path is suitable for projects with limited time, small teams, or no dedicated Semantic Web infrastructure, while still keeping the vocabulary reusable and prepared for possible later SKOS conversion. In a SKOS native path, the vocabulary is managed from the beginning in a vocabulary editor or RDF environment, where concepts, labels, hierarchy, mappings, and identifiers are maintained as part of a semantic resource. 

**Output**: Tooling and implementation profile, selected maintenance path, authoritative working source, annotation tool format, intended release or publication format.

**Format**: Short tooling note, configuration table, README section, spreadsheet documentation sheet, or project documentation page.

[^1]: Recogito Studio is one possible annotation environment for applying or testing the vocabulary. If the selected tool supports only a flat tag list, this list should be treated as a practical derivative of the maintained vocabulary source, not as the authoritative vocabulary itself. Hierarchy, semantic notes, mappings, and documentation should remain in the maintained source.
