relatedItems.label: Répertoire International des Sources Musicales (RISM) - International Inventory of Musical Sources
relatedItems.description:
The Répertoire International des Sources Musicales (RISM) - International Inventory of Musical Sources - is an international, non-profit organization that aims to comprehensively document extant musical sources worldwide. These primary sources are music manuscripts or printed music editions, writings on music theory, and libretti. They are preserved in libraries, archives, churches, schools and private collections.

RISM was founded in Paris in 1952 and is the largest and only international organization that documents written musical sources. RISM records what exists and where it can be found. As a result, by virtue of being cataloged in a comprehensive inventory, music traditions are protected while also being made available to musicologists and musicians alike. Such work is thus not an end in itself, but leads directly to practical applications.

relatedItems.label: Guide to Digital Music Editing
relatedItems.description: The “Guide de l’édition musicale numérique” is a comprehensive, up-to-date manual designed to accompany researchers and practitioners through the intricacies of digital music editing, with a particular focus on scholarly critical editions and the European research context. It is the result of collaborative work within the Huma-Num MUSICA2 consortium in Tours.The Guide addresses the conceptual foundations, technical strategies, and best practices essential for conceiving, producing, and disseminating digital editions of notated music. It systematically distinguishes between “digitized” and genuinely “digital” editions, emphasizing the importance of interoperability, sustainability, and the FAIR principles that dominate the digital humanities landscape.Core topics include the selection and use of notation software, detailed descriptions of encoding formats such as MusicXML, MEI, and Humdrum, and guidance for the conversion, visualization, and long-term archiving of encoded music data. The Guide clarifies legal responsibilities, collaborative workflows, and the integration of metadata and source references—crucial elements for traceability and scholarly citation.It devotes substantial attention to the creation and management of critical apparatus, annotation spaces, and dynamic links between digital editions and primary sources, especially through IIIF protocols and digital “twins”. The text includes a typology of current notation and editing tools, recommendations for quality control, and active encouragement to use open standards and open-access practices to maximize reusability and impact.The Guide situates digital music editing in the wider landscape of European cultural policies, research funding expectations, and technological change, advocating for adaptability and technical literacy among editors. Practical elements include step-by-step checklists for project planning, metadata entry, visualization tools, and the identification of trusted data repositories for long-term preservation.By synthesizing recent research, technological developments, and institutional frameworks, the Guide provides a vital roadmap for both experienced musicologists and newcomers seeking to navigate the dynamic field of digital music publication.

relatedItems.label: Musicology as data science and heritage science
relatedItems.description: This collective guide explores the transformative intersections of musicology with data science and heritage science in theEuropean context. It positions musicological research as both a model for and contributor to broader cultural heritage, analyzingits tangible and intangible dimensions. The report  reviews advances in research infrastructures, including the European Open Science Cloud, ECHOES, and E-RIHS, highlighting challenges and opportunities for integrating music into transnational heritage frameworks. It surveys the complexity of music data — notation, audio, metadata, and visual sources — and emphasizes standardized methods for cataloging and preservation. The text critically assesses legal, policy, and technical barriers to digitizing and reusing musical materials, advocating for legal reforms and open science principles. New publication paradigms are proposed, leveraging digital tools to expand access and impact. The role of musicologists in public engagement, education, and fostering research communities is underscored as crucial for sustainability. Best practices and collaborative models link musicological data to broader digital humanities and preservation strategies. Ultimately, the guide calls for active participation in European policy and research networks to enhance musicology’s role in shaping and disseminating cultural heritage for future generations.

relatedItems.label: Collaborative Digital Edition of a Musical Corpus
relatedItems.description: A project aims to do a digital edition of a musical corpus. The researchers need to be able to encode a broad range of musical documents in a machine-readable structure. The data to be encoded may include the musical content as provided by the composer (notes, pitches, durations, dynamics, etc.), information on the score (incipit, lyrics writer, etc.), information added by a performer when interpreting the content (timing, phrasing, various annotations, etc.), information on the visual appearance of the score (page layout, musical font, etc.) and analyses of the content in any of the other domains. The edition will be structured around a database in order to allow the users to explore it more easily. Furthermore, the project intends to be collaborative, which means it will offer anyone interested the possibility to contribute.

composedOf.label: Define the Corpus and Assess Feasibility
composedOf.description:
A. 
The first step consists of clearly identifying the musical corpus to be edited and evaluating the feasibility of the project. The editor must determine: the nature of the repertoire (plainchant, polyphony, tablature, contemporary music); whether a reconstruction of missing voices is required or whether the work is complete; the existence and accessibility of sources (manuscripts, printed editions, recordings); and the availability of prior editions to be consulted for a critical edition. 

B.
A financial and human resources appraisal must be conducted at this stage, as costs vary substantially depending on the corpus. This preliminary assessment determines whether the project can be conducted by a single researcher or requires a multidisciplinary team, and informs any funding application to be submitted to national or European bodies.

composedOf.label: Consult and Digitize Sources
composedOf.description:
Access to primary sources is a prerequisite for any critical edition and must be addressed before encoding begins. Where sources have not yet been digitized, the editor should follow the IIIF (International Image Interoperability Framework) protocol, which enables standardized sharing, annotation, and long-term preservation of high-resolution images. IIIF allows any rectangular fragment of a manuscript to be directly addressed via a URL, and supports comparative visualization across multiple sources and collections. 

Where digitizations already exist in institutional repositories (libraries, archives), the editor should link to them rather than duplicate them, while verifying the legal conditions of their reuse. Two access modalities are available: a hyperlink to an externally hosted digitized resource, or an IIIF viewer integrated directly into the digital edition interface. 

The availability of digitized sources is particularly crucial for early music, where the faithful transcription of ligatures, mensuration signs, tablature systems, and other notational features requires direct visual reference to the manuscript.

relatedItems.label: IIIF Enablement and Visualization Workflow Using Altamira Viewer and Cantaloupe for Image Repositories
relatedItems.description:
#### Introduction 

The purpose of this workflow is to provide a way to create and serve files in IIIF-compatible (International Image Interoperability Framework) format, which:

- Increase interoperability by standardizing access, as it is open source and widely implemented 

- Enhance delivery time by sending to the end-user only the required parts of the image

- Increase scalability as IIIF is ground-designed to handle large volumes of data

The main goal of this workflow is to streamline the creation process of IIIF-enabled resources. The entire procedure should be as simple as possible. Moreover, saved data should be accessible at will by any user having a proper resource link.

#### Workflow Goals
 
- Enable users to save images (in a given subset of formats) that will be properly converted and saved to the IIIF Server
- Enable users to access saved images at will by IIIF Viewer

#### Workflow implementation
Full documentation available [here](https://gitlab.pcss.pl/dl-team/atrium/iiif/project-files/-/blob/main/README.md)

Mirador provides several workspaces for comparing image-based resources, suitable for use in both cultural heritage and research settings.

composedOf.label: Choose a Notation Software and an Encoding Strategy
composedOf.description:
The second step involves selecting both an encoding format and a notational tool suited to the corpus and the edition's intended objectives. At this stage, the editor must determine whether the project calls for a diplomatic or a critical edition.

Regarding notational tools, MuseScore (open source) stands as the currently recommended choice: it supports direct export to MEI without requiring plugins. Sibelius and Finale, though still widely used in professional contexts, are no longer under active development and cannot be considered viable long-term solutions. For early or non-Western repertoires, specialized tools may prove necessary — among them Gregorio for neumatic notation, LuteScribe and Fronimo for tablature, and the ReTab module for lute tablature in MEI.

The choice of encoding format has major consequences for the interoperability and analytical potential of the edition. MEI (Music Encoding Initiative) is strongly recommended for scholarly digital editions: it allows the coexistence of graphical score visualization and semantic encoding of musical data, accommodates a critical apparatus and a metadata header, and opens the way to computational analysis via tools such as Music21 and Humdrum. MusicXML remains a widely supported interchange format, suitable at the data-transfer stage of the workflow. PDF, by contrast, is appropriate only for dissemination purposes and does not constitute a digital edition in the full sense of the term.

relatedItems.label: MEI Score Editor --MEISE
relatedItems.description: The MEI Score Editor (MEISE) is an Eclipse-based client software for viewing and editing MEI-encoded music documents in CMN (Common Music Notation), facilitating proof reading as well as modifying and correcting MEI files. MEISE was designed to satisfy special requirements of research in musicology, currently unsupported by existing music notation software tools. MEISE should be used especially for working with MEI-data as a processing and editing tool, e.g. for creating variants, generating, completing and modifying MEI-files. As a key merit, MEISE gains of its homomorphic internal data structure to the MEI schema tree, allowing for native support for theoretically all MEI encoding principles. This allows for some unique features arising from the field of scholarly music edition, such as the encoding and visualization of variants of different musical sources in one digital MEI representation.

composedOf.label: Encode the Musical Data
composedOf.description:
Encoding is the central intellectual and technical operation of the digital edition. It involves transcribing musical information into structured, machine-readable data, capturing not only the visual symbols of the score but also their semantic significance. Before encoding, the editor must define which signs are essential and which are complementary: staves, pitches, rhythmic values, dynamics, and measures constitute primary data; ficta accidentals, ornaments, and performance indications may be treated as secondary layers, depending on whether the edition prioritizes analytical use or performer accessibility. Good encoding practice avoids an excessive accumulation of customized or unconventional graphical elements, which compromise file integrity and interoperability. 

The choice between prioritizing logical readability (for analytical purposes) and visual fidelity must be made deliberately and applied consistently. For works with text (vocal music), particular care must be taken to align syllables precisely with their corresponding notes. MEI's attribute allows each element to be uniquely identified, enabling subsequent linkage to sources and audio recordings via thesauruses and reference systems. For some notational symbols (e.g. musica ficta), Python scripts can automate corrections across the encoded corpus, provided the initial encoding has been properly prepared.

composedOf.label: Declare and Enrich Metadata
composedOf.description: Metadata are the foundation of the edition's discoverability, interoperability, and long-term reuse. In MEI format, metadata are gathered in the file header, which must at minimum allow for the generation of an appropriate bibliographic citation. The header is structured into three major sections within : (title, subtitle, composer), (editors, encoders, proofreaders, identified by ORCID), and (source description linked to RISM, VIAF, and other reference systems). A recommended best practice is to register the work with RISM regardless of its historical period: a RISM ID allows the linking of key information including source type, editorial contributions, and holding institution. For projects with substantial metadata needs, the FRBR model (Functional Requirements for Bibliographic Records) can be integrated into the header to establish precise connections with library standards. MEI headers that contain URIs can be directly linked to manuscript images via Verovio. Reference systems to consult include VIAF (persons), Wikidata (works and persons), Geonames (places), Getty AAT (concepts), MIMO (instruments), and RISM (musical sources). For large corpora, Richard Freedman's mei_tools and Mermeid facilitate batch metadata management and visualization.

composedOf.label: Validate the Encoding and Manage File Conversion
composedOf.description: Once the encoding and metadata are complete, the file must be validated to ensure its structural integrity and conformance to the MEI schema. MEIFriend provides real-time validation and allows corrections to be made directly in the browser. Verovio serves as the primary rendering tool, converting MEI files into SVG for web visualization; the editor must verify that the graphical output is satisfactory and that all notational elements are correctly rendered. It should be noted that Verovio does not yet support all aspects of advanced notation (medieval repertories, contemporary graphic symbols): elements not supported are silently ignored and will not be preserved in MEI output. Where multiple output formats are required (MIDI for performers, audio for general audiences, REST API for interoperability), the converter Meico (Java-based) and MEI Garage (web interface) facilitate format conversion from MEI. OCR/OMR tools (Audiveris, Aruspix, the DMOS system developed within the Collabscore project) can assist with the initial transcription of printed or manuscript sources, though their output requires careful scholarly correction.

composedOf.label: Build the Critical Apparatus and Annotation Spaces
composedOf.description: For critical editions, this step involves the systematic encoding of textual variants, editorial emendations, and scholarly annotations within the MEI file or an associated annotation layer. MEI supports a dedicated critical apparatus (using the , , and elements), which enables multiple readings to be encoded within a single master file and linked to their respective sources. The editor must decide in advance on a minimal yet meaningful set of annotation criteria, so that the significance of each source remains clearly perceptible without overloading the file with cross-references. Online platforms implementing collaborative annotation workflows --- such as Gesualdo Online digital edition, both hosted at the RicercarDataLab --- provide established models: annotating users are identified by contributor level, annotations are categorized by type (Duration, Emendation, Pitch, etc.) and validated by an administrator before integration into the master file. The critical apparatus can also incorporate audio files (MIDI or live recordings), provided the relevant rights have been cleared. Synchronization between encoded files and audio recordings remains technically challenging and is currently achieved by only a small number of projects (e.g. the Marenzio edition).

composedOf.label: Address Copyright and Assign a License
composedOf.description: All stages of the editorial process are subject to legal constraints that must be anticipated from the outset. Under European law, the status of a scholarly editor is distinct from that of a creator, but this distinction carries rights implications that can give rise to disputes if not managed carefully. Key legal considerations include: the copyright status of the musical work itself (works enter the public domain 70 years after the death of the composer in the EU); the rights attached to existing printed editions (which may themselves be protected, independently of the underlying work); the rights associated with audio recordings to be integrated into the edition; and the intellectual property of the encoding work and any software used. Creative Commons licenses are strongly recommended for scholarly digital editions: the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license (author must be credited, non-commercial use only, derivative editions permitted) is particularly well suited to critical editions. All contributors must be properly credited, including students who have participated in encoding or proofreading. Where institutions operate under commercial publishing agreements (as in the hybrid model of the Centre de Musique Baroque de Versailles), the financial implications of Open Access must be negotiated at project design stage.

composedOf.label: Design the Presentation Model and Online Interface
composedOf.description: The presentation model determines how users will interact with the edition: which notational layers are displayed by default, how annotations and source facsimiles are accessed, what musical analysis features are offered, and how the interface adapts to different user communities (performers, musicologists, students, the general public). The presentation layer should be designed in complementary fashion to the encoding layer: visual rendering must not be optimized at the expense of machine readability, as a score that is aesthetically pleasing but poorly structured for machines limits the edition's interoperability and analytical potential. Annotation spaces must be carefully architected: setting up a dynamic web interface with collaborative annotation capabilities requires substantial technical expertise and dedicated human resources. The Polish Music Heritage project offers a reference model combining IIIF-based manuscript visualization, MEI score display with multiple export options, and deep metadata links to RISM, Wikidata, and other reference systems. For collections requiring performance history and reception data, Dezède (a relational database for archiving performances) offers complementary functionality beyond what a critical edition's architecture can accommodate.

composedOf.label: Deposit, Archive, and Ensure Long-Term Sustainability
composedOf.description:
The final step of the workflow concerns the long-term sustainability of the edition: the choice of a trusted repository, the conditions of indexing, and the prevention of obsolescence. Data hosting on virtual machines provided by national research infrastructures is recommended for publicly funded projects. In France, Nakala (hosted by Huma-Num) provides a FAIR-compliant repository specifically designed for humanities and social sciences data produced by institutions affiliated with the French Ministry of Higher Education and Research. NEUMA (also hosted by Huma-Num) is a digital music library providing online access to encoded musical corpora. 

Interoperability should be considered from the earliest stages of the editorial project in order to ensure the edition's integration into the larger research ecosystem. The edition must be correctly indexed in relevant discovery portals: the SSH Open Marketplace, RISM, and the IIIF community's shared infrastructures. A stable persistent identifier (DOI via Zenodo, or a handle) must be assigned. Finally, the question of format obsolescence must be anticipated: MEI, like LaTeX, relies on plain text files with tags, a preservation strategy that is more robust than proprietary binary formats.

label: Creation of a TEI-based corpus
description: This scenario explains the steps to take, in order to create a corpus based on the TEI tagset. As of today, the TEI guidelines have become a de facto standard for text annotation, providing solutions for a great variety of text and phrase structures, information on content types, linguistic information on words or phrases, etc. In many digital text collections and digital edition projects annotation has been based on the TEI. Linguistic corpora based on TEI may thus be re-used in projects of other disciplines as well or may themselves benefit from the wide range of already existing resources.

relatedItems.label: Creating an Interoperable TEI Annotation Schema
relatedItems.description:
The process of creating a Digital Edition using the TEI Guidelines is common practice in the Digital Humanities and a cornerstone of creating research data that adheres to the FAIR Principles. However, ambiguous or uninformed usage of annotation elements from the TEI Guidelines can result in interoperability issues and tedious curation effort. 
This workflow promotes the careful creation of a TEI annotation schema by balancing the project-specific needs with existing best practices and tool-related pitfalls. 
By following these steps, you build the foundation for a successful Digital Edition project and can start the annotation process with confidence in your future interoperability.

composedOf.label: Corpus Composition
composedOf.description: For corpus composition a set of canonical decisions should be considered. As a starting point, the corpus type will have to be determined: Is it an opportunistic selection, a balanced corpus, etc.? If balanced, which would be the criteria of balancedness? This is accompanied by the question which domain the corpus should represent (e.g. Should it only contain resources within a specific date range or of a certain text type or from a specific author?). Based on this decision, the resources that should be included in the corpus have to be selected, possibly by reference to a research question. After that, corpus composers have to decide on the type of annotation that should be applied: lightweight or with multiple layers, inline or standoff, etc. The next important step for corpus composition is the determination of a general tagset which the annotation should follow, i.e. the content of the markup planned.

relatedItems.description: This document describes how to produce a customization of the TEI P5 schema. From the start, the TEI was intended to be used as a set of building blocks for creating a schema suitable for a particular project. This is in keeping with the TEI philosophy of providing a vocabulary for describing texts, not dictating precisely what those texts must contain or might have contained. This means that it is likely, not just possible, that you will want to have a tailored view of the TEI.

composedOf.label: Linguistic Annotation
composedOf.description: The corpus texts containing TEI text structuring can be further enhanced by adding linguistic markup, e.g. information on tokens, lemmas, Parts-of-Speech or results of higher level linguistic analysis). Here, a wide range of NLP tools are available to perform the task of linguistic analysis and tagging automatically. For example, the CLARIN infrastructure offers the WebLicht service which allows for data analysis with various NLP tools and for the building of analysis chains. In- and output format here is the Text Corpus Format (TCF; for conversion between TEI and TCF use the TEI2TCF-webservice). Another toolkit is e.g. Apache OpenNLP. As tools you may use e.g. the Stanford Tokenizer or TreeTagger for tokenization, POS tagging and more, or e.g. enrich corpus with Named Entity Recognition annotation (e.g. by usage of Apache Stanbol or Babelfy). Manual annotation may e.g. be performed in WebAnno.

concept.definition: LAF, linguistic annotation framework, is a standard ISO for representing linguistic annotations of language data such as corpora, speech signal and video. The framework includes an abstract data model and an XML serialization of that model for representing annotations of primary data. The serialization serves as a pivot format to allow annotations expressed in one representation format to be mapped onto another.

The resulting TCF document may (possibly after its enrichment with further TCF layers) be converted back into TEI with token information and token IDs. This service was developed at the CLARIN-D center at Berlin-Brandenburg Academy of Sciences and Humanities.

relatedItems.description: The TreeTagger is a tool for annotating text with part-of-speech and lemma information. It was developed by Helmut Schmid in the TC project at the Institute for Computational Linguistics of the University of Stuttgart. The TreeTagger has been successfully used to tag German, English, French, Italian, Danish, Dutch, Spanish, Bulgarian, Russian, Portuguese, Galician, Greek, Chinese, Swahili, Slovak, Slovenian, Latin, Estonian, Polish, Romanian, Czech, Coptic and old French texts and is adaptable to other languages if a lexicon and a manually tagged training corpus are available.

relatedItems.label: WebLicht: Getting Started
relatedItems.description: WebLicht is a service orchestration and execution environment for incremental automatic annotation of text corpora, built upon Service Oriented Architecture principles. Its main components are: \* A set of distributed services for data processing \* A repository containing metadata about the services \* A web application that offers a user-friendly graphical interface for building chains of services and executing them WebLicht's services are hosted on servers distributed throughout Europe, which allows full control of a tool by its developer. Each tool within WebLicht is registered in a repository containing information about its input requirements and its output, among other things. This information is necessary to determine which tools can be added to the processing chain at any given point while building a chain because each tool in a processing chain uses the output of the previous tool in the chain as its input. Only those tools which are able to work with the data are available as choices for adding to a chain. The main focus of this Quick Start Guide is on WebLicht's web application and how it can be used to linguistically annotate text and subsequently to visualize the annotations. We will create and run a very simple tool chain to annotate a text and view the results.

relatedItems.label: WebLicht
relatedItems.description:
WebLicht is an execution environment for automatic annotation of text corpora. Linguistic tools such as tokenizers, part of speech taggers, and parsers are encapsulated as web services, which can be combined by the user into custom processing chains. The resulting annotations can then be visualized in an appropriate way, such as in a table or tree format. 

It is often the case that a tool relies on one or more annotation layers to exist in the input data before it can begin processing. WebLicht can assist the user in building a processing chain by determining which tools are able to operate on the data at any given point and offering only those tools as options to add to the chain. There are 2 modes for building tool chains: Easy Mode lets you choose pre-defined processing chains Advanced Mode allows you to build customized tool chains. 

Login is required to use the tools and corpora. Login with email addresses from most recognized European universities will be automatically accepted. Individuals with a Non-European email address need to create an account with clarin.eu Developed by the German language resource infrastructure (D-SPIN) and Common language resources and technology infrastructure (CLARIN).

composedOf.label: Verification and Cleanup
composedOf.description: It is straightforward to include a phase of verification of results and cleanup after each step towards corpus creation. This step is actually a "hidden" or "stepified" scenario which should take parameters. Verification can be automatic at first, and then manual, done by annotators. This step has the power of looping the entire process back to the previous step (after the/some errors have been corrected). Important: Preserve the data that is about to undergo cleanup (simplest: zip with a date stamp, more intricate: use a versioning system).

label: Customizing the Patrimonium-Editor
description:
This document serves as a guide for customizing the Patrimonium Editor  using the example of the Fercan projects at the University of Graz, that study the Celtic divine names in roman inscriptions in antiquity (see also GitHub https://github.com/DigitalHumanitiesCraft/PatrimoniumEditorFercan/). These projects utilizes the Patrimonium Editor to collect and manage epigraphic data. Supported by the Austrian Science Fund (FWF) through grants. The first project “Celtic Divine Names in the Inscriptions of the Roman Province Germania Inferior. A Case Study on Religion in the Context of Cultural Contacts and Cultural Transfer” researched the Celtic divine names in the Roman provinces of Germania Inferior (P 29274-G25) and the second one “Celtic Divine Names in Latin Inscriptions of the Military Zone in Germania Superior on the Left Bank of the River Rhine. Religious Phenomena in a Cultural Contact Zone“ (P 34422-G) focused on the northern Germania Superior. These two projects examined how local Celtic traditions were integrated into Roman practices, using epigraphic evidence to trace changes and continuities in religious expression. The customization and application of the Patrimonium Editor was done during the second project and retroactively applied to the data management of the first project too.

The Patrimonium Editor is a web application suite designed for academic use, focusing on the encoding, management, and analysis of epigraphic and historical textual sources. It includes an XML editor for text encoding, conversion tools adhering to the Leiden Conventions, and data management capabilities for places, people, and thematic categories. Its modular architecture provides flexibility for customization and leverages the eXist-db XML database. The editor supports TEI (Text Encoding Initiative) and EpiDoc (Epigraphic Documents) guidelines, ensuring compatibility with international standards in digital humanities.

relatedItems.label: Patrimonium-Editor
relatedItems.description: The Patrimonium editor  is an integrated web application, created by Alberto Dalla Rosa and Vincent Razanajao, based on eXist-db and is dedicated primarily to the production and enrichment of epigraphical corpora, from the creation of TEI/EpiDoc files to the building of both the gazetteer and prosopographical data of places and people involved in the documents. The web application has been conceived in a modular and customizable approach, so that it could potentially fit the requirements of any historical project that needs to process textual sources and deal with spatial and prosopographical material.

relatedItems.label: Workflow to work with the PATRIMONIVM-Editor
relatedItems.description:
The PATRIMONIVM-Editor has been created by Alberto Dalla Rosa and Vincent Razanajao (https://patrimonium.huma-num.fr/atlas/editor/) to be a modular, customizable and integrated web application for the management of epigraphic corpora, based on the eXist-db platform. It creates TEI XML on the basis of EpiDoc, allowing the data to be used in digital editions. Based on our experiences with a customized version of the “eStudium. A virtual research environment for Historians” for the epigraphic project “Celtic Divine Names in Latin Inscriptions of the Military Zone in Germania Superior on the Left Bank of the River Rhine. Religious Phenomena in a Cultural Contact Zone“ (FWF funded project P 34422-G), this workflow will document the process both for the scientific, and probably non-tech savvy user, who is filling the editor with information, as well as for the user tasked with postprocessing the information available in the editor for the online publication.

For our first project “Celtic Divine Names in the Inscriptions of the Roman Province Germania Inferior. A Case Study on Religion in the Context of Cultural Contacts and Cultural Transfer” (FWF funded project P 29274-G25) we used single MC Word documents for every entry, which then were consolidated into a single MC Excel document for the conversion to XML by our partners at ZIM (Zentrum für Informationsmodellierung – Centre for Information Modelling) and the following online publication on GAMS (Geisteswissenschaftliches Asset Management System – Humanities’ Asset Management System; https://gams.uni-graz.at/context:fercan ; see picture 10). This method was redundant, cumbersome and prone to errors, especially with regard to required changes. With the PATRIMONIVM-Editor, these redundancies are removed and problems occurring during the postprocessing are easily identified, communicated and solved. (For the process of adapting the PATRIMONIVM-Editor, see either the GitHub documentation https://github.com/DigitalHumanitiesCraft/PatrimoniumEditorFercan/, or "Customizing the Patrimonium-Editor" on SSHOM)

composedOf.label: Setting Up the Environment
composedOf.description:
#### Prerequisites

Ensure your system meets the necessary requirements for running eXist-db and Patrimonium Editor. Install Docker, eXist-db, and Apache Ant.

#### Installing eXist-db with Docker

1.	Download and Install Docker Desktop: Available for Windows, Mac, and Linux.
2.	Run eXist-db Container: Open a terminal and execute the command:
sh
docker run -d -p 8080:8080 existdb/existdb:latest

1.	This command downloads the latest eXist-db image and runs it, exposing port 8080 for web access.
2.	Access eXist-db Dashboard: Navigate to http://localhost:8080/exist/apps/dashboard/index.html in your web browser.

#### Deploying Patrimonium Editor Packages

1.	Required .xar Packages: ausohnum-library (Main program with core functionalities), estudium (Project-specific customizations), estudiumData (Data files, primarily TEI XML documents).
2.	Install Packages via eXist-db Package Manager: Access the eXist-db dashboard at http://localhost:8080/exist/apps/dashboard/index.html and use the Package Manager to upload and install the .xar packages.

composedOf.label: Customisation for Fercan Project
composedOf.description:
#### Modifications to Patrimonium Editor
The Fercan custom editor has been tailored to meet the specific needs of the project, focusing on metadata and transcription editing while omitting certain functionalities of the original editor, such as place and person editors.
#### Customising TEI Elements
Customization of TEI elements is handled through the teiElements.xml file, which defines how different data fields are displayed and managed within the editor.
#### Example Definitions:
##### Deity Name (Göttername):
 deityName /tei:teiHeader/tei:fileDesc/tei:titleStmt/tei:title text 1 Deity Name input  

#### Document Title:

  docTitle /tei:teiHeader/tei:fileDesc/tei:titleStmt/tei:title text 1 Document Title input  
#### Configuration of Document Editor
The document editor is configured using the document-editor.xql script, which defines the input fields and user interface components for editing documents.
#### Example Configuration:
##### Input Field for Document Title:
  {teiEditor:displayElement('docTitle', (), (), ())}  
This function call generates the UI component for the document title based on the definitions provided in teiElements.xml.

composedOf.label: Using the Patrimonium Editor
composedOf.description:
#### Accessing the Editor
Access the editor via the eXist Dashboard at http://localhost:8080/exist/apps/estudium/. Log in as either 'admin' or 'editor'.
#### Creating and Managing Documents
•	Creating a New Document: Select "New Document" and choose a template (e.g., "Germania_Inferior"). Once created, access the document (e.g., inferior467) at http://localhost:8080/exist/apps/estudium/edit-documents/inferior467.
•	Managing Documents: View documents within the Corpora directory at http://localhost:8080/exist/apps/estudium/admin/corpus/germania_inferior.
#### Entering Data into Documents
•	Metadata Entry: Input metadata under "Document Overview". This includes details such as deity names, subtitles, and associated civitas.
•	Text Entry and Formatting: Ensure proper text formatting using the editor's tools, including "Paste as Text" to remove unwanted formatting from sources like MS Word.

composedOf.label: Corpus View and Document Management
composedOf.description:
#### Overview of Corpus View
The Corpus View in the Patrimonium Editor serves as the central interface for managing and viewing various documents related to the Fercan project. Accessible at http://localhost:8080/exist/apps/estudium/admin/, integrating with modules from the ausohnum-library.
#### Document Storage and Naming Conventions
•	Directory Path: Documents are stored in eStudiumData/documents/$corpus.
•	Naming Conventions: Documents are named sequentially (e.g., Doc1.xml, Doc2.xml) for organized storage and easy retrieval.
#### Ingesting Existing Files
•	XML ID Assignment: Assign a unique xml:id to existing TEI documents for identification within the system.
xml

composedOf.label: Advanced Features and Integration
composedOf.description:
#### Thesaurus Management
•	Controlled Vocabularies: Manage thesaurus systems to standardize terminology across documents, facilitating consistent tagging and easier retrieval of related texts.
#### Zotero Integration
•	References and Bibliographic Data: Integrate with Zotero to manage references directly within the editor, ensuring citations and sources are up-to-date during research and documentation.

composedOf.label: Practical Tips and Troubleshooting
composedOf.description:
#### Managing Browser Sessions
•	Incognito Mode: Use incognito mode to avoid caching issues when logging into the eXist-db dashboard.
•	Alternate Browsers: If issues arise with one browser, try accessing the dashboard with a different one.
•	Disable Cache: Disable the cache in your browser settings to ensure changes are reflected immediately during application setup.
#### Common Issues and Solutions
Address common setup and usage issues, providing solutions and workarounds for each.

composedOf.label: Conclusion
composedOf.description: Recap the workflow and its benefits for the Fercan project. Users are encouraged to explore and utilize the full potential of the Patrimonium Editor for their research and documentation needs.

composedOf.label: Workflow for Collecting Data in the Patrimonium Editor - 1
composedOf.description:
#### Step 1: Accessing the Document
1.	URL: Open the document using the provided link (e.g., https://patrimonium.huma-num.fr/documents/superior3).
2.	Navigation: Navigate to the "Document overview" section to begin data entry.
#### Step 2: Entering Metadata
##### 1.	Title:
o	Deity Name (Göttername): Enter the name of the deity, e.g., "Mars Armogius?"
o	Subtitle: Provide additional identifiers or details, e.g., "CF-GeS-1074".
o	Civitas: Select the relevant civitas from the dropdown menu, if applicable.
##### 2.	Editor's Comment: Add any necessary editorial comments or notes for internal reference.
#### Step 3: Apparatus Criticus
##### 1.	Notes: Enter critical notes for each line of the inscription.
	Example:
	Zeile 1: arm(igero?) arm(ato?) – Brambach, Becker; Armigero oder Armogio? – Riese; arm(ato?) – Stauner; aram – EDH, Behrens; Arm() – Weber; (M)arm(ogio?) – EPSG, Scheungraber
	Zeile 7: Am Ende der Zeile ein zusätzliches A: a(d?) – Brambach; a(ra) – Becker
	Zeile 11: l(ibens) l(aetus) – Weber, Stauner, Cubaynes, Scheungraber; l(aetus) l(ubens) – Becker
	Zeile 8: Am Anfang der Zeile (ante diem) – Weber
##### 2.	Autopsie und Editionen: Record observations from autopsies and list the editions and readings of the text.
#### Step 4: Entering Bibliographic Data
##### 1.	Editions and Readings: Enter bibliographic references and IDs for each text.
	Example:
	Text: ILS 3156, ID: 4
	Text: CIL XIII 6738, ID: 3
##### 2.	Citing Online Resources: Record URLs and access dates for online resources such as EDH, Lupa, Clauss-Slaby, and Trismegistos.
	Example:
	EDH: ID: HD055199, Datum: Version von 2019-05-24
	Lupa: ID: http://lupa.at/27080, Datum: Version von 2018-05-18

composedOf.label: Workflow for Collecting Data in the Patrimonium Editor - 2
composedOf.description:
#### Step 5: Entering Descriptive Data
##### 1.	Images: Upload images related to the inscription with descriptions and MIME types.
	Example:
	Dateiname: 1074_front_unklar1.jpg, Beschreibung: Front, Landesmuseum, Mainz, Foto: Ortolf Harl 2016, MIME-Type: image/jpeg
##### 2.	Fund Information: Record ancient and modern find locations, site details, and discovery circumstances.
	Example:
	Fundort antik: Mogontiacum
	Fundort modern: Mainz
	Fundstelle: „in dem Garten des ehemaligen Bischofshofes“ (CIL); Höfchen 2 (EDH)
	Fundjahr: 1832
##### 3.	Storage Information: Record storage details, including the current institution and inventory number.
	Example:
	Verwahrung: Mainz
	Institution: Landesmuseum, Depot Bretzenheim
	Inv.Nr.: S 530
##### 4.	Object Description: Describe the object, material, and condition.
	Example:
	Inschriftträger: Weihestein
	Material: Sandstein
	Zustand Objekt: vollständig
	Maße Objekt: Höhe (cm): 117
##### 5.	Inschrift Description: Describe the inscription's text, condition, and technique.
	Example:
	Schrifttechnik: gemeißelt
	Buchstabenhöhe (cm): 3,0–3,5
#### Step 6: Adding Translations and Comments
##### 1.	Translations: Provide translations in different languages.
	Example:
	Deutsch: Für den Gott Mars Armogius! Iulius Emeritus, Soldat der Legio VIII Augusta Severiana Alexandriana, Schreiber des Statthalters, hat dies geweiht am 19. April unter dem Konsulat des Maximus und des Aelianus und hat ein Gelübde freudig, gern und verdientermaßen erfüllt.
	Englisch: To the god Mars Armogius! Iulius Emeritus, soldier of the legio VIII Augusta Severiana Alexandriana, military record-clerk of the governor, has dedicated this on the 19th April during the consulship of Maximus and Aelianus and fulfilled a vow gladly, willingly and deservedly.
#### Step 7: Reviewing and Saving the Document
1.	Preview: Use the "Preview" option to review the entered data. Ensure the text is formatted correctly and all required fields are completed.
2.	Saving: Save the document to ensure all entered data is stored accurately.

composedOf.label: Creating and Postprocessing TEI XML in the Patrimonium Editor
composedOf.description:
#### Step 1: Initial Data Entry
The initial data entry process in the Patrimonium Editor involves inputting metadata, text annotations, and critical notes directly into the user interface. The information entered here forms the basis of the TEI XML file that will be generated and processed.
1.	Document Overview: Enter basic metadata such as the deity name, subtitle, civitas, and editorial comments.
2.	Text Annotation: Input the text of the inscription using the XML Editor provided in the Patrimonium Editor. Use appropriate tags for text formatting and annotations.
3.	Apparatus Criticus: Add critical notes for specific lines of the inscription. These notes provide context and interpretations from various sources.
4.	Additional Sections: Input bibliographic references, observations, translations, and any other relevant data.
#### Step 2: Generating TEI XML
Once all the necessary data has been entered through the editor's interface, the Patrimonium Editor compiles this information into a TEI XML document. This document conforms to the TEI (Text Encoding Initiative) standards, ensuring consistency and interoperability with other digital humanities projects.

concept.label: TIFF
concept.definition: Tagged Image File Format, abbreviated TIFF or TIF, is a computer file format for storing raster graphics images, popular among graphic artists, the publishing industry, and photographers. TIFF is widely supported by scanning, faxing, word processing, optical character recognition, image manipulation, desktop publishing, and page-layout applications. The format was created by Aldus Corporation for use in desktop publishing. It published the latest version 6.0 in 1992, subsequently updated with an Adobe Systems copyright after the latter acquired Aldus in 1994. Several Aldus or Adobe technical notes have been published with minor extensions to the format, and several specifications have been based on TIFF 6.0, including TIFF/EP (ISO 12234-2), TIFF/IT (ISO 12639), TIFF-F (RFC 2306) and TIFF-FX (RFC 3949).

concept.label: JPEG
concept.definition: JPEG ( JAY-peg) is a commonly used method of lossy compression for digital images, particularly for those images produced by digital photography. The degree of compression can be adjusted, allowing a selectable tradeoff between storage size and image quality. JPEG typically achieves 10:1 compression with little perceptible loss in image quality. JPEG compression is used in a number of image file formats. JPEG/Exif is the most common image format used by digital cameras and other photographic image capture devices; along with JPEG/JFIF, it is the most common format for storing and transmitting photographic images on the World Wide Web. These format variations are often not distinguished, and are simply called JPEG. The term "JPEG" is an initialism/acronym for the Joint Photographic Experts Group, which created the standard. The MIME media type for JPEG is image/jpeg, except in older Internet Explorer versions, which provides a MIME type of image/pjpeg when uploading JPEG images. JPEG files usually have a filename extension of .jpg or .jpeg. JPEG/JFIF supports a maximum image size of 65,53565,535 pixels, hence up to 4 gigapixels for an aspect ratio of 1:1.

concept.label: DUBLIN CORE
concept.definition: The Dublin Core Schema is a small set of vocabulary terms that can be used to describe web resources (video, images, web pages, etc.), as well as physical resources such as books or CDs, and objects like artworks. The full set of Dublin Core metadata terms can be found on the Dublin Core Metadata Initiative (DCMI) website.

label: Digitized Archive Stylistic Analysis with BERT Vector Pooling and K Means Clustering
description: This workflow demonstrates a **reproducible, AI-driven methodology** for analyzing stylistic variation in the **Getty Provenance Index (GPI) German Sales (1900–1945)**, a corpus of ~830,000 German-language auction entries. The process transforms parsed archival fields into a unified language resource, enabling large-scale analysis of commercial connoisseurship as a discursive system.

concept.label: Text Categorization
concept.definition: Wikidata contributors, "Q57771142," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q57771142&oldid=1072020823 (accessed September 4, 2020).

composedOf.label: Data Reconstruction
composedOf.description:
1. **Data Reconstruction**
   - Rebuilds auction entries from parsed GitHub fields (`artist_name_1`, `artist_info_1`, `title`) to restore original catalogue text (e.g., *"Corn. Dusart 1660–1704 Trinker im Freien vor einem Wirtshaus. Leinwand, Größe 50:40 cm. Gutachten Dr. Glück"*).
   - Output: `gpi_auction_entry` (faithful to primary sources).

composedOf.label: Manual Annotation (Gold Standard)
composedOf.description:
- 100-record subsample labeled into **3 stylistic groups**:
     - *Generic*: Sparse, short descriptions (e.g., *"Unknown Artist Shepherd with Flock. Canvas. 19×26 cm"*).
     - *Short/Informative*: Structured object metadata (e.g., *"Wilhelm Kalf Breakfast still life with ham, wine glass, lemon... Oil. Wood. Monogrammed. 46×66 cm"*).
     - *Elaborate/Descriptive*: Rich, contextually dense language (e.g., descriptions with compound nouns, expert attestations).

composedOf.label: Text Encoding & Feature Extraction
composedOf.description:
- **Baseline**: TF-IDF (stopwords/short tokens removed; Roman numerals excluded).
   - **Contextual Embeddings**: GBERT (German BERT) with **4 pooling strategies**:
     - Mean pooling
     - Max pooling
     - CLS token
     - Sentence-BERT (SBERT)
   - **Dimensionality Reduction**: PCA (5–50 dimensions) to mitigate high-dimensional noise.

composedOf.label: Clustering & Evaluation
composedOf.description:
- **Algorithm**: k-means (k=3) for stylistic grouping.
   - **Internal Metrics**:
     - Silhouette Score (cluster separation)
     - Davies-Bouldin Index (compactness)
   - **External Validation**:
     - Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) vs. manual labels.
   - **Qualitative Review**: Identifies biases (e.g., manual annotation’s length-based assumptions) and embedding nuances (e.g., compound noun detection).

composedOf.label: Findings & Reusability
composedOf.description:
- **Max pooling** (PCA=5) achieved highest ARI (**0.40**) and internal cohesion.
   - Revealed **domain-specific patterns** (e.g., German compound nouns like *Jünglingsbildnis* [young man’s portrait] captured by embeddings but overlooked in manual labeling).
   - **Scalable**: Framework adaptable to other GPI language subsets (Dutch, French, etc.) or humanities archives.

#### **Tools & Standards**
- **Models**: GBERT (Chan et al., 2020), SBERT (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019)
- **Libraries**: scikit-learn (k-means/PCA), FAISS (vector indexing)
- **Evaluation**: Silhouette, ARI, Davies-Bouldin
- **Outputs**: Clustered datasets, evaluation metrics, visualizations (PCA plots)

#### **Use Cases**
- **Art History**: Uncover linguistic strategies in auction catalogues (e.g., commercial connoisseurship).
- **Digital Humanities**: Methodology for transforming parsed archives into language resources.
- **AI/NLP**: Benchmarking contextual vs. static embeddings for domain-specific corpora.

composedOf.label: Limitations
composedOf.description:
- Bias in manual annotation (length-based assumptions).
- Potential for hierarchical clustering or metadata integration (auction house, date).
- Extend to multilingual GPI subsets.

**Citation**: Henrickson, M. (2026). *Text Clustering of Fine Art German Language Auction Catalogue Data from the Getty Provenance Index (1900–1945)*. PhD Thesis, University of Leeds.

composedOf.label: Tools used
composedOf.description:
### Tools and Libraries

**Core Tools & Libraries**
- **Python**: pandas, numpy (Data cleaning, reconstruction of auction entries from parsed fields)
- **GBERT (German BERT)**: Contextual embeddings for German-language auction text ([Hugging Face: DBMDZ/bert-base-german-cased](https://huggingface.co/DBMDZ/bert-base-german-cased))
- **Sentence-BERT (SBERT)**: Sentence-level embeddings ([SBERT GitHub](https://github.com/UKPLab/sentence-transformers))
- **TF-IDF**: Baseline static text representation ([scikit-learn TF-IDF](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.feature_extraction.text.TfidfVectorizer.html))
- **PCA**: Dimensionality reduction for clustering ([scikit-learn PCA](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.decomposition.PCA.html))
- **k-means**: Clustering algorithm ([scikit-learn k-means](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.cluster.KMeans.html))
- **Silhouette Score**: Cluster separation and cohesion metric ([scikit-learn Silhouette Score](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.metrics.silhouette_score.html))
- **Davies-Bouldin Index**: Cluster compactness and separation metric ([scikit-learn Davies-Bouldin](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.metrics.davies_bouldin_score.html))
- **Adjusted Rand Index (ARI)**: Comparison of clustering results to manual annotations ([scikit-learn ARI](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.metrics.adjusted_rand_score.html))
- **FAISS**: Efficient similarity search for high-dimensional embeddings ([FAISS GitHub](https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss))

relatedItems.label: Open Data in a Big Data World
relatedItems.description: Four major organisations representing global science, the International Council for Science (ICSU), the InterAcademy Partnership (IAP), The World Academy of Sciences (TWAS) and the International Social Science Council (ISSC), are collaborating in a series of action-oriented annual meetings, dubbed "Science International". These meetings are designed to articulate the views of the global scientific community on international matters of policy for science and to promote appropriate actions. The following accord is the product of the first Science International meeting. The accord identifies the opportunities and challenges of the data revolution as one of today's predominant issues of global science policy. It sets out principles that are consistent with ones being carried out in practice in some national research systems and in some disciplinary fields. It adds the distinctive voice of the scientific community to those of governments and inter-governmental bodies that have made the case for open data as a fundamental pre-requisite in maintaining the rigour of scientific inquiry and maximising public benefit from the data revolution. It builds on ICSU's 2014 statement on open access by endorsing the need for an international framework of open data principles. In the months ahead, Science International partners will promote discussion and adoption of these principles by their respective members and by other representative bodies of science at national and international levels. We will ask that these organizations review the accord and endorse it, and thereby provide further support in global policy venues for these constructive and vitally important principles. An abbreviated version of this accord summarises the issues in section A of this document and presents the open data principles that it advocates.

relatedItems.label: Create the 3D Model
relatedItems.description:
# 3D Modeling
This step involves the creation of an accurate 3D model based on the processed and georeferenced data from the digital survey. Using the cleaned and aligned point clouds or photogrammetric outputs, accurate geometric digital representations of the monument are generated. This process may include surface reconstruction, mesh generation, and texture mapping, depending on the level of detail required. 

# Data Enrichment
Once the base 3D model is created, and depending on the project’s goals, the model is enriched with additional data—such as historical context, material properties, or conservation status—as defined in the project's objectives, resulting in a 3D Data Model.

# Input:

* Processed point clouds / meshes from Step 6
* Historical and architectural data from Step 2
* Metadata from previous steps

# Output:

* Base 3D geometric model → .obj, .fbx, .stl, .ply, .glTF, .3ds
* Textured 3D model → .obj + .mtl + .jpg/png, .glb, .glTF
* Enriched 3D model with annotations or metadata → .ifc, .gltf, .json

concept.label: PNG
concept.definition: Portable Network Graphics (PNG, pronounced PEE-en-JEE or PING) is a raster graphics file format that supports lossless data compression. PNG was created as an improved, non-patented replacement for Graphics Interchange Format (GIF), and is the most widely used lossless image compression format on the Internet. PNG supports palette-based images (with palettes of 24-bit RGB or 32-bit RGBA colors), grayscale images (with or without alpha channel for transparency), and full-color non-palette-based RGB/RGBA images (with or without alpha channel). PNG was designed for transferring images on the Internet, not for professional-quality print graphics, and therefore does not support non-RGB color spaces such as CMYK. A PNG file contains a single image in an extensible structure of "chunks", encoding the basic pixels and other information such as textual comments and integrity checks documented in RFC 2083. PNG files nearly always use file extension PNG or png and are assigned MIME media type image/png. PNG was published as informational RFC 2083 in March 1997 and as an ISO/IEC standard in 2004.

concept.label: JPEG
concept.definition: JPEG ( JAY-peg) is a commonly used method of lossy compression for digital images, particularly for those images produced by digital photography. The degree of compression can be adjusted, allowing a selectable tradeoff between storage size and image quality. JPEG typically achieves 10:1 compression with little perceptible loss in image quality. JPEG compression is used in a number of image file formats. JPEG/Exif is the most common image format used by digital cameras and other photographic image capture devices; along with JPEG/JFIF, it is the most common format for storing and transmitting photographic images on the World Wide Web. These format variations are often not distinguished, and are simply called JPEG. The term "JPEG" is an initialism/acronym for the Joint Photographic Experts Group, which created the standard. The MIME media type for JPEG is image/jpeg, except in older Internet Explorer versions, which provides a MIME type of image/pjpeg when uploading JPEG images. JPEG files usually have a filename extension of .jpg or .jpeg. JPEG/JFIF supports a maximum image size of 65,53565,535 pixels, hence up to 4 gigapixels for an aspect ratio of 1:1.

concept.label: TIFF
concept.definition: Tagged Image File Format, abbreviated TIFF or TIF, is a computer file format for storing raster graphics images, popular among graphic artists, the publishing industry, and photographers. TIFF is widely supported by scanning, faxing, word processing, optical character recognition, image manipulation, desktop publishing, and page-layout applications. The format was created by Aldus Corporation for use in desktop publishing. It published the latest version 6.0 in 1992, subsequently updated with an Adobe Systems copyright after the latter acquired Aldus in 1994. Several Aldus or Adobe technical notes have been published with minor extensions to the format, and several specifications have been based on TIFF 6.0, including TIFF/EP (ISO 12234-2), TIFF/IT (ISO 12639), TIFF-F (RFC 2306) and TIFF-FX (RFC 3949).

concept.label: ASCII
concept.definition: ASCII abbreviated from American Standard Code for Information Interchange, is a character encoding standard for electronic communication. ASCII codes represent text in computers, telecommunications equipment, and other devices. Most modern character-encoding schemes are based on ASCII, although they support many additional characters. ASCII is the traditional name for the encoding system.

concept.label: CSV
concept.definition: A comma-separated values (CSV) file is a delimited text file that uses a comma to separate values. A CSV file stores tabular data (numbers and text) in plain text. Each line of the file is a data record. Each record consists of one or more fields, separated by commas. The use of the comma as a field separator is the source of the name for this file format. RFC 4180 formalized CSV. It defines the MIME type "text/csv", and CSV files that follow its rules should be very widely portable

label: dür.air multimodality process
description:
The dür.air application (see related items) constitutes a **workflow** in its own right, in that it encapsulates a number of activities, some of which could be regarded as a **fully-fledged workflow** in their own right (for example: photogrammetric data acquisition). Developed by Livio De Luca within the UPR 2002 MAP CNRS, dür.air operates at the intersection of heritage sciences and digital sciences, and is designed to manage data from acquisition through to publication. Through **three distinct acquisition modes** (3D by LiDAR, 3D by photogrammetry and 2D by photography), it is possible to digitise an object, process it, enrich it via spatial annotations, and save or publish it in an interoperable manner. These three modes are shown in the **illustration** using colours and an animation. The **diagram** has been designed to illustrate as clearly as possible the **relationships and specific features** of the tool in relation to these three modes. In particular, it highlights the necessary changes (*in situ vs. ex situ* as illustrated in the diagram showing the types of lines and the square brackets, round brackets or curly brackets surrounding the function names) with regard to the relationships between the various stages of a workflow. Feel free to **right-click** on the image to open it in a new tab so you can zoom in and read it whilst following the various stages of the workflow. For interface et in depth documentation see "User manual url" in metadata fields. \
This workflow is not intended to be a precise definition of implementation and usage, but rather a **general overview** of the functions and the relationships between them. In the animated illustration, the letters of the **Latin alphabet** denote the processes of acquisition, processing and enrichment relating to the three modes of dür.air acquisition and the production of data relating to a cultural artefact. The letters of the **Greek alphabet** denote the stages external to the production of the data, especially the ability to upload projects directly from the device to a node (server) specific to an institution. If the workflow **step** linked to the previous one is an iteration or a direct derivative, the numbering remains the same and **‘** / **°** / *, is then added to the letter. Finally, the type of circle for each step is link to a family of activity. \
To provide more concrete explanations of dür.air’s practical applications without limiting the potential of this **workflow-tool**, we prefer to leave it to **users** to envisage usage scenarios that correspond to their own practices. In this sense, a dür.air project may stop at the acquisition stage or extend as far as the curation of customised templates to enrich its annotations. Nevertheless, the application **use cases** (look for "see also" metadata on this page to find examples) will always fall within the scope of all the functions presented here .\
Currently in beta and distributed via an app installed on an iPad/Iphone Pro, this workflow may evolve in the futur.

relatedItems.label: dür.air - digital unfolding of reality through augmented interpretative representation
relatedItems.description:
Dür.air is a mobile augmented reality application conceived as a field-based extension of the scientific and epistemological framework developed within the n-Dame_Heritage project. Its name reflects its core ambition: the digital unfolding of reality through augmented interpretative representation — reconciling observation, interpretation, and documentation at the place and moment where scientific observation is produced, by embedding spatial, temporal, and semantic information directly within in situ investigation.   

In archaeology, conservation–restoration, architectural history, materials science, and landscape studies, knowledge emerges through situated practices: inspection, comparison, measurement, annotation, and the progressive construction of interpretative hypotheses. Where 3D digitisation often separates acquisition and interpretation in time and space, dür.air keeps geometry, semantics, and observation tightly coupled in a single mobile and autonomous environment. 

Combining persistent augmented reality tracking, real-time LiDAR sensing, and on-device photogrammetric reconstruction, the platform supports a progressive “unfolding” of the object or site — an evolving augmented representation built across successive field sessions. On a single device (currently iPad Pro or iPhone Pro with LiDAR) and without network connectivity, it covers the full chain of field documentation: annotation, structured semantic description, metric measurement, dense 3D modelling, orthophoto and profile computation, interactive analysis, and the replay of spatio-temporal observation trajectories. Geometry remains a support for interpretation, memory, and cumulative reasoning.

When connectivity is available, projects can be deposited on a server node for institutional archive, sharing, and web publication — while field work itself stays fully offline.

dür.air is developed at the CNRS MAP laboratory (UPR 2002) within the ERC project n-Dame_Heritage (ERC-2021-Advanced Grant), in connection with the Notre-Dame de Paris scientific action. Complementary support has been provided by CNRS MITI, the French Ministry of Culture, the Fondation des Sciences du Patrimoine, EquipEx+ ESPADON, and E-RIHS ERIC.

composedOf.label: α - Creation and selection of project type
composedOf.description:
*Activity outside the in situ / ex situ framework*

Creating a project is the first step in the workflow required to use dür.air in relation to the process of producing data on a cultural artefact (a material entity). Creating this project  involves a key decision: selecting the type of data acquisition. This choice is closely linked to the artefact being documented and the requirements of the project. In each mode, photography remains central, because (even in LiDAR) all enrichments (audio, metric and graphical annotations) are generated or must be produced in conjunction with a photograph.

* LiDAR (Blue path) is to be used for digitising a space. Based primarily on the digitisation of the space using a laser, the aim is to create a complete 3D scene incorporating enhancements ranging from photographs to spoken annotations, including graphical annotations based on photographs. In this sense, the choice of 3D-LiDAR does not preclude the subsequent production of photogrammetry (see step **a'**) as a specific part of the digitised space.
* Photogrammetry (Purple path) is to be used to digitise a 3D object. Based on the concept of photogrammetry, the project involves creating a 3D background scene to anchor the photogrammetry in space. The aim here is to obtain a result with the background around the object removed, whilst retaining the augmented reality visualisation capabilities offered by the application.
* Photography (Green path) is to be used to digitise a flat document. Similar to photogrammetry, the idea is to enable the documentation of a 2D document (plan, parchment, etc.) by incorporating spatialisation features, particularly for managing double-sided documents.

This stage of project creation involves two systematic and fundamental actions:
1. Choosing a project name, the first piece of metadata that structures the project
2. Creating a visual anchor (an initial photograph) to generate a thumbnail for the project, as well as a minimum number of photos to enable the application to spatialise sessions in relation to one another.

In fact, sessions are fundamental components of a dür.air project. A project is a container comprising one or more sessions, each of which contains data (photographs, annotations, attachments). A session is therefore a new digitisation iteration of the cultural artefact associated with the creation of the project. Consequently, the data associated with a session (primarily annotations) is linked to that session and does not appear in others (at least on the mobile hardware; see steps **ω** and **ω'** for reconciliation between sessions online). Sessions are therefore linked both digitally and spatially through their anchoring to the project’s metadata.
Please note that a project cannot be cross-type. If you select LiDAR when creating the project, you will inevitably have LiDAR sessions. The aim, once again, is to frame the project’s creation within a methodological choice, relating, for example, to temporal or spatial segmentation by sessions.

Finally, a session can be conducted in two modes: *in situ* and *ex situ*.
* The *in situ* mode is the method of data collection in the field. It allows users to scan, take photographs, make verbal annotations, etc. It is therefore the mode of situated observation..
* The *ex situ* mode is the method for enriching and revisiting, after the fact, the data produced on site. This mode offers the possibility of integrating, within the data-collection tool, the ability to retrieve this data in order to enrich it directly, by exploring the cultural artefact remotely (though not exclusively; we shall return to this)
