composedOf.description:
*Activity in the interface external to a project*

  The stage involving the enrichment of metadata and paradata relating to a dür.air project is an activity that can take place at any point in the workflow, but which is of significant importance to your work. Based on the W7 model with a schema tailored for the application (see related items), the dür.air project description model enables you to explore not only the issues relating to the ‘standard’ metadata of digital data production, but also to incorporate documentation of the various micro-activities within the dür.air macro-activity.
  * What documents the cultural artefact and the data produced during the various project sessions
  * Why covers the scopes and stakes of the activity and institutional framework relating to the dür.air project
  * Who describes the individuals who participated in the dür.air project
  * When describes the timeline of the digitisation activity (*in situ*)
  * Where describes the location of the digitisation activity (*in situ*)
  * How documents the research protocol in terms of its quantitative and qualitative characteristics.
  * Which documents the tools that enabled the activity in the broadest sense. Obviously, this includes the iPad or iPhone (hardware) and its specifications, the software (its version, etc.), but also external elements used alongside the main tool during the dür.air activity, such as a lighting system or supports installed around an object.

  Many of the fields in the metadata schema are populated automatically by the application and with data retrieved natively during a session, such as the location, which is linked to the tablet’s GPS position.

concept.label: Preservation Metadata
concept.definition: information that supports and documents acts of preservation on digital materials (Wikidata contributors, "Q7241044," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q7241044&oldid=1202709309 (accessed July 30, 2020).

relatedItems.label: Create a W7 metadata schema
relatedItems.description:
The purpose of this workflow is to describe the production of a **metadata and paradata** schema based on the **W7 description model**. The transcription framework is specific to the implementation of French research projects and is designed to facilitate the use of a tool developed for and by the W7: namely the EquipEX+ Espadon and the **Anamnesis** application (see the "related items" section). Through ongoing experiments, the aim was to formalise the support procedures for the creation and structuring of a metadata and paradata schema specific to **instrumentation** and/or **analysis** techniques in heritage science and digital science.    
The transcription presented here is intended as a proposal for greater generality and reproducibility based on four case studies involving various institutions and key individuals.  This page is a simplified version (both visually and textually) of the detailed workflow (see the ‘User Manual URL’ field). The various sub-steps that make up the main stages have been grouped together to facilitate a general understanding of the key stages of the method.


This workflow therefore documents the creation of a metadata schema, starting from the ground up and as closely as possible to **actual practice**, with a view to using the Anamnesis platform. In this sense, it became apparent that the most impactful “Ws” centered on the “How” (enabling the description of the various actions within an activity) and the “Which” (enabling the description of the tools and settings for the outputs), with the other “Ws” often being more marginal and exhibiting less variability.


Currently structured through an approach involving **cycles of interviews** over time between a technique specialist and a curator,  this chain of actions now allows schemas to be produced in a relatively short time, without considering acculturation to the W7 model, metadata and paradata challenges (which may vary from case to case).

composedOf.label: a - 3D Acquisition by LiDAR
composedOf.description:
*In situ activity only*

  A 3D LiDAR session (of a space) therefore begins after the initial photo has been taken, by accessing the main acquisition interface in dür.air. From this point onwards, you are *in situ*. The hardware’s LiDAR operates continuously until the session is closed, scanning the view from the tablet. It is important not to move too quickly; take your time to scan the spaces slowly.

  Don’t forget to enhance your session by taking additional photos, videos (step **e**), audio annotations (step **g**), or even graphic annotations (step **h**) directly. Each of these functions is available in the *in situ* LiDAR session.

  Please note that it is not possible to add photos (the only method for adding annotations) or videos in the *ex situ* mode of a session. To do this, you will need to carry out a new *in situ* session within the same project, but by ‘restarting’ the scanning of your space. A visual reconciliation of this data is possible, but only via upload to the application’s server node (see steps **ω** and **ω'**).

  Multi-session data acquisition can, for example, enable you to segment your space. Another approach is to carry out an initial general session using LiDAR and a few photographs, followed by subsequent sessions focusing on more specific areas, incorporating, for example, photogrammetry of an object within the space.

concept.label: Scanning
concept.definition: process of creating digital images with a scanner (Wikidata contributors, "Q59155052," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q59155052&oldid=1184040702 (accessed July 30, 2020).

composedOf.label: a' - Photo(grammetric) acquisition
composedOf.description:
*In situ activity only*

  This step, which forms an extension of the LiDAR data acquisition process, should simply be seen as a reminder of the possibility of enhancing a LiDAR scene using photographs and, consequently, photogrammetry. The aim here is therefore not to carry out photogrammetry of a very large LiDAR area, but of a specific portion of a scene: a wall in a room, a column in a church nave, or a sculpture in a museum gallery. The objective of this stage is thus to capture a space and an object within it as a unit necessary for structuring scientific observation.

concept.label: Photographing
concept.definition: art, science, and practice of creating durable images by recording light or other electromagnetic radiation (Wikidata contributors, "Q11633," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q11633&oldid=1237597469 (accessed July 30, 2020).

composedOf.label: b - 3D Acquisition by Photogrammetry
composedOf.description:
*In situ activity only*

  A 3D photogrammetry session (of an object) begins after the initial photograph has been taken, by accessing the main dür.air scanning interface. From this point onwards, you are therefore *in situ*. You can then start taking photographs and carry out your scan. Whether you are using a matrix, rotational or other method, bear in mind that the scan session you are carrying out will be finalised once you switch to *ex situ* mode; it is therefore better to take too many photos than not enough, as you will be able to select which photos to include in your photogrammetry calculation if some are of poor quality.

  Please note that it is not possible to add photos (the only way to add annotations) or video to a session whilst in *ex situ* mode. To do this, you will need to carry out a new *in situ* session within the same project, but by ‘restarting’ the digitisation of your object.

  Feel free to take additional photos during your data collection, including documentary photos (i.e. wide-angle shots of the object), as these general-view photos will be useful for the graphical annotation of features that extend beyond the frame of a photo taken within the workflow of a photogrammetric matrix (which is likely to be zoomed in and fragmented). Without these photos, you will have to crop your annotations from each individual photo depicting the phenomenon.

concept.label: Photographing
concept.definition: art, science, and practice of creating durable images by recording light or other electromagnetic radiation (Wikidata contributors, "Q11633," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q11633&oldid=1237597469 (accessed July 30, 2020).

composedOf.label: b' - Automated acquisition
composedOf.description:
*In situ activity only*

  Automatic capture in 3D photogrammetry mode is a feature designed to simplify your workflow and eliminate the need to take photos manually. Dür.air automatically detects the tablet’s movements in space to generate an efficient shot that meets the overlap requirements for a photogrammetric scan.

  Take care not to move too quickly and to remain relatively steady to ensure the best possible photo quality. Also try to keep in mind the path around the object so that you can mentally visualise which areas have already been documented and which remain to be photographed.

  Once completed, you will be given the option to calculate the mesh directly from your scan or to postpone this calculation until later.

concept.label: Photographing
concept.definition: art, science, and practice of creating durable images by recording light or other electromagnetic radiation (Wikidata contributors, "Q11633," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q11633&oldid=1237597469 (accessed July 30, 2020).

composedOf.label: c - 2D acquisition session by photo
composedOf.description:
*In situ activity only*

  A 2D photo-based session (of a planar object) therefore begins after the initial photo has been taken, when you access the main dür.air interface. From this point onwards, you are *in situ*. You can then start taking your photographs. Bear in mind that the acquisition session you are carrying out will be finalised once you switch to *ex situ* mode, so it is better to take too many photos than not enough.

  Please note that it is not possible to add photos (the only way to add annotations) or video to a session whilst in *ex situ* mode. To do this, you will need to start a new *in situ* session within the same project, but by ‘restarting’ the digitisation of your object.

concept.label: Photographing
concept.definition: art, science, and practice of creating durable images by recording light or other electromagnetic radiation (Wikidata contributors, "Q11633," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q11633&oldid=1237597469 (accessed July 30, 2020).

composedOf.label: c' & c* - Photo acquisition by straightening & mosaic
composedOf.description:
*In situ activity only*

These two specific capture modes for 2D enhance the digitisation process for 2D elements. Accessible on the right-hand side of the main interface in AR mode, these two specific modes allow, in the first instance, a photo to be taken and rectified using a graphical interface that adjusts the angles of the element to be rectified so that it lies flat.
The second, mosaic mode, displays a capture grid to facilitate the capture of an item too large to be captured in a single photograph, thereby allowing the document to be divided into several photographs which are subsequently automatically stitched together to form a complete representation with the "same" high quality as the original document.

Less optional than the respective 3D modes, these two types of capture should really be seen as key stages in a 2D workflow, in that they offer significant added value when it comes to capturing information in 2D.

concept.label: Photographing
concept.definition: art, science, and practice of creating durable images by recording light or other electromagnetic radiation (Wikidata contributors, "Q11633," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q11633&oldid=1237597469 (accessed July 30, 2020).

composedOf.label: d - 3D view screenshot
composedOf.description:
*Ex situ activity only*

  The screenshot stage, which is specific to 3D acquisition modes, should be regarded as a stage for documenting the three-dimensional data and the application’s 3D viewer. In this sense, this function – which, technically speaking, is ultimately ‘merely’ the emulation of a standard device screenshot – serves the scientific purpose of incorporating, within the data structure of a project, the documentation of point clouds and meshes as a distinct body of knowledge within the dür.air project. This data forms part of the dür.air repository and is not third-party data stored in an external library. Thus, this function does not capture the application interface, but only the three-dimensional representation of the cultural artefact. You will be required to end your session *in situ* and initiate the session *ex situ* in order to use this function. It is therefore a relatively late stage in a workflow, but one which, compared to many others, has virtually no prerequisites.

concept.label: Screencast
concept.definition: digital recording of computer screen output (Wikidata contributors, "Q1365447," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q1365447&oldid=1234996090 (accessed September 4, 2020).

composedOf.label: e - Video capture
composedOf.description:
*In situ activity only*

  Video capture, specific to 3D acquisition modes, allows a video of the space in which the acquisition is taking place to be incorporated into a dür.air project and a specific session. Whilst it is not possible to annotate a video, it does allow you to record either a moving activity within the space or to document a large area more quickly, without needing to perform a precise LiDAR scan, or in conjunction with photogrammetry.\
An interesting feature is the reprojection of the tablet’s location into 3D space, which helps to understand and pinpoint the observer’s viewpoint within the 3D scene.

composedOf.label: f & f' - Pointcloud & mesh cleaning
composedOf.description:
*Ex situ activity only & Hybrid activity*

As this is intrinsically linked to LiDAR operations and the generation of a dense point cloud, the ability to clean up a point cloud via the 3D interface in *ex situ* mode allows data processing to be carried out directly via the hardware to remove data from the laser scan that was organically acquired within the scene but is irrelevant and may obscure the understanding of a scene. The aim is therefore to clean up the precise scanning area of the cultural artefact.

Consequently, but at a different data level, mesh cleaning follows the same logic as point cloud cleaning. Inevitably linked to 3D activities, the ability to clean a mesh via the 3D interface in *ex situ* mode allows a processing task to be carried out on the tablet to remove data from the mesh produced by a photogrammetric survey, data which is irrelevant and may obscure the understanding of a scene. The aim is therefore to clean up the precise viewing area of the cultural artefact. This step can be of fundamental importance in the workflow, particularly in the context of orthophotography production, where the fringes of a photogrammetric survey can sometimes produce aberrations that will be visible on an orthophoto if this processing stage is not carried out.

composedOf.label: g - Audio annotation
composedOf.description:
*Hybrid activity*

  Oral annotation is a key function in the process of enriching a 3D scene in dür.air. This feature, available *in situ* and *ex situ*, should be viewed as a form of graphical annotation linked not to an area, but to a point, defined by the centre of your photograph’s frame. This stage of the process can be carried out like a field survey using a voice recorder, but the information is spatially anchored to a representation of an artefact.\
The aim here is to be able to enrich the record of observations about the object, primarily during acquisition (but possibly afterwards as well). Based on the principle of voice dictation and speech-to-text technology, the annotation will then generate a photo to spatially anchor the annotation and attach the audio track and its textual transcription to it. This automatic transcription can, moreover, be edited manually if any errors are found.

concept.label: Audio Recording
concept.definition: mechanical or digital record of a series of audio events (Wikidata contributors, "Q3302947," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q3302947&oldid=1254901544 (accessed September 4, 2020).

concept.label: Audio Annotation
concept.definition: Wikidata contributors, "Q98847703," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q98847703&oldid=1270667708 (accessed September 4, 2020).

composedOf.label: h - Graphic & metric annotation
composedOf.description:
*Hybrid activity*

Graphical and metric annotation is just as important a function as verbal annotation in the process of enriching a dür.air scene. More demanding (in that it requires more than simply dictating), this activity draws on the principles of condition assessment traditionally employed in the documentation of cultural artefacts.\
A graphical annotation is necessarily linked to a photograph; although LiDAR mode offers a method for graphical annotation directly in *in situ* mode—giving the feeling of annotating a 3D object—it is in fact a photograph that is generated from the viewpoint at the origin of the annotation. The reasoning behind this choice is simple: a photograph does not change, whereas a point cloud does. By anchoring annotations to viewpoints that are fixed in time, we ensure the stability of the annotations, regardless of whether the scene or the artefact changes subsequently. In this sense, the reprojection of an annotation from 2D (an image) to 3D (the model) is all the more effective as the images overlap (particularly for spherical objects) and facilitate a step-by-step transfer from one image to another.

A 3D photogrammetry session will inevitably need to be carried out in *ex situ* mode in order to be enhanced with graphical annotations. Here, the approach is to base the *in situ* assessment on photogrammetry, focusing primarily on audio annotations. In a LiDAR session, the concept of capturing phenomena within an area on the fly, in an *in situ* manner, mirrors the way audio annotation works for the 3D photogrammetry session (which will, incidentally, include photos of the object from every angle), in that it allows a fragment of space to be captured – possibly without a photo – from a session based primarily on laser data, without photogrammetric acquisition.

Available via 2D mode and by selecting a photo, metric annotations  and graphical annotations are all tools that enable, respectively, the measurement of an object and the semantic enrichment of information relating to the identification of an element (deterioration, composition, morphology, temporality, third-party techniques such as sampling, etc.) . The aim here is to use manual annotation by emulating the act of drawing directly within the tool. At the same time, the use of colours as an initial form of segmentation—by naming a colour that then becomes a label—enables the enriched information about the artefact to be categorised and organised. A graphical annotation also incorporates descriptors (surface, colourimetry, etc.), a summary of which by class/colour is accessible in the annotation panel, to automatically provide details relating to the condition assessment that can be included in a report (see step **γ**)

concept.label: Visual Annotation
concept.definition: Wikidata contributors, "Q98847784," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q98847784&oldid=1270668347 (accessed September 4, 2020).

composedOf.label: i - Semantic enrichment
composedOf.description:
*Hybrid activity*

Each graphical annotation is accompanied by a description sheet that can be edited or even customised (see step **ε**). The aim of this step is to go beyond simply defining a graphical area associated with a colour, and to enrich the semantics underlying the spatial definition of an element observed on an artefact. The information provided, the level of precision, the complexity and the organisation of the data are not fixed; it is up to each user to experiment and organise their annotations as they see fit to reflect their specific observation of the artefact.

Thus, each annotation can, independently, be supplemented first with a title – the first level of enrichment – and then with an attachment (a report, a technical photograph, a text) that spatially incorporates third-party data into the dür.air scene. However, it is also possible to choose from a number of pre-existing templates loaded natively into the application, or by downloading templates shared by users (see step **ω°**), for example with a view to standardising a particular method of description. This approach to enrichment, tailored to the needs of a specific workflow, allows annotations to be used in a variety of ways.\
The enrichment structure then takes the following minimal form: a colour and its title > an annotation title > a template specific to the annotation

composedOf.label: j - General textual annotation
composedOf.description:
*Hybrid activity*

This type of annotation, specific to a 2D scene (whether acquired via mosaicking or orthorectification), stems from the challenges of graphical annotation and its semantic enrichment. It offers the possibility of adding general enrichment to a document representation, created within a dür.air project, across the entire document without having to add an annotation to the whole photograph and its representations.

composedOf.label: k - Reconstruction & 3D alignment
composedOf.description:
*Hybrid activity*

  3D reconstruction and alignment follow on from photogrammetric data acquisition in that they represent the stage in the workflow where the algorithmic processes for ‘assembling’ the photographs are applied to generate the point cloud and the mesh derived by dür.air. The quality of the mesh should be seen as enhancing the visualisation derived from a dense point cloud, made possible by the quality of the object’s digitisation. Whilst this stage is therefore not mandatory, it offers genuine added value in terms of a detailed, three-dimensional understanding of the artefact.

  It is possible to choose which photographs to include in the dataset used for the calculation, whilst selecting the expected quality level, background masking and the sequencing quality of the acquisition to facilitate a successful calculation. In this sense, dür.air remains an experimental application, suited to a scientific approach, sometimes involving trial-and-error sequences to achieve the desired result, depending on the context, the object, the time available, and the overall workflow relating to the cultural artefact. A mesh can be cleaned up, deleted and recalculated as many times as necessary, regardless of whether the annotations are made before or after its calculation. This is why the photographs serve as anchors for the spatialisation of the mesh, irrespective of the 3D visualisation medium used (mesh or Gaussian splatting).

concept.label: Transformation
concept.definition: process involving change into a qualitatively different form (Wikidata contributors, "Q65757353," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q65757353&oldid=1268189392 (accessed September 4, 2020).

composedOf.label: l - Orthophoto creation
composedOf.description:
*Ex situ activity only*

The creation of an orthophoto is an advanced stage in a dür.air workflow, not only because it can only be utilised (in an operational output) after a mesh calculation has been carried out, but also because it must be designed and integrated into a workflow, taking into account the type of object and a specific requirement (such as generating a ‘plan’ of an area or the geometry of a façade, for example). Naturally, these requirements are linked to a specific data acquisition workflow. The orthophoto-related activities and functions can manipulate the object along its three axes (X, Y, Z) to generate new ‘cameras’ within the scene’s 3D space, based on the viewpoint defined during the framing and generation of the orthophoto. It is then possible to annotate an orthophoto and see these annotations reprojected onto the other photos and onto the 3D object. However, we would like to warn you: this function is unstable in that it depends heavily on the object’s geometry, and the reprojection may therefore malfunction. If you are incorporating the orthophoto into your workflow, we encourage you not to base your entire annotation process on this medium, but to include wide-angle photos in parallel.

This stage can also simply be seen as a means of producing external documentation to facilitate subsequent enrichment. Thus, the workflow is not primarily intended for comprehensive enrichment within dür.air, but rather for using the latter as a mobile application to generate interoperable data (see stage **δ**)

This function also provides an opportunity to specify all the available 3D cross-section mechanisms (here, but also in the 3D visualisation modes of the dür.air scene), which enable the challenges of point cloud and mesh cleaning to be simulated (steps **f** and **f'**), as they allow the definition of a cross-section plane to remove unwanted elements. This also allows for the integration of section generation for hollow objects whose centres have been scanned.

concept.label: Transformation
concept.definition: process involving change into a qualitatively different form (Wikidata contributors, "Q65757353," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q65757353&oldid=1268189392 (accessed September 4, 2020).

composedOf.label: m - Gaussian splatting render
composedOf.description:
*Hybrid activity*

The Gaussian splatting rendering task is a step that occurs at the end of the production chain in the workflow (see the *diagram*), in that this task enriches the project with a specific rendering following acquisition. The quality is finer and more versatile than that of a mesh, particularly in its ability to visualise transparent materials, reflections, etc. This activity is intrinsically linked to a specific preceding workflow in dür.air relating to certain cultural artefacts.

The benefit of anchoring annotations – and, more generally, the semantic layer – to a photograph means that this rendering stage need not necessarily to precede enrichment, but rather serves as an opportunity to enhance the diversity of representations depicting a cultural artefact. Thus, in the same way that a mesh can be calculated, removed and recalculated according to specific parameters, rendering options allow you to enhance the quality of artefact representation in the application’s 3D viewer. The independent annotation enrichment layer will simply be superimposed (or interwoven, depending on your epistemological perspective) onto the visualisation mode you choose when exploring your data. The geometric quality therefore remains unchanged.

A number of parameters are available to enable a user to construct a representation of the model that is of interest for enhancing their dür.air project. The tool’s internal capability for Gaussian splatting, along with its configuration, as an additional layer of information, should be viewed as a combinatorial process that draws upon the various representations of the artefact’s digitisation—not as an end in itself, but as an epistemic capacity to draw upon a particular type of representation and a particular type of data to make a specific contribution to the workflow of a complete dür.air activity.

concept.label: Transformation
concept.definition: process involving change into a qualitatively different form (Wikidata contributors, "Q65757353," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q65757353&oldid=1268189392 (accessed September 4, 2020).

composedOf.label: n - Semantic concept extraction & detection
composedOf.description:
*Hybrid activity*

This final activity in the internal workflow of a dür.air project or session should be regarded as a specific, advanced form of curation and enrichment. Whilst it is not particularly complex – in that it merely involves the automatic detection of terms within fields – its conceptual scope is very significant.

Indeed, it is possible, within the annotation fields (graphics and audio), to extract terms based on shared vocabularies (see step **ω***) and thus, in view of generating a dür.air project’s knowledge graph (see step **ω'**), to establish connections between a project’s semantic enrichment and a repository of standardised terms. From the project’s perspective, the benefit may lie in creating or importing a thesaurus specific to your field of work, so that you can utilise it in your semantic enrichment and thus work with terms common to your disciplinary field. For the data produced, the benefit lies in contributing, whilst carrying out your work as normal, to broadening the scope of your work and its ability to align with and be interoperable if/when you wish to retrieve your data outside the dür.air ecosystem.

composedOf.label: β - Session deletion
composedOf.description:
*Ex situ activity only, relating to the external interface of a project*

This deletion function, which is highly specific and hybrid in that it can be carried out within the *ex situ* interface whilst having an impact on project management within the project’s external interface, is a way of using dür.air’s features to organise your files differently.

It is therefore possible to delete a session if it is of no interest, or even if it causes problems in the organisation of the project’s data. The benefit of a tool such as dür.air is, in our view, that it offers the possibility of producing a coherent, ‘archive-ready’ data container. We therefore consider the curation capability offered here to be essential, particularly as it also allows you to manipulate a project to split its sessions. If you save your ‘.durair’ exchange file (see step **δ**), you can then delete all but one session from a project, so that instead of having one project with four sessions/temporal states for an artefact, you have four projects, with one session per temporal state (by importing the initial file several times and deleting the various sessions in each project). Whether for a state-by-state description of metadata, a specific export requirement, or any other purpose, this function allows you to manipulate ‘.durair’ files.

  Please note that the ‘fusion’ function is not available (at present), so please do remember to keep your original file before deleting anything.

composedOf.label: γ - Report writing
composedOf.description:
*Activity in the external project interface*

Once a project and all related activities have been completed, you can generate a report based on all the information produced during the project. The benefit of the container-based approach, which centralises a set of information, becomes clear, as you can then access a range of data produced within your project (see diagram).

The aim, once again, is to centralise the production of knowledge and data within a workflow tool designed to meet the needs of situated observation, where report writing is often the end goal. We wanted to make the process as straightforward as possible and have integrated, within an LLM embedded in the hardware, the ability to query metadata (see step **α'**) and annotations (both geometric and semantic; see step **h**), by generating text based on the agent’s previous efforts. All the preliminary steps and their integration serve as an incentive here to encourage agents to enrich their general workflow with real-time data and a specific workflow using dür.air.

This step can therefore be seen as the synthesis of a project involving photos, models (see step **d**), annotation areas – in short, a process of curating and editing the data produced

concept.label: Writing
concept.definition: writing designates the activity of creating new texts (instead of capturing existing text). Here, it primarily concerns research papers and reports, but may include other textually-oriented objects.

composedOf.label: δ - Save & export
composedOf.description:
*Activity in the external project interface*

This dual function of saving and exporting is fundamental in that it puts the *F* and *I* elements of the FAIR principle into practice. Indeed, whilst the application is linked to specific hardware, all the data produced can be exported in open formats that can be explored outside the application, allowing you to extend your workflow beyond dür.air

A dür.air export is organised around a project and the sessions it contains. Each session then contains the *digital entities* relating to the data produced by that session.

We will not go into detail here regarding the list of all formats for each digital entity (see the **diagram** and each **DE**), but bear in mind that the DE° incorporates (almost) all of the data produced, the key aspects of which are as follows:

  **DE¹** – scene: contains all the 3D spatial reference frames for a scene, as well as the metadata for this specific DE

  **DE¹** – trajectory: contains data showing the various actions, their spatial locations and their timing during the session’s *in situ* activity.

  **DE²** – screenshot: contains all the screenshots from a session

  **DE³** – video: contains all the videos, their spatial trajectories, and the metadata for this specific DE

  **DE⁴** – audio: contains the audio files, text transcripts and metadata for this specific DE

  **DE⁵** – photo: contains the photographs, all the data required for photogrammetry and the metadata for this specific DE

  **DE⁶** – mesh: contains the mesh data and metadata for this specific DE

  **DE⁷** - ortho: contains the orthophotos and metadata for this specific DE

  **DE⁸** - template: contains the customised templates used in a session

  **DE⁹** - annotation: contains the spatial and semantic reference frames, as well as the initial anchor image for the annotation, for each annotation in a session

  **DE¹⁰** – gsplat: contains the Gaussian splatting models associated with a session’s model

  **DE¹¹** – w7_memos: contains the meta- and paradata document detailing the project

  **DE¹²** – report: contains all reports relating to the project

One of the two unexported digital entities is the **DE¹³** (durair_exchange_file), which is the file used to import a project onto third-party hardware or to load a previously deleted project (see step **β**). This backup step is essential, as bugs, crashes or hardware failure are possible, and as long as the files have not been extracted from the hardware, there is no way to recover them. We therefore strongly recommend that you incorporate the backup of this file into your workflow using a third-party device (computer, external hard drive, server, etc.) to ensure its long-term preservation. This file will (unless specifically stated otherwise in the future) always be compatible with another version of dür.air and/or other hardware running the application.

composedOf.label: ε - Template creation
composedOf.description:
*Activity in the external project interface*

Creating a template for the customised enhancement of a graphical annotation (see step **h**) is an advanced stage of the workflow. It involves, as part of the overall process, the creation of a personalised standardisation of the information to be entered based on the annotation, and therefore requires a significant level of knowledge regarding the issues relating to the cultural artefact. A template can be added to or modified within an annotation at any stage of the annotation’s lifecycle.

It is impossible to anticipate all the different uses and requirements for your data enrichment; however, we can guide you on how to use these templates:

*At field level*
  1. For standardised data, if, for example, you know whether or not a piece of information is present, you can create a Boolean field so that you can select ‘yes’ or ‘no’ in your annotation, rather than entering the value manually
  2. The same applies to fixed values, using a drop-down menu which will standardise terms and prevent inconsistencies or typing errors
  3. You can also use fields to include a link if, for example, you wish to refer to an external database containing data related to an annotation
  4. You can add a date field to specify the timeframe of an annotation
  5. You can include note fields, allowing you to dictate text within a graphical annotation

  *At the template level*
  1. You can use the template to describe not what you observe on the object, but what has been done and how, alongside your digitisation work (a sample taken, a survey, an advanced technique such as an infrared survey, etc.).
  2. You can also use the template as a metadata micro-record specific to an item within a collection.

Bear in mind that this step may influence how you will use dür.air. Whilst this should not be seen as a constraint, giving this stage some thought can help you better prepare the steps and procedures for using dür.air. What you should or should not do during an *in situ* stage, or what other techniques should be employed depending on the information you wish to include in your scene, may be guided by the design of the templates, taking into account your entire workflow relating to an artefact.

composedOf.label: ω - dür.air node connection
composedOf.description:
*Activity in the external project interface*

This function, which can be accessed via the app’s settings, is – although particularly quick, as it simply involves pressing a button and entering an email address – very important to understand within the overall workflow of a project. Whilst so far we have only discussed actions that can be carried out locally on the hardware without a connection, from this stage onwards we connect the hardware to the server node where your user account is authenticated.

The idea here is to enable you to view your data outside the proprietary hardware on which the data is inevitably generated – unless you use the interoperability options in step **δ**, which, however, do not allow for data reconciliation identical to what can be viewed on the hardware itself. The connection to the node seeks to mitigate this issue by offering you access to a set of services external to the hardware, aimed at linking data with its producers – or, more specifically, at linking producers via data that has been made public and accessible.

The server node concept should be understood as the decentralisation of storage and the empowerment of institutions, in that the deployment of a node, its administration and its connection to agents’ hardware (in conjunction with the institution) form an integral part of the dür.air service solution. The aim is to establish sovereignty over data production by enabling an agent, in conjunction with their institution, to retain control over their data, whilst offering them the possibility of making it public and accessible to as many people as possible very quickly within the data lifecycle, and as an integral part of the tool’s workflow.

composedOf.label: ω' - Project upload
composedOf.description:
*Activity in the external project interface*

In relation to the node connection stage, uploading a project allows you, once you have connected to a node, to upload your data to the internet.

Once the process is complete, the choice between private and public viewing rests with the data producer via their own hardware, bearing in mind that they can share a private project via a link. An upload can be revoked at any time.

The clear aim here is to speed up the process of sharing the data produced, and even to move towards a collaborative way of working, in the sense that it becomes possible to work on a site, upload a project and ask a colleague in the office to assess the data, identify any gaps, etc., whilst another data acquisition begins. Of course, the process of visualisation and communication is also a key consideration, because if your project is online, you can easily embed a link or a QR code in a presentation or an article to provide a synchronous view of your work and your data (see an example [here](https://durair.map.cnrs.fr/view/EE4A01AB-79DC-43DC-B283-34F6E5549A85_quasimodo_2026-06-02T14-26-29))

Furthermore, the upload is not intended to replace the hardware’s own functions. The addition of annotations from the server is currently under consideration, in the sense that, in our view, the hardware should retain all functions relating to production and enrichment, whilst leaving visualisation, sharing and online storage to the server. Thus, you can see that in the linked project, all sessions are visible together. This is why we referred to ‘reconciliation enabled by the server’, as it is possible to view the different sessions of a project together in a single view. This is a major strength, as it allows you to view an entire annotation corpus regardless of the sessions in which the annotations were produced.

During the upload, an invisible process also takes place: the generation of the knowledge graph of located observations (based on the our home (MiKADO) ontology). This graph, whose structure is currently evolving, is only visible on the online interface. Its purpose is to represent the 3D scene and its enrichment semantically in two dimensions. In this sense, it links the taking of a photograph to its subjects, its annotations and spatial regions. It reveals previously invisible connections and represents a significant epistemological challenge for us. Whilst it has no bearing on the user—as it is generated automatically from the information provided and the steps carried out in the user’s workflow—its richness is therefore closely linked to the commitment of data producers to their dür.air projects. For example: if you have used an annotation template containing terms semantically linked to a thesaurus, nodes will appear in the graph to connect identical terms with the corresponding thesaurus entries.

As regards updates, if a project is updated on the hardware, a specific symbol (an arrow inside a circle) will appear, indicating that the project needs to be uploaded again as it has been updated. It is not currently possible to work collaboratively on the same file, but it is possible to share a project so that another person can work on an uploaded project on their own hardware.

composedOf.label: ω* & ω° - Thesaurus & template download
composedOf.description:
*Activity in the external project interface*

Connecting to the node does more than simply allow a project to be made public. In fact, it connects the user and their hardware to a data repository linked to the node, which can be accessed on the hardware.

Thesauri (see step **m**) and templates (see step **ε**) are downloadable data sets that can be integrated very easily into a dür.air project. The aim here is to encourage the creation of a community of agents who may work with shared repositories, or who wish to share best practice with the community. As a corollary to project sharing, this function should be viewed as a meta-step within a workflow, in that it does not directly aim at the production of data but rather at aligning it with practices that extend beyond those of a specific user.

Naturally, the administrators of a node have the ability and responsibility to populate their node’s databases with vocabularies specific to their institution. This also applies to templates that have been pre-structured or created on the ground to meet a specific need. Once again, decentralisation via the nodes thus offers flexibility and the capacity for almost immediate action between the person producing the data and the person responsible for its curation.

composedOf.label: ζ - Project Sharing
composedOf.description:
*Activity in the server node interface*

  This final feature is the ability to grant access (or request access) to a project made public on the node, and thus to be able to download it. Whilst this is already possible manually at present (see step **δ** followed by an import onto third-party hardware), the aim here is to introduce a concept of large-scale collaboration into the way we work on dür.air, by offering an agent the possibility not only to view the data produced, but also to be able to access a project in order to enrich it. We are thinking here in terms of interdisciplinary challenges, by simplifying the process of connecting agents, sites and activities via an online interface.

  This feature, which is still at an experimental stage, represents for us the final stage of a workflow on dür.air, as it offers others the opportunity to take ownership of the project and enrich it further: by creating a new session, adding annotations to an existing session, or building on its templates, etc. This therefore marks the beginning of ‘a new chapter’ for a project and a renewed exploration of the entire diagram in terms of the activities that will be carried out on this scientific material.

label: Encode and modelize field surveys for their online          dissemination
description: A researcher wants to preserve and to give access to field surveys and their related materials. Indeed, to provide a consistent context and make the reuse of raw data easier, the documentation has to include not only field materials but also documents about the research process steps, that's to say the preparation of the survey (research project, funding file, etc.), the field collection (interviews, field notebooks, etc.) and the data analysis (summary sheets, drafts, etc.). This corpus can thus cover a great variety of media (paper, digital, picture, audio or video records...) and is organised according to a classification plan. It is supposed that people interested have agreed that data will be made public available (potentially with some restrictions).

relatedItems.label: Organize, describe and conserve the oral sources
relatedItems.description:
Implement preservation measures as soon as field production is complete. Conservation is not a deferred activity: decisions taken at this stage determine the long-term accessibility and integrity of the source.

1. Organise and name files systematically: apply a consistent file-naming convention that reflects the project, the date, and the session identifier. Store files in a structured directory that mirrors the relationship between the field recording sheet and the individual document sheets. Keep all documents produced in a single recording event together.
2. Create preservation copies: produce at minimum: one high-resolution preservation copy (WAV/BWF, 96 kHz, 24-bit for audio; MPEG-4 AVC for video); one local copy on a redundant storage medium (NAS or equivalent); one off-site copy in a secure, trusted cloud repository. Optionally produce a lower-resolution access copy (MP3 or equivalent) for consultation purposes. Never delete original analogue supports after digitisation.
3. Add preservation metadata: attach to each digitised document the following preservation metadata: original support type and conservation state; playback equipment and technical parameters used for digitisation; digital format, codec, sampling rate, bit depth; software and operator information; date of digitisation. Preserve scans or photographs of original physical supports and their containers.
4. Digitise analogue supports (if applicable): for recordings on magnetic tape, vinyl, cylinders, or other analogue media, contract a specialist digitisation centre with documented expertise (public or private). Follow IASA TC-04 for audio and IASA TC-06 for video. The preservation copy must be a faithful transfer of the original signal: introduce no filtering, noise reduction, or signal enhancement. Retain the analogue original after digitisation.
5. Describe sources for discovery and access: describe each oral source within a network of relations: link the recording to its field recording sheet, to the research project, to the agents involved (interviewer, interviewee, archivist), and to any related documents. Use controlled vocabularies and authority files. Consult descriptive software in use at reference institutions (see "Vademecum"). Align description with Dublin Core or EAD standards where applicable, to support interoperability.
6. Identify or select a conservation institution: if you are an independent researcher or a small institution, identify a conservation centre suited to your collection by disciplinary affinity or geographic proximity. Prepare: (a) a project presentation sheet; (b) a transfer sheet specifying access conditions, use restrictions, reproduction rights, and loan terms. Transfer the collection in its entirety: avoid splitting a unified archival complex across multiple institutions.
7. Plan for refresh and format migration: digitisation alone does not guarantee long-term access. Establish a schedule for periodic refresh (copying files to new storage supports before degradation) and for format migration (moving files to new formats before obsolescence). If the collection is deposited in a conservation centre, clearly define which institution or department is responsible for carrying out these long-term preservation operations.

relatedItems.label: jpylyzer
relatedItems.description:
Jpylyzer is a validator and feature extractor for JP2 images. JP2 is the still image format that is defined by Part 1 of the JPEG 2000 image compression standard (ISO/IEC 15444-1).

Jpylyzer tells you if a JP2 image really conforms to the format’s specifications (validation). It also reports the image’s technical characteristics (feature extraction).

Starting with version 2.2, Jpylyzer also supports High Throughput JPEG 2000 (HTJ2K) and its JPH format, which is defined by Part 15 of the standard (ISO/IEC 15444-15).

Jpylyzer can validate raw image codestreams as well.

composedOf.label: Anonymize

Firstly, it has to be noticed that pre-planning and agreeing with participants before collecting data or during the consent process, on what may and may not be recorded or transcribed, can be a much more effective way of handling sensitive data and easier than spending time later removing it from a recording or transcript. Do the anonymization on file copies: use repositionable tapes for paper documents and XML markers for digital documents.

relatedItems.label: Anonymising Research Data
relatedItems.description: This document outlines some thoughts and discussions we have been having about strategies of anonymisation of data to be collected through the ESRC / NCRM Real Life Methods Node Connected Lives project1. It is commonplace for social science research to adopt a policy of 'blanket anonymisation', whereby all names, places and other identifying features are disguised across a data set, including from interview transcripts, diaries and field notes. Here, I consider the practical and theoretical implications of such a strategy and suggest that anonymisation is not a process to be conducted -- and assumed completed -- at just one stage of the research process. Moreover, anonymisation strategies cannot be separated out from other methodological (such as issues around archiving or mixing methods) or indeed substantive issues (such as enabling deeper appreciation of the relationality of networks, or the ways in which space might be constructed). The implications of whatever anonymisation strategy researchers adopt on the future ability to appreciate the social and spatial processes behind networks, neighbourhoods and communities, need to be made clear throughout the research process. In summation, this document argues for a more reflexive, iterative approach to anonymisation and confidential that situates these, and other ethical concerns, in the context of the social process.

relatedItems.label: Research ethical guidelines and anonymity
relatedItems.description: That researchers should give anonymity to research sites and to the individuals involved in research is usually taken as an ethical norm. Such a norm is embodied internationally in most of the ethical guidelines and codes of practice of the various educational, sociological and psychological research associations and societies. This paper challenges this assumption on the basis that it is usually impossible to ensure anonymity and that it is often undesirable to try to do so.

label: EOSC Service Providers Maturity Model
description:
*This is a draft workflow* 

The Service Providers Maturity Model is suggested to assess (or self-assess) the level of integration with the **European Open Science Cloud (EOSC)** for any provider interested to join. 

7 steps are identified in this model that can also be seen as an ideal EOSC integration workflow. 

This workflow has been created as part of the [EOSC-Future project](https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/101017536), and complements the available documentation of the [EOSC Providers Hub](https://eosc-portal.eu/eosc-providers-hub).

composedOf.label: Getting a Basic Awareness of EOSC
composedOf.description:
The first step in the workflow consists in knowing the European Open Science Cloud (EOSC) as an European initiative, and its implementation via the [EOSC Portal](https://eosc-portal.eu/) where the **[EOSC Catalogue & Marketplace](https://search.marketplace.eosc-portal.eu/search/all_collection?q=*)** is also available.
Beyond this knowledge lies the aspiration to join and/or contribute to the EOSC. There are various ways to engage with the EOSC, as a user or as a future provider, we are here interested in "How to become an EOSC Provider?"

Only institutions can register as providers, not individuals. An authorised representative needs to register its organisation as a provider of the EOSC. This is done by filling in a form with information about your organisation. NB: the organisation needs to be a legal entity or to be connected to a legal entity already registered in EOSC

- via the web-based Service Providers Dashboard.
- via the Portal Application Programming Interface (API).

relatedItems.label: 3 ways in which DARIAH contributes to the EOSC
relatedItems.description:
EOSC is a big acronym, representing the bold vision of enabling all European researchers to deposit, access and analyse scholarly resources beyond borders and disciplines. Over the past years, it has become a central component of European science policy and, since its launch in October 2018, a reality as an infrastructure too. Still, due to the scale, the complexity and the multiple dimensions of the endeavour, it is not easy to gain an accurate overview and translate the offerings of the EOSC into one’s own institution or research setting. 

In this series of blog posts, we outline concrete ways in which scholarly and service provider communities around DARIAH can interact with the EOSC and the value it holds for them. We also summarize the many ways in which DARIAH already contributes to the EOSC.

A range of modules with open interfaces support the production, presentation, and archiving of digital assets. The software can be flexibly used for a multitude of digitisation strategies and scalable business models – for in-house projects, purely corporate services, or hybrid endeavours. Kitodo is backed and continually updated by a dynamic user and developer community and the non-profit association Kitodo e. V.

relatedItems.label: Kramerius
relatedItems.description:
Kramerius is an open source software for making digital documents accessible. It is primarily designed for digitalised library collections -- monographs and periodicals. 

It can be also used to make other types of documents accessible, such as maps, sheets of music, or old prints, if need be parts of documents, such as articles or chapters. The system is even suitable for „born digital“ documents, meaning those that come up in electronic form. The Kramerius system is being updated continuously, so that its metadata structure corresponds with the standards published by the National library of the Czech Republic.

The system provides an interface for end users, that enables them to search both in the metadata and in the full texts, to generate multi-page PDF documents from selected pages, download individual pages (JPEG) or print them.

From the management point of view, system Kramerius allows to create virtual collections, change accessibility, import, export, and other operations concerning the saved collection of digital documents.

concept.label: hOCR
concept.definition: hOCR is an open standard for representing document layout analysis and OCR results as a subset of HTML. The goal is to reuse as much existing technology as possible, and to arrive at a representation that makes it easy to store, share, process and display OCR results. This specification defines many features that can represent a variety of OCR-related information. However, being built on top of HTML, hOCR is designed to make it easy to start simple and gradually use more complex constructs when necessary. Consider you have an HTML document that encodes a book: Wrapping page elements in <div class="ocr_page"> tags will convey the page boundaries to hOCR-capable agents and turn the HTML document into an hOCR document.

Utilizing Cheerio for parsing and Simple Statistics for clustering, it determines column counts per page based on OCR line distributions. RBush and rbush-knn enable connecting indented lines to their respective predecessors. Available via npm or as a standalone tool, it offers output formats including JSON and HTML visualization, with configurable options for column count, character width, and minimum lines per column. relatedItems.description:
Interface de géoréférencement pour cartes historiques avec intégration Gallica

Galligeo est une application web développée par Projets Time Machine qui permet de géoréférencer des cartes historiques issues de la bibliothèque numérique Gallica (BnF). L'outil offre une interface intuitive pour créer des points de contrôle et transformer des cartes anciennes en couches géographiques modernes utilisables dans des systèmes d'information géographique.

The Galligeo web app allows you to georeference maps from the Gallica interface of the BnF (national library of France). You can select georeferencing points on both old maps and a current map in order to make a georeferenced map that combines both the modern-day layout and the map.

relatedItems.label: Gallica
relatedItems.description:
Gallica is the online library of the Bibliothèque nationale de France and its partners. Online since 1997, thousands of new documents each week and offers access to many millions of digitized documents. Gallica is one of the major digital libraries available for free via the Internet. It provides access to any type of document: printed documents (books, press and magazines) in image and text mode, manuscripts, sound and iconographic documents, maps and plans.

Most of Gallica's collections have been converted into text format using optical character recognition (OCR-processing), which allows full-text search in the library materials. Users can access high quality zoom via IIIF. 

Each document has a digital identifier, the so-called ARK (Archival Resource Key) of the National Library of France and is accompanied by a bibliographic description. 

Gallica is intended to all readers, whether users just having a look, booklovers, students or academics.

label: Geotagging of texts
description:
The goal of this workflow is to identify historical place names in texts and assign geo-coordinates by linking them to gazetteers (e.g., [ToposText](https://topostext.org/), [Pleiades](https://pleiades.stoa.org/), [GeoNames](https://www.geonames.org/), [World Historical Gazetteer](https://whgazetteer.org/)). By resolving these place references to gazetteer URIs, the workflow enables the retrieval of standardized geographic coordinates, allowing the enriched data to be integrated and published as Linked Open Data (LOD).

This workflow is designed to:
* Combine automatic and manual steps to improve the accuracy of geotagging.
* Explore the application of Named Entity Recognition (NER) for place identification.
* Develop a mechanism to resolve ambiguities.
* Support different input data formats.

relatedItems.label: World Historical Gazetteer
relatedItems.description: A platform for linked open geographical data, enabling discovery and analysis of place attestations across historical periods and world regions. WHG aggregates records from contributed datasets into a union index, supports reconciliation against Wikidata and other authorities, and provides spatial and temporal search, mapping, and API access. Its OpenRefine-compatible Reconciliation Service API allows researchers to match place names against WHG's holdings in batch, with support for fuzzy matching, temporal and geographic filtering, and data extension to enrich tables with geometries, alternative names, temporal ranges, and country codes. An Entity API exposes places, datasets, collections, and areas as Linked Places Format resources under persistent w3id.org identifiers. The project is based at the Institute for Spatial History Innovation (ISHI), University of Pittsburgh.

relatedItems.label: ToposText
relatedItems.description:
ToposText is a mobile application designed to provide users with access to an extensive collection of ancient Greek texts and mapped locations spanning from the Neolithic era through the 2nd century CE. The concept was inspired by the founder's two decades of exploration in Greece and the need to organize information gathered from primary sources like Pausanias. Leveraging the advancement of mobile electronic devices and the availability of ancient texts online, ToposText was developed to index these texts geographically, using a map of Greece as the primary interface.

Upon opening the application, users are presented with a scrolling alphabetical list of over 5000 Greek cities, colonies, sanctuaries, archaeological sites, museums, and other points of interest. These are accompanied by a location-aware map displaying nearby places and the number of ancient references in the database. The application operates offline, storing texts, indexes, and a basic map on the device.

Selecting a site from the list or map provides users with a table of two-line snippets from ancient authors, often supplemented by modern descriptions where available. Users can then access the full text of approximately 240 works in English translation, with some including the original Ancient Greek. The interface allows for filtering by date, genre, and relevance, facilitating quick access to relevant passages.

Translations included in the application are older works in the public domain, stripped of footnotes and scholarly apparatus. Users are reminded that ToposText is not a substitute for the most recent scholarly editions. Each paragraph in the texts is accompanied by a date and event date, though caution is advised regarding historical accuracy.

The application also features links to Travelogues, a sister website offering early traveler illustrations of Greece and its antiquities, complementing the ancient texts.

Places listed in ToposText are categorized by confidence level, with coordinates corrected for accuracy where possible. The application aims for comprehensiveness within the territory of modern Greece, with additional coverage of key areas in the ancient Greek world. Expansion plans include the inclusion of more texts and translations, depending on the availability of scholarly resources.

relatedItems.label: GeoNames
relatedItems.description:
A global geographical database that may be used to identify and tag all references to location. The database contains over 8 million entries, each of which possesses a geographic name (in various languages), latitude, longitude, elevation, population, administrative subdivision and postal codes and information on unique features.

Features:

Built upon web service, enabling transparent look-up and use of content through third-party tools and sites

Browse by geographic location, country name, size of geographic region and other categories.

Full text search support





Extensible, enabling users to expand existing information or contribute new content

Support for the World Geodetic System 1984 (WGS84) co-ordinate system

composedOf.label: Acquire data
composedOf.description:
In this step, digitized texts (TXT, XML/TEI, or PDF) are identified and secured, ensuring they are technically processable and historically and linguistically appropriate, containing references to relevant historical places and in a language supported by the workflow (English, with possible adaptation to other languages). The scholarly value of the texts is assessed, and file formats are verified to meet project requirements. See also [Collaborative Reusable Map Annotation - Step 1](https://marketplace.sshopencloud.eu/workflow/9bQPbB).

In the experiments, the primary test dataset was “Pausanias´ Description of Greece” obtained from the [Digital Periegesis](https://www.periegesis.org/en/reports.php?reportid=1) site.

relatedItems.label: Collaborative Reusable Map Annotation
relatedItems.description:
Historical maps are valuable resources for humanities research, offering insights into past landscapes and patterns of human activity. Maps are more than images; they represent spatial and cultural relationships that may be anchored to the physical world, and often embed narratives of power, identity, and change, such as shifts in place names or symbolic representations. They vary widely in form, type, content, level of detail, and granularity of the information they present. At the same time they are material objects, cultural artifacts, with distinct physical characteristics and complex biographies of their own. Historical maps also come with challenges: they often lack modern geographic precision, may contain outdated or biased perspectives (which are nonetheless of historical significance), or show signs of physical wear, among other issues. Moreover, access to the information they contain is often limited, as searching through map collection catalogues typically relies on record metadata (i.e., basic information, such as title, creator, or date) and not the full content of the map.
Map annotation provides a means to address these issues by enabling scholars to encode features, comment on the content, link place names to gazetteers or other authority files, transcribe text on maps, document historical or cartographic context, etc. Apart from supporting scholarly analysis, this process can transform static maps into searchable and machine-readable resources, by enriching the map metadata and allowing text search indices (Rainer et al. 2019). 
Developed within the ATRIUM project, this workflow supports collaborative annotation and geo-tagging of historical maps, transforming them into rich multilayer resources. It addresses both technical interoperability and data reusability, with outcomes that can enhance catalog records, improve search capabilities, feed into analytical pipelines, and support data visualizations, or even enable the creation of critical editions of maps. While primarily tested in [Recogito Studio](https://recogitostudio.org/), the workflow is designed as tool-agnostic, ensuring flexibility and reusability across different tools, projects and teams. Its steps are not strictly linear; annotation is an iterative process and teams may revisit earlier phases (e.g., revising vocabularies during annotation) or run tasks in parallel or in alternation (e.g., linking to vocabularies and gazetteers). This iterative design allows teams to adapt to evolving insights and technical constraints. 
Note: This workflow is intended for manual annotation.

**References:**
- Reckziegel, M., Wrisley, D. J., Hixson, T. W., & Jänicke, S. (2021). Visual exploration of historical maps, *Digital Scholarship in the Humanities*, 36 (Supplement_2), ii251–ii272, https://doi.org/10.1093/llc/fqaa059 
- Rainer, S., Vitale, V., Kahn, R., Barker, E. & Isaksen, L. (2019). Revisiting Linking Early Geospatial Documents with Recogito, *e-Perimetron* 14 (3), 152–63, https://www.e-perimetron.org/Vol_14_3/Simon_et_al.pdf

composedOf.label: Define goals
composedOf.description:
In this step, it is essential to define a clear and consistent annotation framework. This step establishes what will be annotated, how annotations will be applied, and how results will be interpreted and reused. A well-defined framework ensures consistency across annotators, supports interoperability with external resources, and aligns the annotation process with the broader research objectives. See also [Collaborative Reusable Map Annotation Workflow  - Step 4](https://marketplace.sshopencloud.eu/workflow/9bQPbB).

Define the scope and intended outputs of the annotation to clarify the primary research goals (e.g., identifying and linking historical place names) and determine what the annotation process should produce (e.g., structured geospatial data, enriched metadata, datasets for further analysis and visualization) and how it should be produced (e.g., automated method  (NER), human curated).

* Identify the types of features to annotate, such as places (e.g., cities, regions, villages, mountains, buildings, temples).

* Establish annotation guidelines, assigning specific roles (e.g., annotators, validators) and specifying how to handle issues such as temporal variation (historical vs. modern place names), multilingual forms, spelling variants, and ambiguous references.

* Define reference resources to determine whether annotations will be linked to external authority files like gazetteers (e.g., Pleiades), and ensure that selected tools can support this integration. 

* Select gazetters that align with the chronological scope of your data, ensuring that the chosen resource covers the relevant historical period (e.g., classical, ancient, medieval).

* Assess whether a single gazetteer provides enough coverage or if multiple gazetteers should be combined, and establish rules for resolving overlaps or conflicts between them.

* Set protocols for critical analysis to decide how to document uncertainties, or potential errors in the source material.

composedOf.label: Identify data format
composedOf.description:
This step establishes the technical foundation for the rest of the workflow by determining what type of digital material is being handled. Determine whether the input data is plain text, XML/TEI, or PDF.

Decision points:

**3a.** If the material is in **PDF format**:
  > * Continue with **Step 4** to perform text extraction.
  > * Alternatively, proceed to **Step 5b** if an annotation platform is available, or to **Step 5c** if working with small text samples.

**3b.** If the material is in **XML/TEI or plain text format**:
  > * Proceed to **Step 5**.

composedOf.label: Text extraction
composedOf.description:
In this step, if the documents are not already available as machine-readable text, textual content must be extracted. For scanned PDFs documents an OCR model is required (e.g., [GLM-OCR](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-OCR), [LightOnOCR-2-1B](https://huggingface.co/lightonai/LightOnOCR-2-1B)) or for digital-born PDFs a parser is required (e.g., [pdfminer.six](https://github.com/pdfminer/pdfminer.six)). The resulting text should be checked for encoding errors, broken lines, or layout artifacts that may affect later annotation and Named Entity Recognition (NER). If so, rerun this step using a different model.

In the experiments, the [GLM-OCR](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-OCR) was selected since it is easy to implement, delivers strong performance, and has a relatively compact size of 0.9 billion parameters. Additionally, it offers built-in support for layout detection models, which simplifies the processing of structured documents.

* **Input**: PDF file(s).
    * Perform OCR or parsing on the PDF file(s).
* **Output**: Extracted text in plain text format.
