relatedItems.label: Automatic Text Recognition Workflow
relatedItems.description:
This is workflow for using OCR/HTR itself without  using dashboard, because this workflow is dedicated to mass processing 

The main purpose of the workflow presented here is to recognize a text that has been printed or handwritten. This text was then scanned, photographed, or its image was digitally represented or obtained in any other way (e.g., digitally generated image, NOT text). It is important that we have an image of the text, but not the content of the text itself. What we want to obtain is the content of the text. This will allow us to further process the content obtained in this way, e.g., search for specific words or phrases. NLP tools will allow us to attempt to read the meaning of the text, e.g., NER, sentiment analysis, etc. There is also the potential to translate the recognized text. Recognizing text from images is usually the first step in data processing. This workflow DOES NOT DO this on its own, but it provides input for such processing in other workflows.

This workflow can be part of a larger workflow that receives an image of text at the input and needs the text content (its values) for processing. This workflow can handle both simple text images, i.e., those consisting of a single column, and only that column is on the page. The text can also consist of multiple columns, and the page can contain many different (essentially rectangular) areas with different texts that do not form a single coherent whole. This workflow can be performed for a single page or even a fragment of a page, as well as for multiple pages of an entire document. 

In addition to recognizing the text itself, this workflow can recognize typical page layouts. In this case, it will be the page layout recognized by the OCR/HTR engine. Page layout recognition can also be performed by a dedicated external service.


++Requirements++

1. One or more files that represent a single document. These can be one or more image files in common formats such as jpeg, tiff, or png. If there is more than one file, then all files together form a single multi-page document, and the order in which the files are delivered to the workflow is important and determines the order of the pages in the document.

When we deliver a pdf file, it can be a single file consisting of one or more pages. pdf files can be scanned or digitally created (digital-born). However, text recognition in such files is always performed as if it were an image. This is because some digitally born files may have an internal structure that is not suitable for simple text extraction.

2. When recognizing handwritten text, a trained AI model is required to recognize a specific type of handwriting. This is not necessary for typical printed texts, as most fonts, even if there are differences between them, are well recognized by typical OCR/HTR engines. When it comes to recognizing handwritten texts, it is necessary to train the handwriting model in advance. Training the system is a separate workflow, depending on the software used. In our workflow, we use Kraken software for HTR and recommend using eScriptorium to train models.

3. Optionally, this workflow can use a tool for recognizing page layout.
4. At the output, the workflow delivers:

alto format files   OR
txt (plain text)   files OR
pdf with text layer.

NOTE: Implementation's steps connected with image attached as a media.

relatedItems.label: GLM-OCR
relatedItems.description: GLM-OCR is a multimodal OCR model for complex document understanding, built on the GLM-V encoder–decoder architecture. It introduces Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) loss and stable full-task reinforcement learning to improve training efficiency, recognition accuracy, and generalization. The model integrates the CogViT visual encoder pre-trained on large-scale image–text data, a lightweight cross-modal connector with efficient token downsampling, and a GLM-0.5B language decoder. Combined with a two-stage pipeline of layout analysis and parallel recognition based on PP-DocLayout-V3.

relatedItems.label: LightOnOCR
relatedItems.description: LightOnOCR is an efficient end-to-end 1B-parameter vision-language model for converting documents (PDFs, scans, images) into clean, naturally ordered text.

relatedItems.label: Text Extraction From PDF Files
relatedItems.description:
This workflow describes the process for extracting the textual content of PDF files, and performing some basic segmentation of the extracted text.

The workflow is intended to be used as the first step in larger workflows that process the text (such as geographic named entity extraction etc,) and is unlikely to be particularly useful as a stand-alone workflow. Specifically it was designed in the context of the ATRIUM project to aid in the indexing of English language reports and journal articles describing archaeological investigations and interventions, as supplied by ATRIUM partner Archaeology Data Service (ADS).

composedOf.label: Choose processing path
composedOf.description:
At this step, decide between a rapid annotation pipeline, a multi-step approach that aims for higher accuracy, or a manual annotation pipeline for shorter texts. A fast workflow involves directly importing extracted text into an annotation tool (e.g., [Recogito Studio](https://github.com/recogito/recogito-studio), [INCEpTION](https://github.com/inception-project/inception)) followed by the application of an integrated Named Entity Recognition (NER) component capable of detecting place entities. A more advanced path continues through custom NER, text generation, indexing, and reranking stages.

In this workflow, [Recogito Studio](https://github.com/recogito/recogito-studio) was selected due to its collaborative features, user-friendly interface, open-access availability, integrated NER plugin, and geotagging functionality, which includes an interactive map that enhances spatial visualization.

Decision points:

**5a.** For higher accuracy continue with **Step 6**.

**5b.** For rapid results:

> * Import extracted text(s) or PDF(s) directly into your chosen annotation platform.
> * Run an available Named Entity Recognition (NER) tool or plugin capable of detecting place names to automatically identify relevant entities.
> * Proceed to **Step 11**.

**5c.** For smaller text samples:

> * Import extracted text(s) or PDF(s) directly into your chosen annotation platform.
> * Manually annotate the text according to the annotation guidelines.
> * Export the annotated data in the preferred supported format (e.g., GeoJSON, CSV).
> * Proceed to **Step 12**.

relatedItems.label: Recogito Studio
relatedItems.description: An Extensible Platform for Collaborative, Standards-Based Annotation of TEI Text, IIIF Images, and PDFs. Modern, Open Source, and Easy to Use.

composedOf.label: Named entity recognition (NER)
composedOf.description:
The extracted text is processed with an automated named entity recognition (NER) model (e.g., [NameTag3](https://lindat.mff.cuni.cz/services/nametag/), [Stanford-NER](https://nlp.stanford.edu/software/CRF-NER.shtml)) to identify candidate place entities. If sufficient labeled data is available, a deep learning model can also be fine-tuned using a framework that supports training (e.g., [spaCy](https://spacy.io/), [Flair](https://github.com/flairNLP/flair)).

In the experiments, a deep learning model ([DeBERTa-v3-base](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/deberta-v3-base)) using [spaCy](https://spacy.io/) framework was trained for NER due to its strong performance in delivering accurate results and its efficient resource requirements. The training datasets were obtained from [ToposText](https://topostext.org/texts) with special permission and were all in English.

* **Input**: Plain text file from the output of the  text extraction step.
    * Execute NER model to detect potential place-name mentions.
    * Generate initial candidate entities.
* **Output**: [JSON Lines](https://jsonlines.org/) (JSONL) file with NERed spans.

Example of the JSONL file:

```
{
   "text": "The Peiraeus was a deme from early times, though it was not a port before Themistocles became an archon of the Athenians...",
   "spans":[
      {"start":4, "end":12, "mention":"Peiraeus", "label":"LOCATION"},
      "..."
   ]
}
```

relatedItems.label: Stanford Named Entity Recognizer (NER)
relatedItems.description: Stanford NER is a Java implementation of a Named Entity Recognizer. Named Entity Recognition (NER) labels sequences of words in a text which are the names of things, such as person and company names, or gene and protein names. It comes with well-engineered feature extractors for Named Entity Recognition, and many options for defining feature extractors. Included with the download are good named entity recognizers for English, particularly for the 3 classes (PERSON, ORGANIZATION, LOCATION), and we also make available on this page various other models for different languages and circumstances, including models trained on just the CoNLL 2003 English training data.

relatedItems.label: Flair
relatedItems.description:
Flair is an open-source Python library which allows users to 1) use the trained models provided by Flair and 2) to train their own NLP-models using the provided Python library framework. The tool builds upon the state-of-the-art deep learning Pytorch framework.
Examples of how a model can be trained can be found on their GitHub pages: https://github.com/flairNLP/flair/blob/master/resources/docs/TUTORIAL_7_TRAINING_A_MODEL.md . 
Tasks you can perform include but are not limited to Named Entity Recognition (NER), sentiment analysis, Parts-of-speech tagging (POS) and text classification.
Since the tool is a Python library, you need a programming environment to use it. You can also use it in Colab, Google���s online IDE (example: https://www.analyticsvidhya.com/blog/2019/02/flair-nlp-library-python/). 

**Distribution:**
Library for Python

**User Interface:**
none

**Text Processing:**
Automatically adds some labels (annotation) to your texts, whether it is a sentiment label on the level of a text chunk or an entity label on the sequence level.

**Formalism:**
Universal Dependencies

**Tagset:**
Universal Dependencies. 
PER (person), LOC (location), ORG (organisation), MISC (miscellaneous).
positive, neutral, negative

**Related Papers:**
- Akbik, A., Bergmann, T., Blythe, D., Rasul, K., Schweter, S., Vollgraf, R., 2019. FLAIR: An Easy-to-Use Framework for State-of-the-Art NLP, in: Proceedings of the 2019 Conference of the North. Presented at the Proceedings of the 2019 Conference of the North, Association for Computational Linguistics, Minneapolis, Minnesota, pp. 54–59. https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/N19-4010
- Akbik, A., Blythe, D., Vollgraf, R., 2018. Contextual String Embeddings for Sequence Labeling. Presented at the COLING 27th International Conference on Computational Linguistics, pp. 1638–1649.

relatedItems.label: spaCy
relatedItems.description: spaCy is an open-source software library for advanced natural language processing, written in the programming languages Python and Cython. The library is published under the MIT license and currently offers statistical neural network models for English, German, Spanish, Portuguese, French, Italian, Dutch and multi-language NER, as well as tokenization for various other languages. Unlike NLTK, which is widely used for teaching and research, spaCy focuses on providing software for production usage. As of version 1.0, spaCy also supports deep learning workflows that allow connecting statistical models trained by popular machine learning libraries like TensorFlow, Keras, Scikit-learn or PyTorch. spaCy's machine learning library, Thinc, is also available as a separate open-source Python library. It features convolutional neural network models for part-of-speech tagging, dependency parsing and named entity recognition, as well as API improvements around training and updating models, and constructing custom processing pipelines.

relatedItems.label: NameTag
relatedItems.description:
NameTag is an open-source tool for named entity recognition (NER). NameTag identifies proper names in text and classifies them into predefined categories, such as names of persons, locations, organizations, etc. NameTag 2 recognizes nested entities (embedded entities) of arbitrary depth.

For Czech, it recognizes a [complex hierarchy of categories](http://ufal.mff.cuni.cz/~strakova/cnec2.0/ne-type-hierarchy.pdf). The English model, which is trained on CoNLL-2003 NER annotations (Sang and De Meulder [2003](https://www.clarin.eu/resource-families/tools-named-entity-recognition#Sang%20and%20De%20Meulder%202003)), distinguishes the following four NER classes: person, organisation, location and miscellaneous.

The trained model for Czech is available for through LINDAT: [Czech Models (CNEC) for NameTag](http://hdl.handle.net/11858/00-097C-0000-0023-7D42-8).
A [user manual](http://ufal.mff.cuni.cz/nametag/users-manual) is also available.

composedOf.label: Text generation
composedOf.description:
In this step, each place-mention detected by NER is enriched with contextual information from the surrounding text to support disambiguation. This is done by passing NER outputs to a Large Language Model (LLM) (e.g., [gpt-oss-20B](https://huggingface.co/openai/gpt-oss-20b)) with carefully designed prompts based on the annotation goals and task, which generate concise descriptions for each mention.

In this case, the [Qwen3.5-9B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B) model was used via [llama.cpp](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp) since it offers a balance between performance and accuracy. Other open-source models along with other LLM inference tools (e.g., [Ollama](https://ollama.com/), [MLX-LM](https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx-lm)) or proprietary models can also be used.

Prompt that was used for this dataset:
```
You are an expert historian and archaeologist.

You will receive:
- Mention: a referenced entity (building, temple, city, region, island, country, monument, harbor, person, or object)
- Context: a short text snippet used only for disambiguation

Task:
Identify the most likely real-world entity referred to by the Mention using the Context, and produce a clean, retrieval-optimized Wikipedia-style entity description.

Important:
- Use the Context ONLY for disambiguation.
- Do NOT describe or refer to the Context or source text.
- Do NOT explain reasoning or how the entity appears in the text.
- Do NOT write narrative or historical essays.

Output format:
1-2 sentences describing the entity.

Style rules:
- Be factual and compact
- Include: entity type + location + key identifying feature
- Avoid extra historical narrative details unless essential for identification
- Keep it consistent across all outputs
- Add the proper disambiguated title then ':' and then the description

Output examples:

Kantharos: Kantharos was one of the three ports of ancient Piraeus and Athens. It was the largest of these, and was used primarily as a trading port, although it was also used by the Athenian navy. The port was put into use in the early 5th century BC, and in the 5th century BC it was one of the most important trading ports in the entire Mediterranean.

Athens: Athens was the major urban centre of the notable polis (city-state) of Athens during the classical period (480–323 BC) of ancient Greece, located in Attica, Greece.

Pompeion: The Pompeion (Ancient Greek: Πομπεῖον) was a building made of Hymettian marble located in the Kerameikos of Athens between the Sacred Gate and the Dipylon. The 4th-century BC building was destroyed during the siege by Sulla.
```
* **Input**: JSONL file from the previous step.

    * Prompt LLM to generate a richer and a more specific text for retrieval to reduce ambiguity in place references.
* **Output**: JSONL file with the generated text.


Example of the JSONL file:
```
{

composedOf.label: Indexing & fast approximate retrieval
composedOf.description:
To enable efficient approximate retrieval between textual mentions and known geographic entities, we compare mentions against a vector database derived from a gazetteer. The enriched descriptions produced by the previous step are first converted into vectors using an embedding model (e.g., [Qwen3-Embedding](https://huggingface.co/collections/Qwen/qwen3-embedding)) and then stored into a [FAISS (Facebook AI Similarity Search)](https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss) index. This process generates a ranked list of candidate links for each mention.

In the experiments, the [ToposText](https://topostext.org/) gazetteer was used since it includes the chronological periods present in the test dataset. It was paired with the open-source [Qwen3-Embedding-8B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-8B) embedding model. To store the embeddings, a pre-built [FAISS](https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss) index built from ToposText titles and descriptions was used, enabling fast and efficient similarity searches.

* **Input**: JSONL file from the previous step.
    * Match mentions against an appropriate gazetteer based on your dataset.
    * Create ranked candidate entities.
    * The candidate with the highest score is considered the correct entity.
* **Output**: JSONL file with a list of potential candidates along with a relevance score.

Example of the JSONL file:
```
{
   "text": "The Peiraeus was a deme from early times, though it was not a port before Themistocles became an archon of the Athenians...",
   "spans":[
      {"start":4, "end":12, "mention":"Peiraeus", "label":"LOCATION", "recontext":"Peiraeus: Peiraeus was a deme of ancient Attica that became the primary port of Athens...", "index_results":[
            [
               "379236HPei",
               "0.4406093"
            ],
            [
               "379236UKan",
               "0.61706793"
            ],
            [
               "379237HZea",
               "0.6831315"
            ],
             "..."
         ]},
      "..."
   ]
}

relatedItems.label: ToposText
relatedItems.description:
ToposText is a mobile application designed to provide users with access to an extensive collection of ancient Greek texts and mapped locations spanning from the Neolithic era through the 2nd century CE. The concept was inspired by the founder's two decades of exploration in Greece and the need to organize information gathered from primary sources like Pausanias. Leveraging the advancement of mobile electronic devices and the availability of ancient texts online, ToposText was developed to index these texts geographically, using a map of Greece as the primary interface.

Upon opening the application, users are presented with a scrolling alphabetical list of over 5000 Greek cities, colonies, sanctuaries, archaeological sites, museums, and other points of interest. These are accompanied by a location-aware map displaying nearby places and the number of ancient references in the database. The application operates offline, storing texts, indexes, and a basic map on the device.

Selecting a site from the list or map provides users with a table of two-line snippets from ancient authors, often supplemented by modern descriptions where available. Users can then access the full text of approximately 240 works in English translation, with some including the original Ancient Greek. The interface allows for filtering by date, genre, and relevance, facilitating quick access to relevant passages.

Translations included in the application are older works in the public domain, stripped of footnotes and scholarly apparatus. Users are reminded that ToposText is not a substitute for the most recent scholarly editions. Each paragraph in the texts is accompanied by a date and event date, though caution is advised regarding historical accuracy.

The application also features links to Travelogues, a sister website offering early traveler illustrations of Greece and its antiquities, complementing the ancient texts.

Places listed in ToposText are categorized by confidence level, with coordinates corrected for accuracy where possible. The application aims for comprehensiveness within the territory of modern Greece, with additional coverage of key areas in the ancient Greek world. Expansion plans include the inclusion of more texts and translations, depending on the availability of scholarly resources.

relatedItems.label: FAISS (Facebook AI Similarity Search)
relatedItems.description:
FAISS (Facebook AI Similarity Search) is a library for efficient similarity search and clustering of dense vectors. It contains algorithms that search in sets of vectors of any size, up to ones that possibly do not fit in RAM. It also contains supporting code for evaluation and parameter tuning.

Faiss is written in C++ with complete wrappers for Python. Some of the most useful algorithms are implemented on the GPU. It is developed primarily at FAIR, the fundamental AI research team of Meta.

composedOf.label: Reranking
composedOf.description:
In this step, the preliminary matches obtained from the previous stage are refined using an LLM as a reranking tool (e.g., [gpt-oss-20B](https://huggingface.co/openai/gpt-oss-20b)) that evaluates candidates based on their semantic similarity and contextual relevance to the generated sentence.

In this case, the [gemma-4-E4B-it](https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-4-E4B-it) model was used to reorder results and improve linking accuracy.

Prompt that was used for this dataset:
```
You are an entity matching system.

You are given:
1. A user query
2. A list of candidate entities

Each candidate is a possible interpretation of the query.

Your task is to select the single candidate that is the best semantic match to the query.

Rules:
- Use only the information provided in the query and candidate strings.
- Do NOT guess.
- Treat each candidate as a single label with meaning.
- Choose the candidate that best matches the overall intent of the query.
- If multiple candidates seem similar, choose the one most specifically aligned with the query context.
- If none are a good match, still choose the closest one.

Output format:
- Return ONLY the exact candidate string.
- Do not add explanation, punctuation, or extra text.
```

* **Input**: JSONL file from the previous step.
    * Execute the reranking model to refine candidate ordering.
    * The candidate selected by the LLM is treated as the correct entity.
* **Output**: JSONL file with the reranked candidate selected by the LLM.

Example of the JSONL file:
```
{
   "text": "The Peiraeus was a deme from early times, though it was not a port before Themistocles became an archon of the Athenians...",
   "spans":[
      {"start":4, "end":12, "mention":"Peiraeus", "label":"LOCATION", "recontext":"Peiraeus: Peiraeus was a deme of ancient Attica that became the primary port of Athens...", "index_results":[
            [
               "379236HPei",
               "0.4406093"
            ],
            [
               "379236UKan",
               "0.61706793"
            ],
            [
               "379237HZea",
               "0.6831315"
            ],
             "..."
         ],"reranker_results":
        "379236HPei",
       },
      "..."
   ]
}
```

composedOf.description:
In this step, once the file(s) are imported into the annotation tool, scholars and researchers inspect the annotations inside the tool. This human-in-the-loop phase is essential for ensuring scholarly reliability, correcting existing geotag annotations and adding new geotag annotations where necessary based on the annotation guidelines. After the reviewing of the annotations, export the results into a structured format that preserves both the textual content and the annotation metadata (e.g., CSV, GeoJSON).

In this case, the [Recogito Studio](https://recogitostudio.org/) geotagging plugin was used as a visualization tool where annotations could be modified with the help of a map. For the export, both CSV and GeoJSON formats were chosen.

* **Input**: Structured annotation file from the previous step.
    * Review geotag annotations using the target annotation environment.
    * Modify geotag annotations where needed based on the annotation guidelines.
* **Output**: Exported file containing all geo-annotations, comments, and corrections in a format compatible with your workflow (e.g., CSV, GeoJSON).

relatedItems.label: Collaborative Reusable Map Annotation
relatedItems.description:
Historical maps are valuable resources for humanities research, offering insights into past landscapes and patterns of human activity. Maps are more than images; they represent spatial and cultural relationships that may be anchored to the physical world, and often embed narratives of power, identity, and change, such as shifts in place names or symbolic representations. They vary widely in form, type, content, level of detail, and granularity of the information they present. At the same time they are material objects, cultural artifacts, with distinct physical characteristics and complex biographies of their own. Historical maps also come with challenges: they often lack modern geographic precision, may contain outdated or biased perspectives (which are nonetheless of historical significance), or show signs of physical wear, among other issues. Moreover, access to the information they contain is often limited, as searching through map collection catalogues typically relies on record metadata (i.e., basic information, such as title, creator, or date) and not the full content of the map.
Map annotation provides a means to address these issues by enabling scholars to encode features, comment on the content, link place names to gazetteers or other authority files, transcribe text on maps, document historical or cartographic context, etc. Apart from supporting scholarly analysis, this process can transform static maps into searchable and machine-readable resources, by enriching the map metadata and allowing text search indices (Rainer et al. 2019). 
Developed within the ATRIUM project, this workflow supports collaborative annotation and geo-tagging of historical maps, transforming them into rich multilayer resources. It addresses both technical interoperability and data reusability, with outcomes that can enhance catalog records, improve search capabilities, feed into analytical pipelines, and support data visualizations, or even enable the creation of critical editions of maps. While primarily tested in [Recogito Studio](https://recogitostudio.org/), the workflow is designed as tool-agnostic, ensuring flexibility and reusability across different tools, projects and teams. Its steps are not strictly linear; annotation is an iterative process and teams may revisit earlier phases (e.g., revising vocabularies during annotation) or run tasks in parallel or in alternation (e.g., linking to vocabularies and gazetteers). This iterative design allows teams to adapt to evolving insights and technical constraints. 
Note: This workflow is intended for manual annotation.

**References:**
- Reckziegel, M., Wrisley, D. J., Hixson, T. W., & Jänicke, S. (2021). Visual exploration of historical maps, *Digital Scholarship in the Humanities*, 36 (Supplement_2), ii251–ii272, https://doi.org/10.1093/llc/fqaa059 
- Rainer, S., Vitale, V., Kahn, R., Barker, E. & Isaksen, L. (2019). Revisiting Linking Early Geospatial Documents with Recogito, *e-Perimetron* 14 (3), 152–63, https://www.e-perimetron.org/Vol_14_3/Simon_et_al.pdf

relatedItems.label: Github

GitHub is a web-based repository service which offers the distributed revision control and source code management (SCM) functionality of GIT with a graphical user interface, desktop, and mobile integration. It also provides collaboration tools such as access control, wikis, task management, code review, bug tracking, and feature requests. It offers free accounts, often used to host opensource software projects, and private (paid) repositories.

Projects on GitHub can be accessed and manipulated using the git command-line interface and all of the standard git commands work with it. GitHub also allows registered and non-registered users to browse public repositories on the site. Multiple desktop clients have also been created by GitHub and other third parties which integrate with the platform.

GitHub is mainly used for code but can also be used for non-code files, it supports the following formats and features:

3D render files

Photoshop's native PSD format can be previewed and compared to previous versions of the same file.

Nested task-lists

Documentation and wikis

Small websites can be hosted from public repositories on GitHub. The URL format is http://projectname.github.io.

Issue tracking (including feature requests)

Visualization of geospatial data

Gantt charts

GitHub is a heavily used in the opensource development community but does not require hosted projects to meet the definition of Open Source.

label: How to create a literary bibliography?
description:
This workflow describes the steps needed to establish a digital literary bibliography as an openly and freely available discovery platform. It is not a workflow for improving management of an existing service although it might be beneficial in such cases as well. Hence, this workflow defines steps in a chronological manner, although all of them are intertwined. The steps cover a series of key decisions and implementations starting from defining the scope of a bibliography, applying a governance model, decisions on data-related and software-related issues and establishing proper relationships with existing initiatives and projects. 
The workflow follows primarily the definitions, methodologies and experiences of long-standing projects of Czech and Polish Literary Bibliographies but is adaptable for the needs of any other bibliographic project.

composedOf.label: Define scope, methods and sources
composedOf.description:
Any bibliography should be carefully defined  with regard to its excerption scope, processing methods and available data sources. 
The definition of the excerption scope is a key step and the following characteristics of documents should be taken into account: (a) their language, (b) country/place of publication, (c) year/period of publication, (d) type of document, (e) medium of document, (f) topic, and (g) in case of literary bibliographies primary / secondary content as well as any other relevant criteria.
Another important task is to decide on the methods for how to process the data. Most comprehensive, but time-consuming method is to process the data from the autopsy. In this case a record is prepared with a document in hand and the curator has full control over the content of the record. Another option is to re-use existing sources. This option requires IT resources to extract, enrich and harmonise large datasets (e.g. national bibliographies like German National Bibliography, digital libraries like Gallica, etc.). It enables processing of large datasets within a short period of time, but without the full control of the content of the record. Last option is the retroconversion, which means to convert analog sources (printed bibliography, card catalogue etc.) into the structured data. The most challenging aspect here is to extract as much information as possible either through manual retroconversion or an automated one (e.g. through HTR, OCR or NLP methods).
Based on these parameters, one can better define required technical capacities and skills to make informed decisions on the budget and sustainability of a bibliographic project.

composedOf.label: Define governance model and target user groups
composedOf.description:
Literary bibliographies have historically been units in academic institutions or libraries and have consisted of teams of catalogers (bibliographers) who manually (from autopsy) analysed documents and provided entries to publications or bibliographic databases. Nowadays, however, thanks to the advancements in automated data processing one could imagine establishing and running a literary bibliography without a cataloging team. Although having catalogers on board will probably always be desired.
Literary bibliographies in terms of their governance model might be considered projects supported by the work of departments, centers or teams in academia or libraries. In that case these units are responsible for processing a literary bibliography and it is recommended that such a task is a long-term commitment of an institution.
Good understanding of your governance model is needed from the early stages of the project, i.e. a model which suits your resources at any given time. A governance model is needed both to manage this kind of project, but also to successfully communicate your project’s needs and goals with your funders or management.
Regardless of a chosen legal or institutional status and governance model, a literary bibliography is a research infrastructure: a tool/device/resource which is a service supporting research (for academia, but also the society) and access to knowledge. Running a digital service demands good understanding of your user group and all aspects of digital service management. It is recommended for you be acquainted with IT service management standards which could be very helpful e.g. FitSM, ITIL, ISO etc.
Finally, it is the state-of-the-art approach to treat your bibliographic data as research data and it is helpful to start your project with a good understanding of Research Data Management, especially establishing and updating regularly a Data Management Plan could act as a checklist for you that will allow you to address necessary requirements.

relatedItems.label: Train-the-Trainer RDM Bootcamp
relatedItems.description:
**Date:** 08 to 11 February 2021
**Location:** Online

The SSHOC project and DARIAH-ERIC announce an interactive bootcamp for trainers, data supporters, librarians and data stewards in the humanities and social sciences who provide training in the field of Research Data Management. 

## Highlights

Participants received expert training from leading practitioners and trainers in the field of Research Data Management, and had the opportunity to specialise in a key area of interest and also to receive peer feedback on an assignment to be completed between sessions. The second session concluded with a plenary session focusing on Research Data Management didactics. 

## Course Structure

Day 1 introduced three topics from which participants can then choose a specialisation:

-    Planning to meet the costs of managing research data to be FAIR
-    GDPR and Ethical issues in working with social media data, 
-    Dealing with third-party data coming from Cultural Heritage institutions (galleries, museums, libraries, archives)

Participants received  a ‘homework assignment’ in their chosen subject area. 

On Day 2 participants discussed their completed assignments and attended a plenary session on didactics.

## About the Speakers

**Kerstin Helbig** (Humboldt University Berlin) is research data management coordinator at Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin, Germany. She assists researchers in the management of their research data and organizes training as well as information sessions. In her former position, she was a research associate at GESIS – Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences, where she was responsible for the further development of the used metadata schema and supported researchers in the registration of their research data.

**[Katrin Weller](https://www.gesis.org/en/institute/staff/person/katrin.weller)** (GESIS) is a senior researcher at GESIS - Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences, where she leads an interdisciplinary team within the Department of Computational Social Sciences. Her work is targeted towards developing new approaches to using social media data in social science research, and to support researchers working with these new types of digital behavioral data. Katrin holds a PhD in information science and her research interests relate to social media, data preservation, scholarly communication & altmetrics, web users and communication structures. 

**[Oliver Watteler](https://www.gesis.org/en/institute/staff/person/oliver.watteler)** (GESIS) is a senior researcher at GESIS - Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences, where he works in the area of research data management and data acquisition. He consults projects on organizational and legal matters of research data management, and heads data services projects. Oliver holds a Master’s degree in History and Political Science. He publishes in the areas of research data management and data protection.

**Kristen Schuster**, PhD (King’s College London) is a Lecturer in Digital Curation in the Department of Digital Humanities at King's College London. She completed her doctoral work in May 2016 at the University of Missouri in the School of Information Science & Learning Technologies. Before her doctoral work, she completed her masters in library and information science at Simmons College in 2012.

**Angus Whyte** (DCC) is a Senior Research Data Specialist with the Digital Curation Centre, His focus in DCC, which he joined in 2007, has been on conducting surveys, case studies, and co-designing guidance materials and assessment frameworks. He currently co-leads the Policy and Practice WP in FAIRsFAIR, contributes to establishing the project’s FAIR Competence Centre.

This training workshop on the Data Management Expert Guide (DMEG), organised by the Portuguese Archive for Social Information (Arquivo Português de Informação Social - APIS), was held on 6 November 2019 in Lisbon.
The main goal of the workshop was to explore the research data lifecycle using the DMEG tool provided by the CESSDA Training Team by using training materials developed by the CESSDA Trainers.

composedOf.label: Defining and implementing data models
composedOf.description:
The definition and implementation of the specific data model is of high importance for the further use of the data. The curator should take into account the needs of the specific community, cataloguing standards, and authority files as well as systems of persistent identifiers and descriptive thesauri and ontologies for the needs of the subject description.
The current bibliographic data processing is dominated by the standardised exchange coming from the librarianship sphere. The most popular format is undoubtedly MARC21 and its different variants. MARC21 is a specific hybrid format which might not be easy to understand outside the librarian community. Another option is BIBFRAME, LOD-based format coming from the librarian sphere as well. With regard to the interoperability, the common data standards can be used (e. g. Dublin Core). Specific option is to process the bibliography in the form of linked data/wikidata format. We would not recommend using proprietary data format unless there is no other option available, because it highly complicates the data interoperability.
Next to the format, the list of processed information (database fields) should be prepared. For most of the data, the relevant fields should be available in the standardised formats. There is a possibility to use nationally or locally defined fields as well. If any relevant field is not defined within the standard, it is possible to use e. g. note field in a consistent way.
For the needs of interconnection of the data it is crucial to implement the system of persistent identifiers. These identifiers are crucial for data interoperability and data enrichment from the external sources. National authorities files should be taken into account as PID general knowledge databases adapted for the given country. Individual authorities systems are mapped on the international Virtual Authority File (VIAF) which enables interconnection between various systems of national authority system as well as to wikidata. Subject description might be realised with the set of national authorities as well, but for the needs of specialised discipline bibliographies they might be too general and more granular hierarchy might be needed. The examples of such thesauri might be MESH or AGROVOC.
Finally, a crucial task is to understand the licensing of your data – both those that are being reused and those which are created manually. Proper licensing decision have decisive implications on future data reuse. For open digital literary bibliography Creative Commons licences could be recommended.

relatedItems.label: Dublin Core™ User Guide
relatedItems.description:
This user guide has two parts:
- Creating Metadata:
     - For people who need to create metadata descriptions, such as catalogers.
     - Describes how to use DCMI properties, which are grouped into sections that use similar usage guidelines and similar examples.
     - Links to RDF syntax examples in Publishing Metadata.

- Publishing Metadata
     - For people who need to encode Dublin Core™ metadata in RDF for publication as Linked Data.
     - Provides examples for DCMI properties, listed by name.

As of 2019, DCMI has medium-term plans to restructure the User Guide for better integration of examples into DCMI Metadata Terms.

relatedItems.label: VIAF: The Virtual International Authority File
relatedItems.description: The VIAF (Virtual International Authority File) service provides libraries and library users with convenient access to the world's major name authority files. VIAF Contributors regularly supply authority data that VIAF matches, links, and groups. All descriptions for a given entity are merged into a cluster that brings together the different names for that entity. This service allows researchers to identify names, locations, works, and expressions while preserving regional preferences for language, spelling, and script.

composedOf.label: Define and implement software solutions for data processing and access
composedOf.description:
There are two main software options that support processing of a literary bibliography and they depend on whether a literary bibliography is being created fully automatically or the workflow includes manual creation of entries.
In the first scenario a software for discovery service is needed which does not need to have support for manual creation of entries (e.g. Vufind). It allows importing data into it and the user gets access to the data through a search engine, faceted browsing etc. These kinds of software solutions usually allow for machine access to data (e.g. OAI-PMH, Z39.50, API). For small scale projects solutions like Zotero or even spreadsheets might be of use.
The second scenario demands a software solution that supports manual creation of records and this could be an integrated solution. There is a number of Integrated Library Systems (ILS) on the market available under various business models or one can use open source solutions such as Koha or Folio.  More universal systems such as Wikibase create another option. Finally custom-made solutions are also prevalent, but building such a system from scratch is demanding and comes with sustainability challenges.

relatedItems.label: Open Archives Initiative Protocol for Metadata Harvesting
relatedItems.description: The Open Archives Initiative Protocol for Metadata Harvesting (OAI-PMH) is a low-barrier mechanism for repository interoperability. Data Providers are repositories that expose structured metadata via OAI-PMH. Service Providers then make OAI-PMH service requests to harvest that metadata. OAI-PMH is a set of six verbs or services that are invoked within HTTP.

relatedItems.label: Koha
relatedItems.description: LibLime's Koha is a web-based, open source integrated library system (ILS) that has also been used for virtual library systems (e.g. recreating historic libraries). LibLime Koha offers libraries circulation policies, patron management modules, parent-child relationship for patron records, club and service management features, in-depth "holds" support, single click batch import "undo" option, EzProxy compatibility, self-checkout interface and more.

composedOf.label: Develop relationships with existing initiatives and ensure discoverability
composedOf.description:
When your service is more defined and operating then more collaboration options open up. It is recommended for a literary bibliography to seek collaborations with research infrastructures on national (e.g. DARIAH ERIC nodes, OPERAS nodes), international (DARIAH, e.g. DARIAH Bibliographical Data WG, OPERAS, etc.) and disciplinary levels (literary researchers associations, other infrastructures e.g. CLS etc.). 
Services like literary bibliographies should be presented and discussed both on disciplinary events (conferences, workshops), but also on digital humanities and scholarly communication events. On many occasions poster sessions are a good way to present your tool. 
An operating service might also be an interesting resource for other parts of the research infrastructure ecosystem, e.g. metadata aggregators such as GoTriple or European Literary Bibliography. Making your data available through a protocol like OAI-PMH or API will allow other services to aggregate your data and reach wider audiences. Although, some service providers might also worry about the negative impact of such aggregation on the traffic on their platform. Reuse of your data by services can be, however, monitored if proper relationships with aggregators are established (e.g. allowing for access to some usage statistics).

label: How to create a workflow in the SSH Open Marketplace?
description:
The following workflow helps users understand what a workflow is in the SSH Open Marketplace and how to proceed to create one. 

As described in the [Marketplace’s guidelines](https://marketplace.sshopencloud.eu/about/data-population): ”A research workflow is a (potentially complex/non-linear) sequence of steps to describe how to perform a task within the research data lifecycle (comparable to 'recipes' in [methodi.ca](http://methodi.ca/) and 'scenarios' in the [Standardization Survival Kit](https://hal-lara.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-01513531/)). A workflow can be completed by using diverse tools and resources, connected to each step. As opposed to Training Materials, workflows are a series of steps (which can contain links to other resources) whereas the former are unique resources.”

**This specific workflow guides users, step by step, in the creation of their own research scenario.** Let's highlight first the three main reasons for which you, as a researcher, want to contribute to the SSH Open Marketplace with a workflow:
- to make your research project align with the best practices in your community
- to get peer review and visibility
- to share a project in another form than the usual blog / article (a new way to disseminate your work).

composedOf.label: Identify a good workflow
composedOf.description:
The first step in the creation of a workflow is to **identify and shape** a topic for your workflow. A good workflow is built on use cases, inspired from real life, and aims at supporting and providing expertise to researchers in their use of digital methods.

As stated in the [SSK documentation](https://ssk.readthedocs.io/en/latest/1_tuto.html): “These scenarios can be seen as a living memory of what should be the best research practices in a given community, made accessible and reusable for other researchers wishing to carry out a similar project but unfamiliar with the recommended tools, formats, methods to use, etc”. 

In case of collaborative work, it might be useful to prepare the workflow in a [collaborative template](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Vqk3E0n2_ZY2oYar21x5-ifHhK7KjxiV5X9ZdNAGFfQ/edit?usp=sharing) before creating the workflow in the Marketplace via the edit form.

composedOf.label: Describe your workflow
composedOf.description:
The description of the workflow is the longer text that the contributor has to provide.
- it should explain the scientific problematic and describe the solution put in place.
- it is important to extend the acronyms cited and to briefly present the projects mentioned.

The form of this text should respect the following constraints:
- It shouldn’t exceed 1500 characters (but should not be too short either).
- You can use Markdown syntax to format your description

composedOf.label: Associate metadata to the workflow
composedOf.description:
In order to enhance discoverability and search relevance, the SSH Open Marketplace resources are described with a set of metadata. All available metadata are described and documented in the **[SSH Open Marketplace editorial guidelines](https://marketplace.sshopencloud.eu/contribute/metadata-guidelines#guidance-for-metadata-fields)**, the most relevant to associate with a workflow are highlighted here.

*Categorisation metadata*
- (research) activities to be chosen among the concepts from [TaDIRAH (Taxonomy of Digital Research Activities in the Humanities)](https://vocabs.dariah.eu/tadirah/en/)
- Keyword
- Language

*Context metadata*
- see-also
- helpdesk-url

*Access metadata*
- license

*Actors*
- all authors of the workflow should be added as actors 
- it is possible to add ORCID, Twitter account, email, website... on an actor profile

composedOf.label: Choose an illustration for the scenario
composedOf.description:
- The illustration must closely relate with the purpose of the scenario, i.e. not only with the discipline or the period studied.
- Screenshots are accepted.
- Landscape orientation image are recommended
- It must be published under the licence CC-BY or CC-0.

composedOf.label: Create and describe steps
composedOf.description:
## Steps Writing Guidelines

As in a cooking recipe, you need to **determine the different steps needed** for someone else to perform the workflow and reuse the digital method presented in your research scenario. One step describes an action (or a set of actions) needed to realise the workflow and links useful resources that can be used to perform this action, or to understand the methodology used. Steps are usually temporarily ordered. You can add as many steps as you want, but it is not recommended to exceed 10 steps.

A few recommendations to describe a step:
1. Choose explicit titles starting with a verb or a gerund  

The choice of good titles for steps is crucial. They will be the entry point for the readers, who need to understand at first reading the scope and the aim of a step. To ensure that the message will driven home, consider building titles:
- that starts with a verb or a gerund, describing the process (for a scenario) or the action (for a step) that the user will read about;
- with a number of characters comprised between 10 and 100.

2. Write the description 


When writing workflow steps, follow these principles to ensure clarity, consistency, and usefulness for readers:

### Language Style
- **Avoid personal pronouns**: Do not use “I”, “we”, or “us”.
- **Use the imperative form**: Begin instructions with action verbs such as “Describe”, “Write down”, or “Document”.
- **Prefer active voice**, but passive voice may be used where appropriate. See [Google’s guidance on active voice](https://developers.google.com/tech-writing/one/active-voice).

### Structure and Expression
- Use **“step”**, **“workflow”**, or **“demonstrator”** as the subject:
  - *“This step transforms the data.”*
  - *“The workflow helps convert the format.”*
  - *“The demonstrator exemplifies the process.”*
- When introducing examples:
  - *“The general workflow is exemplified using a specific case.”*
  - *“The process is demonstrated on the following example.”*

###  Content Requirements
- **Explain the purpose** of the action and **how it relates to previous steps**.
- Provide a **high-level overview** of the types of methods and tools the resource refers to.
- **Expand acronyms** the first time they are used (e.g., *Natural Language Processing (NLP)*).
- **Briefly introduce any projects** mentioned, including their relevance or scope.
- The description should be **informative but concise**—**do not exceed 1,500 characters** and avoid overly short texts.
- You may use **Markdown syntax** to format content (e.g., headers, bullet points, emphasis).

composedOf.label: Identify and reference relevant resources
composedOf.description:
Identifying state of the art references is a prerequisite before actually adding the resources to the steps. When we are talking about resources, we mean a tool, service or document helpful for the task completion.
To be linked to the workflow or its steps, these resources need to have an entry in the SSH Open Marketplace.

1. Check if the resource is already referenced in the Marketplace via the search function.
2. If yes, check whether or not the item needs to be enriched with additional metadata. Improve the item description if needed. 
3. If no, create an entry for the resource you want to link to the step, following the editorial guidelines recommendations.

label: How to phonetically transcribe dialects
description: This workflow outlines the main steps involved in the transcription of dialectal speech data, with particular attention to the Italian linguistic context and the Italo-Romance dialects. Although it has been primarily conceived for the Italian reality, the workflow may also be adapted and applied to other geographical and linguistic contexts, provided that the necessary methodological and linguistic adjustments are taken into account. This process is documented by Giovanni Abete in the chapter “Trascrivere il dialetto” (pp. 211–217) of the "Vademecum per il trattamento delle fonti orali" (Tavolo permanente per le fonti orali, 2023).

It can also contain multimodal information like gestures or events and multimedia information like time synchronization and relation to media files.

relatedItems.label: How to Transcribe Phonetically
relatedItems.description: This workflow describes the successive methodological decisions and operations required to produce a phonetic transcription of oral/spoken data for research and documentation purposes in the social sciences and humanities (linguistics, dialectology, sociolinguistics, psycholinguistics, language documentation, conversation analysis, etc.). It is designed for researchers, students, and archivists who need to convert an audio recording into a phonetically annotated resource, whether for a single case study or for a larger, shareable, and reusable corpus. The workflow was elaborated on the basis of practical teaching and research notes on phonetic transcription (auditory and acoustic-supported transcription, use of Praat and ELAN, IPA/SAMPA conventions, inter-annotator agreement, and data publication), and integrates reference information on the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) and its alternative ASCII-based encoding, X-SAMPA. The workflow can be adapted to individual projects or to team-based research infrastructures, and it explicitly foresees the possibility of publishing the resulting transcriptions, together with the source audio, as a citable open dataset (e.g. via Zenodo or a comparable repository).

relatedItems.label: Transcription de données de langage oral
relatedItems.description:
French language workflow on how one can approach the task of transcribing oral recordings, produced by the Consortium Huma-Num Corli2. The French text is followed by its English translation.

Les données de langage oral enregistrées avec un magnétophone ou une caméra vidéo peuvent être transcrites de manière orthographique (pour les langues ayant une écriture) ou phonétique. Ces transcriptions se font en alignant le résultat de la transcription et du son (ou des gestes).  Le résultat des transcriptions est largement utilisé dans la recherche en sciences du langage.

English translation

The oral language data recorded with a tape recorder or video camera can be transcribed either orthographically (for languages that have a writing system) or phonetically. These transcriptions are produced by aligning the transcription output with the sound (or gestures). The resulting transcriptions are widely used in linguistic research.

relatedItems.label: Treating Oral Sources in SSH Research
relatedItems.description:
This workflow, developed in Italy, guides SSH researchers, archivists, and institutions through the full lifecycle of oral sources: from initial legal and ethical preparation, through fieldwork and documentation, to long-term preservation, archival transfer, access, and valorisation, including responsible online publication. It covers the production of audio or audiovisual recordings, their contextual documentation, and their integration into archival systems.

The workflow applies equally to newly initiated oral data gathering campaigns and to the retrospective treatment of pre-existing collections. It draws on the "Vademecum per il trattamento delle fonti orali" (Ministero della Cultura, Direzione Generale Archivi, 2023), a multidisciplinary reference document developed by specialists from different domains, including oral historians, linguists, ethnologists, librarians and archivists.

While it integrates European data protection requirements (GDPR) and established professional standards, it also refers at certain points to the Italian legal framework. Researchers operating in other national contexts should therefore consult the relevant legislation and guidelines applicable in their own country.

relatedItems.label: Vademecum per il trattamento delle fonti orali
relatedItems.description: Starting from a broader definition of oral sources and from the assumption of the unity of the communicative event that generates the source—and, consequently, the archive of oral sources—this Vademecum provides a coherent theoretical framework, not merely prescriptive, to which methods and practices for the treatment of oral documentation can be anchored.

composedOf.label: (Preliminary phase) Obtain high-quality audio recordings
composedOf.description: Transcription quality is directly limited by recording quality. Ensure your recordings are clear, with minimal background noise. Use a professional external microphone when possible, sample at 44.1 kHz / 16-bit minimum, and store files in a lossless or uncompressed format (WAV, FLAC) before beginning any transcription work.

concept.label: Audio Recording
concept.definition: mechanical or digital record of a series of audio events (Wikidata contributors, "Q3302947," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q3302947&oldid=1254901544 (accessed September 4, 2020).

composedOf.label: (Preliminary phase) Define your research objectives upfront
composedOf.description:
The choices you make throughout this workflow — transcription system, level of detail, and prosodic notation — depend fundamentally on your research objectives and your intended audience. The level of phonetic detail, the choice of transcription system, and the extent of prosodic notation all vary according to who your transcription is for and what you intend to use it for. A transcription intended for specialist phonetic research will require different choices from one produced for a general audience or for lexicographic purposes. Clearly identifying your purpose at the outset helps you avoid unnecessary work and ensures that your transcription remains readable and useful for its intended users.

For example, at this stage, you should decide whether your transcription will be broad — recording only the most phonologically distinctive contrasts with minimal diacritics — or narrow — representing as much phonetic detail as possible. This choice should be aligned with your research objectives and explicitly documented.

composedOf.label: Choose a transcription system
composedOf.description:
Multiple transcription systems have been developed for the documentation of Italian dialects. Each reflects different theoretical assumptions and historical traditions of study. The choice of system must be made deliberately, as it conditions both the nature of the categories used and the interoperability of the resulting data.

Widely used among Italian dialectologists is the “Ascoli–Merlo” system. With some modifications, this system was employed in a major documentation project of the Italian dialect heritage known as the “Carta dei Dialetti Italiani”. Substantially different transcription systems were used in works of fundamental importance for Italian dialectology, namely the “Atlante Italo Svizzero” (AIS) and the “Atlante Linguistico Italiano” (ALI). To this plurality of systems, the IPA was added in the second half of the twentieth century, initially facing resistance among Italian dialectologists and only becoming widely established in recent decades. The "Rivista Italiana di Dialettologia" adopts the IPA system. However, its first issue also proposed a simplified transcription system based on Italian orthography.

The existence of multiple systems does not merely represent a variation in symbols: each embodies a different approach to the categorisation and classification of phonetic reality, and must be understood within the historical and theoretical context in which it was developed.

For any new transcription project, the use of the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) is strongly recommended. The IPA is the most widely used phonetic transcription system internationally, grounded in a modern and consolidated phonetic theory. It offers extensive documentation of its symbols and principles, remains relatively stable over time, and provides a flexible yet relatively simple system: the most phonologically relevant distinctions are represented through alphabetic symbols, while diacritics allow for finer phonetic detail. It is also supported by extensive reference materials, including the Illustrations of the IPA series.

If your project is already underway and uses a non-IPA or mixed transcription system, you are not required to convert it to IPA. However, you should provide clear and exhaustive documentation of all symbols employed and of the transcription practices adopted. In this context, the IPA can serve as a metalinguistic reference to clarify the phonetic values of non-standard symbols. If you decide to attempt a conversion to IPA, you should keep in mind that transcription systems are not strictly isomorphic, and that a one-to-one correspondence between symbols is not always possible. Any conversion should therefore preserve the original transcriptions, which users should always remain able to consult.

In some contexts — particularly for dialects with an existing written tradition — transcriptions seek a compromise between orthographic local spelling conventions and phonetic notation; in such cases, all non-standard symbols used must be explicitly listed and linked to their IPA equivalent to ensure interpretability for any reader.

An example of a mixed approach is the orthographic system used to render Neapolitan dialect dialogue in Italian cinema. Stromboli ("Il dialetto sul grande schermo. Il napoletano nella storia del cinema italiano", Firenze, Cesati, 2022) follows the written tradition of Neapolitan, itself based on Italian orthography, while adding a small number of phonetic symbols from different sources. The following extract is from a scene in Massimo Troisi's "Ricomincio da tre":

"E cchéllə ca dico iə, cu tutt' 'a ggènte ca čə sta a Nnapulə pròpio nu móstrə éva vənì 'e cas' affianc' a mme?'"

Here, the schwa symbol [ə] is used to represent the unstressed indistinct vowels typical of Neapolitan, and ‹č› stands for IPA [tʃ] (as in čə = 'there is' where čə = [tʃ]). These conventions must be explicitly glossed in any published transcription.

relatedItems.label: AIS, reloaded: a digital dialect atlas of Italy and Southern Switzerland
relatedItems.description:
In this paper, we will introduce to the scientifi c community, for the fi rst time in printed form, the output of the research project AIS, reloaded (AISr), which yielded the following achievements:
(1) a. a searchable digital version of half of the maps of the Sprach- und Sachatlas Italiens und der Südschweiz (Atlante Italo-Svizzero, AIS, 1928-1940), whose data were collected in 407 survey points in the two countries;
 b. a comparable corpus for the Italo-Romance and Romansh dialects of southern Switzerland (18 points each), corresponding to the original datapoints, consisting of new 
data that have been collected using the same questionnaire in the same localities almost one hundred years later.

The paper is organized as follows. In §2, we provide basic information on the project, which gave rise to the interactive database freely searchable at the website https://www.ais-reloaded.uzh.ch, and present the structure and functionalities of the latter. In §3, we exemplify the ways in which the AISr database can be used to compare subsequent diachronic stages of the same dialects, fi rst (§3.1) discussing some changes – mostly leading towards standardization – which are observed in western Surselva. We then consider changes in the areal distribution of some kinship terms (§3.2), the selection of a gender agreement marker in the dialect of Mesocco (§3.3) and the syntax of negation in Swiss-Lombard dialects (§3.4). Finally, §3.5 addresses (the lexical diffusion of) a sound change in Engadine. By way of conclusion, §4 outlines prospects for further research along this line.

relatedItems.label: Handbook of the International Phonetic Association: A guide to the use of the International Phonetic Alphabet
relatedItems.description:
The Handbook of the International Phonetic Association is a comprehensive guide to the Association's 'International Phonetic Alphabet' . The aim of the International Phonetic Alphabet is to provide a universally agreed system of notation for the sounds of languages, and for over a century the Alphabet has been widely used by phoneticians and others concerned with language. The Handbook presents the basics of phonetic analysis so that the principles underlying the Alphabet can be readily understood, and exemplifies the use of each of the phonetic symbols comprising the Alphabet. The application of the Alphabet
is then extensively demonstrated by the inclusion of over two dozen 'Illustrations' - concise analyses of the sound systems of languages accompanied by a phonetic transcription of a passage of speech. These Illustrations cover languages from allover the world. The Handbook also includes a range of other useful information. The 'Extensions' to the International Phonetic Alphabet cover speech sounds beyond the sound systems of languages, such as those with paralinguistic functions and those encountered in pathological speech . A full listing is given of internationally agreed computer codings for phonetic symbols, including not only those of the International Phonetic Alphabet but also those of other traditions. And there is extensive information on the history of the International Phonetic Association and its current activities. The Handbook is an essential reference work for all those involved in the analysis of speech. The International Phonetic Association exists to promote the study of the science of phonetics and the applications of that science. The Association can trace its history back to 1886, and since that time the most widely known aspect of its work has been the International Phonetic Alphabet. The Handbook has been produced collaboratively by leading phoneticians who have been on the Executive of the Association , and it incorporates (for instance in the case of the Illustrations) material provided by numerous members of the Association world wide.

relatedItems.label: Il sistema di trascrizione dell’Atlante Linguistico Mediterraneo  tra principi teorico-metodologici e prassi trascrittorie
relatedItems.description: This contribution traces the history of the Atlante Linguistico Mediterraneo transcription system, from its first formulation to the subsequent modifications that needed to be made after the fieldwork campaigns. The theoretical-methodological choices made by the promoters of this enterprise are investigated, as well as the phonetic practices of the fieldworkers who often departed from the original prescriptions. In the context of the works for the recovery and publication of the Atlas, and in relation to the strategies of normalization and simplification of the transcriptions that we are planning, it is more than ever appropriate to mature an overview of the evolution of the ALM transcription system and of the theoretical-methodological principles on which this was grounded. Every intervention on the transcriptions must indeed be consistent with these principles, so as to ensure the philological correctness of the operations. The main differences with the IPA transcription system are also summarized. This comparison will help to clarify the specificities of the ALM transcription system, and to correctly evaluate the opportunity and the modalities of a procedure for converting the ALM transcriptions into the IPA system.

composedOf.label: Learn or review your transcription system
composedOf.description: Whichever system you adopt, a solid command of its symbols and conventions is essential before beginning. Study the relevant charts and reference materials carefully, paying particular attention to the sounds present in the dialect you are documenting. If working with IPA — the recommended choice — the authoritative references are the "Handbook of the International Phonetic Association" (Cambridge UP, 1999) and the Illustrations series published in the Journal of the International Phonetic Association, which provides transcribed samples of many languages and dialect varieties. For a broader and more comprehensive understanding of the modern phonetic theory underlying the IPA system, you should also consult J. Laver ("Principles of Phonetics", Cambridge UP, 1994).

relatedItems.label: Type IPA phonetic symbols for all languages
relatedItems.description: This page allows you to easily type phonetic transcriptions in the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA). You can edit your text in the box and then copy it to your document, e-mail message, etc.

relatedItems.description:
Illustrations of the IPA are concise accounts of the phonetic structure of different languages using the Association’s International Phonetic Alphabet, accompanied by audio recordings. 
The latest Illustrations are available to view in order of publication date, title, or article number. After two years from their publication, all Illustrations are made freely available to read.

composedOf.label: Transcribe faithfully
composedOf.description:
The traditional and methodologically recommended approach for dialect data is impressionistic transcription: the transcriber aims to represent, as faithfully as possible, their auditory impressions, mapping them onto the taxonomic categories provided by phonetic theory. This is neither a phonological idealisation nor an attempt to normalise pronunciation toward a reference model. Rather, the transcription records what is actually perceived as produced by the speaker in a given utterance at a specific moment.

Impressionistic transcription requires that the transcriber have a trained ear and a thorough command of the phonetic system being used. The availability of digital recordings and acoustic analysis software (see Tools section below) greatly facilitates this work by allowing the analyst to listen repeatedly to the sequence to transcribe and, where necessary, to complement auditory perception with the visual inspection of acoustic properties.

relatedItems.label: Audacity
relatedItems.description:
Audacity is a free, easy-to-use and multilingual audio editor and recorder. Basic features, as listed on their website, include:



Record live audio.



Record computer playback on any Windows Vista or later machine.



Convert tapes and records into digital recordings or CDs.



Edit WAV, AIFF, FLAC, MP2, MP3 or Ogg Vorbis sound files.



Cut, copy, splice or mix sounds together.



Change the speed or pitch of a recording.

relatedItems.label: Praat
relatedItems.description: Praat is software for the phonetic analysis of speech, including support for articulatory and speech synthesis. It is also a computer program with which you can analyse, synthesize, and manipulate speech, and create high-quality pictures.

relatedItems.label: ELAN
relatedItems.description:
ELAN is a tool for creating annotations on multiple layers on audio and video resources. The textual content of annotations is in Unicode and the transcription is stored in XML.

With ELAN a user can add an unlimited number of textual annotations to audio and/or video recordings. An annotation can be a sentence, word or gloss, a comment, translation or a description of any feature observed in the media. Annotations can be created on multiple layers, called tiers. Tiers can be hierarchically interconnected. An annotation can either be time-aligned to the media or it can refer to other existing annotations. The content of annotations consists of Unicode text and annotation documents are stored in an XML format (EAF).

Main features and characteristics of ELAN:
* provides several ways to view the annotations, each view is connected to and synchronized with the media timeline

composedOf.label: Annotate prosody
composedOf.description: Prosodic annotation in dialect transcription is generally kept to a minimum. Vowel length is typically marked with [ː]; consonant length may alternatively be rendered by repeating the consonant symbol, a solution that many transcribers prefer for readability. Word stress is conventionally indicated with [ˈ] before the stressed syllable, omitted on weak monosyllables but retained on strong ones. For prosodic boundaries, [ | ] and [ ‖ ] are widely used to mark minor and major pauses respectively; silent pauses are often rendered with (.), following Conversation Analysis practice. For spoken-language phenomena not fully covered by IPA — such as hesitation lengthening or abrupt interruptions — additional symbols like ⟨ ⟩ and + are commonly adopted, on the condition that their values are explicitly declared in the conventions document. Words are generally separated by spaces, as this considerably aids the reading and comprehension of the transcription.

concept.label: Transcribing
concept.definition: transcribing describes  the activity of creating a representation of a manuscript or of audio or video recordings. The representation is generally textual for the verbal aspects of recordings and structured for example by speech turns. It can also contain multimodal information like gestures or events and multimedia information like time synchronization and relation to media files.

composedOf.label: Post-process and normalise the transcription
composedOf.description:
After the initial transcription, and having respected the phonetic reality produced by the speaker, it may be appropriate to intervene with simplification and normalisation operations to make the transcription usable for its intended purpose and audience. 

One common case concerns the normalisation of pronunciation variants. Minor fluctuations in the pronunciation of a given segment — which may have been transcribed with slightly different symbols across occurrences in the corpus — can often be unified under a single symbol after analysis, provided that the variation carries no contrastive or analytically significant function. For example, if a vowel is inconsistently realised between two slightly different articulatory positions, the analyst may choose either to preserve this difference by using two distinct phonetic notations, or to transcribe it uniformly using a single notation once it has been established that the variation is not meaningful to the analysis. The decision to normalise must follow, not precede, analysis: only after examining the distribution and function of a variable should you decide whether to represent its different variants with a single symbol. Normalisation should be conservative — when in doubt, preserve the variation.

A “narrow” transcription is appropriate for strictly phonetic research, or for studies in which phonetics constitutes a privileged level of analysis. Even in such cases, however, the transcriber may choose to represent certain phenomena in greater detail when they constitute the direct object of investigation, while paying less attention to other aspects. Although such choices may be acceptable for practical reasons related to time and resources, they must always be made explicit so that readers do not draw inaccurate conclusions from the transcription data. Any deviations from standard IPA symbols and conventions should likewise be clearly explained and properly justified, and should only be introduced when the IPA does not already provide a notation sufficiently adequate for what is being transcribed.

By contrast, in research that does not pursue specifically phonetic objectives, “broad” phonetic transcriptions are generally preferred. These omit most diacritics and tend to normalise minor fluctuations in pronunciation. More generally, every decision taken during transcription and post-processing should be documented clearly and transparently, so that users of the transcription can interpret the data correctly.

relatedItems.description:
Using Praat for Linguistic Research by Will Styler is a practical guidebook and information package designed to help you use the Praat phonetics software package more effectively in Phonetic or Phonological research. Although it was originally written in the Spring/Summer of 2011 for the 2011 Linguistic Institute’s Praat workshop, it’s now available for anybody who’s interested, and is being updated over time, both as Praat changes and as the author adds new information.

The guidebook itself is an 85+ page compilation of walkthroughs, explanations, and tutorials explaining how to use Praat for a variety of measurements and tasks. Although the guide does start with “basic” tasks like opening sound files, measuring duration, formants, pitch, it also covers more “advanced” tasks like source-filter resynthesis, A1-P0 nasality measurement, formula manipulation of sounds and even Praat scripting.
