composedOf.description:
Once the transcription has been reviewed and finalised, it is ready to be shared with its intended audience — whether as part of a published article, a corpus deposit, or an open-access dataset.

Ultimately, a successful transcription process strikes an optimal balance between phonetic reliability and textual readability, ensuring both the accurate representation of dialectal speech data and its long-term scientific interoperability.

label: How to Transcribe Phonetically
description: This workflow describes the successive methodological decisions and operations required to produce a phonetic transcription of oral/spoken data for research and documentation purposes in the social sciences and humanities (linguistics, dialectology, sociolinguistics, psycholinguistics, language documentation, conversation analysis, etc.). It is designed for researchers, students, and archivists who need to convert an audio recording into a phonetically annotated resource, whether for a single case study or for a larger, shareable, and reusable corpus. The workflow was elaborated on the basis of practical teaching and research notes on phonetic transcription (auditory and acoustic-supported transcription, use of Praat and ELAN, IPA/SAMPA conventions, inter-annotator agreement, and data publication), and integrates reference information on the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) and its alternative ASCII-based encoding, X-SAMPA. The workflow can be adapted to individual projects or to team-based research infrastructures, and it explicitly foresees the possibility of publishing the resulting transcriptions, together with the source audio, as a citable open dataset (e.g. via Zenodo or a comparable repository).

relatedItems.label: How to phonetically transcribe dialects
relatedItems.description: This workflow outlines the main steps involved in the transcription of dialectal speech data, with particular attention to the Italian linguistic context and the Italo-Romance dialects. Although it has been primarily conceived for the Italian reality, the workflow may also be adapted and applied to other geographical and linguistic contexts, provided that the necessary methodological and linguistic adjustments are taken into account. This process is documented by Giovanni Abete in the chapter “Trascrivere il dialetto” (pp. 211–217) of the "Vademecum per il trattamento delle fonti orali" (Tavolo permanente per le fonti orali, 2023).

relatedItems.label: Lexical and Non-lexical Tone and Prosodic Typology
relatedItems.description:
Prosodic typology has generally concentrated on those aspects of prosodic representation which are assumed to be represented in the lexicon. It is argued here that non-lexical representation at various levels, underlying phonological, surface phonological and phonetic, can also constitute a basis for prosodic typology. An example is given of a low-level comparison of English and French pitch patterns. A prosodic model integrating these different levels is presented which, it
argued can provide a useful tool for the investigation of prosodic typology and for a more robust basis for establishing the more abstract levels including those of lexical representations.

relatedItems.label: Treating Oral Sources in SSH Research
relatedItems.description:
This workflow, developed in Italy, guides SSH researchers, archivists, and institutions through the full lifecycle of oral sources: from initial legal and ethical preparation, through fieldwork and documentation, to long-term preservation, archival transfer, access, and valorisation, including responsible online publication. It covers the production of audio or audiovisual recordings, their contextual documentation, and their integration into archival systems.

The workflow applies equally to newly initiated oral data gathering campaigns and to the retrospective treatment of pre-existing collections. It draws on the "Vademecum per il trattamento delle fonti orali" (Ministero della Cultura, Direzione Generale Archivi, 2023), a multidisciplinary reference document developed by specialists from different domains, including oral historians, linguists, ethnologists, librarians and archivists.

While it integrates European data protection requirements (GDPR) and established professional standards, it also refers at certain points to the Italian legal framework. Researchers operating in other national contexts should therefore consult the relevant legislation and guidelines applicable in their own country.

relatedItems.label: Vademecum per il trattamento delle fonti orali
relatedItems.description: Starting from a broader definition of oral sources and from the assumption of the unity of the communicative event that generates the source—and, consequently, the archive of oral sources—this Vademecum provides a coherent theoretical framework, not merely prescriptive, to which methods and practices for the treatment of oral documentation can be anchored.

composedOf.label: Become familiar with the IPA transcription system
composedOf.description: Before transcribing, annotators should familiarize themselves with the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA), the most widely used phonetic alphabet, developed and maintained by the International Phonetic Association. The IPA Chart organizes consonants, vowels, and diacritics into tables structured according to phonetic-theoretical parameters (place and manner of articulation, voicing, vowel height and backness, rounding, etc.) rather than as an arbitrary inventory of symbols; understanding this underlying theoretical structure makes the choice of symbols more principled and consistent. The IPA Chart itself, together with downloadable fonts, a phonetic keyboard for Unicode text input, and a broad census of freely available phonetic resources (audio and video illustrations, pronunciation dictionaries, teaching materials), can be consulted and freely downloaded from the International Phonetic Association's website under a CC BY-SA 3.0 licence. A particularly useful external resource is the Seeing Speech portal, which offers interactive IPA tables: clicking on each symbol gives access to an audio example and to visualizations of the moving articulatory organs producing that sound.

relatedItems.label: Illustrations of the IPA
relatedItems.description:
Illustrations of the IPA are concise accounts of the phonetic structure of different languages using the Association’s International Phonetic Alphabet, accompanied by audio recordings. 
The latest Illustrations are available to view in order of publication date, title, or article number. After two years from their publication, all Illustrations are made freely available to read.

relatedItems.label: Seeing Speech
relatedItems.description: This online resource is a product of the collaboration between researchers at six Scottish Universities: the University of Glasgow, Queen Margaret University Edinburgh, Edinburgh Napier University, the University of Strathclyde, the University of Edinburgh and the University of Aberdeen. The resource provides teachers and students of practical Phonetics with ultrasound tongue imaging (UTI) and lip video of speech, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) video of speech, and 2D midsagittal head animations based on MRI and UTI data.

composedOf.label: Define the annotation team structure
composedOf.description: Decide, at the outset, whether the transcription will be produced by a single annotator or by multiple annotators, and make this choice according to the goals of the research rather than as an afterthought. A single-annotator design is faster and more consistent internally, and is often sufficient for exploratory work, small case studies, or projects where one trained phonetician's judgment is the accepted methodological standard. A multiple-annotator design is required whenever the reliability and reproducibility of the transcription itself need to be demonstrated — for example in corpus-building projects intended for external reuse, in studies making claims about categorical phonetic contrasts, or in any context where the transcription will be scrutinized as evidence. Choosing the multiple-annotator design at this stage has downstream consequences: it requires planning time and resources for independent transcription by each annotator, and it anticipates the inter-annotator agreement step described later in this workflow (Step 8). Decide also, at this point, whether annotators will work independently and blind to each other's output (recommended, to preserve the validity of the agreement calculation) or collaboratively from the start.

composedOf.label: Choose the transcription environment and method (auditory vs. acoustic-supported)
composedOf.description: Decide whether the transcription will be hosted and produced within a dedicated software environment, and whether it will be time-aligned to the acoustic signal or kept as a separate text. Two complementary methods of transcription exist. Auditory transcription relies on repeated listening to portions of the recording of varying length, letting the ear judge the identity of each sound. This method should be used with an explicit caveat: human auditory perception integrates a large number of acoustic cues simultaneously (spectral, temporal, and contextual), so isolating too short or too narrow a stretch of audio can distort perception and lead the transcriber to hear segments that are not actually representative of the sound in its natural context. Acoustic transcription complements auditory judgment with visual inspection of the acoustic signal, typically using Praat, which displays the waveform and spectrogram and allows fine-grained visualization and measurement of the signal. Two software tools are commonly used for this purpose. Praat is conceived primarily for acoustic analysis and offers advanced visualization (spectrogram, formants, pitch, intensity) together with an annotation (TextGrid) interface in which IPA symbols are already integrated, making it well suited to segmental and acoustic-phonetic work. ELAN is designed primarily for the annotation of conversational and multimodal data, but can be adapted to phonetic transcription purposes; it also captures the waveform reliably and is often preferred when transcription needs to be integrated with other layers of conversational or gestural annotation. The choice between the two (or the decision to use both) should be driven by whether the project's main analytic interest is fine acoustic-phonetic measurement (favoring Praat) or multi-layered discourse/interactional annotation (favoring ELAN).

Main features and characteristics of ELAN:

composedOf.label: Set up annotation tiers
composedOf.description: Within the chosen software, create the annotation tier(s) (in Praat, a TextGrid tier; in ELAN, a comparable annotation tier) that will host the phonetic transcription aligned to the audio signal. Praat provides built-in support for convenient IPA character entry within the annotation interface. ELAN likewise supports IPA transcription through Unicode input methods and dedicated keyboard mappings, although the workflow differs from Praat's implementation.  Additional tiers can be created in parallel for orthographic transcription, glossing, translation, or prosodic annotation, depending on the project's needs, so that the phonetic tier can later be cross-referenced with these other levels of analysis.

composedOf.label: Choose the transcription system (IPA or other; IPA recommended)
composedOf.description: Before starting to transcribe, decide which phonetic alphabet or transcription system will be used. The International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) is recommended as the default choice: it is the most widely known and used phonetic alphabet internationally, it is maintained and updated by a dedicated scientific association (the International Phonetic Association), it is directly supported by the annotation software commonly used for this kind of work, and it maximizes the readability and reusability of the resulting transcription by other researchers, regardless of their native language or specific subfield. An alternative exists in SAMPA, or its extended form X-SAMPA, a system developed in Europe from 1987 onward specifically to map IPA symbols onto printable 7-bit ASCII characters; guidelines exist for applying it to about two dozen languages, including Italian, and correspondence tables between IPA and SAMPA symbols are freely available online. X-SAMPA can be a reasonable choice in contexts where full Unicode/IPA font support is not guaranteed (for example in certain plain-text databases, older software, or programming/scripting environments where ASCII-only input is required for automated processing), or where the transcribed material must be easily typed on a standard keyboard without diacritic or special-character support. Other, more specialized phonetic notation systems exist for specific research traditions and can be adopted if the project has a compelling reason to do so, but in the absence of such a specific constraint, IPA should be preferred, as it offers the broadest institutional support, the richest set of freely available learning resources, and the greatest interoperability with other researchers' work.

composedOf.label: Learn the specific symbol set of the target language
composedOf.description: Beyond general familiarity with the IPA system, annotators should become practised in the specific, more restricted core set of symbols needed to transcribe the language (or languages) under study, since not all IPA symbols are relevant to any given language. The "Illustrations of the IPA" series, published for a wide range of languages, is a useful reference at this stage, as it presents a language-specific phonemic inventory together with example transcriptions and audio.

composedOf.label: Decide on segmentation
composedOf.description: Segmentation means explicitly marking, on the aligned tier, where each transcribed segment or phonetic element (larger or smaller than the segment, e.g. syllable or stops' VOT) begins and ends within the acoustic signal. Segmentation is not a logical requirement of transcription itself: it is entirely possible to transcribe a stretch of speech phonetically — for instance recognizing and writing the segments [t] and [a] in sequence — without ever specifying the precise instant at which the [t] ends and the [a] begins. However, in many projects segmentation becomes functional to the subsequent analysis: for example, if the research question requires measuring the duration of all instances of the vowel [a] in a corpus, then each relevant segment must be located precisely within the signal so that its temporal and spectral acoustic parameters (duration, intensity, spectral composition, formant structure, etc.) can be extracted. If segmentation is adopted, be aware that some sound sequences are considerably harder to segment reliably than others, even though this does not necessarily make them harder to transcribe. In increasing order of difficulty, segmentation boundaries are comparatively easy to locate for sequences of a fricative such as [s] followed by a vowel; more difficult for sequences involving nasal consonants; more difficult still for liquids; and diphthongs also present specific segmentation challenges due to the continuous, gradient nature of the formant transitions involved. Researchers working with these classes of sounds are encouraged to consult specialized phonetic literature on segmentation criteria before finalizing their protocol.

composedOf.label: Define the type and level of detail of the transcription
composedOf.description: Decide, before transcribing, whether the transcription will be phonological (representing only linguistically contrastive units) or phonetic, and, if phonetic, how much detail it should include. This decision should be driven by the goals of the research and by the intended audience of the transcription, not by convention alone. A narrow phonetic transcription aims to capture the specific realization of a given token as produced in that particular event, including fine phonetic detail and, if needed, voice quality information encoded via diacritics; this level of detail is appropriate when the research question concerns the concrete, individual realization of speech. A broad phonetic transcription instead aims to represent the general, "citation-form" pronunciation shared by a word or phrase across the speech community, abstracting away from token-specific detail; this level is generally sufficient, for example, in a psycholinguistic experiment where what matters is a general contrast (e.g. that half of the target words contain a long vowel and half a short one) rather than the precise acoustic realization of each individual token. As a basic convention, remember that phonetic transcription is always enclosed in square brackets, that no punctuation marks other than the phonetic symbols of the chosen alphabet should appear within the brackets, that orthographic capitalization has no bearing on the transcription, and that spaces between words are optional and can be included or omitted depending on whether the goal is to make the transcription of each individual word transparent or to represent the continuous phonetic realization of a full utterance with a higher level of phonetic fidelity.

composedOf.label: Revise the transcription and, if applicable, compare multiple annotators
composedOf.description: Once a first pass of the transcription is complete, plan a revision phase: the transcriber's intentions and criteria can shift while working through the material, and returning to earlier stretches of the text with a fresh or more experienced ear is normal and expected. Use this revision phase to normalize the transcription, i.e. to make sure that the same phonetic choices have been applied consistently throughout, rather than reflecting a criterion that evolved partway through the work. If the project was designed with multiple annotators (see Step 1), this is also the stage at which their independent transcriptions are compared. Comparing transcriptions serves to legitimate the phonetic transcription methodologically: having several transcribers work independently and then calculating an inter-annotator agreement score shows how much the transcriptions converge and, just as importantly, where and on which specific segments they diverge. Disagreements can be resolved in different ways depending on the project: through qualitative discussion among the annotators, through a negotiated joint decision, or by involving an external adjudicator who reviews the independently produced transcriptions and decides among them based on the reasons given by each annotator. Whichever method is chosen, the resulting agreement rate should always be reported transparently alongside the final transcription, and it should be acknowledged that some residual disagreement is a normal and expected feature of phonetic transcription rather than a sign of failure.

composedOf.label: Extract acoustic-phonetic data from the transcription
composedOf.description: A time-aligned phonetic transcription is not only a qualitative record: it becomes an interrogable dataset. The more segments have been annotated (see Step 4 on segmentation), the more extensive the range of interrogable material becomes. Using a script (for instance, a Praat script), it is possible to automatically extract a defined set of acoustic measurements — durations, intensity values, spectral or formant values, and so on — for every annotated interval or point, with each measurement linked back to its corresponding segment and tier. The output of this extraction step is a structured, interrogable dataset (e.g. exportable to a spreadsheet such as Excel) that can subsequently be used for statistical or quantitative phonetic analysis, closing the loop between qualitative transcription and quantitative acoustic research.

composedOf.label: Publish the transcription and its metadata
composedOf.description: Once the transcription (and, where relevant, its associated acoustic dataset) is finalized, you may consider to plan its publication as a research output in its own right, eventually with the corresponding audio recording, metadata, and documentation, in a suitable repository (for example Zenodo, or any comparable repository for research data). For the purposes of documenting the resulting resource or workflow within a marketplace or repository entry, the following elements should be provided: a title; a short introduction explaining what the workflow or resource allows one to do, in which research context it is meant to be used, and by whom it was elaborated; the title of each step identified in the process; and a description of each step. Publishing the transcription with complete metadata ensures that the resource is findable, citable, and reusable by other researchers, and that the methodological choices made at each stage of the workflow (annotator design, transcription method and software, segmentation strategy, IPA/SAMPA conventions used, level of phonetic detail, and inter-annotator agreement procedure) remain transparent and available for scrutiny or reuse.

label: How to use Github Issues in the Digital Humanities project communication between humanists and developers?
description:
# What is GitHub Issues
_Issues_ is a part of GitHub open platform and a place for reporting bugs, new functionalities, and system vulnerabilities. It could be used to facilitate any Digital Humanities project's communication between coding and non-coding people (like developers and humanists) due to the fact no coding skills are required to use it. 

# What can you do with GitHub Issues
>Create issues, break them into tasks, track relationships, add custom fields, and have conversations. Visualize large projects as spreadsheets or boards, and automate everything with code. 
[Source: GitHub Issues](https://github.com/features/issues)

# When use Github Issues
- In a large digital projects that involves a vast number of participants with various skills to facilitate communication between them, especially between developers and the rest of the team,
- When you would like to have an option to share your communication after the end of project easily and bring open science values to a new level,
- You suspect a lot of testing, bug reporting, new ideas around your digital project will emerge.

relatedItems.label: Transkribus Text Tagging
relatedItems.description:
The workflow describes the strategic development and deployment of a text tagging scheme for transcribed historical prints and / or handwritten resources. It aims primarily at larger collections that consist of relatively homogenous resource types. That means they are similar compared to each other regarding their historic context, structure, extent, language, etc.

If you’ve done transcriptions using Transkribus, it may be the ideal platform to implement your tagging scheme, but the approach is transferable.

Key objectives of the workflow are:
- manage quality and consistency for basic text analysis in the light of limited resources of academic research projects
- make large collections more manageable
- iteratively build up a comprehensible and consistent dataset
- adapt to the specific and generic characteristics of the source material on one side and 
- adapt early to key research questions and analytical dimensions on the other side
- provide the foundation for further data enrichment and higher levels of analysis such as normalized collection dictionaries, NER, Geo-Referencing, etc.
- create a model tagging scheme adapted to your needs for further scalability
- create ground truth data set for domain-specific AI text tagging

Please mind:
1. The workflow was developed in the context of a specific research project at the University of Basel, please visit ["VOCAL POWER"](https://dg.philhist.unibas.ch/de/bereiche/fruehe-neuzeit/snf-professur-macht-der-stimme/) for more information.
2. For the Open Marketplace it was shaped to address challenges that will very likely arise in similar projects. However: We strongly suggest thoroughly discussing all the steps with key stakeholders and project staff in order to adapt the parameters according to your own needs on the ground.
3. Work on data projects is prone to get out of hand easily, so plan your steps carefully, test and iterate small portions early on and finish one step at a time.

relatedItems.label: Github
relatedItems.description:
GitHub is a web-based repository service which offers the distributed revision control and source code management (SCM) functionality of GIT with a graphical user interface, desktop, and mobile integration. It also provides collaboration tools such as access control, wikis, task management, code review, bug tracking, and feature requests. It offers free accounts, often used to host opensource software projects, and private (paid) repositories.

Projects on GitHub can be accessed and manipulated using the git command-line interface and all of the standard git commands work with it. GitHub also allows registered and non-registered users to browse public repositories on the site. Multiple desktop clients have also been created by GitHub and other third parties which integrate with the platform.

GitHub is mainly used for code but can also be used for non-code files, it supports the following formats and features:

3D render files

Photoshop's native PSD format can be previewed and compared to previous versions of the same file.

Nested task-lists

Documentation and wikis

Small websites can be hosted from public repositories on GitHub. The URL format is http://projectname.github.io.

Issue tracking (including feature requests)

Visualization of geospatial data

Gantt charts

GitHub is a heavily used in the opensource development community but does not require hosted projects to meet the definition of Open Source.

For 'Bug' type we recommend:

2. Step by Step to re-create the bug
3. Desired action - how it should work
4. Operational system (on which this bug occurred)
5. Browser (on which this bug occurred)

For the 'new functionality' type we recommend:

composedOf.label: Prepare a set of labels
composedOf.description:
Labels act like tags - you can use to enrich each issue with additional data.
Basic simple set of labels might look like this:
 - backend 
- frontend
- feature
- pending
- urgent

Pending might be used in a context: when there is more contribution from non-coders needed, for example to add more screenshots to visualise the bug.

composedOf.label: Divide project into milestones
composedOf.description:
Milestones are a functionality that can be used to mark each stage/phase of the project. 
Usually we can divide it into: Phase 1, Phase 2 etc. and later add it to the issue.
We recommend use also "Nice to have" milestone, that indicates some issues might be completed in a future (for instance, next funding).

composedOf.label: Set rules for both teams to use Github Issues
composedOf.description:
It is crucial to prepare a set of rules (based on ealier steps) for both teams.
Examplary set might look like this:

1. Screenshots and links are a MUST for bugs issues
2. Be sure that there is no ALREADY existing issue before creating new one
3. Use labels and pay attention to PENDING label

It is up to you, how many rules you want to apply.

composedOf.label: Assign the coordinator of the communication workflow
composedOf.description: Choose a person which will be coordinating whole communication process. It does not matter whether it be coder or non-coder, yet this coordinator should be open to test new digital workflows, act sometimes as a trainer and ensure all people involved act in harmony with established rules and feel comfortable on Github Issues.

#### Introduction 

The purpose of this workflow is to provide a way to create and serve files in IIIF-compatible (International Image Interoperability Framework) format, which:

- Increase interoperability by standardizing access, as it is open source and widely implemented 

- Enhance delivery time by sending to the end-user only the required parts of the image

- Increase scalability as IIIF is ground-designed to handle large volumes of data

The main goal of this workflow is to streamline the creation process of IIIF-enabled resources. The entire procedure should be as simple as possible. Moreover, saved data should be accessible at will by any user having a proper resource link.

#### Workflow Goals
 
- Enable users to save images (in a given subset of formats) that will be properly converted and saved to the IIIF Server
- Enable users to access saved images at will by IIIF Viewer

#### Workflow implementation

concept.label: IIIF
concept.definition: The International Image Interoperability Framework (IIIF) is a set of shared application programming interface (API) specifications for interoperable functionality in digital image repositories. The IIIF is comprised of and driven by a community of libraries, museums, archives, software companies, and other organizations working together to create, test, refine, implement and promote the IIIF specifications. Using JSON-LD, linked data, and standard W3C web protocols such as Web Annotation, IIIF makes it easy to parse and share digital image data, migrate across technology systems, and provide enhanced image access for scholars and researchers. In short, IIIF enables better, faster and cheaper image delivery. It lets you leverage interoperability and the fabric of the Web to access new possibilities and new users for your image-based resources, while reducing long term maintenance and technological lock in. IIIF gives users a rich set of baseline functionality for viewing, zooming, and assembling the best mix of resources and tools to view, compare, manipulate and work with images on the Web, an experience made portableshareable, citable, and embeddable. (source: https://iiif.io/community/faq/)

concept.label: JPEG
concept.definition: JPEG ( JAY-peg) is a commonly used method of lossy compression for digital images, particularly for those images produced by digital photography. The degree of compression can be adjusted, allowing a selectable tradeoff between storage size and image quality. JPEG typically achieves 10:1 compression with little perceptible loss in image quality. JPEG compression is used in a number of image file formats. JPEG/Exif is the most common image format used by digital cameras and other photographic image capture devices; along with JPEG/JFIF, it is the most common format for storing and transmitting photographic images on the World Wide Web. These format variations are often not distinguished, and are simply called JPEG. The term "JPEG" is an initialism/acronym for the Joint Photographic Experts Group, which created the standard. The MIME media type for JPEG is image/jpeg, except in older Internet Explorer versions, which provides a MIME type of image/pjpeg when uploading JPEG images. JPEG files usually have a filename extension of .jpg or .jpeg. JPEG/JFIF supports a maximum image size of 65,53565,535 pixels, hence up to 4 gigapixels for an aspect ratio of 1:1.

concept.label: TIFF
concept.definition: Tagged Image File Format, abbreviated TIFF or TIF, is a computer file format for storing raster graphics images, popular among graphic artists, the publishing industry, and photographers. TIFF is widely supported by scanning, faxing, word processing, optical character recognition, image manipulation, desktop publishing, and page-layout applications. The format was created by Aldus Corporation for use in desktop publishing. It published the latest version 6.0 in 1992, subsequently updated with an Adobe Systems copyright after the latter acquired Aldus in 1994. Several Aldus or Adobe technical notes have been published with minor extensions to the format, and several specifications have been based on TIFF 6.0, including TIFF/EP (ISO 12234-2), TIFF/IT (ISO 12639), TIFF-F (RFC 2306) and TIFF-FX (RFC 3949).

relatedItems.label: Workflow for Annotating and Comparing IIIF resources using Altamira
relatedItems.description:
This workflow enables researchers and members of the public to visually annotate images from various providers that support the International Image Interoperability Framework (IIIF). It facilitates the comparison and integration of annotations across different image sources, allowing users to share their annotations for consultation, review, or collaborative editing.

The solution is particularly valuable in cases where images of a single artifact type are dispersed across multiple providers, and where a streamlined method for sharing annotations is preferred.

Fully compatible with all IIIF-compliant resources, the workflow integrates Altamira, a customized implementation of the Mirador viewer. Altamira has been specifically developed to support the preparation, management, preservation, sharing, and reuse of annotations in accordance with the Web Annotation Data Model.

Altamira is available as a service at the Archaeology Data Service: [link](http://chara-51.man.poznan.pl/mirador/iiif/)

### Implementation
This workflow's functionality relies on both existing IIIF resource sources and the integration of Altamira. Both are indispensable for its operation. Fortunately, these are already deployed across various platforms. If you intend to share your own IIIF resources or utilize a self-managed Altamira instance, please follow the steps detailed in [IIIF Enablement and Visualization Workflow Using Altamira Viewer for Image Repositories](https://marketplace.sshopencloud.eu/workflow/YHAnKE).

### Prerequisite
Altamira can be deployed independently by following [IIIF Enablement and Visualization Workflow Using Altamira Viewer for Image Repositories](https://marketplace.sshopencloud.eu/workflow/YHAnKE), or users may utilize the version deployed as a service by the Archaeology Data Service.

### Detailed documentation 
Detailed documentation with images is available [here](https://gitlab.pcss.pl/dl-team/atrium/iiif/mirador/mirador-atrium)!

relatedItems.label: Consult and Digitize Sources
relatedItems.description:
Access to primary sources is a prerequisite for any critical edition and must be addressed before encoding begins. Where sources have not yet been digitized, the editor should follow the IIIF (International Image Interoperability Framework) protocol, which enables standardized sharing, annotation, and long-term preservation of high-resolution images. IIIF allows any rectangular fragment of a manuscript to be directly addressed via a URL, and supports comparative visualization across multiple sources and collections. 

Where digitizations already exist in institutional repositories (libraries, archives), the editor should link to them rather than duplicate them, while verifying the legal conditions of their reuse. Two access modalities are available: a hyperlink to an externally hosted digitized resource, or an IIIF viewer integrated directly into the digital edition interface. 

The availability of digitized sources is particularly crucial for early music, where the faithful transcription of ligatures, mensuration signs, tablature systems, and other notational features requires direct visual reference to the manuscript.

label: Indexing an Audio Resource
description: Conceived and employed by the ORMETE project (Oralità, Memoria, Teatro), directed by Donatella Orecchia (Università di Roma Tor Vergata), this workflow allows a researcher or curator to produce a segment-based index of an audio or an audiovisual resource. Rather than replacing the recording with a transcription, this process structures the resource into titled, synopsised, and keyworded segments, enabling users to navigate directly to specific points in the interview and locate content by person, place, or institution. By preserving the double voice of interviewer and interviewee at segment level and by using indexing — rather than transcription — as the primary access tool, the workflow supports listening to the original recording as the main mode of engagement with the source, in line with the stated aim of guiding and educating listening. This kind of indexing can be carried out either through OHMS (Oral History Metadata Synchronizer) or without the support of any dedicated application. The output is a reviewed, structured index suitable for publication.

relatedItems.label: Transcribing conversation in ELAN
relatedItems.description:
This workflow outlines the main steps involved in the transcription of conversational data using ELAN, a software environment designed for the annotation and synchronisation of audio and video recordings. ELAN is particularly suitable for multimodal transcription, as it allows the annotation of both verbal and non-verbal phenomena — such as gaze, gestures, pauses, and interactional dynamics — through multiple time-aligned annotation tiers.

The workflow includes the preliminary design of the transcription scheme and annotation hierarchy, the configuration of tiers and segmentation units, the automatic or manual transcription and annotation process, and the exportation of the final transcript in EAF or other formats. 

This workflow is based on Letizia Cirillo’s chapter “Trascrivere la conversazione” (pp. 181–188), part of the "Vademecum per il trattamento delle fonti orali" (Tavolo permanente per le fonti orali, 2020).

relatedItems.label: Annotating Proxemic Features in Audiovisual Document Using ELAN
relatedItems.description:
This workflow describes how to annotate proxemic features in audiovisual corpora using ELAN. It integrates multimodal annotation principles from linguistic and semiotic research, with particular reference to gesture classification frameworks (Kendon, McNeill) and facial annotation protocols (FACS, Ekman & Friesen).

This process is grounded on Meluzzi’s approach to annotation ("Annotare una trascrizione", in "Vademecum per il trattamento delle fonti orali", pp. 227-229).

relatedItems.label: Treating Oral Sources in SSH Research
relatedItems.description:
This workflow, developed in Italy, guides SSH researchers, archivists, and institutions through the full lifecycle of oral sources: from initial legal and ethical preparation, through fieldwork and documentation, to long-term preservation, archival transfer, access, and valorisation, including responsible online publication. It covers the production of audio or audiovisual recordings, their contextual documentation, and their integration into archival systems.

The workflow applies equally to newly initiated oral data gathering campaigns and to the retrospective treatment of pre-existing collections. It draws on the "Vademecum per il trattamento delle fonti orali" (Ministero della Cultura, Direzione Generale Archivi, 2023), a multidisciplinary reference document developed by specialists from different domains, including oral historians, linguists, ethnologists, librarians and archivists.

While it integrates European data protection requirements (GDPR) and established professional standards, it also refers at certain points to the Italian legal framework. Researchers operating in other national contexts should therefore consult the relevant legislation and guidelines applicable in their own country.

relatedItems.label: Timecode Indexing Module - TIM
relatedItems.description: TIM (Timecode Indexing Module) is a tool for indexing and annotation of audio or video recordings, like oral history interviews. TIM facilitates the use of media files and available text (e.g., imperfect transcripts) to create and export timecode index data into existing multimedia display systems, like OHMS and Aviary. TIM also allows for free-form notetaking for casual users or professional researchers to manage a/v content in a timecode-linked environment.

relatedItems.label: Indexing Multilingual Content with the Oral History Metadata Synchronizer (OHMS)
relatedItems.description: No description provided

relatedItems.label: Oral History Metadata Synchronizer
relatedItems.description:
OHMS (Oral History Metadata Synchronizer) inexpensively and efficiently enhances access to oral history by providing users with word-level search capability and a time-correlated transcript or indexed interview connecting the textual search term to the corresponding moment in the recorded interview online.

OHMS is an open source, web-based application designed to improve the user experience you provide for oral history, no matter what CMS or repository you use. There are 2 main components of the OHMS system

OHMS Application: The OHMS application is where the work is done. This is the back-end, web-based application where interviews are imported, and metadata is created. In the OHMS application transcripts are time-coded and/or interviews are indexed. Upon completion, the interview record (including the synchronized transcript and/or time-coded index) are exported as an XML file. When located on a web server, the OHMS XML file is what interfaces with your content management system through the OHMS Viewer.

OHMS Viewer: The OHMS viewer is the user interface of ohms. When an interview is called by the repository, the OHMS viewer loads, calling select interview level metadata and the intra interview level metadata created in the OHMS Application from the corresponding xml file.

relatedItems.label: Vademecum per il trattamento delle fonti orali
relatedItems.description: Starting from a broader definition of oral sources and from the assumption of the unity of the communicative event that generates the source—and, consequently, the archive of oral sources—this Vademecum provides a coherent theoretical framework, not merely prescriptive, to which methods and practices for the treatment of oral documentation can be anchored.

composedOf.label: Listen to the resource
composedOf.description: Listen to the audio/video resource in full, and more than once, before beginning the indexing work.

composedOf.label: Define the segment title
composedOf.description: Divide the resource into segments and assign each segment a title. The title must always reflect the double voice present in the segment (interviewer and interviewee), indicating who is speaking — at minimum through initials/siglum.

composedOf.label: Draft the segment synopsis
composedOf.description: Write a synopsis of the segment in the third person. Short portions of direct speech may be included, placed in quotation marks; extended passages of direct speech should not be used.

composedOf.label: Identify keywords
composedOf.description: Assign keywords to the segment, drawing on a predefined keyword set. This set is generative and organised into fields such as people, places, and institutions, and is expanded over time.

composedOf.label: Repeat for all remaining segments
composedOf.description: Repeat Steps 1–4 (listening, titling, synopsis, keyword identification) for each of the remaining segments of the resource.

composedOf.label: Final review
composedOf.description: Conduct a final review of the indexing by listening to the resource in its entirety once more.

label: In situ FTIR Analysis for the characterisation of          materials on archaeological or cultural heritage objects
description: FTIR spectroscopy is a widely used technique for examining various types of cultural heritage objects, with significant contributions in studies concerning chemical characterization of materials, both organic (binding media, varnishes, adhesives, coatings, consolidants, etc.) and inorganic (pigments, corrosion products, salts, etc.). The main goals are the evaluation of the state of conservation of artworks, characterization of their constituent materials as well as the monitoring of restoration interventions. FTIR spectroscopy can be applied to all the substrates (paintings, metals, stone, paper,...). The FTIR spectroscopy provides quick and relatively straightforward molecular identification of materials under examination, due to the fact that the collective position and pattern of absorption bands in the FTIR spectrum designate the combination of molecular groups found in any specific compound. The method is significantly versatile, therefore different types of equipment are commercially available such as bench top instruments, probes/portable and handheld instruments. These advantages including the simplicity, accuracy and speed of the analysis has made FTIR spectroscopy very successful in the field of cultural heritage. The current scenario presents a methodology for FTIR analysis directly on cultural heritage objects (no sampling).

relatedItems.label: Portable Raman versus portable mid-FTIR reflectance instruments to monitor synthetic treatments used for the conservation of monument surfaces
relatedItems.description: This study aims to evaluate the relevance of portable Raman and portable mid-Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) reflectance instruments in monitoring the synthetic treatments applied on plaster substrates, a crucial issue in a conservation work. Some polymeric consolidants and protectives have a relatively short life owing to their degradation, and after some years the surface should be retreated. It follows that any information about the presence and composition of the products applied, their chemical transformations and their distribution on the surfaces is essential. For these purposes, conservation scientists should seek and test new in situ methods, and this is of utmost importance especially in the case of buildings, considering their large dimensions and consequent extensive mapping. The effectiveness of portable Raman and portable mid-FTIR reflectance instruments has been compared by analysing a set of laboratory specimens prepared and treated with variable amounts of products belonging to three classes of polymers; the spectroscopic investigation highlighted, for the first time, the limits and the advantages of portable Raman and portable mid-FTIR reflectance instruments in the detection of small amounts of products commonly employed for the conservation of plasters.

relatedItems.label: An in situ multi-analytical approach in the restoration of bronze artefacts
relatedItems.description: A multi-analytical approach was adopted to compare different cleaning methods during the conservation works on two bronze artefacts: the Brera's Napoleon by A. Canova and the Florence Baptistery's North Door by L. Ghiberti. An appropriate number of surface areas were identified, and their properties and homogeneity were characterised in situ by means of colorimetry, Eddy Current patina thickness measurements, FTIR spectroscopy and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS). On the Napoleon statue, three sets of laser cleaning parameters were adopted on distinct selected areas. On the North Door, a mechanical and two chemical cleaning methods were applied on two separate areas; both chemical methods were based on Agar gel. The results on surface composition, appearance and corrosion rate of the different cleaning methods were compared with the properties of the uncleaned area with the same set of in situ analytical techniques. Measurements results were statistically analysed to take into account the lack of homogeneity typical of outdoor bronze surfaces. Based on the results obtained on the two bronze artefacts analysed, the role of the analytical techniques adopted is discussed. The effectiveness of the described in situ multi-analytical approach towards a better conservation--restoration methodology for outdoor bronzes is enlightened.

relatedItems.label: Characterization of Pigment-Binding Media Systems - Comparison of Non-invasive In-situ Reflection FTIR with Transmission FTIR Microscopy
relatedItems.description: A novel external reflection FTIR device, which enables nondestructive analyses in the region from 4000-450 cm-1 with a measuring point diameter of approximately 5 mm, was tested for the identification of pigments and binding media in two modern paintings and several mockups with traditional pigment-binding media combinations. Comparative measurements were carried out with minute samples using a diamond cell for transmission FTIR microscopy. The results were interpreted by comparison to database spectra measured in transmission mode. The appearance of distorted peaks in raw reflection spectra impedes a direct comparison with the collected spectra in the transmission mode. Best matches with database spectra were obtained applying the Kramers-Kronig transformation to the reflection spectra of substances showing narrow bands, particularly in the region of about 1900 to 580 cm-1. In the case of modern paintings a good match between transmission and reflection data could be achieved in the fingerprint region. It was possible to identify organic pigments PY 3 (Pigment Yellow 3) and PR 4 (Pigment Red 4) as well as calcite and PVAc (polyvinyl acetate). The identification of materials used for preparation of the mockups was successful for lead white, calcite, Prussian blue, indigo, ultramarine, azurite, malachite, Arabic gum and linseed oil, whereas the transformed spectra of cobalt blue, Naples yellow and especially of smalt and the proteinaceous binding media could not be identified using database spectra

relatedItems.label: Non-invasive identification of plastic materials in museum collections with portable FTIR reflectance spectroscopy: Reference database and practical applications
relatedItems.description: In this work, portable Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) reflectance spectroscopy was used for the contactless, non-invasive, and in situ analysis of historic plastics. For the first time, this paper presents the complete database of polymer spectra of a set of reference materials widely used in the cultural heritage community. Over 100 samples from the ResinKitTM and SamCo (Popart Project) collections, which also include samples such as foams, thin films, dark plastics, and other challenging materials, were analyzed. The extensive database of spectral signatures that was acquired for this work represented the departure point for a field study aiming at the identification of the components of a variety of plastic artifacts in the collections of Architecture and Design and Contemporary Art of the Art Institute di Chicago. Reflectance FTIR spectroscopy was confirmed in situ to be a fast and effective method of identification of historic plastics. In some cases, in addition to the main polymers, it was also possible to identify additives in plastic blends, such as plasticizers and inorganic fillers.

The measurment spot size (dimensions of the analysed spot) and the measurment resolution/accuracy are documented"

composedOf.description: Select the sites of analysis. The point of analysis (3 to 5 mm diameter) has to be optically flat to inhibit diffuse reflection. Acquire high resolution detailed reference images of the entire object or of the part under study (in case of a monument). Use the detailed reference images to document the points of analysis. Possible source of error: Diffuse reflection results from a combined process including reflection, refraction and diffraction of the incident radiation due to interactions with particles of the sample. Diffuse reflection spectra appear to be similar to transmission spectra derived from poorly prepared KBr disks.

A tentative spectrum is obtained on the specimen / area under examination acquiring the number of scans that seems appropriate. The scans may be increased according to the final output. Depending on surface morphology and composition, it may be necessary to optimize the acquisition parameters to improve the spectral profile.

composedOf.description: Recording of the FTIR spectra taken on representative sites on the CH object. First evaluation of the spectrum (assessment of FTIR peaks and eventually distortions). The measurement conditions (number of scans, acquisition specral range, spectral resolution) are documented in a text file for all the measurements or in form of metadata file for each spectrum file. The position of the instrument must be kept as fixed as possible to avoid artefacts and data rejection by the processing system.

concept.label: ASCII
concept.definition: ASCII abbreviated from American Standard Code for Information Interchange, is a character encoding standard for electronic communication. ASCII codes represent text in computers, telecommunications equipment, and other devices. Most modern character-encoding schemes are based on ASCII, although they support many additional characters. ASCII is the traditional name for the encoding system.

relatedItems.label: Revised JCAMP-DX Spectral File Format for Submissions to the Infrared \& Raman Users Group (IRUG) Spectral Database
relatedItems.description: Revised guidelines are presented for the submission of both Raman and infrared (IR) spectra in the JCAMP-DX format to the Infrared and Raman Users Group (IRUG) Spectral Database. The previous guidelines were specific to IR spectra. IRUG uses JCAMP -DX files as the principal source of information for submitted spectra. It remains the chosen file format because it is platform independent, non-proprietary and allows error-free transfer of spectral information between various instruments and users. All information pertaining to a sample and spectrum (as outlined on the IRUG Spectrum Submission Form) is incorporated into the JCAMP-DX file in a consistent format to create a self-contained, complete data record. This format, consisting of JCAMP-DX 5.01 and IRUG defined labelled-data-records (LDRs) and text fields is described. The LDRs for IRUG have been kept to a minimum to facilitate automatic transfer of information when IRUG JCAMP-DX files are imported into user local IR and Raman software packages.

relatedItems.label: MOVIDA
relatedItems.description: MOVIDA is a new and innovative tool for the data management and analysis of non-invasive investigations in the Cultural Heritage field. The software was developed due to the lack of an adequate tool able to manage all the heterogeneous data generated in a in-situ multi-technique investigation of an artwork. It allows to directly manage, store analyse and perform cross-comparison of all the data obtained with the techniques usually employed in a scientific investigation of an artwork.

This analytical technique characterizes material composition by measuring their interaction with infrared radiation. MID-IR wavelengths span 4000 to 400 cm^-1, while FAR-IR extends beyond 400 cm^-1. label: In situ X-Ray fluorescence analysis for the          characterisation of materials on cultural heritage objects
description: X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy is a well-established method for the in situ investigation of archaeological objects and artworks through the characterization of the chemical (elemental) composition of materials. The fact that the method is essentially non-destructive makes it particularly attractive and widely used by heritage scientists, art historians, archaeologists, curators and conservators. The benefits of XRF include fast analysis, applicability to any type of object or composite material of various shapes and dimensions, suitability for the detection of major to trace elements and semi quantitative capabilities.

relatedItems.label: CIDOC-CRM
relatedItems.description: The "CIDOC object-oriented Conceptual Reference Model" (CRM), was developed by the ICOM/CIDOC Documentation Standards Group. Since September 2000, the CIDOC CRM is being developed into an ISO standard in a joined effort of the CIDOC CRM SIG and ISO/TC46/SC4/WG9. Since September 2006 it has been accepted as ISO 21127. The CIDOC CRM represents an 'ontology' for cultural heritage information i.e. it describes in a formal language the explicit and implicit concepts and relations relevant to the documentation of cultural heritage. The primary role of the CIDOC CRM is to serve as a basis for mediation of cultural heritage information and thereby provide the semantic 'glue' needed to transform today's disparate, localised information sources into a coherent and valuable global resource. The CIDOC CRM is intended to promote a shared understanding of cultural heritage information by providing a common and extensible semantic framework that any cultural heritage information can be mapped to. It is intended to be a common language for domain experts and implementers to formulate requirements for information systems and to serve as a guide for good practice of conceptual modelling. In this way, it can provide the "semantic glue" needed to mediate between different sources of cultural heritage information, such as that published by museums, libraries and archives.

relatedItems.label: CRMsci
relatedItems.description: The Scientific Observation Model (CRMsci) is a formal ontology intended to be used as a global schema for integrating metadata about scientific observation, measurements and processed data in descriptive and empirical sciences such as biodiversity, geology, geography, archaeology, cultural heritage conservation and others in research IT environments and research data libraries. Its primary purpose is facilitating the management, integration, mediation, interchange and access to research data by description of semantic relationships, in particular causal ones. It is not primarily a model to process the data themselves in order to produce new research results, even though its representations offer themselves to be used for some kind of processing.

relatedItems.label: An Introduction to X-Ray Fluorescence (XRF) Analysis in Archaeology
relatedItems.description: AbstarctAs I have discussed in the last chapter, our goal here is not to elucidate XRF for the entire scientific community -- this has been done admirably by others -- but to translate the physics, mechanics, and art of XRF for those in archaeology and geoarchaeology who use it as one of the many tools to explain the human past in twenty-first century archaeology. While not a simple exercise, it has utility not only for those like us, who have struggled (and enjoyed) the vagaries of XRF applications to archaeological problems, but for a greater archaeology. First, we trace the basic history of X-rays used in science and the development of XRF for geological and archaeological applications, and the role some major research institutions have played in the science. Following this is an explanation of XRF that, in concert with the glossary, illuminates the technology.

relatedItems.label: Non-Invasive and Non-Destructive Examination of Artistic Pigments, Paints, and Paintings by Means of X-Ray Methods
relatedItems.description: Recent studies are concisely reviewed, in which X-ray beams of (sub)micrometre to millimetre dimensions have been used for non-destructive analysis and characterization of pigments, minute paint samples, and/or entire paintings from the seventeenth to the early twentieth century painters. The overview presented encompasses the use of laboratory and synchrotron radiation-based instrumentation and deals with the use of several variants of X-ray fluorescence (XRF) as a method of elemental analysis and imaging, as well as with the combined use of X-ray diffraction (XRD) and X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS). Microscopic XRF is a variant of the method that is well suited to visualize the elemental distribution of key elements, mostly metals, present in paint multi-layers, on the length scale from 1 to 100 lm inside micro-samples taken from paintings. In the context of the characterization of artists' pigments subjected to natural degradation, the use of methods limited to elemental analysis or imaging usually is not sufficient to elucidate the chemical transformations that have taken place. However, at synchrotron facilities, combinations of μ-XRF with related methods such as μ-XAS and μ-XRD have proven themselves to be very suitable for such studies. Their use is often combined with microscopic Fourier transform infra-red spectroscopy and/or Raman microscopy since these methods deliver complementary information of high molecular specificity at more or less the same length scale as the X-ray microprobe techniques. Since microscopic investigation of a relatively limited number of minute paint samples, taken from a given work of art, may not yield representative information about the entire artefact, several methods for macroscopic, non-invasive imaging have recently been developed. Those based on XRF scanning and full-field hyperspectral imaging appear very promising; some recent published results are discussed.

relatedItems.label: Interferences and Side-effects
relatedItems.description: This chapter focuses on different other possible interactions between electromagnetic radiation and matter, as these can strongly interfere with Raman spectroscopy. It also describes some common approaches to avoid interferences and side-effects such as absorption, fluorescence, thermal effects, photodecomposition, and laser ablation. The selection of an appropriate laser wavelength may be crucial to avoid such interferences. Apart from interferences caused by interaction of the laser light with the sample, background radiation or ambient light may interfere with the measurements.

relatedItems.label: Raman spectroscopy as a means for the identification of plattnerite (PbO2), of lead pigments and of their degradation products
relatedItems.description: The Raman spectra of plattnerite \[lead(IV) oxide, PbO2\] and of the lead pigments red lead (Pb3O4), lead monoxide \[PbO, litharge (tetragonal) and massicot (orthorhombic)\], lead white \[basic lead carbonate, 2PbCO3·Pb(OH)2\] and of their laser-induced degradation products were recorded using a range of different excitation lines, spectrometer systems and experimental conditions. The degradation of PbO2 is more extensive along the pathway PbO2 → Pb3O4 → PbO (litharge) → PbO (massicot) the shorter the wavelength of the excitation line and the higher its power. The Raman spectrum of PbO2, which is black and of the rutile structure, is particularly difficult to obtain but three bands, at 653, 515 and 424 cm−1, were identified as arising from the b2g, a1g and eg modes respectively, by analogy with the corresponding modes of isostructural SnO2 (776, 634 and 475 cm−1). A further oxide was identified, PbO1.55, the Raman spectrum of which does not correspond to that of any of the laser-induced degradation products of PbO2 at any of the wavelengths used. The Raman results are critical to the future use of Raman microscopy for the identification of lead pigments on artworks.

relatedItems.label: Mitigation strategies for radiation damage in the analysis of ancient materials
relatedItems.description: The study of materials in cultural heritage artifacts and micro-samples benefits from diagnostic techniques based on intense radiation sources, such as synchrotrons, ion-beam accelerators and lasers. While most of the corresponding techniques are classified as non-destructive, investigation with photons or charged particles entails a number of fundamental processes that may induce changes in materials. These changes depend on irradiation parameters, properties of materials and environmental factors. In some cases, radiation-induced damage may be detected by visual inspection. When it is not, irradiation may still lead to atomic and molecular changes resulting in immediate or delayed alteration and bias of future analyses. Here we review the effects of radiation reported on a variety of cultural heritage materials and describe the usual practice for assessing short-term and long-term effects. This review aims to raise awareness and encourage subsequent research activities to limit radiation side effects.

relatedItems.label: Raman spectroscopy in cultural heritage: Background paper
relatedItems.description: In the last 30 years Raman spectroscopy has become an essential experimental tool for the analysis of a wide variety of artists' materials, often in a non-destructive, non-invasive manner. The Raman effect provides a quick and relatively straightforward molecular identification of a material under examination. A Raman spectrum can be considered as a fingerprint that could be used for compound identification when a database of standard spectra is available for comparison purposes.

Possible source of error: Diffuse reflection results from a combined process including reflection, refraction and diffraction of the incident radiation due to interactions with particles of the sample. concept.label: PAGE XML
concept.definition: There is a plethora of established and proposed document representation formats but none that can adequately support individual stages within an entire sequence of document image analysis methods (from document image enhancement to layout analysis to OCR) and their evaluation. This paper describes PAGE, a new XML-based page image representation framework that records information on image characteristics (image borders, geometric distortions and corresponding corrections, binarisation etc.) in addition to layout structure and page content. The suitability of the framework to the evaluation of entire workflows as well as individual stages has been extensively validated by using it in high-profile applications such as in public contemporary and historical ground-truthed datasets and in the ICDAR Page Segmentation competition series.

concept.label: PAGE XML
concept.definition: There is a plethora of established and proposed document representation formats but none that can adequately support individual stages within an entire sequence of document image analysis methods (from document image enhancement to layout analysis to OCR) and their evaluation. label: Linguistic annotation of corpora
description: This scenario explains the steps to take to annotate a corpus in order to conduct linguistic and statistical analysis based on it. This scenario wants to provide general information for people starting with linguistic annotation. The aim is to provide a generic scenario with no specific tool in mind: We refer to tools but don't specify how to use them. There are various tools and frameworks to perform the steps in this scenario that can be used depending on the language/s you are working with or your programming environment. A number of tool-boxes for Natural language processing (NLP) exist, which are able to perform several of the annotation steps in an integrated way. These resources are listed below under "Using an existing NLP pipeline". The next step after performing the procedures described in this scenario usually is to put the annotated corpus into a corpus query engine to query and analyze it based on its annotations. Again, some popular query engines already provide a built-in pipeline that is able to perform the basic processing steps in one go, taking most of the burden off the user.

composedOf.label: Tokenizing
composedOf.description: Tokenizing a text refers to the task of splitting it up into identifiable units -- the tokens. Or to state it in less formal terms: to split the text into words and punctuation marks. Tokenization is a prerequisite for basically all other forms of linguistic analysis, as it provides the basic units on which to operate. Though some "higher level" NLP tools would allow to use plain text as input i.e. deal with the necessary tokenization themselves, many tools still rely on tokenized text. Tokenizers are typically quite simple programs: the basic heuristic is to split the text at whitespaces and punctuation characters. An important factor in many western languages is to properly distinguish punctuation characters which are actually part of an abbreviation like in "e.g.". The quality of many tokenizers thus typically relies on the application of language specific abbreviation lists and regular expressions for correctly identifying sequences of characters which form a token. E.g. web and e-mail addresses, date and time etc.

relatedItems.label: TreeTagger
relatedItems.description: The TreeTagger is a tool for annotating text with part-of-speech and lemma information. It was developed by Helmut Schmid in the TC project at the Institute for Computational Linguistics of the University of Stuttgart. The TreeTagger has been successfully used to tag German, English, French, Italian, Danish, Dutch, Spanish, Bulgarian, Russian, Portuguese, Galician, Greek, Chinese, Swahili, Slovak, Slovenian, Latin, Estonian, Polish, Romanian, Czech, Coptic and old French texts and is adaptable to other languages if a lexicon and a manually tagged training corpus are available.

relatedItems.label: Universal POS tags
relatedItems.description: The resource offers a comprehensive overview of Universal POS (Part-of-Speech) tags along with detailed descriptions and examples for each tag. It covers a wide range of linguistic categories including adjectives, adverbs, nouns, verbs, determiners, pronouns, conjunctions, interjections, numerals, particles, proper nouns, punctuation, subordinating conjunctions, symbols, and "other" categories. Each entry provides a clear definition of the linguistic category, examples of words falling into that category, and references for further reading. The resource aims to provide a standardized framework for annotating and analyzing linguistic data across different languages, facilitating linguistic research, natural language processing tasks, and computational linguistics applications.

composedOf.label: Lemmatizing
composedOf.description: Lemmatizing refers to the task which determines the lemma (also known as canonical form, dictionary form, or citation form) for each word form present in the text. It relies on the information extracted in the tokenization and POS tagging steps, and is often integrated into the POS tagging tool. The relevance of the lemma information becomes obvious for morphologically richer languages, where the possibility to simply refer to the canonical form in order to identify all its inflected forms is a real asset. Generally speaking, most lemmatizers rely on some sort of dictionary or word list in the background where mapping between word forms and its lemmas are defined. Because these dictionaries are not able to cover all words of a language you have to expect cases where the lemmatization will miss out.

composedOf.label: Stemming
composedOf.description: Stemming refers to the process of reducing inflected or sometimes derived word forms to their word stem, base or root form. The stem does not need to be identical to the morphological root of the word, nor has it to be a proper word form at all. Stemming can be viewed as a simplified version of lemmatization. In some respects, stemming can be seen as a poor man's version of lemmatizing, c.f. simple affix stripping as the most traditional approach used. However, stemming can relate different lemmata to each other via a shared root, something lemmatization typically does not provide for. Stemming thus is still widely used in the context of information retrieval and by search engines because it allows for generalizations on related words.

relatedItems.label: WebLicht: Getting Started
relatedItems.description: WebLicht is a service orchestration and execution environment for incremental automatic annotation of text corpora, built upon Service Oriented Architecture principles. Its main components are: \* A set of distributed services for data processing \* A repository containing metadata about the services \* A web application that offers a user-friendly graphical interface for building chains of services and executing them WebLicht's services are hosted on servers distributed throughout Europe, which allows full control of a tool by its developer. Each tool within WebLicht is registered in a repository containing information about its input requirements and its output, among other things. This information is necessary to determine which tools can be added to the processing chain at any given point while building a chain because each tool in a processing chain uses the output of the previous tool in the chain as its input. Only those tools which are able to work with the data are available as choices for adding to a chain. The main focus of this Quick Start Guide is on WebLicht's web application and how it can be used to linguistically annotate text and subsequently to visualize the annotations. We will create and run a very simple tool chain to annotate a text and view the results.

relatedItems.label: WebLicht
relatedItems.description:
WebLicht is an execution environment for automatic annotation of text corpora. Linguistic tools such as tokenizers, part of speech taggers, and parsers are encapsulated as web services, which can be combined by the user into custom processing chains. The resulting annotations can then be visualized in an appropriate way, such as in a table or tree format. 

It is often the case that a tool relies on one or more annotation layers to exist in the input data before it can begin processing. WebLicht can assist the user in building a processing chain by determining which tools are able to operate on the data at any given point and offering only those tools as options to add to the chain. There are 2 modes for building tool chains: Easy Mode lets you choose pre-defined processing chains Advanced Mode allows you to build customized tool chains. 

Login is required to use the tools and corpora. Login with email addresses from most recognized European universities will be automatically accepted. Individuals with a Non-European email address need to create an account with clarin.eu Developed by the German language resource infrastructure (D-SPIN) and Common language resources and technology infrastructure (CLARIN).

label: LLM-Powered Mapping of Keywords of a Research Article to Linked Data
description: Suppose you have a research article which is written in a language other than English and you have a set of keywords for that article. How could you grasp the main topics of the article from the keywords? First, you would like to translate them, but this is not a trivial task since words can be ambiguous, and finding the exact sense requires an understanding of the whole article! Moreover, suppose you want to link your article to other resources, for example other articles that share the same topic. Now suppose you want to make your resource accessible so that people can find keywords in different languages. This workflow provides a solution to all this scenarios, since it gives you a way to map keywords to linked data (Wikidata and DBPedia entities).

The second step is to choose the article you want to work.
If you want to work with an article in the GoTriple platform, the tool offers a simple interface to do this! You only need to look for the article in the platform (https://www.gotriple.eu/). By default, each article in GoTriple comes with an ID and a list of keywords. Once you have the article ID, go to the next step.

composedOf.label: Format Keywords and Abstract
composedOf.description:
Now, open a Python notebook (you can use Jupyter or Colab). You can look at the file test_notebook to see a tutorial of how to use the tool. 
In case you are working with a GoTriple article and you have identified the ID (see the previous step), execute the function get_item_by_id with the id of your article as parameter. This formats the abstract and the keywords so that they can be ingested by the other steps of the chain. 

In case your article is not in GoTriple article no problem, we have a solution for you! Execute the function get_item_from_user (see an example in the notebook): this function allows you to manually enter your article data, and automatically formats them in a proper way! You will be asked the article title, the keywords, the abstract. The more info you give, the more keywords will be extracted from your data! But if you don't know some of these things no problem, just enter "unknown" and the tool will work anyway!

relatedItems.label: Introduction to Jupyter Notebooks
relatedItems.description: Jupyter notebooks provide an environment where you can freely combine human-readable narrative with computer-readable code. This lesson describes how to install the Jupyter Notebook software, how to run and create Jupyter notebook files, and contexts where Jupyter notebooks can be particularly helpful.

composedOf.label: Choose your Tool for Linking
composedOf.description:
Now, it's time to choose which tool you want to use to link the keywords to linked data resources! At the present state, the code gives you two options: the first is using DBPedia Spotlight, a simple and light tool which is specialized for named entity linking. This tool is easy and free, but its performance is poor if keywords are not in English.
The second option is to free the power of LLM! You have two choices here: one is to use Mistral, a free model. This method does not require having an account on the OpenAI API, but it is quite slow (nearly 30 seconds to get the answer) and its performance is of course poorer than that of a GPT model. The code also allows you to use your OpenAI key to ask directly to your favourite GPT. In order to execute any of these methods, look at the guide in test_notebook.ipynb. You can choose if you want to give the LLM the content of the abstract, so that it makes more informed choices based on the context.

composedOf.label: Introduction
composedOf.description:
[Zotero](https://zotero.org) is a free and open source reference and bibliography management software. It [ingests structured publication metadata](https://www.zotero.org/support/adding_items_to_zotero) from files in various formats, and through a set of translators also by scraping from websites.

[Wikibase](https://wikiba.se) is a free and open source software solution for storing, editing, and querying Linked Data. It is the software underlying Wikidata.

[Wikidata](https://www.wikidata.org) is today the largest free and open Knowledge Graph. It contains millions of entities describing, for example, scholarly publications and their authors.

ZotWb, the tool presented in this workflow, helps to migrate records from a Zotero group library to a custom Wikibase instance, and performing entity reconciliation against Wikidata and/or the own Wikibase, using [OpenRefine](https://openrefine.org).
