relatedItems.label: MEISE Native note editor for the MEI encoding format
relatedItems.description: The MEI Score Editor (MEISE) is an eclipse-based music notation editor for the musicological XML-based encoding format of the Music Encoding Initiative -- MEI (http://music-encoding.org). It is developed at the Musicology Seminar Detmold/Paderborn, University of Paderborn (http://muwi-detmold-paderborn.de) as part of the german part of the research project "Digital Research Infrastructure for the Arts and Humanities" -- DARIAH-DE (http://de.dariah.eu).

relatedItems.label: MEI Score Editor --MEISE
relatedItems.description: The MEI Score Editor (MEISE) is an Eclipse-based client software for viewing and editing MEI-encoded music documents in CMN (Common Music Notation), facilitating proof reading as well as modifying and correcting MEI files. MEISE was designed to satisfy special requirements of research in musicology, currently unsupported by existing music notation software tools. MEISE should be used especially for working with MEI-data as a processing and editing tool, e.g. for creating variants, generating, completing and modifying MEI-files. As a key merit, MEISE gains of its homomorphic internal data structure to the MEI schema tree, allowing for native support for theoretically all MEI encoding principles. This allows for some unique features arising from the field of scholarly music edition, such as the encoding and visualization of variants of different musical sources in one digital MEI representation.

composedOf.label: Fix and improve the music content
composedOf.description:
In order to modify a MEI file to correct or improve it, you can use MEI Friend or MEISE. Both tools have a musical interface allowing modifying the score like a classic editor. However, the proposed changes remain limited. In order to edit a MEI file locally with MEI Friend, you can use the MEI Friend module in Atom.

To further modify the MEI file, it is necessary to modify the code. To do this, follow the MEI guidelines.

relatedItems.label: MEI-Friend Package for Atom
relatedItems.description: This package for the Atom editor is a friendly companion that helps you edit and improve digital score encodings in MEI format. It makes extensive use of the fantastic engraving engine Verovio. The module can be used locally after installing Atom.

relatedItems.label: Music Encoding Initiative Guidelines
relatedItems.description: The MEI Guidelines, which include the data dictionary, are intended to serve as a reference tool for music encoders. Through the use of natural-language definitions and examples, this document assists users of MEI in achieving effective and consistent markup. Despite translating XML and RNG terminology and concepts into more accessible language, it is still a technical one that presupposes a minimal understanding of XML and music notation.

label: Named entity recognition from transcribed spoken data
description: This workflow is designed to systematically extract structured information from unstructured text. Its primary function is to process transcribed free-text descriptions of archaeological findings and identify relevant named entities. The workflow receives transcribed text from archaeological context sheets as its input and extracts entities related to the archaeology domain. The principal objective of this workflow is to enrich the archaeological records by converting unstructured descriptive text into structured, machine-readable metadata.

label: n-Dame_Heritage digitisation to storage workflow
description:
This workflow addresses the challenges of ensuring the **traceability of practices** within the nDame project and the process of refining methodologies within a framework whose unique nature acts as a magnifying factor. Incorporating standard technical workflows (photogrammetry, lasergrammetry), this workflow aims to outline the practices of UPR 2002 MAP CNRS within the framework of the **ERC n-Dame_Heritage** project. The laboratory was responsible for the digital data working group and thus played a coordinating role for the scientific project's entire output, representing a substantial volume of data. The process described here attempts to cover the **entire scope** (from data acquisition and tool conceptualization to the archiving of data generated during the scientific project. While inevitably incomplete, as it is impossible to detail every specific scenario encountered, we aim to provide a rationalized, retrospective overview of the project team's workflow.

By structuring this workflow and the diagram around **four** major scientific phases (please feel free to right-click the image to open it in a new tab and zoom in on the diagram), we opted for a direct, relational approach. This choice was made despite the fact that timelines often **overlapped** over the project's five-year duration particularly given the volume of artifacts requiring processing and the scientific discoveries made as the restoration work progressed (such as the Jubé and its 1,035 fragments). 

This workflow was therefore applied to both **fixed** elements of the cathedral (chapels, vaults, etc.) and **movable** elements (voussoirs, charred beams, etc.). The context (exceptional and complex in terms of timeframes, technical requirements, and administrative procedures) necessitated extensive preliminary reflection and dedicated research phases to address a project of such unprecedented scale. We chose not to include these methodological steps in the workflow itself, as explaining them would have been difficult; however, it goes without saying that finding a data repository capable of handling such a vast volume of data was a complex undertaking, as was designing a data model that could describe all our outputs. While some of these aspects will be touched upon briefly at various stages, we cannot detail them fully, as they could constitute workflows in their own right. To address this, we attempted to visually indicate the type of action associated with each step: preparation, action, or automatic (or semi-automatic to be more precise) on the diagram (you can right-click it to enlarge it in a new tab).

media.caption: Diagram of the workflow from digitisation to deposit of artifacts from Notre-Dame de Paris.

composedOf.label: 1 - Qualitative / quantitative characterization of the artefact
composedOf.description:
This first stage of the workflow is fundamental because, as part of the reconstruction project for Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris, a wide variety of objects (in the broadest sense) have been made available for digitisation as part of the scientific research programme. This diversity is reflected both in the type of objects (beams, voussoirs, piles of ruins, statues, vault extrados, chapels, archaeological fragments, unique spaces) and in their intended use. Indeed, some artefacts had already been identified as having only one intended use, namely destruction, whilst others were to be preserved. The decision to systematically digitise certain collections (regardless of their intended use) means that this workflow must rationalise requirements and, consequently, the expected quality of the digitisation.

These digitisation tasks were carried out by a lead specialist (for the majority of the digitisation work) for the cathedral ruins and the Jubé collection (discovered during archaeological excavations following the fire), sometimes assisted by one or two additional people. Whether through the most advanced automation or the design and construction of specialised machinery, quantitative considerations also played a significant role in the initial design of the working method. We are sometimes dealing with collections comprising thousands of objects ranging from a few centimetres to several metres in size, or, for example, the cathedral’s chapels as a whole.

The characterisation of the artefacts’ internal features was therefore of significant importance in that it largely determined the working methods and the duration of the assignments required to achieve the scientific objectives, within the framework of the administrative procedures of the scientific project and the material requirements of the reconstruction project.

concept.label: Reasoning
concept.definition: type of thought (Wikidata contributors, "Q1156402," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q1156402&oldid=1265618386 (accessed September 4, 2020).

composedOf.label: 2 - Definition of the digitisation context and objectives
composedOf.description:
Closely linked to the classification of artefacts is a direct consequence: the location of digitisation. Indeed, following the fire, a large number of artefacts had to be removed from the cathedral. Consequently, we can define two main categories and two digitisation pathways (as shown in the diagram): the *in situ* pathway and the *ex situ* pathway. A chapel, for instance, is a fixed part of the cathedral, which requires on-site digitisation. Conversely, a burnt beam from the roof structure requires digitisation at a third-party location. Whilst this movable collection could be partially digitised on site (notably a pile of remains at the transept crossing), it was quickly moved to a secure location outside the cathedral (notably to allow safety works to begin), thus requiring two distinct approaches to the digitisation process.

As part of the *ex situ* digitisation work, the cathedral forecourt served as a temporary storage and digitisation site; subsequently, a dedicated site, situated some distance from Paris, was rapidly established to accommodate the substantial collection of artefacts requiring preservation, restoration and digitisation. This spatial distinction, in addition to highlighting the difference in the nature of the collections, reinforced the distinction between two specific workflows (in terms of the duration of the project, working methods, the tools used and available, and the complexity of access).

The objectives of this digitisation project were therefore to successfully create a ‘digital twin’ that was as faithful as possible to the cathedral’s condition following the fire, whilst also enabling the creation of digital anastyloses that could facilitate both the physical and scientific reconstruction of the cathedral:

- Physical, because understanding the locations of the structures in retrospect was of paramount importance.
- Scientifically, as it provided an opportunity to digitally engage with a symbolic artefact such as Notre-Dame de Paris Cathedral and its remains, and to produce knowledge by contextualising them spatially and temporally, taking into account the building’s entire history.

Clearly, the scientific and methodological challenge lay in assessing the ability to produce such a large volume of data in a reproducible manner and in accordance with FAIR principles, given the sheer quantity of data generated.

composedOf.label: 3a - Comparison of digitisation and restoration schedules
composedOf.description:
*In situ path*

In the context of *in-situ* digitisation, the first step, simple from a methodological point of view but extremely demanding in terms of the digitisation process itself, was to align the digitisation team’s availability with the site’s operational schedule. The latter could not really be adapted to the time constraints of the scientific digitisation team. This practical constraint shaped not only how the scanning assignments were organised, but also the scanning choices made and the timing of these tasks. The compression ring, for example, had to be scanned at a specific time because the scaffolding was due to be removed.

On a broader scale, the overall timetable for the completion of the building works (which differed from that of the scientific project) also had an impact on the scanning missions and their organisation, as once the cathedral reopened, it would become almost impossible to set aside a dedicated space for the digitisations

concept.label: Information Retrieval
concept.definition: activity of obtaining information resources relevant to an information need from a collection of information resources (Wikidata contributors, "Q816826," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q816826&oldid=1228359828 (accessed July 30, 2020).

composedOf.label: 3b - Organisation of short-term on-site assignments
composedOf.description:
*In situ path*

The organisation of the fieldwork trips, which were relatively short given the technical and logistical constraints on site, set the pace for in situ data collection, particularly given the distance between the MAP laboratory in Marseille and Notre-Dame de Paris. The necessity for the digitisation team to travel by train led to a ‘low-cost’ approach to the quantity of equipment required. The structuring of the field missions in line with the site’s schedules and the fact that progress sometimes varied from one week to the next, also necessitated a high degree of flexibility in organising the overall digitisation of the cathedral, and led to an almost constant evolution of the initial framework. Whilst it is virtually impossible to trace these impacts in detail, we feel it is important to highlight this as a contextual factor that influenced the data produced.

concept.label: Information Retrieval
concept.definition: activity of obtaining information resources relevant to an information need from a collection of information resources (Wikidata contributors, "Q816826," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q816826&oldid=1228359828 (accessed July 30, 2020).

composedOf.label: 3c - On-site adjustment based on (re)construction progress
composedOf.description:
*In situ path*

The constant evolution and adaptability mentioned in the previous stage continued on site, in that even though the work and tasks had been organised, the physical reality of a building site, particularly a restoration work-site, and of such a significant structure (in terms of both size and symbolism) meant that the schedules had to be updated almost constantly. With such a large number of workers, different workstations and administrative and technical constraints, the space allocated to digitisation and its schedule also had to be continually adapted. A chapel intended for digitisation might in fact be filled with construction equipment awaiting use, or with workers carrying out tasks there in the morning, only to be cleared out for the chapel next door in the afternoon. The unpredictability of the site therefore had a significant impact on what could be digitised and how: the lighting conditions, the level of cleaning and protection required, the volume of footfall in the space, and the accessibility of the entire area : in short, a multitude of parameters and a degree of momentary subjectivity that we cannot fully convey here, but which greatly influenced the on-site workflow.

It is also important to note the significance that safety issues have taken on in this project, particularly due to the lead contamination caused by the fire, which hampered the team’s ability to work smoothly, especially with regard to the decontamination of personnel and equipment entering and leaving the cathedral.

composedOf.label: 4a - Tasks specifics tool production
composedOf.description:
*Ex situ path

In the context of *ex situ* digitisation, it quickly became apparent that there was a need for rationality and efficiency, given the volume of objects and the staff available to carry out this work. However, given the time constraint (in that the *ex situ* digitisation site had a finite lifespan from the outset), it was necessary to design specialised equipment for the task of digitising thousands of fragments, ranging from beams several metres long to fragments weighing several tens of kilograms.

Consequently, the creation of these tools, although unique in that they were only developed once at the start of the process rather than for each individual fragment, constitutes a defining and fundamental stage in the production of the digitised data. Indeed, this tool development is an integral part of the overall process, as the tools were conceived as necessary conditions for the smooth running of the general workflow. Without these machines (which we explore in steps 4b, 8,9 & 10), the workflow and the results would be entirely different.

composedOf.label: 4b - Organisation of the workplace
composedOf.description:
*Ex situ path*

As mentioned, as part of the *In Situ* digitisation work, a specific location was used to house the portable artefacts whilst awaiting their scientific analysis and, consequently, their digitisation. This location provided access to platforms on which the specially designed equipment mentioned in the previous stage could be set up. This installation (and its maintenance over the course of more than a year) was consistently a key element of the workflow, given the need for robustness and efficiency in the digitisation operations once the missions had begun and become a regular occurrence.

Without going into a full explanation of how the machines are set up, it is worth considering the challenges and constraints they face:
- **The spider** is an automated photogrammetric acquisition rig comprising a series of cameras (between 1 and 4), a series of white LED lights (three rows arranged frontally on a half-dome) and an automatic turntable, all controlled by a Raspberry Pi running the Mercurio Scanner 2.0 application. Fully dismantlable, it consists of three levels of aluminium profiles assembled using 3D-printed corner pieces, giving the assembly its half-dome shape. Complete assembly and disassembly takes 2 hours and has been carried out five times since its creation. Such a device enables the automatic capture of a subject (ranging from 30 cm to 80 cm depending on its maximum diameter) in under 20 minutes, including the time taken to reposition the subject to capture the different sides.
- **L'enjambeur** frame is a semi-automatic photogrammetric data acquisition rig comprising a set of six cameras, a set of white LED lights (three rows arranged in a semi-ellipse) and a strip of specialised red LED lights. Fully dismantlable, it consists of an arch made of aluminium profiles assembled using 3D-printed corner pieces, giving the assembly a semi-dome shape and supporting the six cameras. A tarp printed with automatically recognisable reference markers is used to establish the scale of the scan. Complete assembly and dismantling takes half a day and has been carried out three times since its creation. Such a setup enables the automatic capture of an oblong object (ranging from 30 cm to 7 m depending on its maximum length) in under 40 minutes, including the time taken to reposition the object to capture the various sides.
- **Studio** is an automated photogrammetric data acquisition system comprising a series of cameras (between 1 and 3), a 60cm GODOX lightbox with white LEDs (one square light strip positioned at the front) and an automatic turntable, all controlled by a Raspberry Pi running the Mercurio Scanner 2.0 application. Fully dismantlable, it consists of the lightbox and an assembly of aluminium profiles supporting the cameras, the turntable and the Raspberry Pi. Complete assembly and dismantling takes 30 hours and has been carried out seven times since its creation. Such a setup enables the automatic scanning of a subject (ranging from 5 cm to 35 cm depending on its maximum development axis) in under 20 minutes, including the time taken to reposition the subject to capture the different sides.

composedOf.label: 4c - Application of contextual safety protocols
composedOf.description:
*Ex situ path*

A site such as the one used for digitising the artefacts was subject to certain security constraints, which had an impact on day-to-day work and the implementation of the workflow.

The security constraints related both to the artefacts themselves and to the need to maintain relative secrecy regarding the site’s location for an extended period, particularly given the value of the artefacts. This seemingly trivial point, for example, had an impact on the challenges of metadata documentation, where the digitisation location necessitated temporary obfuscation to avoid revealing confidential information, as well as creating a less practical day-to-day working environment for field staff.

Finally, the same health and safety considerations as those *ex situ* required the daily application of protocols to protect against lead contamination, given the contaminated artefacts extracted from the cathedral. In this regard, the use of full-body protective suits was sometimes necessary in order to approach, handle and digitise the objects, in addition to lead safety training which staff had to complete beforehand.

composedOf.label: 4d - Artefact supply
composedOf.description:
*Ex situ path*

Directly linked to the previous stage, particularly with regard to safety requirements, the issue of handling the artefacts, even if it essentially involves placing them on the various scanning platforms, should not be underestimated. We are talking about collections ranging from beams several metres long, to blocks weighing several tens of kilograms, or collections comprising several hundred objects; the handling of these objects, carried out by the teams (often a single person), accounted for a significant proportion of the working day. This handling became complex due not only to the shape but also to the weight of certain artefacts (120 kg for the heaviest item), requiring more operators. This challenge had been anticipated in the design of the machines, which utilise turntables robust enough to support this load.

composedOf.label: 5 - Metadata integration on scene
composedOf.description:
As part of the process of enriching metadata and ensuring provenance traceability, a major methodological project was launched. Drawing on the W7 model, the aim was to document the techniques employed with greater flexibility and a broader scope than traditional models such as CIDOC or Dublin Core. Indeed, rather than documenting the digitised artefacts, the aim of the work was to construct a hybrid model, based on the correlation enabled by W7 to describe activities, enriched by the PROV-O and CIDOC models to, respectively, ‘fill in’ the gaps in the W7 model (the relationships between activities) and pave the way for broader interoperability in the long term (via prior alignment).

By documenting activities (rather than resources), W7 enables us to keep track of the ‘micro’ workflows implemented in the various digitisation activities and to account for actions whose full scope we can never detail here, even though the document aims to describe the entire process. A simple example: the metadata and paradata record for a photogrammetric acquisition will document the presence of the medium, lighting and filters for each specific acquisition (in addition to the description of the object, location, people and dates). This level of information and its traceability presented a significant challenge.

The other challenge of this work on W7 was to ensure that information was recorded directly within the acquisition data. To this end, QR codes were placed on each scene for every acquisition. By embedding the W7 description JSON files for each activity within the QR codes, we ensured that traceability was no longer external to the digital output but rather intrinsic to and inseparable from the resource produced. Whilst this form of traceability represents an undeniable advantage, it is merely one stage of the work, to which we shall return later when discussing the challenges of data fairness.

relatedItems.label: Create a W7 metadata schema
relatedItems.description:
The purpose of this workflow is to describe the production of a **metadata and paradata** schema based on the **W7 description model**. The transcription framework is specific to the implementation of French research projects and is designed to facilitate the use of a tool developed for and by the W7: namely the EquipEX+ Espadon and the **Anamnesis** application (see the "related items" section). Through ongoing experiments, the aim was to formalise the support procedures for the creation and structuring of a metadata and paradata schema specific to **instrumentation** and/or **analysis** techniques in heritage science and digital science.    
The transcription presented here is intended as a proposal for greater generality and reproducibility based on four case studies involving various institutions and key individuals.  This page is a simplified version (both visually and textually) of the detailed workflow (see the ‘User Manual URL’ field). The various sub-steps that make up the main stages have been grouped together to facilitate a general understanding of the key stages of the method.


This workflow therefore documents the creation of a metadata schema, starting from the ground up and as closely as possible to **actual practice**, with a view to using the Anamnesis platform. In this sense, it became apparent that the most impactful “Ws” centered on the “How” (enabling the description of the various actions within an activity) and the “Which” (enabling the description of the tools and settings for the outputs), with the other “Ws” often being more marginal and exhibiting less variability.


Currently structured through an approach involving **cycles of interviews** over time between a technique specialist and a curator,  this chain of actions now allows schemas to be produced in a relatively short time, without considering acculturation to the W7 model, metadata and paradata challenges (which may vary from case to case).

composedOf.label: 6 & 7  - Manual lasergrammetry & photogrammetry digitization
composedOf.description:
*In situ path*

Let us now turn to the actual digitisation stages. We have decided to group together the steps specific to each of the methods, in that we will not be explaining the photogrammetry or lasergrammetry processes here. These techniques, which are now commonplace, can be found described and explained online in much greater detail than is possible here in writing (you will find an example in the ‘related items’ section for photogrammetry directly on SSHOMP).

Instead, we wish to explain the challenges and the choices associated with these two techniques in relation to the context and the artefacts.

In the context of lasergrammetry and photogrammetry, in the cathedral so, it is important to note at the outset that it was essential to employ efficient, easily transportable techniques that could be adapted to the demands of the construction site :
- A simple **photogrammetry** setup using a Nikon Z72 with a 14mm lens mounted on a pole, allowing shots to be taken from a height of 1 metre to 5 metres. The theoretical convergence point is in the centre of the room to avoid beam divergence issues in enclosed spaces, and we adhered to this as closely as possible. Furthermore, protruding features, such as items of furniture, were captured using their own set of convergent data. Depending on the space, the data capture required between 50 and 150 images.
- For **Lasergrammetry** : photogrammetry enabled us to create an initial model, but as the spaces were very high, we needed a complementary technique to avoid noise effects. We therefore used a Leica BLK306G2 lidar for this purpose. For each space, we took between 3 (simple, empty chapels) and 50 stations (choir galleries). By using the camera pole, we were able to reach a height of 7–8 metres to capture data much closer to the vaults. We have several hundred stations from the cathedral, categorised by type of space (nave chapels, choir chapels, nave and choir galleries, the nave, the western portico, etc.).

concept.label: Scanning

relatedItems.label: Photogrammetry 3D Digitisation
relatedItems.description: This resource is an introduction to the photogrammetry technique to capture visual data about cultural heritage assets and produce associated 3D models.

composedOf.label: 7, 8, 9, 10 - Manual photogrammetry, Spider, Enjambeur & Studio digitisation
composedOf.description:
*Ex situ path*

With regard to *ex situ* acquisitions, we have already discussed in step 4a why we had to draw on specialist expertise and produce specific tools. However, on this occasion we would like to take the time to briefly document the workflow stages relating to each of the machines involved in the digitisation process.

- **Manual photogrammetry**: For each manually digitised subject, a colour calibration chart was captured to aid modelling. Then, once the object has been positioned with a right-angled ruler and two umbrella-mounted flash units angled at 45° from the central surface on a movable surface (turntable, trolley, etc.), a series of photographs is taken; the object is then rotated without moving the flash units, to eliminate most of the shadows. This process is repeated until the object is turned over to digitise its underside. At the end of the process, a number of faces are downloaded and must be renamed and sorted for photogrammetric processing.
- **The spider**: for each object scanned by the spider, a colour calibration chart was acquired to aid modelling. Then, once the object had been positioned using a right-angled scale and the scanning parameters selected (number of images per rotation, number of cameras, extrinsic parameters), the first face of the object was scanned. The object is then turned over, taking care to ensure the safety of both the object and the operator, to scan another face. This process is repeated depending on the complexity of the object being scanned. At the end of the process, a number of faces are downloaded, ready for photogrammetric processing.
- **L'enjambeur** (or Arch) : for each object scanned by the enjambeuer scanner, the device is repositioned on one side of the support tarpaulin. Once the object is in place, the first side of the object is scanned by moving the arch along the tarpaulin. Upon reaching the end, one of the cameras is detached to take specific images of the edges or certain detailed areas. Then, ensuring the safety of both the object and the operator, the object is turned over to scan another side. This process is repeated depending on the complexity of the object being scanned. At the end of the process, a number of scans are downloaded and must be renamed and sorted for photogrammetric processing.
- **The studio**: For each object scanned by the studio, a colour calibration chart was acquired to aid modelling. Then, once the object had been positioned using a right-angled scale and the scanning parameters selected (number of images per rotation, number of cameras, extrinsic parameters), the first face of the object was scanned. The object is then turned over, taking care to ensure the safety of both the object and the operator, to scan another face. This process is repeated depending on the complexity of the object being scanned. At the end of the process, a number of faces are downloaded, ready for photogrammetric processing.

concept.label: Photographing
concept.definition: art, science, and practice of creating durable images by recording light or other electromagnetic radiation (Wikidata contributors, "Q11633," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q11633&oldid=1237597469 (accessed July 30, 2020).

composedOf.label: 11 - Data extraction from tools
composedOf.description:
This new stage, which may seem obvious, struck us as important in that it incorporates specific procedures depending on the tools used. Whilst most machines rely on the use of cameras and therefore SD cards, this nevertheless represents a task that should not be overlooked, particularly given the time required within the production chain.

Furthermore, for lasergrammetry, the extraction stage combines, for us, the extraction of laser data and the initial reconstruction of the scene, particularly with regard to the assembly of the various stations set up as part of a data acquisition session.

There are three possible scenarios: 
- Either the spider or the studio is used, and the Raspberry Pi sorts the data and prepares the metadata automatically, before transferring it to a pre-formatted SSD.
- Either the straddle-type scanner is used or photogrammetry is carried out manually, in which case the data must be exported and sorted manually, sometimes using several SD cards in parallel (the straddle-type scanner has 6), and the metadata is generated from the EXIF data and completed by hand.
- Or the Leica BLK360G2 LiDAR was used, in which case the data is processed in the proprietary ‘Cyclone Field’ software and then exported in .e57 format on a station-by-station basis, and the metadata is created manually.

composedOf.label: 12 - First structuration of files
composedOf.description:
Once the data has been extracted, the first stage of structuring begins. Indeed, we wanted to incorporate stages of progressive structuring into the workflow so that we would not end up having to organise all the data produced at the end of the process, just as we do with the metadata. The main risks were oversight and accumulation, particularly given the time lag between acquisition and deposit; whilst we now present this as a linear process, in reality it did not operate independently for each item from stage 1 to stage 33. The various blocks in the diagram sometimes co-existed depending on the time period, with the storage/publication block actually only beginning in the penultimate year of the project, following several hundred acquisitions.

Therefore, to minimise the issues arising from these differences in timing, it was decided to include a stage for the calibrated structuring of files at the earliest possible stage. Even if this structure were to be modified, its uniformity would ensure that the adjustment from one organisational structure to another could be carried out automatically.
This structure corresponds to what we will encounter later when implementing the repository (see step 28), in that we are here creating the folder for raw resources or, in our repository nomenclature, the ‘sources’.

These folders are structured as follows:\
**File tree for item X** \
**Acquisition folder**/\
 ├─ MEMoS_acquisition.json\
 ├─ subsetA/ # raw image files\
 ├─ ...\
 ├─ subsetX/

**Folder processing**/Metashape/\
 ├─ MEMoS_processing.json\
 ├─ errors/\
  │ ├─ XXX_cameras_errors.csv\
  │ ├─ XXX_project_errors.csv\
 ├─ project/\
  │ ├─ XXX.psz\
  │ ├─ XXX.files\
 ├─ sources/\
  │ ├─ calibration-pp3/\
  │ ├─ linear.pp3\
  │ ├─ subsetA/ # Processed image files\
  │ ├─ ...\
  │ ├─ subsetX/

**Folder results**/\
 ├─ OBJ/\
  │ ├─ FULL/\
  │ ├─ XXX.jpg\
  │ ├─ XXX.mtl\
  │ ├─ XXX.obj\
 ├─ PLY/\
  │ ├─ FULL/\
  │ ├─ XXX.ply\
 ├─ NXZ/\
  │ ├─ FULL/\
  │ ├─ XXX.nxz\
  │ ├─ html # Files for web viewing\
 ├─ POTREE/\
  │ ├─ FULL/\
  │ ├─ html # Files for web viewing\
 ├─ AIOLI/\
  │ ├─ FULL/\
  │ ├─ XXX.zip # Files for import onto the AIOLI platform\

**long-term archive folder**/\
 ├─ XXX.lta # altag3D file for archiving\
 ├─ files/\
  │ ├─ subsetA/ # raw image files\
  │ ├─ ...\
  │ ├─ subsetX/\
  │ ├─ XXX.DAE # 3D model file in standard CINES format

composedOf.label: 13 - Temporary data backup
composedOf.description:
This is a new step that may seem trivial, as it simply involves copying the raw data for each object onto our internal servers. Given the volume of the data, the investment required to produce it and the potential inability to reproduce it in the event of loss (as not all artefacts are intended to be retained), a backup was essential.

The purpose of this point is to draw attention to the cost involved in hosting such a large volume of data, particularly given the significant security and sovereignty issues at stake in a public research project (especially in France, where legal obligations regarding data hosting are relatively strict). Finally, it is worth noting that this stage is also time-consuming, given that the file backup involves not just a few GB, but several TB of data. It therefore carries a significant burden that must be taken into account.

composedOf.label: 14a - Manual processing of data
composedOf.description:
*In situ path*

Let us now turn to the processing stages themselves. As with the data acquisition, we will not be providing a step-by-step guide to using our software (Cyclone Field / Agisoft Metashape) for carrying out the photogrammetric calculations. Instead, we wish to explain the process and its purpose within the workflow in general terms.

Thus, with regard to the artefacts scanned in the cathedral using photogrammetry and lasergrammetry, we first carried out the photogrammetric reconstruction : 
- Photogrammetry (using Agisoft Metashape) of built environments was simpler, as there was only one set of photographs to process; the bulk of the work lay in merging the photogrammetric and lasergrammetric data.
- As regards lasergrammetry, the processing stage is more standard and is used solely on scans of the building structure: first, the stations are aligned with one another (using Cyclone Field), then they are exported to be merged with the photogrammetry data.

concept.label: Transformation
concept.definition: process involving change into a qualitatively different form (Wikidata contributors, "Q65757353," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q65757353&oldid=1268189392 (accessed September 4, 2020).

composedOf.label: 14b - Alignment between laser & photo
composedOf.description:
*In situ path*

Following the initial photo-based reconstruction, the use of laser photogrammetry enabled us to improve the models.

* As mentioned in steps 6 and 7, photogrammetry provided us with an initial spatialisation and modelling of the spaces, but these were subject to noise due to lighting conditions and the acquisition distance. We therefore combined this data with a lightweight LiDAR survey of the same areas to efficiently construct the best usable representation.
* Once the data had been acquired, the assembled LiDAR data was imported into Agisoft Metashape to serve as a complementary resource to the photogrammetry (georeferencing and assistance with the creation of depth maps).
* The hybrid model is exported as a .zip file in AIOLI format (a Micmac project) along with all the photogrammetry images, thereby preserving the 2D-3D-2D interaction of the laboratory’s semantic annotation platform whilst achieving higher-quality modelling in complex and dark areas.

concept.label: Improving
concept.definition: process of a thing moving from one state to another that is considered to be better, usually through some action intended to bring about that better state (Wikidata contributors, "Q21255975," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q21255975&oldid=1264546813 (accessed September 4, 2020).

composedOf.label: 15a - Execution of script for custom tools
composedOf.description:
*Ex situ path*

As for the movable objects, which were digitised outside the cathedral, their number, far greater than that of the objects digitised on site (a ratio of 130 digitised on site to 1,300 digitised in the SRA’s storage facilities), meant we had to find ways to automate the process in order to keep up with the volume of objects to be processed.

It was therefore decided to write and use scripts to automate the processing of data from the tools we had developed for the project. These tools were initially designed to manage photogrammetric reconstruction, but also to merge the faces of objects where multiple separate scans were required to form a single whole (via Rawtherapee / Shaft2 / Agisoft Metashape / PotreeConverter / NexusConverter / Altag3D).

- **Preparatory stages**: colour calibration (of varying complexity using Shaft2 or Rawtherapee), copying of images, creation of a metadata file, initial modelling of each individual face, masking of the background and turntable based on this initial modelling (Agisoft Metashape).
- **Merging of surfaces**: alignment of surfaces using the background and turntable masks, adjustment of the entire set of photos, creation of the dense point cloud / final mesh, export of spatialisation errors (RMSE / SEUW) and scale (Agisoft Metashape) errors, export of the models and preparation of the long-term archive (Agisoft Metashape / PotreeConverter / NexusConverter / Altag3D).

This results in a huge saving in computing time, as processes can be queued for ‘downtime’, such as at night or at the weekend. For example, we digitised 1,081 fragments of the Jubé in 12 months (10 data-collection missions over approximately 20 weeks), and this timeframe includes the acquisition, processing, sharing and long-term preservation of these 1,081 digitised images.

concept.label: Transformation
concept.definition: process involving change into a qualitatively different form (Wikidata contributors, "Q65757353," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q65757353&oldid=1268189392 (accessed September 4, 2020).

composedOf.label: 15b - Manual adjustment for failed projects
composedOf.description:
*Ex situ path*

In some cases (10–15 per cent, depending on the complexity of the data sets), the scripts presented in the previous step may fail to produce a high-quality result, requiring manual intervention to achieve a photogrammetric reconstruction that meets the project’s quality criteria. These issues can range from human errors during preparation to software bugs (Agisoft Metashape can sometimes behave in surprising ways on certain projects).

Initially, the automated process is retried directly; then, if it continues to fail, the project is reprocessed manually, keeping each step as identical as possible to the automated version, whilst running the workflow not in its entirety but phase by phase, in order to understand the source of the initial problem.

This step allows us, by extension, to highlight the systematic verification procedures for automated processes in relation to the responsibilities and ethical considerations of a research project.

concept.label: Debugging
concept.definition: the process of finding and resolving defects or problems within a computer program that prevent correct operation of computer software or a system (Wikidata contributors, "Q845566," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q845566&oldid=1240856516 (accessed July 30, 2020).

composedOf.label: 16 - Export file matching architecture of aioli project
composedOf.description:
This export stage, which is independent of where the objects were digitised and the techniques used, forms part of the requirements outlined previously. Indeed, an export must adhere to a specific structure in order to proceed through the workflow. As part of the nDame project, the use of the Aioli application (developed within our laboratory) was identified, enabling 2D/3D semantic enrichment via photogrammetry. Whilst the application has an integrated processing pipeline via a standard photo upload, this is nonetheless less robust than software specialised in photogrammetry, which offers specific features and capabilities such as automation.

To further speed up the process, it was therefore decided to structure the exports from the processing software so that they correspond to the import requirements on the Aioli platform, via a single folder. The specifications for this folder are therefore to upload a .zip archive, following the MicMac project template, containing:

- a sparse point cloud,
- a dense point cloud,
- an export log file,
- a text file containing the orientation of the images,
- an XML file containing the names of the images,
- a folder containing the individual positions and orientations of the cameras,
- a folder of temporary files,
- and finally the source images.

This structure therefore makes it possible to view the processed scene in third-party software, but within an open ecosystem, whilst once again providing a consistent structure in anticipation of submission (not to create an exact copy of the current file, but to ensure the structure remains identical following a systematic transformation; see step 30)

relatedItems.label: Micmac: Free open-source photogrammetry software tools
relatedItems.description: Micmac is a software tool used for photogrammetry, which is the science of making measurements from photographs. It helps in processing and analyzing images to generate 3D models or other spatial information. Micmac facilitates tasks such as image alignment, 3D reconstruction, and point cloud generation, making it useful for various applications including mapping, remote sensing, and cultural heritage documentation.

relatedItems.label: Aïoli - Reality-based 3D annotation platform for the collaborative documentation
relatedItems.description: Aïoli offers a collaborative digital environment where experts from different disciplines can bring together their observations around a shared 3D representation of cultural heritage objects. By linking spatial annotations to rich external resources, the platform supports integrated analysis, interpretation, and knowledge exchange. Accessible both online and onsite, Aïoli enables efficient, long-term documentation and collaboration throughout the heritage research and conservation process.

composedOf.label: 17 - Temporary data backup
composedOf.description: This step is updated in the workflow and its diagram, but it involves the same challenges as step 13. The file types are different, but once again, the process will require additional time and storage capacity. In this case, it is the processed data (transformed images, camera positions, etc.) and the results (the models) that are stored.

composedOf.label: 18 - Aioli upload
composedOf.description:
The upload stage itself is not particularly complex, as aioli’s web interface allows projects to be imported directly; the most ‘complex’ part is structuring the import correctly.

Nevertheless, this stage once again provides an opportunity to verify the data integrated into the process, particularly given the manual nature of importing each project. This could enable the verification and identification of projects presenting a problem, whether relating to the creation of the archive, unacceptable file names, or other issues linked to the folder structure.

concept.label: Upload
concept.definition: sending of data from a local system to a remote system (Wikidata contributors, "Q7126699," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q7126699&oldid=1267188395 (accessed September 4, 2020).

relatedItems.label: Aïoli - Reality-based 3D annotation platform for the collaborative documentation
relatedItems.description: Aïoli offers a collaborative digital environment where experts from different disciplines can bring together their observations around a shared 3D representation of cultural heritage objects. By linking spatial annotations to rich external resources, the platform supports integrated analysis, interpretation, and knowledge exchange. Accessible both online and onsite, Aïoli enables efficient, long-term documentation and collaboration throughout the heritage research and conservation process.

composedOf.label: 19 - Case study selection
composedOf.description:
Although all projects had to be uploaded to Aioli, not all of them were enriched, and for many projects, the ability to make the digitisation accessible online marked the end of the workflow relating to the production of data and knowledge associated with the digitisation of the artefact itself (we will return to this in stage 22).

For another group (approximately 300 of the 1,800 projects, for which further enrichment may begin following the project’s completion), it was decided to proceed directly to the enrichment pipeline, namely transcription and/or the production of spatialised documentation, via 2D annotation work, reprojected into 3D.

Projects were selected in light of the needs of other research groups and the requirements of the reconstruction project. When areas were identified as of interest (either because they were already documented or required documentation), colleagues often requested access to the digitised data to facilitate the sharing and spatialisation of the available information.

composedOf.label: 20 - Documentation of aioli projects
composedOf.description:
Whether or not we were dealing with a case of ‘enrichment’ via Aioli, the first stage of the work, the preparatory stage, involved documenting the projects. As Aioli remains a research platform, all the functionality required to ensure the traceability of projects had to be implemented outside of it. Given the number of projects and the way they were organised, it was decided to create a spreadsheet to maintain a level of traceability that met the project’s requirements, particularly in view of the practical constraints of the project’s ecosystem (with only one person responsible for this work).

This spreadsheet therefore contains: 
- the names of the projects, 
- the account that owns them, 
- the account that carried out the 2D/3D enrichment, 
- the project IDs, 
- the number of photos, 
- the project upload date, whether or not annotations are present, 
- and the source of these annotations. 

This metadata document is of fundamental importance in that, unlike the data mentioned previously, no decision has been made to store the enrichment work in an external data warehouse.  Given the unique nature of the work and the duplication of data involved in exporting an Aioli project, in relation to data already stored, it seemed difficult to envisage adding this layer of data and knowledge to the submission process. Consequently, the traceability and preliminary structuring, as discussed in relation to data acquisition and processing, were not established to meet the same requirements or levels of documentation for data enrichment, as these requirements were almost exclusively internal to our laboratory.

composedOf.label: 21a - Pre-structuring of semantic enrichment
composedOf.description:
Given that the enrichment and annotation work had to faithfully reflect studies that sometimes fell outside the annotation frameworks developed in our laboratory, a preparatory step was often added to align the documentation with our internal structure.

As Aioli allows users to create layers and groups of layers in which annotations are positioned, in addition to the use of colours and description sheets specific to each layer (which can themselves contain textual or visual data via attachments to the sheet), it was often necessary, on complex projects, to organise the transcription structure of the documentation in advance.

concept.label: Data Mapping
concept.definition: process of linking data objects in distinct models (Wikidata contributors, "Q2330408," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q2330408&oldid=1185372641 (accessed September 4, 2020).

composedOf.label: 21b - Digital transcription of paper documentation
composedOf.description:
*aioli enrichment path*

This stage represents the active part of the enrichment process:
- through the **digital transcription** of paper-based documentation
- through the **direct production** of spatialised documentation

This is a complex process to describe, as it varies greatly depending on the source materials (the artefact, its digitisation and the associated documentation, as well as colleagues’ methods of documentation).

Whether through the sharing of documentation files, which was sometimes the only means of engaging with the knowledge produced by colleagues in other working groups, or within hybrid collaborative dynamics, the stage of assimilating and understanding the knowledge, produced within a highly interdisciplinary framework, was therefore essential as it facilitated the project’s ultimate level of enrichment.

The annotation work itself involves a twofold task:
- **Marking areas** on the photographs that relate to specific information, organising them by colour according to the type of documentation (records of deterioration, spatialisation of stratigraphic/radar analysis, sampling locations, mapping of stone carvings, deformation of vaults).
- **Enriching the annotations** via the description sheets (and their attachments) and by organising and naming layers and layer groups.

This time-consuming dual task was not merely intended to demonstrate the ability to replicate in the digital realm what might already exist on paper. The main and stated objective of producing a ‘digital duplicate’ was to explore the ability to make a vast body of knowledge machine-interoperable, to varying degrees (by drawing on thesauri, for example). This work has opened up, and continues to challenge, scientific thinking regarding the need to pool and cross-reference documented knowledge, and to visualise and utilise it through this new digital paradigm.

composedOf.label: 21c - Cross verification with original documentation producer
composedOf.description:
*aioli enrichment path*

As mentioned earlier, a verification stage was incorporated following the active enrichment stage, mirroring the pre-structuring stage which aimed to understand the work of others. This cross-verification stage seeks firstly to confirm the quality of the transcription work, but also to help highlight the work of the digital group to the initial target audiences. By involving these audiences not only in the dissemination but also in the production of this new form of knowledge, through a joint review process, which may be iterative, the work begins its life outside the confines of the laboratory. Naturally, if a need for adjustment is identified based on feedback from experts, this stage may be repeated iteratively for a given artefact.

composedOf.label: 22 - Internal provision of the project availability through public viewer
composedOf.description:
As part of the research project, a public viewer has been set up to go beyond the internal viewing options available only within Aioli, as the latter requires an account to access the project. This viewer therefore provides access to all the projects that have been published online by Aioli. Beyond its specific role in communication, this hub has also enabled the establishment of informatic routines to aggregate the vast amount of data produced within an environment, thereby providing an initial catalogue of the work carried out outside the digital data set.

At the same time, the communication stage presented here forms part of the dynamic outlined in the previous stage of transmission, as it would be wrong to assume that the completion of the process of acquiring, processing and enriching an object, and its integration into the public viewer, was in itself a significant enough act to naturally mobilise colleagues for whom the digital transcription of documentation is not an inherent part of their workflow.

concept.label: Migration
concept.definition: process of selecting, preparing, extracting, and transforming data and permanently transferring it from one computer storage system to another (Wikidata contributors, "Q1932543," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q1932543&oldid=1212596075 (accessed July 30, 2020).

composedOf.label: 23a - External diffusion of the data & dissemination of knowledge
composedOf.description:
*enrichment path*

This stage is undoubtedly the most unusual part of the workflow, as it does not strictly speaking fall within the scope of our actions. Indeed, here we wish to incorporate (particularly with a view to the rest of the workflow) the idea that the work of analysis and enrichment did not stop when the annotations were completed. This work continued outside our laboratory, outside our workflow, being incorporated into publications, further studies and supplementary experiments (notably in VR). In short, by presenting the artefacts in a new light through digital means. These artefacts (the object and its representation) have been able to take on a life of their own beyond mere digitisation for preservation purposes, serving instead as a direct medium or material for research, in the service of new knowledge that extends beyond the scope of the initial workflow. This new knowledge, the relationships between the data produced, in short, the scientific substrate that has emerged, has thus made it possible to conceptualise a new phase of the workflow, extending the analysis beyond the artefact itself to the knowledge produced around or in conjunction with the artefact’s representation.

composedOf.label: 23b - Terminology extraction and organisation
composedOf.description:
*enrichment path*

Building on the new knowledge generated by our workflow, the process of enrichment and analysis has continued as work on semantic exploration has begun. Indeed, the vast majority of the knowledge produced in connection with the digitisation of artefacts has been set down in writing (primarily through scientific publications).

Therefore, to harness this knowledge, a framework for semantic extraction and the organisation of terms was established, drawing on the published material through the lens of the scientific project. This relatively extensive body of material was explored and synthesised in an attempt to identify the knowledge generated around primary and secondary terminologies, etc. The method used, utilising AI, aimed to extract semantic markers relating to an evolving thesaurus linked to the nDame project

The method, initially tested between the summer of 2023 and January 2024 on various language models, made it possible to identify the conditions required for accurate and controlled extraction. This method was then applied to the 31 articles in Volume 65 of the *Journal of Cultural Heritage*, which is devoted to the scientific study of Notre-Dame de Paris. Each article was broken down according to its structure, then processed paragraph by paragraph using specific prompts. The identified terms were returned in a structured JSON format, converted to CSV, and then imported into an Excel database. A manual curation phase was then carried out to correct classification errors and remove duplicates. In total, this initial operation yielded 5,370 classified terms. In a second stage, the entire set was consolidated and subjected to a further sub-categorisation process. This bottom-up approach enabled sub-categories to emerge from the lists of terms, thereby increasing the semantic granularity of the corpus and providing a structured basis for linking knowledge and constructing domain-specific knowledge graphs.

concept.label: Data Mining
concept.definition: process of discovering patterns in large data sets using computational methods at the intersection of statistics, database systems, or machine learning (Wikidata contributors, "Q172491," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q172491&oldid=1268899513 (accessed September 4, 2020).

composedOf.label: 24 - Integration of the artefact into quasi.modo architecture
composedOf.description:
This key stage in the workflow emerged in response to the project’s initial findings, namely the need for a tool that would not only visualise but also, in turn, enrich knowledge, drawing on the workflow’s previous outputs.

quasi.modo is therefore a tool designed to construct an immaterial representation of a ‘cathedral of data’, by spatialising all the digitised data of the cathedral in the form of the cathedral itself and according to different points in time. It is also possible to continue semantic enrichment and to carry out analysis through the addition of tools enabling the analysis of this new representation of the data. The platform is, first and foremost, a conceptual and technical architecture dedicated to the exploration, integration and interoperability of data and knowledge. With a focus on collaborative work, the platform currently comprises 32 users, 1.6K projects, 17.7K annotations, 415 concepts, 217.3K images, and 6,610.7M 3D points.

As the addition of projects remains a manual process, the structuring of this ‘immaterial cathedral’ represented a singular moment in time, in that a number of projects are not yet accessible in the quasi.modo database. However, the proven value of a unified representation, which allows different views or individualised objects (such as vaults or beams) to be accessed alongside the cathedral, provides a means of reconciling a collection of digitised data originating from diverse paths and timeframes. These objects can ultimately co-exist digitally, even if they have not been restored to their original physical locations.

concept.label: Migration
concept.definition: process of selecting, preparing, extracting, and transforming data and permanently transferring it from one computer storage system to another (Wikidata contributors, "Q1932543," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q1932543&oldid=1212596075 (accessed July 30, 2020).

composedOf.label: 25 - Extraction of singular and representative component from quasi.modo
composedOf.description:
*enrichment path*

The value of quasi.modo in the integrated presentation of data on a single platform lies in the fact that it has been designed to incorporate internal analysis tools, enabling searches not only across projects but also across the entire body of semantic enrichment previously mentioned in Aïoli. However, the ability to access projects goes beyond mere visualisation or a single viewpoint. A single section of a monument can become the focal point for several disciplines, particularly with the possibility of carrying out cross-referenced searches based on annotations and the knowledge graph generated by them.

Tools based on the ability to call up a scene, save the camera’s position in the digital space in relation to a project or a text search, in short, to record a viewpoint or perspective established within the platform, represent a fundamental step in the production of knowledge. Indeed, this is where the transition occurs from exploring a corpus to creating a new resource, generated on the basis of that knowledge and immediately accessible in relation to the digital object.

composedOf.label: 26 - Semantic narrative redaction
composedOf.description:
*enrichment path*

The final enrichment stage combines the work of semantic extraction and the structuring of markers with the extraction of composite viewpoints, as discussed in the previous stage.

Using an additional tool from quasi.modo, it is possible to blend the knowledge produced and referenced throughout the workflow into a new output: a mnemogram. This can be understood as a multidimensional narrative that combines scientific storytelling with an exploration of the three-dimensional model. The narrative is therefore no longer separate from the scientific corpus; it is constructed from it. The mnemogram thus becomes a means of communicating research without losing its spatial and documentary grounding.

In this sense, the uses of these semantic narratives are varied: at times a narrative of scientific practice, at times a transcription of spatial exploration, or even interdisciplinary perspectives on a spatialised dataset. The interplay between perspective, spatiality and narrative leads to a ultimate form of enrichment that is constructed by the data and ‘within’ the data itself.



The creation of a mnemogram begins with writing a narrative. The aim is to gradually build up the narrative and, as it takes shape, to draw on the various resources available. In particular, quasi.scene.capture allows you to record views of 3D models whilst retaining the elements associated with them. Annotations (and the metadata they contain), downloadable images, bibliographic records and other documentary resources can also be integrated into the narrative. These elements are thus selected and arranged according to the argument or journey one wishes to construct. Several layout options then allow the various pieces of content within the mnemogram to be structured and prioritised. A final step involves naming the narrative and adding it to a collection. This method of organisation allows several narratives to be grouped together according to a theme, a subject of study or an editorial project. The method is therefore based on a process of progressive writing and enrichment, in which spatial, documentary and semantic data converge.

To date, 65 mnemograms have been produced. They serve to document the knowledge generated as part of the research project, its interconnections and the interdisciplinary nature of the project, whilst contributing to the promotion and dissemination of the data.

concept.label: Writing
concept.definition: writing designates the activity of creating new texts (instead of capturing existing text). Here, it primarily concerns research papers and reports, but may include other textually-oriented objects.

composedOf.label: 27 - Online publication & storage
composedOf.description:
This stage is undoubtedly the most forward-looking, in that it is still being finalised. As we mentioned, it has been decided not to upload the data from the enrichment and analysis work to Aioli or quasi.modo. However, the display of the outputs from this work remains a point of focus.

At present, quasi.modo already allows the output to be displayed via the tool itself. Indeed, the creation of semantic narratives produces a digital ‘object’ that is directly indexed in the database, utilising point clouds, photographs, annotations, etc. As the matrix formed by the mnemograms can be organised into collections, it can itself be curated and displayed externally via embedding.

It is, in fact, through this approach that another way of publishing and showcasing the laboratory’s work has been devised, by integrating the enrichment work into a specific repository and presenting it in the form of mnemograms. It was through Nakala (see the related item) that the decision was made to move towards externalised display, with a broader reach than that of the research tools themselves.  Furthermore, whilst quasi.modo is primarily a tool for researchers working on a scientific project, Nakala is designed to have a longer-term future, particularly given the attention paid to defining the metadata for the digital objects displayed and stored.

This outsourcing phase is still currently being implemented.
