relatedItems.label: SSHOC Workshop: Copyright Issues in Secondary Data Use
relatedItems.description:
**Date:** 24 to 25 January 2022
**Location:** Online
 
This was a two-day interactive workshop that took place on the 24th and 25th of January 2022.
 
## Event Overview

There is a **misconception in the research community** that the **use of secondary data** does not entail **legal considerations**. Secondary data is an intellectual property of the data owner, so any use of that data may require the data owner’s permission or may be subject to certain terms and conditions. Therefore, this online workshop was specifically designed to highlight these issues and help you overcome these.

In this two-day online workshop, **participants understood what needs to be taken into account when creating, using and sharing data**. It covered the following topics:

-    What is secondary data?
-    Introduction to the copyright
-    Layers and duration of copyright
-    Copyright licenses
-    Copyright in an international context
-    Copyright exceptions
-    Other rights

The two-day workshop included **lectures and presentations** with **individual exercises and group discussions**.
 
## Learning objectives
 
-    Gain a **better understanding of copyright** such as what is copyright, what is covered, who owns it and what is the duration?
-    Identify **copyright exemptions** and gain a better appreciation of fair dealing
-    Be able to differentiate between available **copyright licences** and assess these licences when publishing their own data
-    Be able to identify **country-level diversity in copyright laws** and gain a basic understanding of other types of rights in data
 
## Target Audience

This workshop was intended for anyone who wants to learn about basic copyright principles and is interested in creating, sharing and using data.

## Speakers

**Hina Zahid** is the Senior Research Data Services Officer working in the UK Data Service's Research Data Management section based at the UK Data Archive, University of Essex. She leads on the ethical aspects of research data management, sharing and reuse. She works proactively with researchers, and research centres to provide guidance, advice and training to achieve the implementation of good data management practices, and to optimise the sharing and archiving of data for research.

**Hannah Pyman** joined the University of Essex Library team in September 2016 as a Graduate Trainee, going on to become Interlending and Document Delivery Assistant in April 2017. From September 2019 until July 2020 she was an Information Literacy Co-ordinator. She began her new role as Scholarly Communications Co-ordinator in July 2020. Hannah’s role covers support across the research lifecycle, ranging from literature searching and evaluating resources, to publishing (including open access publishing), copyright, and citations.

**Cristina Magder** manages the UK Data Service's Data Collections Development and Research Data Management teams at the UK Data Archive. She leads the research data management portfolio of support and training for the UK Data Service. Her main teaching interests are data management planning, sharing and archiving data with a specific focus on licencing, data quality assurance, disclosure risk assessment, and reproducibility.

**Maureen Haaker** is a scholar in the field of qualitative methodology. She has worked with the UK Data Service for 10 years as a senior qualitative training officer and is a lecturer in the School of Social Sciences and Humanities at University of Suffolk. Her work has involved the ingest and digitisation of qualitative data, development of training for the management, deposit, and re-use of qualitative data, and the re-use of qualitative datasets for teaching and learning. She is a key contributor to Sage’s Managing and Sharing Research Data (2nd edition) and Qualitative Secondary Analysis. She is currently completing a PhD in Sociology at University of Essex.

composedOf.label: Appraise your data
composedOf.description:
At some point in the research process, you will need to consider how best to organise your data for sharing with others. You may wish to show all the data you collected or only a subset of data that you have enhanced and refined. Some data collected will be useful mainly for shorter-term needs, like raising awareness, managing processes, opening a discussion, or introducing hypothetical questions, while others have enduring long-term value.

There are a few resources available to help guide researchers, data stewards, and repository curators in the process of appraisal which may be useful to consult, such as the Digital Curation Centre published [How to Appraise and Select Research Data for Curation](https://www.dcc.ac.uk/sites/default/files/documents/How%20to%20Appraise%20and%20Select%20Research%20Data.pdf) and the Digital Research Alliance of Canada, Data Curation Network, and Digital Repository of Ireland collaborated on a [Checklist for Appraising Research Data for Long-term Preservation](https://zenodo.org/records/11371489). In the end, researchers often have a high degree of autonomy from funders and institutions when it comes to determining which data have long-term value. 

Consider the following in this step:

1. Put yourself in the place of the person reusing your research: Are the objects, files, or code sufficient to replicate the research (or, in other words, are they enough to answer the original research question)? Is there anything missing that someone would be likely to re-do, whether archival research, interviews, creative design, etc., if you did not share your work?

2. Try to express your research project in narrative form, telling a story with a beginning, middle, and end. It may be helpful to draft a timeline of major decisions (when you stopped archival research, when you decided to add another focus group, when a project member left for other employment, etc.). What are the key plot points in your narrative? Consider that the output of this exercise could be a useful resource to share alongside your dataset upon completion, as a [narrative dossier](https://digitalhumanitiesddp.com/documentation-x-3/the-archiving-dossier-narrative/) or a [datasheet](https://zenodo.org/records/15828222).

3. Once you’ve made your selections, set aside any of the data sources for which reuse licences or credit is unclear so that you can follow-up with individuals and organisations about permission to publish. In the case of data taken from cultural heritage institutions, consider whether it would be more appropriate to provide links to digital sources already available online. Where you might be working with personal or sensitive data, you will also need to determine whether any access conditions need to be set to protect that data. [Please note that if you are working with data that may be sensitive, it is strongly advised to seek help from professionals trained in research ethics and data sharing before determining any access restrictions.]

It may be that at the end of this exercise you have one or several potential datasets to share reflecting different approaches, methods, and outcomes. Will you share them all at once or in the same way? Don’t be afraid to put yourself in the position of both the creator and the audience in this step, seeking to inspire further research later.

concept.label: Managing
concept.definition: influence or authority over something; process of directing the operation of a device, system, or process (Wikidata contributors, "Q29017603," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q29017603&oldid=1238420285 (accessed September 4, 2020).

composedOf.label: Simplify the presentation
composedOf.description:
Simple structures, such as spreadsheets or file directories, are generally recommended for long-term preservation. Repositories widely accept these formats and they can ensure longevity with little maintenance required. Researchers can also download them, query them, and output their results into other formats without also needing to buy expensive software. [The Digital Preservation Coalition Handbook](https://www.dpconline.org/handbook/technical-solutions-and-tools/file-formats-and-standards) has some helpful guidance on file formats suitable for preservation .

If more complexity is required to communicate your research, however, you will need to consider how you can maintain both the data and the presentation format. For example, if your research output is in the form of a website, code, database, visualisation, or other complex artefact, it will be more likely to suffer from obsolescence due to software changes which prevent your code from running, or outright loss (e.g. if you leave your institution where you were hosting a website). Additionally, if you use proprietary tools in your research or to facilitate publication of an output, be aware that you may not be able to archive/deposit that tool with a third party (i.e. a repository or institutional archive) at the end of a project, as this may violate the licence or terms of use. [The Software Sustainability Institute Training Hub](https://www.software.ac.uk/training/training-hub) has some helpful resources on managing and maintaining software and code.

Document your choices carefully so both the data and the platform for communication can be maintained. Some helpful tips include:

1. Start with community-maintained open source tools and methodically document any customisations you make so that updates to software can be carried out if needed. [The Endings Project](https://endings.uvic.ca/principles.html) at the University of Victoria offers advice specific to the sustainability of Digital Humanities websites, such as avoiding links which can break when platforms are migrated to different hosting environments.

2. Utilise an existing data model or format to guide how you present the data. This could be a metadata standard (e.g. [Dublin Core](https://www.dublincore.org/specifications/dublin-core/dcmi-terms/)), a common data format (e.g. [ISO 8601](https://www.iso.org/iso-8601-date-and-time-format.html)), or a linked data vocabulary (e.g. [Wikidata](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:Main_Page)). This ensures the data may be more easily imported into other systems if needed.

3. Consider alternative ways to present your data using those simple structures mentioned above, which would be less likely to suffer from these problems. For example, if your research output is in the form of a web-hosted data visualisation, you might also provide the data as a spreadsheet, along with static images of some of the more interesting charts or visualisations.

concept.label: Transformation
concept.definition: process involving change into a qualitatively different form (Wikidata contributors, "Q65757353," Wikidata, https://www.wikidata.org/w/index.php?title=Q65757353&oldid=1268189392 (accessed September 4, 2020).

composedOf.label: Provide for ongoing stewardship and care
composedOf.description:
Once the scholarly contribution is designed and published, who will responsibly manage continued access or engagement? Many researchers turn to data repositories or archives at the end of a research project to take over the management of their data and provide ongoing access for future public benefit.  

Repositories are not just for storage, they act as key players in research dissemination by keeping the data online, active, and reusable, and they will benefit from early knowledge of both your data and your expectations.  Disciplinary repositories are uniquely positioned to guide and advise on the design of research products within a specific field, which can help you in the appraisal process and even the research study design. The Digital Curation Centre has a helpful guide that includes criteria for selecting appropriate research repositories, [Where to keep research data guide](https://www.dcc.ac.uk/guidance/how-guides/where-keep-research-data).

It may be helpful to map out what you imagine to be the necessary short, medium, and long-term timeframes for your outputs before considering where and how to maintain them: 
- Short-term data may be data that supports a conference paper, which you anticipate might be most relevant for 2-5 years after dissemination. 
- A medium-term dataset could be one which is presented in a custom website that lasts beyond the initial length of the project, and serves as a key engagement resource for exhibitions, talks, or other public events for 10-20 years.
- A long-term dataset may be a compilation of data gathered from a variety of sources and annotated with unique observations that needs to be archived, preserved, and made available for as long as possible.

Consider who your potential partners are that can help you to manage both costs and responsibilities:
1. Researchers at higher education institutions may have resources in place locally to ensure medium-term or long-term storage of their outputs through the institution. Find out early whether these options come with a cost, or are available only for a fixed timeframe.
2. Have a conversation with other potential stewarding organisations as early on in the planning process as possible. Ensure that those best able to invest ongoing time and effort into your data are positioned to understand it and manage it in line with your expectations.

Thinking about long-term stewardship also raises questions about environmental and ethical responsibility, including maintaining open communication with communities or people reflected in your research long after the data is published. Discussions with repository and data management experts at this early stage can, for example, help you to reduce the carbon cost of your data and its presentation format. The environmental impact of data retained may also be a consideration when it comes to formats, platforms, and long-term storage media. The [Digital Humanities Climate Coalition Toolkit](https://sas-dhrh.github.io/dhcc-toolkit/) offers resources to assess the environmental impact of your project workflows and outputs. [The CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance](https://www.gida-global.org/care) were developed to help researchers work with data about and with Indigenous peoples, cultures, and lands around the world. The principles advocate for collaboration and respect in the collection, dissemination, and preservation of data pertaining to those communities.

composedOf.label: Encourage broad reuse of your data
composedOf.description:
If we imagine sustainability as the product of a relationship between data and an audience, then an important consideration in ensuring its ongoing relevance is to encourage reuse. A broad range of people using your data can be a significant asset in terms of securing continued funding, petitioning for technical maintenance or upgrades, and ensuring prioritisation for long-term preservation.

Research data don’t benefit from the same outreach support as publications, where publishers are involved in the distribution and promotion of the content to relevant audiences, and may require some additional investment. One method to ensure continued engagement with your data is to write a [data paper](https://roadtofair.hypotheses.org/364). This will put the data into the publications workflow and make it more discoverable through literature searches.

There are also various approaches to seeking community endorsement which may be borrowed from traditional publishing, such as peer review, submission to awards programs, or collaboration with established entities (e.g. University departments, libraries, local museums, community groups). 

Consider the following in this step:
1. Solicit feedback from your peers using the channels and platforms that helped you most when you were developing your output, encouraging them to share with their networks. 
2. If your output exists on a standalone platform is [open peer review](https://plos.org/resource/open-peer-review/) an option? This may include publishing the review alongside the identities of the reviewers.
3. Publish research outputs as Open Educational Resources (OERs), workflows or datasets on platforms that increase visibility such as [DARIAH-CAMPUS](https://campus.dariah.eu/), [SSHOMP](https://marketplace.sshopencloud.eu/) or [EOSC](https://open-science-cloud.ec.europa.eu/services).
4. Add your research outputs to relevant [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/) communities and [Zotero](https://www.zotero.org/) libraries.
5. Provide a detailed user guide that explains in plain language how to navigate the data or resource, access information about it, or seek help. Ensure that any code outputs are stored in a version-controlled repository such as [GitHub](https://github.com/) or [GitLab](https://gitlab.com/). These platforms not only provide a place to share your code after your project has ended, but allow others to review your code or to collaborate in its development by submitting enhancements and bug fixes.
6. Clearly licence your data so that researchers can reuse and cite your data. A [Creative Commons licence](https://creativecommons.org/share-your-work/cclicenses/) will ensure any reuse is appropriately credited and provides that any further publication must be licensed as well. You’ll not only see your work benefit new research, you’ll be able to reuse that research yourself.

Where feasible, consider making your data available as Open Access, meaning that others can easily view and download it without the need to login to restricted platforms or pay access fees. As wide an audience as possible builds relevance, creates value, and will help to ensure sustained engagement with your data.

label: Semantic change analysis for Ancient Greek lexicological studies
description: A lexicologist wants to study the evolution of a lexical or semantic field in Ancient Greek. Starting with a specific semantic field and a list of words associated with it, they need to determine which words have changed their meaning and which new senses they have acquired or lost, or which of their meanings have undergone some other type of semantic change. This type of study can be carried out by using various resources, including those already available in CLARIN. However, these resources are currently scattered across different CLARIN Resource Families, and do not have enough visibility for people who work on lexical semantic change in different fields. This task would hugely benefit from the creation of a new CLARIN Resource Family for Lexical Semantic Change (LSC), which would collect  all existing resources (and possibly new ones) that could be employed for the study of LSC in this scenario.  This workflow aims at illustrating how such a new CRF could be used for applications in lexical semantic change, by taking the work of a lexicologist on a semantic field as a use-case.

composedOf.label: Set up a corpus
composedOf.description: The first step is for the researcher to set up a corpus (a collection of texts) to perform their analysis on a reference corpus for the target language. Such a corpus should capture variation on the axes that the researcher intends to study e.g. it should be diachronic, or contain texts belonging to different genres or disciplines and this information should ideally be available via the metadata describing each of the texts in the corpus. This corpus does not necessarily need to be sense-annotated, but it should be lemmatised and PoS tagged to reduce data sparsity.

composedOf.label: Split the corpus into different spans
composedOf.description: In order to be able to capture semantic changes, the researcher needs to have the data in the corpus divided into different spans. If the researcher wants to capture diachronic semantic change, they will need to split the corpus into diachronic spans, the size of which will depend on the type of change to be captured. If, on the other hand, the type of change concerns the specialised use of words from everyday language in the technical language of a certain discipline, the segmentation of the corpus will be based rather on the type of texts and their genre (specialist and non-specialist texts).

composedOf.label: Train word embeddings on different spans
composedOf.description: The lexicologist can use word embedding algorithms to determine if and how the semantics of a certain word has shifted and has acquired another sense in a different domain or diachronic span. In order to do this, the lexicologist trains word embeddings on the different sub-corpora or the different diachronic spans obtained in step 2.

composedOf.label: Evaluation against a Gold Standard
composedOf.description:
The lexicologist will need to evaluate the algorithm against the state of the art. In order to do that, they can use existing Gold Standards or create another one for the specific task.
An existing Gold Standard for Ancient Greek lexical semantics is the annotated dataset from the Diorisis Ancient Greek corpus.
If the lexicologist wants to create a new Gold Standard for the evaluation, they will need to create a manually annotated dataset of lexical word senses for the languages included in the study. 
The manual annotation has to be performed by following specific annotation guidelines for manual annotation of word senses. The selection of word senses can build on lexicographic resources, as well as on computational lexical resources such as the Ancient Greek WordNet.
As an output, the researcher will obtain a dataset of occurrences of the target words in context, manually annotated with senses. This dataset can then be used to evaluate the performance of the algorithm.

composedOf.label: Qualitative analysis of the results of the word embeddings
composedOf.description: The researcher compares the closest neighbours of the target words in different time spans in order to determine how the word has changed based on words that occur in similar contexts.

composedOf.label: Additional analysis: qualify the type of semantic change
composedOf.description: The researcher analyses the results of the word embeddings and determines what kind of semantic change affected the words under study, based on literature and studies on semantic change.

label: Semantic change analysis for lexicological studies
description:
This workflow describes the stages of a research process on lexical semantic change, specifically in the field of lexicology. The type of researcher to whom this workflow is addressed is a lexicologist interested in the study of a specific semantic or lexical field. For instance, a lexicologist studying Latin might be interested in semantic lexical changes related to large-scale social and historical events, such as the advent of Christianity. Technical languages (e.g. medical, legal, mathematical lexicon) also offer various examples of lexical semantic change: a lexicologist might study how words in Latin and/or Ancient Greek medical lexicon have changed their meaning from a more general to a more specialised one. Each step of this workflow provides examples of resources for lexical semantic change research in Latin and Ancient Greek, but it can be applied to any language that has similar resources.

Background. Starting with a specific semantic field and a list of words associated with it, the lexicologist needs to determine which words have changed their meaning and which new senses they have acquired or lost, or which of their meanings have undergone some type of semantic change. This type of study can be carried out by using various resources, including those already available in the Social Sciences and Humanities (SSH) Open Marketplace as well as in CLARIN-ERIC. However, these resources are currently scattered across different CLARIN Resource Families, and do not have enough visibility for people who work on lexical semantic change in different fields. This workflow aims at bringing together such resources in a coherent research process, by taking the work of a lexicologist as a use-case.

relatedItems.description: This dataset contains Lemma Embeddings for Latin distributed as follows: OperaMaiora contains embeddings trained on the corpus of Thomas Aquinas (philosophical and religious works); Aligned contains the alignment of embeddings of OperaLatina (corpus of works from different Classical authors) and OperaMaiora; fastText contains embeddings based on the vector representation fastText; word2vec contains embeddings based on the vector representation wor2vec.

composedOf.label: Evaluation against a Gold Standard
composedOf.description:
The lexicologist will need to evaluate the algorithm against the state of the art. In order to do that, they can use existing Gold Standards or create another one for the specific task. Gold Standards for this task are manually annotated datasets in which each lexical item has been assigned a sense by the annotator. Gold Standards for a few lexical items in Latin and Ancient Greek already exist.
If the lexicologist wants to create a new Gold Standard for the evaluation, they will need to create a manually annotated dataset of lexical word senses for the languages and/or semantic fields included in the study. The manual annotation has to be performed by following specific annotation guidelines for manual annotation of word senses.
As an output, the lexicologist will obtain a dataset of occurrences of the target words in context, manually annotated with senses. This dataset can then be used to evaluate the performance of the algorithm.

relatedItems.label: Preliminary guidelines for manual annotation of word senses in Latin and ancient Greek corpora
relatedItems.description:
These guidelines describe how the annotation task should be set up and performed, including: how to determine the sense inventory for each word to be manually annotated; how the annotation would look like (e.g. graded annotation or only one sense selection for each word occurrence); which tool(s) will be used for the manual annotation; how to deal with specific annotation challenges; metaphoric senses; vagueness; sense boundaries.
The guidelines build on evidence from Latin and Ancient Greek, but they are conceived to be as cross linguistically valid as possible.

relatedItems.label: Ancient Greek semantic annotation datasets
relatedItems.description: Datasets containing semantic annotation of the Ancient Greek words mus, harmonia, and kosmos in the Diorisis Ancient Greek corpus. The files are in a tab-separated format.

relatedItems.label: SemEval annotated dataset
relatedItems.description:
This dataset contains the annotations for 40 Latin lemmas taken from the diachronic Latin corpus LatinISE. The dataset was originally created as Latin test data for SemEval 2020 Task 1: Unsupervised Lexical Semantic Change Detection (Schlechtweg et al. 2020).  The choice of the set of lexemes includes lexical units in which a change of meaning is observed in relation to Christianity and other socio-political changes in the late antiquity period. The annotation was performed manually: the annotators had to read each text snippet and assign the dictionary senses to each lemma in context on a graded scale, following a variation of the DuRel annotation framework (Schlechtweg et al. 2018): “1” indicated that the usage of the lemma in the text was unrelated to the dictionary sense, “2” indicated a distant relation between the two, “3” a close relation and “4” was used to indicate that the usage in the text completely overlapped with the dictionary sense. The label “0” was used when the annotator was not able to make a decision.

In Marilyn Walker, Heng Ji & Amanda Stent (eds.), The 2018 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies, Volume 2 (Short Papers), 169–174. Stroudsburg, PA: Association for Computational Linguistics.

label: Semi-automated extraction of information from textual documents in a domain-specific repository
description:
The workflow addresses the **machine processing and enhancement of archaeological textual documents** (e.g., grey literature, excavation reports, field forms) held in a domain-specific repository. It processes both **scanned documents**, through automatic text recognition, and **born-digital documents** (PDF, DOCX) that already carry a text layer. The goal is an integrated solution for **legacy data and new uploads within the selected repository system**: better search and reuse of the documents, and fewer manual steps in archiving and annotation.

The workflow chains **independent tools available as services through APIs**. Each tool performs one step: page classification, OCR quality control, linguistic annotation and named entity recognition, keyword extraction against the domain vocabularies, and translation. Each tool can also be used on its own. The repository calls the services asynchronously and stores every result as an **alternative distribution of the original file**, with a **paradata** record describing the run that produced it (tool version, parameters, licence).

The results of all steps also accumulate in **one JSON record per document** (the ATRIUM document record). Its blocks each have one producing tool, so any step can be re-run alone. The record carries the provenance of every contribution, and the licence of the combined result is derived from the most restrictive licence among them. It can later be exported as an RO-Crate.

The enriched data support:

* full-text and faceted search by page types, named entities and vocabulary keywords,
* assessment of OCR quality before further processing,
* linking of documents to controlled vocabularies and to each other,
* international access through English translations of metadata and texts,
* corpora for natural language processing, including the training and evaluation of models.

The tools were developed in the [ATRIUM project](https://atrium-research.eu/) by the Institute of Formal and Applied Linguistics (Charles University) with the Institutes of Archaeology of the Czech Academy of Sciences in Prague and Brno. They are open source, published as container images, and are described in their own Marketplace records. Their integration into [Galaxy](https://galaxyproject.org/) is being prepared with DARIAH.

The [Archaeological Map of the Czech Republic (AMCR)](https://digiarchiv.aiscr.cz/) repository serves as the **demonstrator** of the workflow.

**Diagram caption**: *Users and data curators work with a data repository (AMCR) that stores each document with its metadata, original file, ALTO XML, document record, enrichments and paradata, and the AMCR vocabularies. A processing orchestration (step 2) passes documents between the repository, a separate automatic text recognition workflow (step 4) and the ATRIUM tool services: page classification (3), ALTO post-processing and quality control (5), NLP enrichment with UDPipe and NameTag to TEITOK (7), vocabulary keywords by LLM (8) and XML translation (10). A dashed born-digital branch (6) replaces steps 4 and 5. NLP enrichment and translation call the LINDAT services; the vocabularies feed keyword extraction and translation. Annotators and data engineers train a custom NameTag model (9). A discovery service (11) serves users and feeds the OAI-PMH and File API, which feeds the ARIADNE Portal.*

relatedItems.label: Task of the XML files translator supporting vocabulary and preserving input files structure
relatedItems.description:
ATRIUM - LINDAT XML Translation Workflow

Overview
The atrium-translator is a modular Python wrapper developed to interface seamlessly with the LINDAT Translation API. This tool is strictly optimized for processing XML documents and their direct derivatives, specifically focusing on ALTO XML documents and AMCR metadata records. It safely translates structural text while maintaining the complex schema and namespaces of the original files.

Core Translation Pipeline Logic
The translation workflow follows a structured pipeline designed to protect context, formatting, and domain terminology:

Language Detection: The text undergoes source language identification using Facebook's FastText models. If the confidence score is below 0.2, the system utilizes an intelligent fallback and defaults to Czech (cs) to prevent pipeline interruptions.

Tag-and-Protect Vocabulary Strategy: To ensure domain-specific terminology is not garbled by the Neural Machine Translation (NMT) model, users can supply a vocabulary CSV. Multi-word phrases are matched via case-insensitive substring matching (favoring the longest match first). Single-word terms are matched by their underlying lemma using the LINDAT UDPipe API. These matched terms are replaced with temporary __TERM_N__ placeholder tags prior to the API call, bypassing translation, and are restored to their specified target language equivalents afterward.

Space-Aware Chunking: When dispatching text to the LINDAT Translation API (v2), the script intelligently segments text larger than 4,000 characters at the nearest space. This protects word boundaries and prevents API truncation errors.

Specialized Operating Modes

1. ALTO XML Mode
Triggered via the --alto flag, this mode is explicitly built for OCR/ALTO transcription documents. It natively traverses down to the String level and extracts the CONTENT attributes. Instead of translating word-by-word (which loses context), it reconstructs the entire TextLine for API submission, and carefully redistributes the translated output back into the individual CONTENT attributes.

2. AMCR Metadata Mode
Designed to safely modify structured archaeological and cultural heritage metadata without breaking XML validation. Target elements are dynamically specified via a list of XPaths (e.g., amcr-fields.txt). It features deep recursive namespace extraction to navigate complex OAI-PMH XML envelopes safely. Outputs can be actively validated against a provided XSD schema (e.g., the AISCR schema) to guarantee structural integrity post-translation.

Quality Assurance & Data Provenance
To support scientific integrity and ease of review, the tool automatically generates comprehensive provenance data:

Line-by-Line CSV Logging: A supplementary QA CSV log (original_filename_log.csv) is written alongside every output file, allowing researchers to manually cross-reference the text_source_lang directly with the text_target_lang on a per-line or per-XPath basis.

Paradata JSON Logs: A ParadataLogger captures run-level provenance metadata, aggregating counts, timing, processed formats, and skipped files into a serialized JSON file within a dedicated paradata directory.

Additional Utilities
Automated Vocabulary Harvesting: The repository includes a helper script (load_vocab.py) that can programmatically download and merge Czech-to-English domain vocabularies from both the AMCR OAI-PMH API and the TEATER GraphQL API into a ready-to-use CSV format.

relatedItems.label: Translator of XML files supporting vocabulary and preserving input structure
relatedItems.description:
A modular Python wrapper specifically designed for the LINDAT Translation API. Following project scope requirements, this tool is strictly focused on processing XML and its direct derivatives (ALTO XML and AMCR metadata records). It identifies the source language using FastText, translates the content to English (or other target languages), optionally overrides domain-specific terms using a Tag-and-Protect vocabulary strategy backed by UDPipe lemmatisation, and safely reconstructs the original XML structure.

relatedItems.label: Vocabulary-driven Information Extraction
relatedItems.description:
This workflow concerns information extraction from textual documents with the aim of enriching existing subject indexing with Linked Open Data (LOD) identifiers for concepts drawn from published controlled vocabularies (such as thesauri) specific to the domain. The overall goal is to improve findability and interoperability in accordance with FAIR principles. 

The primary use-case (in the context of the ATRIUM project) is to suggest enrichments for the subject indexing of English language reports and journal articles describing archaeological investigations and interventions, as supplied by ATRIUM partner Archaeology Data Service (ADS). The workflow accommodates structured text inputs and PDF documents (provided textual data can be extracted). Jupyter notebook demonstrators illustrate the application of the tools developed.

relatedItems.label: AMCR Digital Archive
relatedItems.description: The Digital Archive of the Archaeological Map of the Czech Republic (AMCR) is a web application designed for viewing information about archaeological investigations, sites and finds, operated by the Archaeological Institutes of the CAS in Prague and Brno. The archives of these institutions contain documentation of archaeological fieldwork on the territory of the Czech Republic from 1919 to the present day, and they continue to enrich their collections. The AMCR database and related documents form the largest collection of archaeological data concerning the Czech Republic and are therefore an important part of our cultural heritage.

relatedItems.label: ALTO XMLs post-processing and quality control (text lines categorization)
relatedItems.description:
Turns OCR output into clean, classified text lines. The pipeline splits documents into pages, builds page statistics tables, extracts text in reading order (LayoutReader by default; alto-tools, GLM-4v, JSON-key and plain-text readers as alternatives) and labels every line by language and OCR quality: Clear, Noisy, Trash, Non-text or Empty. The quality score combines structural detectors, perplexity (Qwen2.5-0.5B or distilgpt2) and character-level metrics; the language comes from FastText.

Input: ALTO XML, generic OCR JSON, or any text-bearing file (PDF, DOCX, TXT, HTML, TEI, PAGE XML and more). Output: per-line CSV tables, page statistics, plain text and the ATRIUM document record (JSON), with a paradata JSON log per run.

Command-line pipeline or REST API container image (`ghcr.io/ufal/atrium-alto-postprocess-api`, `/process`).

relatedItems.label: NLP enrichment of OCR text lines into TEITOK (UDPipe 2, NameTag 3)
relatedItems.description:
Adds linguistic annotation to text lines from ALTO post-processing (CSV or XLSX with a `text` column, or plain text). The lines go to the LINDAT UDPipe 2 service for tokens, lemmas, part-of-speech tags and syntax, and to NameTag 3 for named entities. The main output is TEITOK XML, a TEI-based format that keeps the annotation tied to the page layout when the ALTO files are supplied. CoNLL-U files, per-page entity tables, summary CSVs and the ATRIUM document record (JSON) are also written, with a paradata JSON log per run.

Optional keyword extraction per page or document uses YAKE (command-line default), KeyBERT (API default) or the legacy KER method. An optional LLM stage maps text onto the AMČR and TEATER vocabularies; the same engine is maintained as the separate tool atrium-llm-enrich, which the AMČR workflow uses.

Command-line pipeline or REST API container image (`ghcr.io/ufal/atrium-nlp-enrich-api`: `/enrich`, `/enrich_text`, background `/jobs`).

relatedItems.label: Historical documents page classifier - archival scans categorization by content type
relatedItems.description:
Sorts scanned pages of archival documents into 11 content categories, so that each page goes to the processing it needs: OCR or HTR of typed, printed or handwritten text, table extraction, or extraction of drawings and photos. The categories (DRAW, DRAW_L, LINE_HW, LINE_P, LINE_T, PHOTO, PHOTO_L, TEXT, TEXT_HW, TEXT_P, TEXT_T) were formed from archival documents of 1920–2020.

Fine-tuned ViT, RegNetY and EfficientNetV2 models, usable singly or as an averaged ensemble (`--best`), are published on the Hugging Face Hub and were trained on 48,499 manually annotated pages released at LINDAT. The tool covers PDF-to-PNG preparation, top-N predictions for single images or directories, CSV summary tables, training and evaluation, with a paradata JSON log per run.

Command-line tool or REST API container image (`ghcr.io/ufal/atrium-page-classification-api`: `/predict_image` for JPG/PNG, `/predict_document` for PDF).

relatedItems.label: LLM keyword mapping onto archaeological vocabularies (AMČR, TEATER) and born-digital PDF/DOCX conversion
relatedItems.description:
Maps archival text onto controlled archaeological vocabularies with a large language model, and converts born-digital documents into the ATRIUM document record.

**Vocabulary keywords.** Each text line (CSV, TEITOK) or each passage of a whole document (TXT, Markdown) is tagged with a term from the AMČR heslář and the TEATER thesaurus, with Czech and English keywords and a confidence score. The answer is held to the vocabulary: the term list becomes the enum of a JSON schema, decoding follows that schema where the backend supports it, and a category that is not in the vocabulary is dropped, not guessed.

**Born-digital conversion.** PDF and DOCX files with a usable text layer become the document record (JSON) without OCR.

Models run locally (transformers or vLLM, one or more GPUs) or through OpenRouter or Ollama. Every enrichment run writes a paradata JSON log. Command-line tools and container images, including a REST API (`ghcr.io/ufal/atrium-llm-enrich-api`).

composedOf.label: Selection of a target repository and meeting basic requirements
composedOf.description:
The workflow is designed around a **collection of independent services accessible via APIs**, which integrate into the native workflows of a **designated repository**.

To implement the workflow fully, you need **control over the repository implementation**, so that you can adapt its internal workflows and services. The repository must be able to store several **distributions** of one file (the original and the files derived from it), each with its own **paradata** describing how it was produced, and to deliver them with the same access rules as the original. The [Archaeological Map of the Czech Republic](https://doi.org/10.17616/R31NJMYW), based on the [Fedora repository system](https://fedorarepository.org/), is the demonstrator; the approach is adaptable to other repository implementations.

The workflow accepts three kinds of input: **scanned documents** (PDF or page images), which go through automatic text recognition (step 4); **existing OCR output** in _ALTO XML_, which can be processed directly (from step 5); and **born-digital documents** (_PDF_, _DOCX_) with a usable text layer (step 6).

concept.label: 5 - technology validated in relevant environment
concept.definition: The components making up the concept is tested individually in realistic environment.

relatedItems.label: Fedora
relatedItems.description: Fedora is the flexible, standards-based, open-source repository software built to support long-term digital preservation.

relatedItems.label: AMCR Digital Archive
relatedItems.description: The Digital Archive of the Archaeological Map of the Czech Republic (AMCR) is a web application designed for viewing information about archaeological investigations, sites and finds, operated by the Archaeological Institutes of the CAS in Prague and Brno. The archives of these institutions contain documentation of archaeological fieldwork on the territory of the Czech Republic from 1919 to the present day, and they continue to enrich their collections. The AMCR database and related documents form the largest collection of archaeological data concerning the Czech Republic and are therefore an important part of our cultural heritage.

composedOf.label: Integration into the processing workflows of the selected repository
composedOf.description:
To enable the further steps, **develop the repository modules** that send files to the processing services and store the results in the repository.

Processing is **asynchronous**. An orchestration layer (in the demonstrator, [Temporal](https://temporal.io/)) queues the jobs, calls the services in order, retries failed calls, and lets an operator stop, resume and switch individual steps on or off. Large documents are split (page ranges, pages, text chunks) and the partial results are merged, so that no practical limit applies to file size.

The **repository remains the only writer** to its storage. The processing services hold no repository credentials: they return results, and the repository stores each result as a **new distribution of the original file**, together with its paradata.

Every service reads and extends the same **per-document JSON record**. The orchestration passes it from one step to the next, and the repository stores it as a distribution as well. This keeps any single step re-runnable, and the provenance and licence of the combined result traceable.

Processing can be triggered on upload, by a user for selected documents, or in batches for selected datasets.

composedOf.label: Page classification
composedOf.description:
Classify each page of a document by its content type (printed, typed or handwritten text, tables, drawings and photographs, alone or in combination) with the [historical documents page classifier](https://github.com/ufal/atrium-page-classification). The classifier is an ensemble of image-classification models (ViT, RegNetY, EfficientNetV2) trained on manually annotated pages of scanned archival documents, largely archaeological reports.

The service accepts a _PDF_ or a page image and returns the top-ranked categories with their scores for each page, in _JSON_, and writes the page categories into the document record.

The page categories steer the rest of the processing (which pages go to text recognition, which are drawings or photographs) and serve users directly as a search facet.

_Limitations:_ the models are trained on a dataset licensed CC BY-NC 4.0, which the results inherit.

composedOf.label: Automatic text recognition of scanned documents
composedOf.description:
Scanned documents need **automatic text recognition** (OCR/HTR) and layout segmentation before their text can be processed. This workflow does not perform text recognition itself. It relies on dedicated ATR services and workflows, and defines the repository's entry for their output. For planning and running ATR, see the [Automatic Text Recognition Roadmap](https://marketplace.sshopencloud.eu/workflow/o8ilLU) and its linked workflows.

The repository sends the scanned document to an ATR service and stores the result as an alternative distribution in _ALTO XML_ (UTF-8). Output from other ATR engines can also enter as ALTO-compatible _JSON_ with line segmentation. In the demonstrator, an external ATR service is the primary route, with a backup OCR service deployed beside the other tools. Documents that were already mass-digitised enter at this point with their existing _ALTO XML_.

The readiness level refers to the repository entry for ATR output. The ATR services themselves are described in the linked workflows.

relatedItems.label: Automatic Text Recognition Roadmap
relatedItems.description:
**Automatic Text Recognition** (ATR) uses Artificial Intelligence (AI), in particular **machine learning** (ML), to **extract text from a scanned image**. It encompasses two main techniques: **Optical Character Recognition** (OCR), extracting text from printed documents, and **Handwritten Text Recognition** (HTR), extracting text from manusripts.  
This workflow presents the main steps of an ATR workflow and how to integrate it in your research project.

relatedItems.label: Automatic Text Recognition using Object Detection with eScriptorium
relatedItems.description:
_Please note that this workflow is bound to change once the new version of eScriptorium is released._

This workflow performs Automatic Text Recognition (ATR) with an object detection approach. It uses a YOLO object detection model for segmenting regions, the kraken library for line segmentation, and performs text recognition on the eScriptorium platform. Please note that some prior knowledge in the application of these tools is expected, like using a command-line interface or having a free Roboflow account.

relatedItems.label: Performing Layout Analysis for Automatic Text Recognition
relatedItems.description:
Layout analysis is a computer vision tasks that allows us to identify the structure of a document and localize the lines of text. We generate a series of _x_ and _y_ coordinates corresponding to regions/lines on the image, which we associate to a corresponding labels.  

Text line segmentation is mandatory in most ATR systems, but without a good line segmentation, transcription performances will not be sufficient. For example, lines can be missed, read in the wrong order, or even broken down into several lines. 

Synonyms: "segmentation", "zoning", "document analysis", "optical layout analysis".

composedOf.label: ALTO post-processing and OCR quality control
composedOf.description:
Assess whether the recognised text is good enough for further processing with the [ALTO XML post-processing and quality control tool](https://github.com/ufal/atrium-alto-postprocess).

The tool reads the text lines from _ALTO XML_ (or plain text, or ALTO-compatible _JSON_), restores their reading order, identifies the language of each line (fastText), and measures its perplexity with a small language model. From these values it assigns each line a quality category: **Clear**, **Noisy**, **Trash**, **Non-text** or **Empty**.

The output is a per-line table (text, language, scores, category), returned as _JSON_ and stored as a _CSV_ distribution. The same lines, with their positions on the page, form the text layer of the document record, which the later steps read.

_Limitations:_ the categorisation rules are still being calibrated, and a new tool version can move lines between categories. Record the tool version in the paradata, and re-score a corpus when you change the version. Some models used for the layout step carry non-commercial licences, which the results inherit.

composedOf.label: Born-digital branch: text extraction from PDF and DOCX
composedOf.description:
For **born-digital documents** that already carry a usable text layer, this step replaces steps 4 and 5. The born-digital converter of the [ATRIUM LLM enricher](https://github.com/ufal/atrium-llm-enrich) extracts the text lines of _PDF_ and _DOCX_ files, with their positions, fonts and page structure, directly into the document record, in the same form that step 5 produces for scanned documents. The following steps therefore process both kinds of document alike.

Pages without a trustworthy text layer (for example scanned pages inside a born-digital PDF, or text drawn as curves) are flagged, and the document is handed back to text recognition (step 4).

[GROBID](https://marketplace.sshopencloud.eu/tool-or-service/QcBl7a) was considered: it suits born-digital scholarly publications rather than the scan-heavy, loosely structured reports typical of archaeological archives, and it is kept only as a benchmark for scholarly PDFs. For a general PDF text-extraction workflow, see [Text Extraction From PDF Files](https://marketplace.sshopencloud.eu/workflow/nTbkkH).

relatedItems.label: Text Extraction From PDF Files
relatedItems.description:
This workflow describes the process for extracting the textual content of PDF files, and performing some basic segmentation of the extracted text.

The workflow is intended to be used as the first step in larger workflows that process the text (such as geographic named entity extraction etc,) and is unlikely to be particularly useful as a stand-alone workflow. Specifically it was designed in the context of the ATRIUM project to aid in the indexing of English language reports and journal articles describing archaeological investigations and interventions, as supplied by ATRIUM partner Archaeology Data Service (ADS).

relatedItems.label: GROBID
relatedItems.description:
GROBID (or Grobid, but not GroBid nor GroBiD) means GeneRation Of BIbliographic Data.

GROBID is a machine learning library for extracting, parsing and re-structuring raw documents such as PDF into structured XML/TEI encoded documents with a particular focus on technical and scientific publications.

composedOf.label: Linguistic annotation and named entity recognition
composedOf.description:
Annotate the text with the [NLP enrichment tool](https://github.com/ufal/atrium-nlp-enrich). It reads the per-line table from step 5 or 6 (or plain text) and calls two [LINDAT](https://lindat.cz/) services:

* [UDPipe 2](https://lindat.mff.cuni.cz/services/udpipe/) for **tokenisation, lemmatisation, morphological tagging and dependency parsing**, with pre-trained models for the language of the text (e.g., Czech or English);
* [NameTag 3](https://lindat.mff.cuni.cz/services/nametag/) for **named entity recognition**.

The output is a [TEITOK](http://www.teitok.org/) _TEI XML_ file, stored as a distribution. It keeps each token's position on the page image, so that a viewer can highlight tokens and entities on the scan. The entities and the morphological annotation are also written into the document record.

_Limitations:_ the NameTag 3 models are licensed CC BY-NC-SA, and the results inherit this licence. The LINDAT services are remote and limit the size of a request, so long texts are split before they are sent.

relatedItems.label: UDPipe: tool for lemmatization, morphological analysis, POS tagging and dependency parsing in multiple languages
relatedItems.description: UDPipe is a software tool and service that analyzes (plain) text in about 100 different natural languages up to the dependency syntax level. Users specify the desired function (tokenization, segmentation, morphological analysis, lemmatization, POS tagging, dependency parsing), output format, and input text (file(s)). The resulting analysis can be used to index and search documents by lemmas instead of multiple word forms, extract syntactic dependencies with POS information to get relations between words or lemmas, or get grammatical information for every word in the text. While in many cases the results can be used directly (statistical analysis on part of speech, lemmas and words), in many other applications the results of UDPipe serve as intermediate input to more sophisticated analysis, such as information extraction, knowledge representation, term extraction etc. UDPipe software allow to train on any language for which a treebank is available in the CoNLL-U format, such as all the Universal Dependencies corpora.

relatedItems.label: NameTag
relatedItems.description:
NameTag is an open-source tool for named entity recognition (NER). NameTag identifies proper names in text and classifies them into predefined categories, such as names of persons, locations, organizations, etc. NameTag 2 recognizes nested entities (embedded entities) of arbitrary depth.

For Czech, it recognizes a [complex hierarchy of categories](http://ufal.mff.cuni.cz/~strakova/cnec2.0/ne-type-hierarchy.pdf). The English model, which is trained on CoNLL-2003 NER annotations (Sang and De Meulder [2003](https://www.clarin.eu/resource-families/tools-named-entity-recognition#Sang%20and%20De%20Meulder%202003)), distinguishes the following four NER classes: person, organisation, location and miscellaneous.

The trained model for Czech is available for through LINDAT: [Czech Models (CNEC) for NameTag](http://hdl.handle.net/11858/00-097C-0000-0023-7D42-8).
A [user manual](http://ufal.mff.cuni.cz/nametag/users-manual) is also available.

composedOf.label: Keyword extraction against controlled vocabularies
composedOf.description:
Extract **keywords** that match the repository's **controlled vocabularies** with the [ATRIUM LLM enricher](https://github.com/ufal/atrium-llm-enrich). In the demonstrator these are the AMCR vocabularies and the [TEATER](https://teater.aiscr.cz/) thesaurus, harvested from their public sources (the AMCR OAI-PMH API and the TEATER export).

A large language model reads the text line by line or as a whole document, with the vocabulary in its instructions. Its output is constrained so that it can only return terms that exist in the vocabulary. The result is a set of Czech and English keyword pairs, each with a thematic category, the page it comes from and the identifier of the vocabulary concept. Keywords are written into the document record, and entities from step 7 are linked to vocabulary concepts where a match exists.

The model can run locally (on a GPU, or lightweight through [Ollama](https://ollama.com/)) or through a remote provider. Where the texts must not leave the institution, run it locally.

_Limitations:_ the step is experimental, and the quality of the keywords is still being evaluated. The licence of the output depends on the model and, for a remote provider, on its terms of use.

concept.label: 3 - experimental proof of concept
concept.definition: The most critical functions of the new technology is validated by using both analytical and experimental methods.

composedOf.label: Named entity recognition – optional training for enhanced results
composedOf.description:
The NameTag models can be [further trained](https://ufal.mff.cuni.cz/nametag/1/users-manual#training_data) to **recognise custom entities**.

In the demonstrator, the goal is to enable the model to **identify accession numbers**, which link individual descriptive objects and parts of the documentation. The training can also cover **named entities aligned to specialised vocabularies**, such as the [AMCR vocabularies](https://teater.aiscr.cz/) (archaeological dating, types of sites and finds, materials, etc.).

Training needs a dataset of manually annotated texts in [CoNLL format](https://github.com/ufal/nametag3/blob/main/examples/cs_gold_2.conll), with a sufficient number of examples per category (hundreds rather than tens). The documents annotated by step 7 are a starting point for such a dataset.

For recognising vocabulary terms in English archaeological reports and grey literature, and linking them to published vocabularies (Getty AAT, PeriodO), see the ATRIUM workflow [Vocabulary-driven Information Extraction](https://marketplace.sshopencloud.eu/workflow/IrpmkB).

relatedItems.label: Vocabulary-driven Information Extraction
relatedItems.description:
This workflow concerns information extraction from textual documents with the aim of enriching existing subject indexing with Linked Open Data (LOD) identifiers for concepts drawn from published controlled vocabularies (such as thesauri) specific to the domain. The overall goal is to improve findability and interoperability in accordance with FAIR principles. 

The primary use-case (in the context of the ATRIUM project) is to suggest enrichments for the subject indexing of English language reports and journal articles describing archaeological investigations and interventions, as supplied by ATRIUM partner Archaeology Data Service (ADS). The workflow accommodates structured text inputs and PDF documents (provided textual data can be extracted). Jupyter notebook demonstrators illustrate the application of the tools developed.

The archives of these institutions contain documentation of archaeological fieldwork on the territory of the Czech Republic from 1919 to the present day, and they continue to enrich their collections. The AMCR database and related documents form the largest collection of archaeological data concerning the Czech Republic and are therefore an important part of our cultural heritage.

relatedItems.label: NameTag
relatedItems.description:
NameTag is an open-source tool for named entity recognition (NER). NameTag identifies proper names in text and classifies them into predefined categories, such as names of persons, locations, organizations, etc. NameTag 2 recognizes nested entities (embedded entities) of arbitrary depth.

For Czech, it recognizes a [complex hierarchy of categories](http://ufal.mff.cuni.cz/~strakova/cnec2.0/ne-type-hierarchy.pdf). The English model, which is trained on CoNLL-2003 NER annotations (Sang and De Meulder [2003](https://www.clarin.eu/resource-families/tools-named-entity-recognition#Sang%20and%20De%20Meulder%202003)), distinguishes the following four NER classes: person, organisation, location and miscellaneous.

The trained model for Czech is available for through LINDAT: [Czech Models (CNEC) for NameTag](http://hdl.handle.net/11858/00-097C-0000-0023-7D42-8).
A [user manual](http://ufal.mff.cuni.cz/nametag/users-manual) is also available.

composedOf.label: Automated translations
composedOf.description:
Given the volume of texts, translating on the fly would not be efficient. It is more practical to **prepare a basic translation from the minority language** — here Czech — into a widely used language such as English, and to store it.

The [XML translator](https://github.com/ufal/atrium-translator) calls [LINDAT Translation](https://lindat.mff.cuni.cz/services/translation/) on the text content of _XML_ files: metadata records and _ALTO XML_ pages. It detects the source language (fastText), protects domain terms with a vocabulary (using UDPipe lemmas), and rebuilds the original XML structure around the translated text.

The translation is stored as a **separate file** beside the original (for metadata, an English metadata record), not inserted into the original record. The original stays unchanged for the services that already consume it. The translated entities are also written into the document record.

For smaller languages such as Czech, this is a critical step towards genuine international use of the content of domain- and region-specific repositories.

_Limitations:_ the LINDAT Translation service is offered for non-commercial use; its results with the vocabulary resolve to CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. State the licence of the translations alongside them, and arrange production use with the service provider or run your own instance.

relatedItems.label: Translator of XML files supporting vocabulary and preserving input structure
relatedItems.description:
A modular Python wrapper specifically designed for the LINDAT Translation API. Following project scope requirements, this tool is strictly focused on processing XML and its direct derivatives (ALTO XML and AMCR metadata records). It identifies the source language using FastText, translates the content to English (or other target languages), optionally overrides domain-specific terms using a Tag-and-Protect vocabulary strategy backed by UDPipe lemmatisation, and safely reconstructs the original XML structure.

relatedItems.label: ARIADNE Portal
relatedItems.description:
The ARIADNE Portal provides the main point of access for searching and browsing datasets and new services for processing and publishing archaeological datasets online. 

The Portal brings together existing archaeological research datasets from ARIADNE partners so that researchers can browse and access the various distributed datasets for use in their projects. The portal also provides a point of access for the new services developed by the project.

The datasets that are registered in the ARIADNE catalogue are held by its partners and have been created through research, in excavations, in fieldwork, laboratory and other projects. In recent years archaeologists have been making increasing use of sophisticated digital equipment and techniques. During the course of a research project large volumes of data are created and collected, and become part of the research archive. ARIADNE aims to make these archives available through its portal for researchers to consult when starting new research.

relatedItems.label: CIDOC-CRM
relatedItems.description: The "CIDOC object-oriented Conceptual Reference Model" (CRM), was developed by the ICOM/CIDOC Documentation Standards Group. Since September 2000, the CIDOC CRM is being developed into an ISO standard in a joined effort of the CIDOC CRM SIG and ISO/TC46/SC4/WG9. Since September 2006 it has been accepted as ISO 21127. The CIDOC CRM represents an 'ontology' for cultural heritage information i.e. it describes in a formal language the explicit and implicit concepts and relations relevant to the documentation of cultural heritage. The primary role of the CIDOC CRM is to serve as a basis for mediation of cultural heritage information and thereby provide the semantic 'glue' needed to transform today's disparate, localised information sources into a coherent and valuable global resource. The CIDOC CRM is intended to promote a shared understanding of cultural heritage information by providing a common and extensible semantic framework that any cultural heritage information can be mapped to. It is intended to be a common language for domain experts and implementers to formulate requirements for information systems and to serve as a guide for good practice of conceptual modelling. In this way, it can provide the "semantic glue" needed to mediate between different sources of cultural heritage information, such as that published by museums, libraries and archives.

description: This workflow describes the recommended steps for depositing research source code developed within an SSH project, from repository preparation on GitLab, GitHub, or Codeberg to long-term archiving via Software Heritage or Zenodo and declaration in HAL-SHS. It reflects the current French open science infrastructure and its known limitations.

composedOf.label: Prepare the repository (preliminary step)
composedOf.description:
The first step is to create or configure a repository on a version control platform — GitLab or GitHub are the two standard options in SSH research contexts. However, GitHub is not a open-source platform, and it is preferable to use an open-source forge such as Codeberg (https://codeberg.org/). Your repository must include a set of mandatory files at its root, in Markdown format. A README.md file describes your software, its research context, and its usage. An AUTHORS.md file lists all authors with their institutional affiliations; contributors not intended to appear in citation metadata may be listed separately in a CONTRIBUTORS file. 

A LICENSE file specifies the reuse conditions of your source code. Licence selection should be carried out in consultation with the legal or valorisation service of your institution, as intellectual property rights may be shared between you and your employer. A codemeta.json file, generated with the CodeMeta Generator, provides machine-readable metadata that will pre-populate your HAL deposit form automatically. Both the copyright notice and the list of authors must appear explicitly in your repository at this stage, as they condition both citability and archiving eligibility in subsequent steps.

Finally, both Git repositories and Zenodo provide options to configure automatic archiving and synchronization between the repository and Zenodo. This integration enables version management and ensures that each software release deposited on Zenodo is assigned a persistent DOI, thereby facilitating citation, traceability, and long-term preservation of the code.

This resource is supported by Text+. In case of questions you may get in touch with the Text+ helpdesk at textplus-support@gwdg.de.

relatedItems.label: CodeMetaPy
relatedItems.description: Codemetapy is a command-line tool and python library to work with the codemeta software metadata standard. Codemeta builds upon schema.org and defines a vocabulary for describing software source code. It maps various existing metadata standards to a unified vocabulary. Codemetapy allows you to generate codemeta from various sources.

composedOf.label: Archive on Software Heritage
composedOf.description: Once your repository is prepared, submit your source code to Software Heritage using the Save Code Now function, available at archive.softwareheritage.org/save. No account is required. This step preserves the full development history of your repository. Upon completion, retrieve the SoftWare Hash IDentifier (SWHID) from the Software Heritage interface via the Permalinks tab; select the identifier of type "dir" (directory), with contextual information enabled, for use in the subsequent deposit. The SWHID functions as a persistent fingerprint of your source code, calculated directly from the code itself independently of any external registry.

relatedItems.label: Software Heritage Archive
relatedItems.description: The long term goal of the Software Heritage initiative is to collect all publicly available software in source code form together with its development history, replicate it massively to ensure its preservation, and share it with everyone who needs it. The Software Heritage archive is growing over time as we crawl new source code from software projects and development forges.

composedOf.label: Deposit in HAL
composedOf.description:
Carry out your deposit on hal.science — the French national open archive — under the document type "Software". In the "Automatic extraction" subsection, paste the SWHID obtained in Step 2 into the designated field; HAL will extract the metadata from your codemeta.json file and pre-populate the form automatically. This automation is not merely a time-saving convenience: it ensures consistency between the metadata declared in HAL and those archived in Software Heritage, a condition essential to the interoperability of both systems.
Verify and complete the mandatory fields — software name, thematic domain, licence information, and author list with at least one institutional affiliation. These elements form the minimum basis of any scientifically valid record. The optional fields — keywords, production date, programming language, development status, ANR or European project reference, link to the code repository — are far from incidental: they directly determine the visibility and citability of your software across academic information retrieval systems.
At the final stage of your deposit, accept the transfer to Software Heritage. This step is what enables the SWHID to be inscribed in your HAL record and in citation exports, ensuring the long-term traceability of your contribution. Your deposit then enters a moderation phase.

relatedItems.label: HAL-SHS
relatedItems.description:
HAL is the multidisciplinary open archive chosen by the entire French scientific and academic community for the open access dissemination of research results, whether published or not.

HAL is at once:
 - a piece of software,
 - a unique and multidisciplinary repository (see domain list),
 - and a shared platform for more than 130 institutional archives of universities and research organizations; an open repository dedicated to Human and Social Sciences (HAL-SHS) ; an open repository for the dissemination of PhD thesis; and an open repository for visual and audio data (MediHAL).

It is aimed at researchers and their institutions, covering all scientific fields and the different types of documents produced by research (articles published in peer-reviewed journals, conference papers, theses, preprints, software, etc.).

relatedItems.label: Evaluation of the analytical potential of laser-induced breakdown spectrometry (LIBS) for the analysis of historical glasses
relatedItems.description: The novel and---for archaeometrical applications---still rarely used Laser-Induced Breakdown Spectrometry (LIBS) was tested on various standard glasses for its spectrometric performance. LIBS is an almost non-destructive method based on the time-resolved detection of optical emission following direct laser ablation. A frequency-quadrupoled Nd:YAG laser at 266 nm was found to cause a hardly visible crater of c. 200 µm in diameter. The application of an innovative high-resolution Echelle spectrograph allows the fast and simultaneous determination of up to 90 elements in the spectral range from 200 to 780 nm, with a resolution of 10--30 pm under ambient conditions. In principle, LIBS has a high analytical potential for archaeometry; in particular, for the determination of light elements (Li, Be, B and others). Because the measurement parameters (laser energy, delay time and number of pulses) do not independently influence the emission signal, their optimization proved to be complex and is rather a compromise for the range of elements. The effects of sample distance, surface roughness and the accumulation of depth profiles were studied. Problems arose for the determination of sodium and potassium in higher contents due to self-absorption effects. Quantification tests using a silicon line as internal standard yielded a precision range between 3% and 20% relative, but in general no satisfying accuracy for a number of elements. However, these problems might be overcome in the near future by improved spectrometer set-ups and matrix correction approaches

relatedItems.label: Lead determination in glasses by laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy
relatedItems.description: Laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) has been used to determine the lead content of different types of lead silicate glasses commercially designed as sonorous glass (which contain ∼ 10 wt.% PbO); crystal glass (with at least 24 wt.% PbO) and superior crystal glass (with at least 30 wt.% PbO). Seven different types of glass samples were selected, including historic-original, model and commercially available. The selected samples were artificially weathered under neutral, acid and alkaline attack. Analysis by LIBS was carried out in vacuum under excitation at 266 nm and results were compared with those obtained by conventional techniques used for glass characterization. Composition of the bulk glasses was analyzed by XRF (X-ray fluorescence) and the corroded surfaces were characterized by SEM/EDX (scanning electron microscopy/energy dispersive X-ray microanalysis). A linear correlation was obtained between the intensity of selected Pb lines in the LIB spectra and the PbO content. The effect of corrosion could be characterized by comparing successive LIB spectra recorded on the same area; acid attack resulted in a decrease of PbO, CaO and Na2O content in the surface with respect to the bulk of the sample, while minor changes in the composition were noticed under alkaline attack. These results show LIBS as a useful technique to classify the different types of lead glasses by their lead content and to determine and asses the degree and type of corrosion.

relatedItems.label: SOPRANO, Synthetic Organic Pigments Research Aggregation Network
relatedItems.description: SOPs have been widely applied in modern and contemporary painting and are also used extensively in conservation-restoration practice. Nevertheless, historic and scientific interest in the history and characteristics of SOPs has been very limited. While SOPs have already 150 years of history, in which hundreds of different SOPs have been synthesized, these pigments are understudied in comparison to the more classic ranges of natural minerals and synthetic inorganic pigments. Still little is known about the history of SOPs including their stability and degradation characteristics and interaction with the paint binder.

relatedItems.label: Multianalytical characterization of Late Roman glasses including nanosecond and femtosecond laser induced breakdown spectroscopy
relatedItems.description: In the present study, a historical set of Late Roman glasses from a recently unearthed graveyard located in the small city of Cubas de la Sagra, within the Madrid region (Spain) was compositionally analysed using different techniques such as ultraviolet-visible (UV-Vis) and laser induced fluorescence (LIF) spectroscopy, X-ray fluorescence (XRF) and laser induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS). LIBS results, recorded upon nanosecond (ns) and femtosecond (fs) laser irradiation, served for identification of major glass components (to classify them into main historical glass groups) and of minor components (e.g. chromophores, decolouring agents and degradation products). Quantitative information regarding these components was obtained on the basis of calibration curves obtained using glass certified standards and local standards. We have demonstrated that LIBS serves for the non-invasive/micro-destructive, quantitative chemical characterization of most of the analysed historical glasses. Furthermore, this work establishes a comparison between LIBS analysis of glasses in the ns and fs regimes on one hand, and on the other hand with the results obtained using XRF. The procedures and protocols here proposed can be applied for in situ study of historical glass collections, regardless of their size, provenance and chronology

label: Studies on science and higher education system in Poland using the RAD-on platform
description:
In order to answer questions regarding the science or higher education system quality datasets are needed. In this workflow, we guide you through the process of gathering and analysing data about the Polish system of science and higher education using the most up-to-date and reliable open data platform, which is called RAD-on.

The RAD-on system presents reports, analyses, and data on science and higher education in Poland. RAD-on was developed by the National Information Processing Institute in collaboration with the Polish Ministry of Education and Science.

In terms of the data it collects and shares, RAD-on is currently the largest national IT system in science and higher education in Europe. It stores information on nearly all scientific institutions in Poland, as well as their scientists. This includes academic teachers and other individuals who conduct classes at higher education institutions. RAD-on also offers comprehensive lists of scholarly publications, national and international patents, research projects funded by various sources, and institutional investments. It contains extensive information on students, graduates, and on tertiary education programmes.

We hope that the information presented in this workflow will inspire valuable research on science and higher education in Poland. This workflow also serves as an invitation to discuss the future of RAD-on. We are confident that our efforts to promote more widespread understanding of RAD-on will inspire stakeholders to collaborate in the portal’s development and in the enhancement of its efficacy.
