relatedItems.label: How to phonetically transcribe dialects
relatedItems.description: This workflow outlines the main steps involved in the transcription of dialectal speech data, with particular attention to the Italian linguistic context and the Italo-Romance dialects. Although it has been primarily conceived for the Italian reality, the workflow may also be adapted and applied to other geographical and linguistic contexts, provided that the necessary methodological and linguistic adjustments are taken into account. This process is documented by Giovanni Abete in the chapter “Trascrivere il dialetto” (pp. 211–217) of the "Vademecum per il trattamento delle fonti orali" (Tavolo permanente per le fonti orali, 2023).

relatedItems.label: Automatic Transcription of Oral Sources
relatedItems.description:
This workflow guides you through the automatic transcription of oral source recordings in SSH research contexts. It covers the full pipeline: audio preparation, model selection and configuration, transcription, speaker diarisation, quality control, manual post-correction, and the export of timestamped, structured transcripts suitable for archival deposit and open publication.
The central tool is Whisper, a multilingual, open-source automatic speech recognition (ASR) model developed by OpenAI and released under the MIT licence. The workflow also integrates complementary tools for audio preprocessing (Audacity, FFmpeg), enhanced transcription (WhisperX, faster-whisper), annotation (ELAN), and text encoding (TEI-XML). It applies equally to newly recorded interviews and to the retrospective transcription of archival holdings.

relatedItems.label: Transcribe and process the interview
relatedItems.description:
Produce a transcription of the recorded interview in order to enable analysis, indexing, and long-term accessibility. Transcription constitutes a key stage in the enrichment of the oral source, transforming an audio or audiovisual document into a textual resource that can be searched, annotated, and reused.

Define the level of transcription according to the objectives of the research. This may range from verbatim transcription (including hesitations, pauses, and non-verbal elements) to a more edited version that improves readability while preserving the meaning of the discourse. Where relevant, adopt established transcription conventions and ensure consistency across the corpus.

If required, integrate time-coding to align the transcription with the original recording, facilitating navigation between text and audio/video. Consider also the need for translation, particularly in multilingual research contexts.

During transcription, pay attention to the treatment of personal data and sensitive information. Anonymisation or pseudonymisation may be necessary, especially when preparing the material for dissemination or public access. Any modifications should be documented to ensure transparency and reproducibility.

The transcription should be treated as a distinct but related document within the oral source corpus. It must therefore be documented through a dedicated record, including its relationship to the original recording, the tools and methods used, and the identity of the transcriber.

This step may be carried out prior to, or in parallel with, the description and metadata creation phase, depending on the research design and available resources. In all cases, it significantly enhances the findability, accessibility, and reusability of the oral source in line with FAIR principles.

relatedItems.label: Transcribing conversation in ELAN
relatedItems.description:
This workflow outlines the main steps involved in the transcription of conversational data using ELAN, a software environment designed for the annotation and synchronisation of audio and video recordings. ELAN is particularly suitable for multimodal transcription, as it allows the annotation of both verbal and non-verbal phenomena — such as gaze, gestures, pauses, and interactional dynamics — through multiple time-aligned annotation tiers.

The workflow includes the preliminary design of the transcription scheme and annotation hierarchy, the configuration of tiers and segmentation units, the automatic or manual transcription and annotation process, and the exportation of the final transcript in EAF or other formats. 

This workflow is based on Letizia Cirillo’s chapter “Trascrivere la conversazione” (pp. 181–188), part of the "Vademecum per il trattamento delle fonti orali" (Tavolo permanente per le fonti orali, 2020).

composedOf.label: Enregistrement de données de langage sur un support numérique
composedOf.description:
Pour réaliser une transcription avec un outil informatique, il faut disposer d'un support média avec du son et/ou de la vidéo. Ces fichiers doivent être disponibles sur votre ordinateur.

Les formats "son" les plus couramment utilisés sont le Wave (.wav), le MP3 (.mp3).
Les formats "vidéo" les plus couramment utilisés sont le MP4 (.mp4), l'AVI (.avi).

D'autres formats peuvent être utlisés. Le choix dépend des outils de transcription utilisés (voir étape 2).

English translation

To produce a transcription using a software tool, a media file containing audio and/or video is required. These files must be available on your computer.

The most commonly used audio formats are Wave (.wav) and MP3 (.mp3).
The most commonly used video formats are MP4 (.mp4) and AVI (.avi).

Other formats may also be used. The choice depends on the transcription tools being used (see step 2).

composedOf.label: Choix d'un outil de transcription

relatedItems.label: CLAN
relatedItems.description:
The CLAN Programs are downloaded, installed, and used as a single application. Functionally, however, CLAN has two parts. The first part is the CLAN editor which can be used to edit files in either CHAT or CA (Conversation Analysis) format. The editor also provides a wide range of additional functions, such as audio and video playback, linkage to audio and video, fonts for Roman and non-Roman orthographies, data validation, adding codes to files, and shipping data to other programs. The second part of CLAN is the set of data analysis programs. These programs are run from a separate window called the Commands window. The results of the analytic programs are sent to the CLAN Output window.
The tool is only compatible with [TalkBank](https://www.talkbank.org/) corpora that have CHAT annotation.
An [online manual](https://talkbank.org/manuals/CLAN.pdf) is available.

relatedItems.label: Praat
relatedItems.description: Praat is software for the phonetic analysis of speech, including support for articulatory and speech synthesis. It is also a computer program with which you can analyse, synthesize, and manipulate speech, and create high-quality pictures.

relatedItems.label: ELAN
relatedItems.description:
ELAN is a tool for creating annotations on multiple layers on audio and video resources. The textual content of annotations is in Unicode and the transcription is stored in XML.

With ELAN a user can add an unlimited number of textual annotations to audio and/or video recordings. An annotation can be a sentence, word or gloss, a comment, translation or a description of any feature observed in the media. Annotations can be created on multiple layers, called tiers. Tiers can be hierarchically interconnected. An annotation can either be time-aligned to the media or it can refer to other existing annotations. The content of annotations consists of Unicode text and annotation documents are stored in an XML format (EAF).

Main features and characteristics of ELAN:
* provides several ways to view the annotations, each view is connected to and synchronized with the media timeline
* supports creation of multiple tiers and tier hierarchies
* supports Controlled Vocabularies
* allows linking of up to 4 video files with an annotation document
* media support
   * builds on existing, native media frameworks, like Windows Media Player, QuickTime or VLC
   * support for audio and video formats depends on operating system, high performance media playback can usually be achieved
* technical
   * written in the Java programming language
   * distributions available for Windows, macOS and Linux
   * open source, the sources are available under a GPL 3 license 

The solution was developed by the Language Archive of the Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics.

composedOf.label: Choix d'une structure, d'un format, d'une convention pour les transcriptions
composedOf.description:
Les transcriptions seront utilisées pour le travail scientifique. Elles doivent contenir des informations claires et précises, de préférence dans des formats ou avec des conventions partagées par la communauté scientifique.

Les transcriptions contiennent en général l'information sur les locuteurs, une transcription, et éventuellement des informations complémentaires.

English translation

Transcriptions are used for scientific research. They should contain clear and precise information, preferably following formats or conventions shared by the scientific community.

Transcriptions generally include information about speakers, a transcription, and, where applicable, additional information.

composedOf.label: Réalisation de la transcription
composedOf.description:
Faire une transcription exhaustive prend beaucoup de temps. Par exemple, réaliser une simple transcription exhaustive d'un discours ou d'une production de langage de bonne qualité prend de 15 à 20 fois le temps du discours initial. C'est-à-dire que pour un minute de corpus,  il faut de 15 à 30 mn pour faire une transcription. Si cette transcription est vérifiée et controlée, alors le temps peut doubler. Si plusieurs personnes parlent en même temps, le temps de transcription augmente largement. 
C'est pourquoi il faut souvent s'organiser en équipe pour les travaux de transcription de grande envergure.

English translation

Producing a full transcription is time-consuming. For example, creating a simple exhaustive and high-quality transcription of a speech or spoken language recording typically takes 15 to 20 times the duration of the original speech. In other words, for one minute of recorded data, it takes approximately 15 to 30 minutes to produce a transcription. If the transcription is then checked and verified, the required time may double. When several people speak at the same time, transcription time increases significantly.
For this reason, transcription work on large-scale projects often needs to be organised in teams.

composedOf.label: Sauvegarde et diffusion
composedOf.description:
Les transcriptions sont souvent faites pour être partagées avec d'autres utilisateurs. Le coût de leur création incite aussi à ce partage. Enfin les transcriptions réalisées et partagées peuvent être citées comme un travail de recherche et faire partie des travaux d'un chercheur ou d'une équipe de recherche.
Les dépôts et la diffusion de données se font de préférence dans des sites spécialisés comme COCOON, ORTOLANG, ou des sites généralistes comme NAKALA.

English translation

Transcriptions are often created to be shared with other users. The cost of producing them also encourages such sharing. Finally, completed and shared transcriptions can be cited as research output and form part of the work of a researcher or a research team.
Data deposition and dissemination are preferably carried out through specialised platforms such as COCOON, ORTOLANG, or more general-purpose repositories such as NAKALA.

relatedItems.label: ORTOLANG
relatedItems.description:
Plate-forme d'outils et de ressources linguistiques pour un traitement optimisé de la langue française
ORTOLANG permet de déposer, conserver et difffuser tous types de données de langage

Platform of linguistic tools and resources for an optimized treatment of the French language

relatedItems.label: COCOON
relatedItems.description:
CoCoON pour « COllections de COrpus Oraux Numériques » est une plateforme technique qui accompagne les producteurs de ressources orales, à créer, structurer et archiver leurs corpus ; un corpus pouvant se composer d'enregistrements (en général audio) accompagnés éventuellement d'annotations de ces enregistrements.

Les ressources déposées sont dans un premier temps cataloguées et stockées, puis, dans un deuxième temps archivées dans l'archive de la TGIR Huma-Num. L'auteur et son institution restent responsables des documents déposés et peuvent bénéficier d'un accès restreint et sécurisé à leurs données, pendant une période définie, si le contenu de l'information est considéré sensible.

CoCoON for "Digital Oral Corpus COllections" is a technical platform that supports oral resource producers in creating, structuring and archiving their corpuses. A corpus can be composed of recordings (generally audio), possibly accompanied by annotations of these recordings.

The resources are first catalogued and stored, and then archived in the IR* Huma-Num archive. The author and his institution remain responsible for the deposited materials and can benefit from restricted and secure access to their data, for a defined period of time, if the content of the information is considered sensitive.

relatedItems.label: NAKALA, a tool to expose research data

label: Transkribus Text Tagging
description:
The workflow describes the strategic development and deployment of a text tagging scheme for transcribed historical prints and / or handwritten resources. It aims primarily at larger collections that consist of relatively homogenous resource types. That means they are similar compared to each other regarding their historic context, structure, extent, language, etc.

If you’ve done transcriptions using Transkribus, it may be the ideal platform to implement your tagging scheme, but the approach is transferable.

Key objectives of the workflow are:
- manage quality and consistency for basic text analysis in the light of limited resources of academic research projects
- make large collections more manageable
- iteratively build up a comprehensible and consistent dataset
- adapt to the specific and generic characteristics of the source material on one side and 
- adapt early to key research questions and analytical dimensions on the other side
- provide the foundation for further data enrichment and higher levels of analysis such as normalized collection dictionaries, NER, Geo-Referencing, etc.
- create a model tagging scheme adapted to your needs for further scalability
- create ground truth data set for domain-specific AI text tagging

Please mind:
1. The workflow was developed in the context of a specific research project at the University of Basel, please visit ["VOCAL POWER"](https://dg.philhist.unibas.ch/de/bereiche/fruehe-neuzeit/snf-professur-macht-der-stimme/) for more information.
2. For the Open Marketplace it was shaped to address challenges that will very likely arise in similar projects. However: We strongly suggest thoroughly discussing all the steps with key stakeholders and project staff in order to adapt the parameters according to your own needs on the ground.
3. Work on data projects is prone to get out of hand easily, so plan your steps carefully, test and iterate small portions early on and finish one step at a time.

relatedItems.label: How to use Github Issues in the Digital Humanities project communication between humanists and developers?
relatedItems.description:
# What is GitHub Issues
_Issues_ is a part of GitHub open platform and a place for reporting bugs, new functionalities, and system vulnerabilities. It could be used to facilitate any Digital Humanities project's communication between coding and non-coding people (like developers and humanists) due to the fact no coding skills are required to use it. 

# What can you do with GitHub Issues
>Create issues, break them into tasks, track relationships, add custom fields, and have conversations. Visualize large projects as spreadsheets or boards, and automate everything with code. 
[Source: GitHub Issues](https://github.com/features/issues)

# When use Github Issues
- In a large digital projects that involves a vast number of participants with various skills to facilitate communication between them, especially between developers and the rest of the team,
- When you would like to have an option to share your communication after the end of project easily and bring open science values to a new level,
- You suspect a lot of testing, bug reporting, new ideas around your digital project will emerge.

composedOf.label: Know Your Data
composedOf.description:
Before starting, it's important to collect key administrative and descriptive data about your collection. Some numbers will not only be very helpful for estimating the workload, but also to shape the workflow in good balance to your capabilities and resources. It is good advice to be as precise as possible.

Apart from numbers, it’s really important to get a deep understanding of what the data set is all about and to gain a deeper understanding of the material. It may be worthwhile spending some days reading and exploring the collection as a whole, before taking long-term decisions. 

Whether or not you’re a field expert yourself, discussions with staff members and even colleagues from other disciplines may make sense in order to avoid biased decisions and “blindness”. And if you’re solo sailing, this will be even more important...

So try answering the following questions as precise as possible:
- Apart from developing the scheme itself: What will help to make the overall workload as transparent as possible?
- How many documents (or better: individual pages, or countable entities) have to be text-tagged?
- What are collection-wide traits of the material?
- How homo- or heterogeneous is my collection? On what grounds?
- Does it make sense to develop one tagging scheme for the entire collection?
- Are there any similar content element types across the entire collection, such as personal names, locations, time and date entries? What are these?

composedOf.label: Know Your Resources
composedOf.description:
The development and deployment of any text tagging (or annotation / content analysis / data mining scheme) has many dimensions. So, depending on the nature of the material in the text corpus, it bears risks of overdoing, over-interpreting and traps of lengthy discussions about peripheral aspects and detail, that may distract from a focused and analytical approach.

Since time available from you and your staff is the one core limitation in most projects - especially when including manual data entry - it is absolutely crucial to bind pre-defined resources to a transparent and goal-oriented process. When aligned with the desired or externally imposed time frame for the deployment of the scheme (or parts of it as intermediary steps) and reasonable workload-calculations however, the path to the desired outcome becomes a lot more manageable and the scale of the workflow can be adjusted accordingly.

Try answering the following questions as precise as possible:
- How many net working hours (per staff, per week) are effectively available to edit documents and work on tagging on average? Count in: initial learning curves, times on sick leave, vacation time, public holidays, other obligations at work, etc.
- What is the first desired point in time, when the tagging work, or a specific part of it should be finished / is there a deadline to be respected?
- Can tagging work be split up between staff members? How?

How to do this?
- Ask for a reliable self-declaration from your staff about a mid-term possible commitment (weekly hours) or - if you are solo or responsible for the distribution of work - calculate the total available hours yourself.
- Collect feedback on obstacles

composedOf.label: Know Your Progress
composedOf.description:
Separate from the actual text tagging work, the documentation of progress is crucial.

In order to make the documentation helpful and an acceptable effort for everyone involved, it is important to calibrate its granularity: It must not take up too much of the actual working time but it must still be granular enough to bear any reasonable additional value. Whether you set up every entity as a github issue and track it down or you develop a table with a line for every document is entirely up to you, but some sort of progress monitoring must be done. Stick to one functioning system that can display meaningful numbers of the progress at any given point in time.
Ideally, progress is measured in terms of comparable entities with clearly defined  and meaningful statuses, such as "to do", "in progress" "done" or counting hours of work still to be done. Any Project Management tool will contain a basic function like that. If no separate tool is applicable, a Google Docs Spreadsheet will do the job, and if the documentation is rigorously done by all members, it may suit your needs perfectly.

If you implement some sort of review process, with the idea of re-assessing work previously done, you may want to include a mechanism, where staff members change their role in a rotational system.
In order to make this feasible, it is crucial that all members of staff are working on a shared understanding of the tagging scheme, otherwise, different attitudes and interpretations may end up working "against" each other, annihilating previous investments of time and decisions.

At least, review steps must be reflected in the documentation process, i.e. with additional steps "review", or "tagging complete". 

How to do this?
Walk through the entire process at least once and describe every status indicator of the pipeline as precisely as possible. Use only such status indicators, that inform about a relevant difference. 

1. "to do" document is 
- fully transcribed (and checked)
- no tags added yet
2. "in progress" (and “checked out” by a staff member)
- tagging according to tagging scheme is ongoing
- special cases are documented
3. "tagging complete"
- the entire tagging scheme has been applied to the whole document
- open questions are documented
4. "reviewed"
- the tagging choices have been double checked
- open questions ideally solved

You may also want to break down the workload into smaller chunks that can be assigned to different staff members.

composedOf.label: Develop Tagging Scheme
composedOf.description:
The tagging scheme addresses questions that regard the collection as a whole, so it works across the boundaries of individual documents and makes them comparable by clustering information and counting individual occurences. It is therefore important to choose tagging categories that make sense for more or less the entire material of the collection. The paradox here is that you need to define tagging categories that are generic but not too broad, general, yet specific to your material and research needs.

Secondly, text tagging is “positive” in the sense that it is bound to actual written text in the document and it adds a second (and only one) layer of information to a specific string in the text.

Now, re-assess Step No. 2 and think about the collection as a whole:
What clusters of information across the collection are of interest?

In order to generate categories for text tagging, there could be two major initial categories, namely:
1. Place Names / Person Names / Time Information, that is "normalizable" categories, that are 
a) relatively independent from the domain and 
b) have potential references in a controlled vocabulary Wikidata / GND / GEONAMES / AAT / etc.)  

2. "All the rest.", say: More domain-related categories that are a) context-sensitive and b) shaped towards specific research questions

I suggest you define “low-hanging fruits” first: Information from category 1. and then add from category 2. Remember, that every new category adds significantly to the workload. 

Helpful questions may be:
- What does the material itself generically include?
- What are core elements that should be analyzable / countable / comparable later?
- What are domain-specific questions that may become a part within a tagging scheme?

For every tagging category, write a concise definition, and include typical positive and negative examples from your data.

Examples:

Tag: “Natural Disaster” 
Definition: A catastrophic event based on natural forces
Examples: “when the thunderstorm hit the neighbourhood, a flood developed”

Double check, whether the tagging scheme is not too large, since every new tag category multiplies the workload. Double check, whether or not there are clearly defined boundaries between individual tags.

composedOf.label: Deploy Tagging Scheme
composedOf.description:
Once the decision is made for the scheme elements, transfer them to your text tagging environment.
Within Transkribus, this is easily done in the "tags" section of the interface.

It may be useful to deploy the scheme in reasonable parts and start with those categories that are most promising, tied closely to the most important goals.
An iterative approach also lets you estimate more clearly how much of the workload in relation to your resources and given time frame will be possible and it may make much more sense to finish the work in one tagging category throughout the entire collection before starting the next.

One clear suggestion is to start with issues, that are easy to identify.

label: Treating Oral Sources in SSH Research
description:
This workflow, developed in Italy, guides SSH researchers, archivists, and institutions through the full lifecycle of oral sources: from initial legal and ethical preparation, through fieldwork and documentation, to long-term preservation, archival transfer, access, and valorisation, including responsible online publication. It covers the production of audio or audiovisual recordings, their contextual documentation, and their integration into archival systems.

The workflow applies equally to newly initiated oral data gathering campaigns and to the retrospective treatment of pre-existing collections. It draws on the "Vademecum per il trattamento delle fonti orali" (Ministero della Cultura, Direzione Generale Archivi, 2023), a multidisciplinary reference document developed by specialists from different domains, including oral historians, linguists, ethnologists, librarians and archivists.

While it integrates European data protection requirements (GDPR) and established professional standards, it also refers at certain points to the Italian legal framework. Researchers operating in other national contexts should therefore consult the relevant legislation and guidelines applicable in their own country.

relatedItems.label: Transcribing Documents of Ethnomusicological Interest
relatedItems.description:
This workflow describes a structured process for transcribing sound and audiovisual documents of ethnomusicological interest — recordings that may contain musical performances, ritual and festive events, ethnographic interviews, or informal conversations from oral tradition contexts. It is designed for researchers, archivists, and cultural heritage professionals working with collections held in ethnomusicological archives (such as those of national and regional sound heritage institutions) or with field recordings produced by researchers or local cultural actors.

The workflow allows practitioners to determine, case by case, whether a verbal utterance embedded in a sound document should be transcribed as ordinary speech, as sung text, or as musical notation — and to combine these approaches when the material requires it. It is particularly useful when working with oral-tradition repertoires, where melodic, rhythmic, and textual elements interact in complex and sometimes idiosyncratic ways, and where a purely textual or purely musical transcription alone would fail to capture the full technical, formal, and cultural dimension of the performance.

The process was elaborated by Claudio Rizzoni (Soprintendenza ABAP di Genova e La Spezia and ICBSA), drawing on established ethnomusicological transcription methodologies developed over the course of the twentieth century, and is intended to be applied flexibly according to the research context, the purpose of the transcription, and the specific musical culture and repertoire concerned.

relatedItems.label: How to phonetically transcribe dialects
relatedItems.description: This workflow outlines the main steps involved in the transcription of dialectal speech data, with particular attention to the Italian linguistic context and the Italo-Romance dialects. Although it has been primarily conceived for the Italian reality, the workflow may also be adapted and applied to other geographical and linguistic contexts, provided that the necessary methodological and linguistic adjustments are taken into account. This process is documented by Giovanni Abete in the chapter “Trascrivere il dialetto” (pp. 211–217) of the "Vademecum per il trattamento delle fonti orali" (Tavolo permanente per le fonti orali, 2023).

relatedItems.label: How to Transcribe Phonetically
relatedItems.description: This workflow describes the successive methodological decisions and operations required to produce a phonetic transcription of oral/spoken data for research and documentation purposes in the social sciences and humanities (linguistics, dialectology, sociolinguistics, psycholinguistics, language documentation, conversation analysis, etc.). It is designed for researchers, students, and archivists who need to convert an audio recording into a phonetically annotated resource, whether for a single case study or for a larger, shareable, and reusable corpus. The workflow was elaborated on the basis of practical teaching and research notes on phonetic transcription (auditory and acoustic-supported transcription, use of Praat and ELAN, IPA/SAMPA conventions, inter-annotator agreement, and data publication), and integrates reference information on the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) and its alternative ASCII-based encoding, X-SAMPA. The workflow can be adapted to individual projects or to team-based research infrastructures, and it explicitly foresees the possibility of publishing the resulting transcriptions, together with the source audio, as a citable open dataset (e.g. via Zenodo or a comparable repository).

relatedItems.label: Automatic Transcription of Oral Sources
relatedItems.description:
This workflow guides you through the automatic transcription of oral source recordings in SSH research contexts. It covers the full pipeline: audio preparation, model selection and configuration, transcription, speaker diarisation, quality control, manual post-correction, and the export of timestamped, structured transcripts suitable for archival deposit and open publication.
The central tool is Whisper, a multilingual, open-source automatic speech recognition (ASR) model developed by OpenAI and released under the MIT licence. The workflow also integrates complementary tools for audio preprocessing (Audacity, FFmpeg), enhanced transcription (WhisperX, faster-whisper), annotation (ELAN), and text encoding (TEI-XML). It applies equally to newly recorded interviews and to the retrospective transcription of archival holdings.

relatedItems.label: Indexing an Audio Resource
relatedItems.description: Conceived and employed by the ORMETE project (Oralità, Memoria, Teatro), directed by Donatella Orecchia (Università di Roma Tor Vergata), this workflow allows a researcher or curator to produce a segment-based index of an audio or an audiovisual resource. Rather than replacing the recording with a transcription, this process structures the resource into titled, synopsised, and keyworded segments, enabling users to navigate directly to specific points in the interview and locate content by person, place, or institution. By preserving the double voice of interviewer and interviewee at segment level and by using indexing — rather than transcription — as the primary access tool, the workflow supports listening to the original recording as the main mode of engagement with the source, in line with the stated aim of guiding and educating listening. This kind of indexing can be carried out either through OHMS (Oral History Metadata Synchronizer) or without the support of any dedicated application. The output is a reviewed, structured index suitable for publication.

relatedItems.label: “The Egg and Jerry”: Narration and Gesture In L1 and L2 By Italian Schoolchildren
relatedItems.description: In  this paper,we  present  sociolinguistic  research  conducted  on  Italian  schoolchildren  learning  English  as  L2. Following  on  from  renowned  researchers,  we  focused  on  a  less  studied population,  whichis  school-aged  monolingual children.Our participants consistedof15 students of a fourth-grade class at a primary school in Pavia;all aged around 9 years  of  age -7  boys  and  8  girls. Noneof  the childrenpresent  any  recorded  cognitive  problems;they  are  all  Italian  L1 speakers with little or no use of other languages at home, and English has been learnt as L2since the beginning of primary school at age 6. We recorded all the children performing a task of re-narration of a “Tom & Jerry” cartoon, firstly in Italian and then, after one week, in English. The corpus consistsofabout 2h 45’ of recordings, transcribed and annotated in ELAN. Lexical knowledge in English was also tested through a questionnaire before the recordings.The results were analyzed both qualitatively and, partly, quantitatively. During qualitative analysis, two elements were observed: (1) general tendencies in speakers’general  behavior  and  (2)  differences  in  the  relationship  between  syntactic-conversational  system  and  gesture system in relation to L1/L2. The quantitative analysis showsa difference in theuse of beats gestures and iconic ones between L1 and L2, but also between boys and girls. Themain findings of the current research are: (1) frequent use of gesture during L1  recordings,  in  contrast  to  a  general  decrease  of  gesture  during  L2  recordings;  (2)  gesture  as  linguistic  reinforcing  or replacement  of  speech  production  during  L1  recordings,  in  contrast  to  gesture  as a problem-solving  strategy  during  L2 recordings; (3) generally, offline knowledge in L2 is not reflected in online knowledge.

relatedItems.label: Transcribing conversation in ELAN
relatedItems.description:
This workflow outlines the main steps involved in the transcription of conversational data using ELAN, a software environment designed for the annotation and synchronisation of audio and video recordings. ELAN is particularly suitable for multimodal transcription, as it allows the annotation of both verbal and non-verbal phenomena — such as gaze, gestures, pauses, and interactional dynamics — through multiple time-aligned annotation tiers.

The workflow includes the preliminary design of the transcription scheme and annotation hierarchy, the configuration of tiers and segmentation units, the automatic or manual transcription and annotation process, and the exportation of the final transcript in EAF or other formats. 

This workflow is based on Letizia Cirillo’s chapter “Trascrivere la conversazione” (pp. 181–188), part of the "Vademecum per il trattamento delle fonti orali" (Tavolo permanente per le fonti orali, 2020).

relatedItems.label: Annotating Proxemic Features in Audiovisual Document Using ELAN
relatedItems.description:
This workflow describes how to annotate proxemic features in audiovisual corpora using ELAN. It integrates multimodal annotation principles from linguistic and semiotic research, with particular reference to gesture classification frameworks (Kendon, McNeill) and facial annotation protocols (FACS, Ekman & Friesen).

This process is grounded on Meluzzi’s approach to annotation ("Annotare una trascrizione", in "Vademecum per il trattamento delle fonti orali", pp. 227-229).

relatedItems.label: Vademecum per il trattamento delle fonti orali
relatedItems.description: Starting from a broader definition of oral sources and from the assumption of the unity of the communicative event that generates the source—and, consequently, the archive of oral sources—this Vademecum provides a coherent theoretical framework, not merely prescriptive, to which methods and practices for the treatment of oral documentation can be anchored.

composedOf.label: Research Design and Methodological Planning
composedOf.description:
The treatment of oral sources begins with a carefully structured phase of research design and methodological planning, which shapes the quality of the data collected as well as its legal validity, long-term preservation, and future reuse. This phase brings together methodological reflection, technical, and ethical choices, legal awareness, and archival foresight.

At its core lies a solid grounding in the principles and practices of linguistics and oral history. Researchers—and, where applicable, collaborators—should develop a clear awareness of the legal, ethical, and deontological implications of working with oral testimonies. This includes familiarity with relevant international and national guidelines, such as those of the Oral History Society (OHS) and the Associazione Italiana di Storia Orale (AISO), and an understanding of the responsibilities linked to the collection, processing, and preservation of personal narratives. At this stage, the focus is on building awareness within the research team, rather than formally informing participants.

Methodological planning also involves defining the research framework, including research questions, scope, and participant selection. Interviews should be conceived as co-constructed communicative events; therefore, flexible interview guides are preferable to rigid questionnaires, allowing space for digressions that may open new lines of inquiry.

Researchers must also anticipate the conditions of the recording, including the choice of environment and the establishment of a relationship of trust with participants, which directly affects the quality and interpretability of the testimonies.

Technical planning is equally essential. Decisions regarding recording formats (audio or audio-video) and equipment should be made in relation to research objectives and future uses of the data. These choices are methodological as much as technical, as they shape the nature and reusability of the sources.

Finally, this phase includes preparing the documentation resources that will support the workflow, such as interview guides, information sheets, consent and authorization forms, and recording sheets for contextual data. Anticipating legal requirements, preservation strategies, and future access conditions ensures coherence across the process and supports the sustainable reuse of oral sources.

relatedItems.label: Data management planning for long-term preservation
relatedItems.description: Data management planning (DMP) concerns the development, execution and supervision of plans, policies, programs and practices that control, protect, deliver and enhance the value of data and information assets. composedOf.label: Establish the legal and ethical framework
composedOf.description:
Complete all legal groundwork before any recording takes place. This phase is mandatory and non-negotiable.

1. Determine the legal basis for data processing: identify the applicable legal basis under GDPR Art. 6 (e.g. consent of the data subject, public interest, scientific research). Consult applicable national legislation (e.g. Italy: "Codice in materia di protezione dei dati personali"; "Regole deontologiche per il trattamento a fini di archiviazione nel pubblico interesse"). Align your choice with the institutional mandate of the data controller.
2. Draft and distribute the privacy notice: prepare a privacy notice compliant with GDPR Arts. 12–14. Write it in plain, accessible language. Deliver it to each participant before any data collection begins. The notice must specify the legal basis, the purposes and modalities of processing, data retention periods, and participant rights. It may be provided in writing or, where identity is verifiable by other means, orally.
3. Obtain interview authorisation: collect the participant's authorisation to take part in the research — distinct from GDPR consent — either in writing or as a recorded oral declaration at the opening of the session. Confirm the authorisation at the close of the interview. Incorporate this declaration directly into the audio or video recording where possible.
4. Address copyright: clarify authorship and exploitation rights. The interviewer, as the party who structures the encounter and formulates questions, generally holds copyright over the interview as a creative work (Italian Law no. 633/1941; EU Directive 2019/790). Include a rights-assignment clause in the participant waiver, covering both image rights and intellectual property rights. Define contractual terms with any commissioning institution or conservation archive before fieldwork begins.
5. Prepare documentation templates: assemble the following before entering the field: (a) privacy notice; (b) interview authorisation form; (c) participant waiver with rights-assignment clause; (d) field recording sheet; (e) individual document sheet. Use models provided by the "Vademecum".

relatedItems.label: Putting Data Protection into Practice: GDPR and the DARIAH ELDAH Consent Form Wizard
relatedItems.description:
Humanities and social sciences researchers encounter a number of data protection issues in their work.  An example is scientific events where photos and videos are taken and legal participant consent is required in order to comply with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Surveys and other research activities pose similar problems.

To address these issues, ELDAH has developed a tool that provides standardised consent form templates, enabling any user to quickly and easily obtain legal consent valid in all of the European Union. This tool is the [DARIAH ELDAH Consent Form Wizard (CFW)](https://consent.dariah.eu/) 

In this workshop, we discussed the European legal framework for data privacy and processing personal data (GDPR) with the aim of helping participants understand how their research is affected by the GDPR and what issues to pay attention to. 

Topics covered include:

-    A question of ethics and law: processing personal data in research, education and cultural heritage
-    EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR): basic principles and framework
-    GDPR provisions and exemptions for research
-    Introduction to the [DARIAH-EU ELDAH Consent Form Wizard](https://consent.dariah.eu/)

Participants had the opportunity to create their own GDPR-compliant consent form in the context of gathering data from and/or about living people for research purposes; communicating through mailing-lists or other (digital) communication media; and gathering data/consent from participants as host of an academic event.

The workshop was open to anyone interested in GDPR compliance.

## Speakers

Koraljka Kuzman Šlogar (University of Zagreb / DARIAH-HR), Vanessa Hannesschläger (Austrian Academy of Sciences / CLARIAH-AT), Walter Scholger (University of Graz / CLARIAH-AT)

relatedItems.label: SSHOC workshop: SSH Code of Conduct
relatedItems.description:
**Date:** 17 March 2021
**Location:** Online

The SSHOC project announced an interactive workshop for policy makers, practitioners and others working with GDPR, research ethics, and Codes of Conduct. 

Participants gained practical insights into the challenges inherent in establishing a Code of Conduct and learned the how and why from experts in the field.

The outcomes of the workshop will be incorporated into an ongoing project task to set up a Code of Conduct specifically for Social Sciences and Humanities researchers. 

## Agenda

-    Presentation of findings from SSHOC report on the impact of the GDPR and its implications for EOSC, Ina Nepstad and Mathilde Steinsvåg Hansen, NSD - Norwegian Centre for Research Data
-    Anatomy of a Code of Conduct and Implications for GDPR,  Ina Nepstad and Mathilde Steinsvåg Hansen, NSD - Norwegian Centre for Research Data
-    Creation of a Code of Conduct in health research, Michaela Th. Mayrhofer, BBMRI ERIC
-    Plenary and break-out discussion of experiences, challenges, and recommendations  

## Speakers

**Mathilde Steinsvåg Hansen** has a law degree from the University of Bergen. She has been working as an advisor at NSD since 2019, where she provides guidance to health researchers about privacy legislation. She also works as a Data Protection Officer for two external institutions. 

**Ina Nepstad** is senior advisor at NSD, where she assists health researchers to enable high-quality research, while at the same time safeguarding privacy. Prior to this role, she worked at Haukeland University Hospital as a researcher specialising in blood cancer and allergology.  Ina has a PhD from the University of Bergen (Bergen, Norway) and Hopital Cochin, INSERM (Paris, France), and a Master of Science (MSc) from the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (Trondheim, Norway).

**Michaela Th. Mayrhofer** is a political scientist and historian by training. She was educated in Vienna, Louvain-la-Neuve, Essex and Paris. Her PhD thesis was shortlisted for the ‘best thesis 2010’ young scientist award by the Austrian Society for Political Science. Research interests include the governance of life sciences, societal implications of AI and data protection. Michaela has been working for BBMRI-ERIC since 2013, serving as Head of ELSI Services & Research since 2019.

relatedItems.label: DARIAH ELDAH Consent Form Wizard (CFW)
relatedItems.description:
Since the coming into effect of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), humanities researchers have been unsure about how to do certain parts of their research while considering their subjects’ right to privacy. The CFW is here to help.

*What this tool is:* The aim of the CFW is to support humanities researchers within the European Union in obtaining valid consent for data processing in the context of their specific professional activity. This tool will guide you through a questionnaire that will consequently generate a GDPR-compliant form for obtaining consent from data subjects, tailored to your specific purpose and the data categories you intend to collect.  Please be aware that the validity of the generated output will be dependent on the truthfulness and accuracy of the input you provide. Honest and comprehensive answers will improve the quality of the results generated by the tool. After answering the questionnaire, the CFW will output a consent form template specifically tailored to your needs according to your answers in plain text format. You will be able to use this text template for creating consent forms to print out and have signed by data subjects, or to include in online environments. Since we will not store the generated output ourselves, please make sure to save your generated consent form at a location of your choice. If you want to provide your result as an example for other CFW users, please send it to us at eldah@dariah.eu. 

*... and what it is not:* The consent forms provided by this tool will observe the Articles of the GDPR. In some instances, the tool will recommend that you obtain additional legal advice.

It shows how sharing personal data can often be accomplished by using a combination of obtaining informed consent, data anonymisation and regulating data access. The supporting role of ethical review in managing legal and ethical obligations is also highlighted in this chapter.Focus on:	legal and ethical obligations towards research participants and the different legal requirements of EU Member States	how protecting data properly protects against violating laws and promises made to participants	the General Data Protection Regulation and its relevance in research	informed consent, anonymisation and access controls to facilitate creating shareable data	relevant elements in a consent form	anonymisation techniques for quantitative and qualitative data	relevant DMP questions on these topics

relatedItems.label: Data Protection in Research Practice - A Tutorial
relatedItems.description: Since May 2018, the GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) has been in force in all European member states. This affects not only the private sector, but also the academic one. With this tutorial, we would like to introduce you to the most important terms and concepts of the GDPR and also to the ELDAH Consent Form Wizard, a tool that allows you to easily create GDPR-compliant consent forms for personal data collection in a research context.

relatedItems.label: SSHOC Workshop: Data Protection in research practice: The GDPR and the ELDAH Consent Form Wizard
relatedItems.description:
In this workshop, we discussed the European legal framework for data privacy and processing personal data (General Data Protection Regulation, GDPR). The workshop helped participants **understand how their research is affected by the GDPR** and what issues to pay attention to.

The workshop began with a general introduction to the topics of data protection and the processing of personal data in the context of research, education and cultural heritage to summarize the pertinent articles of the GDPR. We then moved on to speak about the **most common scenarios in which humanities' and social sciences' researchers encounter data protection issues**. Examples of this included surveys, interviews and other research activities involving human participants, but also common academic scenarios like communication (mailing-lists, newsletters) and events (e.g. regarding picture and video recordings).

Because researchers have to obtain legal consent from their participants in order to comply with the GDPR for many of their activities, the DARIAH working group [ELDAH](https://eldah.hypotheses.org/) (Ethics and Legality in Digital Arts and Humanities) has developed **a tool that provides standardized consent form templates** for obtaining legal consent from human participants: The DARIAH ELDAH **Consent Form Wizard** (CFW). The CFW enables digital scholars and the wider research infrastructure community to quickly and easily obtain a standardized consent form that is legally valid in all of the European Union.

The workshop participants were introduced to this tool and got a chance to test it by applying it to their own research practices. They used the tool to download templates to obtain research participants’ consent; these templates can be adjusted to their specific needs in a few simple steps. Workshop participants had also a chance to give feedback on the CFW: to point out elements that are missing and suggest additional consent scenarios.

In this poster, we would like to introduce the “consent form wizard” developed by the DARIAH-EU working group “Ethics and Legality in Digital Arts and Humanities” (ELDAH). This tool is currently under development and will be finalized and available in time for the DH2020 conference. It will enable digital scholars as well as the wider research infrastructure community to quickly and easily obtain a standardized consent form that is conforming to the obligations and regulations of the European Union General Data Protection regulation (GDPR) and therefore legally valid in all of the European Union.

Depending on the context for which consent is obtained (e.g. use of images of people at academic events, processing of information shared in surveys, collection / processing of personal data), the wizard users will receive a consent form tailored to their specific needs after answering a series of questions. The different scenarios are the result of discussions with participants of the DH2019 in Utrecht and the DARIAH Annual Meeting 2019 in Warsaw and hence driven by the needs of the research community. Additional meetings with stakeholders from cultural heritage organisations (e.g. ICARUS) and the DARIAH-EU community will ensure a critical evaluation as well as a pragmatic, user-friendly implementation of the tool.

It will be inspired by the code of the CLARIN LINDAT Public License Selector (cf. Kamocki et al. 2016) which offers the same service for license selection that we would like to develop for obtaining a consent form. Software developers, legal experts and (digital) humanities researchers will cooperate in the development of this tool, which - while legally addressing the strict data protection regulations of the European Union - will also be of use for the international research community outside Europe, since the consent forms will provide a best-practice template for ethical research conduct when processing personal data, and hence address the increasingly prominent topic of ethical research practice and scientific behaviour, especially in a largely digital, Internet-based research context (cf. Markham & Buchanan 2012, McKee & Porter 2009).

The presentation of the poster at the DH2020 conference will allow us to present the wizard to colleagues outside our European network, discuss their needs and experiences with the protection of personal data and hence, if appropriate, adapt the wizard to reflect a global rather than European common perspective on research ethics and the processing of personal data.

composedOf.label: Produce and document the communicative event
composedOf.description:
Conduct the interview session with methodological rigour. The recording, together with all simultaneously produced documents, constitutes the founding document of the oral source.

1. Choose and prepare recording equipment: select recording format according to research type and intended preservation use. Recommended audio format: WAV (uncompressed PCM), sampling frequency 96 kHz (minimum 48 kHz, up to 192 kHz), 24-bit resolution. Recommended video format: MPEG-4 AVC (H.264). Recommended photographic format: RAW at maximum camera resolution. Test all equipment before the session. 
2. Prepare and control the recording environment: minimise ambient noise and interference. Choose a space that allows uninterrupted exchange. Position the microphone to capture the speaker clearly. Where video recording is used, frame and light the space appropriately. Notify all parties present of the recording.
3. Open the recording with contextual identification: at the start of each recording, state aloud the date, location, names of interviewer(s) and interviewee(s) (or a pseudonym code if anonymity is required), the research project title, and confirmation of the participant's authorisation. This spoken header embeds essential metadata directly into the audio or video document.
4. Conduct the interview: practise attentive listening. Do not impose rigid structures. Allow for digressions, which often open unforeseen lines of inquiry. Document non-verbal elements (gestures, pauses, emotional tone) in field notes immediately after the session, while memory is fresh.
5. Close the recording: at the end of the session, restate the participant's authorisation and confirm any conditions they have placed on use. Note the close of the recording aloud. Collect any additional materials the participant may share (photographs, letters, objects for digitisation).
6. Complete the field recording sheet: fill in the field recording sheet immediately after the session. Record: event date and location; names and roles of all persons present; equipment used and recording format; contextual annotations impossible to reconstruct later; references to all documents produced during the same session (audio, video, photographs, written materials). This sheet is the archival backbone of the entire oral source package.
7. Complete individual document sheets: for each distinct document produced (each audio file, each video file, each photograph), fill in a document sheet that functions as a sub-unit of the field recording sheet. Record: unique identifier, file name, format and technical parameters, duration or size, relationship to other documents in the same recording event. Preserve the archival bond between all documents of a single event.

composedOf.label: Transcribe and process the interview
composedOf.description:
Produce a transcription of the recorded interview in order to enable analysis, indexing, and long-term accessibility. Transcription constitutes a key stage in the enrichment of the oral source, transforming an audio or audiovisual document into a textual resource that can be searched, annotated, and reused.

Define the level of transcription according to the objectives of the research. This may range from verbatim transcription (including hesitations, pauses, and non-verbal elements) to a more edited version that improves readability while preserving the meaning of the discourse. Where relevant, adopt established transcription conventions and ensure consistency across the corpus.

If required, integrate time-coding to align the transcription with the original recording, facilitating navigation between text and audio/video. Consider also the need for translation, particularly in multilingual research contexts.

During transcription, pay attention to the treatment of personal data and sensitive information. Anonymisation or pseudonymisation may be necessary, especially when preparing the material for dissemination or public access. Any modifications should be documented to ensure transparency and reproducibility.

The transcription should be treated as a distinct but related document within the oral source corpus. It must therefore be documented through a dedicated record, including its relationship to the original recording, the tools and methods used, and the identity of the transcriber.

This step may be carried out prior to, or in parallel with, the description and metadata creation phase, depending on the research design and available resources. In all cases, it significantly enhances the findability, accessibility, and reusability of the oral source in line with FAIR principles.

The results of the analytic programs are sent to the CLAN Output window.

relatedItems.label: ELAN
relatedItems.description:
ELAN is a tool for creating annotations on multiple layers on audio and video resources. The textual content of annotations is in Unicode and the transcription is stored in XML.

With ELAN a user can add an unlimited number of textual annotations to audio and/or video recordings. An annotation can be a sentence, word or gloss, a comment, translation or a description of any feature observed in the media. Annotations can be created on multiple layers, called tiers. Tiers can be hierarchically interconnected. An annotation can either be time-aligned to the media or it can refer to other existing annotations. The content of annotations consists of Unicode text and annotation documents are stored in an XML format (EAF).

Main features and characteristics of ELAN:
* provides several ways to view the annotations, each view is connected to and synchronized with the media timeline
* supports creation of multiple tiers and tier hierarchies
* supports Controlled Vocabularies
* allows linking of up to 4 video files with an annotation document
* media support
   * builds on existing, native media frameworks, like Windows Media Player, QuickTime or VLC
   * support for audio and video formats depends on operating system, high performance media playback can usually be achieved
* technical
   * written in the Java programming language
   * distributions available for Windows, macOS and Linux
   * open source, the sources are available under a GPL 3 license 

The solution was developed by the Language Archive of the Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics.

composedOf.label: Organize, describe and conserve the oral sources
composedOf.description:
Implement preservation measures as soon as field production is complete. Conservation is not a deferred activity: decisions taken at this stage determine the long-term accessibility and integrity of the source.

1. Organise and name files systematically: apply a consistent file-naming convention that reflects the project, the date, and the session identifier. Store files in a structured directory that mirrors the relationship between the field recording sheet and the individual document sheets. Keep all documents produced in a single recording event together.
2. Create preservation copies: produce at minimum: one high-resolution preservation copy (WAV/BWF, 96 kHz, 24-bit for audio; MPEG-4 AVC for video); one local copy on a redundant storage medium (NAS or equivalent); one off-site copy in a secure, trusted cloud repository. Optionally produce a lower-resolution access copy (MP3 or equivalent) for consultation purposes. Never delete original analogue supports after digitisation.
3. Add preservation metadata: attach to each digitised document the following preservation metadata: original support type and conservation state; playback equipment and technical parameters used for digitisation; digital format, codec, sampling rate, bit depth; software and operator information; date of digitisation. Preserve scans or photographs of original physical supports and their containers.
4. Digitise analogue supports (if applicable): for recordings on magnetic tape, vinyl, cylinders, or other analogue media, contract a specialist digitisation centre with documented expertise (public or private). Follow IASA TC-04 for audio and IASA TC-06 for video. The preservation copy must be a faithful transfer of the original signal: introduce no filtering, noise reduction, or signal enhancement. Retain the analogue original after digitisation.
5. Describe sources for discovery and access: describe each oral source within a network of relations: link the recording to its field recording sheet, to the research project, to the agents involved (interviewer, interviewee, archivist), and to any related documents. Use controlled vocabularies and authority files. Consult descriptive software in use at reference institutions (see "Vademecum"). Align description with Dublin Core or EAD standards where applicable, to support interoperability.
6. Identify or select a conservation institution: if you are an independent researcher or a small institution, identify a conservation centre suited to your collection by disciplinary affinity or geographic proximity. Prepare: (a) a project presentation sheet; (b) a transfer sheet specifying access conditions, use restrictions, reproduction rights, and loan terms. Transfer the collection in its entirety: avoid splitting a unified archival complex across multiple institutions.
7. Plan for refresh and format migration: digitisation alone does not guarantee long-term access. Establish a schedule for periodic refresh (copying files to new storage supports before degradation) and for format migration (moving files to new formats before obsolescence). If the collection is deposited in a conservation centre, clearly define which institution or department is responsible for carrying out these long-term preservation operations.

Les ressources déposées sont dans un premier temps cataloguées et stockées, puis, dans un deuxième temps archivées dans l'archive de la TGIR Huma-Num. L'auteur et son institution restent responsables des documents déposés et peuvent bénéficier d'un accès restreint et sécurisé à leurs données, pendant une période définie, si le contenu de l'information est considéré sensible.

CoCoON for "Digital Oral Corpus COllections" is a technical platform that supports oral resource producers in creating, structuring and archiving their corpuses. A corpus can be composed of recordings (generally audio), possibly accompanied by annotations of these recordings.

The resources are first catalogued and stored, and then archived in the IR* Huma-Num archive. The author and his institution remain responsible for the deposited materials and can benefit from restricted and secure access to their data, for a defined period of time, if the content of the information is considered sensitive.

composedOf.label: Transfer archival collections
composedOf.description:
This phase applies when you transfer your collection to an institution, or when an institution acquires an oral archive from an external party.

1. Verify title and ownership: before any transfer, confirm the legal title under which the depositing party holds the collection (ownership, possession, detention). Verify the consent of any co-owners or co-heirs. For donations, obtain documented confirmation of heir consent to prevent subsequent contestation.
2. Prepare an inventory: produce a summary inventory of the entire collection before transfer. Describe: the physical composition and condition of each support; the presence of any damaged materials; the existence of related documents (release forms, field sheets, transcriptions). An inventory is a contractual prerequisite for any form of transfer.
3. Choose the appropriate legal instrument: select the legal mechanism suited to your situation: deposit contract, loan for use, donation, or testamentary bequest. If you are operating in Italy, consult the provisions of the "Codice dei beni culturali e del paesaggio" for collections of certified historical importance. Define in the contract: transport and packaging responsibilities; access and consultation conditions; reproduction and reuse rights; extraction and loan arrangements; scope of any restoration work.
4. Transfer data-processing responsibility: upon definitive alienation of the archive, the data-processing responsibility passes from the original holder to the acquiring institution. The receiving institution must request a written declaration from the interviewer confirming that participants were informed of research purposes and gave their consent. Acquire copies of all existing consent forms. Where copyright was not explicitly transferred in the original transaction, establish specific agreements covering the content rights separately from the physical support.
5. Treat pre-GDPR collections if applicable: for collections recorded before the GDPR entered into force (before 2018, and more broadly before the 2004 Italian privacy law), presume implied consent to the interview. Review existing consents against current GDPR requirements. Where no release form exists, search systematically for rights-holders (interviewers, interviewees, heirs). Demonstrate that you have conducted a diligent search (e.g., through press notices, public announcements, and online postings). If the search yields no result, invoke the orphan works provision (EU Directive 2012/28/EU; Italian Law 633/1941, Art. 69-bis) to authorise publication for cultural and educational purposes.

composedOf.label: Make your oral sources accessible and reusable
composedOf.description:
Make your oral sources accessible to researchers and, where legally permissible, to the wider public. Apply FAIR principles throughout.

1. Structure data and metadata for FAIR compliance: structure metadata to ensure Findability (assign persistent identifiers; use rich descriptive metadata), Accessibility (store in open or widely supported formats; ensure long-term availability of metadata even if access to data is restricted), Interoperability (use shared vocabularies and standards such as Dublin Core, EAD, or domain-specific thesauri), and Reusability (attach clear licence information; document provenance and context). Consult the FAIR Principles documentation for a full specification.
2. Publish online with an explicit release form: where an explicit "liberatoria" exists, publish the oral source online. Protect third parties mentioned in the recording: de-index their names from search engines where the information could damage their reputation; place sensitive content behind a registration-protected access area. Provide rich contextual metadata for all published materials.
3. Apply appropriate access restrictions where no release form exists: where no explicit release exists, choose among the following graduated approaches: (a) exclude the recording from online publication; (b) publish only excerpts already available in other public forms (print, documentary, educational DVD); (c) publish a pseudonymised transcript, ensuring the individual cannot be re-identified through cross-referencing; (d) publish a keyword index (thesaurus-based) omitting personal names; (e) provide authenticated access for research and educational purposes only; (f) state publicly the willingness to remove content on explicit request. Recall that these restrictions do not apply to recordings of public figures whose personal opinions, religious affiliation, or public acts are already widely known.
4. Assign a Creative Commons licence: choose and attach a Creative Commons licence to each published oral source. Select the licence that best reflects the rights-assignment conditions established with the interviewer and interviewee: CC BY (attribution only), CC BY-NC (non-commercial), CC BY-ND (no derivatives), or more restrictive combinations. Note that CC licences govern the circulation of the work online; they do not supersede GDPR obligations, which govern the processing of personal data independently.
5. Deposit in a trusted digital repository: deposit the oral source collection — including recordings, documentation, and metadata — in a trusted digital repository aligned with open science principles. Ensure the repository assigns persistent identifiers (DOI, Handle, or equivalent). Verify that the repository's preservation commitments cover refresh, format migration, and long-term access. Cross-link the deposit record with related publications and project documentation.

relatedItems.label: Tools and Resources for FAIR Data: SSHOC Webinar #6
relatedItems.description:
"Date:" 18 May 2020
"Location:" Online

How can you make your data FAIR? In this webinar, Anca Vlad — data repository administrator at UK Data Service — shared tools and resources applying to the entire data lifecycle.

The knowledge she shared is based on her experience at the UK Data Service. Anca used, among others, the [SSHOC’s EMM Survey Registry](https://www.sshopencloud.eu/news/emm-survey-registry-alpha-version-launched-and-beta-version-development), a consolidated database of quantitative surveys on ethnic and migrant minorities studies, as an example.

Webinar attendees benefited from:

-    A brief introduction to the EMM Survey Registry;
-    An overview of FAIR data publishing standards;
-    Introduction to tools and resources for producing and publishing good quality FAIR data, including a short demonstration;
-    In-depth look at an open-source tool that produces a ‘health check’ report, aiding with curating and anonymising data. 
-    We encourage researchers, librarians or anyone else interested in improving the quality of their FAIR data to attend.

## About the speaker

**Anca Vlad** is a data repository administrator at UK Data Service. She manages data deposits through UK Data Service self-deposit repository (ReShare), advises on data management, data deposit and ethical considerations when archiving data, and conducts data disclosure checks on data deposited.

A diverse set of stakeholders---representing academia, industry, funding agencies, and scholarly publishers---have come together to design and jointly endorse a concise and measureable set of principles that we refer to as the FAIR Data Principles.

Here, we describe FAIR - a set of guiding principles to make data Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Re-usable." (from the Website)

This series of three webinars by Brigitte Vézina helps you develop your open licensing expertise and a deeper understanding of the recommended practices for a better sharing of knowledge and culture, cultural heritage in particular. The webinars provide professional learning opportunities on selected elements of copyright, open licensing in the cultural heritage world, and how to get involved in open movements.
The goals of the webinars are to hold a space for open discussions with the hopes of educating and engaging in a dialog on the many different topics under the umbrella theme of open culture. The CC Open Culture program champions better sharing of cultural heritage collections for the benefit of all and promotes the potential of open access to unlock universal access to knowledge and culture, pursuant to the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals. The webinars aim to offer an opportunity to understand CC’s mission, develop knowledge and skills in copyright and open licensing, and gain visibility among a global open culture community that stands for equity, sustainability, access, and better sharing.

relatedItems.label: The Visible Speech (VISP) research platform
relatedItems.description:
The Visible Speech (VISP) platform is a web-based research infrastructure at Humlab, Umeå University, designed to handle audio recordings of speech in compliance with the national implementation of GDPR and security requirements. VISP provides a centralized environment for research of all disciplines in which recordings of spoken language constitute the primary material, meeting both researchers’ needs for efficient workflows and legislators’ demands for data management.

The VISP platform offers a unified environment for storage, controlled access, direct work, and reproducible speech signal processing. VISP is built on the foundation of earlier research efforts [1,2] and includes a comprehensive set of speech and voice analysis procedures within one framework. Thus, national research groups can collectively store interviews or other spoken language recordings, have automatic transcriptions or other speech processing performed, and access the results for complementary manual annotation or analysis simultaneously and securely. Additionally, VISP facilitates the digital archiving of projects through a uniform, documented, and transparent directory structure, reducing barriers to making data available following the FAIR principles. Research projects dealing with sensitive personal data in audio recording form require review by the Ethical Approval Authority and may subsequently take advantage of the VISP facilities.

A significant feature of VISP is its integration with the Swedish Academic Identity Federation (SWAMID, connected to eduGAIN), which enables researchers across Sweden to have secure, federated logins. This national federated login system allows researchers to access project data and collaborate on material processing in ways that were previously not possible. Moreover, VISP supports projects by lowering the step in to digital signal processing and audio analysis of the collected audio signals. This capability allows researchers to perform hands-on processing and analysis without the risk of disseminating sensitive audio recordings. By leveraging SWAMID, VISP ensures that researchers can work seamlessly and securely on collected materials, enhancing collaboration and data-handling efficiency. By providing tools for the direct manipulation and examination of audio data, VISP ensures that all stages of data handling, from collection to analysis, are conducted within a secure environment, thereby maintaining the integrity and confidentiality of sensitive information.

References:
[1] R. Winkelmann, J. Harrington, K. Jänsch, EMU-SDMS: Advanced speech database management and analysis in R, Comput. Speech Lang. 45 (2017) 392–410.
[2] R. Winkelmann, J. Harrington, EMU-SDMS: R Centric Semi-automatic Speech Database Processing and Analysis. In Sasha Calhoun, Paola Escudero, Marija Tabain & Paul Warren (eds.) Proceedings of the 19th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences, Melbourne, Australia 2019 (pp. 1317--1321).  Canberra, Australia: Australasian Speech Science and Technology Association Inc
