relatedItems.label: Carry out the digital survey
relatedItems.description:
The digital survey phase involves the data acquisition process, where spatial information is captured using technologies such as 3D laser scanning, photogrammetry, Differential GPS (DGPS), and Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs). These tools work together to collect high-resolution spatial and visual data from various perspectives, ensuring comprehensive coverage of the surveyed area or object. During this step, it is essential to record acquisition parameters as metadata, including equipment specifications, camera calibration settings, flight altitude, image overlap, and Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) accuracy.

# Input:
* Work plan
* Calibrated equipment (laser scanner, cameras, UAVs, DGPS)

# Output:

* Raw spatial data:
 * Laser scans → .e57, .las, .pts, .rcs
 * Photogrammetry → .jpeg, .tiff (images), .exif (metadata)
 * GNSS/GPS logs → .csv, .gpx
 * UAV flight data → .log, .csv, .json

* Paradata : equipment settings, flight data, etc.

* Field notes and photo logs

relatedItems.label: Data Collection
relatedItems.description:
Gather relevant information and data on the heritage asset according to the requirements established in step 1 of this workflow. Collection of legal, regulatory, historical, geographical, environmental, social, structural, and material related information is recommended. Collection of geospatial and geometric survey data on the asset is mandatory.

Relevant data, according to information requirements (step 1), should be collected in open standard file formats (e.g., PDF, CSV, JSON, JPEG, TIFF) or processed (step 3), structured and archived in an accessible, secure and frequently updated repository (e.g., PIDs, structured databases, metadata tags).
Absent, purpose specific, relevant data should be acquired (e.g., GIS, materials, structural, and environmental data), especially, digital survey data (on-site survey and reality capture, using either 3D laser scanning or photogrammetry).
Each method used for data collection is expected to follow its own specific workflow, depending on system and information requirements, data sources, object of analysis (e.g., products function, materials properties), and resources (e.g., standards, equipment, software). Examples of basic workflows for geometric survey can be found under the related items.

Preliminary checks for completeness and reporting on data quality should be done, according to the requirements established in step 1. Data processing (step 3) for assuring specified data quality and interoperability (step 1) may be required before data archiving.
A shared data environment is recommended for managing and linking information from various sources to facilitate collaborative work and improve interoperability (e.g., Common Data Environment - CDE in BIM).
Apply naming conventions to all source files and folders.
Populate a central repository with raw data and metadata. Data management documentation should be kept updated.

### Outputs / Deliverables

- Records of data, after quality checks, in open standard file formats (including raw point clouds or raw photogrammetry data, and significant data, as required in step 1, such as, historical, geographical, environmental, social, structural, and material related data)
- Data annotations and structured data
- Interoperable data
- Accessible and secure data
- Preliminary data quality reports
- Data management documentation

relatedItems.label: Data Processing
relatedItems.description:
Process and transform the collected data on step 2, according to data requirements and quality (steps 1 and 2). Different operations, such as cleaning, validation, transformation, enrichment and analysis may be included depending on the data characteristics. Data validation (step 3), harmonization (steps 2 and 3), and storage (step 2) are primary requirements for the seamless integration of multidisciplinary data in step 4.

- Store processed data in the central repository
- Data harmonisation and naming convention report
- Validation report (data quality and completeness)

Unvalidated or poor-quality data should be processed according to the established information requirements (step 1). Some data should also be transformed to streamline 3D-HBIM modelling and enrichment (step 4) using harmonized and interoperable data. Cleaning and merging of point cloud data, improved quality of textured 3D meshes, and related data transformation, assuring the use of consistent coordinate references, are processing stages especially decisive for this broad 3D-HBIM workflow. Examples of basic workflows for 3D data processing can be found under the related items tab.

### Outputs / Deliverables

- Analysed, transformed, and validated data
- Harmonised data and files with standard and open formats (for enhanced interoperability)
- Data processing documentation
- Interoperability strategy report
- LOD Object Matrix
- Model development report

composedOf.label: Georeferencing the surveyed data: Using a GNSS            receiver for precise positioning of Ground Control Points
composedOf.description: Using well materialized Ground Control Points (GCPs) and using the same set in all the performed flights will require the use of topographic instruments only for the first acquisition, as once measured, the GCPs will be re-used for the subsequents flights. It is important to underline the importance of acquiring a trustworthy set of GCPs to be used for all the surveys, instead of measuring new GCPs every time. It is more important, in fact, not to acquire the most accurate GNSS data, but to use the most precise set of GCPs, assuming for (at least locally) the validity of the first data acquired, cause repeating measures over time may lead to non extremely precise co-registration of the generated models. Instruments required: Total station D-GNSS antenna Action to perform: Defining and measuring a topographic network Materialization of the topographical vertices Materialization of the control points Ground control points displacement around and inside the site Natural points selection and digitization for future surveys Control points measurement and recording (via Total station or GNSS receiver) Softwares to use: Topographic network compensation (e.g. MicroSurvey StarNet)

relatedItems.label: Topography
relatedItems.description: Topography is the study of the shape and features of land surfaces. The topography of an area could refer to the surface shapes and features themselves, or a description (especially their depiction in maps). Topography is a field of geoscience and planetary science and is concerned with local detail in general, including not only relief but also natural and artificial features, and even local history and culture. This meaning is less common in the United States, where topographic maps with elevation contours have made "topography" synonymous with relief. Topography in a narrow sense involves the recording of relief or terrain, the three-dimensional quality of the surface, and the identification of specific landforms. This is also known as geomorphometry. In modern usage, this involves generation of elevation data in digital form (DEM). It is often considered to include the graphic representation of the landform on a map by a variety of techniques, including contour lines, hypsometric tints, and relief shading.

In 1997, VRML was ISO certified and continued to attract a large following of artists and engineers. VRML is the most widely supported 3D format for tools and viewers, and it is a direct subset of X3D (where the X stands for Extensibility). In 2001, X3D joined our family as an XML encoding of VRML. X3D added shaders, geo-location, and other cutting edge 3D features along with custom support support for users in medicine, CAD, GIS, multi-user, and other important use areas. You can download a custom editor to interactively and graphically create your X3D world on your PC.

relatedItems.label: COLLADA -- Digital Asset Schema Release 1.5.0 - Specification
relatedItems.description: This document describes the COLLADA schema. COLLADA is a COLLAborative Design Activity that defines an XML-based schema to enable 3D authoring applications to freely exchange digital assets without loss of information, enabling multiple software packages to be combined into extremely powerful tool chains. The purpose of this document is to provide a specification for the COLLADA schema in sufficient detail to enable software developers to create tools to process COLLADA resources. In particular, it is relevant to those who import to or export from digital content creation (DCC) applications, 3D interactive applications and tool chains, prototyping tools, real-time visualization applications such as those used in the video game and movie industries, and CAD tools.

relatedItems.label: OpenCOLLADA

In contrast to other existing COLLADA exporters, these new plug-ins do not store the COLLADA document in an intermidiate data model but writes it directly to file. This leads to a dramatic reduction of memory consumption and to much better performance. For more information about the plug-ins and how to build them, please read the README files in COLLADAMax and COLLADAMaya directories. For information about how to build OpenCOLLADA under linux and mac OSX usings SCons, please read the BUILD file. NOTE: The COLLADA.sln solution, contained in this directory, exists only for development purposes. To build the NextGen plug-ins, please use the solutions in the COLLADAMax and COLLADAMaya directories.

relatedItems.label: Report on the comparison of Tesseract and ABBYY FineReader OCR engines
relatedItems.description: The aim of this report is to compare OCR accuracy of two well known OCR engines: Tesseract 3.0.1 and FineReader10 Corporate Edition. The comparison is based on Polish historical printed documents and ground-truth produced within the scope of the IMPACT project (available at http://dl.psnc.pl/activities/projekty/impact/results/). As a rule defined by the IMPACT project the document is assumed to be historical if it was printed before 1850. Tesseract and FineReader have been selected because both represent high-level solution coming from open-source and commercial community and both were the subject of research works in the scope of the IMPACT project. The idea of the works described in this report was to verify in practice how these two tools can be fine-tuned by the end user in order to improve recognition rate of the historical printed text as well as compare the results of OCR accuracy after fine-tuning of both tools.

relatedItems.label: Språkbanken
relatedItems.description: A free cloud service for OCR The project En fri molntjänst för OCR \`A free cloud service for OCR', funded by the National Library of Sweden (51-KB709-2012), ran from 1st September, 2013 until 31st August, 2014. The project was a collaboration between the University Library of University of Gothenburg and Språkbanken 'the Swedish Language Bank' at the Department of Swedish of University of Gothenburg, its aim to create a prototype Optical Character Recognition (OCR) web service for processing old Swedish texts that are printed in a blackletter (fraktur) or roman typeface, using one of two open source OCR engines. Our ultimate goal is to provide a service for libraries, museums and archives to upload any digitized document and retrieve an OCRed text with high quality, independent on the quality of the print. In the project, we have evaluated two open source OCR engines: OCRopus and Tesseract and further developed one of them, namely OCRopus. Using OCRopus we have set up a open webservice for OCR that can handle Swedish Blackletter print as well as Roman type print. The pilot cloud service and web API can be found here. The material and tools developed in the project are freely available for download from this site under the license CC-BY.

concept.label: PNG
concept.definition: Portable Network Graphics (PNG, pronounced PEE-en-JEE or PING) is a raster graphics file format that supports lossless data compression. PNG was created as an improved, non-patented replacement for Graphics Interchange Format (GIF), and is the most widely used lossless image compression format on the Internet. PNG supports palette-based images (with palettes of 24-bit RGB or 32-bit RGBA colors), grayscale images (with or without alpha channel for transparency), and full-color non-palette-based RGB/RGBA images (with or without alpha channel). PNG was designed for transferring images on the Internet, not for professional-quality print graphics, and therefore does not support non-RGB color spaces such as CMYK. A PNG file contains a single image in an extensible structure of "chunks", encoding the basic pixels and other information such as textual comments and integrity checks documented in RFC 2083. PNG files nearly always use file extension PNG or png and are assigned MIME media type image/png. PNG was published as informational RFC 2083 in March 1997 and as an ISO/IEC standard in 2004.

concept.label: JPEG
concept.definition: JPEG ( JAY-peg) is a commonly used method of lossy compression for digital images, particularly for those images produced by digital photography. The degree of compression can be adjusted, allowing a selectable tradeoff between storage size and image quality. JPEG typically achieves 10:1 compression with little perceptible loss in image quality. JPEG compression is used in a number of image file formats. JPEG/Exif is the most common image format used by digital cameras and other photographic image capture devices; along with JPEG/JFIF, it is the most common format for storing and transmitting photographic images on the World Wide Web. These format variations are often not distinguished, and are simply called JPEG. The term "JPEG" is an initialism/acronym for the Joint Photographic Experts Group, which created the standard. The MIME media type for JPEG is image/jpeg, except in older Internet Explorer versions, which provides a MIME type of image/pjpeg when uploading JPEG images. JPEG files usually have a filename extension of .jpg or .jpeg. JPEG/JFIF supports a maximum image size of 65,53565,535 pixels, hence up to 4 gigapixels for an aspect ratio of 1:1.

concept.label: TIFF
concept.definition: Tagged Image File Format, abbreviated TIFF or TIF, is a computer file format for storing raster graphics images, popular among graphic artists, the publishing industry, and photographers. TIFF is widely supported by scanning, faxing, word processing, optical character recognition, image manipulation, desktop publishing, and page-layout applications. The format was created by Aldus Corporation for use in desktop publishing. It published the latest version 6.0 in 1992, subsequently updated with an Adobe Systems copyright after the latter acquired Aldus in 1994. Several Aldus or Adobe technical notes have been published with minor extensions to the format, and several specifications have been based on TIFF 6.0, including TIFF/EP (ISO 12234-2), TIFF/IT (ISO 12639), TIFF-F (RFC 2306) and TIFF-FX (RFC 3949).

concept.label: PLY
concept.definition: PLY is a computer file format known as the Polygon File Format or the Stanford Triangle Format. It was principally designed to store three-dimensional data from 3D scanners. The data storage format supports a relatively simple description of a single object as a list of nominally flat polygons. A variety of properties can be stored, including: color and transparency, surface normals, texture coordinates and data confidence values. The format permits one to have different properties for the front and back of a polygon. There are two versions of the file format, one in ASCII, the other in binary.

concept.label: OBJ
concept.definition: OBJ (or .OBJ) is a geometry definition file format first developed by Wavefront Technologies for its Advanced Visualizer animation package. The file format is open and has been adopted by other 3D graphics application vendors. The OBJ file format is a simple data-format that represents 3D geometry alone  namely, the position of each vertex, the UV position of each texture coordinate vertex, vertex normals, and the faces that make each polygon defined as a list of vertices, and texture vertices. Vertices are stored in a counter-clockwise order by default, making explicit declaration of face normals unnecessary. OBJ coordinates have no units, but OBJ files can contain scale information in a human readable comment line.

label: Using GoTriple data for your SSH data science tasks
description:
This workflow explains how to use GoTriple data on Social Sciences and Humanities (SSH) for data analytics tasks.

[GoTriple](https://gotriple.eu) is the discovery platform for the SSH: it currently indexes metadata of almost 19,5 million documents, over 25,000 projects and about 22,5 million author profiles. The extreme diversity of SSH is well represented, in its multivaried aspects, in the platform: on the one hand, GoTriple’s documents cover 27 disciplines within SSH, from History to Literature, from Management to Gender Studies. 

Moreover GoTriple is inherently multilingual, indexing documents in over 20 languages but also providing its user interface localised in 10 European languages. Finally, diversity also applies to the nature of its documents, with a high representation of textual content (articles, thesis, reports, books,...) but also a significant amount of datasets, multimedia assets and software artefacts with their number expected to increase in the coming months.

This workflow explains in practice, with code examples, how GoTriple data can be used by Digital Humanists for data analytics tasks.

There are **two ways** to do so:
- by using the data dumps created and published in Zenodo (last update May 18, 2025);
- by using GoTriple APIs, to extract data from the online platform.

**What to use:**
If you just need a subset of GoTriple publications that have a link to their PDF, the data dumps are the quickest way to get you started. Also this is the suggested way if you don’t want to write code to get GoTriple data.

On the other hand, use the APIs if:
a) you need access to the most recent version of the data; 
b) you need to include publications without a full-text; 
c) if you need access to a very specific subset of the data and you want to apply custom filtering conditions.

**Workflow Code**
A Jupyter Notebook with ready-to-use examples is available and it is the base for this workflow [go‑triple_stats‑with‑zenodo.ipynb[(https://github.com/odoma-ch/gotriple-data-utils/blob/main/gotriple_stats-with-zenodo.ipynb).
This Jupyter notebook provides hands-on examples of how to process GoTriple data dumps and integrate analytics workflows via Python or similar tooling. Familiarize yourself with its structure, required dependencies (e.g., pandas, requests), and typical processing pipelines (such as metadata loading, parsing, filtering, aggregation, and visualization).
Also, familiarize yourself with GoTriple data model, which is fully described in the TRIPLE Project deliverable D2.5: [https://zenodo.org/records/7359654](https://zenodo.org/records/7359654).

relatedItems.label: Bibliographical Data Science: from Catalogues to Research Data
relatedItems.description:
Library catalogues have been identified as a crucial resource for studying different aspects of book production spanning from literature to intellectual history and to informatics. At the same time, using them requires addressing challenges of data quality, completeness, and interpretation. Important aspect of bibliographic data science workflow is that it is imagined as a multilingual and transnational way of approaching large humanities and social science data. Data from national libraries for example covers hundreds of years of data and several languages. When we look at the possibility of combining different library datasets from multiple countries, we often face the challenge of dealing with language dependencies and deduplication.

The core of this type of work is to iterate between data harmonisation, analysis built upon different use cases and validating the data against other sources. We should imagine an open science ecosystem of different metadata collections where work on one of them also eases the use of another. Ecosystem thinking is important also because the harmonisation step often depends on other linked sources such as authority files or other library catalogues. An approach through which library metadata catalogues become research data has been coined as bibliographic data science. In this workflow description, we explain what it takes to produce research data out of library catalogues. The workflow can be described as an open science initiative because it takes questions of reproducibility and data quality seriously.

This workflow provides a step-by-step guide for researchers eager to use bibliographical data for research. More specifically, it looks into common issues of data acquisition, preprocessing, harmonisation, analysis and validation as well as an array of dissemination options.

relatedItems.label: Obtain GoTriple abstracts for specific domain
relatedItems.description: Referencing the workflow [Using GoTriple data for your SSH data science tasks](https://marketplace.sshopencloud.eu/workflow/3rVKH7), there are two main methods to obtain abstracts from the GoTriple portal - either via API calls, or via bulk download of GoTriple metadata records (data dumps). The available data dumps are grouped by domain/discipline. The workflow referenced above and the source code associated with this workflow demonstrates how to obtain compressed JSONL GZ format files for the chosen domain. In this case the chosen domain is 'archeo' (Archaeology and Prehistory).

relatedItems.label: GoTriple Discovery Platform
relatedItems.description: The GoTriple platform is an innovative multilingual and multicultural discovery solution for the social sciences and humanities (SSH). It will provide a single access point that allows researchers to explore, find, access and reuse materials such as literature, data, projects and researcher profiles at a European scale. Conceived as an entry point to the EOSC, it is one of the dedicated services of OPERAS, the Research Infrastructure supporting Open Scholarly Communication in the SSH in the European Research Area.

relatedItems.label: Zenodo
relatedItems.description: Zenodo is a catch-all repository for research data. It accepts all research data, with no requirements on format, size, access restrictions, or license. It is intended to support storage, curation, and publication of big research data. It was developed by the OpenAIRE partner CERN, responding to a request by the European Commission to create an open catch-all repository for all EC funded research.

composedOf.label: Using data dumps: 1. Locate and Download Data Dumps
composedOf.description:
Navigate to Zenodo and download the latest GoTriple metadata dumps, updated as of May 18, 2025, at this link: [https://zenodo.org/records/15784401](https://zenodo.org/records/15784401). Here you can find metadata for all publications in GoTriple that have a full-text link, grouped by one of the 27 SSH disciplines of GoTriple. Each file is prefixed with the discipline label and contains a JSON lines gzipped archive. Their dimensions vary from 8MB to over 730 MB: overall the compressed dumps amount to 7.8GB.

If the full text of a publication is not essential for your task, please use GoTriple APIs (see below).

composedOf.label: Using data dumps: 2. Loading and preparing data
composedOf.description:
Load the dumps into your environment by, opening the relevant .json, typically within a Jupyter environment.
Then parse metadata, loading them into data structures using the Panda Python library.
It's time to do some preprocessing and data cleaning. Normalize fields such as document type, language, authors, and disciplines. Handle multilingual text and missing entries appropriately.
Finally you can apply filters to extract and obtain a subset for your purposes. For example, extract relevant items (e.g., documents in a specific discipline, language, or time range).

composedOf.label: Using data dumps: 3. Process data
composedOf.description:
Start, for example, by enriching and aggregating data. Calculate analytics like count per discipline, temporal trends, language distribution, etc.
Finally, you can visualise or export the obtained results. Use plotting tools (e.g., Matplotlib or Seaborn) or export refined datasets for further analysis.

composedOf.label: Using APIs: 1. Getting familiar with GoTriple APIs
composedOf.description:
Start by exploring API Documentation. GoTriple provides Search REST APIs for fetching metadata on three core entities: *documents*, *projects*, and *author profiles*. These are powered by Elasticsearch, enabling flexible query construction. 

Consult GoTriple’s API documentation, which is available here:
- OpenAPI/Swagger description: [https://api.gotriple.eu/ ](https://api.gotriple.eu/ )
- TRIPLE Project Deliverable D6.6: [https://zenodo.org/records/7371832 ](https://zenodo.org/records/7371832 ) ) to understand request formats and parameters.

**Please note** that these APIs can only return a maximum of 10,000 records. If you need to process a larger number of data, you can:
- add extra conditions to your query, e.g. on provider 
- query by datestamp and not by year.  Datestamp is when the “document” has been last updated in the index, so querying by the day/hour etc should allow you a fine grained control over the return data. E.g. datestamp>=2025-01-01T00:00:00Z;datestamp<2025-01-10T23:59:00Z

Now you are ready to use API for data collection.

For REST search queries use endpoints like `/api/documents`, `/api/projects`, or `/api/authors`, with filters for language, discipline, keywords, etc.

APIs can return data in JSON and JSON-LD formats, the latter by making use of the TRIPLE Ontology: [https://www.gotriple.eu/ontology/triple](https://www.gotriple.eu/ontology/triple) . Please note that the JSON-LD is still under development but it is fully available for the `/api/documents` endpoint.

composedOf.label: Using APIs: 2. Process & Analyze data
composedOf.description:
Retrieve and parse API responses in JSON or JSON-LD. Extract relevant metadata fields, and deserialize into dataframes or structured formats.

Clean and transform data similarly to the data dumps method; perform aggregations, cross-entity comparisons, or build time-series insights.

Display analytics outputs through plots, dashboards, or export results for further downstream use.

composedOf.label: Combined Use
composedOf.description: Optionally, merge data from API calls and downloaded dumps. For example, use dumps for bulk coverage, and APIs for updating or enriching with fresh data.

relatedItems.label: Text Extraction From PDF Files
relatedItems.description:
This workflow describes the process for extracting the textual content of PDF files, and performing some basic segmentation of the extracted text.

The workflow is intended to be used as the first step in larger workflows that process the text (such as geographic named entity extraction etc,) and is unlikely to be particularly useful as a stand-alone workflow. Specifically it was designed in the context of the ATRIUM project to aid in the indexing of English language reports and journal articles describing archaeological investigations and interventions, as supplied by ATRIUM partner Archaeology Data Service (ADS).

relatedItems.label: Semi-automated extraction of information from textual documents in a domain-specific repository
relatedItems.description:
The workflow addresses the **machine processing and enhancement of archaeological textual documents** (e.g., grey literature, excavation reports, field forms) held in a domain-specific repository. It processes both **scanned documents**, through automatic text recognition, and **born-digital documents** (PDF, DOCX) that already carry a text layer. The goal is an integrated solution for **legacy data and new uploads within the selected repository system**: better search and reuse of the documents, and fewer manual steps in archiving and annotation.

The workflow chains **independent tools available as services through APIs**. Each tool performs one step: page classification, OCR quality control, linguistic annotation and named entity recognition, keyword extraction against the domain vocabularies, and translation. Each tool can also be used on its own. The repository calls the services asynchronously and stores every result as an **alternative distribution of the original file**, with a **paradata** record describing the run that produced it (tool version, parameters, licence).

The results of all steps also accumulate in **one JSON record per document** (the ATRIUM document record). Its blocks each have one producing tool, so any step can be re-run alone. The record carries the provenance of every contribution, and the licence of the combined result is derived from the most restrictive licence among them. It can later be exported as an RO-Crate.

The enriched data support:

* full-text and faceted search by page types, named entities and vocabulary keywords,
* assessment of OCR quality before further processing,
* linking of documents to controlled vocabularies and to each other,
* international access through English translations of metadata and texts,
* corpora for natural language processing, including the training and evaluation of models.

The tools were developed in the [ATRIUM project](https://atrium-research.eu/) by the Institute of Formal and Applied Linguistics (Charles University) with the Institutes of Archaeology of the Czech Academy of Sciences in Prague and Brno. They are open source, published as container images, and are described in their own Marketplace records. Their integration into [Galaxy](https://galaxyproject.org/) is being prepared with DARIAH.

The [Archaeological Map of the Czech Republic (AMCR)](https://digiarchiv.aiscr.cz/) repository serves as the **demonstrator** of the workflow.

**Diagram caption**: *Users and data curators work with a data repository (AMCR) that stores each document with its metadata, original file, ALTO XML, document record, enrichments and paradata, and the AMCR vocabularies. A processing orchestration (step 2) passes documents between the repository, a separate automatic text recognition workflow (step 4) and the ATRIUM tool services: page classification (3), ALTO post-processing and quality control (5), NLP enrichment with UDPipe and NameTag to TEITOK (7), vocabulary keywords by LLM (8) and XML translation (10). A dashed born-digital branch (6) replaces steps 4 and 5. NLP enrichment and translation call the LINDAT services; the vocabularies feed keyword extraction and translation. Annotators and data engineers train a custom NameTag model (9). A discovery service (11) serves users and feeds the OAI-PMH and File API, which feeds the ARIADNE Portal.*

composedOf.label: Obtain document(s) for input
composedOf.description:
The first step is to identify, obtain and store the document(s) intended as inputs to be processed. The method for obtaining the input documents will of course vary depending on the source - they may originate from the response of an API call, or they may be parsed from fields in a structured text file (e.g. XML, JSON, JSONL etc.), or they may be manually downloaded documents (e.g. PDF reports). 

It is a good idea to keep a note of the original source of the documents and the method(s) used to obtain them, so the same method(s) may be repeated in the future should the documents be updated or appended to. If using a scripted approach, the script may access each file remotely at runtime. Alternatively, you may choose to download and store the required documents to a local folder structure for subsequent processing. 

As an example, use cases for the ATRIUM project include a chosen subset of archaeological reports and journal article PDF documents which are downloaded prior to use, and a JSONL file of text passages, which is downloaded and parsed.

composedOf.label: Extract text contents of the input document(s)
composedOf.description:
The information extraction pipeline works on textual documents, so the next requirement is to obtain the textual contents of the input documents. For extraction of text from PDF files, text extraction libraries (such as [PyPDF2](https://pypi.org/project/PyPDF2/)) can be employed. The output of this step is intended to be a JSON formatted element corresponding to each record or document. This JSON element will hold the text content plus some suitable associated metadata, to be successively enriched in subsequent steps. The expected JSON format for the output of this step is detailed in the schema [Textual Information Data Extraction Schema (TIDES)](https://github.com/cbinding/rematch2/blob/main/tides_schema.json). An example illustrative minimal document is shown below (additional fields may also be present):

```json
{
   "text": "obtained text content to be further processed",
   "meta": {
       "filename": "name_of_file_the_text_was_extracted_from.pdf"
  	   "description": "about the original source of the text and the information extraction process",
  	   "created": "2025-06-26T10:33:36Z"
   }, 
   "tokens": [],
   "spans": [],
   "sections": []
}
```

A [tool created by University of Sheffield](https://github.com/GateNLP/atrium-text_extraction/) performs text extraction from PDF and will create output conforming to this JSON schema. The script also includes an option to re-do OCR on the original PDF document if required.

composedOf.label: Construct and configure the text processing pipeline
composedOf.description:
For maximum flexibility the text processing components have been developed as flexible, configurable and reusable [Python](https://www.python.org/) modules which can be combined within a [spaCy](https://spacy.io/) pipeline architecture to perform various tasks including text normalisation and vocabulary-driven concept recognition. The temporal components accommodate multilingual data, the vocabulary-driven components as described here use English language vocabularies.

Construction and configuration of pipelines is illustrated in a series of exemplar demonstrator [Jupyter notebooks](https://github.com/cbinding/rematch2) accompanying the source code, where more details of the configuration options are also present.

### Configuration

Much of the lower-level configuration is initialised with sensible defaults making the pipeline components usable ‘out of the box’, however as the components can be combined in various ways there are some choices to be made:

- Choose which controlled vocabularies to match on. This involves choosing from a set of pre-defined vocabulary-matching pipeline components. These include:
   - Facets of the [Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus (AAT)](https://www.getty.edu/research/tools/vocabularies/aat/)
      - [AAT Associated Concepts facet](http://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300264086)
      - [AAT Materials facet](http://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300264091)
      - [AAT Objects facet](http://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300264092)
      - [AAT Physical Attributes facet](http://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300264087)
      - [AAT Styles & Periods facet](http://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300264088)
   - Vocabularies originating from the [Forum on Information Standards in Heritage (FISH)](https://heritage-standards.org.uk/fish-vocabularies/)
      - [FISH Archaeological Objects thesaurus](http://purl.org/heritagedata/schemes/mda_obj)
      - [FISH Archaeological Sciences thesaurus](http://purl.org/heritagedata/schemes/560)
      - [FISH Building Materials thesaurus](http://purl.org/heritagedata/schemes/eh_tbm)
      - [FISH Components thesaurus](http://purl.org/heritagedata/schemes/eh_com)
      - [FISH Event Types thesaurus](http://purl.org/heritagedata/schemes/agl_et)
      - [FISH Evidence thesaurus](http://purl.org/heritagedata/schemes/eh_evd)
      - [FISH Maritime Craft Types thesaurus](http://purl.org/heritagedata/schemes/eh_tmc)
      - [FISH Monument Types thesaurus](http://purl.org/heritagedata/schemes/eh_tmt2)
      - [FISH Object Materials thesaurus](http://purl.org/heritagedata/schemes/73)
- Choose a [PeriodO](https://perio.do/) authority identifier. The pipeline component to identify named periods in the text utilises the (entire) PeriodO dataset. When configured with a valid PeriodO authority identifier (e.g. “p0xxt6t” - [Scottish Archaeological Periods & Ages (ScAPA)](http://n2t.net/ark:/99152/p0xxt6t)), the component will identify matches within the text for any of the labels of periods contained in that specified authority. e.g. *Chalcolithic*, *Early Bronze Age*, *Antonine* etc.

- Choose whether to include tokenisation results in the output (default: false). The tokenisation is a key step in the NLP pipeline. The results of the tokenisation can be useful information in diagnosing and understanding how the NLP part of the pipeline has worked. However, these results can be large and detailed and are not required for the overall goal of the workflow, so you may optionally choose to omit them from the output (by default they will be omitted).

relatedItems.label: spaCy
relatedItems.description: spaCy is an open-source software library for advanced natural language processing, written in the programming languages Python and Cython. The library is published under the MIT license and currently offers statistical neural network models for English, German, Spanish, Portuguese, French, Italian, Dutch and multi-language NER, as well as tokenization for various other languages. Unlike NLTK, which is widely used for teaching and research, spaCy focuses on providing software for production usage. As of version 1.0, spaCy also supports deep learning workflows that allow connecting statistical models trained by popular machine learning libraries like TensorFlow, Keras, Scikit-learn or PyTorch. spaCy's machine learning library, Thinc, is also available as a separate open-source Python library. It features convolutional neural network models for part-of-speech tagging, dependency parsing and named entity recognition, as well as API improvements around training and updating models, and constructing custom processing pipelines.

relatedItems.description: PeriodO is a public domain gazetteer of scholarly definitions of historical, art-historical, and archaeological periods. It eases the task of linking among datasets that define periods differently. It also helps scholars and students see where period definitions overlap or diverge.

composedOf.label: Apply the configured pipeline to the input text(s) and produce output
composedOf.description:
The Python spaCy pipeline components perform operations including text normalisation, tokenization, POS tagging, lemmatization, and vocabulary-driven concept recognition. The input for this step will be the JSON file as produced in the first step of the workflow, plus the built and configured pipeline. Various output report formats are available, including TXT, CSV, JSON, HTML and PDF. 

* The CSV output lists the concept entities identified in the text, with their locations in the text.
* The JSON output will be the JSON input enriched with additional fields containing the results of applying the configured pipeline to the input text. This allows for further processing or for flexible aggregation and reporting on the results.
* The HTML output visualises and lists concept entities identified in the text, with summaries of counts for each concept.
* The TXT output is a text version of the HTML output.
* The PDF output is a PDF version of the HTML output.

Examples of applying configured pipelines to data are available as a series of [Jupyter (Python) notebooks](https://github.com/cbinding/rematch2) that accompany the source code.

label: Workflow for Annotating and Comparing IIIF resources using Altamira
description:
This workflow enables researchers and members of the public to visually annotate images from various providers that support the International Image Interoperability Framework (IIIF). It facilitates the comparison and integration of annotations across different image sources, allowing users to share their annotations for consultation, review, or collaborative editing.

The solution is particularly valuable in cases where images of a single artifact type are dispersed across multiple providers, and where a streamlined method for sharing annotations is preferred.

Fully compatible with all IIIF-compliant resources, the workflow integrates Altamira, a customized implementation of the Mirador viewer. Altamira has been specifically developed to support the preparation, management, preservation, sharing, and reuse of annotations in accordance with the Web Annotation Data Model.

Altamira is available as a service at the Archaeology Data Service: [link](http://chara-51.man.poznan.pl/mirador/iiif/)

### Implementation
This workflow's functionality relies on both existing IIIF resource sources and the integration of Altamira. Both are indispensable for its operation. Fortunately, these are already deployed across various platforms. If you intend to share your own IIIF resources or utilize a self-managed Altamira instance, please follow the steps detailed in [IIIF Enablement and Visualization Workflow Using Altamira Viewer for Image Repositories](https://marketplace.sshopencloud.eu/workflow/YHAnKE).

### Prerequisite
Altamira can be deployed independently by following [IIIF Enablement and Visualization Workflow Using Altamira Viewer for Image Repositories](https://marketplace.sshopencloud.eu/workflow/YHAnKE), or users may utilize the version deployed as a service by the Archaeology Data Service.

### Detailed documentation 
Detailed documentation with images is available [here](https://gitlab.pcss.pl/dl-team/atrium/iiif/mirador/mirador-atrium)!

concept.label: IIIF
concept.definition: The International Image Interoperability Framework (IIIF) is a set of shared application programming interface (API) specifications for interoperable functionality in digital image repositories. The IIIF is comprised of and driven by a community of libraries, museums, archives, software companies, and other organizations working together to create, test, refine, implement and promote the IIIF specifications. Using JSON-LD, linked data, and standard W3C web protocols such as Web Annotation, IIIF makes it easy to parse and share digital image data, migrate across technology systems, and provide enhanced image access for scholars and researchers. In short, IIIF enables better, faster and cheaper image delivery. It lets you leverage interoperability and the fabric of the Web to access new possibilities and new users for your image-based resources, while reducing long term maintenance and technological lock in. IIIF gives users a rich set of baseline functionality for viewing, zooming, and assembling the best mix of resources and tools to view, compare, manipulate and work with images on the Web, an experience made portableshareable, citable, and embeddable. (source: https://iiif.io/community/faq/)

The purpose of this workflow is to provide a way to create and serve files in IIIF-compatible (International Image Interoperability Framework) format, which:

- Increase interoperability by standardizing access, as it is open source and widely implemented

- Enable users to access saved images at will by IIIF Viewer

label: Workflow to work with the PATRIMONIVM-Editor
description:
The PATRIMONIVM-Editor has been created by Alberto Dalla Rosa and Vincent Razanajao (https://patrimonium.huma-num.fr/atlas/editor/) to be a modular, customizable and integrated web application for the management of epigraphic corpora, based on the eXist-db platform. It creates TEI XML on the basis of EpiDoc, allowing the data to be used in digital editions. Based on our experiences with a customized version of the “eStudium. A virtual research environment for Historians” for the epigraphic project “Celtic Divine Names in Latin Inscriptions of the Military Zone in Germania Superior on the Left Bank of the River Rhine. Religious Phenomena in a Cultural Contact Zone“ (FWF funded project P 34422-G), this workflow will document the process both for the scientific, and probably non-tech savvy user, who is filling the editor with information, as well as for the user tasked with postprocessing the information available in the editor for the online publication.

For our first project “Celtic Divine Names in the Inscriptions of the Roman Province Germania Inferior. A Case Study on Religion in the Context of Cultural Contacts and Cultural Transfer” (FWF funded project P 29274-G25) we used single MC Word documents for every entry, which then were consolidated into a single MC Excel document for the conversion to XML by our partners at ZIM (Zentrum für Informationsmodellierung – Centre for Information Modelling) and the following online publication on GAMS (Geisteswissenschaftliches Asset Management System – Humanities’ Asset Management System; https://gams.uni-graz.at/context:fercan ; see picture 10). This method was redundant, cumbersome and prone to errors, especially with regard to required changes. With the PATRIMONIVM-Editor, these redundancies are removed and problems occurring during the postprocessing are easily identified, communicated and solved. (For the process of adapting the PATRIMONIVM-Editor, see either the GitHub documentation https://github.com/DigitalHumanitiesCraft/PatrimoniumEditorFercan/, or "Customizing the Patrimonium-Editor" on SSHOM)

relatedItems.label: Patrimonium-Editor
relatedItems.description: The Patrimonium editor  is an integrated web application, created by Alberto Dalla Rosa and Vincent Razanajao, based on eXist-db and is dedicated primarily to the production and enrichment of epigraphical corpora, from the creation of TEI/EpiDoc files to the building of both the gazetteer and prosopographical data of places and people involved in the documents. The web application has been conceived in a modular and customizable approach, so that it could potentially fit the requirements of any historical project that needs to process textual sources and deal with spatial and prosopographical material.

relatedItems.label: Customizing the Patrimonium-Editor
relatedItems.description:
This document serves as a guide for customizing the Patrimonium Editor  using the example of the Fercan projects at the University of Graz, that study the Celtic divine names in roman inscriptions in antiquity (see also GitHub https://github.com/DigitalHumanitiesCraft/PatrimoniumEditorFercan/). These projects utilizes the Patrimonium Editor to collect and manage epigraphic data. Supported by the Austrian Science Fund (FWF) through grants. The first project “Celtic Divine Names in the Inscriptions of the Roman Province Germania Inferior. A Case Study on Religion in the Context of Cultural Contacts and Cultural Transfer” researched the Celtic divine names in the Roman provinces of Germania Inferior (P 29274-G25) and the second one “Celtic Divine Names in Latin Inscriptions of the Military Zone in Germania Superior on the Left Bank of the River Rhine. Religious Phenomena in a Cultural Contact Zone“ (P 34422-G) focused on the northern Germania Superior. These two projects examined how local Celtic traditions were integrated into Roman practices, using epigraphic evidence to trace changes and continuities in religious expression. The customization and application of the Patrimonium Editor was done during the second project and retroactively applied to the data management of the first project too.

The Patrimonium Editor is a web application suite designed for academic use, focusing on the encoding, management, and analysis of epigraphic and historical textual sources. It includes an XML editor for text encoding, conversion tools adhering to the Leiden Conventions, and data management capabilities for places, people, and thematic categories. Its modular architecture provides flexibility for customization and leverages the eXist-db XML database. The editor supports TEI (Text Encoding Initiative) and EpiDoc (Epigraphic Documents) guidelines, ensuring compatibility with international standards in digital humanities.

composedOf.label: Creating a corpus
composedOf.description: Since the Editor is working with Cookies, it is advised to use a browser with the option of an incognito mode, or otherwise the saved cookies could start to cause problems. Once the PATRIMONIVM-Editor has been set up in accordance to the needs of your project and at least one corpus has been set up (please see "Customizing the PATRIMONIVUM-Editor" on SSHOM) , you go to the “eStudium” frontpage and select “eStudium. A virtual research environment for Historians” (picture 1), where you press “Log in” in the upper right corner. After having logged in you will see that on the spot the “Log in” button has been, there now is the name of your user-profile (picture 2). Click on the name and then select “Corpus”, after clicking you will see a list of all available corpora on the left side. New corpora can be added by the IT team (please see "Customizing the PATRIMONIVUM-Editor" on SSHOM). Enter the corpus you want to work on by clicking on it. The content of the selected one will then be shown in the middle of the screen (picture 3). To fill the corpus with entries, you have to create them by clicking on the blue bordered “+New document” icon, which opens a small window, where you first select a template, meaning you set to which corpus the newly created entry is attributed to, and also give it a title (you can correct and even change the title later from within the entry) and then create the document. Once you have created the first document, it will be added to the list in the center. Each document has an intern ID linked to the corpus it belongs to, but the title is what will be visible in the online publication. Beside “Titel” and “ID” the information of the entries displayed in the corpus overview is customizable too. To edit an entry, you have to click on the small blue icon of a pen writing on a block, which appears at the end of the given title, which will open the document in a new browser tab.

composedOf.label: Filling the documents - 1
composedOf.description:
Since the PATRIMONIVM-Editor is modular based and customizable, the exact structure of the editor you are going to work with will be varying between projects. Generally speaking, there are four types of input fields: which are distributed over the different content blocks: 

I. data fields II. regular text fields III.  input-limited fields IV. dropdown fields

The text fields I. and II. are straight forward. Write into them the information according to the category they are attributed to. There are however two important differences in working with them and entering the information.

Fields of the first category need to be enabled for input by clicking on the pencil-on-a-block-icon on the right side first. Once the input is done, save it by clicking on the green icon with the hook. Clicking the red icon with the X will discard all made changes. Please note, that there can´t be any less-than and greater-than brackets (“<”, “>”) in the text field, or saving won´t work. Should you require those, you can use the following work-around: Instead of typing less-than brackets (“<”) use the coding “& lt;” (without space between "&" and "l") and for greater-than brackets (“>”) the coding “& gt;” (without space between "&" and "g"). If you have to edit the text field again, you will have to enter these codes once more, since upon activation of the text field for new input, the code will be automatically turned into the brackets “<” and “>”. If your online publication is also equipped with a searchable index, you will need to set up as many fields of category I. as you have categories in your index. It can happen, that a single category needs to contain several lemmas. In this case you have to mark in the text field where one lemma ends and the other one begins, which is done by placing a semicolon “;” between them. In some cases, it can be necessary to have the ability to add new text fields, or group of fields consisting of this category, to fill in more information to a content block. For those cases you have to create an “Add”-button when setting up the PATROMONIVM-Editor, which then will have the form of a white cross in a blue oval, situated at the right end of the content block (picture 4). In our case we use this for “Apparatus criticus”, “Editions”, “weitere elektronische Ressourcen” (further digital resources), “Abbildungen” (images ) and “Buchstabenhöhe” (hight of letters).

composedOf.label: Filling the documents - 2
composedOf.description:
If you need to add new data fields you first click on the "Add"-button, then there will appear new but shorter text fields at the end of the content block. First you enter the information, then you have to save so the fields will be added (picture 5). If, after several seconds, the fields are still in their shorter form, you have to refresh the page and start the adding process from the beginning. If you want to add a new text field containing the code of any less-than and greater-than brackets, it can happen that the text fireld isn´t saved, we advise to add the new field wihtout the code and then entert he code in the field. Superfluous fields in content blocks with the "Add"-button can be deleted by the orange bin-icon on the right side (pictures 4-6).

The peculiarities of the fields of the second category are, that you don´t need to enable them first in order to write in them. They still require saving though, for which the button is in the lower left corner. They are also saving automatically when you click outside of the text field. It is important, that you can´t save if there are double "spaces" or if a "space" is at the end of a line-break. The easiest way to hunt down the double-spaces in the text field is to enable "CodeView" (the symbol \< / \>) and search for "& nbsp;" (without space between "&" and "n"). Delete this code wherever it appears and the double-spaces are dealt with. In our case we used fields of this type wherever we expected to write down information which needed structuring in paragraphs, as well as for editorial comments we wanted to store close to the published information, but which are set up to not be posted.

The fields of the third category are functionally the same as category I. but are pre-set in the type of information that is to be entered and therefore strictly limited in how to be formatted. Attempting to enter the information in a different format will hinder saving. In our case these are the fields related to dating, measurements, the sequence in "Apparatus criticus" and "Editions" and the MIME-Type of the images.
Finally, the fourth category is dropdown menus. You can set up the available lemmas for each dropdown field and also, if only one or several lemmas can be assigned, case by case. If several lemmas are attributable, then new dropwdowns are added with the "Add"-button, in a similar process as with the text fields of category I. For us this case applies to the dropdowns of "Material" and "Classification".

composedOf.label: Working with the Text annotation -1
composedOf.description:
An important aspect of every epigraphical edition is the application of the Leiden Conventions. In our workflow of the Germania Inferior, the majuscule and minuscule had to be written in "LeedsUniExt" and certain signs of the Leiden Conventions had to be written by use of the "Combining Diacritical Marks" of the "Unicode block". With the text annotation however, the user is enabeled to write not only the majuscule and minuscule, but also the Leiden Conventions directly in XML-format.

But first things first. Once you clicked on "Text annotation", the menu will change and you will see the two categories "diplomatic" and "normalised", both of them containing a toolbar called "Epigraphic annotations" and a text field named "XML Editor 1" and "XML Editor 2". "diplomatic" is where you put in the majuscule, and "normalized" is where you put in the minuscule. If there already exists a majuscule or minuscule in a digital format, you can simply copy it, then click on the blue framed button "Text converter" on the right side of each category. There you can select the language of the inscription, the epigraphic format, and finally paste the text into the first text field and press "OK" (picture 7). You will see to the left the XML coded text you pasted, and to the right the "Preview" of how it will be displayed. Now, even if there is nothing you want to change or to correct in the text itself, you will have to set the lines at least once manually and the second category will then automatically take it over.

To set the line, you first position your cursor in the text field where you want the line to be, then select the "(1)" at the left end of the toolbar, which opens a dropdown menu with "Line beginning" and "Column beginning", each with an additional dropdown menu with numbers beginning with "1" and below the number "- in word". Selecting the "1" will create the code < lb n = "1" / > (with space only between "b" and "n"), selecting the number "2" < lb n = "2" / > (with space only between "b" and "n"). Everything after the code for line 1 and between the code for 2 will be displayed as the first line. Should the last word of line 1 continue in line 2, you select the "- in word" below the "2" and the code will be < lb n = "2" break = "no"/ > (with space only between "b" and "n" as well as "2"" and "b") instead. You repeat this till you have designated all the lines you need. Should the inscription be in columns, you select "Column beginning" instead. Please note, that although the dropdown menus end with "10" for the lines and "5" for the columns, you can set a higher number, simply by copying and pasting the code and correcting the number (pictures 8 and 9).

composedOf.label: Working with the text annotation - 2
composedOf.description:
If the inscription is not in a format allowing for copy and paste, you simply type the majuscule and minuscule in the respective editors and set all needed Leiden Conventions manually by first highlighting the letters you want to be affected and then selecting the according sign in the toolbar above the editor.

While the toolbar consists of the most important Leiden Conventions, the underline for text lost but seen by earlier editors' is missing and has to be coded manually by the user. The required code is < supplied reason = "undefined" evidence = "previouseditor" instant = "false" >XX < / supplied > (with space only between "ed" and "re"; “de”” and “ev”; “or”” and “in”).  In this case the "XX" is a stand in for where the letters in question are to be positioned. In the "Preview" such underlined passages are not shown underlined but represented by a left open square bracket "\]" after the last underlined letter. This also applies to the symbols for centurion and mulier. The code for ">" in the majuscule is “& gt;” (without space between "&" and "g"), while in the minuscule the code is < g type = "centurio" / > (with space only between "g" and "t"). Though there won´t be a preview for the minuscule in the "Document overview", it will be rendered to "((centurion))" on the database after postprocessing. (For mulier, replace "centurio" in the code.)

Once you finished, you need to save both categories "diplomatic" and "normalised" individually by clicking on the blue button with a white disk above "Text Converter", otherwise your work will be lost. As soon as you do any modification, there will appear a red bar above the category you have modified with the message "Text has been modified", which will disappear again after you have saved (picture 9). Furthermore, upon saving, the combined preview of majuscule and minuscule will also be displayed in the "Document overview". For our purposes we put it on the right side and pinned it, so it always stays on the monitor, even when scrolling down in the document, but this is customizable to your preferences and needs (picture 6). Please note, that the "Preview" is only displayed in the document and the "Text annotation" if you have set an action in the XML editor. While being in the "Text annotation", the action must be set in the XML editors individually, for the document preview however, it is enough to have interacted with any of the two XML editors. We advise, to place the cursor at the end of a line, simply press the spacebar once and then delete it again, then press save.

The interface of the Patrimonium Editor also offers an XML file view, exposing the TEI-compliant document structure. This feature enables direct manipulation of the underlying markup, allowing researchers to address unique encoding challenges and implement specialized requirements beyond the scope of standard data fields. By providing access to the raw XML, the editor accommodates complex epigraphic phenomena and project-specific data structures that may not fit within predefined input options.

composedOf.label: Postprocessing the data
composedOf.description:
The postprocessing of data captured by editors involves exporting the information from the editor's database in a predefined TEI/XML format, adhering to a subset of the EpiDoc community standard. This exported dataset undergoes further processing for quality control, enrichment, and alignment with the requirements of the trusted digital repository where it will be published. The postprocessing workflow, executed via XSL transformation, is adaptable to various project settings and application scenarios.

The process encompasses several critical steps aligned with data management best practices. Initially, data undergoes verification and validation to ensure completeness and accuracy, with any detected errors requiring correction and reevaluation. Subsequently, the content is enriched with metadata, annotations, and descriptions, following established field-specific metadata standards. Standardization and normalization procedures are then applied to conform the data to common formats and naming conventions, facilitating interoperability and integration with other datasets.

Throughout the postprocessing, adherence to FAIR principles is prioritized. This entails assigning unique identifiers, providing rich metadata for discoverability, ensuring accessibility through standard communication protocols, using community-agreed standards for interoperability, and associating clear usage licenses and comprehensive provenance information to enable reuse.
Long-term preservation is addressed by transferring the data to a trusted digital repository. This repository assumes responsibility for maintaining data integrity and accessibility over time, implementing regular backups, format migrations, persistent linking systems, and undergoing periodic audits and certifications.

The implementation of these practices necessitates consideration of several factors. Community-driven standards and protocols are adopted to ensure seamless data ingestion by the repository. Open, non-proprietary formats are used for data storage to guarantee long-term access. Detailed documentation of data processing steps and decisions is maintained to ensure transparency and replicability. A robust data management plan is implemented and regularly reviewed to adapt to new challenges and technological advancements.

In the current project, these best practices are applied through the use of standardized metadata schemas such as TEI/XML in the EpiDoc standard, with metadata mapping to other standards like Dublin Core, EDM, and OpenAIRE. Collaboration with a certified digital repository ensures adherence to international standards such as the OAIS model. Detailed metadata on reused image files is recorded, and the project output is provided in a citable and reusable format, including delivery to aggregation services like Europeana and interlinking with other epigraphic resources.

This comprehensive approach to data postprocessing not only ensures long-term preservation but also enhances the accessibility, interoperability, and reusability of the project output, thereby contributing significantly to ongoing and future research endeavors in the field.

relatedItems.description: A free cloud service for OCR The project En fri molntjänst för OCR \`A free cloud service for OCR', funded by the National Library of Sweden (51-KB709-2012), ran from 1st September, 2013 until 31st August, 2014. The project was a collaboration between the University Library of University of Gothenburg and Språkbanken 'the Swedish Language Bank' at the Department of Swedish of University of Gothenburg, its aim to create a prototype Optical Character Recognition (OCR) web service for processing old Swedish texts that are printed in a blackletter (fraktur) or roman typeface, using one of two open source OCR engines. Our ultimate goal is to provide a service for libraries, museums and archives to upload any digitized document and retrieve an OCRed text with high quality, independent on the quality of the print. In the project, we have evaluated two open source OCR engines: OCRopus and Tesseract and further developed one of them, namely OCRopus. Using OCRopus we have set up a open webservice for OCR that can handle Swedish Blackletter print as well as Roman type print. The pilot cloud service and web API can be found here. The material and tools developed in the project are freely available for download from this site under the license CC-BY.

concept.label: TIFF
concept.definition: Tagged Image File Format, abbreviated TIFF or TIF, is a computer file format for storing raster graphics images, popular among graphic artists, the publishing industry, and photographers. TIFF is widely supported by scanning, faxing, word processing, optical character recognition, image manipulation, desktop publishing, and page-layout applications. The format was created by Aldus Corporation for use in desktop publishing. It published the latest version 6.0 in 1992, subsequently updated with an Adobe Systems copyright after the latter acquired Aldus in 1994. Several Aldus or Adobe technical notes have been published with minor extensions to the format, and several specifications have been based on TIFF 6.0, including TIFF/EP (ISO 12234-2), TIFF/IT (ISO 12639), TIFF-F (RFC 2306) and TIFF-FX (RFC 3949).

JavaScript code to be implemented in Google Earth Engine(c).

The multi-scale relief model (MSRM) is a new algorithm for the visual interpretation of landforms using DSMs. The significance of this new method lies in its capacity to extract landform morphology from both high- and low-resolution DSMs independently of the shape or scale of the landform under study. This method thus provides important advantages compared to previous approaches as it: (1) allows the use of worldwide medium resolution models, such as SRTM, ASTER GDEM, ALOS, and TanDEM-X; (2) offers an alternative to traditional photograph interpretation that does not rely on the quality of the imagery employed nor on the environmental conditions and time of its acquisition; and (3) can be easily implemented for large areas using traditional GIS/RS software.

The algorithm is tested in the Sutlej-Yamuna interfluve, which is a very large low-relief alluvial plain in northwest India where 10 000 km of palaeoriver channels have been mapped using MSRM.

label: A Medical History of British India
description:
This dataset forms the first half of the Medical History of British India collection, which itself is part of the broader India Papers collection held by the Library. A Medical History of British India consists of official publications varying from short reports to multi-volume histories related to disease, public health and medical research between circa 1850 to 1950. These are historical sources for a period which witnessed the transition from a humoral to a biochemical tradition, which was based on laboratorial science and document the important breakthroughs in bacteriology, parasitology and the developments of vaccines in a colonial context.

The vivid detail in these reports that makes them a treasure-trove of regional histories, including the effect of diseases on the social fabric of small villages and towns. The accompanying detailed topographical maps and extensive statistics also provide valuable data. In addition, they reveal the development of surveillance systems and the official response to epidemic emergencies within a colonial context, providing vital insights into the role of government and the operation of colonial power. Many of the breakthroughs and advances in the treatment and prevention of communicable diseases are represented in the collection, and a number of the titles are either about or by prominent figures in the field (for example, Sir Ronald Ross, W M Haffkine and S R Christophers). They also provide names of individuals attending medical schools, hospitals, the Indian civil service and other institutions.

Visit the Library’s website for the collection: [A Medical History of British India website](https://digital.nls.uk/indiapapers/)

relatedItems.label: Preliminary guidelines for manual annotation of word senses in Latin and ancient Greek corpora
relatedItems.description:
These guidelines describe how the annotation task should be set up and performed, including: how to determine the sense inventory for each word to be manually annotated; how the annotation would look like (e.g. graded annotation or only one sense selection for each word occurrence); which tool(s) will be used for the manual annotation; how to deal with specific annotation challenges; metaphoric senses; vagueness; sense boundaries.
The guidelines build on evidence from Latin and Ancient Greek, but they are conceived to be as cross linguistically valid as possible.

relatedItems.label: Evaluation against a Gold Standard
relatedItems.description:
The lexicologist will need to evaluate the algorithm against the state of the art. In order to do that, they can use existing Gold Standards or create another one for the specific task. Gold Standards for this task are manually annotated datasets in which each lexical item has been assigned a sense by the annotator. Gold Standards for a few lexical items in Latin and Ancient Greek already exist.
If the lexicologist wants to create a new Gold Standard for the evaluation, they will need to create a manually annotated dataset of lexical word senses for the languages and/or semantic fields included in the study. The manual annotation has to be performed by following specific annotation guidelines for manual annotation of word senses.
As an output, the lexicologist will obtain a dataset of occurrences of the target words in context, manually annotated with senses. This dataset can then be used to evaluate the performance of the algorithm.

label: Archaeometric characterization of Iberian ceramic production from Fontscaldes (Catalonia)
description:
The study of ceramic production plays a key role in understanding technological practices, economic organisation, and cultural dynamics in past societies. In this context, the integration of archaeometric analyses with digital documentation methods offers new possibilities for the systematic study and preservation of archaeological materials. This dataset presents results from the study of ceramic materials from the Iberian workshop of Fontscaldes (Catalonia, 3rd century BC), developed within the framework of the project “Caracterització arqueomètrica de ceràmiques protohistòriques del nord-est peninsular (JDC2023-051995-I)”. The research adopts an interdisciplinary approach combining archaeological investigation, archaeometric analyses, and 3D digitalisation.

The dataset includes WD-XRF results from ceramic individuals, providing major and minor elemental compositions expressed as oxides (mass fraction %, w%), trace elements expressed in mg/kg, and loss on ignition (LOI). These data are used to assess compositional variability, define reference groups, and explore technological choices.

It also includes X-ray diffraction (XRD) data in raw and processed formats (.xrdml and instrument raw files), used for the mineralogical characterisation of ceramic pastes.

In addition, a structured 3D documentation workflow has been implemented, integrating pre-analytical recording, selective digitisation strategies, and post-analytical evaluation. This approach preserves morphological and surface information, including in cases involving destructive or semi-destructive sampling. The resulting dataset includes 3D models (OBJ, STL, MTL) and graphical documentation in PDF format.

All data are organised within a unified digital repository to ensure accessibility, reproducibility, and long-term reuse in accordance with FAIR principles. The combined archaeological, analytical, and digital datasets provide insights into production practices at Fontscaldes and highlight variability within the ceramic assemblage, contributing to a better understanding of local manufacturing traditions. The integration of 3D technologies within archaeometric workflows further demonstrates the potential to balance analytical requirements with the preservation of archaeological information.

label: Archaic to Hellenistic archaeobotanical remains from Little Palace North, Knossos (Crete, Greece)
description: This archaeobotanical dataset from the Little Palace North (LPN) project at Knossos (Crete, Greece) includes sixteen samples dated to the Archaic, Classical and Hellenistic periods. The samples were recovered during the 2001-2002 excavations by flotation. The dataset includes 594 archaeobotanical items: cereal grains and chaff, pulses, fruit and nut remains and wild seeds. Most plant macroremains were charred but a few mineralised/calcified remains were also present, all of them being fruits and possibly nuts. The overall preservation of the assemblage was average while olives exhibited a high degree of fragmentation with only 8 olives found whole and the remaining 236 across the whole assemblage represent the minimum number of individual. The dataset is particularly important as it provides much needed new data on some of the least well represented chronological periods across the Aegean. It is also the first dataset on Classical archaeobotanical remains in Crete.

label: Archaic to Hellenistic invertebrate remains from Little Palace North, Knossos (Crete, Greece)
description:
The archaeomalacological dataset from the Little Palace North (LPN) project at Knossos (Crete, Greece) provides a crucial domestic perspective on Archaic, Classical, and Hellenistic shell exploitation, periods when bioarchaeological data remain remarkably scarce in the Aegean. The assemblage comprises 367 specimens across 53 taxa, consisting of land snails, fossils, and marine invertebrates. Land gastropods, dominate the assemblage. There is also a significant number of fossil shells, of which the diminutive Brachiopoda predominate.

The marine invertebrates, consisting of 108 specimens, features edible taxa including limpets, top-shells, mussels, sea urchins, crabs, and cuttlefish. Banded dye-murex (Hexaplex trunculus) was also found, fragmented and in low numbers. The significance of the LPN shell dataset lies in its reflection of everyday domestic reality, offering a vital counterpoint to the region's heavily studied ritual and feasting deposits. Ultimately, this dataset is fundamental for understanding continuity and change in Aegean coastal resource management, allowing new insights into how historical urban communities locally engaged with their maritime environment.

label: Archives Parlementaires
description: The Archives parlementaires is a chronologically-ordered edited collection of sources on the French Revolution. It was conceived in the mid 19th century as a project to produce a definitive record of parliamentary deliberations and also includes letters, reports, speeches, and other first-hand accounts from a great variety of published and archival sources. FRDA currently contains the AP volumes covering the years 1787-1794, which can be searched using ARTFL's PhiloLogic 4 open source software platform. The texts have been marked up using TEI so that speakers, places, dates, and terms in the published index can be easily found. Users can see both scanned images of the AP pages or just the texts.

The mission of this project is twofold: to meet the specific needs of sound archives, and also to meet the demands of the research field, which often requires many specific skills and kinds of information (multimedia and information technologies, analytical tools, local contextual knowledge, ethnomusicological perspective, etc.). The main purpose is to provide an easy and efficient indexing of sound files. A web platform is also a way to cross borders, to get local populations involved in working on their own cultural heritage and to offer resources to anthropologists and ethnomusicologists around the world.

concept.label: TIFF
concept.definition: Tagged Image File Format, abbreviated TIFF or TIF, is a computer file format for storing raster graphics images, popular among graphic artists, the publishing industry, and photographers. TIFF is widely supported by scanning, faxing, word processing, optical character recognition, image manipulation, desktop publishing, and page-layout applications. The format was created by Aldus Corporation for use in desktop publishing. It published the latest version 6.0 in 1992, subsequently updated with an Adobe Systems copyright after the latter acquired Aldus in 1994. Several Aldus or Adobe technical notes have been published with minor extensions to the format, and several specifications have been based on TIFF 6.0, including TIFF/EP (ISO 12234-2), TIFF/IT (ISO 12639), TIFF-F (RFC 2306) and TIFF-FX (RFC 3949).
